articles.text: Jeremy Bowers has announced he will retire from his post as Piedmont’s Chief of Police this summer. Bowers’ career in Piedmont began Tuesday, September 8, 2014 when he hired as Captain from the San Jose Police Department. Bowers, Piedmont’s highly regarded Police Chief, will wear his uniform for the last time on Tuesday, July 17. Over the last decade, under Bowers’ leadership, Piedmont residents have enjoyed remarkable levels of safety. Bowers came to Piedmont at the recommendation of his predecessor Rikki Goede, with whom he had worked in San Jose. Hired in 2014, he was named Chief on February 6, 2016 following Goede’s retirement. articles.text: Dear PUSD Staff & Families: I am writing to update you on news related to the Department of Education. [On March 20] President Donald Trump signed an executive order to “begin eliminating” the U.S. Department of Education. Whitehouse.gov/ presidential-actions/2025/03/ i m p r ov i n g- e d u c a t io n - o u tcomes-by-empower ing-parents-states-and-communities/ Acknowledging his limitations, he stated that abolishing the department would require congressional approval. However, he emphasized that his administration would take all legal steps possible to “shut down” the agency. During his press conference, President Trump assured that key programs, including IDEA, Title I, and Pell Grants, would be preserved and reassigned to other departments. However, the executive order does not specify these programs or indicate which departments would assume responsibility for them. The order itself provides limited details: • The Secretary of Education must take all necessary steps, within legal authority, to close the Department of Education and return control of education to the states. • Federal education funds must continue to be allocated in compliance with federal law and administration policy. Because PUSD receives only 1% of its funding from federal sources, we do not anticipate any impact on our programs and services. I understand that this news may be concerning to some families, but please be assured that we remain committed to providing an outstanding education to our students. We will keep families informed as new developments arise. Thank you for your continued partnership in supporting our students. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. articles.text: I don’t know if the world needs another sermon or reflection on the Ten Commandments. What matters much more than anything I can say or write about them is what you and I will do with them. Will we take them seriously? Will we follow them faithfully? Will we inscribe them on our hearts? Rare is the week when there is not a news report about an effort to post the commandments on the walls of the public school classrooms of a state, to carve them into the façade of a legislative chamber or to chisel them onto massive blocks of granite to be placed in the public square of a city, town or village. Noted Baptist pastor Marvin McMickle reminds us that “Posting a replica of the Ten Commandments in a public school classroom is a clear a violation of the separation of church and state as can possibly be imagined. What are we saying to Muslim or Sikh or Hindu students when the only religious message posted in their school is from the Judeo-Christian tradition?” Legal and constitutional arguments about the public display of the Ten Commandments aside, the Scriptures direct us always to their life-shaping purpose. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Tony Simons Sophie Hess, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. Ten words of freedom By Pastor Jim Hopkins I don’t know if the world needs another sermon or reflection on the Ten Commandments. What matters much more than anything I can say or write about them is what you and I will do with them. Will we take them seriously? Will we follow them faithfully? Will we inscribe them on our hearts? Rare is the week when there is not a news report about an effort to post the commandments on the walls of the public school classrooms of a state, to carve them into the façade of a legislative chamber or to chisel them onto massive blocks of granite to be placed in the public square of a city, town or village. Noted Baptist pastor Marvin McMickle reminds us that “Posting a replica of the Ten Commandments in a public school classroom is a clear a violation of the separation of church and state as can possibly be imagined. What are we saying to Muslim or Sikh or Hindu students when the only religious message posted in their school is from the Judeo-Christian tradition?” Legal and constitutional arguments about the public display of the Ten Commandments aside, the Scriptures direct us always to their life-shaping purpose. Psalm 119:11 proclaims, “I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you.” The intent of the words God gave to Moses is that they guide us, shape us, direct us, inform us and inspire us. The Ten Commandments are found in both the book of Exodus and the book of Deuteronomy. In Exodus they are given to the people after they have escaped enslavement in Egypt and are poised to begin their journey to the promised land. In Deuteronomy they are given anew to the generation that will leave the wilderness and continue the journey to that land flowing with milk and honey. It is important to understand the commandments, the “Ten Words” in Jewish tradition, are theological in nature, that they are given by the God whose work it is to set people free, that they are a pathway to living in right relationship with God and others and that they are portal to the kind of world most of us would want to live in, the kind of world most of us would like to give to See Religion Corner on page 32 MARIANA NAVARRETE, Piedmont Community Church I’m not a fan of the heat, but today has been a nice change of pace. articles.text: To the Piedmont Community, In September 2014, I joined the Piedmont Police Department after 18 formative years of service with the San Jose Police Department. Nine years ago, I had the honor of being appointed as your Chief of Police. Now, after much contemplation and discussion with my family, the time has come for me to begin a new chapter. I will be retiring on July 17, 2025, concluding 29 years of service in law enforcement as a sworn officer. As my retirement nears, I have been reflecting on my time serving the Piedmont community and the many dedicated individuals I have had the privilege to work alongside—both within the police department and across the broader City staff. I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to serve with the committed, capable, and compassionate members of the Piedmont Police Department, who continually demonstrate their dedication to our shared vision of exemplifying the best of policing. I have learned much from, and thoroughly enjoyed working with, current and former department heads and City staff as we have worked together to provide exceptional service to this community. I am especially thankful for the support, trust, and confidence placed in me by City Administrators Rosanna Bayon Moore, Sara Lillevand, and Paul Benoit, which has allowed our Police Department to operate at the highest levels of policing while continuously striving for improvement. My appreciation also extends to current and past City Council Members, whose dedication to the Piedmont community is truly inspiring. And to the residents of Piedmont—where do I begin? My family and I arrived in this community over ten years ago and were immediately welcomed. I am incredibly grateful for the community’s engagement with our Department, your unwavering support, and the collaborative spirit that has helped us all strive for better. Bowers in 2014 As my time with the City draws to a close, I remain committed to our important work and will do everything I can to ensure a smooth leadership transition. It has been my distinct honor to serve as your Chief of Police. With gratitude and appreciation, Jeremy Bowers Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers (left), with son Andre, wife Patricia and daughter Anjali in 2024. articles.text: Looking for a special adopter for a special dog. Bloom is a sweet and affectionate 9-year-old, 100-pound German Shepherd gal at Oakland Animal Services. Due to shelter overcrowding and the difficulty in adopting out larger dogs, Bloom is an at-risk dog. Shelter staff say Bloom is a devoted companion who enjoys staying close to people and getting pettings. She is very interested in other dogs, but is not reactive to them and could do well in a multi-dog household. Bloom is gentle and knows basic commands. Come meet Bloom at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12-7 pm, or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest returns for its fourth year with an unmissable multicultural celebration Piedmont Food Fest The fourth annual Piedmont Food Fest will take place at Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 19, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Early bird deals on drink and carnival passes are available this month. Beer and Wine Zone passholders can sample local craft beer from Altamont Beerworks, Alameda Island Brewing, Del Cielo Brewery, Headyworks Brewing and Oakland United Beerworks; wine from Deer Hill Vineyards, P. Herrell Winery and Maker Wine; and hard cider from Mount Diablo Cider Company and Blindwood Cider. Early bird passholders save $10 per tumbler. This year’s KidZone will feature a carnival midway, a cultural craft station, frozen treats and a performance by Prescott Circus Theater. Early bird passes save $5 per child. Music and live performance fans can enjoy the Jazz Education Ensemble, Oakland Taiko, Great Wall Youth Orchestra, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance, HiiiWAV Artist Showcase and the Beloved Little Circus aerialist show by the Exedra. All shows are free. The food lineup includes Maine Lobster, Momolicious, La Pituca, Hearth Wood-Fired Pizza and Rock Club Burgers. Returning favorites include The Chairman, Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Aburaya (Japanese Fried Chicken), Tea on Piedmont, Crazy Empanadas and Swahili Spot. Attendee registration and Early Bird passes are available at www.piedmontfoodfest.org. This community event is free to attend and visitors from around the Bay Area are welcome! Photo by Michelle Luo Along with an array of food, there will be games for everyone to enjoy at this year’s Piedmont Food Festival. MUSIC FOOD FROM AROUND THE WORLD! Tom Snyder & Anne Bisagno

articles.text: Piedmont Unplugged and the Piedmont Elementary Parent Education Committee will host Lenore Skenazy, “America’s Worst Mom,” on Thursday, April 3, in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. She was given that title for letting her 9-year-old son ride the subway alone - and now she’s an A-list thought leader in parenting. She is the author of Free-Range Kids, president of Let Grow, and collaborator on The Anxious Generation. She will help parents understand why giving kids more independence, responsibility, and unstructured play can help them thrive. The event is free and open to all. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s Parents Club has a few more tickets left for “Kickin’ it Old Skool.” its school fundraiser on Thursday, March 27. A professional comedian will host the evening’s festivities including a live auction. Party goers will have a chance to eat, drink, and dance the night away to nostalgic 80’s and 90’s music. This is the school’s biggest annual fundraiser and will be held at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Auction items include a private dinner with Michelin 2-Star chef James Syhabout (Commis), Tahoe and wine county vacation rentals, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, plus Warriors and Giants tickets. Old skool sneakers, like Vans and Keds, are not required but highly encouraged to grace the dance floor. There will also be a raffle full of goodies, a Mulberry’s candy bar with nostalgic throwback treats and signature cocktails, including a special “Carnazzo Cosmo” sponsored by Lisa Chan. T he a n nu a l eve nt i s co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several parent parties, including Pub Trivia and Pints, Poker and Pinot. and the Bad Moms Bash. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27 knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Proceeds from the Kickin it Old Skool event raise funds to support school programs, including: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking a few more parent sponsors. articles.text: Stuttering, characterized by involuntary disruptions in speech fluency, often manifests in early childhood. These disruptions, or disfluencies, can manifest as repetitions of sounds, syllables, or words; prolongations of sounds; and involuntary pauses or blocks where the individual is unable to produce sounds. While occasional disfluencies are common in all speakers, stuttering is distinguished by its frequency and the struggle associated with speech production. Stuttering is a complex disorder with multifaceted causes and impacts. Awareness and understanding are vital in creating supportive environments for those affected. With early and appropriate intervention, individuals who stutter can develop effective communication strategies, empowering them to participate fully in social, educational, and professional spheres. Early intervention remains crucial in managing pediatric stuttering. Research reveals a need for personalized therapy plans tailored to each child’s unique needs, emphasizing that no single approach fits all. Intervention can include a variety of elements, such as stuttering modification. Stuttering modification focuses on helping individuals manage and modify their stuttering to achieve smoother speech. This method emphasizes desensitization to stuttering moments and developing techniques to control speech disruptions. Recent studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in school-age children, highlighting its potential as a viable treatment option. Intervention can target fluency shaping as well. Fluency shaping aims to replace stuttered speech with controlled fluency by teaching specific speech techniques, such as slowed speech and gentle onset of voice. This approach has been shown to reduce disfluencies and enhance overall speech fluency in children. Intervention can be indirect as well, empowering parents to support their child’s speech development. Parents can be trained to provide positive reinforcement for fluent speech and create environmental adaptations which enhance fluency. This approach can be particularly effective for preschool aged children. There is a growing shift towards stutter-affirming therapy, which emphasizes a strengthsbased approach. This perspective encourages acceptance and empowerment, moving away from solely focusing on fluency. Such approaches aim to improve the overall well-being and self-esteem of individuals who stutter. The landscape of pediatric stuttering treatment is evolving, with a range of therapeutic approaches tailored to individual needs. Early intervention, combined with innovative therapies and parental involvement, plays a crucial role in supporting children who stutter on their journey toward fluent communication. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Understanding stuttering and effective support strategies

articles.text: Piedmont Scout and PHS Baseball player Sammy Ragones has been working with the City of Piedmont to dismantle and replace the batting cages at Coaches Field with brand new cages, complete with new nets and turf. Ragones planned, organized, led and managed the extensive community service project as his Eagle Scout Service Project – a requirement to become an Eagle Scout, the highest rank in Scouting. Ragones chose the batting cages as the site for his Eagle project to help benefit the Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation (PBSF), who he had played baseball with for 10 years. The project builds on the legacy of Troop 15, where Eagle Scout Alexander Menke built the original batting cage for his Eagle project in 2006. The previous batting cages at Coaches Field were nearly 20 years old and showing signs of heavy damage. Torn fencing and nets allowed potential for baseballs to fly out of the cage, uneven dirt floors posed a possible tripping hazard, and in wet weather it would pool with water. With the cage in dire need of remodeling, Ragones set out to work with the City to install a lasting new cage with multiple lanes. Scouts and parents involved with the new batting cage at Coaches Field Piedmont Scouts from Troop 15 work to dismantle the old batting cages at Coaches Field to make way for a new structure. Scout volunteers double check their work before safely removing the metal framework. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: Eagle Scout project replaces batting cages at Coaches field

articles.text: This summer California College of the Arts (CCA) invites middle and high school students to explore their creativity through dynamic youth art and design programs in San Francisco. With hands-on studio experiences across a variety of disciplines, students can dive into animation, architecture, ceramics, comics, drawing, graphic design, fashion design, film, illustration, industrial design, interaction design, interior design, jewelry making and metal arts, painting, photography, printmaking, screenprinting, sculpture, and textiles. Middle schoolers can engage in interactive studio workshops, while high school students can choose from non-credit and forcredit courses to expand their portfolios. All youth programs are now open for enrollment and tuition includes lunch and all art supplies. Scholarships are available for all programs The Young Artist Studio Program (YASP) is a one week intensive summer program for middle school students currently in fifth, sixth, and seventh grade. The program is hosting three sessions this summer: June 9-13, July 14-18, and August 4- 8. A Pre-College student creates a zine on the drawing tablet. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont defeated Northgate in a dominant 15-2 win, putting an end to a four-game losing streak. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got back in the win column on Thursday, March 20, beating Northgate 15-2 in Walnut Creek. The win ended a four-game losing streak. It was a big game for Peyton Watson, a junior who led the offense with seven goals. Senior Chloe Graham netted four goals and classmate Friedie Schickedanz scored four. She also had three assists, and won five draws in the face-off circle. Piedmont looks ahead to starting its Western Alameda County Conference schedule against Berkeley on Friday, March 28. The Highlanders are hoping to defend last year’s WACC title. The Yellowjackets currently hold a 5-3 record and are also 3-0 against league teams. Berkeley defeated Northgate on March 12 with a 10-6 win. Piedmont got it started with Watson launching one in after three minutes. Friedie Schickedanz scored two and a half minutes later, while Watson netted two more at 4:55 and 3:22. Graham got her first goal with 54 seconds left and Watson got her fifth goal with five seconds left, 9-0. Watson wasted no time getting right back at it, scoring 55 seconds into the third quarter. Friedie Schickedanz scored around two minutes later and added one more with 45 seconds left. In the fourth, Watson scored just 57 seconds into play. Graham got PHS’ last two goals at 9:43 15-2 rout of Northgate Piedmont led 9-0 by the end of the first half with three goals in the first quarter and six in the second. The Highlanders added three more in the third quarter and another three in the final going, while Las Lomas scored twice in the second half. After back and forth possessions for over four minutes, Schickedanz got on the board with 7:43 left in the first quarter. Watson made it 2-0 with 5:07 to go, while Mary Schickedanz scored two minutes later. In the six-goal second quarter, Peyton Watson scored seven goals against Northgate. Chloe Graham (left) scored four goals for Piedmont.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team took to two different events Friday and Saturday, March 21-22. Their distance runners traveled to Dublin HS for the Dublin Distance Fiesta, while sprinters and field athletes took to San Ramon Valley HS in Danville for the Swenson/Werne Invitational. The Dublin Distance Fiesta is one of the marquee events of the spring season for distance runners for 18 years. It brings together hundreds of schools and thousands of athletes. The Swensen/Werne Invitational, meanwhile, is the previous SRV Sprint & Field Festival, marking the first year under its new name. “The Dublin Distance Fiesta is the premier distance event on the West Coast, where athletes from all over California, as well as neighboring states and beyond, make the trek to Dublin to compete against a wide range of distance competition, including the elite of elite,” explained Piedmont coach Pouyan Assadi. Dublin Distance Fiesta Sophomore Sebastien Swain competed in the 800 and 1600 meters with successful runs. He clocked a time of 1:57.96 in the 800 to finish 18th of 972 athletes. He also had a time of 4:23.96 in the 1600 to place 31st among 1331 milers. “The smile on Seb’s face after his 800 is why we as coaches show up and give it our all every day. It’s so awesome that even while sick, he brought it, going up against the top half milers on the West Coast. I’m excited to see what he does with this momentum.” Sophomore classmate Leighton Mand also had successful days in the 800 and 1600. She placed 76th of 598 in the 800 with a time of 2:28.42. Her time was a personal record of two seconds after setting her new PR just six days earlier. In the 1600, Mand was 85th of 709 with a time of 5:22.29. “Leighton is the next woman up in a long history of girls distance success at PHS. Last week she dropped her mile time by 7 seconds, this week it’s her 800 time. She’s super coachable and doesn’t get intimidated. It’s awesome,” Assadi said. Photos by Becky Spies Sam Shelby competed in four events at the Swenson/Werne Invitational. Sebastien Swain ran the 800 and 1600 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta. Leighton Mand also competed in the 800 and 1600 meters at Dublin. Also with a successful day in the boys’ 1600 was junior Noah Sohn, with a time of 4:23.96. In the girls’ 800, sophomore Gladwin Horsley was 169th in 2:36 and Caroline Taylor was 190th in 2:38.39. Taylor also placed 148th in the 1600 in 5:33.94, while freshman Nikita Gorelik was 173rd in 5:38.07. Swenson/Werne Invitational It was a record day for the boys’ 4x100 relay team of Rehan Mumtaz, Sam Shelby, Maddox Ma, and Eric Venner. They placed second in a field of 14 teams with a time of 43.18 seconds. According to online records, their team broke Piedmont’s all-time mark of 43.63 set in 2022. The boys’ 4x400 team also finished second with a time of 3.31.13, with Miguel Long replacing Mumtaz. Shelby also had strong performances in the 100 and 400 meters. He was second of 116 runners in the 100 with a time of 11.12, and was fifth of 88 quarter-milers in the 400, clocking a 50.54. Long is having a banner year. He won the triple jump with a distance of 44 feet, 4.25 inches in a field of 14 athletes. His distance was a personal record and more than 1 foot, 3 inches from last year’s NCS Bayshore Championship. He placed fourth among 18 in the long jump at 20 feet, 10.25 inches. “Miguel had his first monster PR of the season in triple jump going 44’4”, advancing his season best by almost 2 full feet. He continues his streak of winning 1st place in at least one event in every meet this season,” Assadi said. The girls’ 4x100 relay team won their event with a time of 4:14.53 in a field of five teams. Saniyah Johnson finished sixth of 18 in the shot put with a distance of 31 feet. In the other throwing event, Alina Shahid was fifth of 21 in the discus in 94 feet, 6 inches. NEXT UP Piedmont hosts a WACC Meet on Thursday, March 27 at 3:30 p.m. They also visit Castro Valley for the CV Relays on Saturday, March 29 at 9:00 a.m.

articles.text: March Madness is now underway with the Elite Eight on the docket this week. Two former athletes from Piedmont High competed in the NCAA playoff brackets this year: Luke Barrett of St. Mary’s and Natalia Martinez of San Diego State. Here’s a look at their seasons. hitting 45 percent of his field goals. He was third on the team in rebounds with 238, to go along with 48 assists, 25 steals, and 13 blocks. The Gaels finished its season with a 29-6 record. NAT MARTINEZ LUKE BARRETT St. Mary’s Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, finishes as a senior leader on St. Mary’s No. 7 seeded team in the eastern bracket. The Gaels beat No. 10 Vanderbilt 59-56 in comeback fashion on March 21 in the Round of 64, but fell to No. 2 Alabama 80-66 the following round. He played a critical part in SMC’s opening round win over Vandy. He sent a pair of assists for 3-pointers in the second half, including one to Augustas Marčiulionis to give his team a 53-50 lead with 4:33 left. He also knocked down a 3-pointer to give St. Mary’s a 56-50 lead with 2:01 left. Luke finished with a double-double against Vanderbilt with 12 points, 10 rebounds, and two assists. Against Alabama, he played 37 minutes, logging six points, seven rebounds, and an assist. He notched career highs of 20 points and five assists in a 70-60 win over Pacific on December 28, to go along with 10 rebounds for his fourth career double- double. Barrett started all 35 games and leads the team with 1,275 total minutes. He finished fourth on the team in points with 342, San Diego State Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, was impressive in her debut year on the San Diego State Aztecs roster as a freshman They won the Mountain West Conference as the No. 4 seed and earned the No. 14 ranking in the NCAA’s Spokane 1 bracket. San Diego State went up against No. 2 LSU, which had made it to the Elite Eight, losing 103-48. Martinez was in the starting five, playing 27 minutes for seven points, one rebound, and one assist. As the No. 4 seed in the Mountain West Tournament, SD State beat No. 5 New Mexico 63-53, upset No. 1 UNLV 71-59, and won the title against No. 2 Wyoming 72-68. She logged six points and two assists on Wyoming. She set a Mountain West Conference record on January 18’s 85-66 win over Utah State, where she became the first player to ever sink six 3-pointers in a conference game when the, to go along with nine rebounds and seven assists. In her record-setting performance, Martinez finished with 22 points, converting 7/8 from the field and 6/7 for 3-pointers. She also added one steal and a block, and hit one of her 3-pointers from nearly 30 feet. The Aztecs finished its season with a 25-10 record. articles.text: Opera San Jose will present the Northern California premiere of Hector Armienta’s Zorro on April 14, closing its 41st season. The production stars tenor Xavier Prado as Diego de la Vega/Zorro and soprano Maria Brea as Ana Maria Soza. Latino stage director David Radamés Toro will make his Opera San Jose debut, and conductor Jorge Parodi will return after his debut last season on Rigoletto. Armienta’s opera about the masked vigilante combines humor and suspense with mariachi, flamenco and corrido music. Set in an early 1800s Spanish colony, the work follows a nobleman who defends the poor and enslaved while hiding his identity. “I can’t wait to bring Zorro to our audiences,” Opera San Jose General Director Shawna Lucey said. “This mesmerizing opera blends stunning orchestration with high drama, delivering an enthralling experience for both regular opera-lovers and newcomers to the form. From the fierce brass fanfares to the rich strings and sonorous woodwinds, the score pulses with adventure, romance and suspense. With thrillingly challenging vocals and nonstop momentum, Zorro takes us on a heart-pounding ride.” Zorro is the second Spanish-language opera presented on Opera San Jose’s mainstage, following last season’s Florencia en el Amazonas. “So many in our community speak Spanish at home, and we have been delighted to welcome Tenor Xavier Prado is Diego de la Vega/Zorro in Opera San Jose’s Zorro. new audiences who are excited to hear works they can instantly follow,” Lucey said. She added that many California public school students study the state’s history and early settlements, and will gain insight into that era while watching Zorro. “This production will provide an outstanding, and wildly dramatic, look at the political dynamics of that era, making it a great introduction for younger audiences,” she said. The performance will run about 2 hours and 30 minutes with one intermission. Opera San Jose staff will host a pre-show discussion at 1 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. Zorro will be performed on select dates April 19 through May 4. Visit https://www.operasj.org/ productions/zorro to learn more and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Non Stop Bhangra kicks off OMCA’s evening series April 4 OAKLAND, Calif. — The Oakland Museum of California’s free community-gathering evening event series “Friday Nights” returns April 4, kicking off the spring season with performances by Bay Area-based dance crew Non Stop Bhangra. The museum hosts free, family-friendly community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, arts activities and late-night museum access with museum ticket purchase. Non Stop Bhangra crew members have performed Bhangra, traditional Punjabi folk music and dance, for Bay Area audiences for more than two decades. The collective celebrated its 20th anniversary in 2024 and recently presented the Bay Area Holi Festival of Colors in Oakland. Non Stop Bhangra has performed at museums, performing arts centers, festivals, nightclubs, community centers and youth outreach events. The museum’s first Friday Nights event co-celebrates Oakland Fairyland’s 75th anniversary and the opening of “Fairyland @ 75: A Legacy of Magic” near the Gallery of California Natural Sciences. Museum staff will host a puppet-making activity April 4, offering a hands-on way for families to engage with the beloved children’s park. Bring blankets and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s lawn, where live music and entertainment take place. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from food trucks on-site. Vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-nonstop-bhangra/ to learn more. Photo courtesy of Oakland Museum of California Non Stop Bhangra will perform traditional Punjabi folk music to kick off the series. articles.text: Featured artists include Artists Firelei Báez, Masako Miki and Jeffrey Sincich Installation view, Playful Spirits Illuminate the Universe, by Masako Miki, 2024. Miki is one of this year’s featured artists. Tickets for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) Art Bash, its annual fundraising gala, are on sale. Art Bash raises more than $2 million annually, benefiting SFMOMA’s education, family programs and community engagement events, which serve over 150,000 people each year. The gala features a cocktail reception and dinner with live music and immersive art installations. About 2,000 guests are expected at the 6 p.m. reception, designed by New York-based visual artist Firelei Báez. The museum commissioned Báez to create a custom projection for the gala, showcasing her themes of diaspora and afrofuturism. Sotheby’s auctioneer Phyllis Kao will lead a live auction during dinner. Bay Area artists Masako Miki and Jeffrey Sincich will create immersive art installations in other museum spaces. Miki, originally from Osaka, Japan, uses materials including wool, wood, bronze, ink and watercolor to manifest ancient folklore. She has exhibited at museums locally, including solo shows and projects at the de Young Museum in San Francisco and the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA). San Francisco-based artist Sincich, a trained sign-painter, combines his interest in handpainted signage, typography and architecture with handmade quilts. His pop art-style work has been featured in publications including Juxtapoz Magazine and Popeye Magazine. He has shown at the de Young Museum in San Francisco and Charlie James Gallery in Los Angeles. San Francisco soul singer and songwriter Martin Luther and local DJ Lady Ryan will provide live entertainment. Additional performers will be announced. The museum-wide gala ends at 1 a.m. Guests can purchase tickets for the dinner and live auction, or for the late-night party only, which begins at 10 p.m. Latenight party ticket holders receive party access, including immersive art, live music, museum exhibitions and complimentary food and drink. Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/press-release/celebrate-creativity-community-at-sfmomas-art-bash-on-april-23/ to learn more and to purchase tickets. Art Bash 2024 Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

articles.text: Exhibition leaves Asian Art Museum April 7 Courtesy of Asian Art Museum Installation view of Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink at the Asian Art Museum Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink, an exhibition at the Asian Art Museum celebrating the life and work of Chinese ink painter Qi Baishi, closes Sunday, April 7. The exhibition marks the 160th anniversary of Baishi’s birth and features 42 works on paper from the Beijing Fine Art Academy, where he served as the first honorary director. Inspiration In Ink is the first time many of the displayed works have been shown in the United States. “Qi Baishi’s long and storied life witnessed China’s dramatic passage from the Qing Dynasty to the new republic period and the rise of socialism,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “Renowned as the people’s artist, Qi declined retirement. Instead, he explored ink art in his later years, aiming to share his love of nature and help people find enlightenment in everyday life.” Zhang said the artist’s “technical abilities and expressionistic approach imbue his art with a spiritual quality, inviting viewers to contemplate the deeper significance of everyday motifs.” “His work resonates with audiences because he captures his subjects and expresses their spirit through calligraphic, spontaneous strokes, something that requires master brushwork,” Zhang said. In 1960, Baishi became the first Chinese artist to receive a solo exhibition at the de Young Memorial Museum in San Francisco. His “Twelve Landscape Screens” (1925) sold for $141 million in 2017. “His ability to capture beauty in the ordinary contributed to his growing popularity inside and outside China, a legacy that continues to thrive today,” said Rob Mintz, Chief Curator at the Asian Art Museum. “Qi Baishi’s everyday subject matter and whimsical, playful style made his art accessible to audiences, making him the first Chinese painter to capture the attention of American audiences,” Mintz said. The exhibition is on view through April 7. A docent-led public tour will be held Wednesday, March 27, at 1 p.m. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/qi-baishi-inspiration-in-ink/ to learn more and to purchase museum tickets.
articles.title: Last chance to see Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink

articles.text: General admission tickets still available The de Young Museum in San Francisco will welcome artists, luminaries, and museum supporters for its Annual Gala and Late Night after-party, the museum’s largest fundraiser, on Thursday, April 10. Proceeds support educational programming and future exhibitions at the de Young and Legion of Honor museums. The evening will include a seated dinner, an honoree program, and an evening reception featuring full access to de Young galleries, interactive pop-up art activations throughout the museum, and live musical performance. The gala begins at 6 p.m. with cocktails and museum exhibition viewing and ends at midnight. Honorees this year include artist Sir Isaac Julien, whose first major US retrospective will debut at the evening gala, and philanthropist and former trustee of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Dagmar Dolby. R&B vocalist Ravyn Lenae, from Chicago, will perform live in the museum’s Wilsey Court. The 2024 Annual Gala raised nearly $1.5 million and record-breaking net revenue for the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, said the money raised provides “key support for our education programs and ongoing efforts to connect visitors with the art and ideas shaping our time.” Early bird tickets have sold out but general admission tickets are still available. Guests must be 21 years or older to attend. Visit https://www.famsf.org/events/ annual-gala-2025 to learn more and to purchase tickets. The Late Night after-party is hosted at de Young Museum for the San Francisco Fine Arts Museum’s 2024 Annual Gala. The ensemble impressed with its professional approach. Arriving onstage en masse, they displayed efficiency and precision. The program, centered on the 300th anniversary of Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons was compelling. The string orchestra produced a smooth sound. Though billed as an “original instrument ensemble,” their sound was surprisingly robust, delivered with almost unbelievable virtuosity. The audience was enthusiastic. However, the performance had drawbacks. The relentless ferocity of each piece was questionable. While speed and volume may impress, nuance and elegance were lacking. Miles Graber to the rescue In stark contrast was the scene at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday. Pianist Miles Graber, a fixture on local concert stages, joined violinist Sangeeta Swamy, violist Stephanie Ng and cellist Michael Graham for piano quartets by Mozart and Brahms. These musicians rivaled, if not surpassed, the Les Arts Florissants players. Their approach prioritized warmth, vibrancy and musical intelligence over ostentatious displays. Which musical philosophy is superior? The debate continues. Preference isn’t necessarily a matter of one being better than the other.

articles.text: In baseball, perfection is pitching a perfect game. In jewelry, it’s a flawless diamond. In music, does a perfect performance exist? Legendary pianist Vladimir Horowitz, often disappointed in his own work, pointed to Jascha Heifetz. Strangely, Heifetz, a paragon of virtue, claimed satisfaction with only one performance in his career. These days, near-perfection seems commonplace. A recent concert by Les Arts Florissants, led by violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte, exemplified this high level of musical performance. Pianist Miles Graber

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, March 26, 2025 de Young Annual Gala is April 10 General admission tickets still available By Allyson Aleksey The de Young Museum in San Francisco will welcome artists, luminaries, and museum supporters for its Annual Gala and Late Night after-party, the museum’s largest fundraiser, on Thursday, April 10. Proceeds support educational programming and future exhibitions at the de Young and Legion of Honor museums. The evening will include a seated dinner, an honoree program, and an evening reception featuring full access to de Young galleries, interactive pop-up art activations throughout the museum, and live musical performance. The gala begins at 6 p.m. with cocktails and museum exhibition viewing and ends at midnight. Honorees this year include artist Sir Isaac Julien, whose first major US retrospective will debut at the evening gala, and philanthropist and former trustee of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Dagmar Dolby. R&B vocalist Ravyn Lenae, from Chicago, will perform live in the museum’s Wilsey Court. The 2024 Annual Gala raised nearly $1.5 million and record-breaking net revenue for the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, said the money raised provides “key support for our education programs and ongoing efforts to connect visitors with the art and ideas shaping our time.” Early bird tickets have sold out but general admission tickets are still available. Guests must be 21 years or older to attend. Visit https://www.famsf.org/events/ annual-gala-2025 to learn more and to purchase tickets. Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts The Late Night after-party is hosted at de Young Museum for the San Francisco Fine Arts Museum’s 2024 Annual Gala. The Musical Gourmet Better Than Perfection By Joseph Gold In baseball, perfection is pitching a perfect game. In jewelry, it’s a flawless diamond. In music, does a perfect performance exist? Legendary pianist Vladimir Horowitz, often disappointed in his own work, pointed to Jascha Heifetz. Strangely, Heifetz, a paragon of virtue, claimed satisfaction with only one performance in his career. These days, near-perfection seems commonplace. A recent concert by Les Arts Florissants, led by violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte, exemplified this high level of musical performance. Sunday, April 6, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio Please join us for some late afternoon relaxation enlivened by the In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Albert Brooks, MD – celebrating the arrival of Spring — a Time of Renewal with their versions of all your favorite songs and classic jazz and blues! You’ll be able to sit for a couple of hours in a comfortable chair in the intimate club-like environment with complimentary snacks, enjoying the familiar music and perhaps dancing to it. Bring a friend and plan to meet some new ones! Get tickets at https://bpt.me/6214927, or $30 at the door, cash or check only. Seating is limited to 50. Saturday, April 12, 11 a.m. - 2 p.m. Oakland Art Association Group Exhibition Don’t miss the opening artists’ reception for this stunning juried exhibition of Oakland Art Association’s members’ works — varied in style, medium, approach, and size. For the next eight weekends, until June 1, 2025, the gallery will be open and staffed with mermber artists from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday. There is no charge to visit, and of course you can also see the art on display when you attend other fuunctions at PCA! Active since 1957, OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. We encourage artistic endeavor in our community, support public-school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. Exhibits, both group and solo, are often in libraries, banks, John Muir Hospital, Piedmont Gardens, and country clubs. Sunday, April 13, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert René Mandel, Berkeley Symphony’s former Executive and Artistic Director, presents A Viennese Sojourn, highlighting the music that tremendously influenced the Western classical canon. As one of the orchestra’s acting concertmasters, René brings his confident virtuosity into the intimate chamber music setting to envelop the audience in the sounds of the first Viennese school. The Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Series would not be where it is today without the visionary leadership from René’s tenure. Buy tickets at https://bit.ly/4iD9XiU. • • • • • • • • Coming up soon in May and June: Festival Opera Company’s annual fundraising Gala performance event (May 3) Diluvian String Quartet concert Insight Chamber Players Spring celebration Achille Bocus Mandolin Octet concert Benicia Chamber Players concert Berkelium String Quartet showcase recital Left Coast Chamber Ensemble concert … several solo and duo recitals of emerging performers Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events. The ensemble impressed with The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet its professional approach. Arriving onstage en masse, they displayed efficiency and precision. The program, centered on the 300th anniversary of Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons was compelling. The string orchestra produced a smooth sound. Though billed as an “original instrument ensemble,” their sound was surprisingly robust, delivered with almost unbelievable virtuosity. The audience was enthusiastic. However, the performance had drawbacks. The relentless ferocity of each piece was questionable. While speed and volume may impress, nuance and elegance were lacking. Miles Graber to the rescue In stark contrast was the scene 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday. Pianist Miles info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org Graber, a fixture on local concert stages, joined violinist Sangeeta www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org Swamy, violist Stephanie Ng and cellist Michael Graham for piano quartets by Mozart and Brahms. These musicians rivaled, if not surpassed, the Les Arts Florissants players. Their approach prioritized warmth, vibrancy and musical intelligence over ostentatious displays. Which musical philosophy is superior? The debate continues. Preference isn’t necessarily a matter of one being better than the other. Democracy is not a spectator sport! articles.text: Mud a coming-of-age film by Jeff Nichols, follows two boys, Ellis (Tye Sheridan) and Neckbone (Jacob Lofland), living along the Mississippi River. Ellis resides in a river shack with his estranged parents (Ray McKinnon and Sarah Paulson). His mother wants to move to town, while his stern fisherman father resists. Ellis, aligning with his father, declares his love for the river. Ellis and Neckbone discover a motorboat lodged in a tree on a small island. Inside, they find Mud (Matthew McConaughey), a drifter. Mud claims he’s living on the boat and offers it to them in exchange for food. He later reveals he’s a fugitive, awaiting his girlfriend, Juniper (Reese Witherspoon). Ellis, experiencing adolescent hormones, becomes invested in Mud’s romantic story, despite Neckbone’s skepticism. He helps Mud with food, tools and an engine. Meanwhile, Ellis navigates his own romantic interests with an older girl, May Pearl (Bonnie Sturdivant). The boys learn Mud is not only hiding from the law but also bounty hunters hired by King (Joe Don Baker), the father of the man Mud killed. Ellis remains determined to help Mud and Juniper. ing the narrative as a love story through Ellis’ and Mud’s perspectives. Mud is a Southern Gothic tale, emphasizing authentic characters, setting and language, reminiscent of Tennessee Williams and Mark Twain. The film serves as a noir metaphor for Ellis’ coping with his parents’ impending divorce, contrasting with Mud’s idealized love. The narrative culminates in a violent act with a twist. Mud. Written and directed by Jeff Nichols. Lionsgate/Roadside Attractions. Starring Matthew McConaughy, Reese Witherspoon, Tye Sheridan, Jacob Lofland. 2 hours 10 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. articles.text: Catherine Deneuve and Gérard Depardieu in Potiche If you love movies and, over the years, have watched the performances of Catherine Deneuve, then you will find Potiche thoroughly enjoyable. It is a breezy, light-hearted comedy as only the French can construct, and Deneuve, along with Gerard Depardieu, enjoys herself immensely. The year is 1977 and Suzanne Pujol (Deneuve), is a housewife who has been marginalized all of her married life by her wealthy industrialist husband, Robert (Fabrice Luchini). Robert, however, is more than an insufferable male chauvinist pig, to use a familiar parlance, but a skirt-chasing, cantankerous, self-absorbed king of the castle who has no qualms about engaging in dalliances with other women, to include his long suffering secretary, Nadege (Karin Viard). Meanwhile, Suzanne has become, over the years, his Potiche, meaning a type of trophy wife. A Potiche, however, is not a glamorous younger woman who replaces the older wife – she who has devoted decades of her life being supportive as well as bearing and mothering their children. She is and continues to be the woman who has kept his house, looked the other way, ran interference with the children, now grown, while leading a not surprisingly hermetic life. articles.text: Storks, a charming, kid friendly animation, released by Warner Bros. in 2016. It answers the question, “Where do babies come from?” as only Hollywood can: with a delivery service, provided by long beaked and long-legged storks. Prospective parents need only send in their request, and voila!, the little one arrives, wrapped in a diaper. But that was then, and this is now. Apparently, due to a disastrous mix up, the storks are now out of the baby delivery business; instead, they’re in the employment of Cornerstone.com, an online outfit that delivers packages. What happened, long ago, was that a stork grew so attached to an infant that it failed to make the delivery, which created quite a brouhaha. That youngster, named Tulip (Katie Crown), grew up among the storks, and now works for Cornerstone. She’s a ditzy firecracker, full of energy, often accident prone, and sports a mop of red hair. But the head of Cornerstone, Hunter (Kelsey Grammar), is not happy with Tulip’s clumsiness. He calls in Junior (Adam Sandberg), one of the worker storks, and assigns him the task of firing Tulip. But kind-hearted Junior is reluctant to carry out his assignment and doesn’t let Tulip go. But his hesitation has one major unintended consequence: Tulip accidentally activates the unused baby-making machine, which produces an adorable infant. As it turns out, the baby is slated to be the sister of a kid named Nate (Anton Starkman). He has been pleading with his workaholic parents (Jennifer Aniston and Ty Burrell) for a sibling to no avail. Nate even goes as far as writing a letter to the storks at Stone Mountain, asking for a sister. When Junior and Tulip read his intercepted letter, well, they’re confronted with the problem of how to get the little one delivered to the family. Of course, the duo confront a number of obstacles, one being a pigeon named Toadie (Stephen Glickman), and an ominous pack of baby-stealing wolves, led by Alpha and Beta (Keegan-Michael Key and Jordan Peele) that have the ability to shape shift (they even turn themselves into a bridge). Storks is a frenetic story, fastpaced and guaranteed to make the kids laugh. Simply put, it’s a romp that focuses on the many challenges of parenthood and all the accompanying responsibilities. It’s fun from start to finish, all while skirting the question: Where do babies come from? Storks. Directed by Nicholas Stoller, Doug Sweetland. A Warner Bros. animation. Voiced by Andy Sandberg, Katie Crown, Kelsey Grammar. 1 hr., 23 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Now streaming on Prime/apple tv/ Fandango. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s The Great Mouse Detective Disney began its remarkable history of animated stories with a singular mouse, Mickey. So it’s no surprise that once again the animators have returned to The Great Mouse Detective, based on the children’s book series, Basil of Baker Street, by Eve Titus and Paul Galone. Two things took place with this film, both precursors of what was to come: the writers embraced the technology of CGI, realizing that the contemporary audience of kids wanted something a bit more zany. Anthropomorphism alone doesn’t quite cut it. The result is Detective, with a compelling cast of mice and rats, all living in Victorian England in 1897. The tale begins by introducing Olivia Flaversham (Susanne Pollatscheck) and her father Hiram (Alan Young), a master toymaker. Unexpectedly, Hiram, while working in his shop, is kidnapped by a strange bat called Fidget (Candy Candido). He’s a malevolent creature with a broken wing and a peg leg, and bursts in and snatches Olivia’s father. She is at first frantic and at loss as what to do; but then sets out to find the famed mouse detective, Basil of Baker Street (Barrie Ingham), who actually makes his home in the foundation of the home of Sherlock Homes. When Basil learns that the rogue kidnapper was Fidget, the henchman of his nemesis, Professor Ratigan (Vincent Price), a villain he has pursued for years, he immediately takes the case and sets out to solve the mystery of the missing Hiram. And so the hunt begins, a story filled with schemes by Ratigan, whose ultimate dream is to become the supreme ruler of all of England’s Mousedom. The search even includes, surprisingly, Sherlock Holmes’ Basset Hound, Toby (Frank Welker). The plot is exciting, involving Olivia being kidnapped, and a massive dirigible owned by Ratigan that was made for last minute escapes. He even manages to crash the huge ship into the Big Ben tower clock, where, as it turns out, Olivia is being held captive. Kids will enjoy The Great Mouse Detective from the get-go. There is not only a mystery to be solved, but offers nonstop action, led by Basil, magnifying glass in hand, who is in hot pursuit of the villainous Ratigan. At his side, of course, is his trusty assistant Dawson (Van Bettin). The Great Mouse Detective. Directed by John Musker. Disney Animation. 1 hr. 20 min. Rated G. Released in 1986. Now streaming on Disney+/Fandango/prime/ aplle tv. (he makes umbrellas). Suzanne is expected to keep her opinions and criticisms to herself. As circumstances would have it, things abruptly change and Suzanne is forced to step into the role of the C.E.O of the plant, bringing about more changes and demonstrating her latent talent for business and leadership. She turns to the local mayor, Babin (Depardieu), for advice and direction, which he is happy to offer. Of course, things get complicated, in a nice, comedic way, and it seems that these two great actors, national treasures in France to be sure, are having a wonderful time and are the central reason to watch Potiche. Regarding Deneuve, my personal favorite will always be Indochine, set in Indochina during the 1930s. Deneuve portrays a plantation owner and displays, once again, her long-honed dramatic talent. Her filmography is astonishing; she has made countless films, fashioning a magnificent career, her beauty and talent timeless. Few of those films have been comedies, and it is surprising to see how truly funny she can be in Potiche, never letting her role slip into farce and seeming to enjoy what is, at least in part, a satire. Potiche. Directed by Francois Ozon. Starriing Cathrine Deneuve, Gerard Depardieu, Jeremie Renier, Fabrice Luchini and Karin Viard. 1hr, 44 min. Rated R. Released in 2010. Streaming on TUBI/Fandango/ prime/apple tv.

Few of those films have been comedies, and it is surprising to see how truly funny she can be in Potiche, never letting her role slip into farce and seeming to enjoy what is, at least in part, a satire. articles.text: Last Wednesday was the last winter walk of the season for the Walking on Wednesdays group and a parade-like turnout of 52 walkers and six K-9 best friends was on hand. Walker Chuck Oraftik is a train enthusiast and quite knowledgeable about the transit systems that served Piedmont and the East Bay during the first half of the 20th Century. He and Charlene Louie had done a great deal of research on these lines for the group. Chuck had a handout with maps and historical photos to share as he led a tour of three of the four Key System lines that once served Piedmont. In 1870 the Transcontinental Railroad finally reached Oakland and set off a second explosion of East Bay growth. From 1870 to 1890 the Oakland area grew by five times. Many businessmen and speculators sought to make their fortunes by luring customers and workers to the downtowns of Oakland and San Francisco and charging them to get there. More than 30 transit companies were formed during this period. For many years these startups were largely an uncoordinated patchwork of lines with conflicts of egos, politics, track gauges, construction standards plus rapidly evolving power sources: from horsepower to steam power to cable and then to electrical power. Observing this 20-year period of population growth and transit system development, Francis Marion (Borax) Smith saw land investment as a path to wealth and saw efficient transit as a means to increase land values. In the 1890s he formed a Realty Syndicate with Frank C. Havens, and they ultimately bought nearly 20 square miles of land in Piedmont, Berkeley, and Oakland. Smith then managed to acquire ownership of all of the East Bay transit systems. He reorganized and coordinated the system, improved efficiency and schedules and extended routes into his lands to increase their value. Thus, the Key System was created. To further increase ridership and land values he also upgraded trains’ equipment and schedules and also created new destinations and attractions, such Berkeley’s Claremont Hotel and Blair Park in Piedmont. Smith made and lost fortunes twice in the process. After sharing this background, Chuck led the walkers down Highland Avenue to Park Way where they stopped for a group photo. The 10 Line ran down Highland Avenue then turned downhill along the north side of Park Way to Grand and Piedmont Avenues and eventually to downtown Oakland. However starting in 1878 before the 10 Line was created. horsedrawn rail cars came up an unpaved Moraga Avenue from Piedmont Avenue and then along Highland Avenue (then called Vernal Avenue). They In 1890 a cable line also pulled cars up Oakland Avenue to Vernal and then gravity took them back down to Grand Avenue via Carmel and Oakland Avenues. They were all gone by 1902 Chuck Oraftik Talking to Walking on Wednesday Group Among the participants with the Walking on Wedesdays group last week were Margarite Parrone with K-9 best friend Marlin, Mark Laemmle, Maulshree Solanki, Melissa Clark, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Sherry Jacobs, Quincy Dong, Lori Austin, Chuck Oraftik, Peggy Shultz, Helen Dong, Michelle Yang, Priscilla Wanerus, Margie Richardson, Tina Shum, Irene Thompson, Regina O’Connor, Minoo Klayman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Stella Houston, Aabha Kothari, Gayle Young, Debbie Powell, Dave DeRoche, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Phil Witte, Melba Yee, Cathy Laymon, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, June Yee, Noemi Alvarado, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, Nancy Henn, Greg Slatoff, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Jim Kellogg, Tom Lehrkind, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Bob Wong, Mark Davis, Jim Kuo, Brenda Ferrero, Denny McGee, Jasmine Cai, Mike Gallant, Liz Dalrymple, Charlene Louie, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, and Dick Carter. Chuck then took the group down York Avenue, paralleling the Key System’s C Line between York and Riccardo. Along York the group found another pathway near Holly Place that was a C station stop and took it up to Ricardo Avenue. Then it was on to Latham Street where three long, narrow homes were built in 1960 on the right-of-way land on Latham, the only roadway in Piedmont called street. The walkers went to the corner of Oakland and Jerome Avenues, which was the terminal of the C Line and the 12 Line which ran down Fairview Avenue to downtown Oakland via Grand Avenue. There was also a brief discussion of the 11 Line which ran along Linda Avenue past Beach School then up and over to Oakland Avenue via what is now the Linda Avenue Dog Park. Chuck pointed out that the 10 Line was torn out in 1948 and the C Line in 1958 by National City Lines. The trains were replaced by AC Transit. N.C.L. a holding company owned by General Motors, Standard Oil, Firestone Tires, Phillips Petroleum, Goodyear and others. It quickly and quietly purchased all East Bay streetcar lines in 1946, bit in 1949 N.C.L. was convicted of fraud, anti-trust and fined $5,000, (about $60,000 in today’s dollars). Chuck said there are reports that similar interests today are behind the funding of various political and PR campaigns, as well as thousands of lawsuits looking to delay and ultimately kill highspeed rail across America. The walkers expressed their appreciation for all the information and effort Chuck and Charlene put in to make them more knowledgeable about this important part of Piedmont’s history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. and everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. articles.text: • Where should I live? Some states are far more expensive to live in than others. You’ll want to weigh your decision carefully, considering the cost of housing, food, income and real estate taxes, transportation and health care in whatever state you choose. • Have you finished your estate plans? If not, now is the time. You’ll want to work with your legal professional to create whatever documents are needed — a will, living trust, power of attorney — to help ensure your assets go where you want them to go, and that your financial and health care choices will be protected if you become physically or mentally incapacitated. Of course, many of these same issues will apply if you are single, divorced or widowed. But if you are married, you and your spouse will want to discuss all your choices and then decide which steps to take. Once you’ve got your plans in place, you may well find that you can fully enjoy your retirement years. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. articles.text: Once you and your spouse retire, you’ll have some decisions to make. Decisions that could affect your quality of life in your retirement years. What are these choices? Here a few of the most important ones: • How much should I withdraw from our retirement accounts? may have contributed for decades to an IRA and a 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan. But once you retire, you’ll probably need to draw on these accounts to help pay your living expenses. Consequently, both of you will need to be sure that you don’t withdraw so much each year that you risk running out of money later in your retirement. One common guideline is to aim for an annual withdrawal rate of 4%, but everyone’s situation is different based on age, pre-retirement income, lifestyle, health, travel plans and other factors. (Once you turn 73, or 75 if you were born in 1960 or later, you will have to take certain amounts, based on your age and account balance, from your traditional IRA and traditional 401(k) each year.) • When should I take Social Security? The answer to this question depends on many factors, such as your age and other sources of income. You can take Social Security as early as age 62, but your monthly payments will typically be bigger if you wait until your full retirement age, which will be age 67 if you were born in 1960 or later. And if you can afford to wait even longer, your payments will “max out” when you reach age 70. Your decision on when to take Social Security can affect your spouse — and vice versa. If the lower-earning spouse claims Social Security before their full retirement age — again, age 67 — their own retirement benefit and any potential spousal benefit will be reduced. (Spousal benefits are given to the lower-earning spouse if their full retirement benefit is less than half the other spouse’s full retirement benefit.) • Should you downsize? If you live in a big home and your children are grown, you may find it economical to downsize.
articles.title: Key decisions for retired couples

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, March 26, 2025 Key decisions for retired couples Once you and your spouse retire, you’ll have some decisions to make. Decisions that could affect your quality of life in your retirement years. What are these choices? Here a few of the most important ones: • How much should I withdraw from our retirement accounts? By the time you retire, you may have contributed for decades to an IRA and a 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan. But once you retire, you’ll probably need to draw on these accounts to help pay your living expenses. Consequently, both of you will need to be sure that you don’t withdraw so much each year that you risk running out of money later in your retirement. One common guideline is to aim for an annual withdrawal rate of 4%, but everyone’s situation is different based on age, pre-retirement income, lifestyle, health, travel plans and other factors. (Once you turn 73, or 75 if you were born in 1960 or later, you will have to take certain amounts, based on your age and account balance, from your traditional IRA and traditional 401(k) each year.) • When should I take Social Security? The answer to this question depends on many factors, such as your age and other sources of income. You can take Social Security as early as age 62, but your monthly payments will typically be bigger if you wait until your full retirement age, which will be age 67 if you were born in 1960 or later. And if you can afford to wait even longer, your payments will “max out” when you reach age 70. Your decision on when to take Social Security can affect your spouse — and vice versa. If the lower-earning spouse claims Social Security before their full retirement age — again, age 67 — their own retirement benefit and any potential spousal benefit will be reduced. (Spousal benefits are given to the lower-earning spouse if their full retirement benefit is less than half the other spouse’s full retirement benefit.) • Should you downsize? If you live in a big home and your children are grown, you may find it economical to downsize. Of course, this is also an emotional decision, but you may find that you can save money by moving into a smaller home. • Where should I live? Some states are far more expensive to live in than others. You’ll want to weigh your decision carefully, considering the cost of housing, food, income and real estate taxes, transportation and health care in whatever state you choose. • Have you finished your estate plans? If not, now is the time. You’ll want to work with your legal professional to create whatever documents are needed — a will, living trust, power of attorney — to help ensure your assets go where you want them to go, and that your financial and health care choices will be protected if you become physically or mentally incapacitated. Of course, many of these same issues will apply if you are single, divorced or widowed. But if you are married, you and your spouse will want to discuss all your choices and then decide which steps to take. Once you’ve got your plans in place, you may well find that you can fully enjoy your retirement years. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Bowers changed that by having officers on the street, by speaking regularly with City Council and encouraging his officers to become involved in the community. Bowers talked about two different kinds of safety, the actual crime response, crime prevention and investigating, and another, more ethereal sense. “There’s also the perceptions or fear of crime, the feeling of safety in the community,” he said. Bowers mentioned that this sense was recently challenged coming out of the pandemic. The Bowers era of Piedmont police saw new programs emerge, such as Cop on the Block and other partnerships engaging the department directly with residents, including an annual Car Show. “And now, because of the hard work of our officers, we’ve definitely retained that feeling of safety in the community,” he stated. Bowers chose to be part of the Piedmont Police Department even though he was a rising star in San Jose, working as the adjunct to Police Chief Rob Davis and training in the largest Bay Area city. Bowers grew up primarily in Boulder Creek near Santa Cruz, graduating from San Lorenzo Valley High School in 1993 and then went from SF State. At the age of 20, he applied to be in the San Jose Police Department, and left college to begin his career in law enforcement; 18 years later he took the Piedmont job. “I really knew that this was going to be a different chapter in my story, coming to Piedmont. I knew it was going to be fundamentally different,” he said. Bowers said he makes an effort to live in the current moment, and that if he went back to 2014, he wouldn’t have much advice to offer. “I would tell myself, you’ve got the right perspective, be confident in where you are, and be confident in your approach,” he said. “I love this job, I love where I work, this is a good place. I probably added years to my life by coming here and having a healthy working environment,” he said with a smile. Bowers, who will be 50 when he retires, is hoping to see what life has to offer outside of law enforcement. “My wife [a Sergeant with the Santa Clara Police Dept.] is going to be retiring shortly after me. Immediately, we are going to sort of, recalibrate as humans. When I retire I am going to take a break; I have no immediate work or professional plans at this point.” Bowers looks forward to seeing his eldest son graduate from the University of Oregon in June. As the front man of the force, Bowers kept on the cutting edge by making investments in technology, using cameras, and social media as a force multiplier. The City has a couple months to find a replacement, next in command is Captain Chris Monahan who joined Piedmont’s police force in June of 2017. The City has engaged Teri Black & Company, an executive recruiting firm with expertise in law enforcement, to conduct a search for the City’s next Police Chief. articles.text: Retired Beach Elementary School crossing guard, Arthur Ward, passed away peacefully on Sunday, March 16, at the age of 85 after a brief illness. He was surrounded by his friends and family at his home in Oakland. “Mr. Ward made a lasting impact on this community with his connecting energy. I will always remember his smile, his voice, and his kind words,” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “We could not have loved that man more,” said Deborah Dinerman, a close friend of Ward and his family. “He was extraordinary, and his legacy will live on through all of us. There are no words, but we can take solace in knowing that he is now reunited with his love, Summer.” For many Piedmonters, Ward represented a symbol of safety and of joy He was a gift to the community. Chief Bowers got to know Ward as a school crossing guard, protecting kids, teachers and parents, but also “as a person who sought to give a piece of good will as he raised his hand to his hat, gave fist bumps, and exchanged pleasantries with all who passed his way,” Bowers said. His lasting legacy burns on within friends, including former Piedmont Mayor and Beach parent Teddy King, Beach School teacher Claire Stephens, and longtime friend Bruce Joffe. “Arthur’s infectious love for his faith, family, friends and the Beach Community was a source of joy and inspiration for many, he will be sorely missed,” added Dinerman. Arthur Ward lived in Oakland for 60 years with his wife, Summer Ward. They had been married for 58 years when Summer died in June 2023. Ward was a seminal touchstone of the Beach community and neighborhood for nearly 10 years as the beloved crossing guard of the corner of Lake and Arthur Ward (left) and wife Summer Linda Avenues. Ward served in the Marine Corp then worked in the Oakland Naval Supply Center, first as a laborer then promoted to Supervisor of Computer Services, before retiring more than 25 years ago. When he stopped working, he decided to become a school crossing guard in his spare time. When he was first assigned to the City of Piedmont, Summer said they were both a bit skeptical. After the first week, however, all of their apprehension subsided when the community fully embraced them. For years, both he and Summer, a retired special education teacher in Oakland public schools, volunteered at Beach School. Arthur was a gifted musician and always attended the Beach Revue, Pancake Breakfast and the Beach Battle of the Bands. In May 2019, the community worked together to have the corner named in his honor the year before his retirement. The Beach community rallied with a retirement car parade in late spring of 2020. Arthur and Summer were also regular fixtures at many Piedmont events. This included the July 4th parade where they won a trophy for their entry. They proudly displayed the trophy in the Beach School office. In retirement, they also would meet regularly at Mulberry’s Market and Fentons Creamery with their friends from Beach. Arthur’s infectious love for his faith, family, friends and the Beach community was a source of joy and inspiration for many, and he will be sorely missed. Memorial Service A memorial service for Arthur Ward will be on Friday, April 25, at 11:00 a.m. at Chapel of the Chimes on Piedmont Avenue in Oakland.
articles.title: Arthur Ward safely crosses to the other side

articles.text: Eldest member of well respected Scouting family Dr. Jay B. Hann III, MD, passed away peacefully on Friday, January 3, 2025, at the age of 94, surrounded by his family in his Piedmont home. Born on February 27, 1930, in Evanston, Wyoming, he was the son of Jay B. Hann Jr. and Dortha W. Hann (Koebrick). He grew up in rural Idaho, starting his education in a one-room schoolhouse in Challis, Idaho, and later attended Stanford University, where he earned a Bachelor of Science in 1952 and a Medical Degree in 1955. After completing a surgical internship, Dr. Jay served three years in the U.S. Air Force before returning to Stanford for an orthopedic residency, which he completed in 1962. In 1955, he married Helen Hoffman in Bralorne, British Columbia, and shortly afterward they moved to Mountain Home Air Force Base in Boise, Idaho. In 1962 Helen and Jay along with their four children moved to Gothenburg, Sweden, where he trained in hand surgery. Their fifth child was born after their hospital in Palo Alto. Dr. Jay was active in Scouting with both his father and four sons, obtaining the honor of Eagle Scout. His commitment to Scouting earned him the Silver Beaver Award and later the Distinguished Eagle Award for his leadership and contributions. Many considered Dr. Hann a true Renaissance man, with a talent for tackling any project. Whether designing or building, he was known for his skill and ingenuity, often improving on traditional designs. Dr. Hann is predeceased by his beloved wife, Helen (2017), and his daughter, Lisa (2006). He is survived by his four sons: Jay (Piedmont), Byron (Cindy, Moraga), Mike (Denise, Norden), and Robert (Cindy, Santa Barbara), as well as 11 grandchildren, 4 great-grandchildren, and his sister Katherine Rosa of San Leandro. Dr. Jay Hann shared his wisdom, kindness, and creativity with countless individuals. His legacy will live on in the hearts and memories of all who knew him. Dr. Jay B. Hann III, MD of Piedmont dies on January 3. He was 94. move to Piedmont, where they lived for the past 62 years. He was a founding partner of Webster Orthopedics in Oakland and became a prominent hand surgeon in the Bay Area. Beloved by his patients, he specialized in microsurgical nerve repair and finished his career as a teacher and mentor at the Stanford VA
articles.title: Jay Hann dies on January 3 at age 94

The new bridge, prefabricated off-site, was driven into the park and lowered into place by a crane. Footings for the bridge were constructed in advance. The bridge, located at the base of Bushy Dell Creek near the high school softball field, was first identified as in need of replacement in 2015. The previous bridge was over 30 years old and had required substantial repairs twice in the past five years, including the addition of a temporary side rail after the original railings collapsed in 2023 from wood rot. Some finishing work and cleanup is still required, so nearby paths remain closed. Paths are expected to reopen during the second week of April. Construction workers crane the new bridge into place. The Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King was so inspired by the Ten Commandments and the world they envisioned that he developed a list of Ten Commandments for Non-violence that he required of his followers. Among his commandments were “Walk and talk in the manner of love, for God is love,” “Pray daily to be used by God in order that all men might be free,” and “Sacrifice personal wishes in order that all men might be free.” He clearly understood that the commandments were a road map to a goal called freedom, a map to a place named justice. The Ten Commandments are not a formula for fame, fortune or instant gratification. Instead, to pilgrims trying to find a better way, they describe a long and gentle path that leads away from self-destructive behavior and towards what some might describe as heaven on earth. Rev. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.

Piedmont Real Estate Update March 2025 Twenty Years: Then and Now When we started in real estate more than two decades ago, our seasoned colleagues would cite the old adage that “real estate prices double every 10 years. ” Given that we now have data on the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) going back at least 20 years, we thought we would test this precept to see if this is still the case. We looked at all houses that sold in Berkeley, Oakland, Piedmont, and Lafayette that were at least 1,000 sq. ft. We looked at sales data for 2005 and twenty years later for 2024. While we found that there was quite a bit of appreciation in the marketplace, the value of houses did not double every ten years. In fact, over the twenty year period, the median house prices appreciated as follows: Berkeley increased 93% Lafayette increased 86% Oakland increased 77% Piedmont increased 73% Why did the houses in Piedmont appreciate at a lower rate than other East Bay markets? We suspect that the lower appreciation rate might have to do with the higher starting prices beginning in 2005 and residual effects on pricing from the Great Recession. 20 Year Snapshot Median Sales Price ( thousands $) $2.450K 2.5 2.0 1.5 1.0 1.25 0.5 1.0 0.0 0.0 $1.997K $1.562K $1.420K $1.075K $1.015K $810k $810K $575K 93% 93% 86% 86% 77% 73% 77% 73% BERKELEY LAFAYETTE OAKLAND PIEDMONT Welcome, Katie!
