By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: My husband and I have decided that we want to look at senior facilities, as we are in our late 80s (86 and 89), and are finding our house is just too much to manage. Right now, we can get around and go through our day with little or no help, but we feel the day is coming that we will need assistance. We have no children and have no idea where to even begin. Are there things or sources on the internet to help us begin our search? –Sami, Piedmont Dear Sami: This is such a big issue for those of us nearing the age of needing assistance, both physically, and sometimes in the case of a partner with dementia, mentally. I have helped a few clients in their search, because I went through an extensive search for my mother, when I moved her into an assisted living facility in Florida, and then a year later moved her into memory care in San Francisco so she could be closer to me. I spoke with some friends who are nurses, who gave me a list of questions and issues to address in our tours. Of course, not all facilities have the same care services. Some of them are independent living only, others have independent and assisted living, and some have independent, assisted living, and memory care. And very few have all of those and skilled nursing, which is often for those too ill or infirm for the other types of care. Often though, facilities partner with skilled nursing facilities so the transition is not so overwhelming and traumatic. So, it’s important to know that wherever you move, will serve you as you age. Most places that have at least assisted living care have what they call aging in place, which means that they can provide individual care and allow hospice when the time comes. And many are monthly rent, and some are actual buy ins, like a condo. And all that I visited have a move in fee, that does not go toward rent. I have seen that amount from $5,000-$60,000. When I started the search for my mom, it was all new to me, and the first thing I did was start out with, as you ask about, an internet search. Here are a couple of places that you can start your research, with some cautions and my comments. 1 A Place for Mom (aplaceformom.com) This is where many people start. At no cost to you, this organization assigns an agent who interviews you and suggests some facilities based on the criteria of your needs. This is where I started too, but I wouldn’t recommend this. Once you create an account, login, and actually make contact with an agent, they call you all the time. Also, I found the facilities that were suggested by the agent assigned to me were not suitable for my mother. They are like insurance agents. They get paid by the facilities for referrals, so you don’t pay anything. There are some good resources on the website like questions to ask, things to think about as far as the service is provided by facilities. But I felt that they seemed more interested in rushing me to decide, I abandoned this one right away. 2. articles.text: Early Bird passes available now Piedmont Food Fest Mark your calendars for the Piedmont Food Fest, coming to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 19 from 11 a.m. - 4p.m. This annual event builds community by assembling the broadest mix of food, drinks, and performances gathered from around the Bay. Some new additions to the festival include: • Lobster rolls from Maine Lobster (as featured on Food Network), Nepalese momos from Momolicious, Peruvian street food from La Pituca, piping hot pies from Hearth Wood-Fired Pizza, and towering creations from Rock Club Burgers • A special children’s performance in the KidZone by the famed Prescott Circus Theater, a youth circus program that’s worked with local schools since 1984. • An art exhibit on food waste from the Art for Advocacy club from PHS. • An informational booth run by PHS students promoting the Alameda County Food Bank’s efforts to fight food insecurity. Attendees can also enjoy fan favorites such as: • Baos from The Chairman, seafood paella from Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Japanese fried chicken sandwiches from Aburaya, boba from Tea on Piedmont, empanadas, patacon, and arepas from Crazy Empanadas, sambusas from Swahili Spot • Tastings from Deer Hill Vineyards, Mount Diablo Cider Company, Maker Wine, Blindwood Cider, and P. Herrell Winery • Midway games, sno-cones, crafts, and henna tattoos at the KidZone carnival • Live music from HiiiWAV artist showcase, Oakland Taiko, Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Beloved Little Circus aerialists, and many more! Registration and Early Bird discounts on all-day tastings and KidZone passes (through March only) are available at www.piedmontfoodfest.org. articles.text: Amy Fry has been selected to be the next Wildwood Elementary School Principal. Her appointment is scheduled for tonight, during the March 12 School Board Meeting. Fry comes by way of the Pleasanton Unified School District where she is currently serving as the Vice Principal of Hearst and Mohr Elementary Schools. “Her ability to analyze data and implement targeted academic and behavioral interventions stood out as one of many examples of her expert support of student success,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn in a press release. Fry has over 25 years of experience in public education. Before taking on administration responsibilities, Amy spent six years as a Literacy Coach at Oxford Elementary School in Berkeley. While there she provided reading interventions, coached teachers, and facilitated school-wide initiatives to improve literacy outcomes. She has 20 years of classroom teaching experience at Malcolm X Elementary School, in the Berkeley District, where she taught K-5 students. Amy Fry has been selected as the next Wildwood Elementary School Principal, starting this summer on July 1. “Her expertise in literacy instruction, curriculum development, and inclusive education has shaped her commitment to equity and excellence in education,” the release states. Fry has a Master of Arts in Education degree and a Reading Specialist Credential from the University of California, Berkeley. She also earned an Administrative Credential from California State University, East Bay, and a Bachelor of Science in Elemen-

articles.text: For the first time in the tournament’s eight-year history, Piedmont High boys’ soccer team won the Division 5 CIF State NorCal title on Saturday, March 8 at Witter Field with a resounding 4-1 victory over No. 7 Williams as the No. 5 seed. Piedmont defeated No. 4 Orland 1-0 in the first round on March 4 and followed up with a 2-0 win over No. 8 Colusa in the regional semifinals. Their NorCal title run came on the heels of a 2-0 loss as the top seed in the D4 NCS Final to No. 2 Roseland Prep. Their NorCal title is the team’s third championship banner in four years after winning the 2022 and 2023 NCS titles. Their NCS Final appearance was also their third title game in four years.

articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery is inviting the community to join for the 17th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel from March 21-23, 10:00 a.m.-4:00 p.m. The free event welcomes in Spring with a display of blooming Dutch tulips and striking floral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs and students from college floral design class. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to offer suggestions for how to reduce Piedmont’s risk from wildfires, earthquakes, and other natural hazards from now through Sunday, March 23. Community members can share their input at piedmont.ca.gov/MitigationStrategy. Community input will be used to inform the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, a FEMA-required document that studies the specific ways Piedmont could be impacted by natural hazards and creates a roadmap for preventative measures the City can take. • Mitigation actions could include: • Updating or adopting new policies, like strengthening building codes • Infrastructure projects like retrofitting or rebuilding critical facilities • Developing programs to help residents make their properties more resilient Residents may submit as many ideas as they wish and will be able to see suggestions that others have submitted. State and federal grant funding Work to update the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan began last fall, with a deep dive into the natural hazards most likely to threaten Piedmont. The project team has worked to document the specific ways each of these hazards could affect Piedmont if they were to occur, including damage to people and property, critical facilities and infrastructure, and the local economy. This work provides context for the project’s current phase – the development of a mitigation strategy. Effective mitigation – actions taken before a disaster that aim to reduce risk – can reduce damage, minimize disruption, and speed recovery from disasters when they happen. When the mitigation plan is complete, the City will submit it to FEMA and the California Office of Emergency Services for review. Receiving approval from these two agencies positions Piedmont to apply for state and federal grants to fund mitigation projects documented in the plan. Residents can learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the 2019 plan at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMP, or subscribe to email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews.
articles.title: City seeks suggestions for Hazard Mitigation Plan

articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission heard an update at their March 5 meeting on the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which is currently undergoing a re-evaluation process to ensure the City’s resilience in the face of disaster as well as secure state and federal funding. Delivered by Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, the update provided a primer for the conversations the City will be having in the next months about wildfire prevention, risk of natural disasters, and possible changes to the City’s fire code. A Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) is a FEMA required plan in order to receive mitigation funding. The LHMP update seeks to better prepare Piedmont for natural hazards, including evacuation infrastructure, updates to building codes, and attention on critical facilities in the event of disaster. The plan includes a 5-year roadmap of what the City can do to reduce the impact of natural hazards in Piedmont, providing a “North Star” for resiliency efforts in Piedmont. The plan seeks to prepare the City not just for earthquakes and wildfires, but also less obvious disasters such as landslides and flooding. An upcoming conversation for the City will be this year’s fire code update, raising questions of building code modifications, vegetation management requirements and the code enforcement. “Right now, we primarily enforce via education,” said Brannigan. “We talk with homeowners, we respond to requests to come look at properties. Nancy, Nick and I walk the parks and our open spaces to talk about how we can do fuel reduction and fuel mitigation. We get good compliance that way in Piedmont.” Another measure to reduce fire risk could lie in creating fire-resistant landscaping demonstrations in Piedmont’s public spaces. A dry landscape demonstration garden like this could have the potential to show what a beautiful fire-safe area can look like. The presentation ended with a call to action by Chief Brannigan, encouraging residents to get involved in the process by submitting suggestions online at piedmont.ca.gov/mitigationstrategy and subscribing to email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews. In addition, the City will host a Mitigation Strategy Workshop on Wednesday, March 26, from 5:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Brannigan encouraged community members to attend and share feedback on possible mitigation actions.
articles.title: Park Commission hears update on Hazard Mitigation Plan

articles.text: J. Miller Flowers and Gifts, a cherished family-owned florist and gift shop located at 4416 Piedmont Avenue, is thrilled to announce its 55th anniversary. As thanks to its customers and supporters, J. Miller Flowers is inviting community members to join its Spring Open House and Pop-up Art Show with 12 local artists, taking place on March 21-23 from 11:00 a.m.-3:00 p.m. The flower shop was originally purchased in 1970 by Dr. Clinton and Mary Lee, and is currently run by sisters and co-owners Valerie and Robbin Lee. In addition to the Spring Open House this year, the shop will be hosting a Pop-up Art Show with 12 local artists, showcasing unique oil, watercolor and acrylic paintings, handmade soaps and spices. “I think what makes me happiest and most grateful is that, all along we’ve been trying to be a part of the community and incorporate our projects and what we support,” said Valerie Lee. “And so this is a great way for us to give back and support local artists, as well as the joy of flowers.” This year, J. Miller Flowers will celebrate more than five decades of stunning floral Robbin Lee (left), Valerie Lee and Maureen Owens arrangements, exceptional service, and a commitment to quality that has stood the test of time. Active in the community for special events around the Bay Area, J. Miller Flowers has become a beloved part of Oakland’s vibrant community. From weddings to anniversaries, graduations to everyday moments, their flowers have been a part of many milestones for many people in the community. J. articles.text: Havens Lead Coach More than 50 Piedmont fourth and fifth graders zoomed around the track at Witter Field on Wednesday March 5. They represented Beach, Havens, and Wildwood Schools in the third annual Witter Mile Challenge organized by the Piedmont Junior Running Club. Three heats of runners completed four laps on the quarter-mile oval. The top three boys and three girls in each heat received a certificate. In the exciting finish to the final heat, Nicholas Bivens of Beach edged out Troy Wallway of Havens, First place Nicholas Bivens of Beach (left) and second place Troy Wallway of Havens both gad times of 5:55 minutes in the mile run. Piedmont kids in the final heat of the Witter Mile Challenge take off from the starting line for four laps. with both logging a time of 5:55 minutes, the first sub-six-minute performances in the event’s history. The fastest girl of the day was Lamie Wang of Beach, with a time of 7:01. With the five fastest combined individual times among the three schools, Havens earned the team trophy. The Piedmont Junior Running Club is a running program for fourth- and fifth-graders. The program welcomes students of all abilities and strives to instill discipline, teamwork, and, most of all, joy in the sport. Now in its 13th year, the program operates year-round and holds a friendly tri-school competition at the end of each season. In January this year, after 19 years coaching Piedmont runners, program founder Len Goldman retired and moved with his wife to Rossmoor. “I do follow the program from afar now and it will always be something very close to me,” said Goldman. “I hope it will continue to flourish and get kids interested in running.” Spring season will focus on track and field events starting March 24 and continues through May 21. The teams meet immediately after school on Mondays and Wednesdays for 75 minutes. Registration is now open through the Piedmont Recreation Department website. For more information, contact co-coaches Minori Tsuge (mints321@aol.com) or Christine Chapon (cchapon1305@gmail. com). Havens runners participants were awarded the team trophy and popsicles for recording the fastest mile times.

Piedmont Jr. Running Club heats up Witter Track By Paul Lee, Havens Lead Coach More than 50 Piedmont fourth and fifth graders zoomed around the track at Witter Field on Wednesday March 5. They represented Beach, Havens, and Wildwood Schools in the third annual Witter Mile Challenge organized by the Piedmont Junior Running Club. Three heats of runners completed four laps on the quarter-mile oval. The top three boys and three girls in each heat received a certificate. In the exciting finish to the final heat, Nicholas Bivens of Beach edged out Troy Wallway of Havens, First place Nicholas Bivens of Beach (left) and second place Troy Wallway of Havens both gad times of 5:55 minutes in the mile run. Piedmont kids in the final heat of the Witter Mile Challenge take off from the starting line for four laps. with both logging a time of 5:55 minutes, the first sub-six-minute performances in the event’s history. The fastest girl of the day was Lamie Wang of Beach, with a time of 7:01. With the five fastest combined individual times among the three schools, Havens earned the team trophy. The Piedmont Junior Running Club is a running program for fourth- and fifth-graders. The program welcomes students of all abilities and strives to instill discipline, teamwork, and, most of all, joy in the sport. Now in its 13th year, the program operates year-round and holds a friendly tri-school competition at the end of each season. In January this year, after 19 years coaching Piedmont runners, program founder Len Goldman retired and moved with his wife to Rossmoor. “I do follow the program from afar now and it will always be something very close to me,” said Goldman. “I hope it will continue to flourish and get kids interested in running.” Spring season will focus on track and field events starting March 24 and continues through May 21. The teams meet immediately after school on Mondays and Wednesdays for 75 minutes. Registration is now open through the Piedmont Recreation Department website. For more information, contact co-coaches Minori Tsuge (mints321@aol.com) or Christine Chapon (cchapon1305@gmail. com). Hop along the trails, stones and shoreline in this truly unique to the Bay Area environment. Take the dogs and older kids capable of bouldering. The skyride, amusement rides and a brand new electric train are open as well. Buy tickets in advance. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s Parents Club has a few more tickets left for “Kickin’ it Old Skool.” its school fundraiser on Thursday, March 27. A professional comedian will host the evening’s festivities including a live auction. Party goers will have a chance to eat, drink, and dance the night away to nostalgic 80’s and 90’s music. This is the school’s biggest annual fundraiser and will be held at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Auction items include a private dinner with Michelin 2-Star chef James Syhabout (Commis), Tahoe and wine county vacation rentals, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, plus Warriors and Giants tickets. Old skool sneakers, like Vans and Keds, are not required but highly encouraged to grace the dance floor. There will also be a raffle full of goodies, a Mulberry’s candy bar with nostalgic throwback treats and signature cocktails, including a special “Carnazzo Cosmo” sponsored by Lisa Chan. T he a n nu a l eve nt i s co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several parent parties, including Pub Trivia and Pints, Poker and Pinot. and the Bad Moms Bash. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27 knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. articles.text: A creative approach to motivation Sometimes “doing nothing” can be a superpower. We’ve all been there. You plan a fun activity, offer up some great ideas, or even suggest something as simple as going outside, and your kids respond with a solid NO. Or worse—an uninterested shrug. It can be frustrating, especially when you feel like they should be doing something productive, active, or at least engaged with the world around them. But here’s the thing: Sometimes, refusing to do anything is a signal that they need a different kind of approach—or even a little space to be still. So what do you do? Push them? Leave them be? Here’s a creative way to navigate these moments. Reframe “Doing Nothing” as a superpower Instead of panicking that your child is wasting time, consider that rest and boredom are actually important. Boredom fuels creativity, and downtime is essential for mental health. Try shifting your perspective: • If they’re lying on the couch staring at the ceiling, say, “Looks like you’re deep in thought! What big ideas are you working on?” • If they reject all activity suggestions, respond with, “Ahh, the fine art of doing absolutely nothing–you have to practice for that level of skill!” Sometimes, the pressure to be constantly doing can make kids resist even more. A little humor and permission to relax can go a long way. Give them the right kind of choices Instead of asking “Do you want to do something?” (which is easy to say no to), reframe the question: • “Would you rather do something inside or outside?” • “Do you want to pick the activity, or should I surprise you?” • “Should we do something active or something creative?” This small shift puts them in control but still nudges them toward action. Find out what’s really behind the resistance Sometimes, kids don’t want to do anything because they’re: • Tired • Overstimulated • Feeling a little down • Needing connection but don’t know how to ask • Genuinely enjoying stillness If their “no” seems firm, try asking “Do you need a break?” Or, open the door to a conversation about how they are feeling, by asking: “If your feelings were a weather report, what would today’s forecast be?” Let them know it’s okay to

articles.text: Thirty-two members of Highlander Robotics attended the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Regional meet in Orange County the weekend of March 1. With their new robot Kelpie they won the Engineering Inspiration Award, and earned their fourth consecutive qualification to the World Championship to be held this April in Houston. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. A new robot is built for each season and competitions begin six weeks after kickoff. Teams can win awards based on the performance of their robots; the quality, innovation, and creativity of their designs; and the impact they make on their communities. The Highlanders, in the first tournament of the season, arrived as the favorite in a field of 47 teams. After the first day of competition they had a 6-1 record, had set the high score of 170, and were ranked 1st. They lost their final two matches, however, and finished qualifications in third place with a 7-3 record. In the playoff draft, they were first pick of the tournament, selected by the top-seeded Patribots from San Diego. Their three-team alliance was completed by the Firebots from Sunnyvale. In the first round of the double elimination playoffs the Highlanders’ first seeded alliance notched an easy win, 159-64, against the 8th seed captained by Kelpie climbs hanging steel cages in the final moments of a match. Highlander Robotic’s Kelpie qualified for this year’s World Championship Sage Hill Robotics from Newport Coast. In their second round against the 4th seed alliance captained by Dana Point’s Robot Dolphins from Outer Space, the team exited the 15 second autonomous period ahead 51-44. Over the next 2 minutes and 15 seconds however, the Patribots struggled to cope with the opposition’s defense and the alliance lost 141- 164. In the lower bracket, the Highlanders’ alliance adjusted their tactics and the Firebots worked to protect the Patribots from defensive maneuvers. While counter-defense proved ineffective, they still managed to scrape out a 145-115 win and eliminate the 6th seed alliance. In the quarter finals their luck ran out and they lost 151-147 to Atascadero’s Greybots and their 5th seed alliance, finishing 4th overall. In judged awards the Highlanders won FIRST’s Engineering Inspiration award, earning a spot at the World Championship, which celebrates outstanding success in advancing respect and appreciation for engineering within a team’s organization and community. The judges specifically cited their work mentoring middle and elementary school robotics teams, the curriculum they have developed to enable girlscouts to earn robotics badges, the team’s own training systems, and this year’s creation of a full-sized practice field that has been used by 16 other FRC teams. Kelpie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Max Seiden and supported by drive coach Cassie Colby, technician Caetano de Figueiredo, and human player Justin Green. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is composed of 55 students from 17 high schools around the area. They work from the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information visit the team on the web at frc8033.com. This year’s robot, Kelpie, is able to pick up and score 16” kick balls and 4” diameter PVC pipes on a branched steel element called a “reef”. articles.text: Twenty new Eagle Scouts took flight from Scouting America’s Piedmont Council in 2024. Across a wide range of projects benefiting our East Bay community, these Eagle Scouts led 1,870 hours of service. The Eagle rank is the highest honor of the Scouting program, recognizing a Scout’s leadership, service, and character. The rank requires years of effort, requiring completion of twenty-one merit badges, leadership over a community benefitting service project, leadership within their Troop, and continuous demonstration of living by the Scout Oath and Law. Prior to beginning work on their Eagle rank, Scouts must earn six other ranks, demonstrating their knowledge of skills in tool usage, cooking, planning, camping, teamwork, citizenship, and more. The accolade of Eagle is a distinct honor, and one Piedmont Council has always placed great import on recognizing. The Council is proud to continue to support Scouts through their Eagle rank, and to see them achieve one of Scouting’s highest merits. As the saying goes, once an Eagle, always an Eagle.
articles.title: Piedmont Eagle Scouts Soar through 2024

pages.text: Wednesday, March 12, 2025 11 Piedmont Eagle Scouts Soar through 2024 Twenty new Eagle Scouts took flight from Scouting America’s Piedmont Council in 2024. Across a wide range of projects benefiting our East Bay community, these Eagle Scouts led 1,870 hours of service. The Eagle rank is the highest honor of the Scouting program, recognizing a Scout’s leadership, service, and character. The rank requires years of effort, requiring completion of twenty-one merit badges, leadership over a community benefitting service project, leadership within their Troop, and continuous demonstration of living by the Scout Oath and Law. Prior to beginning work on their Eagle rank, Scouts must earn six other ranks, demonstrating their knowledge of skills in tool usage, cooking, planning, camping, teamwork, citizenship, and more. The accolade of Eagle is a distinct honor, and one Piedmont Council has always placed great import on recognizing. The Council is proud to continue to support Scouts through their Eagle rank, and to see them achieve one of Scouting’s highest merits. articles.text: PHS dominates Williams 4-1 to win D5 CIF NorCal title Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team is a champion again, this time winning the CIF State NorCal Division 5 championship. Seeded No. 5, they added another title to the trophy cabinet on Saturday, March 8 at Witter Field, dominating No. 7 Williams 4-1 to claim the school’s first CIF State NorCal title. Two days earlier, they beat No. 8 Colusa 2-nil in the semifinals. “We did our research and had the video analysis before the game. Everything we talked about came out in the game.” said first year head coach Ben Russell. “It definitely paid dividends as the game went on.” A North Coast Section or state title was something difficult to envision midway through the season when they had just two wins through the first 11 games. “I wouldn’t say there was one standout turning point, it was always a step-by-step process. We just tried to piece together every little detail from when we got together. Everything that came out in the Final, especially with the mindset of just getting the next goal,” Russell said. PHS’ boys’ soccer has become one of the most successful programs at the school. They now have three championship banners in four years after winning the 2022 and 2023 D4 NCS titles. They teached this year’s Div. 4 NCS championship game as the No. 1 seed. Senior Jacques Saldanha is in rarified air as a three-time title winner. He was a freshman on the 2022 team, a sophomore in 2023, a captain of this year’s NCS Final runner-up, and now lifts the school’s first-ever CIF State title in the tournament’s eight- year history. “It was just a blessing to get two [opportunities] at a Final this year. We came up short in NCS, but second place goes through to State as well and we really brought it this tournament. This is a big deal for us,” Saldanha said. Piedmont’s NorCal title marked a historic title-game performance by lead striker Gianluca Bini, bagging a hat trick in the first half. He scored his first goal in the 25th minute with a penalty kick, scored again in the 39th minute, and put one more away at halftime. Staff Photos Gianluca Bini scored a 3-goal hat trick in the Div. 5 CIF NorCal Final against Williams. He also scored in the semifinals against Colusa. “Midway through the season I thought I wasn’t ’m not scoring enough goals. But it’s not just me creating these goals, it all comes from my teammates. Having a first-half hat trick was a surreal moment, I couldn’t believe what happened. It came really fast, it went from 1-0 to 3-0 and they were out of the game,” Bini said. It was a strong defensive performance throughout the State tournament with Piedmont scoring seven goals and allowing one. Williams didn’t record a shot on target until the 66th minute and had only had one shot attempt in the first half. Bini thinks their productivity in State is a testament to the team having a full grasp of Russell’s system. “It’s a combination. It took us a long time to understand the tactics that Ben wanted to implement. Once everyone learned their job and their roles to create success, that’s when things clicked. Like Real Madrid, we just found a way to win,” Bini said. The Highlanders’ semifinals 2-0 win over Colusa also featured sophomore Derin Sabuncuoglu scoring the first goal of his varsity career. “I joined the season late and wanted to finish up the season strong for these seniors. I saw the ball bouncing and I know I’m a finisher. I caught it on my left even though I’m a right-footed player. I caught it on the volley and started smiling when I saw it go in,” Sabuncuoglu. 4-1 over No. 7 Williams for title Piedmont scored the game’s opening goal in the 25th minute when Williams committed a foul in the box on a long pass from free kick. Bini stepped to the spot, slotting in his shot. From there, Sabuncuoglu nearly scored in the 31st minute when winning possession in a good area and dribbled around the keeper in a 1-on-1 situation. However, his shot was cleared off of the line by a defender. Bini scored again in the 39th minute when Harper Mand played a great long pass to Gianluca making a run in behind. Then Bini got his hat trick two minutes later at 40+1. This time centerback Max Goldfarb made a slick dribble from the back line toward midfield, evading a tackle in the process before sending a pass up to Bini. With his right foot, Bini sent in another to help kill off the game early. In the second half, Bini nearly scored a fourth goal in the 52nd minute on a header that forced the goalie to make a diving save. The ball deflected to Sabuncuoglu in front of the net, but his shot went high. Four minutes later, Bosco Lorin nearly forced an own-goal when Williams poorly defended a pass in the box. Williams got its consolation goal in second-half stoppage time, but their joy didn’t last long. Lorin scored the game’s final goal at 80+4, leading to the final whistle soon after. Derin Sabuncuoglu celebrates his first varsity goal against Colusa in the semifinals. Bosco Lorin scored the final goal in Piedmont’s 4-1 win over Williams.

articles.text: Highlanders beat Oakland Tech, San Joaquin Memorial Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball season came to an end in the Div.1 CIF State Regional Semifinals. Their two wins at State marks the program’s most since 2015. Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball season came to an end on Saturday, March 8 at No. 4 St. Mary’s of Stockton, losing 61-48.Piedmon t was the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 CIF State tournament. In earlier rounds, the Highlanders defeated No. 16 San Joaquin Memorial in a heated 62-60 Round II victory at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, March 6, and opened the tournament with a dominant 60-29 win over Oakland Tech on Tuesday, March 4. Against St. Mary’s, Piedmont trailed by just four points at halftime down 35-31, but were limited to just six points in the third quarter. Two days earlier against San Joaquin Memorial, Piedmont battled with the Panthers for all four quarters. PHS took a 35-33 lead at the end of the second quarter and never relinquished from there. In the opening round against Oakland Tech, the Highlanders dominated from the get-go, allowing just one point in the first quarter to lead 14-1 and carried a commanding 34-8 lead by halftime. The regional semifinals mark the farthest Piedmont has gone in the CIF State tournament since 2023.competing in the Open Division, the top flight, Piedmont only played one game in State after receiving the No. 1 seed in the Open Division and a first-round bye. This year’s team advanced the farthest since 2015 when it reached the Regional Finals. “The girls played really hard on both sides,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We’ve had big plays from everyone. We went this far in the Open two years ago, but this is a little bit deeper than we’ve gone in the other brackets in recent years,” “I’m just really humbled and grateful. We just worked together really well and had great chemistry. We came together and had a lot of fun,” said freshman Andrea Martin. In their second round win, Piedmont faced No. 16 Memorial which upset No. 1 Folsom 84-74 in the first round, giving PHS the chance to host. “It was all about teamwork, playing together, staying strong and disciplined. We focused on Sienna Evans, she was doing it all. She’s a great basketball player,” Martin said. Their Round II win required a big-game performance by freshman guard Jenelle Solis, who scored 20 points and had eight assists. “Our mentality was just to win. We knew our seniors weren’t guaranteed to play another game, so we just kept pushing for them. It’s a huge accomplishment to make it this far,” Solis said following their win over Memorial. Andrea Martin had 12 points and nine rebounds against St. Mary’s, 22 points and 10 rebounds on Memorial, and 11 points and 11 boards on Oakland Tech.

articles.text: 3-2 win vs. Albany, 7-1 loss to Head-Royce Piedmont’s baseball team had one win and one loss last week. They defeated Albany 3-2 on Tuesday, March 4, but suffered a surprising 7-1 loss to HeadRoyce, on Friday, March 7 at the Jayhawks’ home field in Oakland. The loss to HRS comes as a bit of a surprise after opening the season with a 7-5 win over Acalanes, a top-10 ranked school in the Bay Area and in Division 3. The Highlanders look ahead to a game with El Cerrito on Thursday, March 13 at Humphries DiaThe two sides waged through four scoreless innings before Piedmont broke the deadlock in the top of the fifth inning with two runs, and added one more in the top half of the sixth. The Cougars scored both of their runs in the bottom of the seventh. Piedmont’s starting pitcher was freshman Massimo Mittone, who threw five innings of shutout baseball with seven strikeouts In the Highlanders’ two-run fifth inning, Markos Lagios led off with a double to left field in a heated eight-pitch at bat on a 3-2 count. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end in the first round of the CIF State tournament. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball season came to an end on Tuesday, March 4, losing 84-71 in the Division 4 CIF State first round to No. 8 Natomas near Sacramento. The game concludes PHS’ season with a 15-16 overall record and am appearance in the Div.4 North Coast Section Finals. “I’m proud of the way we battled all season. We were nearly in every single game and fought through a lot of adversity,” coach Ben Spencer said. Their NCS Finals and CIF State appearances marked Piedmont’s second consecutive season year to advance that far in post-season play after reaching last year’s Div. 3 NCS title game. Dillon Casey led the way against the Nighthawks with 24 points, while Ravi Silverberg put up 18 points in the final game of his Piedmont High career. Silverberg leaves Piedmont High as a three-year starter. “Ravi is a gamer I think of all the big games we were in, like being the leading scorer in last year’s NCS Championship. He kept us in that game and is always out there giving his all, diving for loose balls. Ravi’s a winner, he knows how to play at full speed every position. I’m super proud of him and his four-year career,” Spencer said of Silverberg. Looking ahead, Piedmont will watch leading scorer Silverberg graduate with the Class of 2025, along with starting forward P.J. Bayer and backup forward Emmett Asulin. Casey is the marquee returner and should be the next Highlanders’ player to eclipse the 1,000 point mark. joining Silverberg, Brit Burden (Class of 2024), A.J. Harris (Class of 2023), JoJo Murphy (Class of 2022), Luke Harris (Class of 2021), and Luke Barrett (Class of 2020) to reach the achievement under Spencer. 84-71 to Natomas Although Piedmont started with a 7-2 lead, Natomas caught fire with 21 points in the first quarter, but Piedmont hung in there trailing by six with 15. In the opening quarter, Silverberg, Casey, and P.J. Brayer all knocked down 3-pointers. However, PHS was outscored 17-12 in the second quarter to give Natomas an 11-point 38-27 lead by halftime. Casey led the way in the second with seven of the Highlanders’ points. Ravi Silverberg played his final game in Purple and White, scoring 18 points against Natomas.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team is back at it for the spring 2025 season. So far this season, they defeated Bentley School with a 7-0 shutout at the Corey Reich Tennis Center to start the season on Tuesday, March 4. They also went 2-2 at this year’s California Tennis Classic in Fresno on Friday and Saturday, March 7-8. “We lost a lot of good players. But we’re still pretty good. We did pretty well in Fresno and were placed in the second strongest division. It gave us a chance to see our guys play more,” coach Jim Landes said. Piedmont faced some big departures with the Class of 2024, including singles starters Ben Breber and Arun Brahma, along with doubles champion Monte Imburg. Lucas Smolko seems poised for a big junior year at the No. 1 singles spot for a third consecutive year. He was last year’s Western Alameda County Conference singles champion and reached the D2 NCS Individual Tournament’s singles semifinals against University’s eventual-champion Karam Dhawan. “Lucas has been too strong for all of his opponents; he won all four matches in Fresno. He’s playing well,” Landes said. Nate Welch is another junior who looks poised to back up Smolko in the singles order. He won his recent match against Bentley at the No. 1 spot in straight sets. “Nate won some matches in Fresno. He has a great serve when its working. If he can tune that up he’ll be dangerous,” Landes said. New to the team is Gianluca Bini, who is just finishing up the boys’ soccer season with a D5 State Championship. “The soccer star, Gianluca, is joining. He’s rusty but has good fundamentals in tennis, so we think he’s going to get good pretty fast,” Landes said. Nick King and Will Tenney are two senior leaders of the group. Both have appeared at singles and doubles throughout their three years on varsity. “Nick and Will are both seniors. The truth is they are both better in doubles and played really well in Fresno. They both hit big,” Landes said. Freshmen making an impact include Luca LaForte, Emilio Misra, Robert Piniella, and Joseph Assalian. “Emilio has been in a lot of middle school clinics and is a defensive kind of player, he plays really relaxed and is tough to beat. Luca LaForte is also very talented, he’s probably relatively better in doubles right now,” LanStaff Photos Lucas Smolko will lead the tennis ream at No. 1 singles. des said. Piedmont looks ahead to the start of its league schedule against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. After playing non-league College Prep tomorrow, March 12, they visit WACC foe Alameda on Friday, March 13. 7-0 over Bentley Piedmont won all seven matches in straight sets. At singles, Welch won at the No. 1 spot in 6-1, 6-2. Nick King appeared at No. 2, winning 6-2, 6-3. Emilio Misra played at No. 3, winning 6-4, 6-1. Kasper Jansson was No. 4, winning 6-2, 6-1. In doubles, LaForte and Hunter Fasteau appeared as the No. 1 team and won 6-2, 6-2. Assalian and Ben Davis played at No. 2, winning 6-0, 6-1. Torten Olsen and Will Richardson were No. 3, and won 6-0, 6-4. California Tennis Classic Piedmont won half of its four matches at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno. They defeated Clovis East 4-2 and St. Joseph 3-3 with more set victories at 7-6, both on the opening day. They lost to Wilcox 4-2 and Camarillo 4-2. Individual results were not available. Tuesday vs. Castro Valley Piedmont played its first league match on Tuesday, March 11 at Castro Valley. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-2) hosts College Prep on Thursday, March 12 at 3:30 p.m. They also visit Alameda the following day, Friday, March 13 at the same time. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team split its last pair of matches, but remains undefeated at 3-0 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. They beat league foes Newark Memorial 19-5 on Tuesday, March 4 at Witter Field, but lost a heated 13-12 game to Campolindo at Witter “That was fun. The girls had possession of the ball; the first and fourth quarters were entirely different. The girls started to figure it out. We started running an iso with a pick, and it was pretty unstoppable,” coach Carlton Chan said. Their loss to the Cougars came down to the wire. The match was tied at 11-11 with 6:05 left, while Piedmont brought themselves within one at 13-12 with 52 seconds remaining. Despite the loss, it was a type of game Piedmont can hang its hat on. Campolindo plays in a higher division. PHS is looking for answers in its attack following the departure of leading scorer Ruby Guzdar. “It tests us really well on both sides. It tests how well our team can play together, I think we learned that today. Although tonight wasn’t the win that we wanted, we came back by four goals down and that’s an exciting place for us to be,” senior Friedie Schickedanz said. Coach Chan called it a breakout game for junior Peyton Watson, who finished with five goals. “Whenever there’s better team, I can get a little stressed. But this game, I played how I want to play. During the first half, I was trying to find the groove. I think it makes the team more aware of what we can do as a team, we know we can match up against the big teams,” said Watson. Piedmont trailed 5-2 at halftime without a goal in the second quarter, but they turned things around in the second half. “It was adapting to what we saw toward the end of the first half. We couldn’t get our transition down, but second half we got it up the field. We settled the ball and made the right passes,” Schickedanz said. 13-12 loss to Campo Piedmont led the game early at 2-1 with goals from Schickedanz and Chloe Graham, but the CouStaff Photos Peyton Watson scored five goals against Campolindo and six goals against Newark Memorial. Friedie Schickedanz had two goals and five assists against Campo and four goals and an assist in the win over Newark Memorial. Chloe Graham netted five goals against Campo and Newark Memorial. gars scored two straight with 1:53 and 38 seconds left to go up 3-2. They wouldn’t relinquish the lead from there, but Piedmont tied the match on three different occasions. In the second quarter, Campolindo held Piedmont without a goal and extended the gap to 5-2 by halftime. Piedmont quickly scored in the third after winning the draw, where Watson grabbed the ground ball and turned up field to score just 13 seconds in. After that, Campo scored in a shooting space opportunity with 7:34 left, 6-3. A minute later, Graham sent a shot on target that ricocheted back into play, allowing Watson to scoop it up and score in close distance. However, Campo scored again with 5:36 left. PHS scored two straight on a pair of connections between Schickedanz and Graham, making it a 7-6 deficit with 3:29 on the clock. After a Campo goal with 2:36 left, Piedmont tied when Schickedanz scored on a wraparound with 1:58 left and then found Graham with 21 seconds left, tying it at 8-8. In the fourth, Campolindo gained possession and scored in transition with 10:24 remaining. Piedmont tied it at 9-9 on another connection between Schickedanz and Graham. Campo responded quickly, forcing a turnover for a scoop and score. Then Campo charged in for another goal 18 seconds later off the faceoff, 11-9. Piedmont went right back at it when Schickedanz won the faceoff, leading to Watson making a long run to the net with 7:51 left. PHS’ defense forced a big turnover, leading to Watson making another nice individual run for the goal, 11-11 with 6:05 left. Schickedanz won the following faceoff, leading to Watson scoring on a ground shot with 52 seconds left. Luisa Cole helped grab the ensuing faceoff, leading to a shot by Graham going narrowly wide with 20 seconds left. Final stats: Graham had five goals and grabbed five ground balls. articles.text: Goalie Gus Von Metzsch had five saves against Washington and 10 against Amador Valley. Connor Fredericks had two goals and three assists against Washington. He made a big impact in the faceoff circle, winning 26 faceoffs in two games. 20-1 rout of Washington Piedmont scored six goals in the first quarter, four in the second, and five goals in each of the third and fourth quarters. Piedmont finished with goals by eight different players led by Ian Nguyen with five goals and two assists and Timmy Kalamas with four goals, two assists, and three ground balls. Final stats: Connor Fredericks and Brendan Devine both scored two goals and three assists, while Fredericks had six loose balls and Devin had five. Landon Heppner scored twice. Jax Edward Thayer had an assist and three loose balls. Xavier Henderson gathered six ground balls. Goalie Gus Von Metzsch had five saves. 10-4 loss to Amador Valley Amador Valley went up 3-0 in the first quarter, while Piedmont trailed 7-2 going into halftime. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery Garden lovers of all ages will enjoy visiting Ruth Bancroft gardens for a special self-guided tour complete with kid’s activities. Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is gearing up for the spring season with a family-friendly garden tour on Sunday, March 23. “Explore Together” is a family-friendly program designed by garden staff to help visitors of all ages discover the beauty of the Ruth Bancroft Garden while enjoying quality time together outdoors. Visitors can choose to embark on a self-guided tour by grabbing a brochure at the entrance gate or by downloading the tour digitally. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Whether you’re visiting with family, friends or by yourself, the “Explore Together” program invites attendees to explore the garden at an individual pace and immerse yourself in its stunning array of arid and drought-resistant plants and landscapes. Visitors of all ages will learn more about California’s native landscape and members of the Ruth Bancroft Garden can enjoy more offerings including borrowing board games or requesting coloring pages and crayons. Children can borrow an “Explorer Backpack” or “Sensory Backpack” from garden staff for free. Backpacks are filled with hands-on, youth-focused activities and tools to better experience the garden’s offerings. Backpacks are available on a first-come, first-served basis. “Explore Together” hours are from 10 am to 12 pm on Sunday, March 23. The garden is open from 9 am to 4 pm, every Wednesday through Sunday. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/visit/ to learn more.
articles.title: Bancroft Gardens family tour is Sunday, March 23

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) hosts an afterhours event tomorrow, Thursday, March 13, featuring drag performers, trivia and more. The OMCA garage will be open tomorrow until 9 p.m. as part of the museum’s special “Thursday After Hours” event series, which features a rotating selection of artists and performers as well as interactive games and docent-led gallery chats. Tomorrow evening features a spectacular drag performance with Per Sia and friends. Per Sia is one of the originators of the famed Drag Queen Story Hour in San Francisco, and she currently works as a head teacher for first grade at an after-school arts program in the city. In addition to teaching, Per Sia hosts parties and leads workshops and presentations about queer issues to Bay Area residents. Drag performers will take over the OMCA gallery from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. for an evening filled with awesome theatrics, exuberant costumes and high-energy entertainment. Visitors are invited to explore the museum’s award-winning galleries between acts and purchase light bites and drinks from OMCA’s Town Fare Per Sia performs tomorrow at the Oakland Museum of California. Café. Music will be curated by DJ Mark DiVita throughout the evening. The evening’s trivia theme highlights the upcoming Oakland Restaurant Week, which will include more than 150 local restaurants from March 20-30. Test your knowledge on California’s storied food scene and get the chance to win a gift card to the Oakland Museum of California gift shop. Admission tickets are required and attendees must be 18 years or older. Visit https://museumca. org/event/thursday-after-hoursat-omca-drag-performances-trivia-night/ to learn more and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Ruth Asawa: Retrospective, the first posthumous retrospective of the groundbreaking work of Californian modernist artist Ruth Asawa, premieres at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art on April 5. Organized by SFMOMA and New York’s Museum of Modern Art, the exhibition will feature over 300 works of art including looped-wire hanging sculptures for which Asawa is best known, as well as sculptures, drawings, prints, paintings and archival material from public and private collections. “Ruth Asawa: Retrospective is deeply aligned with SFMOMA’s vision to be both local and global—presenting Bay Area artists with profound significance that also have the potential to be highly impactful and relevant on an international scale,” said Christopher Bedford, a director of SFMOMA. “This exhibition provides an opportunity to celebrate the legendary Ruth Asawa, who was both a widely acclaimed artist and a hometown inspiration whose impact can be very much felt today.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective spans over six decades of the artist’s celebrated career and highlights how her longtime San Francisco home and garden served as a muse for her artwork and informed her public sculpture commissions and dedication to arts advocacy in the city. In 1968, Asawa founded the Alvarado School Arts Workshop in San Francisco which laid the foundation for an artists-in-residence program that later expanded to 50 schools. The pioneering artists also helped establish arts festivals and a center for the reuse and distribution of arts materials which is still in operation today. The posthumous retrospective is co-curated by Janet Bishop, Thomas Weisel Family Chief Curator and Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. “It is an immense privilege to present the full range of Ruth Asawa’s life’s work through this retrospective,” said Bishop. “Not only was Asawa an exceptionally talented artist, among the most distinguished sculptors of the 20th century and a major contributor in so many other mediums, but she lived her values in everything she did, modeling the importance of the arts and opening up creative opportunities for others at every turn.” SFMOMA received a $1.5 million grant from Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, in support of the Ruth Asawa: Retrospective. The grant is the largest corporate grant for a single exhibition in the museum’s history, highlighting Asawa’s significance in the Bay Area. “We are grateful to Google.org for their generous support of Ruth Asawa: Retrospective,” said Bedford. “This extraordinary funding will enable SFMOMA to enhance its public programs, community partnerships and free access initiatives in celebration of a legendary artist who continues to have an indelible positive impact on San Francisco.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective will be on view at SFMOMA from April 5 through September 2. The museum will offer free admission on April 13 celebrating the retrospective. Admission is also free to residents of the nine Bay Area counties on the first Thursday of each month. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415. 357.4000 for more information. Sculptor Ruth Asawa
articles.title: Ruth Asawa retrospective comes to SFMOMA in April

articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson Frances Chung and Joseph Walsh in Scarlett’s Frankenstein at San Francisco Ballet. San Francisco Ballet dancers bring Mary Shelley’s classic gothic horror story Frankenstein to life on stage March 20 through 26, closing the company’s 2024- 25 season. Frankenstein, one of San Francisco Ballet’s biggest box office hits, was created as a co-production between The Royal Ballet and San Francisco Ballet in 2016 and 2017. Choreographer Liam Scarlett’s ballet honors Shelley’s narrative but delivers more poetry and scary-monster thrills than the original 19th century novel. Both book and ballet tell a disturbing and tragic tale about the consequences of abandonment and the risks of tampering with human life, centering on titular character Victor Frankenstein and his ghoulish creation. The science-fiction blockbuster features intriguing and innovative choreography, cinematic design, special effects, pyrotechnics, and a haunting original score from Lowell Liebermann. San Francisco Ballet soloist and stager Lauren Strongin said Scarlett’s choreographer allows audiences to see “his deep respect for classical British technique in the footwork and lower body which then allows for freedom in the upper body and port de bras.” “He often spoke of the movement initiating from the back and allowing the arms to react, as if moving through water,” Strongin said. “Liam was a corps dancer in his career, so you will notice the group work is as difficult as the principal work. There are no superfluous movements or ‘filler’ dance sequences for the group, everything is integral to the story.” Strongin added that Scarlett took his inspiration from Shelley’s novel as a jumping-off point and gave more depth to the central characters. “The contrast of the Creature’s birth into painful, primal, awkward contemporary movements quickly transforming into clean technique mirrors the Creature’s rapid learning of language and social mores in the novel,” she said. “For Victor, his dissent into guilt, paranoia, and fear is expressed by increasingly internal movements.” Ricardo Cervera, a ballet master at The Royal Ballet who taught Scarlett’s Frankenstein choreography to San Francisco Ballet dancers, said “theatrical drama” is one of the ballet’s biggest strengths. “At the end of the first act, you can’t wait to see what comes next, and the same thing at the end of the second act,” he says. “Even though you know [the story], you can’t wait to see what [Liam Scarlett] has done with it.” Single tickets to performances may be purchased online at sfballet.org or by calling ticket services at (415) 865-2000, open Monday through Friday, 10am to 4pm. Frankenstein encore performances will be held on select dates between April 26 through May 4.
articles.title: Frankenstein closes SF Ballet’s season with performances March 20-26

articles.text: Sasha De Sola and Joseph Caley in Raymonda Raymonda, San Francisco Ballet’s third production of the 2025– 26 season, opened on March 1 at the War Memorial Theatre. It is a rare sight in the ballet world. Originally choreographed by Marius Petipa for the Imperial Russian Ballet to the music of Alexander Glazunov, the full 180-minute Raymonda is seldom performed today due to its length and complexity. Most companies instead present only the third act. Tamara Rojo’s adaptation, marking the ballet’s North American premiere, is thus an ambitious endeavor—one that highlights the company’s technical and artistic prowess while also showcasing Rojo’s skill as a choreographer. It is a bold attempt to reimagine a classical story ballet in a way that resonates with contemporary audiences, reinforcing ballet’s relevance in the modern world. Yet, despite many delightful moments on Raymonda’s opening night, the overall impression was of a performance that pulled at too many threads without weaving them into a satisfying whole. Rojo’s production replaces the original “damsel in distress” narrative—in which the medieval French countess Raymonda is rescued by her crusader fiancé— with a story of female empowerment inspired by wartime nurse Florence Nightingale. Accordingly, the setting shifts from the era of the Crusades to the 1854 Crimean War, where English, Ottoman, and French forces battle the Russian Empire. Instead of supporting the war effort by sewing alongside her female relatives, the young noblewoman Raymonda (principal dancer Sasha De Sola) defies convention, leaving her family’s estate in England to become a nurse on the Crimean front. There, while tending to the wounded, she becomes entangled in a love triangle with her childhood friend, British officer John de Bryan (guest dancer Joseph Caley), and Ottoman prince Abdur Rahman (Fernando Carratalá Coloma). Her fellow nurses—the free-spirited Henriette (Katherine Barkman) and the dutiful Sister Clemence (Jasmine Jimison)—take sides in the affair, each attempting to sway Raymonda’s choices while delivering some of the production’s most scintillating pas de deux and pas de trois. In the end, Raymonda marries John, leaving Abdur heartbroken. Yet, immediately after the wedding, she walks away from both her husband and her admirer, suitcase in hand, her destination unknown. While the adaptation strives to give Raymonda greater agency and modern relevance, the narrative’s shifts don’t always fully coalesce. Some dramatic moments—like her interactions with Abdur and Constance— flare up vividly but fail to sustain their emotional impact, making it difficult for the dancers to fully immerse in the dramatic arc. These demands were fitting for the ballet’s original comPhotos by Lindsay Thomas missioner, the Imperial Russian Ballet of the 19th century. The choreography includes a cascade of hops en pointe, pirouettes, chaîné turns (half-turns performed while traveling across the stage), and double tours en l’air (jumping turns with two full rotations before landing). The stage is filled with dancers, and the scenes run longer than usual. Taking on a ballet of this scale— one in which many dancers were performing for the first time—is no small feat, even for a company of SF Ballet’s renown. The intricate choreography pushed the dancers to their limits, a challenge they largely rose to, despite a few fleeting missteps in Act III. De Sola danced flawlessly, though perhaps at the expense of emotional depth. Abdur-Hernandez had the only plausible character arc—that of a suffering lover—making his performance the most convincing. For a ballet set during wartime, there was surprisingly little war-related action beyond the Act I brawl between allied troops, which serves as Abdur’s introduction, and the intermittent presence of two wounded soldiers in the left corner of the stage. Despite these shortcomings, Raymonda delivered an abundance of visually arresting sequences. Those include the lantern scene, where scores of nurses carry lamps through darkness (a nod to Florence Nightingale, the “Lady with the Lamp”); the Ottoman dances at Abdur’s camp in Act II; and San Francisco Ballet’s production of Raymonda

There are no superfluous movements or ‘filler’ dance sequences for the group, everything is integral to the story.” Strongin added that Scarlett took his inspiration from Shelley’s novel as a jumping-off point and gave more depth to the central characters. “The contrast of the Creature’s birth into painful, primal, awkward contemporary movements quickly transforming into clean technique mirrors the Creature’s rapid learning of language and social mores in the novel,” she said. “For Victor, his dissent into guilt, paranoia, and fear is expressed by increasingly internal movements.” Ricardo Cervera, a ballet master at The Royal Ballet who taught Scarlett’s Frankenstein choreography to San Francisco Ballet dancers, said “theatrical drama” is one of the ballet’s biggest strengths. “At the end of the first act, you can’t wait to see what comes next, and the same thing at the end of the second act,” he says. “Even though you know [the story], you can’t wait to see what [Liam Scarlett] has done with it.” Single tickets to performances may be purchased online at sfballet.org or by calling ticket services at (415) 865-2000, open Monday through Friday, 10am to 4pm. Frankenstein encore performances will be held on select dates between April 26 through May 4. Tamara Rojo and San Francisco Ballet reimagine Raymonda Sasha De Sola and Joseph Caley in Raymonda By Anastasia Edel Raymonda, San Francisco Ballet’s third production of the 2025– 26 season, opened on March 1 at the War Memorial Theatre. It is a rare sight in the ballet world. Originally choreographed by Marius Petipa for the Imperial Russian Ballet to the music of Alexander Glazunov, the full 180-minute Raymonda is seldom performed today due to its length and complexity. Most companies instead present only the third act. Tamara Rojo’s adaptation, marking the ballet’s North American premiere, is thus an ambitious endeavor—one that highlights the company’s technical and artistic prowess while also showcasing Rojo’s skill as a choreographer. It is a bold attempt to reimagine a classical story ballet in a way that resonates with contemporary audiences, reinforcing ballet’s relevance in the modern world. Yet, despite many delightful moments on Raymonda’s opening night, the overall impression was of a performance that pulled at too many threads without weaving them into a satisfying whole. Rojo’s production replaces the original “damsel in distress” narrative—in which the medieval French countess Raymonda is rescued by her crusader fiancé— with a story of female empowerment inspired by wartime nurse Florence Nightingale. Accordingly, the setting shifts from the era of the Crusades to the 1854 Crimean War, where English, Ottoman, and French forces battle the Russian Empire. Instead of supporting the war effort by sewing alongside her female relatives, the young noblewoman Raymonda (principal dancer Sasha De Sola) defies convention, leaving her family’s estate in England to become a nurse on the Crimean front. There, while tending to the wounded, she becomes entangled in a love triangle with her childhood friend, British officer John de Bryan (guest dancer Joseph Caley), and Ottoman prince Abdur Rahman (Fernando Carratalá Coloma). Her fellow nurses—the free-spirited Henriette (Katherine Barkman) and the dutiful Sister Clemence (Jasmine Jimison)—take sides in the affair, each attempting to sway Raymonda’s choices while delivering some of the production’s most scintillating pas de deux and pas de trois. In the end, Raymonda marries John, leaving Abdur heartbroken. Yet, immediately after the wedding, she walks away from both her husband and her admirer, suitcase in hand, her destination unknown. While the adaptation strives to give Raymonda greater agency and modern relevance, the narrative’s shifts don’t always fully coalesce. Some dramatic moments—like her interactions with Abdur and Constance— flare up vividly but fail to sustain their emotional impact, making it difficult for the dancers to fully immerse in the dramatic arc. These demands were fitting for the ballet’s original comPhotos by Lindsay Thomas missioner, the Imperial Russian Ballet of the 19th century. The choreography includes a cascade of hops en pointe, pirouettes, chaîné turns (half-turns performed while traveling across the stage), and double tours en l’air (jumping turns with two full rotations before landing). The stage is filled with dancers, and the scenes run longer than usual. Taking on a ballet of this scale— one in which many dancers were performing for the first time—is no small feat, even for a company of SF Ballet’s renown. The intricate choreography pushed the dancers to their limits, a challenge they largely rose to, despite a few fleeting missteps in Act III. De Sola danced flawlessly, though perhaps at the expense of emotional depth. Abdur-Hernandez had the only plausible character arc—that of a suffering lover—making his performance the most convincing. For a ballet set during wartime, there was surprisingly little war-related action beyond the Act I brawl between allied troops, which serves as Abdur’s introduction, and the intermittent presence of two wounded soldiers in the left corner of the stage. Despite these shortcomings, Raymonda delivered an abundance of visually arresting sequences. articles.text: Alvin Ailey Dancers The Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater returns to UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall next month for its annual campus residency. It will feature four programs over seven performances and the premieres of four new works and two new productions. The nationally-acclaimed dance company, now in its seventh decade, has regularly performed at Zellerbach Hall, appearing on UC Berkeley’s campus more than any other place in the world outside of their home base in New York City. The company’s current season celebrates the life and legacy of Alvin Ailey Artistic Director Emerita Judith Jamison. UC Berkeley’s Cal Performances dedicates the April 2025 Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater residency and Berkeley/Oakland AileyCamp to her legacy as well. Jamison choreographed performances that led her to international stardom and danced with the company until 1980 when she left to pursue opportunities on Broadway. She returned four years later as a choreographer with her debut work Divining. After company founder Alvin Ailey’s death in 1989, Jamison stepped into the role of artistic director, where she remained until she retired in 2011. She passed away on November 9, 2024. In addition to a dedication to the late Jamison, April’s program also features the Bay Area premieres of four new works, including Jamar Roberts’ Al-Andalus Blues, Matthew Rushing’s Sacred Songs, Hope Boykin’s Finding Free, and Lar Lubovitch’s Many Angels, as well as new productions of Ronald K. Brown’s Grace (1999) and Elisa Monte’s Treading (1979). Alvin Ailey dancers will close with its time-honored tradition, performing the beloved Revelations (1960), on three of the four programs. showtimes below. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30pm and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5pm. articles.text: Shotgun Players’ season opener is Yasmina Reza’s internationally acclaimed play, Art, translated by Christopher Hampton and directed by the visionary Emilie Whelan. The production will run from March 8 to April 6 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley, promising an unforgettable theatrical experience that is both thought-provoking and hilariously entertaining. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Play (1998) and the Olivier Award for Best Comedy (1997), Art is a sharp, witty exploration of friendship, identity, and the value of art. The story revolves around three longtime friends – Serge, Marc, and Yvan – whose bonds are tested when Serge buys an expensive, all-white painting. “The play begins with a guy who buys a white painting with 3 white lines for $200,000 and wants to show it to his friends,” said Director Emilie Whelan. “He’s in the middle of life: the middle of his career, the middle of his divorce, the middle of parenting his two kids who are in the middle of how they feel about him. In this mid-life moment, he doesn’t buy a red Corvette... he buys a $200,000 painting. How will his closest friends - who are in the dangerous middle of their own lives - respond to his purchase? Can we buy a new start? Can we buy a blank canvas?” What begins as merely a debate over aesthetics quickly spirals into an uproarious examination of personal relationships and the fragility of human connections. Marc ridicules Serge’s purchase, while Yvan tries to mediate, leading to intense debates about art, personal values, and their long-standing friendship. Yasmina Reza is a French

articles.text: Four-time Grammy-winning Rosanne Cash, Johnny Cash’s eldest daughter, is the latest celebrity to support one of Oakland’s hidden gems: on Tuesday, April 1, Cash will play an intimate benefit concert for the Northern Light School, a unique PreK-8th grade independent school dedicated to serving children from all socioeconomic backgrounds. Past star supporters have included Bonnie Raitt, MC Hammer, Jackson Browne, Bob Weir, and the late all-star Vida Blue. The event will be held at the Oakland Zoo and emceed by renowned actor and activist Peter Coyote. Ticket prices range from $1,000-$3,000 and can be purRosanne Cash chased by the general public at tinyurl.com/NLSBenefit. At Northern Light School, 75 percent of students receive tuition assistance compared to the national average for independent schools of less than 25 percent. 95 percent of NLS’s students are children of color, compared to the national average of 34 percent, and nearly all graduates matriculate to private or parochial high schools. Tickets are tax-deductible and support a great cause. Northern Light School (NLS) is an independent progressive school in Oakland, CA serving students in Pre-K to 8th grade. NLS is committed to providing an empowering education for children from all socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds. Our faculty and staff create an atmosphere where every child can excel — as learners, leaders, and engaged human beings. Our focus is on academic excellence as well as non-violence, acceptance of differences, respect for the environment, and the moral advancement of humanity — so that the children develop an understanding that they have a responsibility to make a difference in the lives of others.

Friday, March 14, 7:30 p.m. Miles Graber Piano Four-Hands Concert Piano four hands is a type of piano duet involving two players playing the same piano simultaneously. For this concert, Miles Graber and Amy Zanrosso will play PCA’s superb Steinway grand piano together, performing an assortment of pieces by six well-known Austrian, French, and German/Hungarian composers of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries: Ligeti, Brahms, Satie, Ravel, Dvořák, and Schubert. One of the very colorful dishes at Monster Pho restaurant. ing a variety of Vietnamese specialties. In order to make a good review, we needed to get a variety of things. Everything that we ordered was colorful as well as delicious. Needless to say, four of us enjoyed the meal immensely. I am confident that you will enjoy it also. After we had finished we asked to see the owner. He is an extremely friendly fellow and happy to tell the story of his life, which has been very successful. What an inspiration he is. He told us that he was one of the last of the boat people leaving Vietnam in 1987. His family spent two weeks in an overcrowded boat and then after two years of being “in transit” the family arrived in the United States in 1989. Once here, they got to work. Multiple jobs were the order of the day. So was hard work. The mother of the family had absolutely no schooling, but she was an inspiring figure and encouraged all of the kids to get a good education. The entire family stresses being ethical and honest, as well as being generous and helpful. Tee Tran is the owner. Be sure to engage him in conversation. One thing I forgot to tell you is that all of the recipes are family recipes. Simply stated, it’s home cooking. Having a “full plate” sometimes means making some serious choices. articles.text: Hugo, adapted from the Caldecott-winning graphic novel by Brian Selznick, has at first blush the appearance of a film with teens and tweens as the intended audience. And that would be accurate until it isn’t – keep in mind that the film is directed by Martin Scorsese (not a filmmaker associated with kids’ narratives). It stars Asa Butterfield as the 14-year-old orphaned Hugo and Chloe Moretz portraying Isabelle, his contemporary fiend. The setting is a Parisian train station in the early, post-Great War 1930s. Hugo lives up in the eaves of the station, in a small, spare room. His mission, call it a passion, is to wind the enormous station clock and restore an extraordinary mechanical automaton left to him by his late father. A scene from the 2025 Academy Award Best Picture winner Anora When Anora received multiple 2025 Oscar nominations, to include Best Picture, I read with interest several plot summaries prior to the awards ceremony. The film, written and directed by Sean Baker, was characterized as “audacious, thrilling, and a comedic variation on a modern day Cinderella story.” Even references to the iconic film Pretty Woman were included. So far so good. Descriptors like rom-com and meet cute came to mind. However, regarding winning an Oscar, well, as a small indie, it faced stiff competition. Emilia Perez had garnered 13 nominations, followed by The Brutalist and Wicked with 10 nominations each. The pre-Oscar buzz seemed to favor Emilia Perez. Anora had recently won a Palme d’Oro at the Cannes French Film Festival, the highest award given to a film in the official competition. articles.text: Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey is a remake of the 1963 Disney film of the same name. It is based on the 1960 Sheila Burnford children’s story about three animals – Shadow (Don Ameche), a wise old Golden Retriever; Chance (Michael J. Fox), a spunky American Bulldog; and Sassy (Sally Field), a pampered Himalayan cat. The genius of Disney has, since its inception, been the ability to give animals, animated or real, human characteristics, from speech and dress, to facial characteristics. It’s referred to as anthropomorphism. Homeward Bound is a live action feature wherein the animals chat each other up, and make a plan to solve what they perceive to be their dilemma. As Disney has long ago learned, kids find giving human voices to animals completely acceptable, even when animation is blended with live action characters. The plot of Homeward Bound revolves around the decision of the Seavers family to relocate to San Francisco. It’s decided that while making the transition to the new digs, they will leave their three pets with a relative who owns a ranch in northern California. Due to a mix-up in communication, the owner leaves on a cattle drive assuming that the trio will be cared for by a friend, Frank (Gary Taylor). He thinks the pets have been taken along on the drive. The result is that Shadow, Chance, and Sassy believe they’ve, in effect, been left home alone. Shadow decides that he is not going to stay at the ranch, but make his way to San Francisco. Chance and Sassy, at first reluctant, agree to go with him on what will be an epic journey into the rocky mountain wilderness of the Sierra Nevada. And so their adventure begins as these three, who are not prepared for what awaits them, set out on their trek. Of course, they will encounter one crisis after another (Shadow and Chance get separated from Sassy, while crossing a swift-moving river). Of course, Sassy survives and is rescued by an old-timer, Quentin (William Edward Phipps), and is later reunited with Chance and Shadow. The three will encounter mountain lions, bears, and a little girl named Molly who is lost in the woods and they help in her rescue. The rescue party that has been looking for Molly, assuming they’re helping, takes the trio to an animal shelter, from which they eventually escape. Once again the three hit the road so to speak, their destination still San Francisco, hopefully to be rejoined with their owners, the Seavers family. Remember, this is Disney, and after a long and exciting ordeal, the story has right ending. Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey. Directed by Duwayne Dunham. With voices of Don Ameche, Michael J. Fox, Sally Field. Walt Disney Pictures 1 hr., 24 min. Rated G. Released in 1993. Streaming on Fandango/ Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Kiki’s Delivery Service Kiki’s Delivery Service, created by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, who is regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, was adapted from a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home to complete her magic training in another town. She takes with her talking cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, KiKi’s Delivery Service is a wonderful adventure; however, it is also a personal crossroads for KiKi, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. The tale is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With voices of Kirsten Dunst, Debbie Reynolds and Matthew Lawrence. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated G. Released in 1989. Streaming on Fandango/apple tv/ MAX/prime.
