articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met on March 3 at the Community Hall with a record turnout of 26 readers. Participating were Nancy Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Mike Henn, Lois Price, Laura Goldman, Pat McMahon, Nadine Guffanti, Peggy Shultz, Darby Gregg, Melba Yee, Adrienne Hamlin, Bob Hall, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Orrel Lanter, Louise Booth, Sarah Johnson, Hilary Honore, Ken Young, June Yee, Carol Warren, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Gerry Gregg, Martin Levy, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. At their meeting the month before the readers tried something new. The group has grown significantly. Some readers wanted a smaller group experience, so they set up in an alcove for their conversation. It was successful, so at this March meeting four readers led by Lois Price did it again, while Priscilla Wanerus continued to lead the larger discussion. Carol Long once again brought cookies that were enjoyed by all. The group was there to talk about James by Percival Everett. It was published in 2024 and won the National Book Award for Fiction last year. The novel is a reimagining of Mark Twain’s Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, but is told from the perspective of Huck’s friend, Jim, an escaped enslaved person. Readers’ reactions to James were generally positive but varied. They ranged from “loved it” to “liked it, not loved it” to “not disliked it, not loved it.” This should not have been surprising because there are many layers and facets to James. It was felt this is really two books in one. Readers thought the first part of the book was fun and clever, fine for children, but the second is characterized by violence and book. James code-switches and speaks “correct incorrect grammar” to his white tormentors, but uses unlikely, articulate, formal English with other Blacks. Readers recognized the potential for discrimination based on the way people talk. How someone speaks does not reflect their intelligence, and just because someone talks like you, it doesn’t mean the person is like you. Some readers reread Huckleberry Finn for a comparison and saw it as a very different book. It’s “an adventure story of a kid.” They couldn’t see Twain thinking of Jim as James, and his ending was embarrassing for some. Everett’s ambiguous ending for James was unsatisfying for some readers too, but they felt it was probably necessary given James’ uncertain future. The group also asked if Everett’s work would have stood up on its own without Huckleberry Finn. They thought so, but it would be a different book. Everett’s taking of Twain’s classic work and giving it a new perspective was daring. It generated attention and undoubtedly book sales too. After their separate discussions, the two groups rejoin for the selection of their next book. They had previously selected Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz for their April book and Cloudstreet by Tim Winton for May. After Bob Hall’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected How We Got to Now by Stephen Johnson for June. With their business done, the readers went outside the Community Hall for a group picture. The group’s next discussion will be on April 7 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome and there is no fee. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. revenge. The violence directed at James and others is hard to read. Everett’s dark humor may generate an occasional smile, but this is not a humorous story. It presents the South’s “Peculiar Institution” of slavery as a brutal form of repression. It seemed to the group that Everett used the book to channel his anger regarding whites’ mistreatment of Black people. Some readers found his portrayal of the book’s white characters problematic. They are all ignorant and evil. Readers may have to suspend disbelief at times about his story, as realism is not Everett’s game with this book. His message is the game. Everett is a USC English professor, and he wants to forcefully make a point. Black people have been treated very badly in America. They are strong people, who should be respected, and he commands it with James. Readers found the book to be full of imagery. They particularly liked the use of James’ ownership of a pencil to represent the importance of literacy and its power. Enslaved people were not allowed to learn to read or write. It was threatening to whites. Language is also important in the The First Mondays Reading Group meets the first Monday of the month at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park.

articles.text: It’s tax season again — which also means, unfortunately, that it’s time for the annual array of scams aimed at taxpayers. Fortunately, by being alert, you can protect yourself from these attempts to defraud you. Your first line of defense is to recognize the warning signs of potential tax scams. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) cites these common red flags: • Promises of big payments — If you’ve filed taxes for many years, either by yourself or with the help of a tax professional, you probably have a pretty good idea of whether you’re getting a refund, and how much it will be. But scammers, often using social media, may promise huge refunds by essentially encouraging you to claim tax credits to which you’re not entitled and then charging large, upfront fees or a fee based on your refund amount. • Suspicious websites — Watch out for strange-sounding or misspelled web links — these can take you to harmful sites, rather than the official site of the IRS (IRS.gov). • Solicitations from charity imposters — The many natural disasters we’ve experienced in recent years has brought out great support from people wanting to help friends, neighbors and even total strangers. However, these catastrophes have also encouraged scammers who solicit contributions to bogus charitable groups. To determine whether an organization is a qualified charity that can receive tax-deductible contributions, visit the Tax Exempt Organization Search tool on IRS.gov. • Threats or demands — IRS impersonators may threaten you with large fines, or even arrest, if you don’t make immediate payments of what they claim you owe. You can protect yourself from many tax-related scams by knowing how the IRS will or won’t communicate with you. Typically, the IRS will initiate contact with you through regular mail delivered by the U.S. Postal Service. You can verify the legitimacy of any letter by visiting your secure IRS online account, under the “Notices and Letters” section. Other ways the IRS will contact you: • Email — Only with your permission, with a few exceptions, such as criminal investigations • Text – Only with your permission • Phone — Only to discuss your case, verify information or set up a meeting • Fax — Only to verify or request employment information • In-person visit — Rarely done, and typically only following a letter The IRS will not: • Contact you or take payment on social media. • Accept gift cards or prepaid debit cards as payment. • Threaten to call law enforcement or immigration officials. • Take your citizenship status, driver’s license or business license. • Leave pre-recorded voicemails (robocalls). • Mail tax debt resolution advertisements. If you have doubts about any offers or communications, whether supposedly from the IRS or not, you may want to contact a trusted, qualified tax professional. Also, be on guard for your elderly family members, as senior citizens are frequent targets of scammers. If you talk to these family members regularly, see if you can find out about any unusual offers or solicitations they may have received. Finally, if you believe you are a victim of monetary or identity theft, you can report these issues using the IRS website at IdentityTheft.gov. You can also refer to IRS Publication 5027 — l Identity Theft Information for Taxpayers. Tax scams and identity theft are serious threats — so do whatever you can to defend yourself. articles.text: All of the different housing types we use can be divided into two main categories: single-family housing, and multi-family housing. While the vast majority of people in the industrialized urban world live in multi-family housing of one kind or another, in the U.S. an estimated 80% of housing units are single family, and 20-25% as multi family. There are a number of variations and hybrids, along with varying labels for the different types of housing but in my experience, the types shown in the accompanying diagram are common and understood by architects, developers, contractors and planners. For all communities the end result of different housing types is different densities, typically measured in units/acre. There is a huge difference from say, 3.5 units/acre for single family detached homes, to 12 units/acre for attached townhomes, to as many as 90 units/acre for urban high-rise multi-family. There are also many interconnected components to housing density and the resulting look, feel, and functioning of a neighborhood, including open space, roadway size and type, public transportation systems, and infrastructures of various kinds. (And parking, which we will leave for another column.) In my mind, a dividing line in the whole multi-family world can be defined by the entries. Units with their own separate outside entries, such as duplexes, townhouses or garden apartments, have a whole different character than denser types such as mid or high-rise buildings with entries necessarily located off a common corridor. The units in these denser, higher buildings can’t have the individuality, residential character and connection to the street that the lower density units do. The description of different architectural types of housing is sometimes confused with ownership categories. For example, a 10-unit “apartment” building can be owned by one person, in which case the 10 units would be rented out. This is the most common definition of “apartment”. But the same 10-unit building could also be a condominium, in which case the 10 occupants would each own the inside of their own unit with everything else being considered common space owned jointly by the 10 owners. In this case it would typically be called a “condo” and not an apartment building. Other forms of ownership such as co-ops are somewhat similar. In any case, these different types of ownership can be applied to all of the different architectural types, not just multi-family. Special purpose multi-family housing. like student housing, senior housing, affordable housing, or low-income housing, also can be designed in many of the architectural types, under a variety of ownership formulas, with the one-owner “apartment” model probably most common. Next: Multi-family Housing, Part 2 Will Adams was a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who lived in Piedmont for 30 years. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on August 18, 2021. Basic architectural housing types from least to most dense. There are numerous variations and hybrids of these basic types. Outside of central zones, like downtown Oakland or the Lake Merritt area, we are most familiar with single family detached (SFD) housing. Some “attached” single family units can be 4 times as dense as single-family dwellings, although still technically considered single family.

articles.text: Will Adams was an architect, urban designer, and 30-year Piedmont resident who wrote the Piedmont Post’s Walking Piedmont column. He was also a Wednesday walker and led many walks for the group devoted to the different styles of architecture in Piedmont. Last Wednesday, walker and fellow architect Jim Kellogg led a tour of Julia Morgan designed homes, like the first walk Will led for the group in 2021. Jim began the tour with a remembrance of Will’s 2021 walk with information about Julia Morgan and the homes she designed. Morgan’s family moved to the Bay Area from New York when she was two years old, and she spent the rest of her life here. She graduated from the University of California, Berkeley in 1894 with a degree in Civil Engineering. It did not have a School of Architecture then, so Morgan applied and became the first woman admitted to the architecture program at L’Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris and then became the first woman architect licensed in California. Morgan formed her own firm in 1904, after studying with Bernard Maybeck and working for two years with John Galen Howard. She was a constant worker completely dedicated to her profession and never married. She was also an excellent manager and developed a special rapport with craftsmen and artisans working on her projects and managed a hundred people at the peak of her Hearst Castle project. She designed over 700 other California projects including the Berkeley Greek Theater, the Berkeley City Club, the Mills College Campanile, the Carnegie Library, the Monterey Asilomar Conference Center, Piedmont Avenue’s Chapel of the Chimes, Piedmont’s Ransom Bridges School on Hazel Lane, and many others. She was known for delivering projects on time and on budget. Morgan embraced the Arts and Crafts Movement supported by Bernard Maybeck in her architectural work. She strove to reconcile her exposure and training in other styles including BeauxArts formalism, Classical, and Neo-Tudor, while at the same time adding artistry and whimsy to her designs. She was also an excellent engineer pioneering the aesthetic use of reinforced structural concrete as well as inventive custom cement mixes for decorative sculpture and detailing. Morgan designed about 10 beautiful homes that remain in Piedmont. They were all designed within a period of 15 years after Piedmont’s founding in 1907, a time when the city was referred to as “Queen of The Hills” and the “The City of Millionaires.” Her design style and masterpiece projects added to the accuracy of these monikers, as well as the character of Piedmont that we still enjoy today. Jim’s tour would also touch on work by Morgan’s fellow architects of this period. They significantly influenced each other. After providing this background, Jim led the long parade of walkers to see eight of Morgan’s projects. They went up Sierra Avenue for the first two. Several Sierra homes represent the varying architectural styles in the early era of Piedmont’s development and influenced Morgan’s work. They included an arts and crafts home by John Hudson Thomas at 12 Sierra, an elegant beaux-arts classical revival across the street, and a neo-tutor manor house with steep double gable roofs. The first Morgan home was a simple yet beautiful steep-roofed neo-tutor at 49 Sierra built in 1914. It provided an interesting contrast to her house next door at 45 Sierra that was designed in 1925. It represents her mature craftsman’s style with handcrafted detailing. Morgan’s site plan included an elegant, shared porte-cochere driveway and rear yard garage to unify the two homes. The group continued up Lakeview Avenue to Sea View Avenue and stopped at 25 Sea View, an elegantly proportioned classical revival with a Parisian cantilevered glass entry overhang built in 1915. This is not a Morgan house but is an excellent example of Beaux-Arts style that was ingrained in her early education. The walkers continued on Sea View to Hampton Avenue to see. one of Morgan’s masterpieces at 216 Hampton that was built in 1912. The owner agreed to have the group into the yard and go around the house to study the elegant arts and crafts detailing. The house has had only two owners, and they have retained its original layout and character for over 100 years. The beautiful, mature landscaping surrounding the property made the walkers feel they had left modern Piedmont and entered a 1920s “quiet secret garden.” A large turnout of 59 walkers and five K-9 best friends was at the Exedra last Wednesday for a walk by the Walking on Wednesdays group in memory of Will Adams, who died unexpectedly in December. Among walk participants were Debbie Powell, Nancy Henn, Noemi Alvarado, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Karin Fetherston, Helen Dong, Alicia Rivera, tom Lehrkind, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Joyce Ahern, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Cathy Laymon, Laura Dudell-Folley, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kellogg, Peggy Shultz, Jack Fischrup, Mark Davis, Sharona Fischrup, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Edith Lee, Shiela Leunig, Margaret Leunig, Kat Lang, Jim Kuo, Lois Price, Michelle Yang, Abha Kotari, Sherry Jacobs, Camile Scribner, Denny McGee, Regina O’Connor, Liz Dalrymple, Joanne Larson, Margie Richardson, Quincy Dong, Judy Sokoloff, Bob Wong, Chuck Oraftik, Priscilla Wanerus, Bill Ahern, Minoo Klayman, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, June Yee, Kathleen Henrikson with K-9 best friends Finn and Frank, Karen Glasser, Paul Silberstein, Elene Manolis, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Lenka and Larry Glassner, who were walking with them for the first time. The walkers were happy that Will’s wife Linda, daughter Alissa Adams, and granddaughter Chelsea Rose Adams were with them too.

The walkers then turned onto Farragut Avenue to see the final three Morgan homes. The first large home was designed for James Lombard. He was educated at Harrow Public School in England and wanted his home to provide a remembrance of Harrow. articles.text: park, Blair Park now sold refreshments and boasted a restaurant. Venetian Canal The Venetian Canal was popular for old and young visitors alike. Opening in March of 1891, flat-bottomed boats floated in a meandering circular water flume, propelled by a large water wheel driven by an engine. The flume was 1000’ long, elevated to a “considerable height,” and ran over babbling brooks and across small ravines before returning to its start. Riders were given a small pole to ease the boats along when they became stuck. Dancing Pavilion Open on all sides with just a roof above, the Dancing Pavilion was designed as a cooler, more pleasant alternative to the stuffy indoor dancing clubs in downtown Oakland. It was open to the public during the day and could be leased for private parties in the evening. On those occasions the refreshment stand remained open. The 1891 Tribune claimed “…a large electric light in the center of the pavilion abundantly illuminates the structure.” The pavilion was close to the bandstand so visitors could dance to the bandstand music. The French Maze Sometimes called the French Puzzle or the Mystic Maze, the French Maze challenged visitors in Blair Park. Designed after a maze in Paris, it was built with 6-foot tall lattice panels planted with Chinese honeysuckle vines. These panels formed 64 intersecting paths creating a bewildering journey to the center (and back). This maze was only 1600 feet long, but it could be as long as 7000 feet given the wrong turns that one could take. As late as 1954, there was a miniature Japanese pagoda in one of the backyards on Moraga Avenue that reportedly had been in the middle of the French Maze in Blair Park. The Photo Gallery No amusement park would be complete without a photo gallery. The gallery in Blair Park offered mementos by sketch artists in just 10 minutes of one’s visit to the park. Visitors could also buy photographic souvenirs of Blair Park, such as this photo showing the lake in the park and the cemetery monuments beyond. Japanese Tea House Blair Park also had its own Japanese Tea House, an exact replica of an ancient tea house in Japan. It was constructed in Yokohama, then shipped in sections to Piedmont. Rebuilt on the site in the Japanese style, its fitted joints were tightly secured with ropes. Nails were used only to hold the roof tiles. It was This souvenir photo from Blair Park shows Blair’s lake and the cemetery beyond. Japanese Tea House open on three sides with a circular Japanese window. Although the sketch shows ladies seated on chairs, operators originally planned to serve tea in the traditional Japanese manner – to guests sitting on straw mats or standing. There were also plans to bring in two Japanese maidens and their chaperone to serve tea in Oriental gowns. An adjacent Japanese garden was planted with 1000 Japanese lily bulbs. A Family Park Blair Park was planned as a family park. Park operators widely advertised that they maintained a comfortable park where ladies and children could attend without fear of encountering any “objectionable persons.” No wine or liquor was sold in the park, and a deputy constable was present to keep any “toughs” out of the park. In addition to the Venetian Canal for children, there were swings and see-saws scattered throughout the park and a horse-driven merry-goround. articles.text: The bandstand and fountain at the Blair Park entrance. In a previous column, we described the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company, its cable cars and famous gravity loop in Piedmont. The cable car line was expensive to build and expensive to maintain. To encourage more riders on the cable cars, the company leased the Blair Park land and built several popular amusements to draw more riders on their cable cars. The Oakland Daily Evening Tribune described the new “Attractions of Blair Park” on June 20, 1891. (Most of the illustrations here are from that article.) Today it’s difficult to imagine that so many exciting attractions were squeezed into that narrow strip of land on Moraga Avenue. The cable company thinned more trees and shrubs in the 75-acre park, paved the paths throughout the park and planted purple and white wisteria to grow The Venetian Canal Beautiful Bronze Fountain A large 28-foot bronze fountain stood adjacent to the bandstand. The fountain represented the ascending orders of the animal kingdom. Water lilies filled the basin of the fountain. Four dolphins formed the fountain base, each spouting a stream of water into the basin below. Four swans formed the middle tier, Dancing Pavilion. over the large arched entrance. More purple and white wisteria grew near the bandstand. (Could this be the beginning of Piedmont’s purple and white tradition?) As visitors entered the park under this arch, they passed through lawns with benches in a semi-circle and came to a large bandstand, the first attraction the cable company built. pages.text: Wednesday, March 12, 2025 29 History of Piedmont Cable Company attractions in Blair Park The bandstand and fountain at the Blair Park entrance. By Gail G. Lombardi In a previous column, we described the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company, its cable cars and famous gravity loop in Piedmont. The cable car line was expensive to build and expensive to maintain. To encourage more riders on the cable cars, the company leased the Blair Park land and built several popular amusements to draw more riders on their cable cars. The Oakland Daily Evening Tribune described the new “Attractions of Blair Park” on June 20, 1891. (Most of the illustrations here are from that article.) Today it’s difficult to imagine that so many exciting attractions were squeezed into that narrow strip of land on Moraga Avenue. The cable company thinned more trees and shrubs in the 75-acre park, paved the paths throughout the park and planted purple and white wisteria to grow The Venetian Canal Beautiful Bronze Fountain A large 28-foot bronze fountain stood adjacent to the bandstand. The fountain represented the ascending orders of the animal kingdom. Water lilies filled the basin of the fountain. Four dolphins formed the fountain base, each spouting a stream of water into the basin below. Four swans formed the middle tier, park, Blair Park now sold refreshments and boasted a restaurant. Venetian Canal The Venetian Canal was popular for old and young visitors alike. Opening in March of 1891, flat-bottomed boats floated in a meandering circular water flume, propelled by a large water wheel driven by an engine. The flume was 1000’ long, elevated to a “considerable height,” and ran over babbling brooks and across small ravines before returning to its start. Riders were given a small pole to ease the boats along when they became stuck. Dancing Pavilion Open on all sides with just a roof above, the Dancing Pavilion was designed as a cooler, more pleasant alternative to the stuffy indoor dancing clubs in downtown Oakland. It was open to the public during the day and could be leased for private parties in the evening. On those occasions the refreshment stand remained open. The 1891 Tribune claimed “…a large electric light in the center of the pavilion abundantly illuminates the structure.” The pavilion was close to the bandstand so visitors could dance to the bandstand music. The French Maze Sometimes called the French Puzzle or the Mystic Maze, the French Maze challenged visitors in Blair Park. Designed after a maze in Paris, it was built with 6-foot tall lattice panels planted with Chinese honeysuckle vines. These panels formed 64 intersecting paths creating a bewildering journey to the center (and back). This maze was only 1600 feet long, but it could be as long as 7000 feet given the wrong turns that one could take. As late as 1954, there was a miniature Japanese pagoda in one of the backyards on Moraga Avenue that reportedly had been in the middle of the French Maze in Blair Park. The Photo Gallery No amusement park would be complete without a photo gallery. The gallery in Blair Park offered mementos by sketch artists in just 10 minutes of one’s visit to the park. Visitors could also buy photographic souvenirs of Blair Park, such as this photo showing the lake in the park and the cemetery monuments beyond. Japanese Tea House Blair Park also had its own Japanese Tea House, an exact replica of an ancient tea house in Japan. It was constructed in Yokohama, then shipped in sections to Piedmont. Rebuilt on the site in the Japanese style, its fitted joints were tightly secured with ropes. Nails were used only to hold the roof tiles. It was This souvenir photo from Blair Park shows Blair’s lake and the cemetery beyond. Japanese Tea House open on three sides with a circular Japanese window. Although the sketch shows ladies seated on chairs, operators originally planned to serve tea in the traditional Japanese manner – to guests sitting on straw mats or standing. There were also plans to bring in two Japanese maidens and their chaperone to serve tea in Oriental gowns. An adjacent Japanese garden was planted with 1000 Japanese lily bulbs. A Family Park Blair Park was planned as a family park. Park operators widely advertised that they maintained a comfortable park where ladies and children could attend without fear of encountering any “objectionable persons.” No wine or liquor was sold in the park, and a deputy constable was present to keep any “toughs” out of the park. In addition to the Venetian Canal for children, there were swings and see-saws scattered throughout the park and a horse-driven merry-goround. For a small fee, children could also ride donkeys or drive goat carts along the park paths. A Casino in the Park? Future plans called for a casino, possibly three stories high, at the western end of the park. It was to have a large veranda on three sides with easy chairs and refreshments served inside. Trees and shrubs would be cleared to provide vistas of the bay. There is no evidence that the casino was ever built. The next column on Piedmont’s History will explore the balloon ascensions in Blair Park, and the fate of the park. articles.text: On Friday, February 28, Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers was recognized as one of four recipients of the Hometown Hero Award from the San Francisco District Attorney’s Office in celebration of Black History Month. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins honored Bowers and his fellow awardees for their longstanding commitment to the African American community in the Bay Area. Bowers was congratulated for his award by the Piedmont City Council at their March 3 Council Meeting, where he thanked them and described the ceremony as “one of the more meaningful days” in a long career of police work. “As Piedmont’s first African American Chief of Police, your law enforcement career has been nothing short of extraordinary,” said Jenkins while presenting San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins (left) with Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers.
articles.title: Chief Bowers recognized with Hometown Hero Award

articles.text: Since 1968, Beach Elementary School has presented a musical revue. With over 85% of families participating, the Beach Revue is truly a community effort. The Beach community celebrates 55 years of the Revue with this year’s theme of “Runaway Magic.” The audience can expect an exuberant and fun-filled show, featuring many memorable magical worlds presented by Beach students of all ages in full color. Presentations this weekend mark the culmination of a marathon community endeavor of theater, song, dance and fun. “There are dozens and dozens of parents who spend a ton of time on the Beach Revue every year,” said parent volunteer Marty McCall “I’ve been working on it since July. We put our heart and soul into it.” Shows at the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High begin at 6:30 p.m. on Friday, March 7 and Saturday, March 8. The final performance is at 2:00 p.m. on Sunday, March 9. Tickets may be purchased at Piedmont.city/ beachrevue. Tickets are $25 for adults and $15 for students and children. All proceeds benefit Beach Elementary School. Beach School students work on choreography in the school auditorium on January 12 for the Beach Revue.
articles.title: Tickets still available for 55th annual Beach Revue

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council received an update on progress of construction on the Community Pool at their meeting on Monday, March 3. The report stated June 2, 2025 as the completion date for construction, roughly one year later than originally planned. The date does not account for possible further delays due to weather and also does not include a period of four weeks for testing all systems. Key project updates included insulation and drywall on the interiors, solar panel installation, and permanent power turned on by PG&E. Following rains in January and February this year, construction was stalled as workers waited for the site to dry enough to excavate the smaller non-competitive pool. Crews began soil removal on Friday, February 28, and excavation for the activity pool is expected to be completed by the end of March. Once both pools are filled with water, the project will enter a phase known as “commissioning,” when the mechanical, electrical, and building management systems that control the facility are tested to ensure they are working properly. This commissioning process is particularly important for Piedmont’s project, as it is one of the first all-electric municipal pools in California. The first all-electric municipal pool, located in the City of Mountain View, started construction in spring 2022 and had a commissioning process that reportedly took months to complete. An expected opening date for Piedmont’s community pool will not be announced until the commissioning process is underway. Ash Wednesday Prayer By Pastor Jim Hopkins I then turned my face to my Lord God, asking for an answer with prayer and pleading, and with fasting, mourning clothes and ashes. Daniel 9:3 (CEB) Creator of All: As rivers – the Nile in the highlands of Ethiopia, the Amazon in the steep slopes of Peru, the Colorado high in the Rockies, the Sacrament in the melting snows of Mt. Shasta – have a source, we too have a source; our lives begin, as they end, in you. As rivers begin their journeys, they are pristine, pure, unblemished and unpolluted. Over the miles they pick up all kinds of stuff – rocks, sediment, branches, pollutants, ash from forest fires. Yet, rivers still they are. Like rivers we begin our journeys fresh, pure, untainted. Over the days and over the years we pick up all kinds of stuff – prejudices, fears, hates, resentments, wounds. Yet, human still we are. On this Ash Wednesday we pause to consider all the stuff we have picked up. Some of it is helpful. Some of it is not. Some of it is holy. Some of it is not. We confess that we would like some of the stuff to be washed away. We wish we could just let it flow to the sea. Yet, we profess that, smudged though we are, we are human still. Imperfect though we are, we are created in your image. As rivers are created to flow to the sea, we are created to love our neighbors as we love ourselves. No amount of sediment, detritus or pollution can destroy this truth. Ash stained as we are, we are human. We have a source. It is you. We have a guide. It is you. We have a goal. It is you. Amen. All things are from God and through God and for God. May the glory be to God forever. Amen Romans 11:36 (CEB) Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. For more information, see the California Democratic Party website at www.cadem.org Former Piedmont mayor Teddy Gray King was elected on March 3 to represent the 14th Assembly District at the California Democratic Party Convention. Over 30 candidates ran for 14 seats - evenly divided between genders. The leaders in the California Democratic Party help to craft critical policies at the convention and shape the direction of the state Democratic party on numerous public policy issues, which range from education, health care, the environment, and America’s foreign policy. The party is also responsible for voter registration, outreach, mobilization, and getting out the vote. “As a lifelong Democrat, I’m thrilled to represent Alameda County at the state Democratic convention,” King said. “The nation looks to California for thoughtful leadership - for both domestic and foreign policy. Now is the time to build coalitions, listen to common-sense Americans, and bring our special brand of in the light, and I just really think we all felt like it was long overdue,” said Councilmember Long in congratulations of the award. “It is hard to take that acceptance. I do it as a member of an incredible team and an incredible community,” said Bowers. He also thanked the San Francisco District Attorney for providing the space and awareness for such a memorable day. “Brooke Jenkins, the District Attorney in San Francisco, did an outstanding job. Her staff was incredible – incredibly welcoming – and it just shows you again, the leadership, in terms of opening it up across the Bay and having really a regional perspective on it because we’re all in this together,” he said.
articles.title: Teddy King elected to seat at Democratic Party Convention

articles.text: Editor: When I read last week that the Piedmont Walkers went by “to see the disputed 210 address site...with a narrow driveway up the hill”, I was reminded that most people see the narrow “Flagpole” portion of the lot going up the hill as only a driveway. But the reality is that this 11’-0” “Flagpole” slice of land is first and foremost a “pedestrian way” or a “path of travel”. It is the means of egress to Howard Avenue as it provides the only fire exiting system from the proposed condominiums that are over 110’ up the hill on the small Flag portion of the property. I would like Piedmont Post readers to imagine a Flag Lot that has retaining walls on each boundary lot line separating it from a contiguous property. Next, imagine 6-foot high fences without any exit gates or doors in them, built on top of (or next to) these boundary retaining walls. Then, please consider that the proposed paved “Flagpole” slopes up 20% from Howard Avenue and has cross slopes of close to 21% without any Building Code required ramps or stairs in it. Lastly, I would like folks to imagine being trapped on the “Flagpole” portion of the lot when there is a fire on the hill where the condominiums are located. Think about the confusion and panic when people are moving slowly down the steep slope that has no stairs or ramps at the same time the owners of the cars in the 4 car garage are trying to get their vehicles safely down to Howard. At the same time, think about the first responders rushing up this pedestrian way/driveway with hoses to attach to new hydrants on the hill. This project is a recipe for disaster. pages.text: Wednesday, March 5, 2025 3 LETTERS - MAIN The dangers of flag lot at 210 Howard By Bernie Stein Editor: When I read last week that the Piedmont Walkers went by “to see the disputed 210 address site...with a narrow driveway up the hill”, I was reminded that most people see the narrow “Flagpole” portion of the lot going up the hill as only a driveway. But the reality is that this 11’-0” “Flagpole” slice of land is first and foremost a “pedestrian way” or a “path of travel”. It is the means of egress to Howard Avenue as it provides the only fire exiting system from the proposed condominiums that are over 110’ up the hill on the small Flag portion of the property. I would like Piedmont Post readers to imagine a Flag Lot that has retaining walls on each boundary lot line separating it from a contiguous property. Next, imagine 6-foot high fences without any exit gates or doors in them, built on top of (or next to) these boundary retaining walls. Then, please consider that the proposed paved “Flagpole” slopes up 20% from Howard Avenue and has cross slopes of close to 21% without any Building Code required ramps or stairs in it. Lastly, I would like folks to imagine being trapped on the “Flagpole” portion of the lot when there is a fire on the hill where the condominiums are located. Think about the confusion and panic when people are moving slowly down the steep slope that has no stairs or ramps at the same time the owners of the cars in the 4 car garage are trying to get their vehicles safely down to Howard. At the same time, think about the first responders rushing up this pedestrian way/driveway with hoses to attach to new hydrants on the hill. This project is a recipe for disaster. But thank goodness there is the California Building Code and Piedmont Public Works Standard Details to provide building and site health and safety requirements as well as standards for construction which places pedestrian safety before vehicular use on a property. The reality is that after the project’s retaining walls are provided on the Flagpole portion of the 210 Howard lot, I believe the actual paved walking/driving surface between the walls will be between 8’ and 9’ wide, not be the 10’ wide space shown in the applicant’s drawings. It appears that the owner/developer assumed that the neighbors would grant permission to access their properties and build project construction items, such as subsurface geotextile fabric and perforated drain tile (which are shown in the engineer’s structural details) on their properties. By not accounting for these items, only then can the applicant show the pedestrian/vehicular passageway as a 10’ wide space. Piedmont’s own Division 17.54, which the City wrote for SB 9 Lot Splits and Two Unit Housing Developments, requires a minimum 36” wide “path of travel” to any new SB 9 unit from a street. Without getting into the weeds where I identify specific California Building Code divisions and sections, the Building Code considers any walking surface, or “path of travel” with a slope greater than 5%, as a ramp. The developer/owner is showing almost half of the “path of travel”/driveway as having a running slope of 20%. Putting ADA standards aside, the California Building Code requires the construction of either stairs or ramps in the portions of the project’s “path of travel”/driveway where the slope exceeds 5% to allow for a safe, code compliant means of egress to Howard Avenue. Depending on the slope of the ramp, or the number of risers in the stair system, handrails might be required on one or two sides of these egress system components. If a ramp system were to be constructed, in all probability, intermediate landings will be required. Ramps and stairs also may have 4” or 6” high curbs on their edges. So, there is a good chance that the proposed 20% sloping portion of this passageway will have physical elements that prevent a vehicle from going down the “Flagpole” portion. Many Bay Area cities require that the “Flagpole” portion of a Flag Lot have a minimum width of 16’ to 20’ to allow for safe pedestrian and vehicular access at the same time, thus recognizing properties that have sloping terrains. 210 Howard Avenue’s 11’ wide “Flagpole” presents a specific, adverse impact upon its residents health and safety, as well as that of the neighborhood. Short of purchasing land from adjoining neighbors to widen the “Flagpole”, I don’t see a way to mitigate or avoid this specific safety impact. And I don’t think a neighbor will sell a piece of their developed property for this purpose. articles.text: Piedmont City Staff unveiled a new online public record request system at the March 3 City Council meeting, allowing community members to submit, track progress, and review responses to their public records requests entirely online. Use of the online system, called NextRequest, was demonstrated at the meeting by City Clerk Anna Brown. NextRequest is available at piedmont.ca.gov/PRA. The system also allows anyone to view requests and responsive documents submitted by other community members, creating a “one stop shop” for all activities related to public record requests. A demonstration of the system is available on Youtube at https:// www.youtube.com/watch?v=LjKNBPnB-NQ. The platform collects all actions and information related to an individual records request, including clarifying questions and responsive documents, on a single page that can be viewed anytime, by anyone. State law mandates that cities provide records related to operations, activities, and decision-making processes to the public by request within certain timeframes. This can include documents, emails, maps, audio and video recordings, and photographs. Many public records, such as meeting agendas and videos, audited financial statements, and campaign finance reports are already available online. For records not readily available online, the City previously managed requests primarily through email, which could quickly become unwieldy, especially for complex requests. The new system aims to improve the speed, convenience and transparency of public record requests in Piedmont. The launch of NextRequest is part of the City’s ongoing effort to modernize operations, including making more services available online. This is one of several technology upgrade projects planned for 2025, which also include online business licensing and a new City website. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/PublicRecords to learn more about what is considered a public record, and for step-by-step instructions for making a records request. With questions, community members can contact City Clerk Anna Brown at CityClerk@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City unveils online public record request system

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District is accepting nominations for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and have made a difference because of their commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The deadline for nominations is March 14. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, and the winner will be recognized at the May 14 Board of Education meeting, and their good works will be acknowledged. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was the founder of the Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by board member Dewey Watson. Nomination Forms are available in the District Office, by calling Rosalina Barrios, Executive Assistant to the Superintendent, at 594-2614 or via the District website at: Docs.google.com/ document/d/1J92iTb6870oZbIRotoHW8rM3MUmCS8bORuf- 7c1hcCmY/edit?tab=t.0 Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly by Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023) and most recently Sarah Pearson in 2024.

articles.text: I am writing to clear up some misinformation that may be going around regarding the implementation of new programs. At the February 7 Board Study Session, the Board provided direction to staff to pursue the implementation of new programs, including additional courses at the high school (specifically AP Seminar and Vocal Music), world language at the middle school, and additional performing arts at the elementary level along with world language in 5th grade. Ultimately, our goal is to continue to enhance our already outstanding educational programs, and we are grateful for the passage of Measure P, which enables us to advance this goal. At this point in time, we are working with our staff to determine what implementation will look like and a timeline for when new programs can begin. I can appreciate that parents will have many questions about how programs will be implemented and the potential impact of programs. However, we are still in the early stages of program design. We are currently meeting with teachers, administrators, and staff to explore all of the options. Once we have a better idea of program design and a timeline, we will provide an update to families. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School announced that Blue Pinsky, an exceptional 8th-grade student, has successfully passed the regional spelling test and qualified for the upcoming regional spelling bee. This prestigious event will showcase the talents of young spellers from across the region, and Pinsky is excited to compete for a chance to advance to the National Spelling Bee in Washington, D.C. Pinsky demonstrated outstanding dedication and skill during the qualifying rounds, mastering a wide array of challenging vocabulary words. With a passion for language and a commitment to excellence, Pinsky’s hard work has truly paid off, earning a spot among the region’s top spellers. The regional spelling bee is scheduled to take place on Sunday, March 23, and Pinsky will be competing against other talented students for a chance to be one of the top three finishers. The top three spellers from this event will earn the prestigious opportunity to represent the region at the National Spelling Bee in Washington, D.C. “We are incredibly proud of Blue’s accomplishment,” said Karyn Shipp, Principal of Piedmont Middle School. “This achievement reflects not only Blue’s talent but also the supportive environment fostered by our dedicated teachers and staff. We wish Blue the best of luck in the competition.” The entire Piedmont Middle School community is rallying behind Pinsky. Friends, family, and educators are excited to witness this remarkable journey and celebrate Pinsky’s passion for spelling and language.
articles.title: Middle School’s Blue Pinsky advances to Regional Spelling Bee

articles.text: Rewarding tasks motivate us; however, in school students are faced everyday with tasks that are not intrinsically rewarding but still need to be done. To do this requires effort – and effort requires motivation. Research studies show that effort requires the activation of executive functions (e.g. initiating, planning, and sustaining attention). ADHD is associated with dysfunction in the areas of the brain that control executive functions, which results in those with ADHD having a stronger gravitational pull towards a type of cognitive resting state that increases daydreaming or for the mind to be engaged in another task. As a result, for a student to escape from this resting state requires more effort than is typical to shift attention to the task at hand. In other words, a student with ADHD requires more motivation to accomplish tasks that are not intrinsically rewarding such as homework. Many ADHD-related behaviors such as procrastination, inattention, poor planning, and unfinished work are the result of this need for increased motiKids with ADHD can struggle with homework. vation being unfulfilled. By recognizing this brain function, the student can be supported by being given stronger incentives, immediate rewards, and frequent reinforcement to learn optimally. In addition, children with ADHD who are struggling with their ability to accomplish tasks that lack inherent rewards will benefit from prompts and cues redirecting their attention, being asked to repeat back multistep instructions before starting a task, and having a safe environment to ask for directions to be repeated. They also benefit from interventions such as hands-on and arts-integrated lessons that naturally boost the reward (dopamine) systems in the brain. Excitingly, due to the developmental elasticity of the brain, these types of appropriate support and strategies taught by understanding teachers can actually serve to rewire the brain to develop more efficient networks and lead to positive outcomes for those with ADHD. Nancy Rowland is Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at nancy@orindaacademy.org.
articles.title: Adolescent motivation complicated by ADHD

Superintendent Nomination time for Arthur Hecht Volunteer Award Piedmont Unified School District is accepting nominations for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and have made a difference because of their commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The deadline for nominations is March 14. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, and the winner will be recognized at the May 14 Board of Education meeting, and their good works will be acknowledged. We wish Blue the best of luck in the competition.” The entire Piedmont Middle School community is rallying behind Pinsky. Friends, family, and educators are excited to witness this remarkable journey and celebrate Pinsky’s passion for spelling and language. articles.text: On Sunday, February 23, Piedmont’s Circuit Breakers robotics team faced off at the NorCal FTC Championship along with 47 other teams vying to move on to Worlds, the final stage of competition. Half of the teams were there by winning first place at their local tournament, as the Circuit Breakers had. The other half, advancing by winning the award for teams best encompassing the values of the robotics league. The Circuit Breakers, a team composed of middle schoolers, arrived at the NorCal Championship undefeated, but faced stiff competition from the best teams in the Bay Area, largely from Silicon Valley. The tournament started with the Circuit Breakers presenting to the judges about their team, robot, and the journey they took to get there. Then began the actual matches. The Circuit Breakers started out the first two matches with losses against high level teams like Juice (9th in the world in 2024). They won their next match by a hair, as their alliance partner (teams are paired in “alliances” with random teams) showed up to the field three seconds before the match was about to start. They lost their fourth match mostly due to their alliance partner’s robot malfunctioning and scored no points. However, the Circuit Breakers were able to scrape together another win in the next match. They lost their sixth and final match, despite great teamwork, assisting the other team in shuttling them the objects needed to score points. Throughout the competition, they faced mostly high-school teams, many of which have had the same members and been participating in this competition for six straight years. For the Circuit Breakers, a second-year team with mostly new 7th graders, they managed to end the competition with a respectable ranking and proud of their accomplishments. Team members Felix Kansal, Jackson Chu, Kai Snyder, Ethan Grossberg, Theodore Cost, Rory Hull, Jason Zee, and Gabi Stein, with coaches Ben Stein and Jesse Hull and their team banner. Drivers Gabi Stein and Theodore Cost, Coach Felix Kansal, and Human Player Ethan Grossberg await their final score after hanging their robot from the central structure.
articles.title: Circuit Breakers robotic team in NorCal FTC Championship

articles.text: The Califor nia Mobile Museum of Tolerance (MMOT) will be coming to Piedmont schools March 3-7. The Mobile Museum of Tolerance, an initiative of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, is a stateof-the-art traveling museum dedicated to promoting human rights, diversity, and respect. Through interactive and engaging workshops, MMOT challenges participants to confront issues such as intolerance, hate, and discrimination, empowering them to be upstanders in their communities. This is an opportunity for students to experience the impactful work the MMOT is doing to educate and inspire students throughout California. Piedmont middle and high school students will have scheduled visits on the bus while school is in session and we are excited to share that Monday-Wednesday evenings at 6pm and 7pm, greater community members will have the opportunity to experience the powerful workshops as well. Bringing the MMOT to schools is a crucial step in fostering dialogue and understanding among young people. Community presence underscores the importance of this mission and demonstrates a shared commitment to educating future generations on the values of inclusivity and respect. Register at https://tinyurl.com/ MMOTPiedmont. Each session is one hour and can accommodate 30 people. Sessions are free. The Power of Ordinary People Grades 8-12 and older Learning Objectives: This workshop helps participants understand the powerful roles individuals can play in either supporting or opposing hate and violence. This workshop equips participants to recognize their own capacity to be agents of change. Fact or Fiction? (Digital Media Literacy Workshop) Grades 9-12 and older Learning Objectives: This workshop equips participants with skills to critically evaluate digital content for authenticity. This workshop empowers students to become discerning consumers of digital media. More details about the MMOT modules can be found on the mobile museum’s website at www.mmot.com.
articles.title: Mobile Museum of Tolerance visits Piedmont schools now through March 7

Most of all we foster a community.

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School (PMS) Parents Club is now selling tickets for a PMS fundraiser on Thursday, March 27, “Kickin’ It Old Skool.” This is the school’s biggest fundraiser and will take place at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Party-goers will eat, drink, and dance the night away to favorite music from the 80’s and 90’s. The Kickin’ it Old Skool event, formerly known as “March Mingle,” will feature a live auction with special items including a Lake Tahoe vacation rental, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, and sporting event tickets. Old school sneakers like Vans and Keds are recommended. There will also be a raffle and surprises that can be described as “totally radical.” Don’t miss the rare opportunity to relive memories of junior high school days and the culture unique to the era. The event will be co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several Parent Parties, including a Pub Quiz night and Intro to Poker. The PMS Parents Club hopes the parents parties will help raise funds to support school programs. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27, knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Funds will support: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking out a few more Parent Sponsors. Please see Pef. schoolauction.net/marchmingle2025/homepages/show for more details.
articles.title: PMS “Kickin’ It Old Skool” Fundraiser on March 27

pages.text: Wednesday, March 5, 2025 9 Career Day Continued from page 1 two Career Day presentations to attend and had to pick and choose between working adults. The medical field was well represented, as students could choose between hearing from a dermatologist, neurosurgeon, veterinarian or geneticist. Dr. Mark Fedor outlined the pathway to become a pediatric neurosurgeon at Kaiser. Fedor said you have to enjoy the work to become a doctor, after four years at university, four in medical school, seven in residency, doctors then endure what might be the most stressful portion: board exams. “It’s kind of a long road, but it’s worth it,” said Fedor to a full science classroom in the STEAM building. Presenters talked about their career paths, many of which are complex. Jon Essner, a National Security program manager at Lawrence Livermore Labs, switched career paths in 2001 from tech. A student asked Essner for advice on breaking into the current job market. He advised students to diversify their skill set. For example, if pursuing a liberal arts major, consider adding a minor in something technical. Many students asked presenters about the implementation of Artificial Intelligence into their respective fields. Essner talked about a practical application. Some articles in his field would require 2,800 citations; AI could be used to cut down on busy work. David Schleuning delivered a captivating talk on the cutting edge of robotics, and his work on the LiDAR of autonomous Waymo cars. Schleuning admitted the oddity of seeing a car without a driver, but drew a parallel to elevator operators, a job now largely extinct after being commonplace from 1950-1970. Public policy, journalism, graphic design, gaming and architecture were also represented to name a few more categories under review at the impressive event. Parents Alder Yarrow, Kim Hunter, Linda Song Wendel, Sara Ironside and Judy Lin led the event. Shannon Peloquin of McKinsey Consulting, talks with student Elsa Wallway after the presentation. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 5, 2025 HIKING WITH JON Spring waterfall hikes to consider By Jonathan Comeaux The rains from earlier this month have subsided but the impact can still be seen in flowing gulches, streams, and creeks. Winter hiking is the best time to visit the local waterfalls, and The Post has ventured to several in the Bay Area. Here’s a collection of local waterfalls to try: Uvas Canyon, Waterfalls Loop Trail, Morgan Hill In Morgan Hill’s Uvas Canyon County Park are a collection of five accessible waterfalls in 5.2 miles of total hiking. You’ll still require 1,273 feet in elevation gain to see all five in the entire loop—but four of those waterfalls within the first 1.6 miles—making the last long trip to Triple Falls, and optional excursion if you’re worried about tired legs. Cataract Creek, Mt. Tamalpais Watershed The Cataract Falls Trail in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed is a 4.8 out-and-back with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. There are two trailheads, parking on Bolinas Fairfax Road will provide just a 0.5 walk to the first waterfall and another 0.2 to its most famous Helen Markt Falls. Should you walk the entire CataUvas Canyon County Park has five waterfalls to enjoy, including four in the first 1.5 miles. Photo courtesy of AllTrails The waterfall at Murietta Falls in the Dal Valle Regional Wilderness is thriving after snow touched down in the area in late December. Alamere Falls in West Marin is thriving and currently its most active in several years. ract Falls Trail, you will encounter cascades along cataract creek. Murietta Falls, Del Valle Regional Wilderness Murietta Falls in Livermore’s Del Valle Regional Park is considered the highest waterfall in the entire Bay Area at an elevation of near 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness, where a small stream cascades over 100 foot cliff-face—meaning this location should only be taken by experienced hikers looking for a challenge. The entire day required 12.1 miles of hiking and near 5,000 feet in elevation gain; it is considered a good training spot for those interested in Half Dome. Dawn Falls, Mt. Tamalpais We visited Dawn Falls in November, and it was more-so a trickle off a large cliff-face. But fellow hikers online describe its intensity picked up after the rain in the winter months. The walk to the location takes just 1.4 miles at around 500 feet in elevation gain through lush redPhoto courtesy of AllTrails woods. But the walk is popular, we passed 49 people in the trek to Dawn Falls. Alamere Falls, Bolinas The trek to Alamere Falls is a total of 13.6 miles and an elevation gain of 1,811 feet taking the Coastal Trail to the Wildcat Campground. There is a shortcut at 4.5 miles, but it requires scrambling down a steep ravine to the beach and should only be done by experienced hikers who are comfortable with scrambling. articles.text: Piedmont High opens season with strong performance Piedmont High School swim team made a splash in their season opener, securing victories against both Hayward and Bishop O’Dowd in a tri-meet. New head coach Adrien Downey was pleased with the team’s performance, not just in terms of results but also in their camaraderie and focus. “The highlights for me were all about chemistry,” Downey said. “The team did a good job switching it on during warm-ups and psyching each other up. The meet flew by, but our relays and individual racers stayed composed and moved as a team rather than as scattered individuals.” Among the standout performances, Sydney Olson showcased remarkable resilience by competing in back-to-back sprints in the 50 freestyle and 100 butterfly with little rest. “The toughness she showed in keeping up with the fast meet flow stands in for our entire team effort in my eyes,” Downey noted. Tai March-Cunningham and Inaya Majid also stepped up by tackling events outside their comfort zones, demonstrating leadership and team-first attitudes. On the boys’ side, Owen Blanford held on for a thrilling victory in the 100 freestyle, with Nik Costello making a late charge from the outside to secure second place. The junior varsity boys, though a small group, made a big impact with their energy and determination, particularly in relay events. Looking ahead, Coach Downey emphasized the imporOwen Blanford on the blocks Piedmont High School swim coach Adrien Downey tance of adaptability and confidence as the team prepares for tougher competition. “We’ll have a chance to try different events and learn our strengths before heading back into stiffer dual meets. Open-mindedness and belief in ourselves will be key.” Despite losing key swimmers to graduation last season, Downey is confident in the team’s growth. “No one can immediately replace their impact, but our new team members are exactly who we need to keep improving,” he said. Cynthia Wu and Zafar Majid delivered strong individual performances, while Isla McCardell pushed through illness to contribute to key relay races. Additionally, several freshmen made an immediate impact across both varsity and JV, showing versatility and willingness to step up. articles.text: Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg takes a 3-pointer with Piedmont’s student section behind him. He led the team with 33 points against St. Patrick. Piedmont’s No. 1 seeded boys’ basketball team almost battled back for the Division 4 North Coast Section title against No. 11 St. Patrick but fell short of a comeback in a 75-70 loss on Saturday, March 1 at San Leandro High School’s new gym. The Highlanders whittled away a 21 point deficit late in the third quarter to three points but couldn’t take the lead. “I’ve told the guys all year that heart can only get you so far. You can’t spot teams leads, and that’s what we’ve done all year. We don’t come ready and have to battle back. That happened today. But I’m proud of how they battled and how hard they played,” coach Ben Spencer said. Fighting from behind has been a common trend for Piedmont this season. The Highlanders mounted several comebacks this year, including in an overtime win against University on January 11 and a one-point 61-60 victory over San Leandro on January 31. This time, the gap was too far to overtake. “I think it has happened because we’re not locked in enough. If we can build an early lead for ourselves, we can withstand runs from other teams. It’s about how we start the game. We have to get defensive stops and stack them, I think that’s a big factor,” said senior leader Ravi Silverberg. It was one of Silverberg’s highest scoring performances of his high school career with 33 points. “When I saw there were seven minutes left, I thought, ‘I’m going to give it all I’ve got.’ Playing with four fouls, I knew I had to play smarter but still play aggressively without fouling,” Silverberg said. Second-chance points were a big part of the Bruins’ win after nabbing offensive rebounds. “They probably had around 20 second-chance points,” observed Spencer. “If we cleaned up half of those boards, we may have taken the game. Rebounding can be a toughness thing; we didn’t come out tough in that first half,”. But Piedmont’s season isn’t over. With the Finals berth, they Dillon Casey fights for a layup against St. Patrick. clinched a spot in the D4 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed. They play No. 8 Natomas in Sacramento on Tuesday, March 4. Results were not complete by Post time. 75-70 upset by No. 11 St. Patrick St. Patrick opened the game with eight straight points to before Piedmont scored its first basketball when Dillon Casey found Lucian Fang-Ring for a 3-pointer. PHS cut the Bruins’ lead to 17-14 after Casey hit a 3-pointer, but SPSV scored six and allowed two to end the first with a 23-16 advantage. In the second quarter, Casey opened with a pair of baskets to make it 25-20, but St. Patrick then scored five straight to build a 30-20 advantage with 5:50 on the clock. Piedmont chipped away to a five-point deficit at 34-29 when Silverberg converted a pair of free throws but SP scored six of the next seven points to lead 41-30 with 40 seconds left. Casey hit a field goal to make it 41-32 at the half. But PHS went cold in the third. After Silverberg hit a three and Fang-Ring turned a steal into a layup to make it 51-41, the Bruins established its 21-point lead by scoring 12 of the next 13 points including 10 straight. Piedmont began marching down SPSV in the fourth, pulling it to 66-56 with 4:18 left after Silverberg hit a 3-pointer and layup on successive possessions. However, Casey fouled out with 3:52 left, giving SP a 68-56 advantage which extended to 70-57. From there, Piedmont scored nine straight points with threes by Silverberg and Beach Lorin to make it 70-65 with 1:53 left. After a St. Patrick free throw, Lorin converted a layup to make it 71-68 with one minute left— but that was the closest it got. St. Patrick made a layup of its own with 44.8 left, then added a free throw to extend to 74-68. Lorin and Silverberg hit one of two three throws from there, but that was it for Piedmont. Final stats: Silverberg led with 33 points, Casey scored 16, Lorin had six, while Fang-Ring, Brayer, and Cash Panico scored five. Tuesday vs. No. 8 Natomas Piedmont traveled to No. 8 seed Natomas for the first round of the D4 CIF State tournament on Tuesday, March 4. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP With a win on Tuesday, No. 9 Piedmont (15-15 overall) will face the winner of No. 1 Priory or No. 16 Washington on Thursday, March 6.
articles.title: Boys’ Basketball team upset in NCS Finals

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team, the No.1 seed, saw its dream of a third North Coast Section title in four years fell short, losing 2-0 to No. 2 Roseland University Prep in the Div. 4 finals on Saturday, March 1 on a cold and drizzly night at Witter Field. The Knights scored both of their goals in the first half by way of successive corners. In a physical game, Piedmont played 30 minutes with a man-advantage, but still couldn’t find the net. “We just didn’t have enough quality with two set pieces we gave away. We had the numerical advantage and superiority in terms of players positions; we had front four and five at some points. We got frantic and I think the moment got to the boys. But it’s a great learning experience for them and I think the life lessons out of this are huge,” coach Ben Russell said, who is finishing up his first season as head coach. The Highlanders couldn’t replicate its smooth transition play and counter-attacking ability it showed in the early rounds of the playoffs. Bini agreed with Russell that the championship moment psyched some players out. “It got rowdy out there and we got a little rattled; we let the emotions get away from us. It’s tough to see us fall apart like that, but I know it’s a learning moment,” said Bini, a senior and team captain. Roseland’s opening goal came when Piedmont allowed a rolling pass from a corner to the top of the box, leading to a wicked curling shot by Angel Guzman, who scored both of RUP’s goals. Russell would’ve liked to see his team attack the ball to start a counter with the Knights committing a lot of players in the box. “We had the mindset that we’re defending the set piece rather than taking it as a counter-attack pass. Fair play to them, they executed really well. But our mindset needs to be its our counterattack rather than we’re defending their corner. If we can attack the ball instead of following their man, that’s the mindset I want. Obviously it takes time to develop that,” Russell said. Piedmont drew 10 corner kicks on the night, but couldn’t generate a goal on set pieces, This season, PHS has proven to be very productive from set pieces and corners, but it wasn’t the same on Saturday. Piedmont advances to NorCal tourney But Piedmont’s season isn’t over. With the Finals appearance, they clinched a berth in the Division 5 CIF State NorCal tournament as the No. 5 seed. They traveled to No. 4 Orland outside of Chico on Tuesday, March 4, results were not complete by Post time. Staff Photos Harper Mand (35) fights for a corner against Roseland amidst a brief downpour of rain. Gianluca Bini sends a shot against Roseland.

They traveled to No. 4 Orland outside of Chico on Tuesday, March 4, results were not complete by Post time. See Boys’ Soccer on page 29 Dillon Casey fights for a layup against St. Patrick. clinched a spot in the D4 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed. They play No. 8 Natomas in Sacramento on Tuesday, March 4. Results were not complete by Post time. 75-70 upset by No. 11 St. Patrick St. Patrick opened the game with eight straight points to before Piedmont scored its first basketball when Dillon Casey found Lucian Fang-Ring for a 3-pointer. PHS cut the Bruins’ lead to 17-14 after Casey hit a 3-pointer, but SPSV scored six and allowed two to end the first with a 23-16 advantage. In the second quarter, Casey opened with a pair of baskets to make it 25-20, but St. Patrick then scored five straight to build a 30-20 advantage with 5:50 on the clock. Piedmont chipped away to a five-point deficit at 34-29 when Silverberg converted a pair of free throws but SP scored six of the next seven points to lead 41-30 with 40 seconds left. Casey hit a field goal to make it 41-32 at the half. But PHS went cold in the third. After Silverberg hit a three and Fang-Ring turned a steal into a layup to make it 51-41, the Bruins established its 21-point lead by scoring 12 of the next 13 points including 10 straight. Piedmont began marching down SPSV in the fourth, pulling it to 66-56 with 4:18 left after Silverberg hit a 3-pointer and layup on successive possessions. However, Casey fouled out with 3:52 left, giving SP a 68-56 advantage which extended to 70-57. From there, Piedmont scored nine straight points with threes by Silverberg and Beach Lorin to make it 70-65 with 1:53 left. After a St. Patrick free throw, Lorin converted a layup to make it 71-68 with one minute left— but that was the closest it got. St. Patrick made a layup of its own with 44.8 left, then added a free throw to extend to 74-68. Lorin and Silverberg hit one of two three throws from there, but that was it for Piedmont. articles.text: Team now advances to NorCal playoffs Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team, the No.5 seed, solidified itself as a top-five North Coast Section team. On Wednesday, February 26, they beat No. 6 seed Salesian 70-48 in the Open Division’s Fifth-Place Final at Binks Rawlings Gym. The Highlanders never trailed, dominating the boards with 47 total rebounds. Piedmont held a narrow five-point 29-24 lead early in the third quarter and expanded it to 22 by the end of the game. Sophomore Taylor White led the way with 15 rebounds. “We really wanted to focus on rebounds this game and keep Salesian off the boards. In the third quarter, we got things started and it really made a difference. Our energy and ball-movement was really key, we made a lot of cross-court passes to Savannah [Dennig]. We were finding people down low on the block and breaking their press,” White said. It was also a big game for freshman Andrea Martin who had a double-double with 23 points and 11 rebounds despite being in foul trouble. “I thought I wasn’t going to get back in. When I went out, I just thought, ‘Don’t foul.’ Just to calm down and keep my composure. I just left it all on the court tonight,” freshman Andrea Martin said. Also making a strong impression was freshman Savannah Dennig with 18 points. She came off the bench for her strong game. “Knowing where the ball is and IQ on the court is something we really focused on. I don’t think coming off the bench isn’t that bad, it’s a game and we all get to play. We all know we have to put in enough whether you start or not,” Dennig said. Piedmont received the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 CIF State tournament, an impressive feat by a group with four freshmen, a sophomore, and just two juniors and seniors. They faced No. 8 Oakland Tech on Tuesday, March 4—results were not complete by Post time. “I’m really excited for what the season has for us. We just have to keep working, playing hard, executing, and working together,” Martin said. 70-48 blowout of No. 6 Salesian After a close 6-5 start to the game, Piedmont scored 11 and conceded just two to lead 17-7 before Salesian ended the quarter with a free throw. In the second quarter, Salesian inched closer at 22-18 with 4:25 left, but Piedmont rallied from there. PHS scored six straight and added a late free throw to go into halftime holding a 29-20 lead. In the third quarter, Salesian again made things close to trail 29-24 after a pair of baskets, Piedmont answered with 13 of the next 18 points to build a 42-29 lead. PHS ended the third with a 46-35 lead following two straight low post baskets by Dennig. Piedmont continued the outpour in the fourth with Saniyah Johnson hitting an early free throw, then finding Dennig for an assist – 49-35. After a pair of Salesian field goals, PHS scored Staff Photos Taylor White goes in for a layup. She had 15 rebounds against Salesian. Andrea Martin had 23 points and 11 rebounds against Salesian. Briana Webb also had a double-double with 14 points and 10 rebounds.
