articles.text: Piedmont High School’s baseball team is back in action at Humphries Diamond and is starting its season off on a strong note with a pair of wins. They got the season started with a 9-1 win over Salesian in Richmond on Wednesday, February 26 and beat Acalanes 7-5 for their home opener on Friday, February 28. Both wins came against North Coast Section opponents, which will prove vital in North Coast Section’s new seeding system. Salesian is a Division 4 opponent while Acalanes plays in Div. 3 and received a preseason top-10 ranking in the Bay Area. “It just shows you what kind of players we have; they’re not scared of the moment. We have a lot of depth in the lineup and we’re trying to figure out who is going to step up,” coach Eric Olson said. Against Acalanes, Piedmont trailed 5-4 entering the bottom of the sixth inning. With two outs, PHS had the bases loaded after a single by Markos Lagios and walks by Diego Delventhal and Will Parker. That’s when Brandon Dicke hit a hard ground ball to Acalanes’ shortstop and sprinted to force a challenging throw. It proved vital, leading to a throwing error that allowed Lagios and Delventhal to score. “I didn’t even see what happened, I’m just going off of what people told me. It got to a 0-2 count and I thought he had me. We always have the approach to not strike out. I just hit a blooper to the right side and tried to run it out,” Dicke said. The Friday win also featured Will Parker hitting the team’s first home run of the season on a three-run shot to right field. “I was basically hunting the fastball. He threw me a couple of pitches at the beginning and got it to a 2-1 count. He leaked a fastball over the plate and I just turned on it,” Parker said. Delventhal was the winning pitcher after entering in the top of the sixth. The usual infielder struck out the last two batters of the game. “It was stressful for sure, coach threw me in there but I was ready for the moment. They have a lot of good hitters, I just tried to pound the zone with fastballs and curveballs. I trusted Will [Parker] back there to call the right pitches,” Delventhal said. Piedmont has used five different pitchers through its first two games, which is a testament to how the Highlanders will mixand-match to get things done on the mound. With an experienced field of players, the strong point of Piedmont’s team will be its strong bats and dependability of its gloves. “I’ve said we need to play Staff Photos Diego Delventhal celebrates scoring a run. He was the winning pitcher after starting in the field. defense because we’re not going to strike a lot of guys out. The ball is going to be in play, which we love. We know we’re going to hit and play defense, so if we can throw strikes, we’re going to be fine,” Olson said. 7-5 win over Acalanes Acalanes opened the game with one run in the top of the first inning, but Piedmont answered in the bottom half when Parker hit his three-run blast. Before that, Lagios led off with a double and Delventhal drew a four-pitch walk. The Dons scored the next run in the top of the fourth. Brandon Dicke helped bring in the go-ahead run against Acalanes and forcing a difficult throw by the shortstop. Will Parker smacks a three-run homer in the bottom of the first inning.

articles.text: Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg has earned backto-back Athlete of the Month awards. With boys’ basketball, girls’ basketball, and boys’ soccer forging ahead in the North Coast Section playoffs and receiving berths in the CIF State playoffs, we’re awarding Ravi Silverberg of the boys basketball team and Gianluca Bini of boys soccer our boys’ Athlete of the Month, and Jenelle Solis and Andrea Martin of the girls’ basketball team as co-winners of Athlete of the Month. Ravi Silverberg has dominated for the boys’ basketball team. He’s now earned back-toback Athlete of the Month awards after being named our best boys athlete of January. In February, Silverberg carried the way after fellow scorer Dillon Casey suffered an injury at the very end of January. This NCS postseason, Silverberg scored 18 points in Piedmont’s 87-49 win over Ukiah in the first round on February 19, while he put up 25 points in their 78-69 quarterfinals finals win over Bethel on February 22— scoring his 1,000th career point in the process. In their semifinals’ 60-53 win over Windsor on February 26, Silverberg scored 17 points. Gianluca Bini earned one of our Athlete of the Week honors in February, proving vital to the boys’ soccer team’s NCS run in February. This postseason, Bini had one assist in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Justin-Siena in the first round of the D4 playoffs on February 19. In the quarterfinals against No. 9 Urban on February 22, Bini logged two goals and on assist in their 2-0 win. He then scored another brace with two goals in their 2-nil win over San Rafael in the semifinals on February 26. Gianluca Bini earned an Athlete of the Month award for leading the soccer team through the NCS playoffs. Jenelle Solis was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in December and January, now earning the full award. She was recently named the Western Alameda County Conference’s Co-Player of the Year. In February’s NCS postseason, Solis logged 12 points and five assists in their 51-45 loss to No. 4 Cardinal Newman in the NCS Open Division first round on February 20. After that, Solis scored 10 and six assists in Piedmont’s 70-48 win over Salesian for fifth-place in the Open Division on February 26. Freshman Andrea Martin undoubtedly deserves co-honors for Athlete of the Month after her big return to the lineup in February. In Piedmont’s postseason run, Martin logged 10 points and 10 rebounds in their loss to Cardinal Newman. She had a big 23 point, 11 rebound double-double in the Highlanders’ recent win over Salesian. Jenelle Solis earns an Athlete of the Month award for leading the girls’ basketball team and being named WACC Co-Player of the Year. Andrea Martin earns an Athlete of the Month award for logging continuous double-doubles during the post-season.

articles.text: Sam Shelby wins two events Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in two events on Saturday, March 1, traveling to Westmont HS in San Jose for the K-Bell Track and Field Classic, and to Amador Valley in Pleasanton for the Dan Gabor Invitational. It was a strong start if the season for the Highlanders at the K-Bell with the boys’ team finishing second of 24 schools. The girls’ team was 15th of 25, while final team standings were not recorded at the Dan Gabor Invitational. At the K-Bell, Senior Sam Shelby had a monumental run in the 100 meter dash winning the event with a time of 11.05 seconds in a field of 133 runners. His time marked a personal record, shaving .05 off his previous mark. According to online records, Shelby is now just .81 behind Bill Hefter’s 100 meter school record of 10.24 set in 1961. Shelby is now No. 3 All-Time in the 400 meters, just .19 behind Bryan Chiang’s record set in 2008. Shelby also won the 400 meter run with a time of 50.74 against 66 other runners. His time was a four-second personal record, last running the event his sophomore year. “Sam’s a beast, simply put. articles.text: In honor of the 75th anniversary of Children’s Fairyland, the Oakland Museum of California presents “Fairyland @ 75: A Legacy of Magic,” a vibrant retrospective exploring the history, evolution and cultural impact of America’s first storybook-themed amusement park. The exhibit, opening April 4 and on view through December 7, invites visitors to step into nearly eight decades of imagination, creativity and community at an Oakland institution that has shaped generations of childhoods. Museum visitors will discover a timeline of Fairyland’s history tracing the park’s journey from its inception and grand opening in 1950 to today; a “Then & Now” comparison of the attractions and their evolution over the decades; a photo collection of Magic Keys over the years highlighting the design evolution of this iconic Fairyland tradition; and a display of handcrafted miniatures created by local artists depicting scenes fromFairyland’s sets and attractions. Even more features to see at the exhibit include a display of memorabilia featuring rare artifacts, including an original Jolly Trolly car. Families can climb aboard one of Fairyland’s classic attractions and imagine the journey of Fairyland’s past to present. The exhibit opening on April 4 will take place during Friday Nights at OMCA, a vibrant weekly event from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. where visitors can enjoy live music, sample delicious food, participate in hands-on activities and explore the museum’s exhibits into the night. “For 75 years, Fairyland has been a space where children and families escape the ordinary, immerse in imaginative play and bring stories to life,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Children’s Fairyland. “We’re thrilled to partner with another Oakland institution, OMCA, to celebrate Fairyland’s incredible journey and its enduring role in Oakland’s cultural landscape. “A joyful exemplar of Oakland’s vitality, Fairyland has provided delight and wonder to countless East Bay residents and visitors for the past 75 years and counting,” added Lori Fogarty, Oakland Museum CEO. “We are thrilled to host this new installation at OMCA and to partner with our neighbor and beloved cultural anchor.” The Oakland Museum of California (1000 Oak St.) is open 11 a.m. through 5 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday, with later hours for adults on Thursdays 5 p.m. to 8 p.m., and for all on Fridays 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. Tickets (adults $19; seniors $16; youth, students and educators $12; children 12 and under free) and more information are available at museumca.org. “Fairyland @ 75: A Legacy of Magic,” is a vibrant retrospective in celebration of the 75th anniversary of Children’s Fairyland, on view at the Oakland Museum of California April 4 through December 7. ®

articles.text: Impressionism fans, mark your calendars for this one: From Friday, March 21 through July 2026, San Francisco’s Legion of Honor will reunite Claude Monet’s extraordinary group of Venetian paintings. The exhibition will mark the first dedicated exploration of Monet’s luminous Venetian works since their debut in 1912, placing them in context with select paintings from key moments throughout his career, and in dialogue with portrayals of the city by artists such as Canaletto, Édouard Manet, John Singer Sargent, J. M. W. Turner and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. The exhibit will bring together more than 20 of Monet’s Venetian views from public and private collections around the world, including two masterpieces from the collections of the Brooklyn Museum and the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco — The Doge’s Palace and The Grand Canal, Venice. The fact that half of Monet’s Venice paintings are in private collections today makes this project a once-in-a-lifetime experience of the majestic city that inspired one of the most famous artists in the history of Western art. Claude Monet, The Grand Canal, Venice, 1908. From Friday, March 21 through July 2026, San Francisco’s Legion of Honor will reunite Claude Monet’s Venetian paintings for the first time since their debut in 1912. Monet himself once remarked that Venice was “too beautiful to be painted,” and it is perhaps this very beauty, and the city’s fame that has obscured the significance and daring nature of the works he produced there. Often overshadowed by his iconic depictions of the French landscape, Monet’s Venetian works are among the most luminous yet underexplored work of his career. Although Monet visited Venice only once, the city had a profound impact on him. With its fragile beauty and delicate interplay of land and sea, Venice became a site of both formal experimentation and symbolic resonance for the artist. Unlike the bustling, populated scenes of Venetian imagery painted by other artists such as Canaletto, Monet’s Venice is almost uncannily devoid of human presence. His focus was instead on rendering the city’s architecture and canals emerging through and dissolving in the encompassing and unifying color and light that he described as the envelppe. In addition to Monet’s paintings of Venice, the exhibition will present more than a dozen other works created throughout his career that show his lifelong fascination with water and reflections. Paintings from Monet’s time in Normandy, London, and his home at Giverny — including some of his famed water lily canvases — will be on view, drawing connections between the artist’s Venetian experiments and his broader oeuvre. Monet’s trip to Venice was his last major international journey. He returned invigorated, with a new perspective on the water lily paintings he was creating in Giverny. As Monet himself said, “My trip to Venice has had the advantage of making me see my canvases with a better eye.” “In 10 weeks in 1908 Monet captured Venice’s ethereal cityscape in shimmering canvases, creating works unlike anything produced by the centuries of artists who painted the city before him,” described Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Exploring Monet’s alongside other artists’ paintings of Venice deepens our understanding of his innovations in capturing the atmospheric effects of the Venetian lagoon on canvas.” The Legion of Honor (100 34th Ave.) is open 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org, or at the front desk.
articles.title: First exhibit of Monet’s Venice in over 100 years comes to SF

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony, led by Music Director Joseph Young, will continue its 2024–25 Symphonic Series with Spring’s Awakening on Sunday, March 16 at 4:00 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The third of four Symphonic Series performances this season, Spring’s Awakening, a musical commentary on the natural world. This concert will feature Einojuhani Rautavaara’s innovative work Cantus Arcticus, which features recordings of arctic birds; evocative soundscapes.” Berkeley Symphony’s Symphonic Series concludes on June 1 with Triumph, a reflection on the resilience of the human spirit. Gity Razaz’s Methuselah (In Chains of Time), here receiving its Bay Area premiere, evokes ancient bristlecone pines, and rugged South America landscapes come to life in Astor Piazzolla’s fiery Aconcagua, featuring bandoneon player Hanzhi Wang. The program concludes with Dmitri Shostakovich’s Symphony Huang Ruo’s dynamic and introspective Tipping Point, and Robert Schumann’s Symphony No. 1, “Spring,” a jubilant expression of renewal and rebirth. “So many artists, including myself, find inspiration in nature, particularly in Spring,” explained Music Director Joseph Young. “It is a season of boundless energy, renewal, and hope. In this program, three composers capture the excitement, the urgency, and the sheer awesomeness of our natural world in beautiful and Berkeley Symphony conductor Joseph Young. No. 5, a powerful testament to redemption, enduring hope, and triumph over oppression. Subscriptions to Berkeley Symphony are available now. Pianist Utsav Lal and saxophonist George Brooks will fuse Indian classical music and American jazz with contemporary minimalism, crafting innovative new sounds at a concert at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco this Sunday, March 9 at 4 p.m. This extraordinary hybrid concert collaboration will create a genre-defying soundscape that bridges cultures and traditions. The performance will feature a mix of composed and improvised material, inspired by the rich structures of Indian music and American improvisation. Utsav Lal, the acclaimed “Raga Pianist” and Young Steinway Artist, is a visionary Indian pianist and composer who has redefined the role of the piano in Hindustani classical music. With a career spanning two decades, Lal’s soulful renditions of traditional songs have captivated audiences worldwide, with performances at leading venues such as Carnegie Hall, The Kennedy Center, Southbank Centre and NCPA. Blending ancient tradition with innovation, Lal’s unique piano style is influenced by South Indian vocal “Dhrupad” music and artists like The Necks and Thelonious Monk George Brook s is a n award-winning saxophonist and composer renowned for bridging jazz and Indian classical music. He founded influential Indian fusion groups including Summit with Zakir Hussain; Bombay Jazz with Ronu Majumdar and Larry Coryell; Raga Bop Trio with Steve Smith and Prasanna; Kirwani Quartet with Pt. Hariprasad Chaurasia; and Elements with Kala Ramnath and Gwyneth Wentink. Brooks began his jazz studies with Count Basie saxophonist Frank Foster and continued at the New England Conservatory with George Russell, Joe Allard, and Jaki Byard. His journey took him to India, where he studied Indian classical music with Pandit Pran Nath. His albums are considered groundbreaking in the fusion of jazz and Indian classical music. articles.text: The magnificent Vienna Philharmonic returns to Berkeley with three programs of symphonic masterworks with maestro Yannick Nézet-Séguin at the podium, tonight through the Cal Performances 2025 Gala celebration on Friday, March 7. One of the most in-demand conductors in the world, NézetSéguin seems to be everywhere at once. Now at the helm of this orchestra. the Grammy-winner NézetSéguin also leads the Philadelphia Orchestra and the Metropolitan Opera Orchestra, and was musical advisor for the Leonard Bernstein biopic Maestro, for which he also recorded the soundtrack. The March 5 concert matches Mozart’s brilliant Jupiter Symphony with Mahler’s dramatic and ambitious Symphony No. 1. The March 6 performance pairs the sweet lyricism of Franz Schubert’s Symphony No. 4 with Antonín Dvořák’s well-loved New World Symphony, with the orchestra’s brass section featured in the latter work’s haunting slow movement. The final concert in the series on March 7 welcomes esteemed pianist Yefim Bronfman for Richard Strauss’ Ein Heldenleben, Op. 40, and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 3, an intensely dramatic work. “Nézet-Séguin didn’t merely keep time or hold the Philharmonic together; he led them with passion and decisive interpretation …. His finales were so rousing, the audience began to cheer before Nézet-Séguin had even lowered his baton,” wrote the New York Times. Cal Performances Gala This year’s gala, centered around the Philharmonic’s closing night performance on March 7, will feature a cocktail reception at 5:30 p.m. under a grand tent in Lower Sproul Plaza and a 9 p.m. dinner on the stage of the nearby Zellerbach Playhouse. The 2025 Gala dinner is designed by Paul Canales, former chef and owner of the revered East Bay restaurants Duende and Occitania, and former executive chef of Oliveto. Canales, a longtime music fan, ls a friend of composer and MacArthur Fellowship winner John Zorn. International food author Marcella Hazan praised him, writing, “Paul Canales has found and taken unfailing command of what everyone who cooks struggles to discover: the straight road to pure, sincere, deeply satisfying flavor.” Wine for the 2025 Gala is provided by Hess Persson Estates. McCalls Catering & Events, Got Light, Stuart Event Rentals, and Soirée Valet have been engaged to design the event. Following the event Drew Altizer Photography will offer images of it. The honorary chairs and presenting sponsors of the 2025 Gala, Maria Manetti Shrem and Elizabeth Segerstrom, will both be honored with the California Performing Arts Visionary Award at this year’s event. Gordon P. Getty is the 2025 Gala’s Grand Benefactor. Tickets (concert $50-$225; gala $500-$100,000) for these events at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642- 9988. articles.text: Brandee Younger plays new compositions with New Century Chamber Orchestra Tomorrow night through Sunday, March 9 at SFJAZZ, see harpist Brandee Younger present an exciting new set of compositions from her forthcoming album. For this four-night residency at the venue — 7:30 p.m. through Saturday and 7 p.m. on Sunday — Younger will be accompanied by a superb ensemble featuring acclaimed pianist Courtney Bryan and the 19-piece New Century Chamber Orchestra under the direction of bassist, composer and producer Derrick Hodge. SFJAZZ Executive Artistic Director and seven-time Grammy winner Terence Blanchard has said “Brandee Younger is a powerhouse of the harp. Those two words aren’t usually put together. In this case, it speaks to her creative genius and her passion for music.” Carrying on and expanding the tradition of pioneering jazz harpists Dorothy Ashby and Alice Coltrane, Younger made her public debut in 2007 as a grad student at New York University, when saxophonist Ravi Coltrane enlisted the then-23-year-old to participate in a memorial service for his mother Alice. A student of jazz great Jackie McLean, Younger has collaborated with artists from the worlds Tomorrow night through Sunday, March 9 at SFJAZZ, see harpist Brandee Younger present exciting new work with the pianist Courtney Bryan and the New Century Chamber Orchestra. of jazz and hip hop, including Jack DeJohnette, Charlie Haden, Pharoah Sanders, Lauren Hill and Common. In 2021 she released her Impulse! Records debut, Somewhere Different, which earned Younger a Best Instrumental Composition GRAMMY nomination for the track Beautiful is Black, making her the first Black woman nominated for this honor. In 2024, she was the winner of an NAACP Image Award. The New York Times has said of her: “Brandee Younger has almost single-handedly made a persuasive argument for the harp’s role in contemporary jazz.” Rolling Stone has said “Younger’s playing, virtuosic but with a sparkling lightness, invites you to set aside questions of classification, and just savor the sonic finery.” New Orleans native Courtney Bryan is a 2023 MacArthur Fellow and composer-in-residence with Opera Philadelphia. She has composed for orchestras and chamber groups all over the world and collaborated with artists including Kara Lynch, Sharan Strange and Branford Marsalis. Tickets ($25-95) and more details for the shows at SFJAZZ (201 Franklin St.) are available at sfjazz.org, or through the box office at 415-788-7353.

articles.text: The Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No, South African artist William Kentridge’s latest play, will be performed this weekend, Friday through Saturday, March 14–15 at 8 p.m. and Sunday, March 16 at 3 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall. The performances mark Kentridge’s eagerly anticipated return to Berkeley following the success of his production SIBYL. This new work, conceived in collaboration with choral conductor and dancer Nhlanhla Mahlangu and theater maker Phala Ookeditse The Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No, South African artist William Kentridge’s latest play will be performed Friday, March 14 through Sunday at Zellerbach Hall. Phala, is a chamber opera set on a 1941 sea voyage from Marseille to Martinique. The Great Yes, The Great No is rooted in the historic wartime escape from Nazi-occupied Vichy France by the surrealist André Breton, anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss and Cuban artist Wifredo Lam/ It fictionalizes this narrative by adding a colorful cast of historical characters to the passenger list that includes Josephine Baker, Leon Trotsky and Joseph Stalin. Kentridge assembles this menagerie of eccentric thinkers, makers and revolutionaries to make connections between surrealism and the anticolonial Négritude movement, a cultural, political and literary movement founded by a group of African and Caribbean students in Paris in the 1930s who sought to reclaim the value of African culture. Kentridge’s intention in the work is to explore dreamlike, surreal approaches to language and image inspired by both movements. Internationally acclaimed for his visual art, opera and theater productions, Kentridge deploys his signature visual language in the new production, combining animated drawings, video projection, masks, shadow play and bold sculptural costumes with spoken and projected text. Surrealist imagery merges with reallife events and South African choral music, dance and poetry. With its splicing together of recorded events and associative fiction to generate provocative new narratives, Kentridge’s treatment readily opens up to accommodate multiple layers of connection and inquiry about issues that remain urgently significant, including artistic and political critiques of the legacy of colonialism; experiences of political displacement; and what Kentridge terms “the spasms of history”: abrupt moments of personal transformation triggered by the unresolved political events. Rather than offer an “historical reenactment of an event,” The Great Yes, The Great No “becomes a commentary on the themes that were running through the world at that time, as well as contemporary reflections on the historical event,” said Jeremy Geffen, executive and artistic director of Cal Performances. “Though it will be recognizable as a William Kentridge artwork, the style is very different from that of his previous Sibyl,” Geffen added. Because it takes South African artist William Kentridge off from an actual historical event, The Great Yes, The Great No becomes “a much more narrative work, but the Surrealist elements of the piece take you out of the story that it tells in multiple ways … it ventures into absurdity. It’s sometimes difficult to distinguish between what is actual history and what is reflection. There is drama, but there is a lot of humor as well. All of it is so engaging.” Tickets ($43-$130) for this show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642- 9988.
articles.title: The Great Yes, The Great No at Zellerbach Hall March 14-16

Our faculty and staff create an atmosphere where every child can excel — as learners, leaders, and engaged human beings. Our focus is on academic excellence as well as non-violence, acceptance of differences, respect for the environment, and the moral advancement of humanity — so that the children develop an understanding that they have a responsibility to make a difference in the lives of others. At Northern Light, we understand that rigorous academics alone are insufficient to prepare our students for success in a rapidly changing world. Our small class sizes (capped at 20) ensure that students have the opportunity to practice problem solving, collaboration, and inquiry-based learning, while expressing their knowledge in creative and critical ways. At the same time, Northern Light is also deeply committed to social justice, and the importance of developing engaged citizens who, in the words of Paolo Freire, “participate in the transformation of their worlds.” For this reason, social justice lies at the core of Northern Light’s identity. Rosanne Cash Four-time Grammy-winning Rosanne Cash, Johnny Cash’s eldest daughter, is the latest celebrity to support one of Oakland’s hidden gems, the Northern Light School. Past star supporters have included Bonnie Raitt, MC Hammer, Jackson Browne, Bob Weir, and the late baseball all-star Vida Blue. The event will be held at the Oakland Zoo and emceed by renowned actor and activist Peter Coyote. Ticket prices range from $1,000-$3,000 and can be purchased by the general public at tinyurl.com/NLSBenefit. articles.text: The Renegade Orchestra is returning to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, March 8, at 7:00 p.m. Led by conductor Jason Eckl, the orchestra pairs award-winning string musicians with rock-and-roll in a show that encourages the audience to dance and let down their hair. The orchestra mixes top Bay Area string players with a hard-hitting rhythm section to create something that is, in their words, the opposite of elevator music. The strings are a mix of symphony playing, wedding string quartets, Grammy Award winning, Juilliard graduating violins, violas and cellos while the rhythm section consists of a range of players from North Beach jazz musicians to recent college grads. The musicians who take time out of their busy performing schedules to play in the Renegade Orchestra have been entertaining audiences since 2021 with string arrangements of “Purple Haze”, “Bohemian Rhapsody”, “Sweet Home Alabama”, “Enter Sandman” among others. The Bay Area-based rock orchestra came roaring out of lockdown with its first show selling out in Oakland. The group’s second show 24 hours later was at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, playing on the front lawn because of social-distancing rules at the time. “We did one out on the lawn and it went very well, though we couldn’t get the construction to stop initially,” said Eckl, recollecting the orchestra’s first visit to Piedmont. “After a lot of begging, we got everybody to stop jackhammering nearby and all that kind of stuff, and then we did this beautiful outdoor performance on the lawn. We actually haven’t played indoors there yet.” The Renegade Orchestra is coming to Piedmont after performing back-to-back sold out shows – especially impressive considering their difficulty finding a willing venue to play at. “If we call an orchestra venue, the minute they see rock and roll, they get scared. If we call a rock venue, the minute they see orchestra, they get scared. So the hardest part is finding a venue that isn’t afraid of either the orchestra portion or the rock-androll portion,” said Eckl. Tickets are available for $30 at https://bit.ly/RenegadeOrchestra_piedmont or renegadeorchestra.com. The Renegade Orchestra Photo by Frederic Aube

articles.text: Ongoing through March 23 California Watercolor Association California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition — Join us from 11 am to 2 pm on Saturdays and Sundays to celebrate the 85 artists selected by juror Michael Holter, twenty of which will have received awards totaling an estimated $16,000 in cash and sponsor products, as selected by Awards Juror Gary Bukovnik. CWA proudly announces this year’s exhibition, showcasing exceptional watermedia paintings from talented artists around the world. This annual event will be on display from February 15 thru March 23, 2025, free and open to the public as stated above, and of course also viewable when attending other events at PCA. We invite art enthusiasts, collectors, and the community to experience the vibrancy and creativity of watermedia art. Don’t miss this incredible opportunity to view some of the world’s finest works and celebrate the talent of these exceptional artists! Thursday, March 6, 7:00 p.m. Ambroš Duo Concert Founded more than 120 years ago, Sokol SF still celebrates and supports the Czech-Slovak/American community, and here brings us a concert by the renowned mother/ son Ambroš Duo, visiting from the capital city of Prague in the Czech Republic. The concert will feature works by Paganini, Rachmaninov, and Czech composers Dvorák, Janáček, Ježek and Suk, and a piece by John Williams. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” Welcome reception at 6:30, and tickets at https://brownpapertickets.com/e/6556132, or at the door for cash only. By Tony Simons The Renegade Orchestra is returning to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, March 8, at 7:00 p.m. Led by conductor Jason Eckl, the orchestra pairs award-winning string musicians with rock-and-roll in a show that encourages the audience to dance and let down their hair. The orchestra mixes top Bay Area string players with a hard-hitting rhythm section to create something that is, in their words, the opposite of elevator music. The strings are a mix of symphony playing, wedding string quartets, Grammy Award winning, Juilliard graduating violins, violas and cellos while the rhythm section consists of a range of players from North Beach jazz musicians to recent college grads. The musicians who take time out of their busy performing schedules to play in the Renegade Orchestra have been entertaining audiences since 2021 with string arrangements of “Purple Haze”, “Bohemian Rhapsody”, “Sweet Home Alabama”, “Enter Sandman” among others. The Bay Area-based rock orchestra came roaring out of lockdown with its first show selling out in Oakland. The group’s second show 24 hours later was at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, playing on the front lawn because of social-distancing rules at the time. “We did one out on the lawn and it went very well, though we couldn’t get the construction to stop initially,” said Eckl, recollecting the orchestra’s first visit to Piedmont. “After a lot of begging, we got everybody to stop jackhammering nearby and all that kind of stuff, and then we did this beautiful outdoor performance on the lawn. We actually haven’t played indoors there yet.” The Renegade Orchestra is coming to Piedmont after performing back-to-back sold out shows – especially impressive considering their difficulty finding a willing venue to play at. “If we call an orchestra venue, the minute they see rock and roll, they get scared. If we call a rock venue, the minute they see orchestra, they get scared. So the hardest part is finding a venue that isn’t afraid of either the orchestra portion or the rock-androll portion,” said Eckl. Tickets are available for $30 at https://bit.ly/RenegadeOrchestra_piedmont or renegadeorchestra.com. articles.text: Before you watch Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is, in retrospect, two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), having just arrived on his trim 36 foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color, easy-does-it people. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them out and about while embracing an existence far off the grid. Of course, Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45 footer, from Tahiti to San Diego, which is Tami’s hometown. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film, but also something I will avoid mentioning in this review. I’ll say that this is a compellingly entertaining film, especially wellacted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Know that you don’t ever need to have stepped topside on a teak deck to become lost in Adrift. It’s amazing. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on Hulu/Prime/ Apple tv/Fandango. articles.text: Meryl Streep in River Wild River Wild is an engaging, fastpaced adventure-thriller set on a challenging Idaho white water river. The film opens with Gail Hartman (Meryl Streep) preparing to leave with her tween son Roarke (Joseph Mazello) and her husband, Tom Hartman (David Strathairn), packing for their trip west. Gail grew up on the river where she was once a guide, and will act as their principal rower. The getaway trip is clearly a much anticipated and needed family holiday; it’s also a birthday present for Roarke who has heard from his mom all about the roller coaster excitement that awaits him. Arriving, absent Tom, at least initially (he arrives last minute), the family, now including Tom, launches in a typical whitewater raft from a placid starting point. Gail, confident and eager to school her son on the skill sets necessary to navigate the river, takes the oars and so the trip begins. As they drift along, the river current grows stronger and the excitement slowly builds. On their second day, they spot a beached raft and two men on the shore and Gail rows toward the shore to say hello. And it’s at this point in the trip that a tone of tension begins to build. One of the men, Wade (Kevin Bacon), asks Gail if they can follow them on the river, explaining that he and friend are first-timers on the raver and insist they want to attempt a section of the river that is potentially dangerous. What was meant to be a mildly exciting summer holiday trip for the family soon grows in intensity. River Wild features strong performances by Streep and Bacon, as well as Strathairn. It’s a solid thriller. River Wild. Directed by Curtis Hanson. Starring Meryl Streep, Kevin Bacon, David Strathairn. 1 hr., 15 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Netflix/Fandango/Prime/ apple tv. articles.text: To write about Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker is to navigate a minefield of spoilers. Writer-director J.J. Abrams was tasked with telling not only the final chapter of what has been a 42-year, nine-film saga, first brought to the screen in 1977, but he was also asked to neatly tie a knot in an array of plot and genealogical threads. And, of course, it was expected that he would catch lightening in a bottle. Of course. there’s the Star Wars fandom, the meta-audience that will reflexively scrutinize and deconstruct, via social media, every action scene and every brief moment of exposition while simultaneously being pleased and cranky. But taking a step back, it’s impossible not to acknowledge that the Star Wars franchise, in the aggregate, is a work of extraordinary imagination that has, from it first moments, resonated with generations of moviegoers and had a remarkable cultural impact. The long ricocheting narrative is steeped in myth and fable, with trilogies within trilogies and sequels followed by prequels. A family tree, diagramed with all the characters, would be helpful. As well, George Lucas, and a deep bench of writers (well before Disney), gave the film a 17th century look, replete with royalty (lords, highnesses, a princess with ladies-in-waiting, and, of course, the Jedi Knights). For good measure, there were Storm Troopers bedecked in white armor (strangely not black). And there were the commoners (Han Solo and Luke Skywalker to name two), both recruited into what was called the Resistance, prepared to fight against the Dark Side, aka the Evil Empire, led by a malevolent, cadaverous Sith Emperor plus enablers. The tip of the evil spear was the iconic Lord Vader (memorably voiced by James Earl Jones), masked to conceal a deformed visage, his asthmatic inhale forming each ominous baritone comAdam Driver and Daisy Ridley in Star Wars: Episode IX - The Rise of Skywalker

articles.text: William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home The year was 1966 and a Sci Fi series called Star Trek debuted on television, promising to “boldly go where no man has gone before.” Now, more than 50 years later, improbably, Star Trek remains a not forgotten cultural phenomenon. For a time it was not only a television syndication of the original show, but generated books, comics, video games and, for a time, a themed attraction in Las Vegas that drew thousands of what came to be known as “Trekkies.” In other words, Star Trek evolved from those early days in the 60s into a worldwide entertainment juggernaut, resonating with generations of fans, and possessing a cult following wherein hard-core Trekkies perused endless layers of narrative minutiae, characterization and predictive technology. In 1979 the first feature length film was made – Star Trek: The Motion Picture — launching what would become a successful franchise that starred the original multiethnic cast from the television series. Names such as Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Captain Kirk (William Shatner), Lt. Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), and “Bones” McCoy (DeForest Kelley) were a familiar part of our lexicon, as was the phrase, “beam me up.” In fact, NASA named its prototype space shuttle the Enterprise after the fictional starship. Of all the Star Trek films made, including a prequel, perhaps the most accessible is Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, receiving four Oscar nominations. You don’t have to be a Trekkie to enjoy this movie. Though it follows Star Trek III: The Search for Spock, IV easily stands alone. PRESENTS

pages.text: Wednesday, March 5, 2025 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker By Chris Honoré To write about Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker is to navigate a minefield of spoilers. Writer-director J.J. Abrams was tasked with telling not only the final chapter of what has been a 42-year, nine-film saga, first brought to the screen in 1977, but he was also asked to neatly tie a knot in an array of plot and genealogical threads. And, of course, it was expected that he would catch lightening in a bottle. Of course. there’s the Star Wars fandom, the meta-audience that will reflexively scrutinize and deconstruct, via social media, every action scene and every brief moment of exposition while simultaneously being pleased and cranky. But taking a step back, it’s impossible not to acknowledge that the Star Wars franchise, in the aggregate, is a work of extraordinary imagination that has, from it first moments, resonated with generations of moviegoers and had a remarkable cultural impact. The long ricocheting narrative is steeped in myth and fable, with trilogies within trilogies and sequels followed by prequels. A family tree, diagramed with all the characters, would be helpful. As well, George Lucas, and a deep bench of writers (well before Disney), gave the film a 17th century look, replete with royalty (lords, highnesses, a princess with ladies-in-waiting, and, of course, the Jedi Knights). For good measure, there were Storm Troopers bedecked in white armor (strangely not black). And there were the commoners (Han Solo and Luke Skywalker to name two), both recruited into what was called the Resistance, prepared to fight against the Dark Side, aka the Evil Empire, led by a malevolent, cadaverous Sith Emperor plus enablers. The tip of the evil spear was the iconic Lord Vader (memorably voiced by James Earl Jones), masked to conceal a deformed visage, his asthmatic inhale forming each ominous baritone comSee Star Wars IX on page 31 Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home Adam Driver and Daisy Ridley in Star Wars: Episode IX - The Rise of Skywalker William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home By Chris Honoré The year was 1966 and a Sci Fi series called Star Trek debuted on television, promising to “boldly go where no man has gone before.” Now, more than 50 years later, improbably, Star Trek remains a not forgotten cultural phenomenon. For a time it was not only a television syndication of the original show, but generated books, comics, video games and, for a time, a themed attraction in Las Vegas that drew thousands of what came to be known as “Trekkies.” In other words, Star Trek evolved from those early days in the 60s into a worldwide entertainment juggernaut, resonating with generations of fans, and possessing a cult following wherein hard-core Trekkies perused endless layers of narrative minutiae, characterization and predictive technology. In 1979 the first feature length film was made – Star Trek: The Motion Picture — launching what would become a successful franchise that starred the original multiethnic cast from the television series. Names such as Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Captain Kirk (William Shatner), Lt. Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), and “Bones” McCoy (DeForest Kelley) were a familiar part of our lexicon, as was the phrase, “beam me up.” In fact, NASA named its prototype space shuttle the Enterprise after the fictional starship. Of all the Star Trek films made, including a prequel, perhaps the most accessible is Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, receiving four Oscar nominations. You don’t have to be a Trekkie to enjoy this movie. Though it follows Star Trek III: The Search for Spock, IV easily stands alone. articles.text: Classic cars are certainly popular these days. When you go to a museum and see Ferrari and Bugatti cars, it sends shivers through your soul. What do you think of first? Is it the classic style? How about speed and agility? Maybe you’re looking for something that’s beautiful. What about the cost? What do you think of when you see a violin bow? You probably think: “a bow is a bow as a rose is a rose.” Let’s compare classic cars with classic violin bows. There are many similarities. Most people think that a violin bow is just a stick of wood with horse hair between the two ends. You turn a screw at one end to tighten and loosen the horse hair. That’s what most people think. But let me give you something to think about. A violin bow is one of the most astonishing inventions of mankind. It is so cunningly contrived that nothing else can do the work for which it is designed to do. It is a perfect tool. No mathematician, draftsman or craftsman could produce a better tool than the violin bow. It is at the same time unbelievably sensitive to touch. It is truly the work of genius. That genius was a Frenchman named François Tourte. He was to the violin bow what Stradivarius was to the violin – a stupendous genius. What did he do? He designed the violin bow as it is today. And he did this miracle back around 1780 in Paris. Since then, no improvement has been possible. Many great craftsmen have attempted improvements. articles.text: It was one of those winter storms the TV news like to call an “atmospheric river” as my colleague Wayne Marzolf and I drove over the bridge towards Napa. We were headed to one of my favorite wine tastings of the year - the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) at the COPIA Center in Napa on February 1. This year the ZAP organizers had really stepped up their game and had invited some really fine restaurants and chefs to provide food designed to go with Zinfandel. Even with the poor weather the room was packed and full of great aromas and vibrant energy. Zinfandel is not native to California – most ampelographers from UC Davis now believe it came to California from Croatia in the 1800s, but it’s certainly the trademark grape of the state; there was even a bill before the state legislature to declare it the official state wine (the Cabernet and Pinot producers protested). Ninety nine percent of the world’s Zinfandel is grown in California and because there is no French equivalent it is the closest thing we have to a native son. World class Zinfandels are still much less expensive than world class California Cabernets but unfortunately the price is edging upward. Most of the wines listed below retail for between 25 and 50 dollars. These wines can often be found at lower prices at places like the Wine Club in SF or on Wine.com. The wonderful thing about Zinfandel is how versatile it is in pairing with food. It goes great with salmon, steak, burgers, pasta or pizza to say nothing of enjoying a glass all on its own. There were so many old standby producers as well as some new kids on the block that I was excited to meet. The overall quality was extremely high making my job of discerning the best wines very tough. At the end of the day the following wines were the ones that stood out. They are the cream of the crop. • 2021 Seawolf Zinfandel Only one barrel of this Mendocino County micro-Zinfandel was made. The side project for winemakers Jesse and Emma Hall has deep and inviting aromas of tar and earth mingling with red berry fruit and spices. It is fresh and clean with bracing acidity made in a food friendly style. This delicious Zin is worth searching out. • 2022 Miro Zinfandel Bastoni Vineyard Miro Tcholakov who also makes the Trentadue wines is a perennial resident in the top Zinfandel’s circle. This year his Bastoni Vineyard Zin was the standout. The nose is marked by scents of redcurrants and gentle herbal shadings, the palate is full-bodied but taut and juicy, with silky tannins and ample length. • 2023 Perlegos Zinfandel Stampede Vineyard This Lodi based vineyard has given us a wine with a nose of cranberries and blueberries, touches of earth, licorice and orange peel. The palate is medium bodied with dense berry fruits, pleasantly chewy tannins and good freshness on the finish. Excellent effort. • 2023 Once and Future Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard It was not surprising to see Zinfandel master Joel Peterson’s current project Once and Future in the top circle again. He is again producing wine from some of the iconic vineyards that made Ravenswood famous. The Teldeschi Zin jumps out of the glass with aromas of black cherries, A large crowd was on hand for the opening of this year’s ZAP tasting in Napa.

It offers layers of blackberry jam, peach, black pepper and underbrush. The full-bodied palate’s concentrated, mineral-laced fruits are supported by finely grained tannins and refreshing acidity, and it finishes with notable length and elegance. Should improve for a decade in the cellar. Seghesio Winery is a perennial Zin favorite. A large crowd was on hand for the opening of this year’s ZAP tasting in Napa. This year the ZAP tasting was at COPIA in Napa. • 2020 Grgich Hills Zinfandel Miljenko’s Old Vine Deep ruby-purple, this wine explodes on the nose to aromas of boysenberry pie, wildflowers, plums and cinnamon with loads of underlying nuances. The palate is medium to full-bodied and fully fruited with a spicy streak. The frame is juicy and finely grained, and it finishes long and layered. • 2022 Robert Biale Zinfandel Aldo’s Vineyard Napa Valley’s Robert Biale is a perennial Zinfandel superstar. Medium to deep ruby-purple, it has a spicy, layered nose with aromas of nutmeg, black cherries, potpourri and anise. The palate is full-bodied with a firm frame and great freshness, finishing warm and comforting. • 2023 Deauratus Zinfandel Tzabaco Ranchero Vineyard This was a new label to me and the grapes hail from Dry Creek Valley. The wine has a rich perfume of stone fruits and berry jam with notes of cinnamon, earth and floral perfume. The medium to full-bodied palate has well-tempered fruitiness with a pleasant chew, good freshness and a long finish with a hint of warmth. It should thrive for a decade in the cellar. • 2022 Limerick Lane Zinfandel Russian River Valley For years Limerick Lane has been a measuring stick for Russian River Zin. The 2022 features bright cherries, blackberries, dried citrus peel and flowers with accents of dusty earth, exotic spices and stone fruits. Medium-bodied, it’s perfumed in the mouth with soft tannins and mouthwatering acidity. • 2022 St. Amant Zinfandel Mohr-Fry Ranches (Great Value) At $22 this outstanding wine was the best value wine of the tasting. This 100-year-old vineyard in Lodi has produced a wine with aromas of raspberry, tar and earth. These notes give way to blackberries, currants and dried herbs. Medium to full-bodied, it has a spicy character in the mouth, smooth tannins and juicy acidity, finishing long. I would sock this away by the case! • 2021 Bella Zinfandel Maple Vineyards I have written about Bella’s magnificent Zins for many years. The 2021 Maple has a very spicy nose: clove, amaro, eucalyptus and dried herbs with a powerful, flamboyant red and black berry core. Full-bodied, it has firm, chalky tannins and juicy freshness on the savory finish. Try with BBQ or grilled meats. • 2021 Pedroncelli Courage Zinfandel Pedroncelli has been around as long as I have been drinking wine – which is quite a while. They could always be counted on for good value too. The Courage Zinfandel from the Faloni Vineyard in Dry Creek Valley is aged in American oak and has a nose of vanilla, blueberries with leather and black pepper. It is plump and luscious in the mouth finishing long and layered. • 2021 Hendry Zinfandel Blocks 7 & 22 Always dependable Hendry is located at the Carneros end of Napa Valley and benefits from the cooler climate. This bottle is scented with cherries, prunes and spice cake with notions of earth See Wine Corner on page 31

articles.text: Mark your calendars. On the Waterfront, one of the most esteemed of American films, will be playing free to viewers next week at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing a film with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. This month’s offering from 1954 was helmed by Elia Kazan, for whom it won a best director Academy Award. Its compelling story centers on a New Jersey dockworker, Terry Malloy (Marlon Brando), who was an up-and-coming boxer until a vicious local mob boss, Johnny Friendly (Lee J. Cobb), forced him to throw a fight. When a longshoreman is murdered to prevent him from testifying about Friendly’s control of the waterfront, Terry teams up with the dead man’s sister, Edie (Eva Marie Saint), and a streetwise priest, Father Barry (Karl Malden), to testify himself. The scene in which Terry’s older brother Charley (Rod Steiger), tries to dissuade him from speaking up is one the most famous in movie history. It’s the “I coulda been a contender” scene, containing, many have said, the finest example of acting in any American film. It’s heartbreaking. On the Waterfront won numerous awards, including best picture, best actor for Marlon Brando, and best supporting actress for Eva Marie Saint. Leonard Bernstein’s edgy musical score deserved an award, too. On the Waterfront will be screened on Thursday, March 13th, at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is encouraged at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the charming French comedy Amelie, to be screened on April 10th.

February is recognized as Black History Month and it was an opportunity to consider Piedmont’s Black history. The group’s first destination was the Wildwood Avenue former home of the Sidney Dearing family, the first Black family to own a Piedmont house. The group could also later learn about Tom Williamson, who was the first African American student in Piedmont. The walkers went down Magnolia Avenue to 67 Wildwood Avenue and stopped in front of the house where a sad piece of Piedmont’s history was shared. Newspaper articles of the time said Dearing was a successful café owner “whose blood is Indian and white, but sufficient of the black to mark him negro.” Their house was purchased for $10,000 in January 1924 by Dearing’s mother-in-law, who was White. She transferred it to Dearing and his biracial wife. When this was learned, a Piedmont citizens committee offered to buy the home from Dearing for $3,000 more than was paid for it, and he and his family would have to leave the city. Dearing refused. The City said if he didn’t accept their offer, it would start condemnation and eminent domain proceedings so that a supposed extension of Fairview Avenue could be built through to Wildwood Avenue. During this contentious period, a brick was thrown through the window of the Dearing home and a bomb large enough to damage several blocks was found near the home. In May of that year, a crowd of more than 500 people gathered in front of the home and refused to disperse until Dearing agreed to sell the house and leave Piedmont. Dearing finally agreed to accept $25,000, $15,000 of which was for “the surrender of his constitutional rights.” Dearing sold the house in February 1925 and he and his family moved to Oakland. pages.text: Wednesday, March 5, 2025 27 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Piedmont’s racial history It was a warm, sunny, springlike morning last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays group. A large turnout of 54 walkers and two K-9 best friends was on hand. February is recognized as Black History Month and it was an opportunity to consider Piedmont’s Black history. The group’s first destination was the Wildwood Avenue former home of the Sidney Dearing family, the first Black family to own a Piedmont house. The group could also later learn about Tom Williamson, who was the first African American student in Piedmont. The walkers went down Magnolia Avenue to 67 Wildwood Avenue and stopped in front of the house where a sad piece of Piedmont’s history was shared. Newspaper articles of the time said Dearing was a successful café owner “whose blood is Indian and white, but sufficient of the black to mark him negro.” Their house was purchased for $10,000 in January 1924 by Dearing’s mother-in-law, who was White. She transferred it to Dearing and his biracial wife. When this was learned, a Piedmont citizens committee offered to buy the home from Dearing for $3,000 more than was paid for it, and he and his family would have to leave the city. Dearing refused. The City said if he didn’t accept their offer, it would start condemnation and eminent domain proceedings so that a supposed extension of Fairview Avenue could be built through to Wildwood Avenue. During this contentious period, a brick was thrown through the window of the Dearing home and a bomb large enough to damage several blocks was found near the home. The Alameda County sheriff provided protection for the residents, but the Piedmont Chief of police, who as a member of the KKK, did not. In May of that year, a crowd of more than 500 people gathered in front of the home and refused to disperse until Dearing agreed to sell the house and leave Piedmont. Dearing finally agreed to accept $25,000, $15,000 of which was for “the surrender of his constitutional rights.” Dearing sold the house in February 1925 and he and his family moved to Oakland. The Piedmont City Council is developing a Sidney and Irene Dearing Memorial Project in Triangle Park at Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues, across the street Tom Willamson from where the Dearings lived on Wildwood. This project began in May 2022 when the City Council directed the Park Commission to develop recommendations for a memorial. A subcommittee talked with descendants of the Dearings and others to develop a set of guiding project principles. The City has engaged Oakland-based landscape architect Walter Hood to develop memorial designs. The walkers took a group photo in front of the former Dearing and then went to Palm Drive, Wallace Avenue, and past the Wildwood School playground where staff member Mike Carter was getting ready for the noon Tom Willamson high school track photo rush. The group stopped nearby and looked at Witter Field below. A better piece of Piedmont’s Black history was shared, that of Tom Williamson. Walker Nancy Olsen was a 1964 classmate and friend of Tom, and she shared her memories of him. Tom excelled both academically and athletically at Piedmont High, was student body president, and earned letters in football, basketball and track and field. He attended Harvard where he was an All-East defensive back on the football team. He graduated magna cum laude, and was a Rhodes Scholar at the same time as Bill Clinton. He earned his law degree at UC Berkeley in 1974, and had a distinguished legal career marked by public service. Tom died in 2017 at the age of 70 from pancreatic cancer. Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website has an excellent page on Tom, https://www.historyofpiedmont.com/tom. It was then time to go back to the Exedra. The walkers found a steep extension of Requa Road on Wildwood, just past the steps down to Witter Field. The road provides access to four lovely, hidden Requa homes. The Requa extension might be a little like Black History in Piedmont. Many people don’t know about it. Some parts are hard, some parts are beautiful but exploring it can help us get to where we need to be. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on March 16, 2022 The French are proud of the females who are recognized Impressionists. Art historian Henri Focillon, a professor at Académie Beaux Arts, wrote in 1928 that he deemed three women to be serious Impressionists, les trois grandes dames, Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt and Marie Bracquemond. The works of the three females were “revolutionary,” according to Artnet, bringing the feminine sensibility by portraying the real lives of ordinary people. One of the women, the American expat Mary Cassatt, lived most of her life in France and was extraordinarily successful both critically and commercially. Her themes of “mother and child” were universal and insightful forays into women’s inner life. Another of the trio, Marie Bracquemond was a gifted artist who lived “under the thumb” of her artist-husband Félix, the chief saboteur of her art legacy. Their son Pierre later wrote about his parents’ relationship, calling out Felix’s jealousy of his wife’s talent and the successes she enjoyed Balcony, Édouard Manet, 1868. Berthe (left) sat for the artist. Déjeuner sur l’herbe, by Édouard Manet, 1863, the artist’s provocative painting. Berthe at Easel, by Edma Morisot at Salon and the Louvre. They worked together at Havilland, creating porcelain dinnerware and pottery bowls. A 2018 retrospective of Marie’s work reintroduced her to the French public as a major artist. In comparison, the life and work of Berthe Morisot is well known to the French, but The Paris Review noted that Musée D’Orsay’s ushered Berthe Morisot into the collection many decades later than the male artists. The Morisot sisters Édouard Manet was already a cause celebré when Berthe Morisot and her sister Edma were introduced to him by a mutual friend, painter Henri Fantin-Latour who had intimated the sisters were noticeably promising painters. Édouard wrote to Fantin-Latour that, “they’re delightful sisters,” but “what a pity they can’t be men.” He was clearly annoyed by the waste of art training on women. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, March 5, 2025 AMERICANS IN PARIS The Women of French Impressionism By Patricia Forsyth Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on March 16, 2022 The French are proud of the females who are recognized Impressionists. Art historian Henri Focillon, a professor at Académie Beaux Arts, wrote in 1928 that he deemed three women to be serious Impressionists, les trois grandes dames, Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt and Marie Bracquemond. The works of the three females were “revolutionary,” according to Artnet, bringing the feminine sensibility by portraying the real lives of ordinary people. One of the women, the American expat Mary Cassatt, lived most of her life in France and was extraordinarily successful both critically and commercially. Her themes of “mother and child” were universal and insightful forays into women’s inner life. Another of the trio, Marie Bracquemond was a gifted artist who lived “under the thumb” of her artist-husband Félix, the chief saboteur of her art legacy. Their son Pierre later wrote about his parents’ relationship, calling out Felix’s jealousy of his wife’s talent and the successes she enjoyed Balcony, Édouard Manet, 1868. Berthe (left) sat for the artist. Déjeuner sur l’herbe, by Édouard Manet, 1863, the artist’s provocative painting. Berthe at Easel, by Edma Morisot at Salon and the Louvre. They worked together at Havilland, creating porcelain dinnerware and pottery bowls. A 2018 retrospective of Marie’s work reintroduced her to the French public as a major artist. In comparison, the life and work of Berthe Morisot is well known to the French, but The Paris Review noted that Musée D’Orsay’s ushered Berthe Morisot into the collection many decades later than the male artists. The Morisot sisters Édouard Manet was already a cause celebré when Berthe Morisot and her sister Edma were introduced to him by a mutual friend, painter Henri Fantin-Latour who had intimated the sisters were noticeably promising painters. Édouard wrote to Fantin-Latour that, “they’re delightful sisters,” but “what a pity they can’t be men.” He was clearly annoyed by the waste of art training on women. To date, no women had been recognized as serious artists, and yet he was astounded by their confidence and ambition. Edma and Berthe enjoyed all the advantages that the Victorian era could possibly provide. They were intelligent and educated. Their father was an architect in government service and their mother was a distant relative of the rococo Jean-Honoré Fragonard and supported their daughters’ enthusiasm for art instruction. The parents built a studio at home and enlisted A-list artists, especially the Barbizon trailblazer Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot who praised the girls for their quick learning and skills. Berthe qualified for the annual Impressionist exhibition at age 23, and as she matured, she exhibited her work yearly for more than a decade. Her painting style was loose with fast brushwork radiating confidence, but she was shadowed by self-doubt. The year after her older sister Edma married a military officer and moved from Paris, See Americans in Paris on page 32 Woman at her Toilette, by Berthe Morisot, 1875 Eugène with Julie, by Berthe Morisot, 1881.

articles.text: a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: My neighbor was hit by a car today at the corner of Sea View and LaSalle. She was walking her dog and said that it seemed like a car had stopped but then the driver headed into the intersection and hit her. She was taken to Highland Hospital and hopefully it was not something serious. Please keep a watchful eye out when you are out for dog walks. Many of lines on the crosswalks in Piedmont are faded and the City really needs to get out and paint. We need all the help we can get. Growling, –Mark and Tank the Aussie Dear Mark and Tank: I am so sorry that happened. I so hope that your neighbor will be okay and able to regain her strength. I’ve noticed a lot of speeding going on in Piedmont lately. Spring fever? All of us (with or without our canine buddies) must take extra care when crossing anywhere. School children walking to and from school must also be alert and perhaps we need the Police to patrol busy intersections. Word spreads fast when tickets are given. I hope the City can re-paint many of the lines soon before more people are hurt — it seems like the vast majority need to be brightened up so that drivers will remember to stop, and that there is a crosswalk they must pay attention to. I visited the intersection of Sea View and LaSalle and the paint is completely faded. The lines on King by Crocker Park are also faded. By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: My neighbor was hit by a car today at the corner of Sea View and LaSalle. She was walking her dog and said that it seemed like a car had stopped but then the driver headed into the intersection and hit her. She was taken to Highland Hospital and hopefully it was not something serious. Please keep a watchful eye out when you are out for dog walks. Many of lines on the crosswalks in Piedmont are faded and the City really needs to get out and paint. We need all the help we can get. Growling, –Mark and Tank the Aussie Dear Mark and Tank: I am so sorry that happened. I so hope that your neighbor will be okay and able to regain her strength. I’ve noticed a lot of speeding going on in Piedmont lately. Spring fever? All of us (with or without our canine buddies) must take extra care when crossing anywhere. School children walking to and from school must also be alert and perhaps we need the Police to patrol busy intersections. Word spreads fast when tickets are given. I hope the City can re-paint many of the lines soon before more people are hurt — it seems like the vast majority need to be brightened up so that drivers will remember to stop, and that there is a crosswalk they must pay attention to. I visited the intersection of Sea View and LaSalle and the paint is completely faded. The lines on King by Crocker Park are also faded. My sweet Lucy seems to have a cough and is not very energetic. Should I take her to the Vet or just wait it out? Worried, –Cindy and Lucy the Lab Dear Cindy and Lucy: Yes, dogs can get the flu. The symptoms are tricky because they’re similar to other less serious canine respiratory issues. But if your dog has a wet or dry cough, lacks energy, has a fever, loses her appetite, or has a runny nose, take her to the Vet ASAP. Sometimes dog flu can lead to pneumonia and you don’t want to deal with that. You need to see a Vet so you know exactly what she has and how to help her recover. Isolating Lucy from other dogs is also key so that she doesn’t spread it. In this year of one flu after another, don’t wait. Go Dog Go! I still felt that I had enough backstory that allowed me to enjoy what continued to be an epic struggle between good and evil. And though unschooled in plot (at times seeming convoluted) and characters (some aging, some new), I still enjoyed these films as stand-alone installments, each a bridge, however thin, to the next incarnation. The Resistance remained resilient; the Evil Empire ever more venomous; the struggle continued. And so, by the time The Rise of Skywalker arrived, and knowing I had missed some necessary chapters, I expected to be lost in a labyrinth of plot and newbie Resistance fighters, now led by Rey (Daisy Ridley), a fearless Jedi female warrior. Her connection to Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), grandson of Darth Vader (really?)… well, I had no idea what that was all about. But I watched, simply enjoying the wonderful photography, the seamless CGI, and the sustained peril bearing down on an outgunned Resistance. I was surprised to see General Leia (the deceased Carrie Fisher, brought back using previous footage), as well as others I won’t mention. I realized once again that the Star Wars chronicle is an involving, high-tension adventure wrapped in a parable of sorts. To be sure, it is, as a rule, light on exposition; but nevertheless, even as a lapsed fanboy, I decided that it has always qualified as fulsome entertainment, a visual delight, delivered as a grand, heroic poem. Sadly, in its final moments, amounting to a brief denouement, Rey stands alone, looking toward the horizon, watching two suns set. I’m sure watching her as the signature John Williams score surges, there is genuine regret for many. But the Star Wars wish endures: “May the Force be with you.” them to their time. And so they travel back in time, to San Francisco, landing the cloaked Klingon ship in Golden Gate Park. The crew then ventures forth, walking the streets of San Francisco in search of two whales and a nuclear energy source to power the ship. Their time in San Francisco is inspired. The juxtaposition of the crew with the locals makes for some interesting moments. An embedded joke is that even though they are all dressed in Starf leet uniforms (with the exception of Spock, who is wearing a white terry cloth robe and aerobic headband to hide his ears), no one pays them any attention. This is, after all, San Francisco, which is very hip and laid-back. The encounters of the crew with the locals are wonderful, often comedic, and just restrained enough to never slide into parody. There’s also a mild romantic tension (atypical to be sure) between Kirk and a marine biologist, Dr. Gillian Taylor (Catherine Hicks). The conflict in the film stems from the urgency of the hunt. Earth in the future is in peril; time is of the essence. Unlike other Trek films, there are no villains in Voyage Home” – well, perhaps there are, meaning the whalers who have hunted the humpbacks to extinction, a reality that Spock finds “illogical.” But then there is much about the late 20th century San Francisco that Spock finds beyond his understanding. The wine reveals enticing notes of raspberries, kirsch and plums with underlying suggestions of raisins, spice box and fragrant earth. Medium-bodied and opulent in the mouth, it has a plush texture framing the generously spiced black and red fruit preserve layers, with a long and satisfying finish. • 2022 St. Francis Old Vine Zinfandel (Great Value) This wine is also a great value and comes from a variety of old vineyards spread throughout Sonoma County. The wine gives up notes of plums, cranberries and blueberries with touches of dried Provencal herbs and allspice. The decadently fruited, full-bodied palate gives a solid, chewy frame to rein in the boisterous fruit with lovely freshness and a multilayered finish. • 2018 Three Zinfandel Bigelow Vineyard This wine hails from a historic old vine vineyard in Oakley in Contra Costa County. The wine has bombastic aromas of blueberry, cinnamon and underbrush with notes of dried flowers and apricot. The medium-bodied palate gives up explosive red and black fruits with a finely grained frame and fantastic juiciness begging you to come back for another sip. Outstanding effort. • 2021 Capo Creek Zinfandel Eva’s Vineyard The Dry Creek Valley Zin starts with notes of graphite, tar and turned earth. It opens up to luscious scents of cherry jam, fruit cobbler and blueberry preserves with touches of tobacco and eucalyptus. The full-bodied palate is incredibly intense, giving up layer after layer of juicy fruit; it has fine tannins and surprising freshness, finishing very long. • 2022 Tres Sabores Por Que No? This is a fascinating blend of Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Petite Verdot. Medium to deep ruby in color, it has a spicy nose with aromas of pepper, leather, cherries and earth plus notes of grillled meat. Medium-bodied, the palate is juicy and seductive with a comforting round mouth-feel. This well-built wine is delicious now but should last five to seven years in the cellar. articles.text: Dear PUSD Staff & Families: Here we are at the end of February, following a week off. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Recreation Department are facing legal action with plaintiffs seeking to require the City to conduct and implement noise reduction measures at the Linda Beach pickleball courts. A trial date has been set for May 1. The lawsuit deals with the City’s decision to create permanent pickleball courts at the Linda Beach play area without doing any review under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), especially as it pertains to noise impact on residents with homes as close as 30 feet away. Adopted on September 5, 2023, Piedmont City Council approved the dedication and restriping of two Linda Beach Tennis Courts into four courts exclusively for pickleball use. The suit seeks to require the City to implement noise mitigation measures such as noise baffles, noise reducing equipment, possible restriction of hours, and considering alternative locations so that pickleball play can be distributed throughout the city. Neighbors of the area first approached attorney Richard Drury of Lozeau Drury LLP on September 22, 2023, taking issue with the City’s hasty decision. According to the opening trial brief, the sound generated by pickleball is four times louder than that generated by the felt-covered balls used in tennis, with a higher pitch and impulsive quality. This is potentially compounded by the court’s location in a valley, roughly 50 feet below

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) was approved by the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) for a Grants for Arts Projects award of $20,000 last month. Many friends of the choir have been extending their congratulations to PEBCC and their inspiring Artistic Director Eric Tuan. The grant will go to support Echoes of Eureka, a mostly textless choral opera focused on the experiences of Chinese citizens during the Expulsion Acts in the 19th century. The opera, composed by Tuan, will premiere as a part of PEBCC’s Making History Concert this spring on April 12. It will also be performed at a music festival in Eureka in early May. Established by Congress in 1965, the NEA is an independent federal agency and one of the largest funders of the arts and arts education in communities nationwide. “Getting a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts is always a great moment,” said Bob Geary, founding Artistic Director of the choir. “It’s one of the most important things that a composer and an artist can do is to help us experience events or events that are happening, or have happened, that have been covered up or ignored, that have some deeper implications for who we are as human beings and citizens. “The award represents the view, nationally, of the quality of the Piedmont choirs.” The grant-writing process that led to the award was over 18 months in the making and is one of the most sizable grants that the organization has received. “It’s an important story that needs to be told. And we’re very honored to be able to bring this work to life through the support and the recognition by our peers at the national level at the NEA,” said Keri Butkevich, former Executive Director of the choir. The Artist: Eric Tuan Tuan is currently serving his sixth season as the Artistic Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, as well as Eric Tuan at his studio office at PEBCC
