My sister still had school so it was a calm week. When I did go out I played sports with my friends. LETTERS - MAIN More on the problem of 210 Howard Editor: Continuing my discussion of the of 210 Howard Avenue SB 9/ Division 17.54 project, I learned the owner/developer and the City had several meetings and discussions prior to the SB 9/Division 17.54 application submittal, where the owner/developer presented pre-application conceptual dimensioned site plan(s). Typically, at such meetings, Planning Staff will advise a developer that they should make a project application after they got the design correct in terms of safety and health impacts, correct site layouts, proper fire exiting, paths of travel, code compliance, etc. Here, Staff may have also advised the owner/developer that the project would require obtaining neighbors’ permission to access or build on their properties because of the project’s retaining walls on each common property line. Afterwards, the owner/developer submitted their application, perhaps thinking that the neighbors were going to say: “I will gladly grant you permission to come onto my property so that you can construct your out of scale project which may prove to be unsafe, dangerous and might harm my property and house”. Frankly, I don’t understand how this project got so far. This is costing the City money and costing the staff time. This is not right. At 210 Howard, there are many health and safety issues in the current application that would cause a non SB 9/Division 17.54 project to be denied outright, such as code compliance, exiting, means of egress, retaining walls, driveway/walkway, exterior stair, fire issues and the City’s own Division 17.54 “path of travel” provision, etc. On 1/10/2025, the City issued a “Notice of Incompleteness” that accepted the developer’s plans and documents as is, and indicated that certain information needed to be included in the submitted materials in order for City staff to deem the application complete. Several minor clarifications were called out regarding the all-important site plan. Nowhere in this Notice, I believe, is there mention of the need to fix, revise or redesign project site elements that are required to meet standard health and safety standards. Per SB 9/ Division 17.54, the City, within 60 days after deeming the application is complete, will issue an approval or denial of the application based on specific standards. SB 9/Division 17.54 requires that a developer/owner get 2 permits before applying for a Building Permit. The chapter on the Department of Education calls for major changes, most notably: 1) the breakup of the Department of Education with the transfer of most of its programs to other Federal agencies; and 2) providing the option for every parent “to direct his or her child’s share of education funding through an education savings account, funded overwhelming by state and local taxpayers, which would empower parents to choose a set of education options that meet their child’s unique needs.” I spoke to the Piedmont School Board at its February 12 meeting regarding the Project 2025 proposals and the fact that they could have a dramatic impact on public education, most notably in causing decreased enrollment and attendant funding because of the non-public school options that would become economically attractive to Piedmont families with school age children. I made four suggestions to the Board members which were summarized in an email I sent to them the next day and are copied below: 1. If you have not done so already, familiarize yourself with the chapter on the Department of Education from the Project 2025 book. 2. Consider how you will deal with the elimination of the Department of Education (DOE) if/when it happens. 3. articles.text: The City of Piedmont invites residents to complete a brief online survey about their experiences with parking in Piedmont’s Civic Center. Looking ahead to the completion of construction of the new community pool and the city’s 911 dispatch center, the City is conducting a review of public parking on Bonita, Hillside, Highland, Magnolia, and Vista Avenues. When these projects are complete, some parking spaces that had been removed to accommodate construction will become available again. At the same time, the expanded pool facility is expected to draw more visitors to the area. Understanding how community members experience trips to the Civic Center now will provide important context to inform any changes proposed for the future. The short, 9-question survey asks community members to share: • How they generally get to the Civic Center (drive, walk, bicycle) • How long they tend to stay • How easy or difficult it is generally to find parking • How they feel about the current balance of time-limited parking spaces (30 minute, 2 hour) The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ParkingSurvey and will be open through Wednesday, March 12. This comprehensive review follows several years of disruption to historical parking distribution in the Civic Center area, beginning with the construction of the new STEAM building and theater on the Piedmont High School campus, when “Permit A” restrictions were added to existing parking spaces along Magnolia. An additional 57 spaces were lost in 2023 when construction began on the new community pool. Further spaces were removed or redesignated in summer 2024 to accommodate construction on the Police Department’s new 9-1-1 dispatch center. A discussion of parking reconfiguration options in the Civic Center is tentatively scheduled for the March 17 City Council meeting. City staff will present a scenario that maximizes the number of available parking spaces. The Council will provide preliminary guidance to staff for discussion and action later this spring. Survey responses, as well as direct outreach to stakeholders in the area, will provide data to inform this discussion.
articles.title: Piedmont Civic Center parking survey

articles.text: Meet Kendrick, a mellow 3-year-old, 38-pound terrier mix with a striking cow-print coat and natural eyeliner! Kendrick can be a bit shy at first, but staff and volunteers say with a little patience he soon shows his true personality. On a recent field trip from Oakland Animal Services, he was great on leash. He showed no reactivity to dogs, bikes, roller skates, or skateboards that passed by. He enjoyed greeting adults and kids, and was a big fan of ear and muzzle scratches from strangers. With some training, Kendrick could make a great companion for someone looking for a laid-back, loyal friend. He could do well in a home with an appropriately matched dog buddy, or as a solo dog to soak up all the love. articles.text: The Superior Court of Alameda County is seeking residents to serve on the Alameda County Civil Grand Jury. The jury’s primary responsibility is to examine and report on the operations of local government agencies and to investigate citizen complaints, acting as the public’s watchdog. Working as an arm of the Superior Court, the Civil Grand Jury is comprised of 19 citizens authorized to investigate local government to ensure that public agencies are working in the best interests of the public. Its independence gives the Grand Jury a unique role in securing local government accountability and in examining allegations of misconduct. Jury members work to investigate citizen complaints and examine the operations of local government agencies across Alameda County. This work involves reading and analyzing investigative materials, questioning witnesses and writing reports. Serving on the Grand Jury can be a rewarding experience, but also a significant commitment – the jury meets twice a week (Wednesday and Thursday mornings) for a year. Most jurors devote additional time beyond this to their service. Grand jurors are paid $15/day plus mileage and/or public transportation reimbursement. Several Piedmont residents have served on the Grand Jury. Applications for the 2025-2026 term (starting July 1) are due by April 15. To apply, visit the Alameda County Grand Jury website at https://grandjury.acgov.org/ join-us/.
articles.title: Alameda County Grand Jury applications now open

articles.text: The Pardee Home Museum at 672 11th Street in Oakland is hosting a lecture with Richard Schwartz about his new book, The Man Who Lit Lady Liberty, on Sunday, March 16, from 3:00- 5:00 p.m. As the Statue of Liberty stood unlit and unloved by American politicians in 1886, one of her saviors was creating a theatrical sensation at New York’s Fourteenth Street Theatre – Actor M. B. Curtis. As an Actor, producer, real estate developer, promoter, hotelier, benefactor, and murder suspect, Curtis reached the highs of celebrity and fame as well as the lows of failure, illness, and a faltering career. Richard Schwartz’s book The Man Who Lit Lady Liberty rescues his story from the dusty archives of forgotten history and reexamines an actor whose creativity and cultural influence still resonate today. “In this outstanding new biography of that remarkable immigrant thespian M.B. Curtis, Richard Schwartz gives readers a lost episode in the story of the Statue of Liberty and her torch ― that it was Curtis himself who helped pay for Miss Liberty’s first electric lighting bills in November 1886. This is just one of the many absorbing episodes in this biography of one of the most talented character actors of his time,” said Barry Moreno, Historian and author at the Bob Hope Memorial Library at Ellis Island. Richard Schwartz is a historian and the author of Eccentrics, Heroes, and Cutthroats of Old Berkeley, Earthquake Exodus, 1906, Berkeley 1900, and The Circle of Stones. The Man Who Lit Lady Liberty was selected by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Margaret Herrick Library Book cover of Richard Schwartz’s The Man Who Lit Lady Liberty Author Richard Schwartz will host a lecture at the Pardee Home Museum on Sunday, March 16. to be included in their collection. The book was also recently awarded the bronze medal in the 2018 Independent Publisher Book Awards. The lecture will be followed by a question and answer period and a Champagne reception with savory hors d’oeuvres and sweets. Tickets are $25 and all proceeds go to the museum. Attendees can reserve a place as soon as possible by calling Richelle Lieberman (510-381-1973) or booking on Eventbrite at https://pardeehome.us21.list-manage.com/ track/click?u=2ec38cf41e86238fd- 240c454a&id=43335f35e0&e=bb381c4c3e.
articles.title: Pardee Home Museum lecture on rise and fall of actor M.B. Curtis

articles.text: Applications are now open for appointed volunteer positions on six City Commissions or Committees in Piedmont – Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, Civil Service Commission, Park Commission, Planning Commission, Public Safety Committee, and Recreation Commission. Serving in these volunteer positions is an excellent opportunity to learn more about the inner workings of City government. Commissioners help shape City programs, policies and services by providing a valuable resident perspective on upcoming and proposed projects. Applicants can learn more about the work of Commissioners by watching past meetings on the City’s online video archive at https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/kcom-tv/live_content_and_video_archive. Residents can apply online by February 28 at piedmont. ca.gov/Commissioner. Key Dates for Applicants Applicants must be available for a pre-appointment interview with the City Council and a mandatory in-person training at City Hall before assuming their position. • Applications Due: Friday, February 28 5pm • Mandatory interviews: Monday, March 10 (evening) • Required Brown Act Training: Monday, March 31 (evening) • Appointments effective: Tuesday, April 1 (Effective date for Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee appointment is July 1.) For most bodies, members are appointed to 3-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Studies and provides recommendations on annual budget, long-term financial projections, mid-year budget adjustments, and the City’s municipal services tax rate and renewal. Meets as needed Civil Service Commission • 2 Vacancies (1 Incumbent eligible to reapply) Deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. Meets as needed Park Commission • 3 Vacancies (3 Incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to public parks and street trees. Meets monthly on first Wednesdays, 5:30pm. Planning Commission • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to planning and building. Makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. Requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Meets monthly on second Mondays, 5:30pm. Public Safety Committee • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to crime reduction and disaster preparedness. Meets bi-monthly Recreation Commission • 2 Vacancies (1 Incumbent eligible to reapply) Advises on issues regarding recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space and other issues. Meets monthly on third Wednesdays, 7:30pm. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: School districts in California must report a mid-year update of their Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP) before February 28, as required by Senate Bill 114. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich gave the update during the February 12 school board meeting. Of note, Dolowich reported on the progress updating the English Language Arts (ELA) curriculum for elementary students and improved teacher satisfaction with Staff “Professional Development” days. The district is currently in the first year of this three-year LCAP with the following goals prioritized. Goal #1: Creating an Environment to Thrive Goal #2: Investing in Outstanding Academics Goal #3: Partnering Beyond the Classroom Goal #4: Building for Operational Excellence Within Goal #2, Dolowich gave a timeline of the work on the adoption of new elementary level ELA curriculum. The process of switching to either “Benchmark Advance” or “Fishtank Learning” options began in the fall. PUSD, like many other districts, is switching from the curriculum developed by Lucy Calkins, which is now considered outdated. The new curriculum at the three elementary schools will be pilot programs this year. Teachers involved and admin plan to make a recommendation of action by May 7, and plan to seek board approval on May 28. “Previously, the board adopted ‘from phonics to reading [and spellography for]’ K-3,” said Dolowich. “‘Fishtank’ would keep that in place and it would just add a knowledge base, it’s complementary, whereas ‘Benchmark [Advance]’ is comprehensive,” he explained. Dolowich reported a focus on making the district-wide professional development sessions more meaningful. He showed data that this year’s pro-development, with six workshops instead of a keynote speaker, resulted in teachers rating the workdays as helpful in developing a sense of community. “I’m delighted to see the rightward shift in professional development scores,” said Board Vice President Ruchi Medhekar. “I think it’s a testament of how much attention and care you all have taken to put that together.” Dolowich mentioned attendance of the optional, professional development days was paltry when he first arrived in the district, with around 80% of teachers not attending. “The real goal is attendance. What we have seen is more people attending in the last two years,” he said. Board members, student and elected, expressed some apprehension over the results of a portion of the CA Healthy Kids survey which measured student stress. Last year’s data was organized based on how many AP and Honors classes students are taking. PHS student representative to the board Mira Sachs noted that she and her peers took this year’s Healthy Kids survey that same day. “I think a lot of times, they are pretty long tests and ‘I just randomly clicked,’ is sometimes what people say, probably a majority of people take it serious though,” Sachs noted. Board member Max Roman pointed out that language around the words “anxiety” and “worry” in the high school surveys was worth examining. “Some anxiety, I would argue, is good and it gets you to achieve. Do you feel worried? To me it’s a tricky question.” said Roman. Dolowich acknowledged the limitations of surveys and the need for anecdotal feedback and first hand observations to decipher student mental health. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School (PMS) Parents Club is now selling tickets for a PMS fundraiser on Thursday, March 27, “Kickin’ It Old Skool.” This is the school’s biggest fundraiser and will take place at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Party-goers will eat, drink, and dance the night away to favorite music from the 80’s and 90’s. The Kickin’ it Old Skool event, formerly known as “March Mingle,” will feature a live auction with special items including a Lake Tahoe vacation rental, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, and sporting event tickets. Old school sneakers like Vans and Keds are recommended. There will also be a raffle and surprises that can be described as “totally radical.” Don’t miss the rare opportunity to relive memories of junior high school days and the culture unique to the era. The event will be co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several Parent Parties, including a Pub Quiz night and Intro to Poker. The PMS Parents Club hopes the parents parties will help raise funds to support school programs. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27, knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Funds will support: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking out a few more Parent Sponsors. Please see Pef. schoolauction.net/marchmingle2025/homepages/show for more details.
articles.title: PMS “Kickin’ It Old Skool” Fundraiser on March 27

articles.text: Piedmont School Board will meet tonight Wednesday, February 26, in City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. The meeting will be held in a hybrid format, with remote community participation open via Zoom.us/j/89759694815 and it will also be streamed live on KCOM-TV. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s College and Career Center has invited families and students to a Young Professional Panel on Thursday, February 27 in the Alan Harvey Theater from 7:00-9:00 p.m. The following day, Friday, February 28 during the Academy period, students will have access to more than 40 professionals from the community, who will discuss their professions. The speakers will give PHS and MHS students many options to consider. Students can choose to attend any two presentations. Professions represented include neurosurgery, journalism, music, judiciary, and becoming a veterinarian. Career Day speakers include Jonathan Essner talking about national security at Lawrence Livermore Labs, Judge Tom Stevens, David Schleuning describing his work on robotics for Waymo, and Chelsea Sachs discussing her interior design company. Following the presentations students are invited to a Resume Workshop on Friday during lunchtime in Room 24. Led by Stefanie Manalo-LeClair, Director of the College and Career Center, the session offers students assistance in making a resume from scratch or polishing up an existing one. “I’m really excited that the high school is doing this. These sorts of events are so important for our students and their families,” said School Board President Lindsay Thommasson during the last board meeting. Families and students are invited to the panel discussion on Thursday from 7:00-9:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. PHS graduates from 2018- 2020 will share their experiences and insights with PHS Principal David Yoshihara as moderator. A reception with refreshments for speakers and community members concludes the evening. RSVP to Paperlesspost.com/ go/4BQL0ZbhnZVAJ9hVKVow8
articles.title: Career Day and Young Alumni Panel on Feb. 27-28

articles.text: Teens are naturally curious about the world and their place in it. When that curiosity holds a sustained marination around profound questions, it benefits teens in broad and surprising ways. Who am I? What is a good life? How well am I living it? What do I love? What is love? How do I love more? How can I live my best life? Is life about being happy? Am I happy? Why do things happen the way they do? What can I change? Does life have a purpose? What’s mine? Since death alone is certain, and the time of death uncertain, what should I do? What is a human life for? What are the qualities that make my life most worth living? These moments of reflection are not just fleeting thoughts; they are opportunities for growth that can shape their futures in ways many parents may not fully realize. Deep, reflective thinking – or what researchers call transcendent thinking – is when teens engage in abstract and meaningful exploration of their world. This kind of thinking helps them connect the dots between personal experiences, broader societal issues, and complex moral or ethical questions. teens’ development. It activates key brain networks responsible for imagination, empathy, and problem-solving. These networks, like the Default Mode Network, play a significant role in self-awareness and creativity. Teens who engage in transcendent thinking often exhibit: • Greater resilience in the face of adversity. • Increased capacity for empathy and understanding. • Stronger identity formation and self-confidence. • Fosters a stronger sense of self, greater life satisfaction, and healthier relationships. Moreover, this way of thinking physically shapes the brain. Research indicates that when teens reflect deeply on meaningful topics, the connections between brain regions grow stronger, fostering better emotional regulation and decision-making. What can parents do? While schools often focus on rote knowledge and academic achievements, parents can play a pivotal role in fostering an environment that encourages transcendent thinking. Here are a few actionable steps: 1. Invite Open-Ended Questions: Encourage your teen to think critically and share their thoughts. Reference the prior list. 2. articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council is hard at work inventing adventures for its annual Cub Scout Day Camp. Returning to Dracena Park the week after school lets out for the summer, Piedmont Cub Scouts and all youth (1st to 5th graders) will put their creativity to the test with Day Camp’s theme “Invention Convention.” During Day Camp on June 9-13 Piedmont Council will offer a wide range of daily activities including Scout skills, which showcases the Scouting program, sports and games, which get campers running about and staying active, arts and crafts, which challenges creativity, and more. While Day Camp always has new activities, the week will end with a traditional visit by the Piedmont Fire Department to host the traditional egg drop from its 80-foot extension ladder. Camper parents and family are invited to join for a picnic in the park while they watch the eggs fall. Day Camp is planned by a collaborative team of youth from the Council’s five Scout troops and the Community Service crew. The staff leadership team guides campers through all the fun activities they’ve prepared. Returning to oversee Day Camp is the Erin Ashton, in tandem with youth leaders Theo Ferguson and Kajsa Benson. The Council is preparing for a program filled with adventure in Dracena Park, “We’re always excited for Day Camp,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “It brings our youth, both young and old, together for an experience they rarely get. They sing songs, make new friends, work together, and have fun outdoors.” Interested youth can register for Day Camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Community Pass catalog (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). Registration will stay open until the camp is full. Youth interested in joining Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing, or Exploring are encouraged to contact the Piedmont Scout council for more information at 510-844-4752 or contact@piedmontbsa.org. Additionally, you can visit their website at www. piedmontbsa.org, or visit them at the Piedmont Scout Office at 10 Highland Way in Piedmont. The Scout summer day camp opens with a traditional flag ceremony. Staff members and campers hop to it in one of Day Camp’s end of day activities.
articles.title: Piedmont Council to host “Invention Convention” Day Camp

articles.text: Register now for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir summer music camp and sing under the stars with your friends. PEBCC’s popular camp program for singers ages 7-11, Camp Joyful Voices, has added a second week by popular demand and spaces are filling quickly. Designed for young singers, this weeklong sleepaway camp is the perfect opportunity for your child to build confidence, deepen musical skills, and make new friends. With supportive staff and skilled counselors, your singer is sure to make lifelong memories and friendships while nurturing their love for singing. If your kid is always singing in the car and around the house, this is the perfect summer camp for them! Singing in a choir not only helps kids experience the joy and power of making music; it also teaches them teamwork, communication, empathy, and how to be a part of something larger than themselves. Our campers rehearse around 2 to 4 hours a day, grouped into ensembles by age and experience level. All campers participate in small voice classes with vocal experts. Children are encouraged to sing at the lake, on hikes, and around the campfire. Campers can go kayaking and boating, explore the creek bed, make friendship bracelets under a tree, swim, or even encounter a family of deer on the path to breakfast! Singers share cabins, compete for prizes for creative outfits during Spirit Days, and go on hikes to explore nature, watch sunsets, do arts and crafts, and share camp recitals and evening programs. By the time the last day of camp rolls around, the joy and memories are mixed with not wanting to leave. Join us this summer; we can’t wait to sing with you. Camp Dates Session 1: July 21 - July 26 Session 2: July 28 - August 2 Location: Since 2006, Choir Camp is located at Walker Creek Ranch in Marin County: The 1700-acre sleepaway camp site includes forest, chaparral, grassland, 20 miles of hiking trails, and a great 4-acre swimming hole! Cost: $1,775/week – Financial assistance is available. Save your spot now for Camp Joyful Voices: To find out more about Camp Joyful Voices and our other camp programs, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/camp or contact Camp Director Tate Bissinger at tbissinger@piedmontchoirs.org. Campers are excited for the Camp Concert where they show their parents what they learned. Reading the Piedmont Post is also an option at Choir Camp! Campers enjoy creating art and spending time with their new friends.

articles.text: Piedmont educator Chad Hamilton is bringing his beloved Play Ground Sports and Games Camp back for another exciting summer season. As a Havens School teacher and Piedmont native, Hamilton has been nurturing young athletes and fostering community connections through his summer programs for over a decade. “Through my time working A young athlete showcases her skills on the field during Play Ground Sports and Games Camp. The thrill of the chase! Campers dash across the field during an exciting game of Capture the Flag. with children in the competitive sports environment, I saw a need for sports to be inclusive and fun for all, not just the most gifted athletes,” explains Hamilton, who transitioned from teaching third grade to Physical Education at Havens School. “With this in mind, I created Play Ground Sports, where our philosophy is to ‘Build athletes from the (Play) ground up.’” Drawing from his own memories of summers spent in Piedmont’s parks and pools, Hamilton has crafted a program that emphasizes enjoyment over competition. The camp offers a dynamic mix of traditional sports like flag football, basketball, and soccer, alongside creative activities such as Star Wars-themed games, scavenger hunts, and building competitions. What sets this camp apart is its emphasis on unstructured play and personal growth. “It is on the playground that children are allowed to try new things and feel success and failure where there is nothing on the line. No awards, no pressure, and no parents watching,” Hamilton notes. “Play for the sake of play is something that is so often overlooked in youth sports today.” The program is staffed by an enthusiastic team of middle and high school athletes, many of whom are former campers themselves, creating a unique mentorship dynamic. Parents can expect their children to return home pleasantly tired, perhaps a bit dusty, and wearing big smiles – telltale signs of a day well spent in active, engaging play. Featured activities include crowd favorites like dodgeball and capture the flag, alongside innovative team-building exercises and creative games that keep children engaged while developing crucial social and athletic skills. Registration is offered through the Piedmont Recreation Department. For more information follow @play.ground.sports on Instagram or contact Hamilton directly at coachhamiltonofficial@gmail.com. Fun and teamwork take center stage in all activities, where children develop athletic skills through inclusive games. June 2 – August 8 For Grades K-9 ONE WEEK & TWO WEEK CAMPS

articles.text: Piedmont beats No. 9 Urban 4-2 & No. 16 Justin-Siena 2-0 Piedmont celebrates its third goal against Urban. Piedmont High’s No. 1 seeded boys’ soccer team is heading to the Division 4 North Coast Section semifinals. This week at Witter Field they defeated No. 9 Urban 4-2 in the quarterfinals on Saturday, February 22. Previously they shut out No. 16 Justin-Siena 2-0 in the first round on Wednesday, February 19. “It was a great game, back and forth. I’m really happy with the boys,” said first-year coach Ben Russell said following their win over Urban. “They managed to adapt and find different ways to finish things out today. We had some really good goals that we haven’t shown all season,” Their four-goal performance marked the team’s highest since their 10-0 drubbing of league guppies Encinal on January 10. It’s a testament to the Piedmont having a better grasp of Russell’s system, who transitioned the Highlanders from a high-line and heavy press under Todd Sullivan to one who can play opposing offenses into traps and hit them in transition. “Our transition straight away was really good. We went to five in the back and it created some one-on-ones. It’s been a long season and different opponents brings out different moments. We still have some things to work on, but getting the ball to our forStaff Photos wards has been very good,” Russell said. Both Gianluca Bini and Logan Faucher had a pair of goals and assists in the win over Urban, while Jimmy Lagios and Jacques Saldanha had individual assists. Saldanha and Bosco Lorin also scored against Justin-Siena, and Harper Mand and Bini had assists. Faucher scored Piedmont’s second and third goals against Urban. With the game tied in the 55th, Faucher put away a shot from the right side to the far post in a well-worked possession, where Bini found freshman Lagios in the middle of the pitch to lay off one more pass. His second goal was a thing of beauty in the 66th. In the buildup, Jacob Rodriguez found Bini on the outside. On his first-touch, Bini sent a left-footed pass to Faucher a few feet inside the box. Logan took the pass off of his chest and followed through with his right-foot volley into the goal. “That was one of my favorite moments of high school soccer. You can’t really beat that. The first one was a routine play at the back post to go across the keeper. But the second one is probably my pride and joy, I probably won’t do that ever again,” Faucher said. Bini scored the game’s opening goal in the 32nd after SalGianluca Bini had two goals and an assist against Urban, while he also logged an assist on Justin-Siena.

articles.text: 5th straight semifinals appearance for coach Ben Spencer Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team got the job done in its quest for a Division 4 North Coast Section title. In two games last week at Binks Rawlings Gym as the No. 1 seed, Piedmont defeated No. 9 Bethel 78-69 in the quarterfinals on Saturday, February 22 and No. 16 Ukiah 87-49 in the opening round on Wednesday, February 19. The pair of postseason wins sends the Highlanders to the NCS semifinals for the fifth consecutive year. “It should be six if we didn’t have that COVID year with no postseason,” Spencer said. “We were ranked ninth in the Bay Area. It sort of becomes usual that we get hot at the right time and piece things together. Coming into the postseason, we knew we’d be really good. We haven’t had a fully healthy team in 3-4 weeks, which gave other guys more game experience,” he said. Saturday’s win over Bethel also marked a prestigious moment for senior Ravi Silverberg, who scored his 1,000th career point at the end of the second quarter. PHS has had six players reach the achievement during Spencer’s time as coach. “It’s a team reward,” said Silverberg. “I couldn’t have done it without the guys before me. The coaches put me in great position Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg scored his 1,000th career point in Piedmont’s win over Bethel. to succeed and all I have to do is put the ball in the net. It felt great, but I didn’t even know I was close to it. Honestly, the win felt better; I’d rather win games than score points.” Against Bethel, Piedmont clung to a 55-51 lead to start the fourth quarter, and then outscored the Jaguars 23-18 in the final quarter. Sophomore Lucian Fang-Ring had a big game, hitting four 3-pointers in the first half and several key assists in the fourth quarter. “In the beginning of the game, my first shot went in and that built momentum for myself. I just kept shooting and it kept falling. In the second half, I knew I had to help out my teammates, so I just kept passing,” Fang-Ring said. Piedmont will host No. 12 Windsor on Wednesday, February 26 in the semifinals. With a win, the Highlanders will advance to their second straight NCS Final after reaching last year’s Div. 3 title game. A victory will automatically qualify them for the State tournament. Windsor has three common opponents with PHS this season, Gateway, Ukiah and Bethel. Windsor narrowly beat Gateway 59-57 in overtime, which Piedmont dominated 81-54 to start the season on November 30. Windsor also had two close wins over Bethel. If PHS reaches the championship, they will face the winner of No. 2 Middletown vs. No. 11 St. Patrick. 78-69 win over No. 9 Bethel Both teams came out hot in the first quarter with Bethel holding a 26-23 lead through the first quarter, but Piedmont answered in the second quarter to go ahead 43-39 by halftime. PHS held onto a 55-51 lead to start the fourth quarter, but outscored the Jaguars 23-18 in the final going. In the fourth quarter, PHS opened with seven straight points including a layup by P.J. Brayer, Silverberg turned a steal up court to assist Dillon Casey Dillon Casey led scoring with 25 points against Bethel and 24 in the game with Ukiah. Lucian Fang-Ring had a big quarterfinals performance with 17 points, including four 3-pointers in the first half.

articles.text: Piedmont’s top-seeded girls’ soccer team saw its Division 4 North Coast Section postseason come to an end on Saturday, February 22 after falling 2-0 to No. 8 Pinole Valley at Witter Field. PHS couldn’t find the same offensive fluidity as in their 5-1 win over No. 16 College Prep on Wednesday, February 19. “We didn’t do enough to win it tonight. It sort of summarized our season. We’ve had some close games. We didn’t really have any clear chances tonight,” added coach Dan Chubbock. The Highlanders struggled to create dangerous chances against the Spartans, but many passes went too long or were swept up by defenders. “It probably could’ve been a nil-nil type of game,” Chubbock noted. ”We’re just disappointed, especially being the No. 1 seed, but it wasn’t to be. Their center mid was good and their forward was causing us some problems. Their goalie had a good game too,” Both teams remained deadlocked through most of the first half, but Pinole Valley scored the first goal right before halftime at 40+2 minutes. It came when the Spartans sent in a long free kick, allowing the ball to bounce before an attacker pushed it into net. Pinole’s final goal came with about 10 minutes left in the game in the 70th minute on a similar play, where a long free kick was allowed to bounce and fall to an open attacker. Piedmont finished its season with a 7-2-10 (W-T-L) record as it dealt with several key injuries to key players Elsa Wallway, Darcy McKee, Louisa Symkowick, Juliana Thornborrow, Ryo Woltag, and Eliza Hammond. Standout junior Miranda Liu, who was the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year, returned to play against Pinole Valley. “Obviously, the injuries this year held us back. But still, we can’t use it as an excuse. We were the No. 1 seed in Div. 4 and we were fairly ranked. I think we all felt like we could have made a really good run, but we didn’t execute the things we do well,” Chubbock said. Looking ahead, the team will lose 10 seniors to graduation. It could potentially bring back players who earned key minutes, like freshmen Kyla Williams, Teah Suhr and Ayla Blanford, sophomores Wallway and Chloe Toyama, and juniors Elia Kwong, Stephanie Lee, and McKee. No.1 PHS loses 2-0 to No. 8 Pinole Valley In the first half, Kwong had a shot on target in the second minute. Hannah Sullivan then nearly found Woltag from a corner in the 11th minute, but her shot went wide. From there, both teams traded possession without any clear chances until PVHS scored from its long free kick right before halftime. In the second half, Kwong had a shot from atop the penalty area go narrowly wide of the left post in the 45th. Liu had a shot also go wide four minutes later. After several trades of possession, Pinole Valley drew its long free kick that led to their goal. From about 45 yards, they sent in a long pass that was mishandled, falling straight to an attacker for the finishing goal. 5-1 over No. 16 College Prep Williams scored Piedmont’s first goal in the 25th minute when College Prep’s keeper sent a slopped pass to her fullback. Williams pounced on possession, sending in a shot from the left side. College Prep tied the match in the 30th minute, but the Highlanders scored just two minutes later when Thornborrow recovered a ball in the box, launching a shot over the keeper to the far post. Continuing the quick succession of goals, Piedmont was Juliana Thornborrow scored a goal against College Prep. Staff Photos Ryo Woltag had one of Piedmont’s five goals against College Prep.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team returned to toe the line on Saturday, February 22 at the Skyline Invitational, hosted by Skyline HS in Oakland. The Highlanders will have some key athletes missing, like distance runner Xander Schulte-Sasse and girls’ sprinter Breah Bell, but they return a good bulk of talent. “We’re returning 27 of our top 30-point scorers on the boys’ side.” coach Pouyan Assadi said. “Our depth is there and our experience is there. The quantity of rising stars on the boys’ side is fascinating and I’m eager to see who steps up to take the lead. On the girls’ side, the heartbeat of the team is in the 800 and 1600 races,” he added. The 2025 season also marks a return to Witter Field for the track and field team after missing the majority of offseason training last year as Witter Field’s renovation was delayed for nearly one year. Assadi pointed out how the return of their home track has already shown improvement in training and also to limiting injuries. “We are on our own home turf, walking to and from the field from our houses. Our injuries have plummeted and we have access to our weight room. It is so nice to be home,” Assadi said. Skyline results At Saturday’s meet, Piedmont’s boys’ 4x100 relay team won with a time of 44.41 in a close finish with Berkeley and George Washington. Piedmont runners were sophomore Eric Venner, senior Sam Shelby, sophomore Rehan Mumtaz, and junior Maddox Ma. Shelby enters an important season after missing most of 2024 with an injury. Ella Yasar qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in three events last year and is a key returner on the track and field team. Sam Shelby looks ahead to his senior year in track. He helped Piedmont’s 4x100 relay team win at the Skyline Invitational on February 22. “Sam has a chance to rewrite the entire sprinting record book. He’s keen on making an impact this year. He has a lot of opportunities at the collegiate level in football and track. He understands if he puts a nice season together, those opportunities will continue to grow,” Assadi said. Venner and Ma were members of last year’s 4x400 relay team that qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions. Mumtaz is another runner making an impact. With their talent available, Assadi expects Piedmont’s sprinting teams to be among their strong points. “Eric is one of my favorite people to coach because he fully understands what we’re trying to do and he takes it all in. Rehan is also rising with him and Maddox Ma had a substantial PR on the boys’ side on Saturday. That crew is going to do some damage,” Assadi said with a smile. Senior Miguel Long is another key returner. He typically competes in Piedmont’s jumping events and was last year’s leading point scorer for the team. On Saturday, Long competed in three events. He was third in the long jump with a distance of 21 feet, 11 inches; second in the triple jump in 42 feet, 7 inches; and second in the 110-meter hurdles in 16.25 seconds. “Miguel led the team in scoring the previous two years,” Assadi said. Distance runner Sebastien Swain will also make an impact. He’s coming off a strong fall season on the cross-country team, where he qualified for the State Championship in Fresno. At Saturday’s event in Skyline, Swain was second of 57 runners in the 800 meters with a time of 1:59.15. Miguel Long typically competes in the jumping events. He’s another senior on this year’s team. “We all know what Sebastien did as a freshman. Last week, he opened up with a sub two-minute half-mile already,” Assadi said. The girls’ team has some talented distance runners. Sophomores Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray also made headlines last fall for qualifying for the State Championship. “This group of girls’ work ethic is admirable, It’s not a surprise to me that someone like Leighton had a big cross- country season. She’s a heck of a competitor,” Assadi said. Yasar will be a senior leader on the team. She reached last year’s Meet of Champions in three events, the 300-meter hurdles, the 4x100, and 4x400 relay teams. “Ella qualified for the Meet of Champions in three separate events, which is pretty rare to do. With her experience, knowledge, and understanding of my coaching style and the combination of her health, we’re expecting big things from her this year,” Assadi said. Another returner to the field events is thrower Alina Shahid, a senior. At Saturday’s event she was second in the discus with a distance of 85 feet, 7 inches. She also was eighth of 21 in the shot put with 22 feet, 6 inches. With the return of Witter Field, Piedmont will host the first two Western Alameda County Conference Center Meets of the season on March 12 and March 27. NEXT UP Piedmont competes in two events on Saturday, March 1, traveling to the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton, and the K-Bell Track and Field Classic at Westmont HS in San Jose. articles.text: Staff Photos Girls Lacrosse and coach Carlton Chan are back for the 2025 season. Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse returns for the 2025 season as defending Western Alameda County Conference champions. They finished last season with a 14-5 record and reached the second round of the North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seed before losing 9-7 to No. 4 Acalanes. They bring back several key players from last year’s team but will need to fill a void created by the graduation of attacker Ruby Guzdar and middie Hailey Marshburn. “We had really fun players last year and losing them is huge. But the biggest thing for this year is rebuilding out defense. Although it’s a rebuilding year, every year is that way,” said veteran coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont will have experience on its side. Fourteen of its 19 players are seniors. Chan will have senior leaders including Friedie Schickedanz, Chloe Graham, and Luisa Cole, while junior Peyton Watson is another multiyear varsity player. All four players are co-captains this season. “They are outstanding players, so we’re going to be pretty good. This group of girls has played in our system for a while, so they are very familiar with it, but they will have to step up without a Ruby or Hailey to really move the ball,” Chan said. Chan compared this year’s group to the 2019 team that won the D2 NCS title That team relied on their athletic ability to keep teams off balance. “This year, we’re going to go back in time to our 2019 year where there was a lot of cutting and fundamentals. The girls are really good at pick-and-rolls, so we can get a lot of assists. Chloe and Payton also cut really well,” Chan said. Comparing to the 2019 squad, Schickedanz will mirror the school’s All-Time assist leader, Sadie Tschider, who was known for flicking accurate passes to cutters. “We’re looking to get a lot of assists from Friedie. We’re teaching her to be a lot like Sadie, and she’s doing a great job,” Chan said. In goal, senior Sophie Santander steps in as the starter. It allows former goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter to play as a defender on the field. “Sophie Santander is playing tremendous. She was on JV last year and we brought her up,” said Chan. “On the field, Annika is a tremendous player as well. It’s really fun to see her worked into the starting lineup, she earned that spot. She’s transformed into a defender really well.” The Highlanders are looking to compete with Berkeley and Bishop O’Dowd for the league title. Berkeley went 8-10 last year and Piedmont defeated O’Dowd 8-7 in last year’s WACC championship. The Dragons bring back Cornell-commit Lucy Yu, the daughter of former Piedmont High boys’ coach Al Yu. “Not to jinx myself, but we have a lot more returners and better balance than some of the teams. I think Berkeley will be tough and O’Dowd still has Lucy, but they aren’t quite as balanced. I think for our team, everyone can make an impact,” Chan said. Piedmont played its first game of the season on Tuesday, February 25 at Washington in Fremont. They play again at Moreau Catholic in Hayward on February 27 before playing its first home game against Amador Valley the following day, February 28. Friedie Schickedanz is a key player in Piedmont’s attack. Luisa Cole is among this year’s captains.

He was third in the long jump with a distance of 21 feet, 11 inches; second in the triple jump in 42 feet, 7 inches; and second in the 110-meter hurdles in 16.25 seconds. “Miguel led the team in scoring the previous two years,” Assadi said. Distance runner Sebastien Swain will also make an impact. He’s coming off a strong fall season on the cross-country team, where he qualified for the State Championship in Fresno. At Saturday’s event in Skyline, Swain was second of 57 runners in the 800 meters with a time of 1:59.15. Miguel Long typically competes in the jumping events. He’s another senior on this year’s team. “We all know what Sebastien did as a freshman. Last week, he opened up with a sub two-minute half-mile already,” Assadi said. The girls’ team has some talented distance runners. Sophomores Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray also made headlines last fall for qualifying for the State Championship. “This group of girls’ work ethic is admirable, It’s not a surprise to me that someone like Leighton had a big cross- country season. She’s a heck of a competitor,” Assadi said. Yasar will be a senior leader on the team. She reached last year’s Meet of Champions in three events, the 300-meter hurdles, the 4x100, and 4x400 relay teams. “Ella qualified for the Meet of Champions in three separate events, which is pretty rare to do. With her experience, knowledge, and understanding of my coaching style and the combination of her health, we’re expecting big things from her this year,” Assadi said. Another returner to the field events is thrower Alina Shahid, a senior. At Saturday’s event she was second in the discus with a distance of 85 feet, 7 inches. She also was eighth of 21 in the shot put with 22 feet, 6 inches. Girls Lacrosse returns with athletic team Photos by Becky Spies Staff Photos Girls Lacrosse and coach Carlton Chan are back for the 2025 season. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse returns for the 2025 season as defending Western Alameda County Conference champions. They finished last season with a 14-5 record and reached the second round of the North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seed before losing 9-7 to No. 4 Acalanes. They bring back several key players from last year’s team but will need to fill a void created by the graduation of attacker Ruby Guzdar and middie Hailey Marshburn. “We had really fun players last year and losing them is huge. But the biggest thing for this year is rebuilding out defense. Although it’s a rebuilding year, every year is that way,” said veteran coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont will have experience on its side. Fourteen of its 19 players are seniors. Chan will have senior leaders including Friedie Schickedanz, Chloe Graham, and Luisa Cole, while junior Peyton Watson is another multiyear varsity player. All four players are co-captains this season. “They are outstanding players, so we’re going to be pretty good. This group of girls has played in our system for a while, so they are very familiar with it, but they will have to step up without a Ruby or Hailey to really move the ball,” Chan said. Chan compared this year’s group to the 2019 team that won the D2 NCS title That team relied on their athletic ability to keep teams off balance. “This year, we’re going to go back in time to our 2019 year where there was a lot of cutting and fundamentals. The girls are really good at pick-and-rolls, so we can get a lot of assists. Chloe and Payton also cut really well,” Chan said. Comparing to the 2019 squad, Schickedanz will mirror the school’s All-Time assist leader, Sadie Tschider, who was known for flicking accurate passes to cutters. “We’re looking to get a lot of assists from Friedie. We’re teaching her to be a lot like Sadie, and she’s doing a great job,” Chan said. In goal, senior Sophie Santander steps in as the starter. It allows former goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter to play as a defender on the field. “Sophie Santander is playing tremendous. She was on JV last year and we brought her up,” said Chan. “On the field, Annika is a tremendous player as well. It’s really fun to see her worked into the starting lineup, she earned that spot. She’s transformed into a defender really well.” The Highlanders are looking to compete with Berkeley and Bishop O’Dowd for the league title. Berkeley went 8-10 last year and Piedmont defeated O’Dowd 8-7 in last year’s WACC championship. The Dragons bring back Cornell-commit Lucy Yu, the daughter of former Piedmont High boys’ coach Al Yu. “Not to jinx myself, but we have a lot more returners and better balance than some of the teams. I think Berkeley will be tough and O’Dowd still has Lucy, but they aren’t quite as balanced. I think for our team, everyone can make an impact,” Chan said. Piedmont played its first game of the season on Tuesday, February 25 at Washington in Fremont. They play again at Moreau Catholic in Hayward on February 27 before playing its first home game against Amador Valley the following day, February 28. Friedie Schickedanz is a key player in Piedmont’s attack. Luisa Cole is among this year’s captains.

articles.text: Landmark exhibition of China’s Picasso The Asian Art Museum of San Francisco’s is now showing Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink, a landmark exhibition of the renowned Chinese ink painter Qi Baishi (1864–1957), now through April 7. This exhibition marks the 160th anniversary of the artist’s birth and features 42 works on paper lent by the Beijing Fine Art Academy, where Qi served as its first honorary director. This is the first time these works have been presented in the United States. Born during the late Qing Dynasty, Qi was positioned at a unique place in history, living through some of the most transformative shifts in China’s political and cultural history. Despite this changing landscape, the artist’s accessible subject matter and virtuosic style earned him immense respect and popularity, both at home and abroad. In 1960, Qi became the first Chinese artist ever to receive a solo exhibition at the de Young Museum in San Francisco. Sometimes referred to as China’s Picasso, his pieces have achieved record-breaking prices at auctions worldwide — as high as $141 million in 2017 for Twelve Landscape Screens (1925) – underscoring his profound impact on the art market and his status as an international cultural icon. Qi’s legendary career saw the artist rise from humble origins as a peasant carpenter to become one of China’s most revered and best-selling painters. Celebrated for its whimsical approach and technical virtuosity, his works bring to life subjects drawn from the natural world and everyday life. Iconic images of shrimp and crab, among other motifs, reflect his ability to find hidden visual joys and transform the mundane into the magical, resonating with viewers across generations. “Qi Baishi’s technical abilities and expressionistic approach imbue his art with a spiritual quality, inviting viewers to contemplate the deeper significance of everyday motifs,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Barbara and Gerson Bakar Curator of Chinese Art. “His work resonates so widely with audiences because he not only captures his subjects but Flower and Pug Moths, Album of Elaborate Works of Fine Brushwork Insects, No. 1, 1949, Qi Baishi. See the Asian Art Museum’s landmark exhibition of Qi, “China’s Picasso,” the renowned ink painter Qi Baishi, now through April 7. also seeks to express their spirit through calligraphic, spontaneous strokes, something that requires master brushwork.” Considered the most popular painter of 20th-century China, Qi’s semi-abstract, minimalist approach to ink painting not only bridged traditional Chinese ink art with modernist tendencies, but also left a lasting impact on global art movements. He was publicly admired by Picasso and served as an ink art teacher to celebrated Japanese American artist and architect Isamu Noguchi. Today, scholars credit Qi’s combination of mundane subject matter and innovative, multifaceted techniques as having revitalized traditional Chinese ink painting for the modern era. “Qi Baishi’s quotidian subject matter and whimsical, playful style made his art incredibly accessible to audiences at the time, making him the first Chinese painter to capture the attention of American audiences,” said Rob Mintz, Chief Curator at the Asian Art Museum. “His ability to capture the beauty in the ordinary contributed to his growing popularity inside and outside of China, a legacy that continues to thrive today.” In conjunction with the exhibition, visitors will have the opportunity to engage with Qi’s legacy through digital and tactile experiences. Guests can digitally “paint” at a desk at the exhibition that renders their own virtual “brushstrokes” in the style of Qi. Visitors can also take a small piece of the exhibition home with a Letters from the Artist wall, on which guests can find replicas of letters that Qi wrote to his patrons and friends one century ago. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org.

articles.text: De Young opens rare 1963-64 Paul McCartney photo exhibition Paul McCartney. Self-portrait. London, 1963. Paul McCartney Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm presents over 250 personal photos by McCartney, alongside video clips and archival materials, at San Francisco’s de Young Museum this Saturday through July 6. Nearly 60 years after The Beatles performed their final concert at San Francisco’s Candlestick Park, Beatlemania is back in the Bay in a photo exhibit this Saturday, March 31 through July 6. Organized by the National Portrait Gallery of London, and presented exclusively in California at the de Young Museum, Paul McCartney Photographs 1963– 64: Eyes of the Storm will present more than 250 personal photos by Paul McCartney, alongside video clips and archival materials that offer a behind-the-scenes look into the meteoric rise of the world’s most celebrated band. Eyes of the Storm captures a period from December 1963 through February 1964 when The Beatles performed in concert halls across England and in the United States. McCartney’s images reveal the intensity of life on tour as The Beatles were whisked from concerts to hotels, trailed by enthusiastic fans from New York to Miami. Photographs of screaming crowds and paparazzi illustrate the sheer magnitude of the group’s superstardom. In stark contrast, behind-closed-doors images captured by McCartney highlight the humor and individuality of the band members on their days off. Eyes of the Storm invites visitors to witness The Beatles’ journey to stardom, from local venues in Liverpool to the Ed Sullivan Show and worldwide acclaim. McCartney’s photographs of the four band members existed as unprinted negatives and contact sheets for 60 years. Rediscovered in the artist’s personal archive in 2020, these images offer new insight into the band, their fans and the early 1960s, as seen through his eyes. “In this exhibition, we glimpse McCartney both behind and in front of the lens, as he bears witness to a pivotal cultural moment through the camera with a keen artistic eye,” said organizing curator Sally Martin Katz. “From portraiture to landscapes and documentary shots, McCartney demonstrates a deep understanding of the formal styles prevalent in early 1960s photography. Throughout the exhibition, nods to New Wave, documentary filmmaking, and photojournalism underscore McCartney’s multifaceted approach to capturing the spirit of the time,” she added. “In Eyes of the Storm, recently unearthed photographs by McCartney provide a rare time capsule of The Beatles’ world at the moment of their extraordinary rise to fame,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “It is a revelation to discover McCartney’s proficiency as a photographer, documenting everything from the band’s quieter moments and friendships to the ‘Beatlemania’ of the time.” The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive) is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 seniors, $11 students, youth free) are available at famsf.org or at 888-901-6645.

articles.text: The San José Museum of Art announces the opening of the Museum’s first exhibit dedicated to displaying works from its own collection, starting Friday, March 7. Drawing on the Museum’s holdings of over 2,700 works, the inaugural installation Tending and Dreaming: Stories from the Collection will be on view for one year and will include veteran artworks from the collection such as Louise Nevelson’s Sky Cathedral (1957) and Hung Liu’s Resident Alien (1988), as well as recent acquisitions of major artworks by Tishan Hsu, Yolanda López and Sarah Sze, among other artists. Tending and Dreaming will feature paintings, sculptures, photographs, videos, and installations by nearly fifty artists from the Bay Area and beyond. “Since SJMA began collecting art in the 1990s, what began with a regional focus has evolved into a collection that transcends geographic boundaries, tracking the ruptures of the digital age and the complexities of our collective cultural, political, and social struggles and triumphs,” said S. Sayre Batton, Oshman Executive Director at SJMA. “We are thrilled to take the next step in this journey by dedicating permanent gallery space to the stories within our collection,” she added. “By highlighting artists as storytellers, this installation invites visitors to see the Museum not just as a repository of art, but as a dynamic, living space where culture is continually created, interpreted and reimagined.” This marks the first time since the Museum’s collecting program began in 1973 under the guidance of local artists, that dedicated and permanent galleries will showcase the breadth and depth of its holdings. Organized into six thematic groupings, Tending and Dreaming offers visitors a new framework for engaging with the powerful narratives woven through the artworks. The first section considers what it means to be of a place, bringing together artworks that engage local materials such as adobe in the case of performance artist Rafa Esparza and recorded local histories as with interdisciplinary artist Christine Howard Sandoval. The second grouping features artworks that grapple with the stakes of self-making, such as when one migrates to another country as explored by Shilpa Gupta, or by attending to ancestral histories as with the work of Binh Danh. Featuring artists such as Chitra Ganesh, Robert Arneson and Guadalupe Rosales, the third grouping includes artworks that reclaim or disregard dominant perspectives in American culture. The next section explores the connectivity facilitated by technology, such as in Christine Sun Kim’s sound sculpture with recorded lullabies composed in collaboration with an extended network of parent friends, and Martha Atienza’s poetic address to globally rising sea levels. The fifth grouping features a broad range of approaches to engaging the more-than-human world — such as by exploring the cultural continuities of human bodies and land in the case of Laura Aguilar’s photographs, or by attending to the lifespans and intelligences of other organisms as in Gail Wight’s time-lapse video of slime mold. Featuring artworks by Candida Alvarez, Lee Mullican and Harry Powers among others, the final section explores how artists evoke and give form to experiences that are otherwise often unnoticed. The San José Museum of Art (110 South Market Street, San Jose) is open 4 p.m. to 9p.m. Thursdays, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Fridays and 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays. Tickets ($20 general, $15 senior, free for youth 17 and under, free for college students and teachers with ID) are available at sjmusart.org. Drawing on the Museum’s holdings of over 2,700 works including Asawa’s, the San José Museum of Art’s inaugural installation of Tending and Dreaming: Stories from the Collection is on view for one year starting Friday, March 7.
articles.title: San José Museum of Art opens Tending and Dreaming exhibit March 7

articles.text: Left: Anna Ruiz, Institution #2, 2024. Right: If I Give You My Sorrows, dancer Megan Lowe. See The Only Door I Can Open: Women Exposing Prison through Art, an immersive multimedia exhibition co-curated from within prison, at San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts now through June 22. San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts presents a multimedia exhibition exploring the experience of incarcerated women, now through June 22. The exhibition is inspired by a poem by co-curator Tomiekia Johnson, in which she describes her prison bed as “the only door I can open,” while she reflects on her experience of being incarcerated. The Only Door I Can Open: Women Exposing Prison through Art is an immersive multimedia exhibition co-curated from within prison by Johnson and Chantell-Jeannette Black. For the exhibition, Johnson and Black asked eight currently and formerly incarcerated artists to create an artwork that reflects on their relationship to their bed. Within the prison system, a person’s bed is one of the only spaces where they can be alone. For some, the bed is a place of safety and privacy, while for others it is a space of isolation and angst. The exhibition features an array of artworks in diverse media — including murals, paintings and audio narratives — as well as an immersive installation which mirrors a prison cell at Central California Women’s Facility at Chowchilla, where the curators reside. For both Johnson and Black, the exhibition offers a powerful opportunity to encourage visitors to think more deeply about the problematic nature of the prison system itself and take action to enact change. “Prison may be a sentence because of crimes committed, but for those in it, prison is also a state of being,” said Chantell-Jeannette Black. “Art is our platform for human rights, and the outlet through which our voices may be heard. We want viewers to feel inspired to change and grow, to become more than what they were before viewing this artwork.” “I hope that this exhibition allows visitors to picture themselves in my shoes, my bed, on my bunk, feeling the feelings I feel,” said Johnson. “I would like the solution side of people to awaken. I want people to walk away from the exhibit feeling flooded with differing emotions.” “It is important for us to bring our work to where people live, to the neighborhoods and communities that are impacted by the topics we are addressing, and to center the voices of those who are living this experience,” said Jo Kreiter, founder of curation partner company Flyaway Prosponsored by the PEF COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT COMMITTEE Tuesday, March 11 Welcome Reception 5:00 - 6:30 PM $50 per person Piedmont Community Hall Parent Ed Talk 7:30 - 8:30 PM $25 per person Alan Harvey Theater Best Selling Author & PBS Host Wednesday, April 16 7:30 - 9:00 PM Early Bird Tickets: $50 per person Private Piedmont Home

articles.text: Singer-songwriter Martha Redbone leads This Land Is Our Land, a roots music collaboration with the American Patchwork Quartet at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall this Friday, February 28. Roots music singer and songwriter Martha Redbone will lead This Land Is Our Land, a new collaboration between her Martha Redbone Roots Project and the genre-defying American Patchwork Quartet this Friday, February 28 at 8 p.m. at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall. Redbone draws on her heritage as a southeastern Cherokee/ Choctaw and Black American woman to craft songs that celebrate the human spirit, infused with the folk and blues sounds of her childhood in the Appalachian Mountains of Kentucky. Led by Grammy-winning guitarist and vocalist Clay Ross, American Patchwork Quartet is on a self- professed “mission to reclaim the immigrant soul of American roots music.” The ensemble’s repertoire merges folk songs with jazz, country music and sounds from West Africa and Asia, featuring members Falguni Shah (Falu), vocalist; Yasushi Nakamura, bassist; and Clarence Penn, drummer. The Martha Redbone Roots Project consists of Redbone, vocalist and percussionist; Aaron Whitby, pianist and vocalist; Charlie Burnham, violinist and vocalistt; and Fred Cash, bassist and vocalist. The performance continues this season’s Illuminations programming, which explores the idea of “fractured history” through eight performances. Through this series, producer Cal Performances investigates collective memory and the complex evolution of historical narratives to consider what role the performing arts might play in restoring nuance to our understanding of the past, and how that understanding shapes our present and future. For more details for this and other performances in the series, visit calperformances.org/illuminations-2024-25. Tickets ($31-$86) for this show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@ calperformances.org or by phone at 642-9988.
articles.title: Roots musicians at Zellerbach Hall this Friday

articles.text: One of the world’s most distinguished string quartets perform three string quartet pieces at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco this Saturday, March 1. Pro Arte Quartet will perform a contemporary Ukrainian composer’s masterwork along with works by Germaine Tailleferre and Fanny Mendelssohn. The full program features Denys Lytvynenko’s String Quartet No. 2 (2011), Tailleferre’s String Quartet (1919) and Mendelssohn’s String Quartet in E-flat major, H. 277 (1834). Founded by music conservatory students in Brussels in 1912, the Pro Arte Quartet (PAQ) became one of the most celebrated ensembles in Europe in the first half of the twentieth century; in 1932, it was named Court Quartet to Queen Elisabeth of Belgium. Its world reputation blossomed in 1919, when the quartet began the first of many tours that enticed notable composers such as Milhaud, Honegger, Martin and Casella to write new works for the ensemble. Renowned Hungarian composer Béla Bartók dedicated his fourth quartet to PAQ in 1927, and in 1936 PAQ premiered Barber’s Op. 11 quartet with the now-famous Adagio for Strings as its slow movement. PAQ made its New York debut in 1926 and has toured the United States frequently ever since. The quartet was performing in Madison, Wisconsin in May 1940 when Nazi forces invaded Belgium. The University of Wisconsin responded to the emergency by offering the quartet a permanent campus home — the first such arrangement at a major American university. The UW Pro Arte residency became a model of artist residencies, and one now widely emulated throughout the country. The group remains ensemble-in-residence at the UW-Madison School of Music and resident quartet of the on-campus Chazen Museum of Art, performing regularly on the concert series of both institutions. The quartet has performed at the White House and, during its 2012 centennial celebration — being the world’s only quartet to celebrate a centennial — played for the King’s Counselor in Belgium. Suffice all this to say, this is not a show to be missed. The in-person portion of this event will take place at Old First Presbyterian Church (1751 Sacramento Street, San Francisco). Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $10 students with ID, 12 and under free) are available at oldfirstconcerts.org. articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company has announced the program for its fourth Dancing Moons Festival on May 4, an annual celebration of Asian American and Pacific Islander artists. This year the company premieres a major new work inspired by the lives of detainees at Angel Island, the United States’ main immigration facility on the West Coast from 1910 to 1940. In collaboration with the Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation and Angel Island Parks and Recreation, the Angel Island Project features the work of seven choreographers, including Natasha Adorlee, Phil Chan, Lawrence Chen, Feng Ye, Elaine Kudo, Ashley Thopiah, and Wei Wang. In advance of the premiere at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland, on Sunday, May 4, Oakland Ballet Company will present an introduction to the Angel Island Project at the Angel Island Immigration Station. This hour-long event will include a short lecture by Ed Tepporn, executive director of the Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation, on the history of the station, followed by a preview performance of the Angel Island Project and a brief Q&A session with the artists. This preview event will take place on the final two Saturdays in March: March 22 and 29 at 12:45 p.m. Due to the constraints of the site, audiences are limited to 70 people. Tickets ($67- $75) are now on sale at oaklandballet. org/performances-events/angel_ island_project. Ferry passage to Angel Island must be purchased separately. At the premiere on May 4, Oakland Ballet Company will be accompanied by the Del Sol Quartet, under the direction of Charlton Lee, and members of Volti, a choral ensemble, under the direction of Robert Geary. Dr. Wei Cheng will conduct. Tickets, $43 – $86, are now on sale. Featuring an 80-minute oratorio scored for string quartet, 16 singers and a narrator, the music, commissioned by Del Sol in 2020, was composed by Huang Ruo, one of the world’s leading young composers. Born and raised in China, Ruo currently Photo by John Hefti AL Abraham (left), Jazmine Quezada, Lawrence Chen (floor), Florrie Geller (standing) and Ashley Thopiah in Oakland Ballet’s performance of The Seascape by Feng Ye. Photo by John Hefti Jazmine Quezada in Natasha Adorlee’s Last Chinaman from the Titanic, one of seven sections of the Angel Island Project. resides in New York City where he teaches at the Mannes School of Music. This fall, the San Francisco Opera will premiere Ruo’s newest opera, The Monkey King. “With captured imaginations, we take flight on a journey of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved into the walls by detainees at the Angel Island Immigration Station,” said Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig. “The Angel Island Project helps trace who we all are today by remembering our origins and the many perilous journeys made by our ancestors.”
articles.title: Oakland Ballet to premiere Angel Island Project at Dancing Moons Festival

articles.text: The California Watercolor Association held its 55th International Exhibition opening on Saturday, February 15th at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Paintings from 85 artists are now on view. Over 200 people attended the opening reception The Exhibition is open Saturday and Sunday, between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. and will run until Saturday, March 23. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in the center of Piedmont. The California Watercolor Association was started in 1967 and it is passionately committed to advancing the art of watercolors, fostering artistic growth and inspiring creativity in the painting community. Texan Michael Holter was the Juror of Selection. He is known for his dynamic portraits and landscapes. San Francisco’s Gary Bukovnik, the Juror of Awards, is known for his vibrant colors. Both artists have won numerous awards and have shown their work internationally. Piedmont was represented by Bernie Stein in the exhibition. Judge Gary Bukovnik and Carol Huslein, Master of Ceremonies from the California Watercolor Association China Camp, watercolor by Bernie Stein Art lovers at the opening reception of the CWA exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts: Judy Rowe, Tom Lavin, Bernie Stein, Kirsten Theurer and Leslie Wilson A large crowd attended the opening of the annual California Watercolor Association exhibit at Piedmont Center for the Arts.
articles.title: Major art exhibit now at Piedmont Center for the Arts

Tickets ($67- $75) are now on sale at oaklandballet. org/performances-events/angel_ island_project. Ferry passage to Angel Island must be purchased separately. At the premiere on May 4, Oakland Ballet Company will be accompanied by the Del Sol Quartet, under the direction of Charlton Lee, and members of Volti, a choral ensemble, under the direction of Robert Geary. Dr. Wei Cheng will conduct. Tickets, $43 – $86, are now on sale. Featuring an 80-minute oratorio scored for string quartet, 16 singers and a narrator, the music, commissioned by Del Sol in 2020, was composed by Huang Ruo, one of the world’s leading young composers. Born and raised in China, Ruo currently Photo by John Hefti AL Abraham (left), Jazmine Quezada, Lawrence Chen (floor), Florrie Geller (standing) and Ashley Thopiah in Oakland Ballet’s performance of The Seascape by Feng Ye. Photo by John Hefti Jazmine Quezada in Natasha Adorlee’s Last Chinaman from the Titanic, one of seven sections of the Angel Island Project. resides in New York City where he teaches at the Mannes School of Music. This fall, the San Francisco Opera will premiere Ruo’s newest opera, The Monkey King. “With captured imaginations, we take flight on a journey of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved into the walls by detainees at the Angel Island Immigration Station,” said Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig. “The Angel Island Project helps trace who we all are today by remembering our origins and the many perilous journeys made by our ancestors.” Major art exhibit now at Piedmont Center for the Arts The California Watercolor Association held its 55th International Exhibition opening on Saturday, February 15th at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Paintings from 85 artists are now on view. Over 200 people attended the opening reception The Exhibition is open Saturday and Sunday, between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. and will run until Saturday, March 23. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in the center of Piedmont. The California Watercolor Association was started in 1967 and it is passionately committed to advancing the art of watercolors, fostering artistic growth and inspiring creativity in the painting community. Texan Michael Holter was the Juror of Selection. He is known for his dynamic portraits and landscapes. San Francisco’s Gary Bukovnik, the Juror of Awards, is known for his vibrant colors. Both artists have won numerous awards and have shown their work internationally. Piedmont was represented by Bernie Stein in the exhibition. Judge Gary Bukovnik and Carol Huslein, Master of Ceremonies from the California Watercolor Association China Camp, watercolor by Bernie Stein Art lovers at the opening reception of the CWA exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts: Judy Rowe, Tom Lavin, Bernie Stein, Kirsten Theurer and Leslie Wilson A large crowd attended the opening of the annual California Watercolor Association exhibit at Piedmont Center for the Arts.
