articles.text: Life itself is a miracle. How we live it offers a multitude of possibilities. First, there is a question of whether it should be “lessons for life” or “lessons of life.” Whether you are religious or not, the 10 Commandments offers a good jumping off point. A few years ago, I obtained a fascinating book on violin playing. The author was a notable violinist as well as a philosopher of high attainment. At the beginning of his book, there is his version of the 10 Commandments of violin playing. With your kind permission, I will adapt some of these as a recipe for life. The author starts out by instructing us to enjoy music. We should always practice intelligently and examine every aspect of our music critically. Along the way, we should set goals for ourselves and pattern our lives after the greatest geniuses of the past. The author states: “from the genius. We learn what to do. From the fool, we learn what not to do.“ He observes that all of nature has nuance. Therefore, when we make music, we must include nuance as one of the aspects. He explains that a black-and-white photograph has nuance. It is not “black or white“ with nothing in between. In all that we do, we must be honest. And finally, we are told to consider every possibility and then to think for ourselves. Keeping these things in mind has helped me and perhaps it will help you. And finally, we are told to consider every possibility and then to think for ourselves. Keeping these things in mind has helped me and perhaps it will help you. On Thursday, we had a family celebration. The restaurant we chose was not particularly interesting. However, one of the dishes, though mediocre, opened a world of possibilities. Italian pasta, like Chinese food, is very The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet adaptable. We ordered something called cavatappi. The recipe is based on corkscrew pasta, which is mixed with braised short ribs and mushrooms topped with fried mozzarella cubes and Italian seasoning. All you need to do is take some leftover meat such as short ribs, mash it up and mix it with the other ingredients. You can be sure this is a very easy recipe and it won’t cost you $36 per person to prepare. On to music There are many concerts in our area. It is interesting to note that the United States was the first country to offer concerts in churches. In Europe, this never happened. The gigantic cathedral of Saint Mary’s in San Francisco is one of those unique concert spaces. A concert on Sunday afternoon offered interesting performers, as well as a very interesting program. My wife and I enjoyed the music but were disappointed by the dearth of people in the audience. The featured group was the Quantum Trio which included Wendy Loder (soprano and violinist), Joel Cohen (cello), and Jeanette Wilkin Tietze (piano). All of these musicians s have exemplary credentials. I often wonder what it takes to get a full audience. It is sad that huge audiences are often drawn by over-publicized performers, who fail to deliver high level musicianship. Throughout the concert the performances were very sensitive. The musicians breathed life into everything they played and paid careful attention to the balance of the three instruments. Even though the huge cathedral is notable for its echoes, the result was more than satisfactory. Perhaps our over publicized superstars could learn something about nuance. After the concert, I chatted with the performers, one of them express concern that they needed more rehearsal. I responded: “do not worry. Your inspiration and nuance more than made up for the lack of rehearsal.” Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts The Quantum Trio after their concert in St. Mary’s Cathedral in San Francisco: pianist Jeanette Wilkin Tietze (left), cellist Joel Cohen, and Wendy Loder, soprano and violin. articles.text: All the Pretty Horses is based on the Cormac McCarthy novel of the same name. First a few words about McCarthy. He will always be one of my favorite authors, a writer who moved from narrative to setting with a gifted agility. His dystopian book, The Road, winner of the Pulitzer Prize in literature, is a spare and unforgiving story, deeply complex, yet The film, starring Viggo Mortensen, is grim and dark, which, like the novel, offers a portrait of the love of a father for his young son as they face what proves to be a harrowing struggle to survive in an apocalyptic world where hope is all but impossible All the Pretty Horses is an exceptional film, with excellent performances by Matt Damon as John Grady Cole, Penelope Cruz in the role of Alexandra, and Henry Thomas portraying Lace Rawlins. The year is 1949 and circumstances have not been John and Lacey decide to leave the Cole ranch, which has been willed by his deceased father to John Grady’s estranged mother. On horseback, they head south, crossing the Rio Grande and drift further into Mexico. Soon they meet up with a kid called Blevens (Lucas Black), riding alone, a strange and quirky kid Lacey believes is a runaway. Matt Damon and Penelope Cruz in All the Pretty Horses And so begins in earnest what proves to be a compelling adventure. Though Texas and Mexico merge in terms of landscape, Mexico is a very different country as the two friends will soon learn. They find work on an immense cattle ranch, hired to break horses. And it’s there that John Grady meets Alexandra, the beautiful daughter of the wealthy owner (Ruben Blades). Inevitably, a wonderfully rendered romance develops between them, forbidden by custom and closely watched by Alexandra’s aunt. Feeling luck has found them, the two set about breaking horses. It is, however, at this point that the narrative takes an unexpected turn for John Grady and Lacey as well as the surprise return of Blevens. The sound track is gorgeous, the encounters between John Grady and Alexandra heartfelt and sad. And there is a long, engaging denouement that has a fine cameo appearance by Bruce Dern as a Texas Justice of the Peace. All the Pretty Horses. Directed by Billy Bob Thornton. articles.text: Kids will love How to Train Your Dragon. It’s one nifty movie. Let’s start not at the beginning but with an inspired and breathtaking scene: a young Viking named Hiccup, seated securely on the back of Toothless, an ebony dragon, soars through the clouds in a prolonged flight that is breathtaking. The colors are lush and gorgeous, the sky a startlingly blue in contrast to the enormous cumulus clouds. Hiccup, eyes wide, is exhilarated and terrified. This scene, like so many in this film, is testimony to the depth and breadth of the imagination of the filmmakers, and graphically illustrates how stateof-the-art animation, combined with the technology of 3-D, has made quantum strides in the last several years. Of course, neither technology nor 3-D can save a film if the story lacks serious mojo. How to Train Your Dragon has all the right stuff: a sweet if recognizable story that will resonate with youngsters, tweens and likely early teens. And the characters are, to a person, perfect. Briefly, there’s young Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), the son of Stoick the Vast (Gerard Butler), who lives on the small island of Berk, off the coast of Scotland. For 300 years dragons have been attacking their village, making off with their livestock. The Vikings have fought back and along the way developed an abiding hatred for and fear of dragons. Hiccup, a newbie adolescent, rebelling against his chieftain father and his community, resists learning to fight dragons. Stoic is both frustrated and angry with his son. Clearly Hiccup, lean in stature (the Vikings are all more than hefty), and not inclined to fight back when the dragons attack, is not cut out to be a dragon slayer. articles.text: Troop 4 Open House on March 3 As proud members of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 4, we’d like to share what makes the troop so special. Being part of Troop 4 has been one of the most rewarding experiences of our lives. Every meeting, every camping trip, and every community service project has taught us something new about nature, teamwork, and ourselves. “Troop 4 is amazing, filled with various activities and adventures to go on. Personally, I enjoy Troop 4 because of the many opportunities to go out and explore, talk to people, and work on requirements. It provides an overall friendly and welcoming atmosphere, and the outings we go on are a joy to be in. People here are all very kind, supportive, and constructive, and it is an amazing Troop through and through, for anyone interested in joining,” said Patrol Leader, Francis Guo From our very first day, we were captivated by the sense of adventure that filled our meetings and outings. we’ve hiked rugged trails, set up camp under endless starry skies, and learned invaluable outdoor skills like map reading and knot tying. Each adventure challenges us in different ways and deepens our love for the great outdoors. Whether it’s navigating a tricky path or mastering a new survival skill, every experience pushes us to grow and become more confident. “Troop 4 is a small troop which gives a lot of personal attention to the Scouts,” said Scoutmaster Eric Mellers. “We’re scout-led, which gives scouts a lot of opportunities. Scouts get to decide what we do, and it really allows us to do things that would be difficult as a larger troop. But we still offer a full program, we still have regular trips, and we’re trying to have a lot of fun”. One of the best parts of being a member of Troop 4 is the hands-on learning. We’ve had the opportunity to learn essential skills, from first aid and wilderness cooking to leadership and problem-solving. These skills aren’t just for the outdoors; they’re lessons that apply to everyday life, teaching us to face challenges head-on and trust our abilities. “My daughter visited all troop open houses. She knew right away that Troop 4 was the right one for her,” noted parent organizer Stacy Lau. “She was drawn to how fun and casual everything was. She could just come in and let out some steam. Some of her den mates joined another troop, but Troop 4 feels more laid back. The activities were a lot of fun, I really enjoyed getting to know the parents. It felt much more welcoming to her and had much more of a laid-back atmosphere”. What truly sets our troop apart is the sense of family and camaraderie among us. We’ve made friends here who share our love for adventure and who always have our back, both in the wild and out in everyday life. pages.text: Wednesday, February 26, 2025 27 Features Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wed. group keeps exploring city By Dick Carter It wasn’t supposed to rain last Wednesday morning. A drizzle turned into a light rain for the Walking on Wednesdays group, but it was not enough to stop 41 walkers and four K-9 best friends from being at the Exedra and enjoying their weekly walk. Before they got started, it was announced the group’s walk on Wednesday, March 5th will be in the memory of Will Adams, who died unexpectedly in December. Jim Kellogg will lead a walking tour to Julia Morgan designed homes, like the first Wednesday walk Will led in 2021. It was Ski Week and students were on break, so it was a good week for the walkers to visit Beach School. They could also see the Linda Beach Tot Lot that is going to be upgraded by the City. On the way to the school, there were historic homes on Nace, Howard, and Lake Avenues to see. Additionally, morning Piedmont Post readers learned there is a controversy at City Council regarding a proposed development at 210 Howard Avenue. A developer wants to build two structures divided into four condominium units on a flagshaped lot that has a long, narrow driveway into the property. The walkers could see the site. Off the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue to the upper portion of San Carlos Avenue. They went down Greenbank Avenue where they stopped in front of a charming Queen Anne Victorian at 225 Greenbank, the former home of State Assembly member Audie Bock. Ole Berg built this home in 1896. He was a 45-year-old Norwegian stevedore who worked on the Oakland docks and may have done much of the work himself. It was a simple, one-story home, and Ole added a garage in 1926. In the 1990s the house was raised to add a second floor. Today, there is a white picket fence and two inviting chairs in the front yard. The group could have gone straight up Howard to Lake Avenue and Beach School, but despite the light rain, they wanted to see and learn about the homes on Nace. In 1906, Laura Fenton, the granddaughter of the founder of Fenton’s Creamery, married Maxwell Franck, a young civil engineer, and they moved into the new, classic Craftsman house at 52 Nace. One of the oldest houses on Nace is the “Gibson House” at 46 Nace. Before the Gibsons, the owner was the dairy man Fenton. In 2024 this house was the winner of the City’s Excellence in Integrated Garage Design and the walkers took a group photo in front of its good-looking garage. The walkers went to Howard Ave, to see the disputed 210 address site. There is no home, only a curb cut with a narrow driveway up the hill. The group assumed the site for the proposed condominiums is up there, and it seemed understandable the neighbors have issues. The group went back to Lake and were soon at Beach School’s main entrance. Egbert Beach Elementary can tie its history back to the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. On that April 18th morning, thousands of people fled San Francisco for the East Bay, and Piedmont grew ten times over the next year. Piedmont was incorporated in 1907 and City leaders decided to build two schools to serve the growing community. The “Bonita Avenue School,” later renamed after its land donor, Frank C. Havens, opened in 1911. The “Lake Avenue School” was built in 1913 and renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in 1917 to honor of the first Piedmonter and first Californian officer killed during World War I. The group walked through the playground to the tot lot which is scheduled to be upgraded, As light rain continued, it was time to return to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. He also served for twelve years as founding Artistic Director of the chamber chorus Convivium and Director of Music at Christ Episcopal Church in Los Altos. Growing up in Oakland, Tuan began his musical journey in Piedmont’s choirs as a young chorister at the age of six, after a teacher recommended that he join the choir. The Artistic Director of the choir at the time, Bob Geary, would become one of Tuan’s mentors after noticing his talent. “I think at the age of about 10, I called his parents because I wanted to get a feeling for whether they understood how special he was,” said Geary. “And that was the point at which I realized of all the many, many students we’ve had – and many of them have gone on to marvelous lives and careers, both in the arts and in other disciplines – that Eric was one of the very, very few who was the most gifted.” Tuan spent 10 years singing with PEBCC before pursuing higher education. He received a B.A. in Music with Honors from Stanford University and a Master of Music in Choral Studies with Distinction from the University of Cambridge in England, which he obtained with the support of a Gates Cambridge Scholarship. Returning after college, Tuan joined PEBCC faculty in 2015 as conductor of the high school age Ecco group and as composer-in-residence before beginning his tenure as Artistic Director in July 2019. Tuan’s current choral training program serves more than 350 youth singers and leads its top ensembles in concerts throughout the world. Tuan’s dedication to musical exploration has led him to write more than 30 works, with compositions being performed by Luther College Collegiate Chorale, Lux, Vino Ensemble, Volti, and others. Tuan’s musical catalogue shows a long history of works displaying wisdom, social justice, and spirituality, such as his 2023 works “Vision in the Coast Range” and “Let Them Not Say.” “I really like telling stories that bring humanity into some of the more contentious social issues that we face now,” said Tuan in an interview with the Post. “I feel like the world is so polarized and that people and issues can become very abstract. I’m interested in my music telling individual stories very deeply so that people can feel the human connection and experience.” Choral music, undoubtedly beautiful for the audience, seems to give its greatest treasures to its singers and musicians. Tuan spoke at length about the deep connections of choir music as an art form. “I think singing together is a deeply primal thing,” said Tuan. “I think it’s one of these things that make us human. Singing together – I mean, it literally synchronizes your body and your breath and your heart because you’re all breathing together. So there’s this wonderful feeling of connection.” Youth choir and community For Tuan, singing is more than just sound – it’s community. For students in the program, singing together allows them to make friends across a wide range of people and cultures. “Our singers often say that it’s a safe place for them. It’s a place where they’ve made their deepest friends and cherished lifelong experiences,” said Tuan. “The level of musical training that they receive and the opportunities that affords is huge.” The program is also centered around student growth, with a number of programs designed to support youth engagement and youth leadership. The leadership team, elected by the choir, is in charge of creating choir sweatshirts, tour T-shirts, and even sending weekly emails. PEBCC also has a teaching assistant program, where high school aged singers go back into their elementary choir classrooms and assist with teaching. This is often the first job for many singers in this program. When asked if he had any advice for young people looking to pursue their passions, Tuan encouraged youth to look for new experiences. “Don’t be afraid to take risks because often every experience, whether it’s positive or negative, teaches you something,” said Tuan. “Don’t be afraid to make mistakes. Don’t be afraid to try new things… Nourish yourself as a person, because that feeds into your art.” Echoes of Eureka Of all his works to this point, Tuan is most proud of his opera, Echoes of Eureka. “I took a lot of risks in writing it. And I’ve really enjoyed reaching out to and collaborating with community members in Humboldt County and the API community there and historians who have been really generous in sharing their work with me to create this piece,” said Tuan. Echoes of Eureka promises to be a moving opera with a message that is especially relevant in the current American landscape. “It’s almost therapeutic to be rehearsing it right now because the story it tells is so relevant,” said Tuan. “It reminds me both of the contemporary challenges we face and also of the really powerful resistance for civil rights that these Chinese immigrants showed in the 1880s and 1890s. I hope that it allows us both to learn from and be inspired by the past right now.” Echoes of Eureka will premiere as a part of PEBCC’s Making History Concert on April 12, as well as being performed at a music festival in Eureka on May 2-4. But adolescence is also a time to nurture the deeper, reflective capacities that help teens become compassionate, thoughtful adults. By encouraging transcendent thinking, you’re not just supporting your teen’s brain development; you’re equipping them with the tools to navigate life with purpose, empathy, and resilience. And who knows? They might just inspire you to think a little deeper too. articles.text: This becomes all too clear when, wandering in the forest, he comes across a fallen dragon, Toothless. Instead of killing the dragon he befriends him. And that budding friendship sets the story in motion. Hiccup not only helps Toothless regain his ability to fly (he designs and then makes him a prosthetic tail), but, with the assistance of Astrid (America Ferrera), a wonderful tweenteen-tomboy (first it’s boy meets dragon, then it’s boy meets girl), they begin to work out a plan that will change the attitudes of the village toward dragons. Hiccup soon discovers that he and Astrid are not alone. With the help of his friends – Tuffnut, Fishlegs, Snotlout – they transform the future of Berk. What is also so much fun is that the dragons are marvelous – Hideous Zippleback, Monstrous Nightmare and the uberdragon, Night Fog. As well, all the kids speak in hip teen vernacular (“Vikings have stubbornness issues”), absent the brogue of his father and Gobber the Belch, and they dress like they buy their clothes from the Gap’s Viking annex, to include Ugg boots. Very cool. Astrid has a nifty hairstyle, leggings, short skirt and tons of ‘tude. They’re a goofy but delightful group and youngsters will identify with them and their situation. So, if the gremlins are hanging out this week complaining there is nothing to do, sit them down to see How to Train Your Dragon. They will enjoy themselves. How to Train Your Dragon. Piedmont Real Estate Update February 2025 The Less Glamorous Aspects of Home Ownership With heavy rains and atmospheric storms hitting the East Bay, homeowners face flooding, sewer backups, and pest infestations. While rain is beneficial, it can also expose vulnerabilities in your home. Taking action now can help avoid costly repairs. Preventing Sewer Backups Atmospheric storms can overwhelm East Bay sewer systems, leading to backups. Reduce the risk by: Inspecting Your Sewer Lateral – Many homes have aging pipes with cracks or root intrusion. A professional camera inspection can detect problems early. A number of East Bay plumbers will run this inspection for free. Call us for a referral. Protecting Against Tree Roots – Tree roots can infiltrate pipes, causing blockages. Consider a root barrier or replacing old pipes with root-resistant materials. Reducing Water Use During Storms – Limiting laundry and dishwasher use can ease strain on the system. Installing a Backwater Valve – This prevents sewage from backing up into your home during heavy storms. Water Weeps & Drainage Water weeps (drainage spaces in stucco and windows) prevent trapped moisture from building up. However, blocked weeps or poor drainage can lead to mold, leaks, and foundation issues. Check & Clear Weep Holes – Ensure they’re not clogged with dirt, paint, or debris. Improve Drainage – Redirect downspouts at least 5' from your foundation. If water pools, consider a French drain or sump pump. Inspect Doors & Windows – Leaky seals allow rain to seep in. Reapply caulking and weatherstripping as needed. Rodent-Proofing Your Home Colder temperatures and rain drive rodents indoors, especially in neighborhoods near open fields, creeks, and wooded areas. Prevent infestations by: Sealing Entry Points – Close gaps around vents, pipes, and foundation cracks with steel wool or caulking. Mice can squeeze through holes as small as a dime! Cleaning Gutters & Trimming Trees – Clogged gutters and overgrown branches provide shelter and easy access for pests/rodents. Eliminating Food Sources – Store food in airtight containers, secure pet food, and rodent-proof compost bins. Checking Crawl Spaces & Attics – Look for droppings or gnawed materials. If you suspect an infestation, act quickly. You can hire a rodent company to assist you. Here are a few with 4+ star Yelp reviews: Omega Pest Control (510) 777-6664 Capable Pest Control (510) 688-8471 Crossfire Pest Termites & Rodents (800)496-9914 Stay Ahead of the Rain! With more storms expected, now is the time to act. The East Bay’s aging infrastructure and hilly terrain make flooding and drainage issues a real concern. Contact us for referrals to trusted local service providers. Stay safe this season! articles.text: Residents of Lake Avenue, Nace Avenue and Howard Avenue in Piedmont are expressing concern about a proposed development at 210 Howard Avenue, which threatens to be a repeat of the construction on Wisteria Way last year. A developer seeks to build on a flag lot, with a long and narrow driveway leading into the property. The proposed building includes two structures roughly 30-feet tall, divided into four condominium units with a fourcar garage. After learning of the project, six neighborhood residents spoke out in opposition of the development at the January 21 City Council Meeting. They voiced concerns about the expedited process of SB9 construction, and cited safety issues with visibility when leaving the driveway at 210 Howard Avenue. “The street is directly across the street from Beach Elementary, so there’s a great deal of pedestrian traffic,” said Howard Avenue resident Ben Lim at the Council meeting. “My concern is, with the safety issue not being resolved or maybe even ignored, that there’s a potential for disaster and tragedy,” said Lim. According to architect and long-time Nace Avenue resident Bernie Stein, multiple projects have been denied at 210 Howard Avenue over the years. “There have been six attempts since 1977 to develop the lot. And every time it’s been either denied at commission level or planning at council level or the project just died after talking to people in the City, in planning,” said Stein. Stein talked about the driveway’s steeper-than-average slope, narrow clearance, and sightline blocked by fencing on both sides. Beyond safety, Stein doesn’t think that the proposed project would fit with Piedmont’s architectural history and design sensibilities. “If you want to see something that’s a very good example of what multifamily housing should look like in Piedmont, go down to the bridge over Oakland Avenue,” commented Stein. “There’s a development that was put in like four or five years ago. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to nominate their favorite tree to become a City of Piedmont Heritage Tree. To nominate a tree or group of trees from Piedmont’s parks and public spaces, residents can complete an online nomination form by Friday, March 21. Nominations will ask for: • A brief description of the tree and what makes it noteworthy • Address or general location • Photos of the tree, if available The Park Commission will consider trees for the title based on aesthetic, educational, or historical qualities. Any tree in Piedmont’s parks or public spaces is eligible for consideration. Trees on private property will not be considered. This year’s Heritage Trees will be announced at the April 2 Park Commission meeting and highlighted at the City’s annual Arbor Day celebration, which will take place on Thursday, April 24 at Community Hall. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized as part of the Arbor Day program and receive a limited-edition Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. Interactive map Explore all of Piedmont’s Heritage Trees on an interactive map. RELIGION CORNER The sin of being naïve By Pastor Jim Hopkins This is the way The Message Bible translates one of the most important teachings of Jesus. It’s easy to see a smudge on your neighbor’s face and be oblivious to the ugly sneer on your own. Do you have the nerve to say, “Let me wash your face for you,” when your own face is distorted by contempt? It’s this I-knowbetter-than-you mentality again, playing a holier-than-thou part instead of just living your own part. Wipe that ugly sneer off your own face and you might be fit to offer a washcloth to your neighbor. (Luke 6:41-42) This is important counsel. While we are to be discerning, we are not to be judgmental. We are to be as aware of the obstacles to our own perception as we are of the shortcomings of others. We are recognize that the advice we are so ready to give may not be as helpful in every situation as we think it is. I hear Jesus saying that it is a sin to be arrogant, to be unaware of our imperfection, to believe that we are fundamentally superior to the other human beings with whom we share this planet. That being noted, while it is a sin to be arrogant and unaware, it is also a sin be naïve, to think that we can only speak, act or lead when we have achieved perfection ourselves. In his book The Wounded Healer the great teacher Henri Nouwen puts it this way. “Nobody escapes being wounded. We all are wounded people, whether physically, emotionally, mentally, or spiritually.” In every situation, especially those in which we would advise, instruct, teach or direct, we do well to be aware of our brokenness while not letting that brokenness paralyze us or prevent us from active engagement with the world, from speaking truth to power, from standing up for those who have been knocked down, from taking the side of the most vulnerable. If perfection were a requirement for stepping out in faith, Jesus would never have let his disciples go out on their own. If perfection were a perquisite to being a “drum major for justice,” Martin Luther King Jr. would never have joined the parade. If sinlessness were needed before one could make a public call for ethical action, the public square would be a quiet place. articles.text: Editor: I went to the City’s Objective Design Standards (ODS) Open House last week. It was billed as a presentation demonstrating how the ODS were being tailored just for Piedmont’s SB 9, ADU and other City projects, and were intended to provide “clear and consistent expectations of high-quality design for new projects in Piedmont”. But it came off to me as a sales pitch indicating that the City has embraced the State’s SB 9 regulations that will no doubt destroy the wonderful urban beauty and texture of Piedmont that has existed for over 100 years. In response to the State’s SB 9 heavy handedness, Piedmont has augmented and created its own Division 17.54 Urban Lot Split and Two-Unit Housing Development regulations to work in conjunction with the State’s SB 9. However, I believe there are things the City can do to mitigate some of the negative issues associated with SB9/Division 17.54. SB 9 and the City’s Division 17.54 are a developer’s delight. In tandem they will destroy the unique character of each and every single family home neighborhood in Piedmont. They take away hearings and reviews by the Planning Commission and the City Council. There is no public notice about an upcoming SB 9/ Division 17.54 project. I came away from last week’s meeting thinking that the effort was like putting lipstick on a pig. SB 9/ Division 17.54 have just a very minimum ministerial review by the Planning Director based on a few planning/zoning standards that in turn, result in a process that is unfair to Piedmont’s residents. Combined together, SB 9 and Division 17.54 are very deceptive regulations. Here’s an example of why SB 9 is a dangerous and unfair law. A Building Permit Review is the place where a project gets looked at for health and safety impacts. Under SB 9/Division 17.54, a project is reviewed for a Building Permit in the 2nd part of a project’s process. But to get to this 2nd part health and safety review, the project must first get approved for a Lot Split and a 2 Two Unit Development. It’s also important to understand that once a project gets this 1st part approval, it’s all downhill for a neighborhood because the developer can go to the County and file for a tentative parcel map. So, where there was once only one parcel, there are now two and a Building Permit is just around the corner. SB 9/ Division 17.54 would like people to think a project can be denied for health and safety impacts, but it requires this very review for health and safety to occur after the project gets approved for a lot split and along with the right to build up to 4 residential units. This is a little bit outrageous. Again, SB 9 and Division 17.54 do not protect Piedmont’s resiproject clearly doesn’t meet current Piedmont and California Building and Fire code safety and health standards. I say this as a retired architect who is familiar with these regulations. I’ve lived on Nace Avenue for 35 years and I’ve seen 6 attempts by developers to put something on the 210 Howard Flag Lot. Each and every time, these proposals failed because 210 Howard was and remains a very dangerous property to develop for the potential residents of the condominiums, and to the neighborhood residents, especially the neighborhood parents and the kids walking to Beach School. Past Piedmont Planning Commissions and City Council have deemed 210 Howard an unsafe property and have denied projects on the 210 Howard flag lot. But with the invent of SB 9 and Division 17.54, now after almost 25 years of seeing no applications or proposed projects, a developer is back trying to build 4 condominium units, a 4 car garage, 2 30’+/- structures, on a property that a fire truck can’t access. Is there any wonder as to why this application just popped up now? This project may be just the start of an onslaught of SB9/Division 17.54 projects. Can any other Piedmont resident imagine staring at two 30’+/- boxes 4 feet away from their property? tional information. –Bernie Stein als and information on the [permit application form] and must submit additional information before City review of compliance with applicable standards begins. Once the application is deemed complete, the City will review the application and determine compliance with the standards for approval.” The Post reached out for a comment to Councilmember Tom Ramsey, who served on the Planning Commission for seven years. At press time no response had been received. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver

pages.text: Wednesday, February 19, 2025 3 SB9 is a developer’s delight; 210 Howard fails on all counts Editor: I went to the City’s Objective Design Standards (ODS) Open House last week. It was billed as a presentation demonstrating how the ODS were being tailored just for Piedmont’s SB 9, ADU and other City projects, and were intended to provide “clear and consistent expectations of high-quality design for new projects in Piedmont”. But it came off to me as a sales pitch indicating that the City has embraced the State’s SB 9 regulations that will no doubt destroy the wonderful urban beauty and texture of Piedmont that has existed for over 100 years. In response to the State’s SB 9 heavy handedness, Piedmont has augmented and created its own Division 17.54 Urban Lot Split and Two-Unit Housing Development regulations to work in conjunction with the State’s SB 9. However, I believe there are things the City can do to mitigate some of the negative issues associated with SB9/Division 17.54. SB 9 and the City’s Division 17.54 are a developer’s delight. In tandem they will destroy the unique character of each and every single family home neighborhood in Piedmont. They take away hearings and reviews by the Planning Commission and the City Council. There is no public notice about an upcoming SB 9/ Division 17.54 project. I came away from last week’s meeting thinking that the effort was like putting lipstick on a pig. SB 9/ Division 17.54 have just a very minimum ministerial review by the Planning Director based on a few planning/zoning standards that in turn, result in a process that is unfair to Piedmont’s residents. Combined together, SB 9 and Division 17.54 are very deceptive regulations. Here’s an example of why SB 9 is a dangerous and unfair law. A Building Permit Review is the place where a project gets looked at for health and safety impacts. Under SB 9/Division 17.54, a project is reviewed for a Building Permit in the 2nd part of a project’s process. But to get to this 2nd part health and safety review, the project must first get approved for a Lot Split and a 2 Two Unit Development. It’s also important to understand that once a project gets this 1st part approval, it’s all downhill for a neighborhood because the developer can go to the County and file for a tentative parcel map. So, where there was once only one parcel, there are now two and a Building Permit is just around the corner. SB 9/ Division 17.54 would like people to think a project can be denied for health and safety impacts, but it requires this very review for health and safety to occur after the project gets approved for a lot split and along with the right to build up to 4 residential units. This is a little bit outrageous. Again, SB 9 and Division 17.54 do not protect Piedmont’s resiProposed Development Continued from page 1 Stein about the flag lot. According to the City Council Minutes on September 7, 1993, the previous attempt to build on 210 Howard was denied. The Council that year found the proposed bulk and height excessive, found the design of the home to have substantial adverse effect on privacy and views of neighbors, and said that the driveway turnaround was too great an intrusion on the neighborhood. In fact, the 1993 Council found that the design adversely affects vehicular traffic and pedestrian dents because it places the health and safety review second. I want to mention how SB 9 and Division 17.54 affects my neighborhood. We are currently seeing an extremely unsafe and dangerous project proposed for the 210 Howard Avenue flag lot advance through the City. This project clearly doesn’t meet current Piedmont and California Building and Fire code safety and health standards. I say this as a retired architect who is familiar with these regulations. I’ve lived on Nace Avenue for 35 years and I’ve seen 6 attempts by developers to put something on the 210 Howard Flag Lot. Each and every time, these proposals failed because 210 Howard was and remains a very dangerous property to develop for the potential residents of the condominiums, and to the neighborhood residents, especially the neighborhood parents and the kids walking to Beach School. Past Piedmont Planning Commissions and City Council have deemed 210 Howard an unsafe property and have denied projects on the 210 Howard flag lot. But with the invent of SB 9 and Division 17.54, now after almost 25 years of seeing no applications or proposed projects, a developer is back trying to build 4 condominium units, a 4 car garage, 2 30’+/- structures, on a property that a fire truck can’t access. Is there any wonder as to why this application just popped up now? This project may be just the start of an onslaught of SB9/Division 17.54 projects. Can any other Piedmont resident imagine staring at two 30’+/- boxes 4 feet away from their property? See next week’s Post for additional information. –Bernie Stein safety. As recorded in the minutes: “The driveway access is troublesome because of its excessive slant, its lower-end retaining walls, and the creation in effect of an unsafe 85-foot long ‘tunnel’ for drivers to navigate with only 18-inch clearance on each side.” “The application for SB 9 Urban Lot Split and Housing Development at 210 Howard Avenue has been determined to be incomplete,” said Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson. “This means that the applicant has not submitted all the materials and information on the [permit application form] and must submit additional information before City review of compliance with applicable standards begins. Once the application is deemed complete, the City will review the application and determine compliance with the standards for approval.” The Post reached out for a comment to Councilmember Tom Ramsey, who served on the Planning Commission for seven years. articles.text: Aprè-ski Week event on Fire Science set for Sunday, Feb. 23 The League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) and the Piedmont Fire Department invite the community to a discussion on fire science and family preparedness on Sunday, February 23, from 4:30-6:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. This free event offers a unique opportunity to learn about wildfire risks, home safety strategies, and emergency preparedness directly from Piedmont’s fire safety experts. Whether you’re a longtime resident or new to the area, this discussion will provide valuable insights to keep your family safe. All are welcome, light refreshments will be served and RSVPs are requested. The League of Women Voters, a nonpartisan organization, has been a vital part of the Piedmont community, working to empower voters and advocate for effective public policies for over a century. This event will highlight the importance of local engagement in addressing today’s pressing issues. RSVP to: https://lwvpiedmont.org/content.aspx?page_ id=4091&club_id=601389&item_ i d = 2 539 535. Fo r m o r e information contact Lisa Gardner at Lgardner555@gmail.com.

articles.text: Young Wooly is a one-yearold cream-colored husky mix with a playful and engaging personality who loves both human interaction and canine companionship. He is available to be fostered temporarily or for adoption. Given his young age, Wooly surprises those who meet him because of his calm and gentle demeanor. Shelter staff and volunteers say Wooly is very affectionate and social with adults and children. He adores being pet and adjusts his energy level to whomever is interacting with him. He participates in a daily doggie playgroup and gets along well with other canines. Wooly knows the sit command and walks fairly well on leash, although he may zig-zag at times. Wooly would make a fun and loving addition to any home, temporarily or forever. Come meet him at Oakland Animal Services. If interested in fostering you can fill out a foster form on the shelter’s Meet Wooly, a one-year-old cream-colored husky mix. website and pick him up this Thursday from 12-7 pm. If interested in adopting, you can meet him Thursday 12-7 pm or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Wooly must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about the fostering or adoption process, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting residents to help make a selection of new playground equipment at Linda Beach Tot Lot. A brief online survey is now available. The survey builds on two recent events at the tot lot where staff spoke to playground users about their preferences and priorities for new playground equipment. The survey invites community members to share: • how often they visit Linda Beach Tot Lot • what age children they bring • what they like most about the Tot Lot • which types of equipment are most important to include • whether they prefer matting or playground “turf” for the new playground surface The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/BeachTotLotSurvey and will remain open through February 21. In addition to replacing the aging playground equipment, this project will: • create ADA access from Linda Avenue to the playground • resurface the playground with ADA compliant matting or turf • install a new water fountain or bottle filling station Funding for the project was included in the 2024-25 City budget and includes a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Kids feel samples of the proposed new turf for Linda Beach Tot Lot.

articles.text: Salvation Army of Alameda County’s annual gala, The Way Out 2025. A Night for Others, will be held on Sunday, March 30, at the Claremont Country Club. Debbie Kelley and members of the organizing committee are especially pleased to announce that this year’s Volunteer of the Year award will be presented to Alice Waters, the founder of the iconic Chez Panisse Restaurant in Berkeley and the visionary leader of the Edible Schoolyard Project. Alice has pioneered a model that integrates gardening and cooking into school curricula, providing students with fresh, healthy meals and essential nutritional education. Her commitment to offering free meals and fostering a deeper understanding of food’s role in health and well-being exemplifies the values we hold dear at The Salvation Army of Alameda County. To attend and for tickets, contact Debbie Kelley at TheWayOut.SalvationArmy@gmail.com. Alice Waters is this year’s Salvation Army of Alameda County Volunteer of the Year award recipient. An interactive map of all 30 Heritage Trees is available on the City’s website at piedmont. ca.gov/HeritageTrees. The Heritage Tree program aims to raise awareness and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Each year, the Park Commission selects up to 5 trees from a pool of community nominations to receive the Heritage Tree designation. Previously selected trees include the evergreen dogwoods that bloom each spring in front of City Hall, the grove of dawn redwoods surrounding the lawn area in Dracena Quarry Park, and the row of autumn blaze maples lining the 400 block of Wildwood Avenue. articles.text: Applications are now open for appointed volunteer positions on six City Commissions or Committees in Piedmont – Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, Civil Service Commission, Park Commission, Planning Commission, Public Safety Committee, and Recreation Commission. Serving in these volunteer positions is an excellent opportunity to learn more about the inner workings of City government. Commissioners help shape City programs, policies and services by providing a valuable resident perspective on upcoming and proposed projects. Applicants can learn more about the work of Commissioners by watching past meetings on the City’s online video archive at https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/kcom-tv/live_content_and_video_archive. Residents can apply online by February 28 at piedmont. ca.gov/Commissioner. Key Dates for Applicants Applicants must be available for a pre-appointment interview with the City Council and a mandatory in-person training at City Hall before assuming their position. • Applications Due: Friday, February 28 5pm • Mandatory interviews: Monday, March 10 (evening) • Required Brown Act Training: Monday, March 31 (evening) • Appointments effective: Tuesday, April 1 (Effective date for Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee appointment is July 1.) For most bodies, members are appointed to 3-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Studies and provides recommendations on annual budget, long-term financial projections, mid-year budget adjustments, and the City’s municipal services tax rate and renewal. Meets as needed Civil Service Commission • 2 Vacancies (1 Incumbent eligible to reapply) Deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. Meets as needed Park Commission • 3 Vacancies (3 Incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to public parks and street trees. Meets monthly on first Wednesdays, 5:30pm. Planning Commission • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to planning and building. Makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. Requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Meets monthly on second Mondays, 5:30pm. Public Safety Committee • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to crime reduction and disaster preparedness. Meets bi-monthly Recreation Commission • 2 Vacancies (1 Incumbent eligible to reapply) Advises on issues regarding recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space and other issues. Meets monthly on third Wednesdays, 7:30pm. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District has announced it is offering April Adventures, enriching programs for local students April 7-11 at Havens Elementary School providing a week of learning and fun. Mornings will focus on academic enrichment, while afternoons will feature creative and recreational activities, special performances, and Piedmont Park scavenger hunts. Program hours are 9:00 a.m. -3:00 p.m. with extended care available from 8:00-9:00 a.m. and 3:00-5:00 p.m. Summer Adventures Summer Adventures will return for another exciting season, serving students in TK through 6th grades with two sessions at Havens School. • Session 1: June 10-20 • Session 2: June 23-July 3 Students can enjoy morning academic enrichment classes, followed by afternoon recreation options including art, sports, science, and cooking. Full-day and half-day options are available, with extended care from 8:00- 9:00 a.m. and 3:00-5:00 p.m. Welcome to TK & Kindergarten Designed for students entering these grades in fall 2025, these sessions provide young learners with a sneak peek into their upcoming school experience. Children will engage in fun and developmentally appropriate activities led by teachers and staff, helping them adjust to a structured school schedule while making new friends. Welcome to 6th Grade This program is designed to help incoming sixth graders transition smoothly to middle school. Students will familiarize themselves with their new campus, daily schedules, and expectations while engaging in writing activities and team-building games to build confidence for the fall. Junior CIT Program (Grades 7-8) The Junior CIT (Counselor-in-Training) Program is open to students in 7th and 8th grades interested in developing leadership skills and gaining experience assisting with activities. Junior CITs will have the opportunity to help in both morning and afternoon sessions, learning valuable skills while making a difference. Participants can register for either the morning (9:00 a.m. - 12:00 p.m.) or afternoon (12:00 - 3:00 p.m.) sessions. Registration for both programs opens February 14 for April Adventures and February 25 for Summer Adventures. To register and for more details visit the PUSD website: www.piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: Astronomers of every stripe are looking forward to next month’s total lunar eclipse, which will be visible from the Bay Area if skies are clear. According to Chabot Space & Science Center astronomer Gerald McKeegan, “There will be a total Lunar Eclipse (a.k.a. Blood Moon) late on the night of Thursday, March 13. The visible part of the eclipse will begin at 10:09 p.m. Pacific Daylight Time. The mid-point of the eclipse will be at 11:59 p.m. (one minute before midnight.) The visible part of the eclipse will end at 1:48 a.m. Friday morning, March 14. NASA’s website advises the best way to view the eclipse: “You don’t need any special equipment to observe a lunar eclipse, although binoculars or a telescope will enhance the view. A dark environment away from bright lights makes for the best viewing conditions. “The same phenomenon that makes our sky blue and our sunsets red causes the Moon to turn reddish-orange during a lunar eclipse. Sunlight appears white, but it actually contains a rainbow of components—and different colors of light have different physical properties. Blue light scatters relatively easily as it passes through Earth’s atmosphere. Reddish light, on the other hand, travels more directly through the air. A “Blood Moon” lunar eclipse is coming in March. When the Sun is high on a clear day, we see blue light scattered throughout the sky overhead. At sunrise and sunset, when the Sun is near the horizon, incoming sunlight travels a longer, low-angle path through Earth’s atmosphere to observers on the ground. The bluer part of the sunlight scatters away in the distance (where it’s still daytime), and only the yellow-to-red part of the spectrum reaches our eyes. During a lunar eclipse, the Moon appears red or orange because any sunlight that’s not blocked by our planet is filtered through a thick slice of Earth’s atmosphere on its way to the lunar surface. It’s as if all the world’s sunrises and sunsets are projected onto the Moon. Chabot Space & Science Center will host a public lunar eclipse viewing event from 9 pm Thursday, March 13, through 1 am Friday, March 14 on its observation deck and telescopes with astronomer presentations, activities for all ages and hot cocoa. For more information and tickets. See http://www.chabotspace.org.

articles.text: Piedmont School District is accepting nominations for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and have made a difference because of their commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The deadline for nominations is March 14. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, and the winner will be recognized at the May 14 Board of Education meeting, and their good works will be acknowledged. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was the founder of the Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by board member Dewey Watson. Nomination Forms are available in the District Office, by calling Rosalina Barrios, Executive Assistant to the Superintendent, at 594-2614 or via the District website at: Docs.google.com/ document/d/1J92iTb6870oZbIRotoHW8rM3MUmCS8bORuf- 7c1hcCmY/edit?tab=t.0 Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly by Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023) and most recently Sarah Pearson in 2024.

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, February 19, 2025 By Jay Russell On February 1st a group of 20 exchange students from Galicia, Spain arrived in Piedmont for an 11-day educational and cultural swap. Students, and a few Spanish teachers stayed with Piedmont host families, allowing Spanish students to attend classes with their hosts. Students in grades 8-12 brought their life experiences from 5,500 miles away and nine time zones ahead. The exchange, in its first year, was spearheaded by Piedmont High Spanish teacher Deysi Sahagon, “Deysi (along with Bryan Smith, French teacher) came to Ariel Dolowich and me last year with this idea of a cultural exchange that would bring students from Spain to Piedmont, and it would take students from Piedmont to Spain,” explained School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Hawn, and Dolowich were immediately enthusiastic about a cultural exchange, and the Piedmont School Board enthusiastically approved the program as an example of a strategic priority “Partnering Beyond the Classroom.” Spanish students stayed with their Piedmont partners, whom they had been communicating with since last October. Ten Spanish students paired with upperclassmen, even attended Piedmont’s Winter Ball on Saturday, February 8. Spanish exchange students open some eyes and minds Two days earlier the students from Spain made an outing to San Francisco that included visiting the Golden Gate bridge. “Spanish students were happy to be in California and stay with American families that took them to different activities after school and places such as ice skating, dining out, and Warriors games,” said Sahagon. Sahagon reported that the Spanish counterparts thought school in Piedmont was more fun, when compared to their school in Spain, and were surprised at how many sports Piedmont kids play. Spanish students were also universally surprised at how early the dinner bell tolls in these parts, around 5:30 or 6:00 p.m., as compared with 9:00 or 10:00 p.m. at home. “I really believe that when we connect our students, our communities together, even students from other countries with other languages, that we really build bridges; and that’s how we become better humans.” said Superintendent Hawn. In addition to enhancing their language skills, Sahagon noted the benefits of the program. “[This exchange program] broadens global perspectives, builds international networks, enriches educational systems academically, achieves personal growth while adapting to a new environment, and creates the opportunity to make lifelong friendships,” she said. articles.text: Nearly a dozen Girl Scouts from Troop #33521 celebrated their recently completed Silver Awards at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Wednesday. The 11 Scouts are 9th graders who spent the past three years working towards their Silver Award. The highest honor a Girl Scout Cadette can receive, the Silver Award encourages them to take action and make an impact on their community. articles.text: A teenage pedestrian was stuck by a vehicle at the intersection of Grand and Greenbank Avenues on Tuesday, February 11, around 6:00 p.m. The incident turned into a hit-andrun when the driver of a Ford pickup truck fled the scene after striking the girl. According to police and eyewitnesses, the teenager was hit by a white 1998 Ford F-250 truck. She ended up on the ground 15-feet from where she had been on the sidewalk. The truck proceeded to flee the scene, traveling on the wrong lane of traffic without stopping. The girl was brought to a hospital by paramedics and is in stable condition. The suspect vehicle was quickly identified using the Piedmont Police Department’s Public Safety Camera System and Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras, and the driver was later arrested at his home in San Leandro by two Piedmont Police officers. The suspect, Alfredo SotoReyes, was arrested and sent to Santa Rita Jail. Casey Bivens, a resident of the area, was unloading his car nearby when the collision occurred. “I saw her, just a few feet above the ground, land on the ground. It took maybe three seconds to register what actually happened and what I was looking at,” said Bivens. Bivens provided immediate aid and stayed with the teenager until the paramedics arrived. She was treated and later released. Piedmont Police utilized license plate cameras and public safety cameras to locate the suspect. At 6:33 p.m. the police log shows the suspect vehicle, with front end damage, was located on Lark Street in San Leandro. The registered owner of the truck was contacted at 7:23 p.m. and arrested. The suspect is charged with a felony hit-and-run along with reckless driving and was taken to Santa Rita Jail. Piedmont Captain Chris Monahan gave credit to the use of technology in making the arrest. “It’s another example of the value-add that both the license plate cameras and the public safety cameras bring in our ability to apprehend offenders or those committing crimes in our city,” said Monahan. articles.text: Basketball team falls to Alameda, CV to end regular season Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up its regular season with a pair of losses against Western Alameda County conference competition, falling by one point, 59-58, to Castro Valley at home on Friday, February 14, and losing 66-57 to league champions Alameda two days earlier. The pair of games closes Piedmont’s regular season with a 12-14 record. PHS benefitted from its difficult schedule and going 4-0 against other Division 4 schools, earning the No. 1 seed in the D4 North Coast Section bracket. The last time PHS received the top seed was when they won the D4 title in 2020, which was coach Ben Spencer’s first year at the helm. Since winning the D4 title, Piedmont has at least reached the semifinals in three straight tournaments. PHS lost to Branson in the 2022 and 2023 D3 semifinals, while they narrowly lost 65-55 in the D3 Finals to University last year. This marks their first time playing in the D4 bracket since winning it all in 2020. Prior to their game against Castro Valley, Piedmont honored its two seniors on the roster in Ravi Silverberg and Emmet Asulin. Piedmont will host No. 16 Ukiah tonight, February 19, for the opening round. With a win, the Highlanders will host the winner of No. 8 Hayward and No. 9 Bethel. Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg, a three-year starter, played his final regular season game for Piedmont High. 59-58 loss to Castro Valley Piedmont trailed 15-14 through the first quarter, but took a 29-28 lead by halftime. Castro Valley got back to the front in the third quarter by scoring 15 points and allowing 13, making it 43-42 for the Trojans. In the final going, both teams scored 16 points. The Highlanders also lost their first game against Castro Valley by just one point, 50-49, on January 29. Despite the loss, it was an important return for the team’s second-leading scorer, Dillon Casey, who suffered an injury against San Leandro on January 31. Final stats: Ravi Silverberg led with 15 points, Casey scored 13 points, Beach Lorin had 11, Emmet Asulin, a two-year varsity member, wrapped up his regular season career at Piedmont. Dillon Casey returned to Piedmont’s lineup in time for the North Coast Section post-season playoffs.

articles.text: Girls’ basketball team gets No.5 seed in NCS Open Division Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team closed out its regular season at Binks Rawlings Gym with a 72-24 win over Castro Valley on Friday, February 14 and a 74-60 victory over Alameda two days earlier. The pair of wins means they will share the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division first-place banner with Bishop O’Dowd. The Highlanders finished its season with seven straight wins to post a record of 21-4 and 7-1 against league competition, proving to be one of the best teams in the North Coast Section. As a result, they received the No. 5 overall ranking in the Open Division. PHS will travel to Santa Rosa tomorrow to face No. 4 Cardinal Newman tomorrow, February 20. Piedmont’s recent win over Alameda came after holding a 37-31 lead at halftime. The Hornets got the No. 10 seed in Division 1, but in the Open Division, Piedmont will face the section’s best of the best. “What we talked about at halftime and after the game is when we play an Open team, if you’re not alert and ready to play, you can go down by 15. They execute at a higher rate, you have to match that intensity and execution,” said PHS coach Bryan Gardere. It’s an impressive achievement for a team with three freshman as starting varsity players – Jenelle Solis, Andrea Martin, and Savannah Dennig. The team also Shakila Zuberii is a four-year varsity player. Staff Photos Briana Webb, a senior, is finishing up her first year on the varsity squad. includes sophomore Taylor White and first-year varsity starter Briana Webb. “We’re going to play better teams in the Open, so we need to prepare ourselves for this competition. We’re just taking things game by game,” Solis said. Piedmont celebrated Webb and four-year varsity player Shakila Zuberi as its two seniors on the roster prior to their game against Castro Valley,. “It marks the end of my journey, but it’s more of a celebration. Now that its so close, I want to delay it and want more games at home,” Zuberi said. “It means a lot to me. It’s sentimental, but it’s been a hard journey and there’s been a lot of happy moments,” Webb mentioned, who came to Piedmont from Moreau in Hayward.

articles.text: Upper Falls is about 15 feet tall; it is situated closely to Basin Falls. [Reprinted from February 2021] Morgan Hill is home to a 1,147 acre park known for its collection of easily accessible waterfalls. On the eastern side of the Santa Cruz Mountains is Uvas Canyon County Park, found at the very end of the private Sveadal community on Croy Road. Hikers will be greeted to the sound of bubbling brooks immediately when entering the park on the Waterfall Loop trail along Swanson Creek. The first and smallest cascade, Granuja Falls, provides a fitting welcome to visitors after the first bridge. After another half mile, hikers will find the base of the Black Rock Falls on the right. Follow the water up the narrow path to find the roughly 20-foot tall waterfall that passes over a black rock face barring its name. Returning back to the Waterfall Loop Trail for just 0.2 of a mile brings walkers to an intersection with the base of Upper Falls on the left, and a walkway to Basin Falls—which seemed to be the most thriving of the park after the rain. Basin Falls stands around 15 feet, flowing down stones as it feeds into Swanson Creek. A fallen tree sits in its center to provide a clear perspective of its size. Returning to the Waterfall loop reunites you with Upper Falls, a two tiered cascade that is also around 15 feet tall. Passing the falls means you are nearing halfway through your day as you venture onto the Contour Trail. The Contour Trail goes for about 1.1 miles and provides some uphill climb to your day, meaning it’s not just a scenic nature hike, but a fitting lower body workout. The trail also surrounds you with the aroma of California Bays, the sprawling red bark of Manzanita, and a towering second-growth redwood here and there. Intersecting with the Alec Canyon Trail, turn right to head just slightly less than a mile to Triple Falls. It’s the final landmark of the day and the tallest of the waterfalls at around 50 feet, but a small trickle compared to the other four. A sixth waterfall is on the right during the main trek in on the Waterfall loop, but it isn’t all the noteworthy given it is a similar small stream and farther away from hikers. Our Uvas Canyon loop to hit every waterfall is approximately 5.2 miles and topped out at 1,273 feet in elevation gain. The Post passed 44 hikers on the day, but over 36 of which came on the initial walk on the Waterfall Loop given its popularity. It is also one of the few dogfriendly parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains, so it is safe to bring your pooch. The park requires 24-hour advance reservations for parking, otherwise you’ll be parking on the road leading in. For parking information, visit https:// parks.sccgov.org/santa-claracounty-parks/uvas-canyon-county-park or search “Uvas Canyon County Park” in your device – it will be the first option in search engines. Punch in “Uvas Canyon County Park” to your GPS device to access this South Bay park. A view of Swanson Creek. You’ll walk over the creek to continue on the Contour Trail.

Intersecting with the Alec Canyon Trail, turn right to head just slightly less than a mile to Triple Falls. It’s the final landmark of the day and the tallest of the waterfalls at around 50 feet, but a small trickle compared to the other four. A sixth waterfall is on the right during the main trek in on the Waterfall loop, but it isn’t all the noteworthy given it is a similar small stream and farther away from hikers. Our Uvas Canyon loop to hit every waterfall is approximately 5.2 miles and topped out at 1,273 feet in elevation gain. The Post passed 44 hikers on the day, but over 36 of which came on the initial walk on the Waterfall Loop given its popularity. It is also one of the few dogfriendly parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains, so it is safe to bring your pooch. The park requires 24-hour advance reservations for parking, otherwise you’ll be parking on the road leading in. For parking information, visit https:// parks.sccgov.org/santa-claracounty-parks/uvas-canyon-county-park or search “Uvas Canyon County Park” in your device – it will be the first option in search engines. Punch in “Uvas Canyon County Park” to your GPS device to access this South Bay park. A view of Swanson Creek. You’ll walk over the creek to continue on the Contour Trail. Staff Photos Uvas Canyon County Park in Morgan Hill has a collection of waterfalls that are easily accessible for hikers. Pictured here is Basin Falls. The first of the group is the smallest Garunja Falls. Black Rock Falls is around 20 feet tall and feeds into Swanson Creek. Triple Falls is our final of five thriving waterfalls in the park. It’s the tallest at around 50 feet in height.

articles.text: The Batsheva Dance Company will take the stage at Zellerbach Hall with the Bay Area premiere of MOMO this Saturday at 8 p.m. and Sunday at 3 p.m. In the world-renowned company’s own words, this staggering new work by its choreographer Ohad Naharin “has two souls. One sends long roots to the depths of the earth — a soul that embodies archetypes and myths of hardened, raw masculinity, and the other is in a constant search for an individual and distinct DNA. One moves within its own autonomous and independent force field and the other is a constellation of elements that spin around the same nucleus — alternately drifting away and towards it, making room for necessary tenderness and catharsis.” The performance includes recordings of Laurie Anderson and Kronos Quartet’s Landfall, Philip Glass’ Metamorphosis and a song-prayer by the Venezuelan musician Arca, with additional music provided by Naharin himself under the name Maxim Waratt. Of the work, the French newspaper Le Figaro write, “Ohad Naharin’s latest piece is unlike any of his other works … Mesmerizing. And as always, captivating.” The Batsheva Dance Company was founded in 1964 by Baroness Batsheva de Rothschild. Notably, the company was the first outside of American dance maverick Martha Graham’s own troupe to perform her choreography. In its first decades, the company was led by various artistic directors from Israel and abroad. The company has long nurtured a space for creative process and artistic interpretations. Many of its dancers have emerged as creators and choreographers including Bobbi Jene Smith and Or Schraiber, who performed in Olivier Messiaen’s Harawi at Zellerbach Hall earlier this season. Over the course of his years with Batsheva, Naharin has won many awards and honors, among them Chevalier de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres from the French government, the Samuel H. Scripps American Dance Festival Award for Lifetime Achievement, a Doctor of Philosophy honoris causa by the Hebrew University, and an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree from the Juilliard School in New York. In 1990 Ohad Naharin was named artistic director and led the company into a new era. Thanks to his bold choreography, Batsheva Dance Company has been critically acclaimed as one of the foremost contemporary dance companies in the world. The company’s awards and accolades include receipt of the New York Dance and Performance Bessie award, and the Yair Shapira Prize for their contributions to the world of dance. Tickets ($42-$108) are available online at calperformances. org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642-9988.
articles.title: Legendary Batsheva Dance Company to perform MOMO at Zellerbach this weekend

articles.text: The madcap musical comedy Nobody Loves You opens at the American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco on February 28 for a one-month run. The game of love is on: This play features a wildly popular reality dating show by the same name, in which eager contestants compete for love and social media stardom, while audiences are taken on a behind-the-scenes ride through reality television and into real life. When Jeff (A. J. Holmes), a philosophy grad student, snags a spot on the show to win back his ex-girlfriend, he breaks all the rules and tries to blow the game wide open; that is, until he falls for Jenny (Kuhoo Verma), an enticingly prickly producer of the show who yearns to leave the drama to make serious films. In a world where every kiss comes at the end of a selfie stick, can two people really connect? Bay Area hometown heroes Itamar Moses (Tony Award winner for The Band’s Visit, Drama Desk winner for Dead Outlaw) and Gaby Alter provide uproarious screenwriting, witty lyrics, and a winsome pop score in this madcap musical comedy helmed Catch the madcap musical comedy Nobody Loves You at the American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco from February 28 through March 30. by Tony Award winner and A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “Nobody Loves You is a hilarious and heartfelt musical quest for authenticity through the ridiculously inauthentic world of a reality dating show,” said MacKinnon. “You will root for your favorites, cringe at their foibles and, by the end of the show, feel that you too should step into the world as yourself and take your chance at love. “Seldom do I laugh as hard as when I get to direct a world created by Itamar Moses,” she added. “I can’t wait to share Nobody Loves You with the Bay Area.” Showtime information and tickets ($25–$130) for the performances at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theatre (415 Geary St., San Francisco) are available at the ACT Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf.org/NLY.

articles.text: French-Israeli Mezzo-Soprano Naama Liany perform her unforgettable new album Daydream in a hybrid show at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco this Friday, February 21 at 8 p.m. Hailed as “One of today’s most promising singers” by Dutch media site Jonet.nl, Liany’s acclaimed programs of the 20th century musical repertoire span styles and decades, finding common ground between Darius Milhaud and George Gershwin, Federico Mompou and Leonard Bernstein. Her performances communicate the emotional heart of the music with audiences across the world. Her new album, Daydream, is a stunning example, bringing together works on the subject of dreams. The program of songs for her concert, includes Samuel Barber’s Despite and Still (1968), Leonard Bernstein’s I Hate Music: A Cycle of Five Kid Songs (1943), Federico Mompou’s Combat port of an award from the country’s Ministry of Culture. The program came together during the COVID-19 lockdown, as the notion of being a singer without an audience took on surreal and dreamlike proportions. Dreaming is an apt subject for Liany, whose parents recall her waking up at the age of four and recalling a dream where she sang in front of a crowd of joyful listeners. Liany studied at the Mannes School of Music and the Conservatory of Music of Brooklyn College and has performed at Carnegie Hall when living in New York. Europe beckoned when Liany was one of ix vocalists chosen worldwide to participate in the Gstaad Menuhin Festival & Academy, directed by legendary opera singers Cecilia Bartoli and Silvana Bazzoni. She settled in Paris, where her performance career took off with international acclaim. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $10 students with ID, 12 and under free) are available at oldfirstconcerts.org. Get a copy of The Mouse That Roared, then enjoy the movie starring Peter Sellers. But this is a music column, so I might suggest that you get the book Ah Julian. It is a combination of Wibberley’s autobiographical aspirations along with a beautiful memoir of his violin teacher Julian Brodetsky. Along the way, you gain insights into passions for music, and, more than anything else, advice on how to live your life. One of the most compelling chapters was an in-depth description of why the violin bow is one of the greatest, and most sensitive, instruments invented by mankind. This chapter should be taken out of context and made required reading to every violinist. The famous composer Rossini was also one of the most famous gourmands of all time. To people who like food, his name has been applied to “Tornadoes of Beef à la Rossini.” A restaurant in our area took this idea and created the “Rossini burger.” Who would have thought that a humble hamburger could be turned into a true work of art? That is exactly what the folks at Perle Restaurant in Montclair Village did. At first glance the price of $45 for a Rossini burger might scare you. Don’t be afraid. It’s worth it. A giant hamburger topped by a generous portion of black truffle paste, duck, butter, marsala onions, and a large green salad is what you get. It was one of the two best hamburgers I’ve ever eaten. Other items on the menu are equally good. Prices tend to be on the high side, but the quality is equally high. Service was friendly and efficient though a little bit slow. In musical terms, a finale is often called a “Coda.” It turns out that our four legged rodent friend, the mouse, is often a talented singer. There might even be examples of mice singing opera. While this thought is intriguing, I couldn’t find any examples. However listen to Rossini’s delightful “Duet of the Two Cats.” Priceless.
