articles.text: There’s a lot more to mice than you might think. My predecessors have made exhaustive studies on them. Don’t worry… this story is easy to read even though it delves into philosophy, biography/autobiography, music, and violin making – among many things. Let’s begin by mentioning an important author named Leonard Wibberley. I’ll bet you don’t recognize the name. He was a very interesting character and a brilliant writer to boot. He wrote the book The Mouse that Roared which became a very successful movie and begat many other mouse tales. Wibberley is the subject of this column simply because he was a very interesting character and because I knew him. He was a truly quixotic genius. Being an Irishman, he had many of the characteristics of a leprechaun. As for his gift of words, he was brilliant. Think of Mark Twain in the costume of a leprechaun and you get an inkling. It didn’t matter what the subject was – the result was compelling. Political satire made a lot of money for him. In addition, there were biographies, autobiographies, and many aspects of music. He always wanted to be a violinist, but he was more of a failure than a success. That didn’t seem to matter to him. I used to see him on Saturday mornings in the violin shop of Mario Frosali where he was an apprentice. Most people enjoy being complimented, but not Wibberley. When I told him that I was acquainted with his work and enjoyed it very much you’d think he would be happy. His demeanor changed as if I had insulted him. It didn’t Leonard Wibberley, author of The Mouse that Roared
articles.title: Sage advice…from mice

articles.text: Thursday, Feb. 20 Lage will begin his four-day residency with a 7:30 p.m. solo recital, showcasing the breadth of his guitar mastery in the most revealing setting — one in which his peerless musicianship is presented without restrictions, undiluted and unadorned. The evening will harken back to Lage’s landmark 2015 release World’s Fair, a solo guitar session of original compositions focused on the exploration of the song styles that shaped his own aesthetic, inspired by the work of a formative influence, classical guitar genius Andrés Segovia. Friday, Feb, 21 Night two brings a concert of duets with Jorge Roeder, a longtime collaborator with Lage and among the most acclaimed bassists in modern music. Hailing from Lima, Peru, Roeder began classical cello and bass studies at age 14 and was the assistant principal bassist for the Lima Symphony by 21. Among the first musicians he met when arriving in New York in 2007 were Julian Lage and virtuoso pianist Shai Maestro, who have been long-term musical partners ever since. Saturday, Feb. 22, 7:30 p.m. Lage will bring a program of music including material from his new album Speak To Me with his current working trio including longtime bassist Jorge Roeder and drummer Kenny Wollesen. For this special night, the band is joined by keyboard master John Medeski, best known as one-third of the jazz-funk trio Medeski Martin & Wood and for his work with John Scofield, John Zorn, Robert Randolph, and the Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Speak To Me is Lage’s fourth album for the Blue Note label, produced by the acclaimed singer-songwriter and guitarist Joe Henry and featuring an expansive new set of original songs with guest appearances from saxophonist Levon Henry and keyboard wizard Patrick Warren. Sunday, Feb. 23 Lage’s final night pairs him with the iconoclastic guitarist Marc Ribot. A singular instrumentalist, Ribot follows his muse wherever it leads, resulting in a career that has ranged across free jazz, no-wave, rock, film music and Cuban rumba. Beyond his wildly eclectic output as a leader — which has veered from the rollicking Los Cubanos Postizos to avant-rock to a solo guitar score to accompaniments for Charlie Chaplin’s silent classic The Kid — Ribot is best known as a key collaborator with Tom Waits, Elvis Costello, John Zorn, the Lounge Lizards, Diana Krall, Robert Plant and Alison Krauss.

The evening will harken back to Lage’s landmark 2015 release World’s Fair, a solo guitar session of original compositions focused on the exploration of the song styles that shaped his own aesthetic, inspired by the work of a formative influence, classical guitar genius Andrés Segovia. Friday, Feb, 21 Night two brings a concert of duets with Jorge Roeder, a longtime collaborator with Lage and among the most acclaimed bassists in modern music. Hailing from Lima, Peru, Roeder began classical cello and bass studies at age 14 and was the assistant principal bassist for the Lima Symphony by 21. Among the first musicians he met when arriving in New York in 2007 were Julian Lage and virtuoso pianist Shai Maestro, who have been long-term musical partners ever since. Saturday, Feb. 22, 7:30 p.m. Lage will bring a program of music including material from his new album Speak To Me with his current working trio including longtime bassist Jorge Roeder and drummer Kenny Wollesen. For this special night, the band is joined by keyboard master John Medeski, best known as one-third of the jazz-funk trio Medeski Martin & Wood and for his work with John Scofield, John Zorn, Robert Randolph, and the Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Speak To Me is Lage’s fourth album for the Blue Note label, produced by the acclaimed singer-songwriter and guitarist Joe Henry and featuring an expansive new set of original songs with guest appearances from saxophonist Levon Henry and keyboard wizard Patrick Warren. Sunday, Feb. 23 Lage’s final night pairs him with the iconoclastic guitarist Marc Ribot. A singular instrumentalist, Ribot follows his muse wherever it leads, resulting in a career that has ranged across free jazz, no-wave, rock, film music and Cuban rumba. Beyond his wildly eclectic output as a leader — which has veered from the rollicking Los Cubanos Postizos to avant-rock to a solo guitar score to accompaniments for Charlie Chaplin’s silent classic The Kid — Ribot is best known as a key collaborator with Tom Waits, Elvis Costello, John Zorn, the Lounge Lizards, Diana Krall, Robert Plant and Alison Krauss. Sage advice…from mice By Joseph Gold There’s a lot more to mice than you might think. My predecessors have made exhaustive studies on them. Don’t worry… this story is easy to read even though it delves into philosophy, biography/autobiography, music, and violin making – among many things. Let’s begin by mentioning an important author named Leonard Wibberley. I’ll bet you don’t recognize the name. He was a very interesting character and a brilliant writer to boot. He wrote the book The Mouse that Roared which became a very successful movie and begat many other mouse tales. Wibberley is the subject of this column simply because he was a very interesting character and because I knew him. He was a truly quixotic genius. Being an Irishman, he had many of the characteristics of a leprechaun. As for his gift of words, he was brilliant. Think of Mark Twain in the costume of a leprechaun and you get an inkling. It didn’t matter what the subject was – the result was compelling. Political satire made a lot of money for him. In addition, there were biographies, autobiographies, and many aspects of music. He always wanted to be a violinist, but he was more of a failure than a success. That didn’t seem to matter to him. I used to see him on Saturday mornings in the violin shop of Mario Frosali where he was an apprentice. Most people enjoy being complimented, but not Wibberley. When I told him that I was acquainted with his work and enjoyed it very much you’d think he would be happy. His demeanor changed as if I had insulted him. articles.text: Ralph Fiennes in Conclave Conclave, the recipient of eight 2025 Oscar nominations, to include Best Picture, achieves what film does best: it takes the audience inside one of the world’s most secretive and centuries-old traditions. The church’s Cardinals, dressed in black and scarlet vestments, each with a large Pontifical cross, have been called to the Vatican from around the world. There they will gather behind locked doors in a cloistered conclave, tasked with the responsibility of selecting a new pope. Chosen to manage this densely ritualistic process is Cardinal Lawrence (Ralph Fiennes); his responsibility, we soon realize, is no small endeavor. The position of Pope is not only one of shepherding the millions of Catholics word wide, but one of power. Which Cardinal will be chosen, using paper ballots, while solemn is, as the narrative reveals, also Machiavellian, even touched by scandal and deception. With quiet sidebars, it can seem closely similar to a political gathering of sorts, these small huddles taking place behind closed doors or small huddles. These men of insistent faith are also just men who deal in the currency of secrets, touched by temptation, often conflicted when tested. Conclave is, ultimately, a captivating character study of Cardinal Lawrence who must reach beyond the conclave as he urgently attempts to discover the truth behind two whispered mysteries. This takes place while ballots are filled out and counted as the conclave waits to reach that necessary majority, and a plume of white smoke can be released from the much-watched chimney, signaling that a new pope has finally been elected. Conclave . Directed by Edward Berger. Starring Ralph Fiennes, John Lithgow, Stanly Tucci. 2 hrs. Rated PG. Released in 2024. Streaming on Netflix/ Prime/Fandango/apple tv.

No Way Back has an epic feel, and it transcends what may, at first blush, seem a rudimentary plot. The year is 1940 and a rag tag group of men improbably escape a Russian gulag work camp. Against all odds they trek more than 4,000 miles across some of the most inhospitable country imaginable. Their destination, as it turns out, is British-controlled India. This is not a road trip. articles.text: Kevin Costner in For Love of the Game For Love of the Game is, indeed, about baseball. But, like so many sports films, the field of play is also a perfect crucible in which the character of those who play are tested. The opening scenes find Billy Chapel (Kevin Costner), veteran Detroit Tigers’ pitcher, waiting in his NYC hotel suite for Jane Aubrey (Kelly Preston). They have agreed to have dinner and (it’s implied) perhaps reconnect after what has been a tumultuous five-year relationship. Jane fails to show up, which is only obliquely explained the next morning. She tearfully tells Billy that she is leaving, having taken a job in London. And it’s at this point that the structure of the film is revealed, one that is ideal for storytelling. Billy is slated to pitch against the Yankees that evening and it’s when he takes the mound to begin what might be the conclusion to an extraordinary career that the writers, using a seamless story-telling device, the flashbacks, which consist of vignettes, beginning with how Jane and Billy meet-cute. This is, after all, far more than a baseball story. And so the actual game begins to take form, inning after inning, the momentum broken only by Billy’s almost meditative reflections on the past. All of this is framed by the inevitable decision facing Chapel regarding his career. He loves the game, deeply, a game he has played almost all of his life, to include 19 years in the big show with the Tigers. To go beyond what I’ve written above would deprive you, the audience, of the enjoyment of watching what I judge to be such a remarkable story, one that transcends the field of play. At the same time, know that the game unfolding, with Billy on the mound throwing hard to his long-time friend and catcher, Gus Simski (John C. Reilly), is standalone riveting. For Love of the Game. articles.text: Moana 2, a Disney musical, is set on a lovely tropical island in the blue waters of the South Pacific, the sand is white, grass huts are ubiquitous along the shore. Suddenly the screen is filled with the latté image of Moana (Aulii Cravahalo), effortlessly sweet and engaging. She lives in the embrace of her community and is adored by her mother and father and worshiped by her small sister, Simea. Moana, a skilled sailor, has spent her days sailing to the surrounding islands in search of other tribes that might be connected to her own people. She has heard the myths and legends and is determined to make contact. In a community ceremony, her father (Temuera Morrison) bestows on Moana the title “The Way Finder.” Restless to begin her quest searching for other islanders, she organizes her next journey that will take her beyond the horizon. Because of the distance, Moana decides to assemble a crew of locals to include, of course, her loyal bug-eyed chicken and a small white pig. And so, with the community gathered on the shore, she departs into the unknown, filled with hope and song and holding an etched coconut shell found on a neighboring island that confirmed her belief that there are others out there. If only she can find them. A comment about the animation: it’s extraordinary, and reveals the breadth and depth of the Disney artists. The characters are so good as to seem almost real, with A scene from Disney’s Moana 2

articles.text: The Formosa Quartet will perform a concert sponsored by Four Seasons Arts, on Saturday, February 22 at 3:00 p.m. at St. John’s Presbyterian Church, 2727 College Ave, Berkeley. The quartet, which formerly included violinist Wayne Lee, performed a number of times at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The quartet now includes Jasmine Lin, Violin, David Bernat, Violin, Matthew Cohen, Viola, and Deborah Pae, Cello. Guest artist Chieh-Fan You, viola will replace Mathew Cohen for this performance. This Quartet’s cultural identity includes Taiwanese, broader American, pan-Asian and Eastern European roots. The name “Formosa” is taken from the Portuguese for “beautiful.” J.S. articles.text: Ongoing through March 23 California Watercolor Association Exhibit California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition — Join us from 11 am to 2 pm on Saturdays and Sundays to celebrate the 85 artists selected by juror Michael Holter, twenty of which will have received awards totaling an estimated $16,000 in cash and sponsor products, as selected by Awards Juror Gary Bukovnik. CWA proudly announces this year’s exhibition, showcasing exceptional watermedia paintings from talented artists around the world. This annual event will be on display from February 15 thru March 23, 2025, free and open to the public as stated above, and of course also viewable when attending other events at PCA. We invite art enthusiasts, collectors, and the community to experience the vibrancy and creativity of watermedia art. Don’t miss this incredible opportunity to view some of the world’s finest works and celebrate the talent of these exceptional artists! Friday, February 21, 7:00 p.m. Michael Jones Trio – Postponed Concert postponed to a future date. Thursday, March 6, 7:00 p.m. Ambroš Duo Concert Founded more than 120 years ago, Sokol SF still celebrates and supports the Czech-Slovak/American community, and here brings us a concert by the renowned mother/ son Ambroš Duo, visiting from the capital city of Prague in the Czech Republic. The concert will feature works by Paganini, Rachmaninov, and Czech composers Dvorák, Janáček, Ježek and Suk, and a piece by John Williams. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” Welcome reception at 6:30, and tickets at https://brownpapertickets.com/e/6556132, or at the door for cash only. Saturday, March 8, 7:00 p.m. Renegade Orchestra Concert If you don’t know about the Renegade Orchestra, just imagine what happens when you take a bunch of amazing musicians and remove all the rules. Classic rock, zydeco, 60’s favorites and more. The last 2 shows sold out, so catch us here. This concert will be performed by our string sections, but will still bring you virtuoso musicians breaking all the rules — with the Heart of a Symphony, and the Soul of a Rock Band! Leave your expectations at the door and come to be surprised and excited! Advance tickets at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/964647987097. Sunday, March 9, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Concert Piedmont Center for the Arts and the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra present A Sunday Serenade: Music of Haydn and Mozart. Piedmont’s popular local chamber orchestra returns with an intriguing program of smaller works by Haydn and Mozart, featuring Mozart’s Serenata Notturna K.239 and the Wind Serenade in Eb, K.375 plus the curious Symphony No. 83, (La Poule - “The Hen”) by Haydn. Conductors Martha Stoddard and Andrew O’Donnell will share the podium, and featured soloists are Shauna Revelli and Gar Wei Lee, violins; Thomas Chow, viola; and Jay Soule, contrabass. This concert is free admission but reservations on Eventbrite are strongly encouraged due to seating limitations – go to https://www.eventbrite. com/e/1246829543729. More to come Friday, March 14, 7:30 p.m. Four-hands Piano Concert, Miles Graber & Amy Zanrosso Sunday, March 16, 4:30 p.m. St. Patrick’s Day in the Classic Jazz Club, by In the Tradition Friday, March 21, 7:00 p.m. Early Music Concert by Baltimore Consort Trio Sunday, March 23, 3:00 p.m. Mozart & Brahms Piano quartets — Miles Graber

articles.text: Life’s work of famous Iranian-American artists on view Through this Sunday, February 23, see two solo exhibitions at San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts that offer investigative portraits of artists whose lives and creative outlets become inextricably linked to political revolution. In the presentation of distinct bodies of work through Nicky Nodjoumi: The Personal is Political and Nahid Hagigat: Etched in Time, visitors will explore the practices of two of the most influential Iranian-American artists today, ranging from Nodjoumi’s surreal and kaleidoscopic paintings exploring manifestations of political power, to Hagigat’s evocative and intimate etchings about women and their ongoing struggle for freedom in Iran. Both exhibitions will be framed by an introductory gallery featuring family photos and archival material shedding light on the personal and shared struggles that shaped these artists’ lives. Nicky Nodjoumi presents a series of paintings created over the past 15 years. In these works, Nodjoumi presents layered narratives that reiterate his staunch commitment to democracy. Exploring the dynamics of power, often through satire, Nodjoumi transforms his lived experiences in Iran and the U.S. into scenes that resonate beyond specific geographical boundaries. His works are like theatrical stages where compositions of figures, both serious and ridiculous, are brought together into stories that illuminate both Nodjoumi’s personal history, and historical experiences of political struggle. Nahid Hagigat offers an evocative selection of paintings, prints and etchings that span six decades. Hagigat explores the constraints of politics and ideologies on women, through works that portray female Iranian figures through a feminist lens. Among these works is a series from the 1970s inspired by photographs sent to Hagigat in New York by her sister in Tehran. Drawing on these images, Hagigat creates scenes of women, children and everyday life, synthesizing history with her personal experience in Iran and New York, moving seamlessly between the personal and the global using images of pain, uncertainty, light, and clarity as a way of moving between the past, present and future. The dual exhibitions are inspired by the film A Revolution on Canvas, an HBO documentary produced by Nodjoumi and Hagigat’s daughter Sara Nodjoumi and her partner Till Schauder. The film begins by investigating the disappearance of 120 of Nodjoumi’s artworks in Tehran after his 1980 exhibition, which led to his family’s exile from their native country. Through an attempt to find the missing paintings, Sara Nodjoumi and Schauder present a layered exploration of her family’s history, her parents’ individual work as artists and the indelible impact of politics on their lives. “These two exhibitions invite us to reflect on the role of artists and the power of creative expression, especially during times of political upheaval,” said YBCA curator Amy Kisch. “How do their voices ground us in our shared humanity? What are the sacrifices they make and the impact across generations? How do we support legacies of creativity and free expression? This show pays tribute to Nodjoumi’s and Hagigat’s incredible commitment to art and democracy, even under times of great duress.” The Yerba Buena Center for the Arts (701 Mission St., San Francisco) is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($10 general admission, $5 students and seniors) are available at the front desk; details are available online at ybca.org/visit, over email at boxoffice@ybca.org and by phone at 415-978-2787. articles.text: A look back at The Maze, now Witter Field English gardens designed as mazes were highly popular in the early 20th Century. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on June 10, 2020. The ninth and final marker in Piedmont Park’s history trail may be the most exotic of them all, The Hedge Maze. The Maze perplexed its visitors in the location now occupied by Piedmont High School’s Witter Field. Marker 9: The Maze The marker is located near Wildwood Ave. overlooking Witter Field. As Frank C. Havens began to expand Piedmont Springs Park, he added The Maze, a playful feature on a grand scale in 1904. The living hedge maze was modeled on the maze at England’s Hampton Court, the home of Henry VIII. Gardeners planted hedges and let time grow them tall to make the maze even more mysterious. Havens developed a lower entrance pathway to Piedmont Park shrouded by palm trees from Grand Avenue, what is now Palm Drive. The prime feature from the lower entrance was The Maze, situated in the natural bowl shaped ravine. A field of roses stood next to The Maze, making this area of Piedmont Park ideal for strolling visitors. The finish line of The Maze was its center, occupied by a red-roofed pagoda. Ladders were placed throughout The Maze to give direction to those who had become lost. Getting to the center was only half the challenge; making it back out could take just as long. A 1914 article in the Oakland Herald noted, “At the western end of the park on the low grounds is situated the “Maze” where the visitor can find much enjoyment trying to find his or her way out to the open path. articles.text: Saturday, February 8th, marked the 20th Girl Scout Pinewood Derby. Racers from Piedmont, Oakland and San Francisco gathered at the Piedmont Community Church to race creative model cars. Eighth Grade Piedmont Middle School Troop 33587 hosted the Girl Scout Derby again this year. In addition, they also hosted a car making workshop two weeks prior to the race where they helped racers build their cars from start to finish. Racers ran their cars accordGirl Scouts Daisy Rose Burnham, and Pearl Burnham, check their derby cars in. Girl Scouts are wowed by the cars racing down the track. A wide range of colorful and creative cars were entered to race. Brownies watch their cars race, on the edge of their seats to see the result. A group of Girl Scouts celebrate their friend’s victory. Cadettes and Up Category: Clara Keilch won Most Artistic Car, Skye Prata Baack won 2nd Place, Zoe Schoen won 1st Place and Troop Leader Sally Baack is holding Lucy Allen’s 3rd Place car. ing to their level of Girl Scout from Daisies to Cadettes and Up. Each category received award certificates, a special derby patch and fastest cars received 1st place trophies, 2nd place trophies, 3rd grade medals. “It’s competitive, but a great way to experience engineering first hand,” said Brownie Winnie Pickavance. The judges’ favorite car designs included a horse car named “The Flying Filly”, a couple of cheese wedges, and an Uno card. “It was fantastic to see how enthusiastic the GS pinewood derby racers were to try out their unique and innovative designs,” said Troop 30713 leader Sally Baack. “The room was filled with the sound of cheers, laughter and excitement as Girl Scouts and families enjoyed the afternoon.” Troop 33587 offers thanks to the troops that hosted the Derby in the past, race participants, the Piedmont Community Church, Piedmont Boy Scout Council and Nancy Brahm at PUSD for making the car workshop and race day possible.

articles.text: Frederic Vignobles finish. This lovely wine would pair well with shrimp, grilled chicken, roasted vegetables, or The year was 1989. We were veal in a cream sauce. It was our at a blind tasting together at The top rated white. Wine House in West Los Angeles. Among roughly 20 wines, one stood out: Ridge York Creek Petite Sirah. Holy smokes. Sure, the varietal has never been especially well known, but this wine was outstanding – head and shoulders above the other contenders. And it only cost six bucks. A great wine value had been discovered, and thus began our decades long search for exceptional value in wine. Our motto has become “anybody with 50 bucks can buy a great wine, but it takes effort and knowledge to buy a great wine for 15 bucks.” We come from the European school, where delicious food and good wine grace the family dinner table as a matter of evening ritual. So, affordability matters. Wine should not be just for the rich or ostentatious. We have dedicated our most recent tasting to discovering good wines for under $20. We started with wines we thought were contenders, then searched the Wine.com website for other wines that were highly rated by both critics and customers. These we added to the mix and picked a dozen for tasting. Three wines failed to make the mark, but we found nine to recommend, the best red, best white and best value being truly outstanding. Try one, or try them all, and enjoy. The Pine Ridge Chenin Blanc/ Viognier was the best value of the tasting. • 2023 Pine Ridge Chenin Blanc/Viognier, $12.99 (Best Value) Better known as the mainstay of Vouvray and as a leading white varietal in South Africa, almost all of the Chenin Blanc in California was replaced with other varietals in the 1970s. Pine Ridge was one of the few wineries to stay with it. This wine is an unusual blend of 80% Chenin Blanc and 20% Viognier, which works well. The wine opens with slight floral notes then white peach, apple and pear fruit. Light to medium body, there is a hint of tart grapefruit before a clean, dry finish. The wine is not complex, but enjoyable and at $13 per bottle it wins the best value award for the whites. • 2023 Mapreco Vinho Verde, $12.99 This bright, refreshing wine from Portugal opens with lemon-lime, then apple notes and just the right amount of effervescence. It is light bodied, clean and crisp. Enjoy by itself on a hot summer afternoon, or pair it with fresh seafood. Delightful. • 2022 Côtes Du Roussillon Bila Haut Blanc. $15.99 This wine is an appealing blend of 60% Grenache Blanc, 20% Roussanne, 10% Grenache Gris, and 10% Macabeu. It opens with a complex nose of stone fruit with floral notes, then citrus and honey. Medium bodied, it left us wanting a bit more fruit in the middle but had a lovely finish. A good value that would pair nicely with smoked ham.

articles.text: Italian Sausage and Garbanzo Bean Soup Photo by Deborah Quok • It’s still soup season, although it’s fair to say soup is welcomed pretty much year-round here in the Bay Area. With those record cold days lately, we’ve been enjoying this simple and satisfying soup, especially at lunchtime. We enjoy it for lunch since it comes together with just a few ingredients you may already have on hand. It’s ready in about 30 minutes, or less, from chopping to serving. My pantry always has low-sodium chicken stock or broth and canned beans on the shelves. Similarly, I always keep a few varieties of fully cooked sausage on hand. The ones I buy are vacuum packed so they store well in the refrigerator, and an even longer life in the freezer. Having these on hand mean I have myriad options for pulling together a tasty meal in short order. Don’t be shy about “doctoring” a store-bought broth. Adding aromatics (onion, garlic, leeks, ginger), fresh or dried herbs, and spices is pretty much mandatory for a soup of any cuisine. For this soup, a bay leaf, oregano and thyme would be delicious additions. Using different sausages, beans, and greens is highly encouraged. Adding cubes of butternut squash would be right in line, too. I highly recommend adding a crunch-factor in the form of croutons (see photo) to bring a tasty, textual component. Making your own is easy; fair warning: you may never go back to store-bought once you’ve made your own. • • • • • • • • 1 can garbanzo beans, rinsed and drained 2 cups lacinato kale, sliced in 1/2-inch strips 1 white onion, small, diced; about 3/4 cup 3/4 cup fresh tomato, diced (Substituting canned diced tomatoes is fine.) 1 clove garlic, minced 1 quart chicken broth, preferably homemade, but low-sodium if store-bought 1 tablespoon olive oil Red chile flakes, to taste Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste. INSTRUCTIONS Italian Sausage and Garbanzo Bean Soup Makes about 2 quarts INGREDIENTS • 2 links Italian sausage, fully cooked, sliced Heat the olive oil over medium heat in a 3-quart saucepan for about one minute, add the sliced Italian sausage and spread into a single layer. Let brown slightly, then turn to brown the second side, about 3–4 minutes. Add the diced onion and minced garlic and stir to combine. Continue cooking over medium heat until the onion turns translucent. Do not over-brown and be especially watchful of the garlic. Add the diced tomatoes, garbanzo beans and chicken broth. Bring to a gentle boil for at least five minutes to cook the tomatoes. Add the kale and cook until just wilted. Taste and season to taste. Easy Croutons This soup is rustic and begs for big, crunchy croutons atop to provide a textural contrast. For one cup of rustic croutons, simply hand pull 1/2 – 1-inch chunks of bread from your favorite loaf and toss in about 1–2 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

It has good roundness and structure to balance the fruit and it finishes with soft supple tannins. • 2022 Cline Ancient Vines Carignane, $16.99 Cline has long had access to some historic 100-year-old vineyards in Contra Costa County that are some of the best places in California to grow Rhone varietals. This Carignane is bursting with cranberry, strawberry, cedar and dusty earth. It was aged 10 months on French oak and has some vanilla notes. Well-made and perfectly balanced this wine is a delight to drink now and should last 6 or 7 years in the cellar. This wine is an incredible value. Italian Sausage and Garbanzo Bean Soup Photo by Deborah Quok By Deborah Quok • It’s still soup season, although it’s fair to say soup is welcomed pretty much year-round here in the Bay Area. With those record cold days lately, we’ve been enjoying this simple and satisfying soup, especially at lunchtime. We enjoy it for lunch since it comes together with just a few ingredients you may already have on hand. It’s ready in about 30 minutes, or less, from chopping to serving. My pantry always has low-sodium chicken stock or broth and canned beans on the shelves. Similarly, I always keep a few varieties of fully cooked sausage on hand. The ones I buy are vacuum packed so they store well in the refrigerator, and an even longer life in the freezer. Having these on hand mean I have myriad options for pulling together a tasty meal in short order. Don’t be shy about “doctoring” a store-bought broth. Adding aromatics (onion, garlic, leeks, ginger), fresh or dried herbs, and spices is pretty much mandatory for a soup of any cuisine. For this soup, a bay leaf, oregano and thyme would be delicious additions. Using different sausages, beans, and greens is highly encouraged. Adding cubes of butternut squash would be right in line, too. I highly recommend adding a crunch-factor in the form of croutons (see photo) to bring a tasty, textual component. Making your own is easy; fair warning: you may never go back to store-bought once you’ve made your own. • • • • • • • • 1 can garbanzo beans, rinsed and drained 2 cups lacinato kale, sliced in 1/2-inch strips 1 white onion, small, diced; about 3/4 cup 3/4 cup fresh tomato, diced (Substituting canned diced tomatoes is fine.) 1 clove garlic, minced 1 quart chicken broth, preferably homemade, but low-sodium if store-bought 1 tablespoon olive oil Red chile flakes, to taste Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste. INSTRUCTIONS Italian Sausage and Garbanzo Bean Soup Makes about 2 quarts INGREDIENTS • 2 links Italian sausage, fully cooked, sliced Heat the olive oil over medium heat in a 3-quart saucepan for about one minute, add the sliced Italian sausage and spread into a single layer. Let brown slightly, then turn to brown the second side, about 3–4 minutes. Add the diced onion and minced garlic and stir to combine. Continue cooking over medium heat until the onion turns translucent. Do not over-brown and be especially watchful of the garlic. Add the diced tomatoes, garbanzo beans and chicken broth. Bring to a gentle boil for at least five minutes to cook the tomatoes. Add the kale and cook until just wilted. Taste and season to taste. Easy Croutons This soup is rustic and begs for big, crunchy croutons atop to provide a textural contrast. For one cup of rustic croutons, simply hand pull 1/2 – 1-inch chunks of bread from your favorite loaf and toss in about 1–2 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: It was a cool and overcast afternoon on February 3rd when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their monthly discussion at the Community Hall. There was a good turnout of 21 readers on hand for the meeting. The readers tried something new at this meeting. The group has grown significantly since it started in January 2019. Currently, 68 people are registered with the Recreation Department for the activity. There have been as many as 25 participants in individual discussions, and some readers had a desire for a smaller group. As an experiment, chairs were set up in the Community Hall alcove for a smaller conversation. Six readers went off to the smaller session, and the rest of the group stayed in the hall’s main room. Lois Price led the smaller discussion, while Priscilla Wanerus continued to lead the bigger group. The English cookies that Carol Long brought were enjoyed by both groups. The readers were there to talk about their February book, Endurance: Shackleton’s Incredible Voyage by Alfred Lansing. It was written in 1959 and is the story of the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, led by Sir Ernest Shackleton, and its failed attempt to cross the Antarctic continent in 1914. Lansing tells the story of an almost two-year struggle for survival endured by the Endurance’s twenty-eight man crew. This exploration ship became stuck in and eventually crushed by Antarctic ice, leaving the men stranded on the pack ice. The crew drifted on ice floes for over a year in desperately cold conditions. They lived off the ship’s dwindling provisions and the seals and other animals they killed. Finally, Shackleton and a few of his crew barely reached South Georgia Island 650 nautical miles away. Shackleton then led two of them on the first successful overland crossing of South Georgia. Three months later, he was able to rescue the remaining crew members. Almost every diary from the expedition was made available to Lansing, and almost all the surviving crew members provided lengthy interviews. Lansing drew on these resources to make the book’s characters very personal and his account very real. This is a survival story. Almost all the book deals with the hardships the Endurance’s crew experienced. Their constant suffering can be hard for the reader, but the book was well received by the group. For some it was a surprise. They wouldn’t have picked the book, but once they started it, they couldn’t put this adventure story down. Some felt the book might not be great literature, but it is well-written, absorbing, and a little gruesome. The frigid cold and hardships that Shakleton and his crew experienced were an endless procession of misery. The Endurance’s crew were seamen. They knew they were signing up for a long and dangerous expedition, and they were well prepared, but this voyage was more than anyone expected. The readers admired and were amazed by the ability of all these men to survive their ordeal. How did they stay sane? How did they avoid hypothermia? How did they stay focused and together? Shakleton’s leadership was a major part of their survival. The readers were impressed by him and his determination to save his crew. Endurance is a good study of leadership. The readers were asked, “Could a crew today do Alfred Lansing’s Endurance tells the story of an almost two-year struggle for survival endured by the Endurance’s twenty-eight man crew. what these early 20th Century men did?” Yes, they thought, if they were the right crew and had the right leadership. After separate discussions the two groups rejoin for the remainder of the meeting for a recap and the selection of their next book. The participants in the smaller group discussion felt it was a success. It was flexible, conversational, and the acoustics were better. So, the intent is that a smaller, separate group will be part of future meetings. The group had previously selected James by Percival Everett for March, and Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz for their April book. After Laura Goldman’s presentation of three fiction candidates for their May book, the readers selected Cloudstreet by Tim Winton. The group’s next discussion will be on March 3 at 1:30 p.m. at the Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. Participating in the First Mondays Reading Groupon February 3 were Bella Almanzan, Nancy Henn, Sarah Johnson, Carol Long, Carol Warren, Orrel Lanter, Louise Booth, Peggy Shultz, Sue Backer, Laura Goldman, Ken Young, Hilary Honore, Lorrell Plimier, Lois Price, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Martin Levy, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Bob Hall, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus.

articles.text: A strong turnout of 48 walkers and three K-9 best friends were on hand at the Exedra to get their steps before the rain. Pala, Mesa, and Monte Avenues, just above Highland Avenue, were nearby streets the group could walk, and they could then climb the steps between Pala and Scenic Avenue to see views of the Bay and the looming clouds. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, turned up Oakland Avenue, and stopped in front of the house on the corner. This Victorian was built by John Rackliffe and his wife Ellen in 1899. Rackliffe was 73 years at the time but needed a large house for his family that included his two adult children and a grandson. The Rackliffes were one of the few families listed in the 1900 Piedmont Census. The house’s cross gabled roof and octagonal corner turret with gables of different sizes and a witch cap roof are typical of Queen Anne designs of the period. Jim Kellogg pointed out the seamless addition that architect Grier Graff later designed for the home. The area above Oakland and Highland Avenues was a bit of a bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters, including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there and before them land developer Frank C. Havens also resided in this area. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake. After Piedmont became an incorporated city in 1907, home construction boomed. The homes were built above an early pathway that went from Moraga Avenue to the one-room cabin of Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area. Blair named the path “Vernal” because of the abundant ferns and shrubs that grew around a nearby spring. That roadway was renamed “Highland Avenue” in 1911. The homes built above the street were part of the Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development of Wick ham Havens, Frank C.’s son. The walkers wondered if Wickham’s “Alta Piedmont” resulted in later references to “Baja Piedmont” for the streets below Highland. The group went up Oakland Avenue, turned left on the oneblock Hardwick Avenue, and walked to Blair Avenue. They went up Pala, turned on Mesa and enjoyed the attractive homes built in Bungalow, American Foursquare, Colonial Revival, and Craftsman styles. Seven homes on Mesa’s were built in 1907, The walkers took special notice of the home at 17 Mesa. Its exterior ornamentation is unique with lovely, miniature columns supporting large, curved brackets on the porch. The group went up Moraga Avenue to Monte and back to Pala. The homes along Monte were built between 1906 and 1960. The walkers stopped to appreciate another beautiful home, this one at 110 Monte. Its design is interesting and complex with a hipped roof, twin towers, stained glass windows, and a red tiled roof in an unusual L-shaped design with varied roof heights. The walkers went up Pala to the Scenic-Pala Steps, 161 feet to the top. On Scenic they enjoyed an expansive, cloudy view of the Bay. They continued up the street and marveled at homes built on Scenic’s steep ridge above Blair Park and Moraga Avenue below. Even more surprising were story poles on a vacant lot indicating a new home is planned for the steep slope. Further up Scenic the group passed the longest path in Piedmont, the 281-foot steps down to Blair. The group’s return to the Exedra was via Alta Avenue, Blair, Pacific, Mountain, and Highland Avenues with more beautiful, cloudy views along the way. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Last week’s gathering of the Walking on Wednessdays group included Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Denny McGee, Jim Kuo, Gail Truman, Priscila Wanerus, Greg Keller, Charlene Louie, Lorek Haghnazarean, Jasmine Cai, Tina Shum, Bob Wong, Nancy Olsen, Alicia Rivera, Nancy Henn, Martin Levy, Mike Gallant, Rick Eigenbrode, Larry Olsen, Julia Chin, Phil Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Stella Houston, Lori Austin, Michelle Yang, Liz Dalrymple, Melba Yee, Peggy Shultz, Pat Keller, Lois Price, Judy Love, Margie Richardson, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kellogg, Lauren Dudell-Folley, Chuck Oraftik, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Edith Lee, June Yee, Irene Thompson, Bill Ahern, Terry Tom, Lisa Euphrat, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Minoo Clayman walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: Jorge Alberto Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Jr., age 54, passed away at home in Fairfield, California on February 3, 2025 of natural causes. A native of Piedmont, Jorge was born on February 20, 1970, in San Francisco, California, to Linda Fraizer Suarez Rivas and Jorge Alberto Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Sr. He was a graduate of Piedmont High School and received his Bachelor of Arts degree in History from Saint Mary’s College in Moraga. A dedicated employee of Southern Wine & Spirits for nearly 20 years, he was the East Bay District Manager at the time of his passing. In his youth, Jorge worked as a bartender in the Bay Area and Pasadena, and was well known as a craft cocktail specialist (before anybody knew what that meant), creating many oneof-a-kind drinks, including the classic, “Jorge’s Headbanger.” Jorge was fiercely proud of his Cuban heritage and served as the unofficial family armchair genealogist and collector of stories. He often spoke with great admiration of his father, Jorge, and Uncles Eduardo and Juan, for their participation in the Bay of Pigs Invasion in 1961. All three men were captured and tortured by Castro’s forces and spent nearly two years in Cuban prisoner camps. Jorge was a salesperson extraordinaire. winning countless awards and accolades. He was a loving and fun grandfather, and drenched participants in the notorious El Cerrito Avenue water balloon fights on Memorial Day weekends of long ago. Christmas Day will never be the same without Jorge hosting the annual family dinner at a Chinese restaurant in Walnut Creek. Most importantly, he was a devoted husband, father, grandfather, son, brother, Piedmont native Jorge Suarez Rivas, Jr. died on February 3 at age 54. uncle and friend. Jorge was beloved by family, friends and colleagues, and his sudden passing has been devastating to all who knew him. He is survived by his wife, Diane Suarez Rivas, daughters, Jennifer (Riki) Barulich and Julia (Patrick) Mullaney; son, Daniel Brown; grandchildren, Quinn Barulich, Emilia Barulich, Kiera Mullaney, Jack Mullaney, Rudy Brown, Logan Brown, and Callie Brown; mother, Linda Fraizer Ruby; sister, Tana Suarez Rivas (David Shall); brother, Matthew Ruby (Lisa Billings); nephew, Rocco Ruby; godson, Parker Gneckow; beloved dog, Charlotte, and many aunts, uncles and cousins. He was predeceased by his father, Jorge Alberto Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Sr.; stepfather, Robert L. Ruby; and grandparents, Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Ofelia Munroe, and Margurite and Keith Fraizer. A Celebration of Life will be on Friday, March 14, at 2:00 p.m., at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont.

articles.text: On Saturday, February 8, Wildwood Kindergarten Girl Scouts Troop 32605 had an exciting visit to the Piedmont Fire Department. The firefighters gave an engaging presentation about their daily responsibilities, the heavy gear they carry, and the key differences between a fire truck and a fire engine. The girls were most excited about being able to tour the fire engine. During their visit, Daisy Girl Scouts earned their Respect Authority badge and had a fantastic time meeting the firefighters – the community’s true heroes. Wildwood Kindergarten Girl Scout Troop 32605, with snacks in-hand, pose with four Piedmont firefighters in front of a fire engine. Match Recap Piedmont got on the board quickly when Sullivan lofted a shot over the Jets’ goal keeper in the 12th minute from the right side of the penalty area. From there, Piedmont had four shot attempts and drew three corners, but couldn’t find the back of the net prior to halftime. The Highlanders got things rolling in the second half. Hammond had a header go wide after receiving a pass from a corner in the 45th, while Symkowick had a long shot from a free kick on target in the 47th. Piedmont drew a penalty kick the very next minute, leading to Symkowick rolling in a shot to the left of Encinal’s keeper, making it 2-0. Hammond scored Piedmont’s final goal in the 63rd minute when retrieving a pass from a corner in the box. Initially having her back facing the goal, Hammond took her shot on a quick turn to send it in. Stephanie Lee nearly scored in the 66th minute after receiving a nice through-ball by Sullivan, but her shot was saved. Symkowick had two more shot attempts miss the mark in the later minutes. articles.text: ria; find, against all odds, Lake Baikal; cross the plains of Mongolia; survive the heat and sandstorms of the Gobi Desert; and face the snows and spires of the Himalayas, the gateway to Tibet. Beyond is India. How they accomplish this remarkable feat makes for an astonishing tale, not unlike in some strange way the survival tale 127 Hours. Both experiences are testimony to the depth of the very human desire to survive. While 127 Hours is relatively static and claustrophobic, No Way Back is all about movement and space, filling the screen with vistas that are startling in their seemingly benign beauty, though clearly malevolent in their raw harshness and inherent deprivations. The performances by the international ensemble are outstanding, led by Harris as a stoic American engineer who came to a background on land and sea that is lush with a rainbow of colors. Regarding the characters, each is a wonderful creation of movement and expression. But with that said, and filled with anticipation and promise, Moana 2 abruptly shifts and becomes just another movie, much to my disappointment. The slow island story morphs into a series of slapstick scenes, some verging on the manic. Indeed, the crew now includes the familiar presence on board of Maui (Dwayne Johnson), covered in his familiar animated and responsive tattoos. It’s as if the writers decided that in order to hold the attention of the young audience, well, they needed to pump up the volume and increase the pace, beginning with the crew arriving at an island inhabited by a gnarly, angry tribe of half-shelled coconuts called Kakamonas. articles.text: Prior to 1922, a largely neglected park with a rustic Japanese tea house and a bandstand sat on land that had originally been owned by Frank C. Havens. That year, the City of Piedmont acquired the land and engaged architect Albert Farr to design a civic center. His elaborate plan featured a Spanish Colonial design that included the Community Hall, a rose garden, expansive lawns, and the iconic Exedra. Funded by a bond issue, the construction of both the Exedra and the Community Hall began in 1924 and was completed in 1925, marking their 100th anniversary this year. Unfortunately, the Great Depression soon followed, halting the completion of Farr’s grand design. How fortunate for Piedmont to have these two incredible structures. The term “Exedra,” originating from ancient Greek, is defined by Webster as “a room, building or outdoor area with seating, where conversations were held.” Piedmont’s Exedra is that, and much more than just a place to sit and talk. The front of the Exedra has remained unchanged, still featuring its distinctive iron gates and blue vase. The area behind the Exedra, however, has seen significant improvements over the years and much of that is thanks to the dedication of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. ing signs of age. That September, the City accepted a generous gift of over $26,000 from PBF to restore the Exedra “to its original elegance”. PBF also agreed to oversee the project. Under the leadership of PBF President Barbara Magee, a committee was formed with Bob Leefeldt, former Chair of the Park Commission, at the helm. The restoration work was meticulous, including the use of epoxy injections to patch and seal cracks in the walls. It was believed this material would be more flexible and durable than plaster. Research was also undertaken to find a paint that would be resistant to graffiti. The most challenging part of the project was repairing the iron gates, which required an additional $15,000 in fundraising. The project was so delicate that Leefeldt had to present his plans to the City Council for approval. Leefeldt told the Council, “The gates were assembled like a fine Swiss watch.” The gates were removed carefully, treated with brushed steel material, and then reinstalled. Forty-five years later, the restoration has stood the test of time. During this period, PBF has played a significant role enhancing the area behind the Exedra with several important projects. In 2001 the Matthew Lempres Memorial Fund and the Marianne Lempres Memorial Fund provided support for a beautiful fountain and a terrace of tiles, as well as seating areas. These additions have transformed the space into a delightful spot for conversation – true to the Exedra’s ancient Greek meaning. In 2008 the Barbara Magee Overlook was dedicated with steps down to the plateau overlooking Bushy Dell Creek and the canyon. This project honored Magee’s contributions to both the Exedra’s renovation and other initiatives during her presidency of PBF and many years as an advisor. Shortly afterwards, a special moonlighting installation from the Exedra to the Magee Overlook was completed in memory of Frances Bishopric, another longtime PBF advisor. But the most special thing about Piedmont’s Exedra is that it has become much more than a place to sit and have conversations. Today the Exedra is a symbol of the City itself—rivaling the thistle which adorns the City’s white flag. Its location in front of a graceful crescent of Highland Poplar Trees (named as Heritage Trees in 2019) together with the planting circle, often filled with purple and white flowers, stands as a perfect focal point as one walks or drives down Highland Avenue to the center of town. In 2002, under the leadership of then President Betty Shapiro, PBF adopted the Exedra as its logo. Various depictions had appeared on earlier PBF documents, but in 2002 the present version became official. {More recently a brandnew on-line newspaper chose the name “The Exedra.”} In fact, images of the Exedra pop up here and there all over the City. The author gives special thanks to Sharon Hom and Gail Lombardi, who provided much historical background for this article and for the four preceding articles about significant PBF projects. Thanks also to The Post, which provided generous coverage for the articles and their accompanying photos. Visit the PBF website for information about current projects: www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org The front of the Exedra has remained unchanged, still featuring its distinctive iron gates and blue vase.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to share their thoughts on a proposed structure and pricing model for use of the new community pool. Residents can provide input by speaking at a Pool Advisory Committee study session tomorrow, Thursday, February 13, at 6:00 p.m. at City Hall. Community members unable to attend the meeting can submit comments by email to cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Email comments received by 4pm on February 13 will be shared with Committee members at the study session. The proposed model, called “Build a Pass,” is designed to offer community members broad flexibility to purchase annual or seasonal (summer) passes that meet the unique needs of their household. In contrast to the limited pass options available at the old pool, this framework creates opportunities for everyone to access passholder benefits without paying for features they don’t need. Proposed options and pricing The model begins with a choice of base category (adult, senior, family, student), then offers add-on options (adult, senior, youth, guest) that can be mixed and matched as-needed. Visitors could choose from an annual pass, which offers the largest discount, a seasonal summer (4 month) pass, or drop-in day passes. The proposed rates are benchmarked to adult pass pricing for 2019, the last full year of pool service. Proposed pass rates would begin at 15% above 2019 levels, with annual adjustments based on inflation. Across all pass options, non-resident rates are proposed at 20% above resident pricing. Other considerations and next steps The Committee will also discuss additional benefits being considered for passholders, including: • priority access to pool use during peak hours or days (all passholders) • priority registration for swim lessons, summer swim camps, and junior lifeguarding (annual passholders) • priority reservations for Poolside Room and Pavilion rentals (annual passholders)

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club hosted its 38th annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 8, at the Veterans Hall in an energetic celebration. The fundraiser for Wildwood Elementary School drew 150 parents, community members and crab lovers together for an evening of all you can eat, drink and dance. The parents club supplied dozens of volunteers to help plan, decorate and deliver the feast, along with the help of sponsors donating wine and cocktails. The “Island Vibes” theme was well adhered to, with many patrons wearing traditional crab bibs to protect their well coordinated outfits. Dads Club volunteers spoke on stage briefly, as event leaders Scott Zengle and Sergio Serna addressed the crowd dressed in grass hula skirts and Hawaiian shirts. As always, the star of the show was the crab– in this case 250 pounds of fresh Dungeness crab. “It’s just a really great opportunity for everybody to get together, have a fun time, meet new parents and support the kids Matt Derrigo (left) fills a plate alongside other shellfish fans at the Wildwood Dads Club Crab Feed.

articles.text: Editor: Piedmonters should take a good look at the depiction of housing the city is proposing be built under the Objective Design Standards (https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/objective_ design_standards_open_house_ feb_2025). That figure shows 4 units – two wall-to-wall duplexes on a lot divided 60/40 under SB9 – and is applicable to every single-family residence in Piedmont. This is a “Wistaria Way” accident waiting to happen to many residents in Piedmont. State law allows developers to build this 4-unit scenario with only 30 days of staff review and no public notice. Residents should participate in these ODS public meetings. Start by watching the YouTube video at the link. There’s an interesting semantic exercise wherein a subjective definition for front entry way is redefined in objective terms. Perhaps staff can develop objective definitions for massing, parking requirements, view, noise and yard setbacks so we can maintain the neighborhood character and privacy that Piedmonters enjoy. The Planning Department should use ODS development to preserve existing design guidelines, as best it can. -Garrett Keating 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Tony Simons Sophie Hess, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz offers ideas for New Year’s resolutions Happy New Year! Each January, the turning of the calendar offers a reset - an opportunity to embrace new lifestyle choices. But for many of us, when the month draws to a close our most ambitious resolutions have already fallen by the wayside. Today, I offer four suggestions for simple yet impactful alternatives – planet-friendly lifestyle adjustments you can start working into your routine at any time. • Buy local Buying local can have two meanings. The first is centered on purchasing locally sourced goods - like gathering supplies at a farmer’s market or craft fair. The second is the support of small or community-based organizations. Shopping at these businesses strengthens community rapport, solidifies jobs, and improves the local economy. Buying local lowers transportation emissions that would come from traveling longer distances for goods or from services for online purchases. • Drive less As of 2022, 46% of Piedmont’s total greenhouse gas emissions came from passenger vehicles. One easy way to cut back on emissions is carpooling. Team up with a group of neighbors to rotate school drop-off trips in the morning. Fewer cars on the road means lower emissions, less congestion, and saves money on gas. There are also significant social benefits to carpooling that can foster new friendships for kids and parents alike. Alternatively, try mixing up your routine by walking, biking, or taking public transportation occasionally instead of driving. • Purchase second-hand goods Instead of ordering a new book online, browse used bookstores or the library. Instead of purchasing fast-fashion, look for vintage, upcycled, or thrifted clothes. Like shopping local, buying second-hand lowers transportation emissions. Shopping second-hand also eliminates emissions and resources used in manufacturing and packaging. • Be water conscious The simple act of turning the faucet off while brushing your teeth can save 3.75 gallons of water. Shorter showers and fewer dishwasher cycles are other easy Piedmont Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz ways to conserve water at home. To calculate your water use, refer to the East Bay MUD Watersmart Calculator at https://www.ebmud. com/water/conservation-and-rebates/residential/watersmart-calculator. Bonus: being water conscious is more than just a sustainable practice – it also lowers monthly utility bills! The beauty of these resolutions is they can be attempted at any time. Even if you find yourself being inconsistent, each step you take is progress toward a sustainable future. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting residents to help make a selection of new playground equipment at Linda Beach Tot Lot. A brief online survey is now available. The survey builds on two recent events at the tot lot where staff spoke to playground users about their preferences and priorities for new playground equipment. The survey invites community members to share: • how often they visit Linda Beach Tot Lot • what age children they bring • what they like most about the Tot Lot • which types of equipment are most important to include • whether they prefer matting or playground “turf” for the new playground surface The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/BeachTotLotSurvey and will remain open through February 21. In addition to replacing the aging playground equipment, this project will: • create ADA access from Linda Avenue to the playground • resurface the playground with ADA compliant matting or turf • install a new water fountain or bottle filling station Funding for the project was included in the 2024-25 City budget and includes a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. articles.text: Applications are now open for appointed volunteer positions on six City Commissions or Committees in Piedmont – Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, Civil Service Commission, Park Commission, Planning Commission, Public Safety Committee, and Recreation Commission. Serving in these volunteer positions is an excellent opportunity to learn more about the inner workings of City government. Commissioners help shape City programs, policies and services by providing a valuable resident perspective on upcoming and proposed projects. Applicants can learn more about the work of Commissioners by watching past meetings on the City’s online video archive at https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/kcom-tv/live_content_and_video_archive. Residents can apply online by February 28 at piedmont. ca.gov/Commissioner. Key Dates for Applicants Applicants must be available for a pre-appointment interview with the City Council and a mandatory in-person training at City Hall before assuming their position. • Applications Due: Friday, February 28 5pm • Mandatory interviews: Monday, March 10 (evening) • Required Brown Act Training: Monday, March 31 (evening) • Appointments effective: Tuesday, April 1 (Effective date for Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee appointment is July 1.) For most bodies, members are appointed to 3-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Studies and provides recommendations on annual budget, long-term financial projections, mid-year budget adjustments, and the City’s municipal services tax rate and renewal. Meets as needed Civil Service Commission • 2 Vacancies (1 Incumbent eligible to reapply) Deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. Meets as needed Park Commission • 3 Vacancies (3 Incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to public parks and street trees. Meets monthly on first Wednesdays, 5:30pm. Planning Commission • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to planning and building. Makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. Requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Meets monthly on second Mondays, 5:30pm. Public Safety Committee • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to crime reduction and disaster preparedness. Meets bi-monthly Recreation Commission • 2 Vacancies (1 Incumbent eligible to reapply) Advises on issues regarding recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space and other issues. Meets monthly on third Wednesdays, 7:30pm. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm
articles.title: Commission & Committee Applications open now until Feb. 28

articles.text: Construction is scheduled to begin on Friday, February 14 on a project to replace the pedestrian footbridge over Bushy Dell Creek in lower Piedmont Park. There will be path closures and detours in Piedmont Park for 4-6 weeks while the project is underway. This project, supported by State of California Proposition 68 grant funds, will replace the existing bridge with a long-term durable bridge in the same alignment, composed of a weathered steel frame with pressure-treated wood decking. A new bridge has been fabricated off-site and will be delivered to the park then installed by a crane. New footings are being constructed in advance which requires the area around the bridge. Three benches near the base of Bushy Dell Creek will be removed temporarily in order to allow truck access and will be re-installed once construction is complete. The bridge, located in the southwest portion of Piedmont Park near the PUSD softball field, was first identified as in need of replacement in 2015. The bridge is over 30 years old and has required substantial repairs twice in the past five years. Holes in the wood decking have been temporarily patched with plywood, and temporary side rails were constructed in 2023 after the original protective railings collapsed due to rotten wood. The City asks residents to respect detour signs and avoid closed paths when visiting the park.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 12, 2025 5 Pardee Home Museum Musicale: Moonglow Trio By Tony Simons The Pardee Home Museum is hosting an afternoon of music with the Moonglow Trio on Sunday, February 23, from 3:00-5:00 p.m. Back by popular demand, the museum invites community members to enjoy a lovely afternoon in the museum garden. The program will feature music from the Great American Songbook plus some gypsy jazz. A champagne reception with sweets and savories will follow. The Moonglow Trio consists of Richard Chon on violin and vocals, John Nichols on guitar, and Bing Nathan on bass. Reservations are required. The cost of admission is $25. Tickets can be purchased at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ pa rde e -home -mu seu m-musicale -moonglow-t r io -t ickets-1236288565379?aff=oddtdtcreator. Call Richelle Lieberman (510-381-1973) for more details. All proceeds go to the museum. The Moonglow Trio will be at the Pardee Home Museum on Sunday, February 23, from 3:00-5:00 p.m. Bridge on Bushy Dell Creek closed for repair By Tony Simons Construction is scheduled to begin on Friday, February 14 on a project to replace the pedestrian footbridge over Bushy Dell Creek in lower Piedmont Park. There will be path closures and detours in Piedmont Park for 4-6 weeks while the project is underway. This project, supported by State of California Proposition 68 grant funds, will replace the existing bridge with a long-term durable bridge in the same alignment, composed of a weathered steel frame with pressure-treated wood decking. A new bridge has been fabricated off-site and will be delivered to the park then installed by a crane. New footings are being constructed in advance which requires the area around the bridge. Three benches near the base of Bushy Dell Creek will be removed temporarily in order to allow truck access and will be re-installed once construction is complete. The bridge, located in the southwest portion of Piedmont Park near the PUSD softball field, was first identified as in need of replacement in 2015. The bridge is over 30 years old and has required substantial repairs twice in the past five years. Holes in the wood decking have been temporarily patched with plywood, and temporary side rails were constructed in 2023 after the original protective railings collapsed due to rotten wood. The City asks residents to respect detour signs and avoid closed paths when visiting the park. It’s time to book your exterior painting project! Contact us now and beat the summer rush. Lic. Serving in these volunteer positions is an excellent opportunity to learn more about the inner workings of City government. Commissioners help shape City programs, policies and services by providing a valuable resident perspective on upcoming and proposed projects. For most bodies, members are appointed to 3-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. articles.text: Celebrations Hawn authored another update to the school community in her bi-monthly Piedmont Pulse newsletter on Monday, February 10. An abridged version is below. View the full collection of school news and updates at Piedmont.k12.ca.us/ref/superintendent#fs-panel-9259. Dear PUSD Families & Staff: At last week’s Board Study Session, the Board provided direction to staff to pursue a number of program options to implement for the fall, including additional performing arts in grades 4 and 5, additional world language in grades 5-7, and additional courses at the high school level, including AP Seminar and Vocal Music. Staff are now collaborating on what the implementation looks like. Slide deck for the budget study session: Docs.google.com/ presentation/d/1AyPbjn_DPjmkoVmBWjuK3MowvjsNSNk0cIm3aj-P8eg/edit . If you have thoughts on these options, we sent out a survey several weeks ago where you can still submit ideas, via Docs.google.com/forms/d/e/ 1FAIpQLScsmlpVTbJyLxCXlFV6Y1TJTYm1ARWmaPiPf HmYHvIbs7dTOg/viewform. Following collaboration and input from staff and families, we will present information to the Board in the months to follow. Thank you for your partnership in supporting our students. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Once Upon a Mattress One of the many outstanding aspects of our district is our performing arts programs, including use of the Alan Harvey Theater. Congratulations to Amy Moorhead and our students for a fun production of Once Upon a Mattress, the comedic adaptation of The Princess and the Pea. As always our students were wonderful, with an array of costumes, and an enjoyable evening for all ages. Students from Spain arrive It was great to attend a reception on February 2 for students and staff from Spain (Galicia) who are part of a cultural exchange program for our high school students. Thanks to Deysi Sahagon, Ken Brown, Joanne Guillen along with parent supporters who have made this wonderful exchange program happen. Our Spanish visitors will be here through February 11, and our students and staff will visit Spain over spring vacation. Art, Literature Thanks so much to the Beach staff, including Ms. Harris for letting a Board member and me drop into her K art class where kids were creating art based on Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are–wonderful! Later in the week, I visited high school English classes, including Dr. Marks’ AP Literature class where students were studying Milton, and Mr. Wolbert’s 9th grade English class where students were working on their I-Search projects. Many of you know I taught high school English for many years, and visiting our expert teachers amazing work! Students learn the power of words I happened upon a lesson at Havens last week in which our students were learning about the power of language, including the meaning and impact of racial slurs and discriminatory language. Thanks to Jean Takazawa for her leadership, along with our high school Affinity Mentors who facilitated the lesson for our elementary students. Thanks also to our Havens teachers for their collaboration on teaching students the importance of appropriate language and behavior. Threat Management Team - Committee members needed Pa rent s/Gu a rd ia ns: We launched a committee last year to establish safety procedures for threats to the campus. Since the launch, we have collaborated with PPD, PFD, and our staff on developing a process for threats that we hope we never need. At this point, we have a draft document that we would like to refine and finalize. We are looking for 1-2 experts in mental health threat assessment who would be willing to join our committee and advise on our internal procedures. We anticipate two additional meetings this year, and an annual meeting thereafter. The next meeting is scheduled for February 25 at 11 a.m. in person. If you would like to join us, please let us know Docs.google.com/ forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSccvZ4MrB0245O1P5ZeV0coABgQszIp- 8pJjEMakKQVSA5_RHQ/viewform . Thank you for your consideration.

articles.text: 557 McReynolds Rd., Sausalito (415) 339-3900 Located in the shadow of the Golden Gate Bridge at Fort Baker, the Bay Area Discovery Museum is worth the trip west to Sausalito. Both indoor and outdoor spaces are open. The outdoor portion of the museum boasts 7.5 acres of exhibits, landscapes, activities and installations. There’s a gravel pit, crow’s nest, fishing boat and a shipwreck for kids to play on. Designed for infants, toddlers and younger kids. Museum of Art and Digital Entertainment (MADE) MADE is the only all-playable video game museum in the world. Featuring 11,000 games kids and adults will have a great time and get educated on video game programming as well. Play thousands of games on original hardware and check out one-of-a-kind pieces of gaming history. MADE is open into the evening 9:00 p.m. Friday and Saturday The Oakland Zoo sets the standard for world-class animal care in captivity. There are so many species at the zoo to marvel at, while learning about conservation in the wild. The Zoo is open every day from 9:30 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. Take the gondola to the amazing boardwalk of the California Trail, for viewings of wolves, buffalo and bears. The skyride, amusement rides and a brand-new electric train are open as well. Buy tickets in advance. 2140 Mandela Parkway, Oakland, 903-6722 Pacific Pipe Climbing Gym is the perfect space for rock climbing excitement and instruction kids love. Does the rain have your kids stuck inside and bouncing off the walls at home? Take them somewhere where they can literally climb the walls. The expansive space has 46,000 square feet of climbing, with enormous climbing walls up to 55 feet and many programs for climbers of all ages and skills. It is also a great place to host a birthday party. Pacific Pipe has extensive hours of operation seven days a week.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District has announced it is offering April Adventures, enriching programs for local students April 7-11 at Havens Elementary School providing a week of learning and fun. Mornings will focus on academic enrichment, while afternoons will feature creative and recreational activities, special performances, and Piedmont Park scavenger hunts. Program hours are 9:00 a.m. -3:00 p.m. with extended care available from 8:00-9:00 a.m. and 3:00-5:00 p.m. Summer Adventures Summer Adventures will return for another exciting season, serving students in TK through 6th grades with two sessions at Havens School. • Session 1: June 10-20 • Session 2: June 23-July 3 Students can enjoy morning academic enrichment classes, followed by afternoon recreation options including art, sports, science, and cooking. Full-day and half-day options are available, with extended care from 8:00- 9:00 a.m. and 3:00-5:00 p.m. Welcome to TK & Kindergarten Designed for students entering these grades in fall 2025, these sessions provide young learners with a sneak peek into their upcoming school experience. Children will engage in fun and developmentally appropriate activities led by teachers and staff, helping them adjust to a structured school schedule while making new friends. Welcome to 6th Grade This program is designed to help incoming sixth graders transition smoothly to middle school. Students will familiarize themselves with their new campus, daily schedules, and expectations while engaging in writing activities and team-building games to build confidence for the fall. Junior CIT Program (Grades 7-8) The Junior CIT (Counselor-in-Training) Program is open to students in 7th and 8th grades interested in developing leadership skills and gaining experience assisting with activities. Junior CITs will have the opportunity to help in both morning and afternoon sessions, learning valuable skills while making a difference. Participants can register for either the morning (9:00 a.m. - 12:00 p.m.) or afternoon (12:00 - 3:00 p.m.) sessions. Registration for both programs opens February 14 for April Adventures and February 25 for Summer Adventures. To register and for more details visit the PUSD website: www.piedmont.k12.ca.us.
