articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School (PMS) Parents Club is now selling tickets for a PMS fundraiser on Thursday, March 27, “Kickin’ It Old Skool.” This is the school’s biggest fundraiser and will take place at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Party-goers will eat, drink, and dance the night away to favorite music from the 80’s and 90’s. The Kickin’ it Old Skool event, formerly known as “March Mingle,” will feature a live auction with special items including a Lake Tahoe vacation rental, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, and sporting event tickets. Old school sneakers like Vans and Keds are recommended. There will also be a raffle and surprises that can be described as “totally radical.” Don’t miss the rare opportunity to relive memories of junior high school days and the culture unique to the era. The event will be co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several Parent Parties, including a Pub Quiz night and Intro to Poker. The PMS Parents Club hopes the parents parties will help raise funds to support school programs. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27, knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Funds will support: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking out a few more Parent Sponsors. Please see Pef. schoolauction.net/marchmingle2025/homepages/show for more details. Parents are encouraged to attend while dressed as they did in their middle school days.
articles.title: PMS “Kickin’ It Old Skool” Fundraiser on March 27

articles.text: Why it matters even in difficult times In life’s toughest moments, joy can feel out of reach. Yet creative expression—through art, music, writing, and more—often brings light to even the darkest places. Why does creating spark joy, and why is that joy essential when Creative expression connects us to something deeper. The process itself, not just the outcome, is 1. Flow State: Creative activities induce a sense of flow—a state where you become deeply absorbed, losing track of time and gaining a sense of fulfillment. 2. Emotional Release: Art externalizes feelings we can’t always verbalize, offering relief and clarity. 3. Playfulness: Creativity encourages experimentation and discovery, reigniting childlike curiosity and wonder. 4. Sense of Accomplishment: Completing a creative project, whether big or small, can spark pride and satisfaction Why joy matters during hardships Joy doesn’t erase pain but provides balance, resilience, and hope when we need it most: 1. Emotional Strength: Positive emotions replenish mental and emotional reserves, making challenges feel less overwhelming. 2. Hope and Optimism: Small moments of joy remind us that beauty and possibility coexist with hardship. 3. Connection: Sharing creativity fosters human connection—whether through community performances, collaborative projects, or heartfelt creations gifted to others. All kinds of creativity, including taking an art class, helps to spark joy in one’s life.
articles.title: Finding joy through creativity

articles.text: In March each year Piedmont’s five Scout troops host an open house for youth in fifth grade and up and their parents. It allows them to choose which troop to join. A total of 20 percent of youth in Piedmont participate in a Scouting program – a record high on a national standard. But what if you aren’t sure why your family should even be considering this option? Throughout the week of February 10th, Piedmont Scout Council is hosting information sessions Each informational meeting is open to all, though we welcome parents of 5th grade kids from Piedmont’s specific elementary schools on the following dates at 7:30 pm: February 10, Wildwood parents; February 11, Beach parents info session; February 12, Havens parents. Glen Tripp, Vice President of Scouts BSA, will lead each session. For seven years he served as Scoutmaster of Troop 15 and is the father of two Eagle Scouts. He has seen the incredible transformative impact that Scouting has on the lives of youth. For the location and details of each informational session, please contact Glen at glentripp@ gmail.com or visit the open house landing page: https://www.piedmontbsa.org/2025/01/21/troopopen-houses-2025/
articles.title: Scout Council hosts Info. sessions in advance of Troop Open Houses

articles.text: Fairyland’s new 75th Anniversary sign was Installed on January 28. Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, is celebrating its 75th anniversary in 2025. Leading up to the park’s official anniversary on Tuesday, September 2, 2025, Fairyland will celebrate all year with exciting special events for visitors of all ages. “Fairyland’s 75th anniversary celebrates the timeless magic of imagination, the boundless wonder of childhood, and the resilience of our community,” said Executive Director Kymberly Miller. “For generations, Fairyland has been an oasis where families escape the ordinary, craft cherished memories, and discover life’s simple joy of connection and belonging. As we honor 75 years of history and look to the next 75, we are committed to preserving Fairyland as a welcoming, joyful space where the spirit of imaginative play continues to shine.” To kick off its historic year Fairyland has unveiled a sparkling new lawn sign on Fairyland Hill overlooking Lake Merritt. The updated sign invites the community to join the yearlong festivities. Fairyland has planned a year filled with exciting events, new experiences, and collaborations to celebrate its 75th anniversary: park exploration and imaginative play and offers fun rewards yearround. 75th Anniversary Special Museum Feature: Opening Friday, April 4, 2025, a new collaborative installation titled “Fairyland @75: A Legacy of Magic” will be on view at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA), highlighting Fairyland’s rich history, cultural impact, and enduring magic. New, Original Puppet Shows: Two brand-new productions will debut in 2025, adding to Fairyland’s renowned storytelling tradition. • What Makes a King (July 11– August 24): A story inspired by Maya myths that explores themes of leadership and courage. • Tío Conejo’s Big Wish (August 30–October 26): Fairyland’s first bilingual puppet show, based on a Cuban folktale about self-acceptance. Exclusive 75th Anniversary Merchandise: Including a limited-edition Magic Key (now on sale), Willie the Whale plushie (now on sale), and more to come. Fairyland’s Passport Card: Launching March 21, 2025, this in-park activity encourages 75th Birthday Party: On Labor Day, Monday, September 1, 2025Fairyland is hosting a Jubilee celebration featuring cakes from local bakeries, performances, arts & crafts activities, and other family-friendly activities—more details to come later in the year. Happily After Hours Events for Adults (21+): Fairyland’s four adult-only nights invite guests to experience the park after hours, without kids. Each themed evening features unique activities, entertainment, and the release of exclusive collectible prints created in collaboration with local artists. Full Calendar of Family Events: Explore every event happening throughout the year by visiting Fairyland’s Calendar of Events at https://fairyland.org/ assets/1672d2d183/FL.2025.CalendarofEvents.pdf. While the new sign celebrates this milestone year, Fairyland remains deeply committed to its collaboration with the Sogorea Te” Land Trust and its mission to honor the Ohlone people, the original stewards of this land. The “Children’s Ohloneland” sign, which first appeared in November 2024, will return later this year. In addition, Fairyland and Sogorea Te’ Land Trust are working on exciting future projects, including a puppet show debuting in 2026 that will highlight a story from the Ohlone culture.
articles.title: Children’s Fairyland celebrates 75 years of Imagination, Education, and Magic

The fresh cracked crab nearly silenced the large and festive crowd, save for slurps and the sound of crab claws being tossed into the metal waste buckets on each table. The side dishes were up to the high standard with melted butter, toasted bread and lemons on each table. The ovenbaked salmon, New Orleans spicy spinach, and creamy mac ‘n cheese were consumed heartily as well. A lineup of live entertainment included Dads Club DJ Ben 2025 Crab Feed volunteers Erik Knutson (left), Adam Cunha, Shor Bowman, Matt Derrigo, and Joel Tornatore There were no crabby daddies at the event; everyone was well fed. Kathy Derrigo (right) got to the front of the line early, in ravenous wait for the buffet to open. Wildwood Dads Club President Jake Strzelecki (left), with DJ Ben Anderson, Scott Zengel and Sergio Serna Robin Stearns (left), Jovie Strzelecki, Linn Hillestad, and Kathy Derrigo Anderson, who brought along a DJ from the Burning Man collective Space Cowboys. Multiple PHS Jazz band combos took over Max Roman (left), Mike Stearns, and Rohit Giri on stage, some of whom were wearing their Winter Ball tuxedos and formal wear. All in all, everyone left the event full, happy and merry, as another rousing success for the Wildwood Dads went in the books. Piedmont Veterans Hall was transformed from top to bottom for the 38th annual Wildwood Dads Club Crab Feed.

articles.text: John and Sue Malick on a visit to Croatia. As residents of Piedmont for over 40 years, Sue and John Malick have demonstrated a love of the city rivaled only by their love for each other. John and Sue met on a blind date in 1972. Sue was an undergraduate at Wheaton College in Massachusetts studying political science and John had just started graduate school studying architecture at Yale. The couple dated for three years before getting married in 1975, two weeks after John finished his Masters degree. They married in Harvard, Massachusetts, a little town 30 miles west of Boston and unrelated to Harvard University. They lived in Portland for a while when John worked for global architectural and urban planning firm Owings and Merrill. Moving to Piedmont in 1983 for its schools, the couple planted roots in town to raise their three children – Andrew, Mollie, and Nick. After celebrating many Valentine’s Days together, Sue Malick still has every Valentine’s card her husband John has given her – well over 40 now. This year, the couple plans to enjoy a Valentine’s dinner for themselves and six friends that they purchased at a benefit for Piedmont Choirs this past Fall. “We’re going to be served and serenaded by one of the high school sections of the choirs, and by Eric Tuan, their artistic director,” said Sue. “And I hope we’re going to be celebrating Eric getting an NEA grant for the opera he’s been writing.” Sue doesn’t mind having extra company on the most romantic of holidays. In fact, Valentine’s Day is a great opportunity to enjoy the bonds of community that the Malicks have fostering for many years. “It’s a day of just appreciation – for not just my husband, but every one in my life who I love,” said Sue. “There’s so much to love about this town and my life,” said Sue. “And that’s part of Valentine’s Day, too – just the world we’ve built here.”
articles.title: John & Sue Malick – A song of love for each other and community

articles.text: The Post caught up with Max and Tory Roman to learn about the Piedmont couple’s wedding and what a husband must do for a wife who has a birthday the day before Valentine’s Day. The Romans were wed in Dunbar, Scotland in 2014, and last summer they celebrated their 10th anniversary in Scotland as well. Max is a Piedmont native who has returned to his roots to raise his two children in town. He jumped into serving the community and is now in his first term on the school board. The couple met in Los Angeles in 2012. “We met on EHarmony. I completely lied and said I lived in Los Angeles and I liked hiking. Then we went on dates, and I neither lived in Los Angeles nor enjoyed hiking,” acknowleged Tory. Max eventually learned Tory was only temporarily in L.A. She was heading to Chicago and then New York to be in the musical Kinky Boots, which was to be produced at a theater on Broadway. Upon learning of the little fib, Max said that they made it work anyway. “We had gone too far at that point. She was smart and it was a good strategy,” he said. Max was smitten and picked Valentine’s Day to surprise Tory. “He sent me the most beautiful bouquet of roses to the rehearsal studios. And I think the whole cast and creative team of Kinky Boots lost their minds, and were like, you better marry this guy,” recalled Tory. Tory, then Tory Ross, actress Max and Tory on their wedding day July 5, 2014, in Dunbar, Scotland. and Broadway performer, wasn’t subtle about her intentions. “Well, she started harassing me to propose pretty early and sort of created a sense of inevitability around it. Six months in I had a pretty good idea,” said Max with a smile. Soon enough the wedding date was set for June 5, 2014 in Scotland, where many of Tory’s family still resides. In 2016, Max returned to Piedmont with wife Tory and their 8-month old twins. For the couple, Valentine’s Day holds many memories and is not to be confused with another important day, February 13. “I made it very clear when Max and I were dating that my birthday and Valentine’s Day are separate occasions, therefore, I am to receive separate gifts,” said Tory. Tory, taking the Piedmont Post’s call from 12,000 km away while boarding a plane in Israel, took the opportunity to remind her husband, of her request for a robust toaster oven and air fryer unit for her birthday tomorrow. “We’re living the Piedmont dream, because Max is now Mr. Piedmont on the school board,” said Tory with a smile.
articles.title: Max & Tory Roman on Valentine’s Day

articles.text: Kate Benson is the Executive Director of the Piedmont Scout Council. She and her husband Neil’s relationship first took flight while the two worked at the Portland Airport, loading freight planes as they prepared for their future careers. Seeing each other’s work ethics through the physical labor their hearts began to soar as they talked about the deeper subjects of life while waiting on late planes to arrive. The couple married in 2003 at a picturesque Scout Lodge on the east side of the Portland with a view of the mountains. “It had a huge picture window that framed Mount Hood, and was a beautiful building,” Kate reminisced. With their two daughters in tow, Kate and Neil moved to Piedmont at the end of 2020 in the middle of the Covid quarantine. “It was a hard time for our whole family to move and try to make new friends and community connections. Sometimes we still find something we’ve missed that would otherwise be obvious to new arrivals,” said Neil. In time, the couple was able to find a home in Piedmont for themselves and their daughters, now in 10th and 7th grade. Kate and Neil Benson have been married for 22 years. The family has managed to find a church home, a scout troop, sports that they love, and Kate even found a book club to join. Kate and Neil prefer to enjoy a simple and modest Valentine’s Day. They sometimes celebrate it with a dinner for the family. But the Bensons’ favorite Valentine tradition is an at-home date night while sharing a giant candy bar together. “It’s a low-key holiday for us. We’re more likely to find something special in the everyday rather than save it for later,” said Kate. “We’ve walked through some significant health issues with each other, and know how important it is to say and show ‘I love you’ to each other as often as possible.” Neil and Kate continue to count their blessings, recognizing their love for each other every day. “We’ll ask each other, ‘Are you blessed?’ No matter what’s going on, the answer is ‘Off the charts.’”
articles.title: Kate and Neil Benson

Person not trespassing at time of initial contact and is advised to leave area. 20 minutes later, another resident reports man jumping fences & in the backyard of houses on Crocker and King Ave. Person located and detained; is arrested for loitering. Parole officer contacted; man is transported to Santa Rita Jail. 4:12 p.m. Harvard Rd. articles.text: PHS girls on track to split league title with 2 games left It was a triumphant week for Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team, claiming two wins against to whom they had previously lost. The Highlanders defeated Bishop O’Dowd 50-47 in the Dragons’ home gym on Wednesday, February 5, and also beat Antelope 61-47 at home in Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, February 8. PHS lost to O’Dowd 56-47 on January 14 and fell 53-51 to Antelope on January 25. Their victory over the Dragons means Piedmont is on track to split the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division title with O’Dowd for the second straight year. Piedmont still must take care of its final two regular season games – against Alameda tonight, February 12, and Castro Valley on February 14. The recent two wins bring their record to 19-4 and 5-1 against league opponents. O’Dowd rallied to tie the game 46-46 in the fourth quarter, but Staff Photos Piedmont players celebrate after the final whistle of their win over Bishop O’Dowd. were held to just one point in the remaining minutes. “We have four losses and each of them have been very similar, where we didn’t find ways to figure it out in the fourth quarter. They came back and tied it, but we are progressing,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Briana Webb led Piedmont’s scoring with 15 points against Bishop O’Dowd. We lost by nine last time, so we wanted to come out strong. We played for each other and that’s how we won. There was no other thought than to go home with a win, we were talking about this game all week,” senior Briana Webb said. “We lost [the earlier game] at home, and that helped motivate us [in the second game]. We heard a lot of chatter from people saying O’Dowd should blow us out. I think that motivated everyone to push harder,” Solis said. 50-47 victory over Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont closed the first quarter with an 11-10 lead, moving to the front when Taylor White found Savannah Dennig for a layup with 27 seconds left. There were four lead changes in the second quarter with Piedmont leading 24-20 thanks to a 3-pointer by Solis in the final seconds. In the third, Piedmont established a 10-point lead with 3:15 left after a layup by White while they carried a seven-point advantage into the fourth up 40-33. Things got nervy in the fourth with the Dragons battling back to tie it at 46-46 with 3:27 left in the game. But Piedmont turned up the defense from there, allowing just one point via a free throw. Webb hit a big layup to make it 48-46, then Solis hit one of two free throws. Webb closed the game with a free throw with 16.4 seconds left. Final stats: Andrea Martin had five points, 10 rebounds, three assists, and six blocks. Dennig had eight points, 10 rebounds, two assists, and a steal. White had four points, seven rebounds, two assists, two steals, and a block. Webb led with 15 points, two rebounds, and two steals. Cleo Afsar had two points and a steal. articles.text: Staff Photos Niko Markopoulos (no. 22) scored Piedmont’s first goal against Alameda. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team split its recent pair of league matches to brings its record to 5-4-8. It handed Alameda a 2-nil loss on Tuesday, February 4 under the lights at Witter Field, but lost to league leaders Berkeley 2-1 on the road on February 7. Match details against Berkeley were not available. Against the Hornets, Piedmont scored both of its goals in the first half when Niko Markopoulos scored in the 19th minute and Bosco Lorin put away a penalty kick in the 39th. It was also a strong performance by goal keeper Daniel Malecki to keep the clean sheet, recording five saves on the night. The Highlanders have just one match left in its regular season as they look to fight for a North Coast Section berth, visiting Castro Valley on Thursday, February 13. Piedmont last defeated the Trojans 1-0 on January 21. 2-0 shutout of Alameda Early in the game, Piedmont goal keeper Daniel Malecki came up big with a string of saves in the eighth minute. After saving an initial shot, Alameda recovered in Piedmont’s penalty area. Malecki then made a diving save, which rebounded back into play for another shot attempt that was stopped. Alameda stayed on the front foot with a few shot attempts going wide or blocked. But against the run of play, Piedmont broke through in the 19th minute. In the buildup toward goal, Max Goldfarb played a long pass up to Gianluca Bini, who took on two defenders before laying off a pass to Markopoulos standing unmarked a couple of yards inside the penalty area. On his first touch, Markopoulos sent a hard shot toward the left post—sending a laser past Alameda’s keeper. Both teams traded possession from there with Lorin taking the next shot attempt from a long free kick from 30 yards out in the 28th minute. Roman Ahearn had a shot deflected wide in the 31st. Piedmont then drew a free kick a yard above the penalty area in the 38th, leading to Lorin taking a shot that hit off an Alameda defender’s outstretched hand— drawing a penalty kick. Lorin stepped to the spot, firing it to the left of the keeper for the goal. In the second half, Malecki did well to rush off his line to push a shot wide in the first minute back in action. Malecki came up with another save on a slow shot in the 50th minute. Alameda then had a shot from close distance narrowly go high in the 68th. Both teams traded possession in the remaining minutes without generating anything overtly challenging. Tuesday vs. Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont hosted Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 11. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-4-8 overall, 3-3-4 league) visits Castro Valley on Thursday, February 13 at 7:00 p.m. Staff Photos Bosco Lorin put away a penalty kick against Alameda to make it 2-nil. Photo by Scott Stratford Goalkeeper Daniel Malecki had five saves against Alameda for the shutout.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team had a difficult run over the last week with two losses to Western Alameda County Conference opponents. They lost 72-63 on the road at Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, February 5, and took a 76-67 loss to Berkeley at home two days later. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 12-12 and 2-6 in the Foothill Division. Against O’Dowd, PHS narrowly inched back into the game and trailed 50-42 with one minute left in the third quarter. However, the Dragons took control from there. “O’Dowd’s an extremely wellcoached team and they have a lot of size. They got up to [a19-point] 19 points and we cut it to eight points in the third. Our kids have heart and the fight is there. For our younger guys who haven’t played here at O’Dowd, there’s always a learning curve,” coach Ben Spencer said. The Highlanders had to do its work without the team’s No.2 scorer, Dillon Casey in both games, leaning on senior leader Ravi Silverberg—who scored 23 points against O’Dowd and 24 against Berkeley. “To not have Dillon was huge. He has started every game for the last two years. Ravi is a warrior and has college potential. He can score against the best of them,” coach Spencer said. The Highlanders have two games left in its regular season, visiting league-leaders Alameda tonight, February 12, while they try to break the hearts of Castro Valley on Valentine’s Day, February 14, at Binks Rawlings Gym. 72-63 loss to Bishop O’Dowd O’Dowd got out to an 18-9 lead in the first quarter and extended the gap to 37-21 by halftime. BOD continued their 16-point advantage through the third up 60-44, while Piedmont was able to cut it to nine points in the fourth quarter with 19 points. In the third quarter, Piedmont went on a 16-5 scoring run to cut the Dragons’ lead to 50-42 with less than a minute to go, but that was the closest things got for the Highlanders. From there, BOD ended the third with eight unanswered points. O’Dowd established a 19-point lead in the fourth. Piedmont chipped it down to 11 points with 2:02 left, but it was too little too late. Lucian Fang-Ring closed the game with a 3-pointer to make it a nine-point loss. Final stats: Ravi Silverberg led with 23 points, Fang-Ring had 12 points, Emmett Asulin Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg led Piedmont’s scoring against O’Dowd and Berkeley with 23 and 24 points respectively. Lucian Fang-Ring knocks down a 3-pointer against Bishop O’Dowd with Piedmont’s student section behind him. P.J. Brayer had nine points against O’Dowd and 16 vs. Berkeley. had two, Beach Lorin had six, Cash Panico scored 11, while P.J. Brayer had nine. 76-67 victory over Berkeley Berkeley came out scorching hot to establish a 27-9 lead in the first quarter and extended the lead to 45-24 by halftime. Piedmont out-scored the Yellowjackets in both quarters of the second half, trailing 57-40 through the third, while scoring 27 points and conceding 19 in the fourth. Final stats: Silverberg led with 24 points, Brayer had 16, FangRing had 10, Lorin had eight, Panico scored six, and Johnny Lee had three. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team looks ahead to the season-finale against Encinal. Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team suffered a narrow 1-nil loss to Castro Valley while playing on the Trojans’ home field on Wednesday, February 5. The result brings their record to 5-2-8 (W-T-L) and 2-1-5 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. It’s been an injury-riddled season for the Highlanders, suffering extensive injuries throughout the season. Since January PHS has gained just one win in nine matches after finishing 2024 with three wins and a draw through six matches. Three-year starting midfielder and captain Louisa Symkowick has missed multiple weeks, and the Highlanders were without leading scorer Elsa Wallway against Castro Valley after she suffered what is likely to be a season-ending injury the previous week. Piedmont’s been without starting defender Darcy McKee for most of the season while fellow defender Eliza Hammond missed a stretch of time. Although the Highlanders are below a .500 winning percentage, it can qualify for a North Coast Section playoff berth given that they are 1-0-0 against other Division 4 schools. Piedmont notably defeated Div.4 foe Cardinal Newman 2-1 on December 10. PHS has just one match remaining in its regular season, hosting Encinal on Thursday, February 13. Piedmont will honor its nine seniors on the roster, including Friedie Schickedanz, Juliana Thornborrow, Samantha Ronen, Eliza Hammond, Hannah Sullivan, Kyra Trombi, Louisa Symkowick, Ava Sauer, Ryo Woltag, and Genevieve Hiller. Eliza Hammond had a shot on target from a free kick against Castro Valley.

Since January PHS has gained just one win in nine matches after finishing 2024 with three wins and a draw through six matches. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team is back in the gym for their off-season weight lifting program led by assistant coaches Oski Tauaho (middle, left) and Bo Tauaho (middle, right). Early in the morning for the past four years a swarm of Piedmont High football players lines up at the school’s weight room to prepare for the season. Getting to Witter Field bright and early to lead the workouts are the offensive and defensive line coaches, Oski and Bo Tauaho. After winning two consecutive Western Alameda County Conference titles and the school’s first North Coast Section win since 2017, there’s no doubt about the success of the training program the Tauaho brothers have constructed. “We met head coach Seiden when he was running weights in the morning the season before we came on. We revamped how we lift weights; it’s just teaching them the mechanics behind it,” Oski said. “The results have been pretty good, just to see the development of the kids when they start with us. When we get toward the summer, you start to see the changes with them moving better and getting stronger,” mentioned Bo. Oski and Bo came to Piedmont High as members of coach Jordan Seiden’s staff in 2023, one year after his arrival when the school had to drop its varsity due to a small roster. Injuries were a major part of the 2022 team’s downfall, but after the arrival of Bo and Oski’s weight-lifting program, the number of injuries significantly dropped. “It’s been amazing to watch the football team grow. We came after the 2022 season and Jordan was telling us about the program. His plan was to just keeping it growing and we told him that we could run the weight-lifting; it’s a good way to get the kids out there. It’s not just playing football, you have to work out and have a good offseason too,” Bo said. “You lift weights in the offseason to prevent injuries when the season comes. You have to strengthen all of your muscles to prepared to rock and roll when the season comes,” Oski said. Since then, Piedmont won the 2023 WACC Shoreline title, receiving a berth in the D7 NCS playoffs. After a promotion to a more competitive division, they won the 2024 WACC Mission title and were undefeated against league opponents. With that, the sport’s popularity at the school has revived. It’s something that makes both coaches proud. “I’m proud of the guys. It starts with the players and if they lock in, they’ll see the results. Winning games starts in the offseason and the guys have been pretty good at committing to that. The weight room builds confidence, they believe in what they are doing,” Bo said. “The 2025 class was the one leading the team, a big part of it was just having that leadership. It’s a proud statement of staying the course and building; you see the results from the past two seasons,” Oski said. On the heels of their WACC title run, Piedmont will have a staggering 16 seniors graduate. They’ll have to replace the bulk of their starting cast, including at quarterback, receiver, running back, and the majority of defensive roles. articles.text: Honorable Mentions: Andrea Martin & Lucas Malecki Staff Photos Jenelle Solis was named Athlete of the Week after leading Piedmont to big wins over Bishop O’Dowd and Antelope. We have named Jenelle Solis of the basketball team and soccer player Bosco Lorin as Athletes of the Week, with honorable mentions to soccer goalie Lucas Malecki and basketball player Andrea Martin. Jenelle Solis appears as our Athlete of the Week once again after being an honorable mention for January. Over the past week, Solis was a major part of Piedmont’s wins against Bishop O’Dowd and Antelope. Against O’Dowd she scored 12 points and had three assists, and had 15 points and six assists against Antelope. Bosco Lorin makes his first appearance as Athlete of the Week honors after making a big difference in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Alameda. In the game he drew a penalty kick after his hard shot on a free kick made contact with a defender’s hand. Staff Photos Bosco Lorin earns Athlete of the Week after scoring and drawing a penalty kick against Alameda. took the PK and scored the goal to put his team ahead by two. Honorable Mention Andrea Martin last appeared as our Athlete of the Month in December but then missed nearly two weeks in January with an illness. She had a strong return to the starting lineup over the past week in Piedmont’s big wins over O’Dowd and Antelope. She led with 10 rebounds in their big victory over O’Dowd. Against Antelope, Martin led the way with a double-double, logging 24 points and 10 rebounds. Lucas Malecki earns an honorable mention after helping Piedmont keep the shutout in their 2-nil win over Alameda. articles.text: [Reprinted from February 2023] There is no better time for viewing bodies of water following the recent rains. Just nine miles from Piedmont is a trail that will make you forget that you’re in the hustle and bustle of the Bay Area with the Kings Canyon Loop off of Canyon Road on the way to Moraga. Parking at East Bay MUD’s Valle Vista Staging Area, the Kings Canyon Loop is a moderately challenging trail that walks alongside the Upper San Leandro Reservoir. Hiking the loop requires 6.4 miles of walking and around 950 feet in elevation gain. The reservoir is the most full it’s been in years, providing fantastic views for the majority of your hike. Walking along the northern portion of the reservoir, there’s a continuous great view of the rolling East Bay hills as you walk along the winding trail. It’s a great location for birding or catching sight of little critters. On multiple occasions, California newts were spotted passing by on the trail. As for the difficulty of the trail, about 75 percent of the trail was manageably flat, but once California newts can be spotted along the Kings Canyon Loop trail. you hit the 4.5 mile mark, the trail noticeably ramps up in elevation gain—providing 460 feet in ascent in just half a mile—so roughly half of the day’s elevation gain is in one portion of the trail. It’s worth mentioning that several portions of the trail were oversaturated with mud, making it difficult to walk through without slipping. Be advised to use caution and patience when passing over slippery surfaces. After walking alongside the reservoir for those 4.5 miles, the trail takes into the hills and narrows down from over 10 feet wide to just a few feet in some sections. It traverses underneath groves of Oak trees and eventually provides an overhead view of the reservoir. At the 6-mile mark, you come to an intersection to continue on Electric power towers are overhead on the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Watch out for several muddy and slippery areas. articles.text: Uncle Vanya, a heartbreaking comedy about the eternal battle between futility and change, opens at Berkeley Repertory Theatre February 14 through March 23. Olivier Award-winner Conor McPherson’s acclaimed adaptation of Anton Chekhov’s masterpiece will be directed by Shakespeare Theatre Company Artistic Director Simon Godwin, in a co-production with Berkeley Rep. Joining Golden Globe and Emmy Award nominee Hugh Bonneville as Vanya is Tony Award winner John Benjamin Hickey (Astrov), Ito Aghayere (Yelena), and Melanie Field (Sonya) When a distinguished elderly professor and owner of a rural estate returns home with a new young wife, Yelena, chaos erupts. Tensions run high, marriages reach their limits, as confessions and vodka flow freely. Two friends – Vanya, brother of the professor’s late first wife, who has long managed the estate, and Astrov, the local doctor – Golden Globe and Emmy Award nominee Hugh Bonneville plays the lead role as Vanya in a new adaptation of Chekhov’s haunting comedy Uncle Vanya at Berkeley Repertory Theatre, February 14 through March 23. both fall under Yelena’s spell while bemoaning the ennui of their provincial existence. Sonya, the professor’s daughter by his first wife, who has worked with Vanya to keep the estate going, suffers from her unrequited feelings for Astrov. Matters are brought to a crisis when the professor announces his intention to sell the estate, being Vanya and Sonya’s home, with a view to investing the proceeds to achieve a higher income for himself and his wife. Although Chekhov’s play had previous small runs in provincial theatres in 1898, its metropolitan premiere took place in 1899 at the Moscow Art Theatre, where the play became a permanent fixture. Tickets ($25-$134) and showtimes for performances at Berkeley Rep (2025 Addison St.) are available online at berkeleyrep. org, or by phone at 647-2949 (Tuesday through Sunday, 12 p.m. to 7 p.m.).
articles.title: Uncle Vanya opens at Berkeley Rep this Friday

articles.text: Opera San José Emeritus Artist-in-Residence Maria Natale sings the role of Judith and Zachary Nelson is Duke Bluebeard in a new production of Béla Bartók’s opera Bluebeard’s Castle Saturday through March 2. This Saturday, February 15 through March 2, Opera San José presents an all-new production of Béla Bartók’s chilling one-act opera Bluebeard’s Castle. This psychological thriller, directed by Opera San José (OSJ) General Director and CEO Shawna Lucey, follows Judith, a woman who uncovers terrifying corners of her new husband’s dark past while unlocking rooms in his eerie home. “Bluebeard’s Castle” will feature Emeritus OSJ Artist-in-Residence soprano Maria Natale — whose recent acclaimed portrayals at OSJ include the title role in Tosca and The Countess in The Marriage of Figaro — as the unwitting bride who comes to live in the haunted realm of a mysterious duke. Acclaimed baritone Zachary Nelson will make his OSJ debut as Duke Bluebeard, and OSJ Music Director Joseph Marcheso is set to conduct this powerful work. OSJ is collaborating with the Silicon Valley dance company New Ballet to feature three dancers as the previous wives of Duke Bluebeard: Delaney Ewert, Alysa Reinhardt and Sorcha Tate. The piece, including a libretto by Béla Balázs, will be performed in English, with both English and Spanish supertitles projected on stage. Bartók’s staggering opera premiered at the Royal Hungarian Opera House in Budapest in 1918. Based on, and departing from, the tale of Bluebeard from French folklore, the opera delves into psychological themes of love, trust and the unknowable depths of the human soul. The work is acclaimed for its lush and evocative orchestration, which conveys the dark, mysterious atmosphere of Bluebeard’s castle, and its dramatic vocal writing for the two characters, Bluebeard and Judith. Bartók’s innovative use of Hungarian folk music influences and modernist techniques creates a gripping narrative soundscape and has remained a cornerstone of 20th century opera, praised for its emotional intensity and symbolic depth. “I can’t wait to bring this mesmerizing opera to our audiences,” said Lucey. “Besides its stunning orchestration, the work is emotional and unforgettable. From fierce brass sections to rich strings and sonorous woodwinds, the music and terrifically challenging vocals take us on a truly chilling thrill ride for a little over an hour. Fasten your seat belts for this memorable one-act work.” “Classically Curious” night for Bluebeard’s Castle will be held Friday, February 21, bringing together people who have a passion for deepening their involvement with opera. This program was created to introduce new audiences to opera, offering access to discounted tickets, exclusive behind-the-scenes opportunities and social events that connect emerging opera lovers. More information can be found at go.operasj.org/ClassicallyCurious. To buy tickets ($58–$215) for the performance at California Theatre (345 S 1st St., San Jose), visit operasj.org, or call the box office at 408-437-4450.
articles.title: Bluebeard’s Castle at Opera San José through March 2

articles.text: Smuin Contemporary Ballet will present its Choreography Showcase in San Francisco, this Friday through February 23. Ten premieres will be unveiled ranging from humorous to heartfelt and featuring a variety of dance styles and musical selections. Presented at the Smuin Center for Dance, these intimate performances will provide audiences with an invaluable glimpse at the rising choreographic voices within the company. Smuin will also host preshow talks and post-show Q&As, in which audiences will enjoy insights into the program and creative process behind the ballets. This thrilling opportunity for audiences to experience never-before-seen world premieres by first-time and rising dancemakers was inspired by founder Michael Smuin’s commitment to put the artistic reins into the hands of dancers, providing them with the time, space and talent to develop their choreographic skills. “Choreography is a honed skill that takes practice, mentorship, and training,” said Smuin Artistic Director Amy Seiwert, a nationally acclaimed choreographer, as well as a former dancer. “Creating dance requires resources that aren’t always easy to access, such as skilled dancers and a dedicated space. Opportunities are rare in the ballet field but are so important in fostering the next generation of creative leaders.” Smuin Director Emerita Celia Fushille formalized the tradition by launching the company’s firstever Choreography Showcase in 2008. Since then, the opportunity has repeated annually or once every two years, with several of the works developed in the Showcase process adapted for mainstage premieres at Smuin. Experiences such as these are uncommon, particularly in the field of ballet, as they are logistically and financially difficult to organize. “We are investing in our dancers to become stronger collaborators,” added Seiwert. “The experience is incredibly valuable as they gain an understanding of what it takes to create a piece, and strengthens their skill set as a dancer working on premieres by other creators.” Tickets ($35-$55) and schedule information for the shows at Smuin Center for Dance (1830 17th Street, San Francisco) are available online at smuinballet. org, or by phone at 415-912-1899. Smuin Contemporary Ballet’s Choreography Showcase will be performed in San Francisco this Friday through February 23. Pictured are Maggie Carey and Brennan Wall in A Harlem Night from a production in 2023.
articles.title: 10 ballet world premieres to be unveiled in San Francisco

Sonya, the professor’s daughter by his first wife, who has worked with Vanya to keep the estate going, suffers from her unrequited feelings for Astrov. Matters are brought to a crisis when the professor announces his intention to sell the estate, being Vanya and Sonya’s home, with a view to investing the proceeds to achieve a higher income for himself and his wife. Smuin Dance Showcase in SF Feb. 14-23 10 ballet world premieres to be unveiled in San Francisco By Selen Ozturk Smuin Contemporary Ballet will present its Choreography Showcase in San Francisco, this Friday through February 23. Ten premieres will be unveiled ranging from humorous to heartfelt and featuring a variety of dance styles and musical selections. Presented at the Smuin Center for Dance, these intimate performances will provide audiences with an invaluable glimpse at the rising choreographic voices within the company. Smuin will also host preshow talks and post-show Q&As, in which audiences will enjoy insights into the program and creative process behind the ballets. This thrilling opportunity for audiences to experience never-before-seen world premieres by first-time and rising dancemakers was inspired by founder Michael Smuin’s commitment to put the artistic reins into the hands of dancers, providing them with the time, space and talent to develop their choreographic skills. “Choreography is a honed skill that takes practice, mentorship, and training,” said Smuin Artistic Director Amy Seiwert, a nationally acclaimed choreographer, as well as a former dancer. “Creating dance requires resources that aren’t always easy to access, such as skilled dancers and a dedicated space. Opportunities are rare in the ballet field but are so important in fostering the next generation of creative leaders.” Smuin Director Emerita Celia Fushille formalized the tradition by launching the company’s firstever Choreography Showcase in 2008. Since then, the opportunity has repeated annually or once every two years, with several of the works developed in the Showcase process adapted for mainstage premieres at Smuin. Experiences such as these are uncommon, particularly in the field of ballet, as they are logistically and financially difficult to organize. “We are investing in our dancers to become stronger collaborators,” added Seiwert. “The experience is incredibly valuable as they gain an understanding of what it takes to create a piece, and strengthens their skill set as a dancer working on premieres by other creators.” Tickets ($35-$55) and schedule information for the shows at Smuin Center for Dance (1830 17th Street, San Francisco) are available online at smuinballet. org, or by phone at 415-912-1899. articles.text: Works of women composers to be performed livestreamed The Shoreline Piano Trio presents “Exploration of Love and Art,” a concert celebrating the works of women composers this Valentine’s Day, Friday at 8 p.m., at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco. The concert will also be livestreamed by the trio – violinist Sui-mi Shin, cellist Katie Youn and pianist Menghua Lin. The program includes works by Caroline Shaw, Maria Theresia von Paradis, Jessie Montgomery, Amy Beach, Pulitzer Prize-winner Jennifer Higdon, and the iconic Romantic composer Clara Schumann. Sue-mi Shin is an avid chamber violinist, orchestral performer and music educator. She was one of the founding members of Yule Piano Trio and Sonnet Ensemble, where she served as the artistic director for many seasons. As an active orchestral performer, she plays with the Opera San Jose orchestra, Symphony San Jose and Monterey Symphony among many others. She holds degrees from Manhattan School of Music and Yale University. Katie Youn has appeared as a cellist in concerts throughout North America, South America, Europe and Asia, in venues including Boston’s Symphony Hall and Jordan Hall, Japan’s Suntory and Minatomirai Hall, Vancouver’s Orpheum Hall, and Vatican City’s St. Peter’s Basilica. She regularly appears with Sound Impact, Chamber Music Silicon Valley, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra and Sonnet Ensemble. She holds Bachelor and Master of Music degrees from the New England Conservatory and a Doctorate of Musical Arts form Boston University. Menghua Lin began her piano studies at four, winning prestigious competitions including the Pittsburgh Concert Society, Steinway Society West Pennsylvania, Chautauqua Music Festival Concerto Competition and YAMAHA Piano Competition. She holds a degrees in piano performance from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Carnegie Mellon University and the Manhattan School of Music. articles.text: Immersive science and art exhibition runs Feb. 15 through April 27 This Saturday through April 27, experience our solar system like never before at the breathtaking exhibition “Look Up: Eclipse, Moon, and Mars,” at the Exploratorium in San Francisco. Feel the thrill of space exploration as you immerse yourself in the beauty of a total solar eclipse, marvel at monumental realistic sculptures of the Moon and Mars and explore the rovers supporting NASA’s latest breakthroughs in space exploration. This cosmic experience will spark curiosities of all ages and inspire your imagination of our solar system and humanity’s next great frontier — space “‘Look Up’ brings the excitement of space exploration to life through art, science and technology,” said Rob Semper, chief science officer at the Exploratorium. “This exhibition is a rare opportunity to explore the tools and results of our ongoing exploration of the solar system’s most breathtaking phenomena, right here on Earth.” “Perfect for explorers of all ages, ‘Look Up’ is more than just a visit – it’s an invitation to discover, share, and be inspired,” said Sylvia Algire, Director of Museum Experience. Exhibition highlights include: Immersive eclipse experience Step into the awe-inspiring phenomenon of a total solar eclipse. Produced in collaboration with Montreal-based multimedia production studio Supply + Demand, this prototype experience uses state-of-the-art visuals and soundscapes to capture the magic of this celestial event. The Moon and Mars Marvel at breathtaking largescale planetary sculptures by British installation artist Luke Jerram. His featured work, “Museum of the Moon and Mars,” is inspired by Jerram’s childhood in Bristol, UK, where the moon-tugged tides are the second-highest in the world. This artwork, printed from 120 dpi NASA imagery, shows the moon’s every cliff and crater at an approximate scale of 1:700,000; one inch of the sculpture equals about 11 miles of the lunar surface. NASA’s Mars Rovers and Orbiters Meet NASA space explorers Perseverance, Sojourner, Odyssey and more, and discover how these groundbreaking missions are helping us learn about Mars, the Red Planet. These remarkable instruments are on display thanks to a special loan from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The exhibition also builds on the Exploratorium’s decades-long partnership with NASA to livestream total solar eclipses from across the globe, making this a uniquely rich and immersive experience for visitors. The Exploratorium (Pier 15 Embarcadero at, Green St, San Francisco) is open 10 a.m. through 5 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday (with additional Exploratorium After Dark hours from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. on Thursday), and 12 p.m. through 5 p.m. on Sunday For more information and to purchase tickets ($39.95 for adults 18-64, $29.95 for youth 4-7, teachers, students and seniors), please visit exploratorium.edu/ space or call 415-528-4444. This Saturday through April 27 experience our solar system like never before at the breathtaking exhibition “Look Up: Eclipse, Moon, and Mars,” at the Exploratoriumin San Francisco.

articles.text: Production delights audience and dancers Tamara Rojo’s inaugurated her third season as Artistic Director of the San Francisco Ballet with Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon, an evocative ballet about the dangers of desire. Set in pre-revolutionary France, the ballet charts the transformation of Manon from a naïve girl on her way to join a convent to a passionate lover, courtesan, and ultimately a prisoner transported from Paris to New Orleans, offering an exploration of the challenges faced by a woman in a society constrained by class and wealth. Far from a fairy tale, this is a story of passion and despair, portrayed through profoundly expressive choreography. Despite the demanding nature of their roles, the dancers clearly reveled in performances, their enthusiasm matched by those of the audience. MacMillan, of Scottish descent, transformed British ballet, steering it away from the refined lyricism of Fredrich Ashton and the structured classicism of Ninette de Valois, his predecessors at the Royal Opera House. Known as the “angry young man” of dance—akin to John Osborne in literature— MacMillan is celebrated for ushering The Royal Ballet into an era of psychological realism and intense emotional storytelling. Manon, which debuted at the Royal Opera House in London in 1974, showcases a fusion of modern dance shapes with classical ballet lines. The ballet moves at a fast cinematic pace, transitioning between continents and times periods, yet always firmly rooted in the characters’ psychological reality. On January 31st, the last evening performance of the season, the title role of Manon was danced by Nikisha Fogo, the Company’s first black female principal dancer—and a new tour de force whose athleticism and technical brilliance is magnified by her radiant onstage presence. Aaron Robison danced the role of Des Grieux, a young student who falls in love with the beautiful Manon. Their on-stage chemistry was palpable, adding a layer of complexity to an otherwise standard naïve young lovers’ conceit. They were brilliantly paired with Fernando Carratalá Coloma as Manon’s brother Lescaut and Katherine Barkman as his mistress. All four dancers transcended typical ballet character archetypes, emerging as fully realized individuals while demonstrating remarkable command of their discipline. Two scenes were particularly striking. First, the drunken dance in Act 2, where Lescaut, portrayed by Coloma, must navigate a lavish party while inebriated. MacMillan’s choreography brilliantly captures his intoxication as an artistic feat—his movements are unpredictably off-kilter; his legs buckle, he lunges as if gravity betrays him, and he collapses into his mistress’s arms, only to be jerked upright again. This pas de deux strikes a precarious balance between humor and menace, showcasing Coloma’s impressive technical and artistic skills. Second, the more sinister scene in Act 3 features Manon being assaulted by a Louisiana prison guard. Earlier tender moments between Manon and her lover give way to the brutal force of a man who views her as merely an object. Fogo’s portrayal of Manon in this scene is harrowing—she flails and convulses, sometimes from almost impossible positions, like lifting her legs nearly 90 degrees while lying face down. Her frantic, desperate resistance leads to heavy, uncontrolled falls that deviate from classical ballet’s grace, underlining the realism of her terror and accentuating her vulnerability. The compelling dancing is complemented by dynamic, sumptuous sets and exquisite costumes. Both evoke scenes of extreme poverty and decadent wealth—the two worlds between which the characters oscillate. Lavish gowns crafted from lace and tulle dazzle the eye, set in stark contrast to the ragged clothing of the poor. San Francisco’s performances of Manon revive the iconic 1974 sets and costumes Photo by Lindsay Thomas Jasmine Jimison in Manon originally created for the Royal Ballet by the renowned designer Nicholas Georgiadis. Within the costume waistbands, one can find the names of all the cast members who have worn them since 1974. “It is an incredible honor when you get to wear a costume that perhaps was once on the stage, on the body of an artist you admire,” Rojo remarked. Among those names on the bands was Rojo’s own, as she has also danced the lead role in Manon. The seemingly effortless beauty and elegance of the San Francisco Ballet’s Manon, which belies the long weeks of strenuous rehearsals, costume fittings, and set management, was not lost on the audience. The theater was packed, and the applause at the end was longer than usual. Manon represents a strong start to the 2025 season for the San Francisco Ballet and is yet another gift to the city from this renowned company. It is especially valuable at a time when beauty and enjoyment are hard to come by. Anastasia Edel is an American writer and arts critic for the Piedmont Post. San Francisco Ballet in MacMillan’s Manon. Photo by Lindsay Thomas

articles.text: Don’t miss an artful weekend with the California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition this Saturday. Return on Sunday to the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) for Music by In the Tradition jazz trio. Watercolor exhibition Join the California Watercolor Association (CWA) in celebrating the 85 artists selected by juror Michael Holter for this year’s international exhibition on February 15, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. at PCA. The awards, totaling an estimated $16,000 in cash and sponsorships, will honor the top 20 paintings selected by Awards Juror, artist Gary Bukovnik. CWA’s free annual event, honoring exceptional watermedia paintings from talented artists worldwide, will be running from Saturday through March 23. It will continue to be free from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, and will also be viewable for attendees of other events at PCA. Organized in 1967 as East Bay Watercolor Society, it changed its name in 1996. Throughout the decades, the organization has continued to support artists and students working in watermedia through community outreach programs, workshops, public exhibitions, scholarships and student workshops. Don’t miss this opportunity to see this exhibition of some of the world’s finest new watercolor works. No tickets are necessary. In the Tradition Join Bill Jackman, Albert Brooks and Michael Jones in celebrating Valentine’s Day with “In the Spirit of Love!” at PCA on February 16 at 4:30 p.m. This skilled jazz piano trio will play all your favorite love songs from the 1910s through the 1960s including ballads, swing, a little Latin flavor and even some blues — sweetened by complimentary refreshments. This Sunday’s lineup of jazz and pop standards includes “You Made Me Love You” (1913), “Someone to Watch Over Me” (1926), “I Only Have Eyes for You” (1934), “I’m in the Mood for Love” (1935), “Like Someone in Love” (1944), “That’s Amore” (1952), “Never on Sunday” (1960) and many more. Bill Jackman, playing with the trio for the past 30 years, was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher, who for several decades presided over the grand piano at the former Solomon Grundy’s (now Skates) on the Berkeley Marina. Jackman is also a Lupita Records musician who has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Michael Jones is a bassist and band leader who has played throughout the Bay Area for over 30 years. After studying music at the University of Northern Colorado, he moved to the Bay Area in the mid-1970s, where he played with many icons including Al Tanner, Faye Carroll, Ed Kelley, Donald Bailey, Pharoah Sanders and Buddy Montgomery. As a sideman and bandleader, Jones has served as the music director for the Golden Gate Library Summer Concert and Jam Session series in Oakland for the past 23 years. Albert Brooks grew up dancing to Latin music in the South Bronx, playing these rhythms on any percussion instrument he could get his hands on. Alongside Latin drumming, he added trap drums to his musical offerings several decades ago and fluently melds these with swing rhythms. articles.text: Bounce opens in a Chicago airport, the weather heavy snow, flights are delayed or cancelled. Three waiting passengers are gathered around a small table near a crowded bar. Strangers, they exchange names and professions: Mimi (Natasha Henstridge). Buddy (Ben Affleck), and Greg (Tony Goldwyn). Mimi is on her way to Dallas, Buddy and Greg are waiting for their L.A. flights to open up. Greg learns that his flight was just cancelled, and he shows them his gifted hotel voucher. Mimi and Buddy are still hopeful their flights, though pushed, will depart. Buddy has been told that his flight will be the last to L.A. They are three personable, attractive and eager to get home. Greg shares that he is married with two young boys (it is the holidays and he has promised his wife, Abby (Gwyneth Paltrow), that he will hurry back to take them Christmas tree shopping). Gwyneth Paltrow and Ben Affleck in Bounce All of the above is just a brief introduction to the next two acts that follow. To say more would deprive the audience of a story that becomes incrementally compelling. It’s enough to say that with each scene the question is asked: will Buddy seize the moment? Of course he doesn’t. Bounce brings to mind the Sydney Pollack film Random Hearts, also layered with multiple questions that are only partially resolved. It stars Harrison Ford and Kristen Scott Thomas as two strangers who share a devastating tragedy that changes their lives forever. Now Streaming on apple tv/prime/Fandango. Bounce. Directed by Don Roos. Starring Gwyneth Paltrow, Ben Affleck, and Tony Goldwyn. 1 hr., 46 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2000. Now streaming on Paramount+/Fandango.

articles.text: Talent and musical genius often runs in the family. Johann Sebastian Bach had 20 musical children and a very large and talented extended family. We remember Frederick the Great for his military genius. Perhaps we need to remember him for his musical genius. And believe it or not, his two sisters were equally Other famous musical families include the brother and sister duo of Felix and Danny Mendelssohn, and three generations of Mozarts. In our area we are happy to mention the Menuhin family with a brother and two sisters, and the Ricci family with two brothers More recently, the Hansen family has been active on the music scene. The father was a noted band conductor, and son Eric Hansen has been the subject of this column on many occasions. He continues as the brilliant conductor of the Prometheus Eric‘s younger sister Robin Hansen is a noted violinist in our area. As such, she is a stalwart performer in many orchestras. For her concert yesterday afternoon in the Berkeley City Club she gathered some important musicians for a chamber music concert. Joining her were pianist John Wilson, violinist Ani Bukujian, violinist Elizabeth Prior, and cellist Saul Richmond-Rakerd. The program itself was out of the ordinary. It began with a Piano Trio by Amy Beach, then a String Quartet by Mozart, and finished off with a Piano Quintet by Samuel Coleridge-Taylor. The musical proficiency of the performers was obvious from the very beginning. I was particularly interested in the tone that Robin Hansen draws from her violin. The instrument was made by the great violin maker Mario Frosali, who was a very good friend of mine. Violinistically speaking, Violinist Robin Hansen the performance was notable for its subtle virtuosity abetted by an underlying lyricism. These aspects graced the playing of the other musicians. The music of Amy Beach is seeing a rebirth. Her music, like the music of Samuel College-Taylor which concluded the program, is exemplified by great technical skill and a dearth of memorable melodies. I liken these two composers to the musical skill of Cilea, albeit without his melodic gifts. Throughout the concert, technical precision was at the forefront. Impressive though this was, what I missed were nuances of dynamics. As I surveyed the audience, I did not see any musicians in attendance. All five of the featured players are well known throughout the Bay Area. This alone should have encouraged their friends and colleagues to attend. Sorry to say, these friends and colleagues were notable for their absence. When I was a student, my professors, most notably Jascha Heifetz and Gregor Piatigorsky, encouraged all of us to attend the concerts of our colleagues. They said that we owed it to our colleagues, and added that perhaps we might learn something from their performances. They were right. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

articles.text: Yesterday opens with Jack Malik (Himesh Patel), wannabe rocker, trying to explain to his manager/best friend, Ellie (Lilly James), that he has decided to accept the handwriting on the wall, meaning the empty-room gigs he’s been playing. It’s time to give up music and resume his career as a schoolteacher. Ellie argues that he should continue. Shortly thereafter, riding home one night on his bike, guitar on his back, there is a strange, worldwide blackout wherein everything goes dark. Unseen, riding through an intersection, Jack is struck by a bus and ends up in the hospital with Ellie at his bedside. Essentially undamaged, he is soon released and given a welcome home party beachside where Ellie presents him with a new guitar. She asks him to play a song and Jack, reluctantly, plays and sings “Yesterday” by the Beatles. Ellie and their friends listen, agape, Ellie asking, breathlessly, “What was that?” And when did he write it? All agree it was wonderful. Puzzled, looking at them for signs that they are teasing him, Jack insists that of course they know that song. It’s one of the most iconic by the Beatles. All of them shake their heads. “Who?” they ask. “The Beatles. You know, the Beatles.” Still nothing. And it’s in this moment that the predicate/premise of Yesterday is offered up. Jack is gradually made to understand, with the aid of Google, that he is living in a world that has never heard of the Beatles, or their songs, causing Jack to say, “This is the most complicated joke I’ve ever heard.” What exactly happened during that blackout, causing his accident, is never explained. Which is all to the good. The point is that the story should be happily embraced, enjoyed, and definitely not overthought. Sure it’s a bit Sci-Fi, mind bending. But all that follows this slightly off center reality distortion is remarkably entertaining. Jack, song after song, reframes most of the Beatles’ catalog from memory and it’s in this new world context, that the stand-alone genius inherent in the music is affirmed. Again and again. articles.title: The History of Piedmont

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 12, 2025 The History of Piedmont Cable Cars in Piedmont By Gail G. Lombardi A cable car ride to the country was the perfect way to spend a Sunday afternoon in the 1890s. From 1890 to 1893, riding the cable car to the Piedmont hills was a favorite pastime. Cable cars provided convenient transportation for residents in the Piedmont hills to downtown Oakland and San Francisco, and almost more importantly, they brought visitors and future residents into the hills. In 1873, Andrew Hallidie built the first cable car line in San Francisco, and by 1889, there were eight cable car lines in the city. The first cable car in Oakland was running in 1886 along San Pablo Avenue. “8,000 passengers rode the cable cars [into Piedmont on the opening day of the cable car company in 1890].” A cable car stops at the passenger shelter at Oakland and Vernal Avenues before turning north on the turntable towards Blair Park. Note the vacant In 1890, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company began operating a cable car line into the Piedmont hills. The company built a large brick powerhouse to run two cables. One cable ran from the powerhouse up Oakland Avenue to Vernal Avenue (now Highland). The other cable ran to 8th and Clay Streets in downtown Oakland. Steam from the powerful engines heated the water for the popular Piedmont Baths next door. The opening day for the cable car to Piedmont was August 1, 1890. The cable company reported that 8,000 passengers rode their cable cars that day. While some cars were open, new green cable cars were designed with large windows and roofs “six to eight inches higher than those of other cars, so as to give passengers a better view of the scenery on route.” This was quite an improvement from the old horse cars. Dressed in their Sunday best, land in 1890. passengers enjoyed the picturesque ride up the hill to Piedmont. From the powerhouse, cable cars traveled at a swift eight miles per hour up Oakland Avenue through grassy fields and down, up more hills and across the wood trestle over the Linda Avenue ravine. As the cars ascended the final hill, passengers enjoyed views of downtown Oakland, Lake Merritt, and then the Bay and Golden Gate. Many rode the cable cars for the view alone. The cable car reached its apex at the turntable at Oakland and Vernal Avenues, an elevation of 341 feet. The cable car stopped at the turntable, and passengers bound for the Piedmont Springs Hotel disembarked and took the short walk south to the hotel. Five dining rooms, a wide veranda, a main salon and saloon offered pleasant places to enjoy an afternoon. Two years later, 1892, Piedmont Springs Hotel burned down. After arriving at the end of the line, the cable car conductor would rotate the car on the turntable to the north and release the cable, allowing the car to coast gently down Vernal Avenue to Moraga Road and Blair Park. Here, the remaining passengers enjoyed a larger, more improved Blair Park. To encourage ridership, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company added more attractions to the park, transforming it from Blair’s small picnic haven to a popular amusement park. (These new attractions will be explored in a future column.) The Piedmont cable car line was famous for its gravity loop, and some passengers rode the cable car for its exciting return ride. From Blair Park, the cable car coasted diagonally toward Oakland Avenue, gaining speed, sometimes reaching roller coaster speeds, on a winding course across Blair’s wheat fields. The conductor recaptured the cable near what is now Carmel Avenue, and the car proceeded at a more sedate speed to downtown Oakland. In her memoir, Evelyn Craig Pattiani remembers the famous “gravity loop” as “that most thrilling ride through the grain fields.” The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company was financially unsuccessful. It went into receivership in 1893 and was sold at auction in 1895. It was expensive to build and expensive to run. The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company built the powerhouse (right) and cable car barn (left) on Harrison Street near Lake Merritt in 1890. The engines that drove the cable ran on coal creating the black plume of smoke from its 136-foot smokestacks. The building was remodeled as a Cadillac showroom by architect Clay Burrell in 1925. It has been the Whole Foods building since 2007. An open air cable car in front of Blair Park on Moraga Road. Passengers wore their Sunday best outfits, complete with hats for this trip in the country. The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company ran five cable cars on Oakland Avenue every day and seven cars on Sunday. The tracks were set in solid concrete with a trench for the cable. To encourage more riders, the cable car company leased Blair Park and added many attractions including a bandstand for concerts on Saturdays and Sundays. Later, balloon ascensions with daring aerialists drew visitors to the park by cable car. These attractions also were expensive, and the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company failed to make a profit each year it ran. Though the cable car company did not prosper, it was a boon to early Piedmont real estate. Cable cars brought efficient public transportation to Piedmont. Many weekend visitors enjoyed the views and the climate and decided to build their homes here. A good number of Piedmont’s early 20th century houses were built near the cable car line on Oakland Avenue. It’s not surprising that the early horse cars, cable cars and electric streetcars were built by real estate investors. If you enjoy reading these biweekly columns on the history of Piedmont, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving its annual newsletter. More information on Piedmont’s history and membership is on the website, Piedmonthistorical.org. For additional information, contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@ pacbell.net. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on July 11, 2018.

Walkers learn history of Bear Park By Dick Carter The previous two Wednesdays the Walking on Wednesdays group had visited projects that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation has supported over its 60 years of serving Piedmont. There was a strong turnout of 56 walkers and five K-9 best friends forth e final tour of PBF projects. The first contributions, the Exedra Blue Vase, Exedra Plaza, and McGee Overlook, were right in front of them. Patty shared that this site was originally the location of the Piedmont Springs Hotel that Walter Blair built in 1871. After the hotel burned down in 1892, Frank C. Havens developed his Piedmont Park, a park café, a Japanese Tea House, and other attractions. After Havens died in 1918, the City purchased most of the park and hired Albert Farr in 1922 to design a City Center Master Plan. The Exedra and Community Hall were part of it and were dedicated in 1925. PBF’s first Exedra renovation began in 1972 with Blue Vase Triangle plantings, major structural and decorative repairs, iron gates, and lighting. In 2000, PBF also made major donations to the development of the Exedra Plaza, which is at the backside of the vase. The McGee Overlook was added with the Centennial Oak Grove. The Plaza was a great background for a group photo. The group then went across the top of the park to the Tea House where Cameron Wolfe and former Piedmont mayor and PBF president Valerie Matzger were waiting for them. Valerie and Cameron said this is not the original tea house that Havens built in 1907 as an attraction for his Piedmont Park. When the City acquired the land in the 1920s, the original tea house and many other park features were torn down to make room for the new Civic Center. In 1976 the Leander Redmon estate at Hillside and Magnolia Avenues was razed to build the new Piedmont Middle School. The estate had a tea house that was donated to the city and moved on a flatbed truck to its current site on a Sunday morning with many citizens watching. Next, the walkers went to the top of the park and the Highland-Guilford Steps where Gayle Lambert was there to tell them about this project. On a rainy winter day before Covid, she and Ruthie McCloud were walking down this path and found the railroad tie stairs uneven and slippery with no handrails. They met Chester Nakahara, the public works director, and Nancy Kent, the parks and project manager, and a renovation project was developed. It was approved by the City Council in 2021 with $55,000 from PBF and the Piedmont Garden Club and $100,000 from the City. The wooden steps were replaced with colored concrete, landings, metal handrails, landscaping, six benches, and a small plaza. The walkers continued to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues and up to the Hall Fenway, a scenic path that connects Wildwood and Crocker Avenues. Down the path was Sharon Hom ready to share more PBF history. This area once served as the right-of-way for the early 20th Century Key System’s #10 line streetcar, which ran through Piedmont until 1948. When the line was terminated, much of the right-of-way was sold for infill home developments. AC Transit even briefly used the land to park buses. However, Herbert Edwin Hall, a nearby King Avenue resident, convinced the City to obtain the property and he worked with neighbors to raise funds to acquire it in 1963. When PBF was established in 1964, it adopted the Fenway as one of its first major projects and raised more funds to complete its transformation. To honor Herbert Hall’s pivotal role, the path was officially named “Hall Fenway.” To ensure its long-term beauty, PBF has contributed $4,000 annually for plant maintenance. The group then went to Crocker Crocker Park. Cathy Glazier was at the Bear and Nursing Cubs sculpture in the middle of the park. She explained that this sculpture was the work of internationally renowned sculptor, Benny Bufano, and was a gift from Jerry S. Mosher to the citizens of Piedmont. Its placement in the park followed four years of negotiations between the PBF, the Piedmont City Council, and the Bufano Society of the Arts. This acquisition, valued at between $40,000 and $50,000 at the time, was installed in 1980 by Rigging International, a company owned by Piedmont resident Denny McLeod. It is number nine in a limited addition of 25 Bufano sculptures and is composed of polished ground granite that weighs 2 1/2 tons. PBF, led by then President Norma Wells, raised $4,700 to help with installation and landscaping. The bears were restored and cleaned in 2000, and a wrought iron bench was renovated in 2009. The group expressed thanks to Cathy, to PBF President Patty Dunlap and to PBF for all it has done for Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Cancer League celebrated its 51st annual Holly Ball on Friday, December 6th at Claremont Country Club. The event, chaired by Janet Nunan, was attended by 135 generous supporters who came together to raise over $300,000. These monies will be used to fund numerous “Seed-Stage” grants, focused on breakthrough cancer research and treatments. Flickering candles adorned surfaces covered in red tablecloths and opulent greenery. The guests sparkled in their red evening gowns and black tie. Delicious food and excellent wines donated by local businesses and wineries created a warm and elegant atmosphere. The Raise the Paddle event at evening’s close cemented a successful night of fundraising. As guests moved into the Lounge to dance, Chair Janet Nunan commented, “What a joyous night to celebrate the kindness of our guests who loyally support us every year in this quest to fund cancer research.” Holly Ball has helped raise over $7million in its 51 years. The mission of The Cancer League is to support accredited non-profit organizations dedicated to the fight against cancer. Since our inception in 1973, we have raised and donated over $7 million toward the fight against cancer. We have an average yearly allocations budget of over $300,000 and our average grant size is between $10,000- 50,000. Our work takes on a special significance given that each of our members has coped with cancer either personally, within their family, or in their circle of friends. The Cancer League is a charitable 501 (c)(3) organization. For more information see https://thecancerleagueinc.org.
