articles.text: On February 11, 1980, Benny Bufano’s iconic sculpture, Nursing Bear and Cubs, found its permanent home in Crocker Park. The successful installation was made possible through the generosity of Denny McLeod and his company, Rigging International, after a three-year campaign by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Nursing Bear and Cubs is Number 9 of a limited edition of 25 sculptures, with only five pieces thought to be in the Bay Area. The sculpture is made of ground granite, stands over five feet tall, and weighs 2.5 tons. At the time of its arrival, its estimated value was $40,000. About Beniamino Bufano Beniamino Bufano, the creator of “The Bears,” as we often refer to the sculpture, was born in Italy in 1890. He moved to the United States with his family in 1910, first settling in New York City, and then relocating to San Francisco in 1915. Bufano’s first public commission in San Francisco was for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in 1915, where he created a piece for the Court of the Universe on the Arch of Triumph. In his early years, Bufano became known for his sculptures with themes of peace and, in later years, animal-themed works like the Nursing Bear and Cubs. His art can still be seen in various public places in San Francisco. Bufano died in August of 1970, more than ten years before Nursing Bear and Cubs was installed in Crocker Park. The gift and community effort The sculpture was a gift from Jerry S. Mosher, a longtime collector of Bufano’s works and principal owner of Mosher Investment Services, based in Lafayette. As an Oakland resident and Piedmont neighbor, Mosher hoped that the community would appreciate the sculpture and that he would be able to enjoy it as well. Upon hearing about Mosher’s offer of the sculpture, Norma Wells, who was President of PBF at the time, was keen to make the project a reality. She enlisted Jean Wolfe, with whom she had previously worked on the Tea House project in Piedmont Park. They contacted Bob Leefeldt, a former Chair of the Park Commission and a long-time champion of Crocker Park, to join the cause. However, the timing was difficult. Proposition 13 had just passed, and local governments throughout California were thrown into financial chaos. Piedmont, like many cities, was struggling with budget constraints, and there were concerns about how to fund the sculpture’s acquisition and maintenance. Some were skeptical of PBF’s ability to raise the required funds. The project was also met with debates about where the sculpture should be placed. Despite the challenges, Wells, Wolfe, Leefeldt, and other PBF trustees worked tirelessly over three years and eventually secured the necessary funds on behalf of PBF. These funds spared the City unwanted expenses and provided the crucial support needed. After a contentious City Council meeting, the decision to proceed with the acquisition was narrowly approved by a 3-to-2 vote, and the project moved forward. sculpture was installed, and a grand celebration followed. The Piedmonter newspaper shared a heartwarming moment from the event. A young girl said, “I hope no one ever hurts it.” She is not named in the article, but this author has a suspicion. Lilla Wells, then 8 years old, attended the celebration with her grandmother Norma Wells who was presiding. Lilla, the daughter of former Mayor Susan Hill, and now an adult living in Piedmont, recently said she “is proud that many residents now call it ‘Bear Park’ rather than Crocker Park. Walk through the park on any given day and you will see small children playing around and on the Bears. It is a happy ending to an “only in Piedmont” story. A sculpture by Benny Bufano, Nursing Bear and Cubs, is located permanently in Crocker Park in Piedmont. Benny Bufano’s image is courtesy of the San Francisco History Center at the San Francisco Library. Mosher, a longtime collector of Bufano’s works and principal owner of Mosher Investment Services, based in Lafayette. As an Oakland resident and Piedmont neighbor, Mosher hoped that the community would appreciate the sculpture and that he would be able to enjoy it as well. Upon hearing about Mosher’s offer of the sculpture, Norma Wells, who was President of PBF at the time, was keen to make the project a reality. She enlisted Jean Wolfe, with whom she had previously worked on the Tea House project in Piedmont Park. They contacted Bob Leefeldt, a former Chair of the Park Commission and a long-time champion of Crocker Park, to join the cause. However, the timing was difficult. Proposition 13 had just passed, and local governments throughout California were thrown into financial chaos. Piedmont, like many cities, was struggling with budget constraints, and there were concerns about how to fund the sculpture’s acquisition and maintenance. Some were skeptical of PBF’s ability to raise the required funds. The project was also met with debates about where the sculpture should be placed. Despite the challenges, Wells, Wolfe, Leefeldt, and other PBF trustees worked tirelessly over three years and eventually secured the necessary funds on behalf of PBF. These funds spared the City unwanted expenses and provided the crucial support needed. After a contentious City Council meeting, the decision to proceed with the acquisition was narrowly approved by a 3-to-2 vote, and the project moved forward. By February 20, 1980, the sculpture was installed, and a grand celebration followed. The Piedmonter newspaper shared a heartwarming moment from the event. A young girl said, “I hope no one ever hurts it.” She is not named in the article, but this author has a suspicion. Lilla Wells, then 8 years old, attended the celebration with her grandmother Norma Wells who was presiding. Lilla, the daughter of former Mayor Susan Hill, and now an adult living in Piedmont, recently said she “is proud that many residents now call it ‘Bear Park’ rather than Crocker Park. Walk through the park on any given day and you will see small children playing around and on the Bears. It is a happy ending to an “only in Piedmont” story. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) reviewed its annual police report for 2024 and the results of a Police Staffing Study at the City Council meeting on Monday, February 3. The report was presented by Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. The PPD Annual Report showed a significant reduction in property crimes in 2024, primarily larceny. Burglary and robbery had risen from previous years, with vehicle theft staying relatively the same. Part of the downturn in larceny can be attributed to the drop in catalytic converter theft after arrests of significant sellers of the stolen goods, also known as “fences,” by an Alameda County task force. The report also included an update on Piedmont’s Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras. These cameras, expanded in recent years to number 48 across the city, have directly resulted in 16 arrests and have helped recover 65 vehicles throughout the year. The annual report, however, showed a reduction of ALPR “hits” – when the cameras identify a license plate reported as stolen or criminal. Bowers noted that this seeming decrease in Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers presents the 2024 PPD Annual Report to the city council.

Religion Corner - Main Low points and turning points By Pastor Jim Hopkins As Jesus and company were leaving the Jerusalem Temple one day, an unnamed disciple marveled at the magnificence of the temple complex. His sense of wonder was not misplaced for historians of the era such as Flavius Josephus and Tacitus commented on its beauty. Jesus, however, gave a shocking response. He informed everyone who was listening, “Before long, it will all come tumbling down.” When they were out of the city and looking at the temple grounds from the Mount of Olives, Jesus explained his comments to the leaders of his disciples. “Hard times are coming. There will be trouble at every turn. Supposedly trustworthy leaders will prove untrustworthy. Friends you thought you could count on will let you down. Your foundations will be shaken. It will seem like the world is coming apart at the seams. The scale of human suffering will be immense. Yet, mark my words, this is but the beginning of the birth pangs. This low point will be a turning point.” How can this be? How can our low points be turning points? It may be that low points can be turning points because they cause us to turn anew to the only one who can tell us who we are, the only one who can teach who we are born to be, the only one who holds us when the world breaks us, the only one who stills us when our foundations shake. Long before Jesus, long before there was a temple at Jerusalem, maybe even long before there was a Jerusalem, there was a woman of deep faith named Hannah. Hannah was broken. In a world that defined women by their ability to have children, Hannah did not have a child. She went into her temple at the old city of Shiloh and prayed earnestly, yet silently, for a son. The priest at the temple, Eli, observed her and rebuked her. “Go home. You are making a spectacle of yourself. Look at you. Drunk in a sacred space.” This low point for Hannah proves to be a turning point. Her longing to give birth serves as the birth pangs for a new way of being. She challenges Eli, who represents male dominated religion, “I am pouring out my heart and you accuse me of pouring in the wine. It is you who needs to repent.” She trusts God. “I believe you have heard me. articles.text: Piedmont City Council issued a proclamation in recognition of Black History Month at the Council meeting on Monday, February 3. The proclamation, signed by Mayor Betsy Andersen, affirms the importance of black history and honors the efforts and insights of African Americans throughout the history of the United States. “Whereas Black History Month was formally adopted in 1976 to honor and affirm the importance of black history throughout our learning experience, and whereas the history of people with African heritage goes back tens of thousands of years, and includes some of the greatest and most advanced and innovative societies in the history of the human experience, and whereas African Americans have played a significant role in the history of the United States from the early days of the Pioneers to our present-day leaders in such industries as aerospace, finance, government, and international trade, and whereas during Black History Month all Americans are encouraged to reflect on the rich history and teachings of African Americans and bear witness to the progress, beauty and achievements they have made throughout society, now therefore we proclaim that the City Council of the city of Piedmont hereby designates February 2025 as Black History Month throughout the city.” Council members invited Samuel Bahala to speak. Bahala is a foreign exchange student from Mali, originally from the Congo. “Let’s celebrate our strength and togetherness,” said Bahala, before reciting his poem titled Echoes of Labor. Piedmont City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore (left), City Attorney Deepa Sharma, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Piedmont Student Samuel Bahala, Councilmember Lorrell Plimier, and Councilmember Tom Ramsey more dispatch and analytical support for the department through a crime analyst. The next step for Piedmont Police following the staffing study is to build a work plan to properly address the study’s findings with what resources are available. The hearing of the PPD Annual Report ended with a question from the City Council, asking for insight on the recent replacement of the Alameda County District Attorney. Like many local law enforcement agencies, Bowers reported that Piedmont police were “ecstatic” about the replacement. “For years we enjoyed a professional, objective seat by [the District Attorney] and so we’re excited to have that again,” said Bowers. The full police report is available for download at piedmont. ca.gov/PPDAnnualReport2024. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver

pages.text: Wednesday, February 5, 2025 3 City Council issues Black History Month proclamation By Tony Simons Piedmont City Council issued a proclamation in recognition of Black History Month at the Council meeting on Monday, February 3. The proclamation, signed by Mayor Betsy Andersen, affirms the importance of black history and honors the efforts and insights of African Americans throughout the history of the United States. “Whereas Black History Month was formally adopted in 1976 to honor and affirm the importance of black history throughout our learning experience, and whereas the history of people with African heritage goes back tens of thousands of years, and includes some of the greatest and most advanced and innovative societies in the history of the human experience, and whereas African Americans have played a significant role in the history of the United States from the early days of the Pioneers to our present-day leaders in such industries as aerospace, finance, government, and international trade, and whereas during Black History Month all Americans are encouraged to reflect on the rich history and teachings of African Americans and bear witness to the progress, beauty and achievements they have made throughout society, now therefore we proclaim that the City Council of the city of Piedmont hereby designates February 2025 as Black History Month throughout the city.” Council members invited Samuel Bahala to speak. Bahala is a foreign exchange student from Mali, originally from the Congo. “Let’s celebrate our strength and togetherness,” said Bahala, before reciting his poem titled Echoes of Labor. articles.text: Piedmont City staff introduced the new KCOM-TV Station Manager, Jeff Shaw, at the February 3 City Council meeting. Shaw worked for 25 years as Production Manager for Davis Media Access, starting a lowpower FM radio station in his time there. Shaw has also worked with 50 other organizations across the country, helping them navigate through the FCC process to start their own non-commercial radio stations. As KCOM-TV Station Manager, Shaw oversees all video production for the City and the broadcast system and Council Chambers AV equipment replacement. Shaw will also be upgrading the KCOM-TV cable systems so that residents without cable TV will soon be able to view KCOM-TV through connected TV apps or online. “I’m very happy to join the City of Piedmont staff,” said Shaw. “I look forward to working with City staff, and maybe Council members also, in using our audio/video tools to sort-of help increase public participation and civic engagement.” Staff photo Piedmont Communications Manager Echa Schneider (left) introduces new KCOM-TV Station Manager Jeff Shaw to the city council.

articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted on January 21 to award a contract to Rapid Grading Services for a project that involves repaving the length of Grand Avenue in Piedmont, adding bulb-outs and installing green infrastructure. The contract was approved for an amount of $1,414,102 with a construction budget of $1,555,513. A significant portion of the funding – $500,000 of it – is coming from an Alameda County Transportation Commission grant that the City applied for in the summer of 2002. Key elements of the project include a two-inch grind and resurfacing of the pavement, installation of ADA compliant curb ramps and bulb-outs, bicycle markings, and a bioretention basin that provides soil-filtering of storm water. Additionally, this pavement rehabilitation project would meet all of the Green Infrastructure needs that are required under the City’s municipal permit, satisfying Alameda County requirements. The soil-filtering areas of the project will be furnished with drought-resistant plants such as salvia, sea lavender, California gray flush, and coyote mint. When asked by City Council about the effectiveness of the proposed bulb-outs, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales cited observations of traffic officers that vehicles moved slower after their installation. Although there were no statistics cited, Gonzales offered to come back with more data if requested. “Narrowing a roadway is the single most effective tool that is recommended for traffic calming, and so this design is very much consistent with that,” said Gonzales. The bid documents allow for 90 working days, or 18 weeks, of construction time. Not including possible delays from weather, the City estimates construction should be completed this summer. articles.text: In an effort to stay on top of federal telecommunications law, Piedmont City Council voted to approve the first reading of an ordinance that amends design standards for wireless communications facilities (WCFs) at its meeting on Monday, February 3. WCF is an encompassing term for equipment and structures that broadcast and receive wireless frequencies such as antennas, connection cables, broadband equipment or wireless tower structures. After a series of study sessions with the Planning Commission and City Council, City Staff developed a set of proposed standards with the aim to strike a balance between the need for modern wireless infrastructure and the preservation of Piedmont’s landscape setting and building standards. Piedmont’s Planning Department outlined three key goals to guide the new standards: minimize visual impact, enhance wireless coverage, and comply with applicable laws. The standards highly encourage “stealth” designs which conceal wireless equipment to appear as an everyday feature. The presentation showed examples of concealed designs in Piedmont such as equipment integrated into lamp posts, hidden in building towers, or disguised as chimneys. Revised standards include updated height limits, strengthened visual impact mitigation, incorporated city standards for right-of-way facilities, and establishment of a 10-year permit term. Residents may review the new standards in the agenda report for the January 13, 2025 Planning Commission Meeting. A list of meeting agendas and recordings can be found on the City’s Live Content and Video Archive at https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/ kcom-t v/live_content_and _ video_archive.

School board members Michael Malione and Thomasson are on the committee. articles.text: As standardized testing continues to evolve, many families wonder how AP exams, which take place each May, fit into their student’s college roadmap. We want to help sift through the enormity of information available on the internet, and provide insight into some of the questions we are most frequently asked… • Do AP exams matter for college admissions? The short answer is yes! AP exams can be impactful for college admissions. Depending on exam scores, students may be eligible for specific merit scholarships or receive college credit. AP exams allow schools to evaluate a student’s readiness for the rigor of college courses. • My student signed up for an AP exam back in October; must they take the test? They do not have to take the test, but, unless there is an extenuating circumstance, most students should. articles.text: The East Bay Hills FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) League celebrated its first season with a tournament held at Piedmont Middle School on Sunday, January 26. The event showcased the ingenuity and dedication of 16 teams from across the region (including 8 from Piedmont), highlighting the remarkable talent in youth robotics. Tournament Highlights: • Champion: Circuit Breakers (Team 21419) from Piedmont, CA, emerged as the tournament champion, demonstrating exceptional engineering and strategy throughout the competition. Serving as the captain of the winning alliance, they have secured advancement to the regional tour nament. Throughout the league meets, the Circuit Breakers maintained an impressive record, achieving 10 wins and zero losses. They maintained their unbeaten streak throughout the tournament, winning all 5 of their qualification matches and each of their three playoff showdowns. • Finalist: Piedmont Pioneers (Team 11201) from Piedmont, CA, secured the finalist position, showcasing impressive performance and teamwork. • Inspire Award: The Patriots (Team 3470) from Brentwood, CA, were honored with the Inspire Award for embodying the ‘challenge’ of the FTC program and serving as a role model for other teams. As winners of this award, the Patriots will also advance to the regional tournament. This season’s events included three league meets leading up to the league tournament, each providing teams with opportunities to refine their robots and strategies. The league extends its gratitude to all mentors, parents, volunteers, sponsors, and participants who contributed to the success of this season. Their unwavering support and commitment have been pivotal in providing students with a platform to explore and excel in robotics. “It was fun to compete in four different matches against teams from all over the East Bay, and see the same faces each time,” said Gabi Stein, an 8th grader on the Circuit Breakers team. “I’m so excited to now go compete in the Regionals against teams from all over California.” The East Bay Hills League, part of the Northern California FTC, is sponsored by the Piedmont Makers. The ensemble of Once Upon a Mattress sings in whispers to avoid waking up the princess. Ali Atanasio, and seniors Beatriz Donohue, Fiona Chen, and Clare Warner singing “The Swaps of Home.” Ben Wakefield (center) with the ensemble sing “An Opening for a Princess.” Four performances of the Piedmont High production of the musical Once Upon A Mattress were greeted by large audiences last weekend in the Alan Harvey Theater. Amy Moorhead directed and produced the musical, which is a comedic tweaking of the fairy tale The Princess and the Pea. The lead role of Princess Winnifred the Woebegone was performed by senior Clare Weiss, with senior Caitlin Boothby as Queen Aggravain and Ben Wakefield as Prince Dauntless the Drab. “The student performers, spanning grades 9-12, did a fantastic job with the comedy, as well as sang and danced beautifully in the musical Once Upon a Mattress,” said Moorhead. “Our student orchestra brilliantly handled a difficult musical score, and our stage crew swiftly managed the set changes.” Trevor Meseroll was Musical Director and conductor of the student orchestra. The fabulous costumery of the show was provided by The Theatre Company of Upland, CA. “While Mattress is at first glance a light musical, like most fairy tales there are darker themes at play,” wrote Moorhead in the program. “One of the darker themes is a mother’s fear of losing her son.” Juniors Theo Ferguson as the Jester (left), Caleb Canada as King Sextimus, and freshman Zayd Mahmood as the Minstrel, singing “The Minstrel, the Jester, and I.” Senior Payton Cole (left) as the Wizard and junior Ali Atanasio as Princess No. 12. articles.text: Troop 15 In January Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 had an excellent trip to Pinnacles National Park, near Soledad, for a weekend of hiking and car camping. Everybody started with their packs and a healthy dose of energy; then drove two and a half hours to the park. We dropped our packs off at the campsite and brought our daypacks and lunches to the shuttle that took us to the trailhead. Due to the limited shuttle capacity and long shuttle wait time, we split into two groups. Thirty waited for the buses, and 14 of us decided to make the 3-mile walk to the trailhead. The gravel path followed a riverbed, eventually leading into a canyon filled with moss-covered boulders. After an hour, we made it to the most exciting part of Pinnacles – the caves. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: League title fight tonight at Bishop O’Dowd Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team picked up three easy wins last week and squares up for a WACC Foothill title-fight against Bishop O’Dowd tonight. Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team got the job done with three expected wins last week. They beat Castro Valley 73-28 on the road on Wednesday, January 29, handled San Leandro a 61-20 pounding in the Pirates’ new gym on Friday, January 31, and then obliterated Weston Ranch 54-12 the following day at Binks Rawlings Gym. Their record improved to 17-4 overall and 4-1 in league. It all builds to the most important game of the regular season for the Highlanders tonight, squaring up against Western Alameda County Conference leaders, Bishop O’Dowd tonight in the Dragons’ home gym. Piedmont needs to win its remaining league games to split the WACC Foothill title with O’Dowd after dropping their first meeting 56-47 back on January 14. “The biggest thing is to just play the way we’ve been playing and lock in for all four quarters,” said coach Bryan Gardere. ”In each of our losses, we’ve fallen behind in the late third quarter or fourth quarter. Everyone got experience in that first O’Dowd game, now they know what to expect.” Last year, Piedmont won Savannah Dennig had a double-double against San Leandro. the opening meeting against the Dragons but lost the second game, settling for a shared WACC title with O’Dowd. Senior Shakila Zuberi has been a varsity member all four years of her high school career, while her eight other teammates are in the midst of their first year at PHS. Zuberi knows about the intensity this game brings. “We’re taking in our desire and how much we want it. Now that we’ve felt that defeat, we don’t want it to happen again. I want to see us recognize who scores for O’Dowd, how they score, and to take those points away,” Zuberi said. Although it’s a big game with a league title on the line, Dennig cautions against psyching themselves out. “We’ve learned to treat it as another game, we’re going to play hard the whole game and be aggressive. I’ve learned a lot of people treat it much larger than the typical high school game, but we just need to treat it with the same intensity as these other games,” added freshman Savannah Dennig. 73-28 win over Castro Valley Piedmont led 14-5 through the first quarter and jumped out to a 35-15 lead by halftime. PHS extended the gap to 53-24 by the start of the fourth quarter, adding 20 more points in the final going while only allowing four. Final stats: Jenelle Solis led with 21 points, three rebounds, six assists, and a steal. Briana Webb had 13 points, six rebounds, and four steals. Taylor White had nine points, 16 rebounds, eight assists, and two steals. Dennig Shakila Zuberi is a senior on the girls’ basketball team.
articles.title: Piedmont girls win three more

articles.text: Lose 50-49 to Castro Valley in another league thriller It’s been a week of drama for Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team, which split results in two league games, each by one point. The Highlanders recently spoiled the party for San Leandro in the Pirates’ brand new $60 million gym on January 31, winning 61-60 with the a go-ahead basket with 25 seconds left. Two days earlier they lost 50-49 to Castro Valley in the Trojans’ gym. Piedmont has proven to be a gritty team when their backs are against the wall, outscoring San Leandro in both the third and fourth quarters. “It was nice to get this win after the loss to Castro Valley, especially when we’re down a few starters. We shot the ball extremely well despite not being super crisp; the heart was there, the energy was there,” coach Ben Spencer said. “It was almost the same situation against Castro Valley. We took the loss against CV, so we were hungry this time. We played great defense, got steals, and knocked down free throws in the clutch,” said senior captain Ravi Silverberg. Silverberg hit the go-ahead score late in the fourth to put PHS up 59-58. Finishing with 19 points, Silverberg and teammates had to do it without their leading scorer, Dillon Casey, who suffered an injury early in the fourth quarter. Starting forward P.J. Brayer also missed the game. “We were down a bunch of starters and then Dillon goes down. I never felt like the day was lost. Everyone was ready to play—from the last guy off of the bench to the first guys on the court,” Silverberg said. It was a big moment for sophomore Beach Lorin, a new starter on the varsity roster. He nabbed a steal at midcourt after Silververg’s basket, drew a foul and converted two critical free throws for a 61-58 lead. It proved to be especially important when SL scored a field goal as time expired. “It was exciting, I saw the pass and just went for it. To know we had the lead and got the ball, it felt great,” Lorin said. 61-60 over San Leandro Piedmont and San Leandro were tied 14-14 through the first quarter and trailed 32-30 at halftime. The Pirates came out hot Staff Photos The moment Ravi Silverberg scored the go-ahead basket against San Leandro’s best player with about 25 seconds left. Beach Lorin with his big steal at the end of the game to help solidify the win over San Leandro.

articles.text: 2 goals wiped in 1-0 loss to Berkeley with poor officiating Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team walked out of last week with a win and a loss in two road games against Western Alameda County Conference foes. They beat Encinal 2-0 at Estuary Park in Alameda on Wednesday, January 29 but lost 1-0 to Berkeley two days later on a cold and rainy night, and a game marred by poor officiating. Piedmont waswithout four key players: midfield captain Louisa Symkowick, Kyla Williams, Kyra Trombi, and Chloe Toyoma. articles.text: Staff Photos Harper Mand (35) celebrates his goal against Hayward. Also pictured is Gianluca Bini (left) and Callum Long. The Highlanders answered a two-game skid to get back in the win column on Thursday, January 30, beating the visiting Hayward Farmers by a 3-1 score. Two days earlier, Piedmont lost a high-scoring 3-2 to match to Mt. Eden, also at Witter Field. The pair of results brings PHS’ record to 5-3-7 (W-TL) and 3-2-3 in league. “I’m happy for the boys to finally get a result. I was pleased to see some concepts we’re looking for. We talk about playing conscious and subconscious thinking; we were very conscious in the first 10 minutes and then you see fatigue, then bad habits kick in,” said coach Ben Russell. Piedmont has proven to be its most productive during set pieces so far this season with four goals on set pieces in the last three games. Two of their goals against Hayward came by way of passes from free kicks; they scored one from a corner against Mt. Eden, while their score in a 3-1 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on January 24 was from a lofted ball by Roman Ahearn. “Set pieces have been something we’ve worked on since the start of the season, it’s a good foundation for us. It’s something the boys have taken to. We have a lot of height on the team; it’s just turning it into more games. I think the chance creation is there,” Russell said. The center back pairing of Elias Reed-Miguel and Max Goldfarb produced assists on goals on free kicks against Hayward. “We have a lot of height with our attackers. We know if we can get the ball into the box, then we can create goals pretty easily. It’s great to get results in games like this so we can build confidence for the harder teams,” Reed-Miguel said. It took just two more minutes for Piedmont to score when Reed-Miguel launched a free kick from the left sideline to freshman Jimmy Lagios at the far post for a header goal. Hayward scored by way of a corner in the 24th while Piedmont went into halftime with a 2-1 lead. Eden Piedmont scored quickly in the second minute after drawing a corner. Ahearn sent a cross in a cross targeting Bini, who headed a ball centrally to Mand, volleying it out of the air into the net. articles.text: Last summer the U.S. men’s 4 rowing team won a gold medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics. The monumental feat sent shockwaves through the nation and set a new bar for U.S. rowing. The four rowers didn’t just end up there due to talent; it took years of hard work and dedication to reach the highest level of the rowing world. I had a chance to interview gold medalist Nick Mead, the bow seat of this impressive crew. Mead, who was born in Pennsylvania and graduated from Princeton, started rowing as a freshman in high school and instantly fell in love with the sport. His passion and early success laid the foundation for everything that followed. In college, he became a team captain of the Princeton Tiger Crew, leading them to win gold at the 2017 IRA championships. After college, Nick competed in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where the U.S. men’s 8 placed fourth. That close victory in Tokyo made Mead even more determined to make it to Paris. When asked about their pre-Olympic training, Mead said the crew would row 260,000-260,000 meters a week. To put that into perspective, for an Olympic athlete, rowing 1,000 meters takes about 3.5 minutes, meaning these athletes were putting in some serious hours. This astounding level of dedication is part of what made this crew so good, but what sets them apart is the strive for perfection. Being in sync with three other rowers requires poise, patience, and a strong mind. To help them with this, their crew used telemetry. They put this device on the oars to track every little detail of their stroke, giving them realtime feedback during training, helping them find the perfect rhythm. Another factor was the chemistry established between the four. Being able to train in the same boat for over 25 hours a week requires personal connection, respect, and trust. Regarding how they dealt with conflict, Mead said they always stayed humble and put their egos aside, adding: “We never had conflict that lasted past practice.” What pushed this team over the edge, though, was their preparation for race day. “Preparation has been happening for so long that, the day before, you’re not listening to music to lock in. It’s been building for months,” Mead said. What resonated with his crew for the Olympics was visualizing the race as race day got closer, talking over every detail. After winning the Paris Olympics, Nick shared that he feels fulfilled and ready to retire from the sport. He is excited to pass the torch to the young athletes like me, hoping we can rise to the challenge and eventually fill the big shoes he and his crew have left behind. Evrim Duransoy is a junior in Piedmont High School and a member of the Oakland Strokes junior rowing program. articles.text: A photo of Lower Yosemite Falls, an added attraction near the Firefall viewing area. Staff Photos Yosemite National Park’s annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls is starting this week and stretching through the end of February. The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracting light shining off of Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 through the end of the month, requiring clear skies around sunset in order for the marvel to be seen and sufficient water flowing from Horsetail Falls. In order to manage the popularity of the Firefall, Yosemite National Park is enforcing reservations to enter February at www.Recreation.gov. Current weather forecasts shows mostly sunny skies February 9-11 with rain and snow predicted the following two days before a mostly sunny Valentines day, February 14. Mostly partly cloudy skies are forecasted from February 16-22, while the final week of February could have ideal conditions with clear skies from February 25-27. Those interested in lodging at Yosemite, reservation information can be found at www.travelyosemite.com. As of writing this on Tuesday, February 4, there is still availability at the Curry Villiage, Yosemite Valley Lodge, and The Awahnee. As for camping, many sites remain closed during the winter, but Camp 4’s first-come, firstserve site is still open. The Upper Pines Campground is open and still has some availability through the end of the month. Camping information can be found at www.Recreation.gov. The Post would love to see your photos of the annual Yosemite Firefall, send your shots to news@piedmont-post.com and Jonathancx525@gmail.com. pages.text: Wednesday, February 5, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Firefall season at Yosemite National Park A photo of Lower Yosemite Falls, an added attraction near the Firefall viewing area. Staff Photos By Jonathan Comeaux Yosemite National Park’s annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls is starting this week and stretching through the end of February. The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracting light shining off of Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 through the end of the month, requiring clear skies around sunset in order for the marvel to be seen and sufficient water flowing from Horsetail Falls. In order to manage the popularity of the Firefall, Yosemite National Park is enforcing reservations to enter February at www.Recreation.gov. Current weather forecasts shows mostly sunny skies February 9-11 with rain and snow predicted the following two days before a mostly sunny Valentines day, February 14. Mostly partly cloudy skies are forecasted from February 16-22, while the final week of February could have ideal conditions with clear skies from February 25-27. Those interested in lodging at Yosemite, reservation information can be found at www.travelyosemite.com. As of writing this on Tuesday, February 4, there is still availability at the Curry Villiage, Yosemite Valley Lodge, and The Awahnee. As for camping, many sites remain closed during the winter, but Camp 4’s first-come, firstserve site is still open. The Upper Pines Campground is open and still has some availability through the end of the month. Camping information can be found at www.Recreation.gov. The Post would love to see your photos of the annual Yosemite Firefall, send your shots to news@piedmont-post.com and Jonathancx525@gmail.com. Photo courtesy of Aaron M Photogrohpy Provided is a forecast for the best times to see Yosemite’s Firefall. articles.text: The first U.S. solo exhibition of work by Amol K Patil, a visual artist whose work explores issues of class and caste in his native Mumbai, India, will be on view at Berkeley Art Museum now through April 27. “MATRIX 286 / Amol K Patil: A Forest of Remembrance” will feature paintings and sculptures by Patil, all newly commissioned for the BAMPFA presentation. The exhibition marks the latest installment in BAMPFA’s signature contemporary art exhibition series “MATRIX,” an experimental platform for artists to make and show new work. Over the past decade, Patil has established himself as a premier voice in India’s contemporary art scene through a multidisciplinary practice that includes painting, sculpture, video installation and live performance. In both abstract and figurative forms, Patil illuminates the experience of marginalized communities in India’s highly stratified urban settings, where poverty and caste discrimination have led to massive levels of inequality. Patil’s work often references Mumbai’s chawls — the century-old social housing originally built for mill workers and other laborers, where the city’s working classes have since managed to create vibrant shared living spaces against a backdrop of economic precarity. In Patil’s BAMPFA-commissioned series of painting and sculptures, the chawl is reimagined as a space of historical memory and present resistance, highlighting the resilience of the multigenerational families who persevere there. Working with cast bronze sculpture, Patil has crafted a series of five figurative sculptures that obliquely reference the tangled bodies and cramped living conditions of chawl households — where families often live in units as small as 120 square feet. These sculptures will appear alongside a new series of 19 paintings that expressionistically render everyday life in the The first U.S. solo exhibition of work by Amol K Patil will be on view at Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Fine Arts now through April 27. chawls, drawing on the personal and communal histories of these sites. “We are thrilled to present this newly commissioned body of work by Amol K Patil for his first U.S. solo exhibition,” said BAMPFA’s Chief Curator Margot Norton. “Patil’s poetic and deeply moving sculptures and paintings bring the everyday experiences of those living in India’s chawls into vibrant relief, depicting intimate moments to reveal urgent societal concerns.” Patil is a conceptual and performance artist based in Mumbai. Following his education in the visual arts from Rachana Sansad Academy of Fine Arts and Crafts, Mumbai, he has made work that explores the intersection of performance art, theater, music, kinetic art, and video installation. He was a 2022-2024 resident at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam. In 2023, he received his first international solo exhibition at the Hayward Gallery in London. Patil’s grandfather was a noted interpreter and poet, and his father was an avant-garde playwright. Berkeley Art Museum is located a 2155 Center Street and is open 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($18 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa.org. articles.text: This Saturday, February 8 through March 9, see the Northern California premiere of 2023 Pulitzer Prize finalist Lloyd Suh’s The Heart Sellers at Aurora Theatre in Berkeley. The humorous and heartwarming play about the Asian immigrant experience offers a personal portrait of the impact of the landmark 1965 Hart-Celler Act that revoked certain barriers to immigration and citizenship in favor of a skills-based preference system. Set in 1973 during the aftermath of Watergate, The Heart Sellers centers on two Asian women navigating their first American Thanksgiving. Starting out as strangers who meet in the grocery store, Luna (Nicole Javier) from the Philippines and Jane (Wonjung Kim) from South Korea find common ground in their shared experiences of often absent medical resident husbands, missing families and friends back home and discovering the joys and challenges of life in America. As the women attempt to cook Thanksgiving dinner for the first time, they dream of discotheques, Disneyland and the future. Acclaimed director, actor and playwright Jennifer Chang, who directed the World Premiere of the show at Milwaukee Repertory Theater, will co-direct the show Aurora Theatre in Berkeley is presenting The Heart Sellers, an acclaimed new play being shown February 8 through March 9. Pictured are Nicole Javier and Wonjung Kim in the lead roles as Luna and Jane. with Lloyd Suh. “I have long been a fan of Suh’s work and ‘The Heart Sellers’ is the epitome of everything we aspire to present on our stages,” said TheatreWorks Artistic Director Giovanna Sardelli. “It’s so funny and filled with heart. Pinpointing the personal during a pivotal moment in our history, this uplifting play offers a moving tribute to those who make America their home. This is a beautiful story that needs to be told.” The New York Times called the play “beautiful” and “politically astute.” “My first thought after I read this play was that we must produce it,” said Michael Stevenson, Artistic Director of production company Capital Stage. “The beautiful story of these women’s friendship made me fall in love with these immigrants and their first Thanksgiving journey. Lloyd’s extraordinary writing touched my heart and made me laugh out loud – and made me think anew about the idea of America and what it means to so many people.” Tickets ($41 general, $15 college student, $10 high school student) for this production at Aurora Theatre (2081 Addison St., Berkeley) are available online at auroratheatre.org or by phone at 843-4822.
articles.title: The Heart Sellers comes to Aurora Theatre Feb. 8

articles.text: Provocative political drama Waste opens February 6 Waste, a provocative Edwardian drama about devious behindthe-scenes political machinations, comes to Marin Theatre in Mill Valley for four weeks opening February 6. Although “Waste” was written in 1906 by the accredited English actor, director and playwright Harley Granville-Barker, a colleague of G.B. Shaw, its public debut was delayed more than 20 years due to outrage over its content. This new production, adapted and directed by Carey Perlof, artistic director emerita of American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco, is a fresh take on the century-old play that shines a spotlight on the issue of reproductive rights. The play follows an ambitious politician on the cusp of bringing his life’s work to fruition. The flawed Henry Trebell, played by Marin Theatre Artistic Director Lance Gardner, finds his promising career curtailed by the threat of scandal over an illicit affair which has led to dire consequences for his wife. Rather than showing sympathy, outrage or even condemnation for the women, the play cynically focuses on the insiders who scheme to use the scandal to manipulate a political outcome. “I am very excited that our audiences will get to experience this remarkable play in my first season as artistic director at Marin Theatre,” said Gardner. “I look forward to returning to the stage, and collaborating with Carey Perloff who returns to direct in the Bay Area for the first time since her tenure at A.C.T.” Waste opened in 1906 in London but was swiftly censored due to its controversial subject matter and critique of societal norms. Finally presented publicly in 1936, Waste earned critical acclaim for its sharp-witted commentary and compelling drama, hailed by The Times as “A masterpiece of its time.” Nearly 100 years later Waste was revived Off-Broadway in 2000. Director Carey Perloff is no stranger to the work of Harley Granville-Barker, given Perloff’s acclaimed production of the playwright’s similarly prescient work about business ethics, The Voysey Inheritance, which was later adapted by David Mamet and received the San Francisco Chronicle’s highest rating. Tickets ($30-$85) for the show at Marin Theatre (397 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley) are available online at MarinTheatre.org or by phone at 415-388-5208. Marin Theatre Artistic Director Lance Gardner will star in the provocative political drama Waste at Marin Theatre from February 6 through March 2.
articles.title: Rare century-old play comes to Marin Theatre

articles.text: The Year of the Serpent brings in the 25th anniversary of Lunar New Year celebrations at Davies Symphony Hall with a concert and banquet this Saturday. This elegant commemoration of the holiday will draw upon vibrant Asian traditions, past and present. The celebration will begin at 4 p.m. with pre-concert lobby festivities open to all ticketholders, featuring an array of entertainment and activities including lion dancers, dragon’s beard candy making, fortune readers, calligraphy artists and cultural performances. Conductor Francesco Lecce-Chong and the orchestra will then open the 5 p.m. concert with An-Lun Huang’s “Saibei Dance” from Saibei Suite No. 2, featuring styles of wind and percussion from Northwest China, and Tian Zhou’s “Indigo” from Concerto for Orchestra, which received a Grammy nomination for Best Contemporary Classical in 2018. Zhou describes “Indigo” as “a musical postcard from a walk in the forest one late summer night.” The program continues with the world premiere of a new San Francisco Symphony commission by award-winning composer and pianist Shuying Li. Assistant Principal Cello Amos Yang will play selections from Chen Gang and He ZhanJoin San Francisco Symphony conductor Francesco Lecce-Chong and celebrate the Year of the Serpent at Davies Symphony Hall with a concert and banquet this Saturday. hao’s famous The Butterfly Lovers Concerto, based on an ancient Chinese legend about two people who fall in love but cannot be together, ultimately transforming into butterflies. Pipa player Wu Man will join Lecce-Chong and the orchestra to perform Zhao Jiping’s Pipa Concerto No. 2. The pipa is a traditional Chinese plucked instrument that has been played for almost 2,000 years. Concluding the program is Huan-zhi Li’s energetic and popular Chinese orchestral work Spring Festival Overture. The post-concert Lunar New Year Banquet will begin at 6:30 p.m. in Zellerbach Rehearsal Hall, located at 300 Franklin Street at the rear of Davies Symphony Hall. The evening will feature a lucky draw and live music. The décor for the event will include hanging screens that highlight the various ways that Lunar New Year is celebrated across different cultures. VIP dinner packages include access to the pre-concert reception. Tickets for the concert ($75- $150) at Davies Symphony Hall (201 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco) and information about individual and full banquet table reservations can be found for purchase at sfsymphony.org, or through the box office at 415- 864-6000.
articles.title: SF Symphony celebrates Lunar New Year this Sat.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra’s (YPSO) will celebrate its 88th Season with a Spring Concert on Saturday, February 8, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The program includes Marine Safari/Whale Watch by Jeremy Cavaterra; Violin Concerto in D Minor, 1st Movement, 1 by Jean Sibelius; and Symphony No. 9 in E Minor, New World Symphony by Antonín Dvořák
articles.title: YPSO Concert this Saturday

articles.text: When Ariel Pawlik-Zwiebel takes the stage at the Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) Winter Concert on February 8 at First Church Berkeley, it will be more than a celebration of classical music. As a senior at Campolindo High School in Moraga and YPSO’s co-concertmaster, he is one of the winners of YPSO’s annual Concerto Competition. He will perform the first movement of Jean Sibelius’s Violin Concerto in D Minor, a masterpiece of emotional depth and virtuosity. Beyond music, Ariel is a key member of Highlander Robotics, a student-led team based at Piedmont High School that brings together students from multiple schools to design, build, and program competition-ready robots. As a strategist and drive coach, he played a pivotal role in the team’s success at the FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) World Championship, where they were a division finalist. Just as in an orchestra, success in robotics depends on teamwork, adaptability, and creative problem-solving. His ability to excel in both fields reflects a broad and deep commitment to learning and achievement, as well as the power of collaboration across disciplines. A dedicated soloist and recitalist, Ariel has performed across the Bay Area and beyond, including a recent appearance at the San Francisco International Piano Festival, collaborating with his father, pianist Markus Pawlik. This season, YPSO violinist Ariel Pawlik-Zwiebel he will also perform the Sibelius Violin Concerto as a soloist with the Livermore-Amador Symphony in February and the Prometheus Symphony in May. Julie Kim, YPSO’s first violin coach, highlights Ariel’s extraordinary commitment: “Ariel’s dedication to his craft and his willingness to grow as a musician are truly remarkable. He brings such passion and focus to his playing, and it’s inspiring to see him excel not only in music but in other areas as well.” YPSO’s Winter Concert will include Marine Safari/Whale Watch from the Monterey Suite by YPSO Composer-in-Residence Jeremy Cavaterra’s, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 9 in E Minor, “From the New World.” Tickets are $20 for general admission, and students can attend for free by registering at ypsomusic.org/events.
articles.title: Music meets Robotics: Piedmont connection in YPSO Winter Concert

articles.text: Twyla Tharpe troupe to dance with Philip Glass percussion score For the first time in 10 years, Twyla Tharp’s dance company will return to Zellerbach Hall at UC Berkeley for three performances on Friday, February 7 and 8 at 8 p.m. and February 9 at 3 p.m. The program, celebrating Tharp’s six-decade career as one of the most influential and popular American choreographers of her generation, features the West Coast premiere of Slacktide. The performance will be danced to a score by composer Philip Glass which will be performed live by Chicago’s Grammy-winning Third Coast Percussion, featuring flutist Constance Volk. Tharp will also revive “Diabelli,” a signature ensemble work from 1998 inspired by Beethoven’s Diabelli Variations with music performed live by pianist Vladimir Rumyantsev. In close collaboration with Tharp, Third Coast Percussion has arranged Glass’ hypnotic score Aguas da Amazonia which they will perform live on a collection of custom-designed percussion instruments. Volk will join the group performing a series of flute solos she has composed for the arrangement. Slacktide reunites two titans of contemporary performing arts for the first time in nearly 40 years, since Tharp and Glass’ exhilarating 1986 creation In the Upper Room. Tharp’s choreography captures the layered rhythms and propulsive energy of Glass’ iconic music, here reflecting on the crisis of climate change. In Diabelli Tharp’s choreography highlights the intense humanity of Beethoven’s fiendishly challenging composition, bringing out its humor, pathos and tenderness. The technically demanding work asks dancers to shift effortlessly from ballet to jazz and contemporary dance, even incorporating folk dance. Russian-born pianist Rumyantsev joins the dancers as accompanist and sparring partner for this choreographic and musical journey. Tharp is renowned for creating technically precise works that have pushed the boundaries of ballet and contemporary dance. She founded Twyla Tharp Dance in New York City in 1965; in addition to creating dances for her company and for American Ballet Theatre, she has choreographed Tony-winning Broadway shows, Emmy-winning television specials and blockbuster Hollywood films including Amadeus and Ragtime. Chicago-based Third Coast Percussion is the first percussion ensemble ever to win a Grammy award. Celebrating its 20th anniversary this year, the quartet is best known for interpretations of works by John Cage, Steve Reich and Philip Glass. Tickets ($42-$120) for the show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642-9988. For the first time in 10 years, American choreographer Twyla Tharp’s dance company will return to Zellerbach Hall at UC Berkeley for three performances February 7-9.
articles.title: West Coast premiere of Slacktide at Zellerbach Feb. 7-9

Beyond music, Ariel is a key member of Highlander Robotics, a student-led team based at Piedmont High School that brings together students from multiple schools to design, build, and program competition-ready robots. As a strategist and drive coach, he played a pivotal role in the team’s success at the FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) World Championship, where they were a division finalist. Just as in an orchestra, success in robotics depends on teamwork, adaptability, and creative problem-solving. His ability to excel in both fields reflects a broad and deep commitment to learning and achievement, as well as the power of collaboration across disciplines. A dedicated soloist and recitalist, Ariel has performed across the Bay Area and beyond, including a recent appearance at the San Francisco International Piano Festival, collaborating with his father, pianist Markus Pawlik. This season, YPSO violinist Ariel Pawlik-Zwiebel he will also perform the Sibelius Violin Concerto as a soloist with the Livermore-Amador Symphony in February and the Prometheus Symphony in May. Julie Kim, YPSO’s first violin coach, highlights Ariel’s extraordinary commitment: “Ariel’s dedication to his craft and his willingness to grow as a musician are truly remarkable. He brings such passion and focus to his playing, and it’s inspiring to see him excel not only in music but in other areas as well.” YPSO’s Winter Concert will include Marine Safari/Whale Watch from the Monterey Suite by YPSO Composer-in-Residence Jeremy Cavaterra’s, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 9 in E Minor, “From the New World.” Tickets are $20 for general admission, and students can attend for free by registering at ypsomusic.org/events.

articles.text: Ian Cheung is a quiet young man, quiet and unassuming. And profound. He was the violin soloist last weekend for the Prometheus Symphony concert. Let’s set the scene as if it were a baseball game. Ian is dressed in a jacket and a tie as he approaches home plate. He doesn’t take any practice swings. The pitcher winds up and Ian hits a long one to the deepest reaches of centerfield. The announcer screams: “home run!” Ian rounds the bases and takes a bow when he reaches home plate. The announcer says, “We’ve never seen such calmness in any player.” That was the scene last weekend. Ian Cheung’s vehicle was the First Violin Concerto by Prokofiev. I have never seen a soloist so calmly composed. He walked to his position in the midst of the Orchestra, and then, without any warm-up, proceeded with an interpretation of this unique violin concerto that was masterful. Prokofiev’s First Violin Concerto breaks all the rules. It begins and ends quietly and magically. Only in the second movement is there a display of virtuosity. That Ian Cheung was up to every challenge is putting it mildly. The audience responded enthusiastically. Oh, how I wish he had given us a solo encore. Violin soloist Ian Cheung (center), his teacher Chen Zhou, and Eric Hansen (right), conductor of the Prometheus Symphony after a recent memorable concert.

articles.text: Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling in La La Land I admit that I have always possessed a bias against Hollywood musicals. When dialogue abruptly shifts to singing and music from the background to the foreground, I have found it difficult to suspend my disbelief. And so it was with some reluctance that I sat in a darkened theater and waited for La La Land to begin. I admit that even the title gave me pause. When it started, the opening scene, while energetic, seemed a bit retro (I flashed on Grease). I was already growing restless. Young, beautiful people, stuck on an L.A. freeway in bumper to bumper traffic, suddenly leave their cars and start singing while standing on the hoods and roofs of their cars, the song, Another Day of Sunshine. Palm trees dot the horizon, the colors lift off the screen. A perfect day in L.A… But singing? Dancing? And then something completely unexpected and surprising happens. La La Land becomes almost magical, quickly morphing into a creative and seamless story that is incredibly winning. At the risk of sounding hyperbolic, it is magnificent and wonderful, crafted by writer/ director Damien Chazelle, composed by Justin Hurwitz with lyrics by Benji Pasek and Justin Paul. And what lyrics they are. Together they have created an astonishing collaboration that is transformative and delightful, most especially the theme song, a wistful ballad called City of Stars. So I sit here, with my computer, looking at the screen, asking myself how to write sentences that will encourage moviegoers to discover this film and allow themselves to be swept away by the music and the superb performances of Emma Stone as Mia and Ryan Gosling as Sebastian. Both are denizens of L.A., and both possess dreams yet to be fulfilled. His is to use his talent on the piano to play pure jazz in a club of his own. Hers is to audition (which she does time after time, to heartbreaking effect) for a part that will allow her to not only display her deep reservoir of talent but to truly unleash it. Sebastian and Mia meet briefly, then meet again, and, inevitably, they begin a journey that is heartfelt and sad and wonderful, their moments together enriched by songs and thematic music that will echo for days after you leave the theater. There are moments in this film that are breathtaking, they are so original and filled with artistic risk-taking. At its core La La Land is a simple story: boy meets girl, fall in love, and finally sing and dance as the early evening lights of L.A. appear like so many thousands of surreal stars, the horizon still a gauzy red-purple glow as the sun reluctantly sets. Sensational. Don’t hold back. Trust me. This film is far more than an attempt to pay homage to oldtimey Hollywood musicals that were once so ubiquitous. Chazelle has crafted something glorious and he has elicited from Stone and Gosling startlingly good performances – I mean they are really good. Sit back and open your heart and let La La Land charm you and make you smile, sadly, especially at the end. If given a chance you will be enchanted, I promise. La La Land. Directed by Damien Chazelle, Starring Emma Stone, Ryan Gosling, John Legend. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2016, Now streaming on Prime/Fandango/Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS La La Land a winner, start to finish

articles.text: One of the deep pleasures of movies is seeing one with companions and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, meeting on the second Thursday of each month offers; a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. January’s Flix Fest offering is the international favorite from Italy, the bittersweet comedy/ drama, Cinema Paradiso. Winning the Academy Award for Best Foreign Film in 1989, the film is often credited with reviving Italy’s film industry. Directed by Giuseppe Tornatore, it was filmed in his small hometown in Sicily. Set a few years after World War II, it focuses on eight-year-old Salvatore (Salvatore Cascio), the bright, mischievous son of a war widow. Nicknamed Toto, he discovers a love for movies and spends every free moment at the local movie house, Cinema Paradiso. Although they initially start on tense terms, he forms a friendship with the middle-aged projectionist, Alfredo (Philippe Noiret), who often lets him watch from the projection booth. The boy finds in the images on the screen the perfect escape from life in his war-torn village. When he grows up, he falls in love with a beautiful local girl (Agnese Nano) and takes over as the Paradiso’s projectionist. Alfredo sets out to persuade Salvatore to leave his small town and pursue his passion for filmmaking. Cinema Paradiso received widespread critical acclaim. Making Tornatore internationally known, it’s regarded by many as a classic. The movie is particularly renowned for the ‘kissing scenes’ montage at its end. The critic Roger Ebert gave it four stars out of four. Cinema Paradiso will be screened in Piedmont on Thursday, February 13, at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis or register at https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next offering in the Piedmont series is one of the most honored of American films, On the Waterfront, directed by Elia Kazan and starring Marlon Brando and Eva Marie Saint, with a stirring score by Leonard Bernstein. It will be shown on March 13th. Watch Cinema Paradiso at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Thursday, February 13th at 1:00 p.m.

Sebastian and Mia meet briefly, then meet again, and, inevitably, they begin a journey that is heartfelt and sad and wonderful, their moments together enriched by songs and thematic music that will echo for days after you leave the theater. There are moments in this film that are breathtaking, they are so original and filled with artistic risk-taking. At its core La La Land is a simple story: boy meets girl, fall in love, and finally sing and dance as the early evening lights of L.A. appear like so many thousands of surreal stars, the horizon still a gauzy red-purple glow as the sun reluctantly sets. Sensational. Don’t hold back. Trust me. This film is far more than an attempt to pay homage to oldtimey Hollywood musicals that were once so ubiquitous. Chazelle has crafted something glorious and he has elicited from Stone and Gosling startlingly good performances – I mean they are really good. Sit back and open your heart and let La La Land charm you and make you smile, sadly, especially at the end. If given a chance you will be enchanted, I promise. La La Land. Directed by Damien Chazelle, Starring Emma Stone, Ryan Gosling, John Legend. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2016, Now streaming on Prime/Fandango/Apple tv. It is a lively Polynesian story about a strong-willed, adventurous girl named Moana (Auli’i Cravalho), 16, the daughter of her tribe’s chief, Tui (Temuera Morrison). Set on the pacific island of Motunui, an emerald paradise, the story begins with Moana, looking toward the horizon, ever curious, wondering what’s beyond, understanding that for years her tribe has been afraid to venture past the reef that surrounds the island. But a strange cloud now hangs over the island. The fish are not as plentiful and the coconuts dry A scene from Disney Animation studios’ Moana and tasteless. Moana’s grandmother, Tala (Rachel House), tells her that the ocean has chosen her to return the island’s goddess, Te Fifi, an idol stolen by the demigod, Maui (Dwayne Johnson), a millennia ago. Late at night, in the pale moonlight, Moana takes a beached canoe, called a camakan, and sets out, beyond the reef, in search of the hulking, overly confident demigod Maui (Dwayne Johnson). Her mission is to break the spell cast over her people. Moana is clearly Disney’s attempt to feature a young woman who does not need to be rescued by a prince, an almost iconic story line. Instead, the studio approaches the character of Moana with a light hand, the inherent feminism subtle but compelling. Moana is independent, courageous and never burdened with an oppressive patriarchy. Actually, it is her destiny to become the eventual chief of her tribe. There is also no love story, no rugged islander waiting to marry her. Moana is simply a story of an empowered teenage girl on a quest. The directors of the film, John Musker and Ron Clemens (The Little Mermaid, Aladdin) consulted with South Pacific locals, regarding their history and folklore. They also cast a wide net in search of the Hawaiian teen Auli’i Cravalho as the voice of Moana. As well, Dwayne Johnson, adding star power, has Samoan heritage. Voicing Moana’s father, chief Tui, is New Zealander Temuera Morrison of Maori background. Know as well that Moana is sprinkled with 10 songs, sung by Moana and Maui (as it turns out, Johnson has a solid voice).The music was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who wrote Hamilton. Plus, the animation is rich in tropical colors. Moana. Directed by John Musker and Ron Clemens. Disney Animation studios. articles.text: It was Lunar New Year on Wednesday last week, but there was another reason for the Walking on Wednesdays group to celebrate. As part of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s 60th anniversary, the walkers wanted to see the second of three sets of projects that the PBF has supported during its years of service to Piedmont, the Ramona/Ronada Triangle, the Dracena Park tot lot, and Storyteller Bridge. At each location a PBF volunteer would tell the walkers about the project. A big turnout of 49 walkers and a record eight K-9 best friends were on hand. The morning started off with Matt Gerhardt and PBF President Patty Dunlap telling the group about PBF and what they were going to see that morning. They headed off in a long line going down Highland, Moraga, and Estrella Avenues to Ramona Avenue. Molly Ashford, who lives nearby, shared the Ramona/ Ronada Triangle’s history while a video team from KCOM taped her talk. In the early 2010s residents on Ronada and Ramona Avenues thought this corner was a traffic safety hazard for children going to school. The neighbors felt the crosswalk was too wide and traffic coming off Moraga Ave. was dangerously fast. The residents came to the Park Commission and presented their case for the intersection’s improvement. They had raised money and were willing to financially support improvements. The City appreciated their commitment, and PBF campaigned to raise money to develop this triangle park. It was determined that a small park projecting out from 109 Ronada along with a stop sign would slow traffic. Landscaping with drought tolerant plants and handsome masonry were done, and the park’s opening celebration was Arbor Day 2014. This was also the 50th anniversary of PBF. Molly noted the plants have grown and matured beautifully over the last 10 years. This little park is in the middle of a busy street, but it is also a sanctuary. The walkers headed off down Ramona, up a hidden set of stairs to Arroyo Avenue, and down Ricardo Avenue to the foot of Dracena Park. The walkers went up to the tot lot in Dracena Park where Nancy Kent, the City’s Parks & Project Manager, shared the park’s history. Dracena Park’s site was part of Walter Blair’s land purchase in 1852. Blair was the first European settler in the area. This land had a basalt outcrop, a dark-colored formation of volcanic rock, and Blair created a quarry to extract it. This material was used to pave early Oakland and Piedmont roads. However, in 1890 Blair’s diggers struck an underground stream. A lake formed and the quarry work stopped. In 1903 Frank C. Havens bought the land and it was left as a natural area until 1916 when Piedmont voters approved a bond to purchase the land. The site was used in 1924 by the City as a corporation yard and nursery. It took over 200 truckloads of dirt to flatten the area. For over 40 years the old quarry was fenced off for public safety, but in 1975 the City started to develop the former quarry site. In 2004 PBF was a major contributor to the development of the play area, tot lot, and landscaping, and in 2006 the tot lot was renovated with new equipment, matting, lighting, and paths. pages.text: Wednesday, February 5, 2025 23 The Wine Corner A Taste of Sonoma County Part Two By Pierre DuMont and Frederic Vignobles Pax Wines On a bright, crisp January morning we drove the back roads through rolling, sunlit vineyards from Healdsburg to Sebastopol listening to Bill Evans on cassette tape and soaking in the landscape. It was the kind of morning that makes you want to count your blessings. We were on our way to meet Pax Mahle, co-owner of Pax Wines. After stints as a sommelier and wine buyer, Pax and his wife Pamela founded Pax Wines and began making cool-climate Syrah in 2000. We met Pax at his urban winery in its modern “tasting room meets wine bar” space in Sebastopol filled with overstuffed leather couches and chairs. A record player and old vinyl collection stood ready, dozens of bottles with different Pax labels lined the walls, too funky and cool to have been designed by a corporate brand manager. It didn’t take long to figure out that Pax is someone who marches to the beat of his own drum. He eschews Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir as varietals because what is accepted as “high-quality” has become calcified and formulaic. His winemaking style is European, traditional and minimalist, with great attention to the soil. Grapes are crushed by foot, fermented using ambient yeasts, and free from unnatural additives. As we conversed – while tasting more than a dozen wines ranging from Vermentino and Trousseau Gris to Gamay Noir and Syrah – it became clear that he values diversity of varietals, supports small scale efforts, and is committed to making good wine that doesn’t break the bank. Once a dominant varietal it was almost completely pulled out in the 70’s. This classy wine enchants with mineral essences and citrus blossom aromas. Medium bodied, the wine offers a fresh, spicy palate with a touch of bitterness on the finish, leaving a mineral impression. It’s a wine that begs to be paired with seafood or shellfish and reminds one of a classic Savennieres from the Loire Valley. • 2023 Pax Trousseau Gris Fanucchi-Wood Vineyard, $30 This rare grape comes from the Jura region in eastern France and produces this distinctive rose wine. It has a clean and expressive nose with notes of roses and wild herbs. It is characterful, elegant and precise, full of strawberry fruit with more complexity than one usually finds in a rose. • 2022 Pax Syrah Griffin’s Lair, $75 Our favorite of the Pax Syrahs the initially shy nose began to saunter out of the glass with some aeration. It shows some mint and herbal notes followed by waves of lush cassis and blueberry fruit. Some leather and earth on the palate, but the emphasis is on rich, concentrated dark fruit. This is full-bodied, earthy and long on the finish remaining fresh and vibrant throughout. It reminds me of a fine Cornas from Clape or Verset. • 2022 Pax Sonoma Hillsides Syrah, $60 This is a selection of the best barrels from a variety of Sonoma vineyards and shows off the house style well. Notes of violets and raspberries appear on the nose, while the full-bodied palate is concentrated yet well structured, rich and velvety leading to a long softly tannic finish. The wine is delicious now but built to last decades in the cellar. prominently displayed, a testament to her excellence as a winemaker and her justifiable pride in her work. Referred to as the Queen of Zinfandel, Carol is one of a handful of women who blazed a trail for female winemakers in California. After attending UC Davis and working her way to become winemaker at Windsor, Carol and her husband/business partner decided to venture out on their own. Over the last two and a half decades, she has specialized in single vineyard Zinfandels. Perhaps her most widely recognized wine is Wild Thing Zin – a fruit forward, crowd-pleasing Zinfandel that belongs at a casual backyard barbeque. We found her most interesting and best wines being released under the Carol Shelton label. We also appreciate the winery’s moderation in wine pricing. Carol has avoided the sky-high prices of many wineries and her wines are all great values in the market. • 2022 Coquille Blanc, $28 Concocted from Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Viognier, and Marsanne grapes mostly from the Paso Robles area this complex and deeply layered wine presents a huge mouthful of flavor. It has notes of crushed stone and jasmine followed by peach and citrus flavors and a round long finish. • Rockpile Reserve Zinfandel, $42 Our favorite of the Shelton wines, this is the kind of wine the winery has built its reputation on. It displays gorgeous aromas of black cherries and blackberries, a touch of briar patch and a hint of stone fruit. It is full bodied and powerful yet also silky-textured and elegant from start to lengthy finish. Perfect partner to a lamb or beef stew. • 2019 “Wireless” Old Vine Carignane, $30 The Wireless name comes from the fact that these are old head pruned vines not trained on wires and looking like small bonsai trees. Carignane is one of the Languedoc’s workhorse grapes and is rarely seen in California. Here Shelton has crafted it into a big, luscious juicy wine oozing with dark blueberry pie flavors and baking spice notes. It is an opulent wine yet has the acid and structure to avoid being cloying. If you’re tired of the same old same old give this interesting wine a try. • 2018 “Bluetooth” Alicante Bouchet, $34 We wrote about this wine in the Alicante Bouchet article last year and were glad to retaste it. It is as good as we remember. It shows a beautifully complex nose of blackberries, currants, and leather, and is hugely mouth filling on the palate but not ponderous or over the top. Layered, complex and balanced it has structure to last for decades in the cellar. Beautiful job. One of the many outstanding Carol Shelton Zinfandels. Carol Shelton Wines We met Carol at her winery in a light industrial space near several other wineries and a brewery in Santa Rosa. The small tasting room has an informal, family-owned vibe.
