articles.text: Beginning in 1974 and culminating in 2011 two major projects have made the Japanese Tea House a beloved part of Piedmont Park, serving as a focal point for weddings and other celebrations. Notably, the Tea House is located on the same site where Frank C. Havens originally built another tea house in 1907. Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi describes the first chapter in the story succinctly: “The construction of the new Junior High School called for the demolition of the Leander Redman estate next door. The estate was built in 1906 and had a Japanese tea house in the garden. The Board of Education offered the tea house to the City, and in 1974 the tea house was pulled onto a trailer, (and) moved to Piedmont The idea to acquire, relocate and restore the tea house came from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Garden Club. Both organizations made it their Bicentennial Project. Community leaders Jean Brown Wolfe, Marnie Winsor and Norma Wells helped make the idea a reality. Wolfe, President of the Garden Club and who had already served as Chair of the Park Commission and President of PBF, convinced the City Council to accept the School District’s offer of the tea house. Through PBF, funds were raised to cover the cost of moving the tea house, preparing the site to receive it, and restoring it to its original condition. To complete the first project, in 1976 a Japanese architect was engaged to design the circular dry rock pond, construct the first decking and complete the landscaping. Installation of the dry rock pond was almost as difficult logistically as moving the building but was ultimately accomplished by Rigging International thanks to Piedmont resident and Rigging President Denny McLeod. On June 27, 1976, City leaders were invited to a Japanese style tea ceremony hosted by Wells and Wolfe to celebrate the completion of Piedmont’s own Japanese Tea House and garden. PBFs continued support showing signs of wear and tear. Both the decking and the Tea House needed repair, and some of the landscaping had deteriorated. At that time, former Mayor Valerie Matzger was President of PBF, and she launched a campaign to restore the Tea House and replace the decking and surrounding garden. In addition to the current decking that anchors the Tea House, several lovely benches were offered as tributary opportunities, providing a significant portion of the funding for the project. Contributions from many Piedmont families The Japanese Tea House today Photo courtesy of Scott Fitzgerrell Photo of the Leander Redman Tea House en route to Piedmont Park The tea house in the gardens of the Redman Estate, pre-1974 were recognized with a brass plaque near the entrance to the garden. At the impetus of Mayor Matzger, and following a unanimous vote of the City Council, the name “Jean Brown Wolfe Tea Garden” is inscribed at the top of the plaque to honor her more than 50 years of service to the City. Wolfe had passed away in February of 2010. On September 27, 2011, the newly restored Tea House and the Jean Brown Wolfe Tea Garden were formally dedicated. PBF President Valerie Matzger emceed the celebration, with a diverse crowd in attendance, including Vice Mayor John Chang, Council member Margaret Fujioka, Public Works Director Chester Nakahara and Japanese Consul General Hiroshi Inomata and his wife Midori. Consul Inomata spoke to the crowd and congratulated the City on the authenticity of the Tea House and Garden. Many members of Wolfe’s family were in attendance, including her son Cameron who stated that “the volunteerism of its citizens is the key to the wonderful character of Piedmont.” Matzger and Wolfe continue to be valued advisors to PBF to this day. PBF further enhances Piedmont Park The Tea House and Tea Garden are not the only PBF projects near the Community Hall. The circular planting bed and Magnolia Tree are among PBF’s earliest projects having been completed in 1967. Landscaping and planting along Cherry Tree Walk soon followed in 1971. PBF recently finished fundraising for the Highland - Guildford Steps and Handrails at Cherry Tree Walk, a project made possible by a generous gift in memory of Denny McLeod made by his wife Ruthie McLeod and their family. McLeod was a past President of the Piedmont Garden Club and served as an Advisor to PBF. Perhaps PBF’s most beloved and long-standing gift to the City is the annual Holiday Tree Lighting, which was first established in 1969 and has since become a cherished tradition in Piedmont. This celebration has recently been expanded to include other winter holidays as “Lights Up Piedmont”. Special thanks to Sharon Hom and Gail Lombardi, whose historical research was instrumental in the creation of this article.

articles.text: Piedmont Springs Grotto and Eucalyptus Amphitheater Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on May 27, 2020 This week the Post examines two of Piedmont Park’s most social features from the early part of the 20th century. The Piedmont Springs Grotto and the Eucalyptus Amphitheater served as locations for entertainment, connection and rejuvenation, facets of life our current society yearns for. Take notice of these community locales that enriched and united the community in the days of yore. Doesn’t an outdoor amphitheater for summer Shakespeare plays sound fun about now? Marker 7: Piedmont Springs Grotto The maker is located near the center of the park, on the southside of the creek. When Piedmont celebrated its centennial in 2007, the City honored Piedmont Park in two ways, with the history trail markers and restoring the Piedmont Springs Grotto. The historic sulfur springs grotto became dilapidated since being built in the 1890s by Frank C. Havens. Designer Mark Feldkamp utilized the remains of the grotto and created a plaza seating area alongside Bushy Dell Creek and connects the grotto to a fern garden and the rest of Piedmont Park. In Piedmont’s infancy Walter Blair capitalized on the springs by bottling the mineral water and erecting a decorative gazebo over the spring for those passing by. The springs were a popular destination, and in 1869 lured a visit from Mark Twain when he was on a lecture tour in San Francisco. After the Piedmont Springs Hotel burned in 1892, the sulphur springs remained as the lead tourist attraction. Frank Havens built a concrete faux rock folly around the lower spring. Chicken wire laid the framework for the concrete structure. Concrete niches inside this grotto held the bubbling sulphur waters, with a tin drinking cup to “take the waters.” A second grotto was built near the site of Piedmont Community Hall. A reporter with the Overland Monthly Magazine, Carlotta Sessions, described the grotto in 1901 as follows: ”What appears as a tremendous boulder has been built deep in hills, and there, in the twilight of concealed electricity, ferns cluster around springs of sulphur and magnesia water, while within a tiny aquarium inserted in the rocky wall, fish dart about, flashing light from their golden fins. It all seems so natural that it is hard to realize that the artistic ingenuity of man had planned and executed such a lovely picture.” The new stonework’s cubby holes give glimpses to the original stone grotto behind it. The original grotto lasted for decades until the 1950s when residents complained of the smell of rotten eggs. The city capped the springs then; they still exist underground. Marker 8: Eucalyptus Amphitheater Located in Piedmont Park beyond the outfield of the Softball Field. Frank C. Havens pioneered the importation of eucalyptus to California, evidenced by the Eucalpytus Amphitheater within a grove of the trees at the bottom of Piedmont Park. A patch of Eucalyptus The sulphur springs in Piedmont were exalted for their restorative capabilities, including relief from rheumatism, skin conditions, and pain. Above the current high school softball field is a trail marker for the Eucalyptus Amphitheater, that shows a program from a 1908 performance of Shakespeare’s Love’s Labor’s Lost. The restored stonework grotto in Piedmont Park offers some serenity and a place to listen to the water in Bushy Dell Creek. still remains by the field house at Witter Field. The amphitheater, however, is a specter of the past. The first play performed in the Eucalyptus Amphitheater in the spring of 1908 was Love’s Labor’s Lost, a comedy by William Shakespeare. The amphitheater existed within a grove of eucalyptus. Some of the giant trees even sprouted through the floorboards of the stage. Florence Nace, the first superintendent of the park, fashioned the open-air venue in a rustic stickwork style similar to the rest of the park’s bridges and benches. Through the 1910s, Shakespearian plays continued at the summer theater in Piedmont. The youth were not neglected here however, as the amphitheater was truly a meeting ground for the entire city. Swings and hobby horses entertained the young theater goers as did the performances of Alice in Wonderland and Peter Pan. On August 29, 1915, the Oakland Tribune provided this description of a play: “With the sun rays as a spotlight, a pantomime unfolded with the appearance of two maidens in Greek garb slowly wending their way holding braziers from which thin wreaths of incense smoke ascended heavenwards. Then followed the processional of Egyptian, Greek, Roman, Monk The Eucalyptus Amphitheater was dozens of rows deep and featured balcony seating.

articles.text: One of three new mountain lion cubs found in San Mateo County, are now temporarily at Oakland Zoo. On Sunday, January 26, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) brought three orphaned mountain lion cubs to Oakland Zoo for rehabilitation and care. This marks the 30th mountain lion rescue for the Zoo through its close collaboration with CDFW. Oakland Zoo’s advanced Veterinary Hospital has enabled the Zoo to assist in numerous mountain lion rescue cases for those who were sick, injured, burned, or orphaned. The three mountain lion cubs, now named Fern (female), Thistle (male), and Spruce (male), are currently recovering at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. They were found in Portola Valley, San Mateo County. In January, Portola Valley residents spotted the kittens wandering in the neighborhood, and the cubs were later found hiding under a car. CDFW looked for the kittens’ mother for two weeks, using trail cameras and reports from the Midpeninsula Open Space District. There have been no confirmed sightings of an adult female searching or calling for her cubs. Due to their disoriented behavior, lack of a mother for two weeks, and proximity to where an adult female was hit by a vehicle, CDFW decided to capture the kittens for evaluation with help from the Open Space District. Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff conducted a thorough health examination on the three cubs, now named Fern, Thistle, and Spruce, including treatments and bloodwork. The Two of the three mountain lion siblings were transported to Oakland Zoo on January 26. cubs arrived at Oakland Zoo relatively healthy but thin after being without a mother and not receiving adult care for a fortnight. Zoo veterinarians have estimated them to be approximately three months old. Mountain lions in California face many threats, including car strikes and wildfires. These factors contribute to human-wildlife conflict, increasing encounters as mountain lions encroach on urban areas and developments. “As human development has significantly enhanced the wellbeing of our communities, it has simultaneously taken a toll on wildlife and their natural habitats. As we continue to thrive as a species, it is essential for coexistence that we also take action to ensure the survival of others,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. “We must continually advocate for establishing wildlife corridors, such as the recent overpass in Los Angeles, to maintain the biodiversity of our Golden State.” To support Oakland Zoo’s efforts to rescue and rehabilitate animals in need, please donate at oaklandzoo.org/give An Oakland Zoo veterinarian examining the three cubs on arrival to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. The already large paws of a three month old mountain lion; the big cat also known as panther, puma, and cougar.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 5, 2025 29 Troop 15 Continued from page 10 bat season, so we had to go on a short low-hanging passage to the exit. By then, our stomachs were rumbling so we quickly headed to the reservoir and had lunch. After a drizzly 45 minutes, we started on the rim trial for a return. We saw beautiful views of the whole canyon – mesolithic rocks erupting from the sides. In what seemed like no time, we made it back to camp. After a whole day of hiking, the Scouts craved a large meal. We split into our patrols and cooked dinner, including burgers, ramen, pasta, and other meals. After dinner, something interesting was happening with people’s snacks. Out of view, a gang of mischievous raccoons were plotting a heist of a colorful Cotopaxi backpack that apparently caught their eyes. They started by sending out two goons near the dumpsters across the road. The raccoons made their movements clear, rustling in the bushes and edging as close as possible to human territory. It was only a matter of time before a young Scout spotted their activity. Our forces quickly assembled to yell and bang on pots and sticks to prevent the two raccoons from infiltrating and causing havoc. Little did we know that the rest of the raccoon forces were laughing at us from a safe location 80 meters away. Some Scouts fell for such an elementary decoy. With things going their way, the raccoons finally retrieved a bag with snacks, scampering into the bushes to open their stolen food. But unluckily for them, our young Scout came to the realization that the raccoons stole the bag in a flash. The Scouts organized a hunt and found the bag of food in the bushes. The only signs of the raccoons after that eventful evening were dozens of pairs of beady illuminated eyes from across the road. Troop 15 outsmarted the raccoons this time, but we will surely encounter more wildlife in the future. articles.text: Piedmont City Council honored the Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) during their January 21 council meeting with a proclamation and announcement highlighting PAAC’s upcoming Annual Lunar New Year Celebration at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse from 5:30- 7:30 p.m. on Friday, January 31. The event will feature student performances, crafts, food, drink, and a Lion Dance. LETTERS - MAIN A serious look at fire prevention in Piedmont By Pamela Starr Hadley Editor: This letter is in response to a letter from Rebecca Perlman. I think she has some good ideas. I believe they could be expanded by also covering fire resistant vents, such as those offered by Vulcan, gutter guards, metal roofs, and the like. These relatively simple and cost effective steps could make a big difference in most fires. I was in Piedmont during the 1991 firestorm (same house). I remember being aware that if we had had one more day of Diablo winds, the entire city could have burned down. And that was before we had such extreme fire behavior as we just had (and are having) in Southern California. I think we have not yet fully comprehended the scope of the problem, or the particular vulnerability that Piedmont has. The fires in Southern California are not really wildfires in the usual sense. They are urban conflagrations according to research scientist Jack Cohen. They spread from house to house by direct heat, often ignoring the greenery between houses. While it is always a good idea to keep brush under control it would not have made any difference in this instance. The particular problem in Piedmont is that the houses are often very close together. The new state laws regarding ADUs and lot division will make this worse. Narrow winding roads in many places in Piedmont make access by fire equipment difficult. If we should have a similar incident in Piedmont, we could easily lose the entire city, with the possible exception of some houses, like Hampton house, that are on unusually large lots. What to do? I think there should be a conclave of the relevant heads of departments, such as the fire chief, the head of planning, the head of building, along with fire scientists, architects and engineers to figure out what changes need to be made in our building codes to protect our homes and our community. This is a much bigger project than we have previously imagined. Once we have figured out what we want to do, then we have to figure out how to do it. We can start with codes for new homes. articles.text: Piedmont City Council and City Staff gave a surprise proclamation at their January 21 Council Meeting, honoring Michael Szczech for his work as the City’s Finance Director and wishing him a relaxing retirement. A long-time resident of Piedmont, Szczech served as Finance Director for over seven years and worked his last day on Thursday, January 23. As Finance Director, Szczech administered the City’s fiscal operations, including budgeting, investments, financial transaction processing, record-keeping and reporting, payroll, accounts payable and accounts receivable. In recognition of his performance as Financial Director, the City Council officially declared Friday, January 24, 2025 as Michael Szczech Day. Originally from Chicago, Szczech is a 27-year resident of Piedmont and has raised two daughters in the city. Szczech’s wife Wendy joined the meeting to congratulate him, along with his daughters Emily and Molly joining remotely. “It’s been a great seven-and-ahalf years. I’ve worked with one of the best teams ever,” said Szczech, who described his coworkers as “the most conscientious group of employees I’ve ever worked with.” Szczech was recruited to apply for the role of Finance Director by former Mayor Bob McBain. “He far exceeded any of my expectations,” commented McBain. “He’s one of the finest professionals I’ve ever worked with, and he’s a great Finance Michael Szczech Director and a very high quality person of character and integrity.” A slew of congratulations were given by Szczech’s daughters Emily and Molly, Budget Advisory Committee Chair Frank Ryan, and every member of the City Council. Szczech is leaving big shoes to fill. The City currently is recruiting for a permanent replacement. To serve during the transition, the city council voted on November 18, 2024 to appoint Lisa Malek-Zadeh as Interim Finance Director. Malek-Zadeh will take over as Finance Director on an interim and temporary basis while the city decides on a permanent appointment. In a conversation with Szczech, the Post asked about his decision to retire. How much of a change will retirement be for you? “It will be a big change as I have been working for 52 years. It’s time to relax and find my beach!” Will you miss the short morning walk to work? “I will continue my morning walk, except I will now be accompanied by my hound dogs.” What will you miss most about working at City Hall? “I will miss the people. It is the best group of people I have ever worked with.” Do you have any advice for Piedmont’s next Finance Director? “Keep a close eye on Pension liabilities and Infrastructure needs. Make sure you dive into the details.” City Attorney Deepa Sharma (left), City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, former Mayor Bob McBain, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Finance Director Michael Szczech, Wendy Szczech, Council Member Jennifer Long, Council Member Lorrell Plimier, Council Member Tom Ramsey, and Budget Advisory Committee Chair Frank Ryan Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission has begun a project to replace playground equipment at the Linda Beach Tot Lot. City staff presented an update at the January 14 Park Commission meeting with details of the project. The work will include replacing aging playground equipment as well as adding ADA access from Linda Avenue to the playground. The Tot Lot is currently surfaced with sand, which will be replaced with either ADA compliant matting or turf in order to install a new water fountain or bottle filling station. Funding for the project was included in the current city budget and includes a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. The Park Commission looked into measures to create shade at the playground as well, but were unable to find a solution within the project’s current budget. “With this generous but tight budget we just couldn’t find appropriate equipment and shade structures – either incorporated with the equipment or independent of the equipment are almost double our budget right now,” said Nancy Kent. In preparation for the project, the city’s staff will gather community input at the Tot Lot on January 30 and February 1 from 10 a.m.-12 p.m., asking questions to gauge the most important pieces of playground equipment. The City will ask attendees to share their thoughts on topics like: • What they like most about coming to the Tot Lot • Which types of equipment are most important • Balance of active versus quiet play • Choice of playground surface (samples of options will be available) For tot lot users who are unable to attend either event, an online feedback opportunity will be available next week. Linda Beach Tot Lot

Say hello to Beebee, a bright and bouncy 4-month-old shepherd-mix puppy available through Oakland Animal Services. Beebee is crate trained and house trained, knows her “sit” and “down” commands, and is making great progress with loose-leash walking. She’s a quick learner who’s eager to please. Currently weighing 35 pounds, she’s sure to grow into a strong, athletic dog who’ll need plenty of exercise. Beebee is super friendly and playful with people. Her foster family says she gets along great with her pittie foster sister and should do well with other dogs, including another dog in the home, after a slow introduction. Her foster family describes her as intelligent, energetic, and loving. This spirited pup is looking for an active home with plenty of space to run, play, and explore and for people who can continue her training to keep her happy and well-behaved. articles.text: Piedmont City Council heard an informational report on the City’s budget at their council meeting on Tuesday, January 21. The report contained some good news – a projection of an $800,000 budget surplus. The surplus could result in a lower amount given increased cost projections, that could result in a $400,000 surplus. The surplus would likely be used to refill the Facilities Capital Fund to provide for maintenance and building of public facilities. Piedmont saw an increase in revenue due in part to higher than expected real property transfer tax receipts, increased Recreation Department revenue, Mutual Aid wildfire support, Building Permits and Planning Related Fees, and property taxes. City staff also projects an increase in budget expenditures by a figure of approximately $150,000. The increase in expenditures is primarily due to: • Increased Workers Compensation claims • Higher overtime costs in the Fire Department due to mutual aid wildfire assistance and one vacant position • Higher costs in the Recreation Department due to higher-than-expected program interest and third-party contract program costs. These expenditures are more than offset by the corresponding program revenue. • Offset by lower aquatics subsidy and retiree medical costs According to the report, General Fund revenues are budgeted at $41.5 million, with General Fund expenditures being budgeted at $39.8 million. The Street Funds are expected to be slightly under-budget, due in part to the City adopting the practice of bundling street repair projects together in order to get better overall deals when sending the project out to bid. According to the mid-year report, the ongoing Community Pool project budget is $34.9 million. Through December 31, 2024, $24.6 million has been expended so far, with any funds not expended by the end of the project to be returned to the Facilities Capital Fund. “The General Fund remains in a sound position, with revenues exceeding expenses,” said Finance Director Michael Szczech in his final budget report for the city before his retirement. “This is the result of conservative budgeting and prudent management of day-to-day operations.” However, Szczech continues with caution in the report: “There can be no assurance these trends will continue as the economy continues to face high interest rates and moderate inflation.” For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. Wildfire History Beginning with an acknowledgement of families affected by the ongoing Los Angeles and Palisades Fires, Brannigan gave a brief history of notable wildfires in California. In 1991, the Oakland/Berkeley Hills Fire burned from Tunnel Road in Oakland, destroyed over 5000 structures and killed over 25 people. The fire blazed up to the border of Piedmont in a time of about 5 hours, only stopping because of a wind change. In 2017, fires in Napa and Sonoma County blackened over 35,000 acres of land and destroyed thousands of homes, reaching Santa Rosa’s doorstep in about an hour. Although occurring far from Piedmont’s backyard, this fire is noteworthy because it impacted cities in a similar way that PFD anticipates could happen to Piedmont – starting as a vegetation fire and quickly jumping from structure to structure. Today, the Los Angeles Fires continue to burn throughout Southern California. The fires, including the Palisades Fire to which PFD firefighters were sent on mutual aid in the past weeks, have greatly impacted multiple communities in their areas. “What all of these fires have in common,” stressed Brannigan, “is that they were dense, structure-to-structure fires at some point, socio-economic impacts, both of the residents and demographics of the area, are similar to what we have in Piedmont, and the dollar-amounts were catastrophic.” Brannigan continued to go over in detail the four steps of the City’s Disaster Management Cycle – Preparedness, Response, Recovery, and Mitigation. Preparedness The Fire Dept. begins with preparedness in the event of an emergency. This includes ongoing training, an Emergency Operations Plan, regional coordination, neighborhood preparedness meetings, and general public education on the risk of fires. In terms of what the Piedmont Fire Department is working on to stay prepared, PFD is currently working with a consultant to design an evacuation exercise for May 2025 to showcase practical evacuation procedures for neighborhoods likely to be impacted in the event of a disaster. PFD also plans to work with the Piedmont School District this year to communicate about citywide at-home activities for wildfire preparedness. Response In the event of a fire, PFD would not be operating in a vacuum. In the event of windy and dry conditions, such as during a Red Flag Warning from the National Weather Service, Piedmont works to make sure PFD is fully staffed, coordinated with nearby fire departments, and patrolling the hills for potential fires. PFD sends out emergency messages via AC Alert, an emergency alert system that residents can sign up for at acalert.org. Recovery Funding for the recovery process in the wake of a disaster is primarily sourced through the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and through insurance. FEMA funding is channeled to help pay for the efforts of local fire departments in partnership with the California Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). Although FEMA does not provide direct support in the form of apparatus or personnel, FEMA is a reliable and steady stream of funds in the event of natural disaster. From the insurance perspective, much of the specific details of coverage were out of the scope of the Fire Chief’s presentation. However, it was noted that insurance companies assess possible risk of properties, neighborhoods and communities, and so mitigation strategies to reduce risk have potential to affect recovery and insurance coverage in Piedmont. Wildfire History Beginning with an acknowledgement of families affected by the ongoing Los Angeles and Palisades Fires, Brannigan gave a brief history of notable wildfires in California. In 1991, the Oakland/Berkeley Hills Fire burned from Tunnel Road in Oakland, destroyed over 5000 structures and killed over 25 people. The fire blazed up to the border of Piedmont in a time of about 5 hours, only stopping because of a wind change. In 2017, fires in Napa and Sonoma County blackened over 35,000 acres of land and destroyed thousands of homes, reaching Santa Rosa’s doorstep in about an hour. Although occurring far from Piedmont’s backyard, this fire is noteworthy because it impacted cities in a similar way that PFD anticipates could happen to Piedmont – starting as a vegetation fire and quickly jumping from structure to structure. Today, the Los Angeles Fires continue to burn throughout Southern California. Preparedness The Fire Dept. begins with preparedness in the event of an emergency. This includes ongoing training, an Emergency Operations Plan, regional coordination, neighborhood preparedness meetings, and general public education on the risk of fires. In terms of what the Piedmont Fire Department is working on to stay prepared, PFD is currently working with a consultant to design an evacuation exercise for May 2025 to showcase practical evacuation procedures for neighborhoods likely to be impacted in the event of a disaster. PFD also plans to work with the Piedmont School District this year to communicate about citywide at-home activities for wildfire preparedness. Response In the event of a fire, PFD would not be operating in a vacuum. In the event of windy and dry conditions, such as during a Red Flag Warning from the National Weather Service, Piedmont works to make sure PFD is fully staffed, coordinated with nearby fire departments, and patrolling the hills for potential fires. PFD sends out emergency messages via AC Alert, an emergency alert system that residents can sign up for at acalert.org. Recovery Funding for the recovery process in the wake of a disaster is primarily sourced through the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and through insurance. FEMA funding is channeled to help pay for the efforts of local fire departments in partnership with the California Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). Although FEMA does not provide direct support in the form of apparatus or personnel, FEMA is a reliable and steady stream of funds in the event of natural disaster. From the insurance perspective, much of the specific details of coverage were out of the scope of the Fire Chief’s presentation. However, it was noted that insurance companies assess possible risk of properties, neighborhoods and communities, and so mitigation strategies to reduce risk have potential to affect recovery and insurance coverage in Piedmont. Mitigation Every year, the City mitigates fire risk most notably through vegetation management, otherwise known as weed cutting. The goats brought in to reduce flammable plant matter do a large part in reducing fire risk in areas like Moraga Canyon. Areas like Piedmont Park and Bushy Dell Creek are regularly checked by PFD and Public Works staff to check for hazard risk, removing brush if needed. PFD conducts courtesy and complaint-based inspections if requested, sending out personnel trained in fire prevention and vegetation management to assess the area. For the future, PFD will be receiving updated Fire Hazard Severity Zone Maps, which they will need to adopt via City Ordinance within 120 days after they are received from Cal Fire. This year is also a Fire Code Update year. With new incoming information on fire hazard severity, Brannigan notes the opportunity to open the conversation on what to change or not change within City building and fire codes. Guiding the City through these talks would be the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which the City is required to update this year. A Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) is a FEMA required plan in order to receive mitigation funding. The LHMP update seeks to better prepare Piedmont for natural hazards, including evacuation infrastructure, updates to building codes, and attention on critical facilities in the event of disaster. Future Steps For future measures to take against wildfires, Brannigan spoke about measures that can be taken to reduce fire risk to structures. Residents getting roofing work done can look into making sure they have a Class-A fire rated roof or simply clear out all flammable objects and plants in a 5-foot radius around structures, to give some examples of measures that citizens can take themselves. Another possible measure would be to form a Firewise Community – a neighbor-driven fire prevention organization. Contact with neighbors, a Community Risk Assessment, and a 3-year Action Plan would allow a community to apply for certification as a Firewise Community, which PFD can assist with if the community is interested. Citywide Piedmont could even look for a certification as a Fire Risk Reduction Community. This is a California classification that requires a very high fire hazard severity zone, which Piedmont would qualify for, and Fire Code Adoption and Vegetation Management Adoption that is above and beyond the minimum codes. Currently, Berkeley is the only Northern California city to achieve this status. Before answering questions, Brannigan gave the community a call to action, encouraging the community to get engaged with the hazard prevention process and sign up for AC Alert. “Don’t be a stranger,” encouraged Brannigan. “We’re going to be talking about all these things. Get to know your neighbors, look into becoming a Firewise Community Neighborhood, and we can beat this thing. We can beat fires.” Community members can sign up for AC Alerts at acalert. org. A full recording of the presentation can be viewed at https:// piedmont.granicus.com/player/ clip/3020?redirect=true. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District has announced that nominations are now being accepted for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and have made a difference because of their commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The deadline for nominations is March 14. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, and the winner will be recognized at the May 14 Board of Education meeting, and their good works will be acknowledged. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was the founder of the Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by board member Dewey Watson. Nomination Forms are available in the District Office, by calling Rosalina Barrios, Executive Assistant to the Superintendent, at 594-2614 or via the District website at: Docs.google.com/ document/d/1J92iTb6870oZbIRotoHW8rM3MUmCS8bORuf- 7c1hcCmY/edit?tab=t.0 Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and National School Board Recognition Month I shared at last week’s Board Meeting that January is National School Board Recognition month. Thank you to our PUSD School Board, including Board President, Lindsay Thomasson; VP, Ruchi Medhekar; Board Member, Michael Malione; Board Member, Max Roman; and Board Member, Susy Struble. Thank you also to our student Board members, including Shakila Zuberi, Meher Bachher, Grace Rego, and Mira Sachs. Board positions are elected and voluntary, with no compensation. Thank you to our Board for your service! AI Community Input In our effort to develop a framework for our use of Generative AI, we have created a Board Policy that centers our efforts. We have brought a draft to the Board for a first and second reading; however, we know we will benefit from additional input. Our draft Emerging Technologies Board policies is available at Docs. google.com/document/d/14ZRxkqKs6bxk3Gyz1wArFfIOV_ Wu K P G Q n x H k K A z 8 T1Q / edit?tab=t.0. An additional policy we recommend you review before providing input on the Emerging Technologies policy is our Acceptable Use Policy, which includes a Board Policy, Administrative Regulation, and Exhibit related to student and staff technology use. The Acceptable Use policy is available at Docs.google.com/document/d/1zfeIKcMxnGuozbPt8U5lZD6xWO28zumtWS82I-vO7zg/edit?tab=t.0 We invite your input on our technology policies, particularly with AI in mind. You can share your thoughts at Docs.google.

articles.text: Celebrations Partnering Beyond the Classroom...in Spain & France Toward the end of last year, French teacher Bryan Smith and Spanish teacher Deysi Sahagon proposed a student cultural exchange program allowing our students to travel to France and Spain, and students from those countries to visit PHS/MHS. Fast forward to next week. We will host 21 exchange students and two adult chaperones visiting our community from February 3-11. Thank you to Bryan Smith and Deysi Sahagon, Dr. Yoshihara, Mr. Marik, along with the PHS staff and students for supporting this cultural exchange program, which also aligns with our strategic priority, Partnering Beyond the Classroom. Wildwood Spelling Bee Winners Congratulations to Anya Giri and Parker Chu for their achievement in the Wildwood Spelling Bee competition. After four days and 16 rounds, Giri and Chu achieved the honor of being chosen from the 15 fourth and fifth grade finalists to represent Wildwood School in the Regional Qualifier Test, with Giri as the winner and Chu as the runner-up. Students with the top 45 scores in the Regional Qualifier Test will be invited to compete in-person at the San Ramon Valley Regional Spelling Bee on February 23 at 10:00 a.m. The champion of that event will advance to the 2025 Scripps National Spelling Bee in Washington, D.C., which begins on May 27. Congratulations and good luck to Giri and Chu, and a special thanks to Martin Lewis who coordinates the Wildwood Spelling Bee.

articles.text: After it rains, sometimes we get the chance to see a rainbow in the sky. But what causes a rainbow to form? Rainbows are created when sunlight is refracted by water droplets in the sky, resulting in a colorful display for us to observe. Did you know that this phenomenon can also be seen at night? However, instead of a rainbow, it is known as a moonbow. What causes a Moonbow? A moonbow is produced by the same process that forms a rainbow, with the Moon acting as the light source instead of the Sun. Earlier this year, observers were able to witness a moonbow in Oakland. When the right conditions align, it is a stellar sight to witness. However, such sightings are rare. Why is a Moonbow rare? Moonlight is significantly fainter than sunlight, which is why the circumstances in which you can see a moonbow, especially one with color are so rare. For a moonbow to appear, specific conditions must be met: a full or nearly full Moon, light rain, or sufficient moisture in the atmosphere to refract light, and clear skies to allow the Moon’s light to shine through. What if the moon is not completely full? A moonbow may still appear, but instead of displaying the typical colors we are familiar with, the moonbow will appear white or grey. While rainbows color our daytime sky, moonbows bring magic to our nighttime sky. They show us that even simple things like sunlight, moonlight, and raindrops can create something truly spectacular. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a nonprofit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Colorful skies: Moonbows and rainbows

articles.text: This week Girl Scout Troop 33587 of Piedmont Middle School visited the site of their Silver Award project. The troop is building a general store in a tiny homes community. During their site visit they mapped out what needed to be done for their project. The tiny homes community is called Youth Spirit Artworks. The people there live in small houses, with a communal kitchen close to every house. The organization offers transitional housing for teens and young adults that have aged out of foster care, and they utilize art as therapy. They celebrate youth empowerment and embrace community, land, history, and freedom. The mission of Youth Spirit Artworks is to create spaces for safety and belonging for growth and healing. articles.text: Rob James has been named a Distinguished Eagle Scout upon nomination by the Piedmont Council and Scouting America. The award is granted to Eagle Scouts who, after over 25 years, have distinguished themselves in their life work and have voluntarily shared their talents with their communities. Rare as Eagle Scouts are, Distinguished Eagles are even rarer still, with an inaugural class dating back to 1921. Recipients include President Gerald Ford, Senators Bill Bradley and Sam Nunn, Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, admiral Elmo Zumwalt, Astronaut Commanders Neil Armstrong (Apollo 11) and Jim Lovell (Apollo 13), film director Steven Spielberg, and Justice Stephen Breyer. Rob James has distinguished himself through his legal career and through continued service to others by following the principles of the Scout Oath and Scout Law. Now a partner with the international law firm of Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, Rob began practicing law with them in 1983. He specializes in energy, construction and infrastructure projects. He was recognized as one of the Top 100 Lawyers in California (SF and LA Daily Journal, 2006) for his work on the Chevron-Unocal merger, which thanks to an unsuccessful competing takeover bid by the Chinese National Offshore Oil Company (CNOOC) was termed by Fortune magazine as the “most politicized takeover battle in American business history.” Rob was counsel to the largest sponsor on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, with extensive travel to Russia and Kazakhstan from 1993 to 2000. “Rob was my anchor in this ground-breaking project,” wrote Michael Waller, the lead lawyer for the largest Russian company. “He was the one who I cornered, always outside the limelight, to explore the possible and chart courses to avoid the catastrophic. This transaction could have run off the rails countless times without Rob’s steady hand at the wheel. “Balancing all of the competing concerns in a multinational, multi-faceted transaction such as ours was no easy task. You have precious few opportunities to observe in real time a counterpart walk through such circumstances with such grace and dignity. Working alongside Rob James was one of those precious few opportunities for me.” Rob’s other projects as counsel have included the design and Rob’s most significant contribution is his work on Artificial Intelligence in Renewable Energy, combining two of the most transformative currents of our time. (https://www.pillsburylaw. com/images/content/1/7/178431/ AI-in-RE.pdf). He is the energy lead for the Artificial Intelligence Trust Foundation. Not surprisingly, Rob also has a deep history of pro-bono legal work, and other volunteer activities. In the field of climate change, he is Senior Research Fellow of the Institute for Responsible Carbon Removal and founding counsel of the California Resilience Challenge. He was a San Francisco Bar Association Volunteer of the Month in October 1989 for his pro bono legal services after the Loma Prieta earthquake. He contributed to legal planning for relief efforts following hurricane and superstorm damage on the Atlantic Coast and the Gulf of Mexico in the 2010s. For seven years he served in a variety of roles, including chairman of the board for the Easter Seal Society of San Francisco Bay Area. During his tenure, Rob served children and adults with disabilities through administering direct service provider programs and led fundraising campaigns for research and development of assistive devices for the disabled. Rob has also served in a remarkable array of positions as a Scouting volunteer. He earned his Eagle Scout rank in 1975 in Salinas, California. Starting in 2008, he returned to Scouting as a parent in Piedmont, serving as den leader, assistant scoutmaster, and eventually as president of the Piedmont Scout Council. He continues to serve as the Leadership and Governance lead for the territory serving all of California and Nevada. National Executive Board members Wes Smith and Anne-Marie Lamarche of Piedmont supported the local council’s nomination of Rob. “We have worked closely with Rob at the Council, Area and Territory levels and have found him to be an admirable Scouting Leader… Rob elevates every organization he touches. We believe Rob James exemplifies the DESA award through his accomplishments, impact and service to the Scouting community, as well as the high moral standard to which he holds himself and others,” they wrote. Bob Coleman, Piedmont’s most recent Distinguished Eagle, said, “It is thrilling to add Rob’s name to the list of Piedmont DESA’s. His resume adds great luster to our group.” “In addition to his skill as a leader, Rob also brings thoughtfulness, humor, and humility,” added Piedmont Council Scout Executive Kate Benson. “His willingness to serve has had a wonderful positive impact on our community.” The National Eagle Scout Association Committee, as part of Alumni Relations at the Scouting America’s national office, selected 18 recipients from throughout the U.S. this year. Members of the selection committee are all recipients of the Distinguished Eagle Scout Award. Scouting America, chartered originally as Boy Scouts of America in 1910, is the nation’s foremost youth program of character development and values-based leadership training. The Piedmont Council Scouting America runs programs within the footprint of Piedmont. Programs include Cub Scouts (youth k-5th grade), Scouts BSA (youth 11-18 years old), Venturing (youth 14-20 years old), and Exploring (career based, for youth 14-20 years old). About 1 in 4 Piedmont youth are in scouting programs, and girls are a third of the council’s membership. The character, fitness, leadership and adventure of Scouting America here in Piedmont are open to all youth. To learn more, visit www. piedmontbsa.org, or reach out to contact@piedmontbsa.org. Longtime Piedmont Scout volunteer Rob James construction of the San Francisco Giants baseball (Oracle Park), the first exclusively privately-financed baseball stadium in over three decades (1996-2000); supply of critical United States-origin rare earths for electric vehicles to the American automobile industry (2020-present); $7 billion in Stanford Hospital expansions (2011-present); divestitures of Chevron’s mining operations worldwide (2001-2019); and procurement of the new fleet of Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) railcars (2010-2014). Along the way, he helped the Getty Museum acquire a Vincent Van Gogh painting that at the time was the most expensive work ever sold at auction (1990); negotiated product placement in a James Bond movie (1989); and wrote the world’s shortest courtcited law review article (one word of text) (1982, republished 1999). “He was a brilliant legal strategist, able to lead teams in highly complex transactions,” wrote Mary Cranston, Pillsbury firm chair from 1999-2006. “It was always wonderful to work with Rob. He is as kind as he is brilliant…He was an exceptional leader: growing revenue, introducing creative new legal offerings and developing the next generation of leaders in the firm.” The leadership that may be Questions? He was recognized as one of the Top 100 Lawyers in California (SF and LA Daily Journal, 2006) for his work on the Chevron-Unocal merger, which thanks to an unsuccessful competing takeover bid by the Chinese National Offshore Oil Company (CNOOC) was termed by Fortune magazine as the “most politicized takeover battle in American business history.” Rob was counsel to the largest sponsor on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, with extensive travel to Russia and Kazakhstan from 1993 to 2000. “Rob was my anchor in this ground-breaking project,” wrote Michael Waller, the lead lawyer for the largest Russian company. “He was the one who I cornered, always outside the limelight, to explore the possible and chart courses to avoid the catastrophic. This transaction could have run off the rails countless times without Rob’s steady hand at the wheel. “Balancing all of the competing concerns in a multinational, multi-faceted transaction such as ours was no easy task. You have precious few opportunities to observe in real time a counterpart walk through such circumstances with such grace and dignity. Working alongside Rob James was one of those precious few opportunities for me.” Rob’s other projects as counsel have included the design and Rob’s most significant contribution is his work on Artificial Intelligence in Renewable Energy, combining two of the most transformative currents of our time. (https://www.pillsburylaw. com/images/content/1/7/178431/ AI-in-RE.pdf). He is the energy lead for the Artificial Intelligence Trust Foundation. Not surprisingly, Rob also has a deep history of pro-bono legal work, and other volunteer activities. In the field of climate change, he is Senior Research Fellow of the Institute for Responsible Carbon Removal and founding counsel of the California Resilience Challenge. He was a San Francisco Bar Association Volunteer of the Month in October 1989 for his pro bono legal services after the Loma Prieta earthquake. He contributed to legal planning for relief efforts following hurricane and superstorm damage on the Atlantic Coast and the Gulf of Mexico in the 2010s. For seven years he served in a variety of roles, including chairman of the board for the Easter Seal Society of San Francisco Bay Area. During his tenure, Rob served children and adults with disabilities through administering direct service provider programs and led fundraising campaigns for research and development of assistive devices for the disabled. Rob has also served in a remarkable array of positions as a Scouting volunteer. He earned his Eagle Scout rank in 1975 in Salinas, California. Starting in 2008, he returned to Scouting as a parent in Piedmont, serving as den leader, assistant scoutmaster, and eventually as president of the Piedmont Scout Council. He continues to serve as the Leadership and Governance lead for the territory serving all of California and Nevada. National Executive Board members Wes Smith and Anne-Marie Lamarche of Piedmont supported the local council’s nomination of Rob. “We have worked closely with Rob at the Council, Area and Territory levels and have found him to be an admirable Scouting Leader… Rob elevates every organization he touches. We believe Rob James exemplifies the DESA award through his accomplishments, impact and service to the Scouting community, as well as the high moral standard to which he holds himself and others,” they wrote. Bob Coleman, Piedmont’s most recent Distinguished Eagle, said, “It is thrilling to add Rob’s name to the list of Piedmont DESA’s. His resume adds great luster to our group.” “In addition to his skill as a leader, Rob also brings thoughtfulness, humor, and humility,” added Piedmont Council Scout Executive Kate Benson. “His willingness to serve has had a wonderful positive impact on our community.” The National Eagle Scout Association Committee, as part of Alumni Relations at the Scouting America’s national office, selected 18 recipients from throughout the U.S. this year. Members of the selection committee are all recipients of the Distinguished Eagle Scout Award. Scouting America, chartered originally as Boy Scouts of America in 1910, is the nation’s foremost youth program of character development and values-based leadership training. The Piedmont Council Scouting America runs programs within the footprint of Piedmont. Programs include Cub Scouts (youth k-5th grade), Scouts BSA (youth 11-18 years old), Venturing (youth 14-20 years old), and Exploring (career based, for youth 14-20 years old). About 1 in 4 Piedmont youth are in scouting programs, and girls are a third of the council’s membership. The character, fitness, leadership and adventure of Scouting America here in Piedmont are open to all youth. To learn more, visit www. piedmontbsa.org, or reach out to contact@piedmontbsa.org. Longtime Piedmont Scout volunteer Rob James construction of the San Francisco Giants baseball (Oracle Park), the first exclusively privately-financed baseball stadium in over three decades (1996-2000); supply of critical United States-origin rare earths for electric vehicles to the American automobile industry (2020-present); $7 billion in Stanford Hospital expansions (2011-present); divestitures of Chevron’s mining operations worldwide (2001-2019); and procurement of the new fleet of Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) railcars (2010-2014). Along the way, he helped the Getty Museum acquire a Vincent Van Gogh painting that at the time was the most expensive work ever sold at auction (1990); negotiated product placement in a James Bond movie (1989); and wrote the world’s shortest courtcited law review article (one word of text) (1982, republished 1999). “He was a brilliant legal strategist, able to lead teams in highly complex transactions,” wrote Mary Cranston, Pillsbury firm chair from 1999-2006. “It was always wonderful to work with Rob. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

Against Alameda, they clung to a 38-36 lead to start the fourth, but outscored the Hornets 16-8 in the final minutes. “It’s always an adjustment when you have played down. But we weren’t sharp in the first half; we had 12 turnovers by halftime that was silly or unforced. The fourth quarter, I was really proud of them for how they responded,” said coach Bryan Gardere. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team walked out of the last week with two wins out of its last three games. Although the Highlanders lost 74-60 to Western Alameda County Conference foes Alameda on Thursday, January 23 at Binks Rawlings Gym, they followed up with a dominant road win over Novato 66-35 two days later and had a high-score 91-44 display over Capuchino at home on Monday, January 27. The batch results bring Piedmont’s record to 11-9 with six games left in the regular season. The win over Capuchino came against a Division 4 school of the Central Coast Section, making PHS 4-0 against other D4 schools. Piedmont got all of its players on the score sheet in their 91-point drubbing of Capuchino, including double-digit points by five different players. “This is what you want for team morale late in the season. To see your starters cheering on guys just for team spirit feels pretty good. I thought our on-ball defense was aggressive and any time you can score 91 points is an accomplishment. It’s another D4 win and we could end up as high as D2 with the new NCS seeding system. When we can beat another D4 team by 40, it shows the quality of our team,” Spencer said following Monday’s win. It was a strong group of games by senior leader Ravi Silverberg, who scored 15 against Alameda, 27 vs. Novato, and 22 against Capuchino. “I’m just trusting the game plan and my teammates. My coaches are putting me in great positions. I just go out there and try to do my job. It’s a test, we have hard league games coming up, so we have to get ready for those,” Silverberg said. 74-60 loss to Alameda Alameda came out hot in the first quarter up 25-7 but Piedmont played them tight in the remaining three quarters. The Hornets held a 39-22 point lead at halftime, extending the gap to 57-38 in the third. Piedmont scored 19 points in the fourth but conceded 20. Final scorers: Silverberg and Lucian Fang-Ring scored 15 points. Dillon Casey scored 13 points, P.J. Brayer had 10, and Cash Panico scored seven. 66-35 rout of Novato Piedmont held Novato to under 11 points in each quarter, including limiting them to eight points in the second and six points in the fourth. PHS outscored them 22-10 in the first quarter and added 17 more in the second to lead 39-18 by halftime. The Highlanders scored 15 more in the third and 12 in the fourth quarter. Final scorers: Silverberg led with 27 points, Casey scored 14, Brayer had 13, while Beach Lorin and Fang-Ring had six each. 91-44 blowout win vs. Capuchino Piedmont scored over 20 points in all four quarters, but played to a tight 20-13 first quarter. The Highlanders exploded in the second quarter with 23 points while allowing 11 to go up 43-24 Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg scored 27 points on Novato and 22 on Capuchino. Dillon Casey with a layup against Capuchino.

Alameda took a 35-34 lead in the third quarter with 1:47 left, but it was the only time the Hornets held a lead. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team suffered a heartbreaking 2-1 loss to Alameda on Wednesday, January 22, after conceding the game-winning goal in second-half stoppage time with less than one minute to play. Piedmont opened with a goal in the 15th minute, but struggled to find fluidity in the remaining 65 minutes of action. “It was tough. Alameda is obviously delighted with that result. It probably should’ve been a draw,” said Piedmont coach Dan Chubbock. “They managed to get that final chance and it fell to their best player who hit the shot. We just look beat up and bruised, but we have a strong enough squad where we should be able to get this game under control. We weren’t good enough tonight, simple as that.” The result brings Piedmont’s record to 4-2-6 (W-T-L) and 1-1-3 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. To qualify for North Coast Section, PHS must finish with a .500 winning percentage on its overall record, league record, or record against fellow Division 4 schools. PHS has now lost three matches in a row, including two one-goal losses to Alameda after falling 4-3 on January 17. Piedmont was playing considerably well before winter break, including 2-1 wins over D4 school Cardinal Newman and Cal High of D1, while they went toe-to-toe with defending D1 state champions Archbishop Mitty in a 2-1 loss. Piedmont was notably without its leading scorer Elsa Wallway. Its back line has suffered considerable injuries. “We had those ups and downs last year, like how we lost to Encinal. It’s a little different now; playing Alameda so close together with the same injuries made things tough. I’d love to see how we compete when we’re at full strength,” Chubbock said. With six matches left in the regular season, the Highlanders still have an opportunity to turn things around and re-find its form. Match Recap After back and forth action to open the game, Piedmont broke through in the 15th minute when Elia Kwong broke through the defense to whip a hard shot on target. Kwong’s shot was saved and rebounded perfectly to Ryo Woltag at the left post, tapping it into the empty net. From there, both teams traded possession without anything overtly challenging. Samantha Ronen had a shot blocked in front of net in the 31st minute and had another shot trickle wide five minutes later. Alameda scored on its first good look of the game in stoppage time of the first half at 40+1 when the Hornets’ right winger sent a low cross to her forward in front of the net—slotting in the goal. Louisa Symkowick had a shot go wide at 40+3 before halftime. Piedmont struggled to create in the second half with a lot of empty long passes. Hannah Sullivan had a shot blocked in the 47th, while Woltag also had an attempt blocked in the 52nd. Sullivan had one more look in a good position in the 65th when Kyla Williams sent a cross that deflected to Sullivan, but she couldn’t make square contact on the volley attempt. The Highlanders drew just one corner in the second half in the 72nd minute, but couldn’t take advantage. Alameda’s game-winner came with around 30 seconds left in second-half stoppage time Staff Photos Ryo Woltag perfectly positioned for her goal into Alameda’s empty net. Elia Kwong pictured here taking her shot attempt which led to Ryo Woltag’s goal.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Laney Athletics Four former Piedmont High students are currently competing on Laney College’s women’s basketball team: Erinn Gardere (front row, second from left), Adrienne Blackwell (front row, second from right), Maddie Hill (front row, right), and Lindsey Wirgler (top row, second from right). Piedmont High’s basketball programs have possibly been the best at the school at sending players off to compete in college. Four former players on Bryan Gardere’s girls’ basketball team are currently competing at Laney College: Adrienne Blackwell, Maddie Hill, Erinn Gardere, and Lindsey Wirgler. The team is currently 18-3 with seven games remaining in the season. Blackwell, PHS Class of 2023, was a member of Piedmont’s Division 4 North Coast Section title and Western Alameda County Conference title-winning team in 2023. She transferred to Piedmont for her senior year after spending two years at Santiago High in Corona in Southern California and her freshman year at St. Mary’s in Stockton. She’s now a sophomore at Laney College where she has played both years. This season, Blackwell has appeared in 20 games, scoring 118 points by converting 32.8 percent from the field and 30.8 percent for 3-pointers. She has also recorded 76 rebounds, 24 assists, 10 steals, and one block. As a freshman, she appeared in all 29 games of Laney’s 24-5 Staff Photos Adrienne Blackwell shown during her senior year at Piedmont High in Staff Photo Erinn Gardere (left) and Lindsey Wirgler on Senior Night at Piedmont High in 2024 2023. season, helping them reach the CCCAA State Quarterfinals. She finished with 186 points, 59 rebounds, 23 assists, 22 steals, and one block. Hill, a PHS classmate in 2023, was another member of NCS and WACC titles in her senior year of 2023. She was a four-year starter at PHS and was our 2020 Honorable Mention for Freshman of the Year. At Laney Hill has appeared in 14 games this season. She has recorded 157 points while shooting 34.2 percent from the field and 33 percent for 3-pointers, to go along with 31 rebounds, 13 assists, and 17 steals. She initially joined Rocky Mountain University in Montana following graduation from PHS. As a freshman at RMU, Hill appeared in 11 games for 18 points, while hitting four 3-point attempts. Wirgler, PHS Class of 2024, emerged as a starter her senior year at Piedmont after sitting out the previous season when she transferred to Piedmont High. We named her among the school’s breakout starts of 2023/2024 after becoming the school’s second-leading scorer behind Natalia Martinez. As a senior, Wirgler was a part of Piedmont sharing the WACC title with Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont’s second straight WACC banner. With the Laney Eagles Wirgler has appeared in 14 games. She’s scored 22 points, including eight field goals and five 3-pointers, adding 15 rebounds, 10 assists, nine steals, and a block. Erinn Gardere, PHS Class of 2024, never appeared for Piedmont High on the basketball court due to transfer policies ruling her ineligible, but she was able to compete on the Highlanders’ flag football team. She is coach Bryan Gardere’s niece. She’s showing the quality the Highlanders missed out on as a freshman at Laney. So far this season, Gardere has appeared in 20 games, scoring 234 points by converting 79 field goals at 32.5 percent, to go along with 56 threes at 29.9 percent. Erinn has also logged 45 rebounds, 14 assists, and 26 steals.

articles.text: We return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021, where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Aside The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. A downed redwood tree at Portola Redwoods State Park.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 29, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Walk along old growth trees at Portola Redwoods State Park By Jonathan Comeaux We return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021, where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Aside The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. A downed redwood tree at Portola Redwoods State Park. The Old Big Tree at the end of the Old Tree Trail is estimated to be 1,200 years old. The redwood is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter. from the awe striking size, the thousand year old tree is among the few old growths to make it through the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent through the hill sides for near two-miles and gaining 550 feet in elevation until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail—turning left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. Turning right starts a 1.5 mile hike to a historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turned left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with a T—turning right to make our way to Upper Escape Road, turning right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car—making it a 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that we crossed 18 patrons on the 0.6 out-and-back Old Tree Trail. Aside from towering redwoods in every direction, you can often spot chickadees chirping about, an occasional banana slug wriggling beneath you, and the knocking of woodpeckers off in the distance. From January 2021 Staff Photos Hikers can still spot burn marks from previous decades along the many first- and second-generation redwoods of Portola State Park. Downed trees line your path on many of the 18 miles of hiking trails at Portola Redwoods State Park. DISCOVER REAL STRENGTH IN 2025! articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will ring in its first show of the year with the Northern California premiere of Exotic Deadly: Or the MSG Play, performing this Thursday, January 30 through March 8. Set in 1999, Japanese American high schooler Ami is trying to fit in with her American peers and she is devastated to discover her family helped create MSG, the purportedly addictive and dangerous ingredient that’s gained infamy. When a mysteriously cool new girl arrives at school, Ami vows to find the truth and save the world from MSG. Spiced with anime and ‘90s pop culture inf luences, this whimsically wacky time-traveling adventure is a riotous romp through teenage crushes, family legacies and the delicious properties of instant ramen. Exotic Deadly: Or the MSG Play received its world premiere at The Old Globe in San Diego, where it was called “wildly funny. Smart and hilarious” by The San Diego Union-Tribune. San Francisco Playhouse has assembled a cast of talented actors for this imaginative new play. Ana Ming Bostwick-Singer makes her Playhouse debut as Ami. articles.text: Catch the world premiere of The Thing About Jellyfish, opening at Berkeley Repertory Theatre this Friday, January 31 for a run through March 8. It features 12-year-old Suzy Swanson who, during the final week of summer vacation, is devastated to learn that her best friend Franny has drowned. Struggling to comprehend this tragic loss, Suzy retreats into her imagination, embarking on journeys around the globe, diving into the ocean’s deepest realms and pondering the enigmas of distant, collapsed stars. Based on a novel by Ali Benjamin and adapted for the stage by Keith Bunin, The Thing About Jellyfish is directed by Tyne Rafaeli. This visually stunning and deeply moving coming-of-age story delves into love, loss, friendship, and the boundless resilience of the human spirit and invites audiences on a journey that transcends the boundaries of grief and illuminates the resilJanssen, Colby Kipnes, Lexi Perkel, Rebecca Schweitzer, Robert Stanton, Kayla Teruel and Antonio Watson. “Ali Benjamin’s astonishing novel is a story about the most essential of human experiences— love, loss, and how to embrace the greatest mysteries of the universe,” added director Tyne Rafaeli. “Through the eyes of the singular Suzy Swanson, we are taken on a journey that allows us all to reflect on the extraordinary gift of being alive. articles.text: Celebrated actor, director and filmmaker Robert Townsend takes audiences on a one-man rollercoaster ride through show business in Living the Shuffle, performing now through February 2 at The Marsh in Berkeley. The Marsh Berkeley presents the return of Living the Shuffle, a captivating one-man show by renowned actor and director Robert Townsend, being performed through February 2. Written, performed and directed by Townsend and produced by both Don Reed and Townsend, this rollercoaster of a play takes audiences through the highs and lows of show business, as Townsend shares his trailblazing career. From navigating the dangerous streets of Chicago to performing Julius Caesar at a gangster convention in New York City, Townsend chronicles his path to creating the groundbreaking film Hollywood Shuffle (1987), which launched his career and established him as a pioneer in Black cinema. In the movie, aspiring actor and hot dog stand employee Bobby Taylor (played by Townsend) catches the ire of his grandmother (Helen Martin) for auditioning for a role in the regrettably titled exploitation film Jivetime Jimmy’s Revenge. When production company Tinseltown Studios casts Taylor in the title role, he has a series of conflicted dreams satirizing African-American stereotypes in Hollywood, and must reconcile his career goals with his desire to remain a positive role model for his little brother (Craigus R Johnson). When Living the Shuffle first debuted at The Marsh Berkeley in 2019, it received rave reviews from critics and audiences alike. Theatrius wrote: “Townsend expertly weaves deeply personal moments with laugh out loud comedy,” asserting that it was “an experience unlike any [they’ve] seen before.” BroadwayWorld applauded it as “Fascinating and inspirational, 90 minutes of captivating tales and good humor.” Nicknamed one of the “godfathers of the independent film world,” Townsend is an actor, director, writer and filmmaker with over 30 years in show business and a recurring role on the FX/Hulu Emmy Winning juggernaut dramedy The Bear. Noticing the difficulty Black actors had finding jobs and the lack of consistent work available in the film industry led Townsend to create opportunities for himself and fellow artists. He co-wrote, directed, produced and starred in his first film, financed by his personal credit cards and a miracle—the critically acclaimed Hollywood Shuff le, a satire depicting the trials and tribulations of Black actors in Hollywood. Nominated for 30 NAACP Image Awards, Townsend’s prolific television work has been seen on Disney, Fox, NBC, MGM, HBO, WB and MTV. Reed, the play’s co-producer, was the 2016 Theatre Bay Area winner for Outstanding Solo Production for East 14th, and has earned recognition from the San Francisco Bay Area Theatre Critics Circle, as well as three nominations from the NAACP for Best Actor and Best Playwright. Tickets ($40 regular, $50-$100 VIP) and showtimes for performances at The Marsh Berkeley (2120 Allston Way) are available online at themarsh.org, or by phone at 415-282-3055.

articles.text: SF Ballet’s 92nd Opening Gala brings magic, glamour to New Year San Francisco Ballet in Balanchine’s Symphony in C choreography by George Balanchine Tamara Rojo, the artistic director of the San Francisco Ballet, may have been right in her on-stage remarks at the Company’s 2025 opening night gala at the War Memorial House this past Wednesday. From the spectacular 90-minute performance by some of the world’s finest dancers to the audience’s chance to take the floor during the after-party at the transformed City Hall, the Gala was a marvel of a celebration, one that made you proud to live in a city like ours. Say what you will about San Francisco, but there’s still plenty of art, style and revelry. The combination was particularly intoxicating on January 24th, as it all came together at the city’s Civic Center. SF Ballet’s biggest fundraising event of the year that serves as a major source of financial support for the company’s artistic and educational initiatives, the opening night gala is both an introduction to the Company’s upcoming season and an opportunity to thank patrons with exclusive performances available only that evening. As in previous years, the Gala began with a red-carpet reception and dinner at City Hall, where tables sold well in advance. The event, regularly profiled in the Town and Country magazine, drew San Francisco’s elite, including politicians, former and current mayors, banking executives, philanthropists, fashion designers, and other notable figures. This year’s honorary chair was Ayesha Curry, wife of San Francisco Warriors basketball star Stephen Curry. For the rest of the public, the doors of the War Memorial Theatre opened at 7 pm, and the foyer quickly filled with festively dressed ballet enthusiasts, laughing, chatting, and toasting. A black-tie affair, the SF Ballet’s Gala is undoubtedly the most fashionable event in town. The theatre’s marble-and-gold foyer, adorned with a dramatic red gauze canopy for the occasion, made for a natural runway. Colorful trains of elegant gowns trailed gracefully up the stairs, sparkling necklines glistened under the chandeliers, and the rhythmic click of stilettos echoed across the space. Hats, feather trims, and even the occasional (gasp) furs also made their appearance. Men’s fashion centered on classic tuxedos, though there were bold exceptions—after all, who says pumps and tutu-inspired dresses are just for women? Most importantly, everyone seemed to be enjoying themselves. Even the ushers looked pleased. At around 8 p.m. the performance chimes rang for the third time, summoning people into the auditorium. The national anthem, performed by the San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under the baton of music director and principal conductor Martin West, added a note of gravitas to the evening. It was followed by the intense and inspiring pre-curtain video short for Rojo’s third year as artistic director, whose tagline, “Transcend the ordinary!” felt right on point. Then came the first dance number: a bedroom pas de deux from Act I of Manon by Sir Kenneth MacMillan, marking its San Francisco premiere. Danced brilliantly by the SF Ballet’s rising star Jasmine Jimison and Max Cauthorn, it was a perfect foray into the company’s new season (Manon opens this Friday, January 27th). Before the next number, a vibrant Hungarian Dance from Raymonda choreographed by Tamara Rojo after Marius Petipa, honorary gala chair Ayesha Curry addressed the audience. A businesswoman, chef, author and actress, Ms. Curry is also an eloquent advocate for the art of ballet. “These dancers are top of the top of the top athletes. What they do with their bodies is unmatched,” Curry, radiant in her glittery strapless black gown said as she stood alongside Tamara Rojo, also stunning in a fitted black-and-gold tunic. “Ballet,” Curry continued, “gives you a safe space to be creative, to imagine…. I’m excited to be able to feel something tonight.” Judging by the frequent cries of “bravo” ringing through the auditorium, there was no shortage of emotion. The Three Preludes (choreographed by Ben Stevenson) perfectly illustrated Curry’s remarks about the athleticism of ballet. Classical ballet is Jasmine Jimison and Max Cauthorn in the bedroom pas de deux from MacMillan’s Manon challenging on its own, but performing on top of a ballet barre, as lead ballerina Frances Chung did in part of the piece, takes it to another level. Chung was in excellent hands with Harrison James as her partner, whose performance was flawless. Their minimalist costumes, paired with Rachmaninoff’s piano score, kept the focus squarely on the precision and beauty of their movements. Following this, Esteban Hernández, dressed in black, delivered a dramatic solo from 5 Tangos by Hans van Manen—a predictable crowd-pleaser that did not disappoint.
