articles.text: Acclaimed pianist Malcolm Martineau joins at Zellerbach Hall Cal Performances presents soprano singer Lise Davidsen in recital with pianist Malcolm Martineau this Tuesday, February 4, at Zellerbach Hall. Norwegian soprano Lise Davidsen will make her nationally anticipated Bay Area debut on Tuesday, February 4 at 7:30 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. She will be joined by one of the world’s most renowned collaborators on piano, Malcolm Martineau, who appeared at Cal Performances last season with soprano Erin Morley. It takes a lot to stir up the New York City classical music world, where an endless stream of virtuosic artists passes through on a weekly basis, performing in some of the world’s most iconic halls. But Davidsen pulled off the operatic equivalent of a mic drop last fall, when — following a string of acclaimed roles at the Met — she dazzled a sold-out house on that grand stage in her New York solo recital debut. Her program in Berkeley will include selected arias and songs by Giuseppe Verdi (“Tu che le vanità” from Don Carlo), Henry Purcell (“Thy Hand, Belinda… Dido’s Lament” from Dido and Aeneas), Richard Strauss (“Es gibt ein Reich” from Ariadne auf Naxos, and others), Edvard Grieg (“Dereinst, Gedanke mein”), Franz Schubert (“Ellens Gesang III (Ave Maria), and Richard Wagner (“Liebestod” from Tristan und Isolde.) articles.text: Winter Wandering Festival in SF Jan. 31- Feb. 2 This Friday through Sunday, join the Left Coast Chamber Ensemble for its Winter Wandering Festival, a weekend musical adventure. The festival will feature performances of “Schubert Quintet: Hay que caminar,” “On the Threshold of Dreamland,” “A Dark Matter” and “Winter Journey.” “Schubert Quintet: Hay que caminar” strikes a meaningful balance between beginning and ending, life and death. Left Coast violinists Anna Presler and Liana Bérubé will take on Italian avantgarde composer Luigi Nono’s late work “Hay que caminar… soñando” (“One must walk dreaming”), a piece defined equally by its being written in the final years of Nono’s life and at the height of his political activism. The piece is simultaneously dark and light, beautiful and uneasy — a glimpse into the mind of a composer unsatisfied with the world he is soon to leave behind. Featured side by side with the Nono masterwork is Franz Schubert’s String Quintet in C Major, a piece often cited as Schubert’s greatest achievement in all of his chamber music. It is an honest reflection on the human experience written in the final months of Schubert’s life; its iconic melodies give just as much voice to joy as sorrow, in which the end of a life sounds less like death than it does transcendence. “On the Threshold of Dreamland” combines the efforts of Left Coast and renowned Bay Area chamber choir Volti SF. World premieres by American composers Todd Kitchen and LJ White — alongside works by Laurie San Martin, Huang Ruo and Benjamin Britten — make for an eclectic, beautiful, and sometimes unsettling sonic journey. This performance will be preceded by a pre-concert talk by LJ White in Berkeley and by Todd Kitchen in San Francisco. “A Dark Matter” is sure to leave listeners refreshed as they continue on their journey. This program includes the world premiere of an eponymous piece by Bay Area composer Addie Camsuzou, and a performance of composer Gilad Cohen’s winning piece from Left Coast’s 2023 Composition Contest. “ Wi nt e r Jou r ney,” a n unabridged performance of Franz Schubert’s iconic “Winterreise,” invites listeners to think deeply about the journey they’ve undertaken. Guest tenor Kyle Stegall notes that the central figure of this piece’s narrative is a man “not fully aware of what he’s looking for … that ‘getting lost’ feeling is part of the character of this piece, which is so unique.” In all its tumult and frigidity, the piece offers listeners the freedom to get lost along the way, to leave their journeys open-ended or to go on wandering. Festival passes are $120 for general admission and $60 for students. Tickets for individual concerts are $38 general and $18 for students at the door, and $35 general and $15 for students in advance. articles.text: Noir City — the world’s largest annual film noir festival, now in its 22nd year — is in full swing at the Grand Lake Theatre every day through this Sunday, February 2. The theme for this year’s festival, hosted by Film Noir Foundation founder and Turner Classic Movies (TCM) host Eddie Muller, features 24 movies in 10 days and nights, shining a spotlight on women whose cinematic legacy is entwined with the rise of film noir. Many of this year’s films star the six actresses profiled in Muller’s 2002 book Dark City Dames: The Wicked Women of Film Noir, which is being reissued through a TCM book series in April 2025, in a newly revised and expanded edition. Jane Greer, Marie Windsor, Audrey Totter, Evelyn Keyes, Coleen Gray and Ann Savage are the core cadre of women featured in this year’s Noir City program, which includes many of their signature films, including, respectively, Out of the Past (1947), The Narrow Margin (1952), Tension (1949), The Prowler (1951), The Killing (1956) and Detour (1945). In addition to those acclaimed favorites, the program also highlights films starring nine other actresses notable for their performances in crime films of the era: Joan Bennett, Peggie Castle, Rhonda Fleming, Marsha Hunt, Ella Raines, Ruth Roman, Jan Sterling, Claire Trevor and Helen Walker. Not coincidentally, the expanded edition of Muller’s book includes new profiles of these women. “One thing I’ve learned after doing programs for 25 years,” Muller said, “is that you need to circle back and re-show the classics – the bedrock of the genre. Some of these films are wellknown to the hardcore, but for younger fans, who may have been in grade school when I started doing festivals, this will be the first time they’ve seen many of these movies … and certainly the first time on a big screen with an enthusiastic audience.” Muller noted that extra effort was made this year to secure as many 35mm prints as possible: “It’s harder than ever to show film prints, so it feels sort of Billy Wilder’s 1951 film Ace in the Hole, featuring Jan Sterling and Kirk Douglas, is just one of the many double-featured films running through this Sunday for this year’s femme fatale-themed Noir City festival at Grand Lake Theatre. valedictory.” Fourteen of the festival’s 24 offerings are film prints. “It’s remarkable to realize that when I began these festivals, everything was on film. No digital versions existed. Now, this might be the first — and last — time that younger viewers will see a 35mm film print, ”Miller added. “I’m very enthused about this year’s program because I had friendships with many of the women we’re celebrating and I’ll have plenty of stories to share — as well as being able to see these women again in all their glamorous glory,” Muller said. One sample of the double feature programs in the festival’s remaining week includes: Sunday, February 2 • The Prowler (Joseph Losey, 1951), 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Losey’s greatest American film, from a script by legendary screenwriter Dalton Trumbo, has a cop (Van Heflin) stalking a lonely, affluent housewife (Evelyn Keyes) and deciding to win her in time-honored noir tradition: by knocking off her husband. Don’t miss this opportunity to see one of the rarest — and most unusual—of all films noir in its original 35mm glory. • Ace in the Hole (Billy Wilder, 1951), 4 p.m. and 9 p.m. On its release, critics called this the most bitter, cynical and mean-spirited movie ever made. It still may hold the honor. What’s certain is how frighteningly prescient Wilder’s tale of mainstream media manipulation turned out to be. Kirk Douglas is stupendously rotten as a disgraced reporter reclaiming the spotlight by prolonging the plight of a trapped miner. A genuine masterpiece. Presented digitally. A full list of film schedules and tickets ($22.80 for a double feature) for the festival at Grand Lake Theatre (3200 Grand Avenue, Oakland) is available at noircity.com.

articles.text: Thursday, February 6, 7:00 p.m. William Gee Wong Book Talk Join Bill Wong, native-born in Oakland’s Chinatown, now a Piedmont resident, who will have a riveting discussion with colleague Bruce Koon about Chinese American history during the Chinese Exclusion Era, centered around Bill’s recently released book, Sons of Chinatown. A slide show will be followed by a discussion. A light reception will close the evening. Bill has spent a fruitful career as a newspaper journalist who broke barriers as one of the few Chinese Americans in the mainstream American press, starting in the early 1960s, including time with the San Francisco Chronicle, the Wall Street Journal, and the Oakland Tribune. This event is free; donations are accepted. Saturday, February 15, 11 a.m.–2:00 p.m. California Watercolor Association California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition opening reception and awards presentation. Join us to celebrate the 85 artists selected by juror Michael Holter. Awards, totaling an estimated $16,000 in cash and sponsor products, will honor the top 20 paintings, with decisions made by Awards Juror Gary Bukovnik. This annual event will be open through March 23 and available to the public from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. Sunday, February 16, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio Join Bill Jackman, Albert Brooks, and Michael Jones in celebrating Valentine’s Day with a concert titled In the Spirit of Love. Enjoy the music in the intimate PCA Classic Jazz Club with this skilled piano trio providing all your favorite love songs from the 20s (It Had to be You) and 30s (My Funny Valentine) right up into the 60s (Never on Sunday; Lara’s Theme), with some ballads, some swing, a little Latin flavor, and even some blues, along with complimentary refreshments. Advance tickets are $25 at https://bpt. me/6214927, or $30 at the door, cash/check only. Friday, February 21, 7:00 p.m. Michael Jones Trio Jazz Concert Michael Jones is a bassist and band leader in the Bay Area who has performed for over 30 years with jazz and blues. After studying music at the University of Colorado, Michael migrated to the San Francisco Bay Area where he has played with Al Tanner, Faye Carroll, Ed Kelley, Donald Bailey, Pharoah Sanders, Denise Perrier, Calvin Keyes, and Buddy Montgomery. For this concert, the Trio will be joined by Azure McCall, an award-winning vocalist known as Hawaii’s first lady of jazz. She has sung with Ray Brown, Freddie Hubbard’s band, Dizzy Gillespie, and many others. Tickets for this special event will be available soon on the PCA website. articles.text: Events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are always festive. The room is usually decked out with art and the food is always great. The same can be said for the entertainment. Unbelievable variety! Italian-American pianist Cristiana Pegoraro is in our area for a series of concerts. Usually, touring musical artists are in town for a concert and then leave the next day. Fortunately, Cristiana and I had the opportunity to talk about the philosophy of music and what is missing in today’s performers. I try to arrive early to listen to the artists warm-up. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 29, 2025 The Musical Gourmet The Midas touch By Joseph Gold Events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are always festive. The room is usually decked out with art and the food is always great. The same can be said for the entertainment. Unbelievable variety! Italian-American pianist Cristiana Pegoraro is in our area for a series of concerts. Usually, touring musical artists are in town for a concert and then leave the next day. Fortunately, Cristiana and I had the opportunity to talk about the philosophy of music and what is missing in today’s performers. I try to arrive early to listen to the artists warm-up. It is a fascinating experience, I assure The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet you. Her first warm-up piece was Robert Schumann’s Traumerei, which was truly dreamy as the name implies. This is the way the composer wanted it, but unfortunately, the dreamy mood usually evades the majority of pianists. Pegoraro found the right mood and imparted it to the music. It was a transcendental experience. Her entire program was out of the ordinary. It got off to a rousing start with Rossini‘s great aria “Largo Al Factotum”. All of the pieces were grouped by special mood, a brilliant idea and brilliantly delivered, I might add. The insight that Pegoraro gives to her programs is one of the things that is lacking in programs of other musicians. It is obvious that she loves what she does and this love is conveyed to the audience. The program continued in the similar fashion from one high point to another. All of the playing was truly inspired. The tone was rich and full and well nuanced. The special element was Cristiana’s well-developed musical personality. The two of us had a chance to discuss many things. It is amazing how many things she can do in every area of music. She is a concert pianist par excellence, she acts as her own impresario. Most impressive of all is that she runs a large weeklong music festival every year in the famous Italian town of Narnia, where she lives. If you’re thinking of traveling to Europe in July, think about going to Narnia. The area is beautiful- just an hour north of Rome. The cuisine is beyond reproach. Cooking classes are available, and music is everywhere. A variety of concerts and dance and acting performances are all free to the public. Yep, all entertainment is free. Everyone is welcome from elementary school through senior citizens. Check it out. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, January 29, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore results of Beautification projects Linda and Kingston Avenue in 1910 By Dick Carter It was another great mid-winter day last Wednesday when the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group met at the Exedra for their weekly walk, but there was a special reason to be there on this lovely morning. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is celebrating 60 years of supporting projects that have made Piedmont even more beautiful. The Wednesday walkers were going to see sets of them this week and the following two weeks and recognize PBF’s contributions to Piedmont. The different projects that PBF has been a part of is impressive and can be seen at https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation. org. Current PBF President Patty Dunlap and past Park Commission Chair Patty Siskind were on hand as was Piedmont’s new KCOM Station Manager Jeff Shaw. The City of Piedmont wants to publicize PBF’s great work, so Jeff’s video team was going to tape the walk at the project sites. Patty Dunlap briefly told the walkers about PBF. It has been working since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces in Piedmont that build a strong sense of pride and community. The inspiration for PBF came from the Piedmont Garden Club, which continues to nominate the PBF officers. They are joined by the Piedmont mayor, vicemayor, and the chair of the Park Commission to provide advice on projects. Matt Gerhart had created three route maps to show the walkers this week and the next two. At each location, a PBF volunteer would be there to tell the walkers about the project. The first destination was the Jerome Triangle where Jerome and Fairview Avenues meet just below Oakland Avenue. The group went on Jerome in a long line to the triangle. The film crew was waiting for them and so was Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich, who described the creation of the triangle. The hazardous condition at the interseection of Jerome and Magnolia was first identified by nearby resident Ralph Marinelly. As a tribute to his efforts, the triangle and landscaping were dedicated to him. Nick told the walkers how the project to create the triangle started 37 years ago in 1988 and was completed in 1990. Eight 10-to-12-foot-tall redwoods in 24” boxes were planted and have grown into the large trees in the triangle today. Azaleas and rhododendrons were also planted, but the redwoods have a way of sucking moisture and nutrients from the soil that minimizes other trees and plants. Nick also said that redwoods’ shallow roots grow together tightly and make the ground around them hard. Redwoods should be in groves of at least three trees. They support each other and this reduces the risk of their being blown over in windstorms. Then it was off to their second PBF destination, the Linda/ Kingston Triangle. The group went down Oakland Avenue and after two cycles of traffic signals crossed Grand Avenue. They went up Howard Avenue, down Lake Avenue past Beach School, and up Linda Avenue to the triangle at Kingston Avenue. Jeff Shaw’s video crew was there to meet them. At the triangle Patty Siskind told the group how this community-suggested intersection improvement was created. Neighbors were concerned about children’s safety at this corner and pushed for the project. It took from 2014 to 2017 to complete, and PBF dedicated funds in 2016 for it. The north edge of the triangle is in Oakland and the project was coordinated with the City of Oakland. City of Piedmont Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent did the landscaping, and a bio-swale was incorporated to collect and percolate ground water. A handsome stone wall surrounds the triangle with two stone benches built into it and two bronze signs. One has the triangle’s name and history while the other proclaims, “Mom’s A Mensch. She Deserves A Bench. The Siskind Family.” Patty’s family members were rightly proud of her Park Commission work on this wonderful project. The long walk to the triangle and the city’s border had taken longer than was anticipated in Matt Gerhart’s route, so the walkers made their way back to the Exedra by a shorter route up Linda, Grand, Wildwood, and Magnolia Avenues. They enjoyed seeing these two PBF projects, appreciated Patty Dunlop, Patty Siskind, Jeff Shaw, Nick Millosovich, and Matt Gerhadt’s participation, and were looking forward to seeing more of PBF’s generous contributions to Piedmont in the next two weeks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A large group of 54 walkers and five K-9 best friends were on hand. articles.text: Frederic Vignobles The Hartford Far Coast Chardonnay tops the list. The first two were run of the mill but when we got to the third one, we looked at each other and said “Wow.” Most of the Hartford Family vineyards are nearby in the Russian River or Dry Creek appellations. The Far Coast Vineyard is an hour’s drive north on the top of the Sonoma Coast Mountain range near Annapolis. The wine opens with a perfumed nose of honeysuckle and jasmine with pear and apple notes along with a hint of forest floor. On the palate it shows more apple fruit but teamed with butterscotch or toffee like a caramel apple. Well balanced and finely tuned each sip is inviting, making you reach for another. This delightful wine is one of the best Chardonnays we have had in years. • 2022 Hartford Family Pinot Noir Fog Dance Vineyard, $78 This wine stood out in the flight of three Pinots. It hails from the Green Valley AVA and rather than the usual strawberry or cherry aromas for Pinot Noir it had a distinct raspberry nose. Unusual and charming. In the mouth it was packed with opulent fruit and layers of red berry flavors. It had good balance and structure with no earth or oak notes. The finish was long and savory. Would make a great partner to grilled salmon.
articles.title: A Taste of Sonoma County

articles.text: It was the kind of day that demanded the top down on the convertible. One of those clear sky, crisp, perfect temperature winter days that reveal the incredible beauty of Sonoma County. We cruised the back roads outside of Healdsburg and turned off Martinelli Rd. onto the narrow winding path up to Hartford Family Winery. It was evident upon seeing the winery that great care had been taken in its planning. It is a beautifully proportioned classically styled building nestled in a small amphitheater of vines with an installation of solar panels showing the respect for the environment. We were escorted to a flagstone patio covered by a vine trellis that overlooked the vines. The Hartford Family winery was founded in 1994 by Don and Jennifer Hartford. They located their winery in the town of Forestville about 15 miles from the cool Pacific Coast. The Hartford Family Winery specializes in making wines from single vineyard sites believing small and low-yielding vineyards deliver expressive and personality-rich wines. “High risk, High reward” is their philosophy. In addition to their single vineyard wines, they have bottlings of Russian River Chardonnay, Pinot and Zinfandel that are made in larger quantities and are widely distributed across the US. Pete Wilkie, a trained sommelier, was our knowledgeable host as we tasted through the Hartford portfolio. The following wines were the highlight and are available through their website. • 2022 Hartford Family Chardonnay Far Coast Vineyard, $70 To be honest we are kind of over Chardonnay - nearly members of the ABC (Anything But Chardonnay) club. So, expectations were not high as Pete started the tasting with a flight of three single vineyard Chardonnays. Mauritson Winery in Healdsburg.

Since Nancy Kent became Piedmont’s Parks and Projects Manager in 2016, she has maintained the Fenway along with the City’s other parks. Her stewardship, supported by Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, has kept the path in excellent condition. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, January 29, 2025 By Cameron Wolfe in Celebration of Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s 60th Anniversary Piedmont is fortunate to have a Fenway, a term denoting a marshland pathway, uncommon in most cities. Perhaps the bestknown Fenway in the U.S. is Boston’s Fenway Park, home of the Red Sox, named for its location in a marshy area of Boston—a “path through the meadow” akin to what English walkers once called paths through marshes. In California, Yosemite Valley boasts a well-known Fenway: a partially elevated path between Camp Curry and the John Muir Trailhead, winding through a marshy area. articles.text: On Friday, January 17, a group of the Piedmont Seniors ventured on a day’s outing to visit two of the East Bay’s most historic sites – the Berkeley City Club and the Claremont Club & Spa. The Berkeley City Club, a historical landmark organized in 1927, was one of the area’s earliest attempts by women to contribute to social, civic and cultural progress. The building, constructed in 1929, is one of the outstanding works of noted California architect Julia Morgan, whose successful interpretation of Moorish and Gothic elements in this monumental 6-story structure created a major landmark of California design. Julia Morgan, who grew up in Oakland, is perhaps best known as the architect of Hearst Castle at San Simeon, and the post-1906 earthquake rebuilding of San Francisco’s Fairmont Hotel. Morgan was also the architect of several houses in Piedmont. When the Piedmont Seniors arrived at Berkeley City Club, they were divided into two groups, each with a docent to guide them through the property. In the 1920s, women across the country were enjoying a new sense of civic involvement and educational interest. The women’s club movement offered educational, civic, recreational, and philanthropic opportunities. This “little castle” with its grand ballrooms, dining room, a variety of meeting rooms, residence rooms, and a beautiful swimming pool was just what the founding group had envisioned. Since 1962 this club has welcomed men and women alike, and in 1965 the name was changed from the Berkeley Women’s City Club to the Berkeley City Club. Today, along with its social club activities, the Berkeley City Club provides an elegant location for weddings, reunions, conferences, and meetings of civic groups. Once the tour was concluded the group met in the Club’s dining room for an elegant lunch. The restaurant renamed Julia’s, is open for lunch, dinner and weekly high teas. After lunch the Piedmont Seniors ventured to the Claremont Club & Spa, where they were greeted by docent, Laura Pictured inside the Berkeley City Club are Piedmont Seniors Larry and Patti Singer, Gloria Wilmer, Mona Jamieson, Ann Chandler, Loretta Vanderveen, Arlene Garfinkle (seated), Greg Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Sue Getreuer, Carole Jones, Nancy Hinsch, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Elene Manolis, Lilly Guardia-Labar, and Jim Ayotte. Shown in front of the historic Claremont Hotel are Jim Ayotte(left), Lilly Guardia-LaBar, Carole Jones, Elene Manolis, Arlene Garfinkle (seated), Mona Jamieson, Gloria Wilmer, Sue Getreuer, Nancy Hinch, Loretta Vanderveen, Ann Chandler, Janet Epstein, and Greg Jurin. Visiting the Berkeley City Club’s historic swimming pool are docent Karen Yencich (left), Elene Manolis, Loretta Vanderveen, Janet Epstein, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Sue Getreuer, and Lilly Guardia-LaBar. Christensen, who gave the group a 45-minute tour of the many rooms of the main floor of the hotel, including those not open to the public. It is an historic American hotel that is situated at the foot of Claremont Canyon in the Berkeley Hills. It has 279 guest rooms, a 20,000-square-foot spa, 10 tennis courts, and 22 acres of landscaped gardens. It is situated on the Oakland/Berkeley border and is a designated Historical Landmark and a member of Historic Hotels of America. The site was developed initially by early settler William Butler Thornburgh, who constructed a large home on the site in 1870, which he called a “castle”. After a wildfire in the hills, the house burned to the ground, and on November 10, 1905, the property was acquired by Louis Titus on behalf of the Claremont Hotel Company for approximately $37,500. The Claremont Hotel Company was a group of investors that included, among others, Frank C. Havens of Piedmont. Construction was temporarily halted due to the 1906 earthquake, but resumed in 1910, and was completed in 1914. It finally opened in 1915 as the Claremont Hotel. The Claremont faced destruction in the 1991 Oakland firestorm, but firefighters and the lessening winds stopped the flames short of the hotel. In 2007 the Claremont was acquired by Morgan Stanley, but the resort filed for bankruptcy due to losses attributed to the ongoing recession. In 2014 it was purchased by the Fairmont Hotel chain and financier Richard Blum. Finally, in May 2023, the hotel was. Purchased by Ohana Real Estate Investors for $163 million. Overall, the Piedmont Seniors had a wonderful day going back in time. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, including future excursions, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area.

articles.text: Piedmont Seniors enjoy a festive holiday luncheon at the Claremont Country Club on December 13. On Friday, December 13 the Piedmont Seniors held their annual Holiday luncheon at the Claremont Country Club. The Club was all decked out in holiday decorations with white reindeers, ornaments, and tall Christmas trees throughout the facility. Originally founded as Oakland Golf Club, it was located by Lake Merritt in the Adams Point area of Oakland. In 1904 it relocated to its present site. Early in 1927 tragedy struck the thriving Claremont Country Club when a four-alarm fire completely destroyed the clubhouse. Two years later it was rebuilt largely to its present shape. The Seniors enjoyed a delicious three-course luncheon consisting of butternut squash bisque, and a choice of cordon bleu chicken breast or spinach and mushroom crepes, vanilla ice cream with chocolate sauce and a homemade cookie. There was a delightful pianist in attendance, who played holiday tunes in the Garden Room of the Club. Forty-three members and guests celebrated this event. There was a special tribute to Flo Bryan, who celebrated her 100th birthday with the group. After the meal the group exchanged gifts which is always a highlight at the party. The event put people in the holiday spirit and was most enjoyable for all. For more information about the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors’ group has monthly meetings on the 4th Wednesday of each month at 10 am at the Piedmont Community Hall. They also go on monthly excursions to diverse locations throughout the Bay Area. Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein presents a poinsettia plant to celebrate Flo Bryan’s 100th birthday.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama, I am trying to get my estate in order so I can update my trust. One of my friends recommended I keep myself organized on my computer. I have no idea how to even get started. My attorney wants my updated beneficiary list and changes. How do I begin? Lissa R., Oakland Dear Lissa, When you realize how valuable a tool a computer can be to get yourself organized for things like managing your beneficiary list for your trust and will, managing your medical expenses, etc., it helps with the stress of getting ready for the inevitable. Since I am assuming you don’t plan to try to create your will and trust by yourself without an attorney, here are some ways to get organized. 1. Create a folder for all of the documents you need. You might label it Trust and Will 2025. In this folder, you can keep scanned documents to help you get organized: bank account, account numbers, and any documents that you create. 2. Get your documents in order It’s very likely that your financial planner or stockbroker has a guide how to organize your documents to make it easier for your executor or family members to proceed in the event of your death. You should organize things like investment accounts, bank, accounts, and assets. If you are making a trust for the first time, you should know the limits of what you can have before things go to probate. If you have a lot of money in your checking account, for example, you should make sure it doesn’t exceed the limit to necessitate probate. Assets are subject to probate if they are not in trust, jointly held, or if a beneficiary designation is not in place. As a reference, decedent estates had to be probated when assets subject to probate exceeded $184,500 for persons who passed away in 2023. And assets aggregate maximum value threshold for 2023 was $25,000. Each item’s value cannot exceed $5000. So if you have artwork worth more than $5000 apiece, you want to make sure that is put in the trust. Again, it’s important to talk to your financial advisor about the state of your accounts. You can keep copies of investment statements, bank statements, etc. in your organizational folder. 3. Create a spreadsheet Your Mac comes with spreadsheet, word processor, and presentation software. The spreadsheet software is called Numbers. Of course, many of us have Microsoft products, and that case you can use Excel if you have that on your computer. Then you can make headings for the types of beneficiaries that you may have. The headings can be family, friends, and nonprofits and charities. For the nonprofits and charities, you will need their addresses, their EIN numbers phone numbers and or email. If you’re not even sure which charities to choose, you can use a well-known site like charitynavigator.org. This very useful site gives you ratings for the charities, as well as all of their contact and Tax ID information.

Instruction will focus on body awareness to increase coordination between one’s body and mind, while developing strength, flexibility and breath control. Each class will include relaxation, standing meditation, basic movement, and the Tai Chi routine. Tai Chi from the Ground Up will be taught by Evelyn Lee, a 13th-generation disciple of Chen-lineage Tai Chi. Born in San Francisco, Evelyn has lived in Oakland since 1980. articles.text: Widely respected plastic surgeon who created large floats for Piedmont 4th of July Parade It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, and grandfather, Dr. Ronald P. Gruber, who left this world peacefully on Saturday January 18th, surrounded by his loving family. Born on April 13, 1941, in London, England to parents fleeing the holocaust, his family emigrated to the U.S. when he was five. Following the family’s early years in New York, they moved to Oakland. Ron graduated from Oakland High School in 1958, UC Berkeley in 1962, and UCSF School of Medicine in 1966. He began surgical training at Montefiore in New York but was interrupted to serve as a Captain in the U.S. Army where he did research in wound ballistics and learned to fly planes. Returning to California, he completed his plastic surgery training at Stanford University. In 1975 Ron returned to the East Bay, settled in Piedmont, and opened his plastic surgery practice in Oakland. He worked tirelessly to become a world-renowned rhinoplasty surgeon and was considered a leading authority in the field. Although his practice was based in the Bay Area, patients from all over the world traveled to be in his care. Ron understood that “successful results are the product of years of training, skill, compassion, honesty, and the blending of two disciplines – science and artistry.” Selfless and tireless, he gave back to the plastic surgery community and rhinoplasty in particular. Author of Rhinoplasty State of the Art and over 100 articles on the subject, he explained to the novice rhinoplasty surgeon basic and advanced techniques to provide superior results. He was generous with sharing his knowledge as Adjunct Professor of Plastic Surgery at Stanford and at UCSF. Ron was a founding member and President of the Rhinoplasty Society. In his zeal to improve and invent, Ron designed and created The Gruber Rhinoplasty Set – a surgical instrument set being used by many surgeons today. But this was just a footnote in Ron’s amazing life. Ron was a polymath. He had a passion for so many things and excelled not only in medicine, but the sciences and the arts. He undertook any new subject and dissected it cleanly until he fully understood where he could make a difference. Ron was fascinated by the aspect of the time continuum. With Albert Einstein as his inspiration, he delved into the elasticity of time and was published in the field of Astrophysics. If you were fortunate enough to attend one of his lectures about Relativity you would walk away with a good basic understanding of an incredibly complex topic. He probed into the relationship of physics and psychology, authoring 16 articles on the subject, and a book, Time is an Illusion. He co-chaired a symposium at Stanford on the Nature of Time. His latest experimental venture was using virtual reality to resolve the dilemma of this illusion. Ron’s contributions extended beyond his career and family. He was an active member of his community, often lending his time and expertise to charitable and community causes. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, January 29, 2025 Obituary It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, and grandfather, Dr. Ronald P. Gruber, who left this world peacefully on Saturday January 18th, surrounded by his loving family. Born on April 13, 1941, in London, England to parents fleeing the holocaust, his family emigrated to the U.S. when he was five. Following the family’s early years in New York, they moved to Oakland. Ron graduated from Oakland High School in 1958, UC Berkeley in 1962, and UCSF School of Medicine in 1966. He began surgical training at Montefiore in New York but was interrupted to serve as a Captain in the U.S. Army where he did research in wound ballistics and learned to fly planes. Returning to California, he completed his plastic surgery training at Stanford University. In 1975 Ron returned to the East Bay, settled in Piedmont, Dr. Ronald Gruber dies at 83 Widely respected plastic surgeon who created large floats for Piedmont 4th of July Parade and opened his plastic surgery practice in Oakland. He worked tirelessly to become a world-renowned rhinoplasty surgeon and was considered a leading authority in the field. Although his practice was based in the Bay Area, patients from all over the world traveled to be in his care. Ron understood that “successful results are the product of years of training, skill, compassion, honesty, and the blending of two disciplines – science and artistry.” Selfless and tireless, he gave back to the plastic surgery community and rhinoplasty in particular. Author of Rhinoplasty State of the Art and over 100 articles on the subject, he explained to the novice rhinoplasty surgeon basic and advanced techniques to provide superior results. He was generous with sharing his knowledge as Adjunct Professor of Plastic Surgery at Stanford and at UCSF. Ron was a founding member and President of the Rhinoplasty Society. In his zeal to improve and invent, Ron designed and created The Gruber Rhinoplasty Set – a surgical instrument set being used by many surgeons today. But this was just a footnote in Ron’s amazing life. Ron was a polymath. He had a passion for so many things and excelled not only in medicine, but the sciences and the arts. He undertook any new subject and dissected it cleanly until he fully understood where he could make a difference. Ron was fascinated by the aspect of the time continuum. With Albert Einstein as his inspiration, he delved into the elasticity of time and was published in the field of Astrophysics. If you were fortunate enough to attend one of his lectures about Relativity you would walk away with a good basic understanding of an incredibly complex topic. Dust will make its full San Francisco premiere in February 2025. The three pas de deux that followed also showcased contemporary works, with the most dynamic being Chroma by Sir Wayne McGregor. Starring principal dancer Nikisha Fogo, the first Black principal dancer in the history of the San Francisco Ballet, Chroma has been described as a groundbreaking ballet, “a shock to the system,” merging cutting-edge choreography with a rhythmically complex, rock-inspired score. Fogo had already captivated audiences during the Company’s production of The Nutcracker this past Christmas season; In Chroma, she stepped into the role previously performed by the iconic Yuan Yuan Tan for the San Francisco Ballet. Fogo’s interpretation was both powerful and precise, which was no small feat given the ballet’s demanding choreography. The evening concluded with the finale from Symphony in C. Choreographed by George Balanchine to Bizet’s score, the piece dazzled with its scale and energy, featuring 50 dancers—a near-complete showcase of the entire troupe. For those pining for the elegance of tutus amidst the contemporary costumes of the night, this performance delivered. Balanchine’s bold interpretation of the classical technique shone through, creating a sense of unity and spectacle. With its scale and majesty, the Gala’s closing number evoked the grandeur of Swan Lake, albeit with a more jubilant tone. The perfect finale, it was met with a thunderous ovation. The beauty of the Gala is that when the curtain falls, the celebration doesn’t stop. All it takes is a short walk across Van Ness to continue the festivities at City Hall. (Of course, you’ll need an after-party ticket, but at $175 each, it’s a solid deal given the amenities: several open bars, multiple food stations offering everything from sushi and dim sum to charcuterie and desserts, and three dance stages, some illuminated for added flair.) There’s no better place to flaunt a gown than on City Hall’s grand staircase—long, broad, and offering a perfect vantage point of the foyer and central stage. At times, it felt like you were stepping into a movie or a Broadway show with Vegas lights, and yet, you don’t feel like an outsider. That’s the magic of art: as long as you’re a fellow traveler, you belong. There was plenty of dancing, live music and singing to the likes of “Sweet Dreams.” While the DJ’s choices may have at times felt conventional, as lamented by one of the party’s more eccentric attendees, for those on the dance floor, myself included, they proved riveting enough. Given that the festivities, which began at 10 pm, extended into the early morning hours, a lounge was thoughtfully arranged in the South Light Court. Here, on plush blue velvet couches, guests could converse with friends – — assuming they had the foresight to attend—or simply observe the lively scene while enjoying a cocktail or two (or perhaps three or four—nobody was counting). Throughout the night, boredom was conspicuously absent, and unsurprisingly, no one departed early. As I made my way to my car, I found myself already anticipating the 2026 Gala. The greatest part, of course, is that San Francisco Ballet’s season has just begun. Over the next few months, all you need to do is cross the Bay Bridge to the Civic Center (BART is another option, with walking groups to the theater before and after shows). From the Gala, it’s clear that Tamara Rojo’s new season will be an exciting one, featuring both classical and contemporary, genre-bending works, while showcasing plenty of talent. You can buy individual and season tickets at sfballet. org. I’ll certainly be returning to experience the pieces glimpsed at the Gala in their full glory, and I hope to see you there. And don’t forget to mark January 24, 2026, the night of the opening gala, on your social calendar. After all, it is the best party in town. Anastasia Edel is an American writer and arts critic for the Piedmont Post. The work is commonly known as the Jupiter Symphony, named after the Roman god for its grand scale. Mozart completed the monumental piece in a brief two-month period over the summer of 1788, along with his Symphonies Nos. 39 and 40, creating a final trilogy of works that has puzzled scholars: it’s unknown for what occasion he wrote them, since they were not commissioned by any patron for any specific performance, an anomaly in Mozart’s career. And that’s what I always strive for – honesty, in my music.” Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez was inspired by the gardens at the Royal Palace of Aranjuez, rebuilt in the 18th century. Rodrigo wrote that the concerto captures “the fragrance of magnolias, the singing of birds, and the gushing of fountains.” The piece has been performed and recorded numerous times in many forms since its premiere in 1940 — including as part of Miles Davis’s Sketches of Spain and by jazz pianist Chick Corea as part of his composition Spain. California Symphony’s featured guitar soloist, Meng Su, has performed in over 30 countries and is on the faculty at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Classical Guitar Magazine reports that she has the “star potential to serve as inspiration for new generations of guitarists to come.” Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Symphony No. 41 in C Major is his final symphony, and his longest and grandest. The work is commonly known as the Jupiter Symphony, named after the Roman god for its grand scale. Mozart completed the monumental piece in a brief two-month period over the summer of 1788, along with his Symphonies Nos. 39 and 40, creating a final trilogy of works that has puzzled scholars: it’s unknown for what occasion he wrote them, since they were not commissioned by any patron for any specific performance, an anomaly in Mozart’s career. A majestic, intricate, exuberant masterpiece, Mozart’s Symphony No. 41, his final symphony, is one of his most celebrated and frequently performed works, showcasing a genius at the height of his powers. “In choosing music to precede a great milestone such as Mozart’s final symphony, I decided that it was best to showcase music of a completely different and opposing style and aesthetic,” California Symphony Artistic and Music Director Donato Cabrera said. “Simon’s Breathe is contemplative and meditative music that speaks softly but carries a big stick,” he continued. “It has a natural forthrightness to it that is beguiling and gently invites one to just be present in the moment. With everyone in such a heightened state of mind, the beginning of Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez should be particularly magical and poignant.” “There are many reasons why Mozart’s Symphony No. 41 has been considered one of the greatest achievements of Western classical music, but most of these reasons are best left in the textbooks,” he added. “For me, and I believe for the listener, the magic that this piece possesses is that it somehow contains a facet of every aspect of human existence and experience.” For tickets ($50 general, $25 students 25 and under) and more information about the concerts at Hofmann Theater at the Lesher Center for the Arts (1601 Civic Dr., Walnut Creek), visit LesherArtsCenter.org or call the box office at (925) 943-7469. articles.text: At the January 8 school board meeting Superintendent Jennifer Hawn delivered a “State of the District” report going over the health of Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD). Hawn highlighted changes, successes and future projections for the entire district, in her concluding iteration of the “State of School” series. “I think we should make time for gratitude more often. We have so much to be grateful for. The good news in our district is, we are not broken. We’re actually quite remarkable,” said Hawn. Hawn highlighted the district and all three labor groups have agreements in place after much hard work. “We passed a parcel tax at over 80%. Oh my goodness. It just amazes me that our community shows up and provides the support for our teachers, for our community, and for our kids to get the finest education that’s out there,” said Hawn of Measure P. PUSD’s leadership has worked to standardize their newsletters and communications. “I started the practice of sending out my newsletter – sending out any kind of communication that might impact staff – to our staff first before I send it to parents,” explained Hawn. The superintendent highlighted that the district has a balanced budget and a slight increase in the reserve. “In years past we really had not saved up and I think that didn’t serve us well,” said Hawn. PUSD is now a model of success in Title IX equity, which Hawn called a huge win for the community. “When I came in there was a great deal of distress, distress from parents, distress from some of our female athletes and distress from the previous board around Title IX and our lack of ability to get in compliance,” she said. “We are now in compliance and in fact we are so strong in this area that our consultants have asked if they could use our school district as a model for Title IX compliance,” Hawn stated. The district report acknowledged they lost a principal midyear at Wildwood but Hawn reported that Interim Principal Beth Rhine’s work has been outstanding. One of the new laws requires California public schools to notify parents of upcoming active-shooter drills ahead of time and right after one occurs. Another law mandates that students learn about the treatment of Native Americans during the Spanish colonization of California and the gold rush. Once implemented, secondary students will need to be educated on how excessive alcohol consumption can lead to depression and anxiety. Lastly, an Assembly Bill gives further protection for California students’ anonymity around their gender-identity and sexuality. State’s gender-identity disclosure rules already match PUSD Public-school districts and school boards are barred from sharing a student’s sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression without their consent. Public schools across California must now align with Assembly Bill 1955. PUSD is already in compliance with this requirement. RELIGION CORNER Starting a Conversation By Pastor Jim Hopkins Though there were other roads he could have taken, Jesus chose to pass through Samaria on his way to the Galilee in order to start a conversation with a Samaritan woman. He met her at Jacob’s well. Though there was significant enmity between observant Jews, like Jesus, and the Samaritans, Jesus thought it was time to build some bridges. Stopping at the storied well, Jesus asked a woman who had come to draw water for a drink. This request started a conversation about spiritual thirst, living water, true worship, the woman’s life and connections between groups that didn’t want to admit that they had much in common. The woman is an active participant in the conversation and, when she identifies Jesus as a prophet, he does what prophets do, he speaks important truth. In this case he makes it clear that the spiritual destinies of the Samaritan people and the Jewish people are intertwined and promises that, together, they will worship the One God in “spirit and in truth.” He started a conversation to lift up a vision of shared worship, shared values, shared truth and shared hope. In a similar fashion a follower of Jesus, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., attempted to start a conversation with the American people about our common destiny, race and racial justice. As early as 1962 this American prophet was saying, “We must learn to live together as brothers or we will perish together as fools.” Some in the United States were, like the woman at the well, willing participants in the conversation. Many were not. Many are still not. Central to this conversation were Dr. King’s beliefs that: • There was a great need to abolish the idea of superior and inferior races • Though laws don’t change people’s hearts, they were still need to regulate their actions • That the American dream is the dream that all can live together The vision Jesus shared with the woman at the well for their time, is startlingly similar to the vision Dr. King lifted for his time. articles.text: No public process seen in city’s plans for development of lots Editor: Through this letter, I am reaching out to all fellow Piedmont residents who may not yet fully understand what our City leaders intend to do to our neighborhoods – without advance notice to us and without giving us an opportunity to be heard. Attached below is a listing of vacant, single-family residential lots in Piedmont, as reported by the City Council in its “6th Cycle Housing Element” plan. These lots are next door to many of us, or perhaps right down the street or just around the corner. They are appropriately zoned for single-family homes. The City Council and its Planning Department, however, want each and every one of these lots to be developed with up to four homes per lot. The City has seized upon a controversial state law, known as “SB 9,” as the vehicle by which developers are being invited in to split and rapidly build out these lots with multiple family dwellings – via a rubber-stamped, “ministerial” approval process that is intentionally designed to not tell us what is happening until it is too late. Don’t take my word for it. Just drop by 77 Wistaria Way (one of some 60 lots on the City’s hit list) and view the concrete monstrosity being erected there. The developer is shoehorning three dwelling units into a steep, treacherous lot that until now had been a wooded sanctuary with a creek running through it. A creek that the City itself promised to preserve. Instead of following normal design and building code public review for a single-family home, this multiple family development was allowed to bypass all those requirements and was blessed by junior Planning staff, without Planning Commission or City Council consideration. And without timely notice to neighbors, or any fair opportunity for neighbors to raise important safety and environmental issues. This despite the fact that even SB 9 does not prohibit the City from affording residents this modicum of fairness. Snap a few pix if you wish and take the Wistaria Way image with you and then look at the addresses on the City’s hit list, shown below. See any location there near your home? (How about you folks on Howard and Nace Avenues?) Then ask yourself: Do I think that having multiple family units built there without public notice or comment reflects the level of respect for residents I expect from my City leaders? I have asked the City Council and the City Attorney at the very least to provide minimal notice and opportunity for residents to be heard whenever an SB 9 multi-family lot split and development application is filed. But even this modest request has been met repeatedly with stony silence. Maybe when more of us end up with this in our own backyards, enough voices will be heard to make a difference. But please, don’t wait to see something to do something. By then it will be too late. Respectfully, Harvey L. articles.text: Editor: A headline on the front page of the December 11, 2024, Piedmont Post incorrectly states that the new community pool project has a cost overrun of 79 percent. This is misleading and erroneous. The Post arrives at this number by using the $19.5 million face value of the Measure UU bond measure as the basis for computing the cost overrun percentage. It is more appropriate to use the December 5, 2022, City Council approved project budget of $28.9 million as the basis, resulting in a 20% cost overrun – not 79%. We, the members of the Measure UU Pool Bond Oversight Committee, have been meeting regularly since October 13, 2022, and have carefully followed spending for the Piedmont Community Pool Project. We believe that it is important to correct the record. Here are the facts. 1. The total pool project cost was estimated at $23 million on July 20, 2020, with a recommended face value amount of $19.5 million in bonds to be issued. The actual net proceeds of the $19.5 million bond measure came in at $24.4 million because they were sold at a premium. 2. The City Council approved a total project budget of $28.9 million on December 5, 2022, when it awarded the construction contract. This includes both hard costs (construction) and soft costs (project management, architectural design, engineering). A major contributor to the increased budget was the unprecedented 32% spike in the California construction cost index from July 2020 (initial pool cost estimate) to January 2023 when construction began. 3. The City Council has approved three subsequent increases to the pool project, bringing the total budget to $34.9 million. These increases have been due to weather related project delays, utilities and undergrounding requirements, the discovery of two buried fuel tanks at the site, remediation costs, soil disposal, the complexity of pool electrification, and other factors.
articles.title: Setting the record straight on pool cost overrun

articles.text: Editor: There is a 4-unit duplex project with a 4-car garage in two 30-foot high structures proposed for 210 Howard Avenue under SB 9. It is a very different animal than 77 Wisteria Lane. The Wisteria neighborhood tried to stop the project based on CEQA concerns. Our concern is about safety and possible serious injury to kids going down the sidewalk to Beach School, going alone or running ahead of their parents. In normal times, prior to the advent of SB 9, a similar project would have been shut down from the get-go. But SB 9 will allow someone to walk a 4-unit condominium, 4-car garage project through a City with a very rushed, expedited review process with no public hearings or review. SB 9 is going to change Piedmont forever and there’s very little a resident can do. This is a very dangerous, small flag lot with a very long flagpole/driveway that doesn’t meet Piedmont standards for width and exiting sight lines/visibility and has cross slopes that exceed 20% as one would move down the driveway. articles.text: Preview sale on Jan. 26; open to the public on Jan. 29 The Oakland Museum of California’s widely-popular White Elephant Sale returns for its 66th year next week with a preview sale on Wednesday, January 26. With over 90,000 square-feet of shopping space and more than 19 departments, there’s something for everyone at the White Elephant Sale. Gently used, good-quality items, including furniture, bicycles, plateware and antiques, are donated from the public year-round and sold at the rummage sale with proceeds benefiting the museum’s exhibitions and educational programs. The sale, touted as Northern California’s biggest rummage sale, is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board and remains the museum’s largest fundraising event. The sole purpose of the Women’s Board, a group of over 100 yearround members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959 it has raised more than $30 million for the museum. The White Elephant Sale provides a significant amount of funding for the museum. The sale includes many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Order tickets for admission now and get ready to shop when doors open on January 26. Open warehouse days are held on select weekdays through February 22, and a discounted “clearance weekend” is held Saturday and Sunday, March 1 and 2. Visit https://www.whiteelephantsale.org to learn more about the event and to purchase tickets. The White Elephant Sale truck picks up donations for free throughout the greater Bay Area. To schedule pickups, call 510- 839-5919. To volunteer on sale days, visit https://www.whiteelephantsale.org/volunteer. A shopper browses at Oakland Museum’s annual White Elephant Sale.
articles.title: Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns

articles.text: Introducing Mila and Becky, two Chihuahua-mix sisters. This bonded pair of 30-pound 3-year olds got a temporary break from Oakland Animal Services shelter at a foster’s home. The foster reports Becky is a quick learner who went from not knowing any commands to quickly learning a half dozen. Mila is the calmer of the two and enjoys snuggling and lazing on furniture or in her crate. The foster has left both pups at home for up to 4 hours. Becky is a toy enthusiast who loves her chewing time. Although she mostly confines her munching to her toys, she does need to be crated when you’re away to prevent unwanted nibbling. These girls don’t require a lot of space. They love a calm environment and a walk each day. Come meet Becky and Mila and Becky, two Chihuahua-mix sisters. Mila at Oakland Animal Services this week on Thursday from 12-7 p.m., or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than the pair must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan will deliver a presentation on wildfire readiness in Piedmont at the Public Safety Committee meeting in City Hall on Thursday, January 23, at 5:30 p.m. Community members are encouraged to attend and speak at the meeting in person. Video of the presentation will be available for viewing afterwards on the City’s website. Chief Brannigan will describe the City of Piedmont’s work to prepare for, respond to, and mitigate risk from wildfires, including both City-specific initiatives and collaborative regional work. The presentation will discuss the ongoing wildfires in Los Angeles, the risks a similar event could pose to Piedmont, and two Fire Department initiatives currently in progress that aim to address these risks – an update of the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan and a community wildfire evacuation exercise planned for May 2025. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update, which began last fall, is a data-driven process to develop a roadmap for actions the City can take now that could prevent or reduce potential impacts of a wildfire or other disaster, such as: • creating programs to help residents make their properties more resilient • strengthening building codes • retrofitting/rebuilding critical infrastructure and facilities Documenting these projects in a formally adopted mitigation plan will position Piedmont to apply for state and federal disaster assistance and mitigation grants. The wildfire evacuation exercise allows the City to test organization-wide emergency response protocols and identify any gaps in procedures or training, while also providing community members a practical opportunity to test their own household’s preparation. Community participation is critical to the success of both efforts. The presentation will highlight upcoming opportunities to get involved, including a public workshop scheduled for Wednesday, March 26, where participants will collaborate to brainstorm and prioritize mitigation projects or programs. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP to learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, sign up for email updates, and provide input to the project team. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/disaster for information on preparing your household for wildfires and other disasters, including creating an evacuation plan, packing a go-bag, and managing vegetation to reduce risk on your property. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) has been awarded a $20,000 grant by the National Endowment for the Arts for its project Echoes of Eureka, a mostly textless choral opera focused on the experiences of Chinese citizens during the Expulsion Acts in the 19th century. The opera, composed by Piedmont Choirs Artistic Director Eric Tuan, will premiere as a part of the choir’s Making History Concert on April 12. Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns Preview sale on Jan. 26; open to the public on Jan. 29 By Allyson Aleksey The Oakland Museum of California’s widely-popular White Elephant Sale returns for its 66th year next week with a preview sale on Wednesday, January 26. With over 90,000 square-feet of shopping space and more than 19 departments, there’s something for everyone at the White Elephant Sale. Gently used, good-quality items, including furniture, bicycles, plateware and antiques, are donated from the public year-round and sold at the rummage sale with proceeds benefiting the museum’s exhibitions and educational programs. The sale, touted as Northern California’s biggest rummage sale, is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board and remains the museum’s largest fundraising event. The sole purpose of the Women’s Board, a group of over 100 yearround members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959 it has raised more than $30 million for the museum. The White Elephant Sale provides a significant amount of funding for the museum. The sale includes many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Order tickets for admission now and get ready to shop when doors open on January 26. Open warehouse days are held on select weekdays through February 22, and a discounted “clearance weekend” is held Saturday and Sunday, March 1 and 2. Visit https://www.whiteelephantsale.org to learn more about the event and to purchase tickets. The White Elephant Sale truck picks up donations for free throughout the greater Bay Area. To schedule pickups, call 510- 839-5919. To volunteer on sale days, visit https://www.whiteelephantsale.org/volunteer. Fire Chief to give presentation on wildfire readiness Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan will deliver a presentation on wildfire readiness in Piedmont at the Public Safety Committee meeting in City Hall on Thursday, January 23, at 5:30 p.m. Community members are encouraged to attend and speak at the meeting in person. Video of the presentation will be available for viewing afterwards on the City’s website. Chief Brannigan will describe the City of Piedmont’s work to prepare for, respond to, and mitigate risk from wildfires, including both City-specific initiatives and collaborative regional work. The presentation will discuss the ongoing wildfires in Los Angeles, the risks a similar event could pose to Piedmont, and two Fire Department initiatives currently in progress that aim to address these risks – an update of the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan and a community wildfire evacuation exercise planned for May 2025. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update, which began last fall, is a data-driven process to develop a roadmap for actions the City can take now that could prevent or reduce potential impacts of a wildfire or other disaster, such as: • creating programs to help residents make their properties more resilient • strengthening building codes • retrofitting/rebuilding critical infrastructure and facilities Documenting these projects in a formally adopted mitigation plan will position Piedmont to apply for state and federal disaster assistance and mitigation grants. The wildfire evacuation exercise allows the City to test organization-wide emergency response protocols and identify any gaps in procedures or training, while also providing community members a practical opportunity to test their own household’s preparation. Community participation is critical to the success of both efforts. The presentation will highlight upcoming opportunities to get involved, including a public workshop scheduled for Wednesday, March 26, where participants will collaborate to brainstorm and prioritize mitigation projects or programs. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP to learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, sign up for email updates, and provide input to the project team. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/disaster for information on preparing your household for wildfires and other disasters, including creating an evacuation plan, packing a go-bag, and managing vegetation to reduce risk on your property. Mock active-shooter lockdowns have become more common in recent years as school shootings have proliferated. California had the most school shootings in the country between 1970- 2022 (214). School-focused organizations have raised concerns over the risk of trauma for students, following school shooter drills. “None of the ‘Lockdown Drills’ which PUSD has conducted, where [Piedmont Police Department] staff were present, included any element of ‘high intensity drills’,” confirmed Bowers. Expanded Native American history AB 1821 requires California public-school history classes to include the treatment of Native Americans during Spanish colonization of California and during the Gold Rush when teaching students about those eras. This change is in the process of implementation. Introduced by San Bernardino Assemblymember James Ramos, AB 1821 mandates history courses in elementary, middle and high schools include “the treatment and perspectives of” indigenous Californians during those aforementioned periods “to the extent instruction is provided.” “For far too long California’s First People and their history have been ignored or misrepresented,” said Ramos. “Classroom instruction about the Mission and Gold Rush periods fails to include the loss of life, enslavement, starvation, illness and violence inflicted upon California Native American people during those times.” Lessons on alcohol abuse AB 2865 was introduced by former Los Angeles Assemblymember Wendy Carrillo. It requires public middle and high schools to provide instruction about the short- and long-term effects of alcohol consumption. It is also in the process of implementation. All California public schools were already required to teach students about the consequences of alcohol, narcotic and recreational drug use; the new law mandates the inclusion of how excessive alcohol use can lead to depression, anxiety, and death. Carrillo was charged with a DUI in 2023 when she crashed into parked cars in Los Angeles with a blood-alcohol level twice the legal limit. Carrillo’s behavior directly led to her advocacy for alcohol-prevention education in public schools.

School-focused organizations have raised concerns over the risk of trauma for students, following school shooter drills. “None of the ‘Lockdown Drills’ which PUSD has conducted, where [Piedmont Police Department] staff were present, included any element of ‘high intensity drills’,” confirmed Bowers. Expanded Native American history AB 1821 requires California public-school history classes to include the treatment of Native Americans during Spanish colonization of California and during the Gold Rush when teaching students about those eras. This change is in the process of implementation. Introduced by San Bernardino Assemblymember James Ramos, AB 1821 mandates history courses in elementary, middle and high schools include “the treatment and perspectives of” indigenous Californians during those aforementioned periods “to the extent instruction is provided.” “For far too long California’s First People and their history have been ignored or misrepresented,” said Ramos. “Classroom instruction about the Mission and Gold Rush periods fails to include the loss of life, enslavement, starvation, illness and violence inflicted upon California Native American people during those times.” Lessons on alcohol abuse AB 2865 was introduced by former Los Angeles Assemblymember Wendy Carrillo. It requires public middle and high schools to provide instruction about the short- and long-term effects of alcohol consumption. It is also in the process of implementation. All California public schools were already required to teach students about the consequences of alcohol, narcotic and recreational drug use; the new law mandates the inclusion of how excessive alcohol use can lead to depression, anxiety, and death. Carrillo was charged with a DUI in 2023 when she crashed into parked cars in Los Angeles with a blood-alcohol level twice the legal limit. Carrillo’s behavior directly led to her advocacy for alcohol-prevention education in public schools. 8 Wednesday, January 22, 2025 MLK Day Continued from page 1 Berkeley, was scheduled to speak at the event but was ill. The event began with opening remarks by PADC President Ellen Lee and Event Founder Lois Corrin, followed by an Acknowledgement of Native land by Jean Takazawa, Director of Diversity for Piedmont Unified School District. Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen addressed the audience after the opening, speaking about Piedmont’s fight against racism and exclusion, including the City’s plans to create a memorial to Sydney and Irene Dearing. “Dr. King knew that change doesn’t happen within our comfort zones,” said Andersen. “It happens when we are willing to listen, to learn, and to push forward together. That is why events like today matter.” Congresswomen Lateefah Simon offered much to think about in her speech on peace, responsibility, and accountability in the upcoming days of administration at the national level. Her message to keep moving and keep “fighting against the oppressions that will come” seems more pertinent than ever, especially after reports of tech billionaire Elon Musk performing a Nazi salute after the presidential inauguration later that same day. “We’re supposed to talk about joy and love today, but King was a serious man and he said consistently that he was about His Father’s business,” said Simon. “We will keep moving. I understand the charge,” said Simon. “The dream is big but we will get there.” Piedmont High School student Hunter Fastau, co-President of the African Affinity Student Union, introduced the keynote speaker, Ericka Huggins, before Fastau sat down for a “fireside chat” with the lifelong activist. Huggins spoke about her experience as an educator and activist, her husband’s assassination and her subsequent incarceration by the FBI, and the role of young people in social activism. “Please know that the underpinning of social justice is serving humanity with love,” advised Huggins. History is a river. And what I think, or feel, about Martin Luther King is that he showed us how to step into that river,” said Huggins. The 4th annual Art & Writing Showcase presented youth works created for MLK Day as a slide show. Destiny Arts Dance Company and the Oakland Youth Chorus singers both held performances between the speeches. Destiny Arts mixed dance and spoken-word poetry as they struck powerful ensemble poses throughout their routines. The Oakland Youth Chorus sang songs of light and togetherness which got the audience standing and singing along to their final song of the night, “Lift Every Voice and Sing” by James Weldon Johnson. Piedmont Students Samuel Bahala and Naylah Kasaun of the PHS African Affinity Student Union addressed the audience before the closing song with a call to action. “Let’s stand up and show the world that we’re more than the colors and negative descriptions that are seen, because I believe in each of us are deep stories that can shine,” said Bahala reading from a poem titled “Until When?” “Let the world see us not as our limits, but as a bright light. For in the diversity of who we are, we shine strong and bright like diamonds.” Students Samuel Bahala (left) and Naylah Kasaun of the African Affinity Student Union give a Call to Action before the last performance. articles.text: To support Highlander Robotics’ goal of encouraging girls and women in STEM, this year’s outreach program was expanded to Girl Scouts by hosting two new workshops. Brownies and Cadettes both learned about robotics and engineering in the PHS Makers Fab Lab at PHS, an experience that also earned the girls their requirements for engineering badges. The first workshop, held in early November for Brownies aged seven to nine, was based around building a spring bot using basic principles of physics and energy. After a short presentation by 8033 members Cassie Colby, Tristen Milsum, Athena Li, and Lewy Seiden, the younger scouts got to build and test their own designs. Experimenting with different variables and recording the results is key to problem solving, just as a real scientist or engineer would. Brownies test out their spring bot and record the results while earning their Engineering Badges. The second workshop, geared for older middle school Cadette scouts, went deeper into the design process of robotics, challenging them to design and build their own catapults. They also had a brief lesson about the science behind catapults and the engineering process. Each group got to design and build their own catapults, and then also had the opportunity to tour the robotics lab for a closer look at Team 8033’s Crescendo robot. Girl Scout Cadettes observe Highlander Robotics Team 8033’s Crescendo robot. Questions? Contact District Executive Eris Turner eturner@piedmontbsa.org 510-844-4752

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee.
