articles.text: Piedmont head coach Ben Spencer achieved his 100th win at Piedmont in a game with Terra Linda on January 18. Pictured are Beach Lorin (left), Nicholas Riordan, Johnny Lee, Dillon Casey, Cash Panico (back), Lucian Fang-Ring, assistant coach Jason Harris, head coach Ben Spencer, assistant coach Kalen Davison (back), assistant coach Shamaree Worley, Emmet Asulin (back), Akash Bornstein, P.J. Brayer, and Ravi Silverberg. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team finished up a busy week with four games. The 61-54 victory over Terra Linda on Saturday, January 18 marked a milestone for PHS coach Ben Spencer. It was the team’s100th win since he became the head coach. “It came faster than I expected,” Spencer said. “It’s nice to get it off your back but we’re just focusing on the next game. It’s a small goal, but it’s about winning NCS, league, and State. It’s exciting to get to 100 and I’ve been lucky to have great players,” Spencer said. Spencer and his assistant coaches Shamaree Worley and Jason Harris took over the varsity squad in the winter of 2019-20, and led the school to the Division 4 North Coast Section championship, the school’s first section title. They also reached last year’s NCS Finals as a Div.3 team.. “I think we’ve gotten a lot better at teaching. We were privileged early on with that NCS team that had nine seniors. That year, we could just roll the ball out. The last few years, we had good players and teams, but the talent wasn’t as great as that NCS year. With our strength of schedule, we’ve focused on the fundamentals. I think that’s been the biggest thing toward building tough and smart basketball players,” Spencer said. The Highlanders had a pair of Western Alameda County Conference losses over the past week, 78-53 to Bishop O’Dowd at home on Tuesday, January 13, and 65-51 to Berkeley two days later. PHS battled to a 73-64 loss to Branson at the MLK Showcase at Merritt College on Monday, January 20. In each of the games, PHS fell behind early and couldn’t recover. “It’s been our Achilles heel with the young team, we come out slow when we’re just as good or better than the team we’re competing against. Berkeley, they started with an 11-0 run. Bishop O’Dowd went on a 12-nothing run to start the second half. Terra Linda started off 11-3 and today we started 11-0. We’re spotting teams points and we’re not coming out ready to play. It’s frustrating, but the fight is there,” Spencer said. 73-64 to Branson Branson came out hot with an 11-0 lead and carried a 24-14 lead through the first quarter. In the second, Piedmont clawed back to a 26-24 deficit, but the Bulls carried a 34-29 lead into halftime. Branson carried a nine-point 52-43 lead into the fourth, but Piedmont was able to cut it close in the final going. In the late minutes of the fourth, Piedmont cut the deficit to just three points when Lucian Fang-Ring found Ravi Silverberg for a 3-pointer to make it 64-61, but that’s the closest things got with the Bulls going on a seven point run to pull ahead by 10, 71-61. Final scorers: Silverberg led with 22 points, Casey had 16, Fang-Ring had nine, Cash Panico had eight, P.J. Brayer had seven, and Beach Lorin had two. Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg led the scoring against Branson and Terra Linda. Dillon Casey had 16 points against Branson, 14 against Terra Linda, and 16 against Berkeley.
articles.title: Ben Spencer achieves 100th career win

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team wrapped up a rough week, winning one of their last three games to bring its record to 13-3. They lost to Western Alameda County Conference rival Bishop O’Dowd 56-47 at home on Tuesday, January 14, defeated Menlo School 52-33 on Saturday, January 18 in the MLK Shootout at St. Mary’s of Stockton, and lost 81-66 to Centennial of Las Vegas at the MLK Classic at Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, January 20. Their loss to the Centennial Bulldogs came against a topthree rated team in Nevada, and a team expected to compete for its state title. They possessed several players over 6-feet tall. “They were a good team and aggressive. If we fell asleep for one second, they would make you pay. We shot decently but then we let them off the hook. They are ranked as one of the best teams in Nevada. We just have to find a way to compete longer,” coach Bryan Gardere said. 81-66 loss to Centennial The two sides battled to an 18-18 tie through the first quarter, while Centennial carried a narrow 40-37 lead into halftime. Piedmont cut the deficit to 59-57 to start the fourth quarter, but the Bulldogs height and athleticism was too much for the Highlanders in the final going—getting outscored 22-10 in the fourth. Piedmont held a lead late in the third quarter after Jenelle Solis found Andrea Martin for a 3-pointer to take a 54-53 lead with 1:43 left, but it was the last time PHS held an advantage. Centennial took a 55-54 lead with 1:07 left and never relinquished. Centennial forward Nation Williams, listed at 6 feet, 2 inches, led the Bulldogs with 24 points. and 6-foot guard D’Arrah Mitchell added 22 points. Final stats: Briana Webb led scoring with 22 points and seven rebounds. Martin scored 10 points, seven rebounds, three assists, and one block. Savannah Dennig had five points, four rebounds, three assists, and one steal. Solis scored 10 points, six assists, and two steals. Shakila Zuberi had nine points, one rebound and assist. Taylor White scored seven points, five rebounds, two assists, two steals, and a block. Cleo Afsar had three rebounds and three assists. 52-33 win vs. Menlo School Piedmont led 18-6 through the first quarter, but only scored seven points in the second quarter to cling onto a 25-22 lead at halftime. PHS turned up the intensity in the second half, outscoring Menlo School 17-6 in the third to lead 42-28, then added 10 more points in the fourth and only allowed five. Final stats: Martin scored 15 points, six rebounds, three assist, and four blocks. Dennig had two points, nine rebounds, and one assist. Solis had nine points, four rebounds, five assists, and a steal. Zuberi had two points, six rebounds, and one assist. White scored six points, six rebounds, four assists, two steals, and two blocks. Webb had seven points and nine rebounds. Afsar had nine points and three rebounds. Saniyah Johnson had two points, two rebounds, two steals, and one block. Staff Photos Briana Webb led the scoring against Centennial with 22 points. Andrea Martin had 10 points against Centennial, 15 vs. Menlo School, and eight points against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Piedmont tied San Leandro 1-1 and fell 2-0 to Berkeley. Staff Photos The Highlander boys’ soccer team had mixed results in games last week. They lost 2-0 to Berkeley at Witter Field on Friday, January 17 and drew 1-1 with San Leandro at Burrell Field two days earlier. The team is still searching for its first win against league competition. Coach Ben Russell is hoping the team can establish its attacking fluidity. “Berkeley has good quality and has a big talent pool. But it was good to see the boys’ motivation. We competed and had little moments where things could’ve boiled over. Defensively, just one little lapse against teams with good quality can hurt us. We haven’t been able to build our offensive structure into the game just yet. Hopefully we can continue this competitive mindset into the next game and avoid dropping quality,” Russell said following the loss to Berkeley. Their tie to San Leandro came after bashing the Pirates in a preseason game in November. Russell thinks the result was a testament to Piedmont taking its foot off the gas in a game against lesser competition. “We just dropped out standard and felt like it was going to be too easy. We allowed them to get back into the game and it was difficult to get back to the high level. We can’t go in and out of games, we have to maintain a standard,” Russell said. PHS looks ahead to visiting WACC rivals Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Friday, January 24, while they host Mt. Eden for another league game on Tuesday, January 28. 2-0 to Berkeley Berkeley controlled the action with tons of possession in the first half, limiting Piedmont without any shot attempts in the opening 40 minutes. In fact, PHS only had one shot on target for all 80 minutes of regulation and never drew any corners. Goalie Lucas Malecki saved a hard shot straight at Goalie Lucas Malecki was busy against Berkeley with five saves.

Staff Photos By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlander boys’ soccer team had mixed results in games last week. They lost 2-0 to Berkeley at Witter Field on Friday, January 17 and drew 1-1 with San Leandro at Burrell Field two days earlier. The team is still searching for its first win against league competition. Coach Ben Russell is hoping the team can establish its attacking fluidity. “Berkeley has good quality and has a big talent pool. But it was good to see the boys’ motivation. We competed and had little moments where things could’ve boiled over. Defensively, just one little lapse against teams with good quality can hurt us. We haven’t been able to build our offensive structure into the game just yet. Hopefully we can continue this competitive mindset into the next game and avoid dropping quality,” Russell said following the loss to Berkeley. Their tie to San Leandro came after bashing the Pirates in a preseason game in November. Russell thinks the result was a testament to Piedmont taking its foot off the gas in a game against lesser competition. “We just dropped out standard and felt like it was going to be too easy. We allowed them to get back into the game and it was difficult to get back to the high level. We can’t go in and out of games, we have to maintain a standard,” Russell said. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet premiere of Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon opens the company’s 2024/25 Repertory Season this Friday, January 24. Inspired by the 1731 novel Manon Lescaut by Abbé Prévost, Manon is considered one of MacMillan’s most notable and widely-celebrated works. The ballet chronicles the rise and fall of its titular heroine, beginning near Paris and ending in New Orleans. The three-act ballet was first performed by The Royal Ballet in London in 1974 with Antoinette Sibley and Anthony Dowell in principal roles. “MacMillan was an artist who infused novelty and depth into his choreography,” San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo said. “Manon exemplifies how he brought new life to a classic story, transforming it into a timeless narrative.” Principal casting for Manon includes Dores André, Jasmine Jimison, Sasha De Sola, and Nikisha Fogo as Manon. The principal dancers also include Harrison James, Max Cauthorn, and Aaron Robison as des Grieux. San Francisco Ballet welcomes principal guest artist Alban Lendorf to the War Memorial Opera House stage for select performances as des Grieux. The War Memorial Opera House bars will serve a specialty cocktail inspired by the themes of Manon and 18th-century France. Manon is performed on stage through February 1. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling ticket services at 415-865- 2000, open Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Scene from San Francisco Ballet’s production of Manon > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC Photos to pull from Marketing Hub image library FAP-1942O-A-AD AECSPAD 24176164

articles.text: Italian pianist Christiana Pegoraro Italian pianist and composer Cristiana Pegoraro returns to Piedmont for another inspired solo performance on the PCA’s Steinway grand piano, This renowned pianist will perform the same program she played at Carnegie Hall in November. Acclaimed as one of the most gifted musicians of her generation, since her formal debut in Messina at age 10 she has received more than forty international awards, has released over 30 CDs, of which six are her own compositions. She has performed with major orchestras and in renowned concert halls all over the world, including Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall. In addition to a full-time teaching schedule in Rome and New York, she is the founder and of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of the annual Narnia Festival in her hometown of Narni, in Umbria, Italy. articles.text: Speaker event at museum also live-streamed Feb. 1 Curators at the de Young Museum will host a discussion on the iconic artist Tamara de Lempicka and how she used fashion as a way to craft her own artistic identity. The retrospective Tamara de Lempicka, the first exhibition in the United States dedicated to the artist’s full oeuvre, includes more than 150 works on view as well as a number of rarely seen drawings and still lifes. “Considering San Francisco’s history as a great Art Deco capital of the world, the exhibition, aptly presented in close proximity to landmarks of the period such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Coit Tower, adds to our understanding not only of Lempicka’s work specifically, but also this influential art and design period at large,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Artwork from Lempicka’s early Parisian years feature melancholic interiors and a selection of Art Deco objects, sculptures and dresses from the Fine Arts Museums’ permanent collection. Through her world-renowned paintings, Lempicka celebrated the changing world of women’s fashion in the 1920s and 1930s. Patrons view the retrospective Tamara de Lempicka exhibit at de Young Museum. The artist also wore designs by contemporary fashion powerhouses like Jean Patou and Marcel Rochas, and used fashion to craft her own artistic and public identity. The speaker event will be at 1 p.m. on February 1 in the museum’s Koret Auditorium and is free to ticket-holders. Seating is first-come, first-served. The discussion will also be live-streamed at the same time and is free on the museum’s website. The discussion will be led by museum curators Furio Rinaldi, the Lempicka exhibition co-curator, and Laura Camerlengo, the fine arts museum’s textile and costume expert. “Lempicka’s drawings reveal both the artist’s outstanding technical refinement as a designer and her breath of visual sources,” said Rinaldi. “The core of her unique style [draws] from Italian Mannerism to the French Neoclassicism, the Russian avant-garde and the innovative graphic language of fashion illustrators like George Barbier, Helen Dryden and Georges Lepape.” Camerlengo is curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, and since 2010, has organized and presented numerous costume and textile exhibitions for the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/events/conversation-lempicka-fashion.
articles.title: De Young hosts conversation on Tamara de Lempicka exhibit

articles.text: Past Lunar New Year celebrations at Children’s Fairyland traditionally feature a lion dance performed by local groups. Celebrate the Year of the Snake and the diverse Asian cultures of the Bay Area by joining in one of the Lunar New Year festivities being offered at museums and venues. Oakland Museum annual Lunar New Year on Feb. 8 The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) has celebrated Lunar New Year for over two decades with a day of family-friendly festivities, art, music and folkloric dance. The museum celebrates the year of the snake on Saturday, February 8, beginning at 11 a.m. Local Asian and Pacific Islander chefs will be onsite serving food for purchase throughout the day, while drinks and quick bites inspired by Lunar New Year will be available at the Museum’s outdoor Town Fare Patio. A lucky lion dance performed by LionDanceME takes place on the outdoor stage at 12 p.m. and Children’s author Oliver Chin will real aloud The Year of the Snake: Tales from the Chinese Zodiac. Art activities include puppet-making, crafting and decorating traditional red envelopes and tea-making. Local artist Chelsea Ryoko Wong and OMCA’s Senior Curator of Art Carin Adams will lead patrons through the museum’s galleries from 1 p.m. to 2 p.m. LionME closes out the day’s events with a traditional dance at 3:45 p.m. Visit https://museumca.org/ event/24th-annual-lunar-newyear-at-omca-year-of-the-snake/ to learn more and purchase tickets online. Limited tickets will be available at the door. Asian Art Museum Lunar New Year lecture series starts Feb. 5 The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco will host a Lunar New Year virtual lecture series on Wednesday, February 5 for museum members. Attendees will learn about the fascinating and colorful traditions of Lunar New Year, celebrated by various Asian cultures, including the symbolism behind lanterns, firecrackers, red envelopes, and traditional food. The one-hour lecture is held online via Zoom and led by one of the Asian Art Museum’s community speaker docents. The lecture will be followed by a halfhour Q&A. Visit https://calendar. asianart.org/event/virtual-lecture-series-lunar-new-year-yearof-the-snake/ to learn more and to reserve your spot. Fairyland celebrates Year of Snake Jan. 24-26 Children’s Fairyland in Oakland celebrates both Lunar New Year and the park’s 75th anniversary this Friday through Sunday, January 24 to 26 with special arts and crafts activities and traditional dance. From 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. this weekend, staff will serve festive sampling of fruit jelly, good luck candies, and traditional rice balls with sweet soup to park visitors. Kids will enjoy learning how to Lion Dance and play with handmade rattle drums. Park visitors are encouraged to wear red this weekend for good luck. Visit https://fairyland.org/ events-and-performances/lunarnew-year/ to learn more. Connie Han performs at Filoli House and Garden Jan. 29 - 31 Pianist Connie Han will perform a concert in Filoli Historic House and Garden’s elegant ballroom January 29 through 31 for a special series honoring the traditions of Lunar New Year. Han was born in Los Angeles to Chinese parents, both of whom were professional musicians, and was taught piano from the age of five. Han first discovered jazz in high school when she heard “Chance” by Kenny Kirkland from his album and decided to pursue the genre in her own musical career. Her album Crime Zone seized the attention of the jazz world and established herself as a fast-rising star on the scene. Her follow-up, Iron Starlet, also gained critical acclaim. All performances begin at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://filoli.org/ lunar-new-year/ to purchase tickets. ®

articles.text: Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink, an exhibition celebrating the life and work of renowned Chinese ink painter Qi Baishi, is now on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The exhibition marks the 160th anniversary of Baishi’s birth and features 42 works on paper on loan from the Beijing Fine Art Academy, where he served as the academy’s first honorary director. Inspiration In Ink is the first time many of the displayed works have been presented in the United States. “Qi Baishi’s long and storied life witnessed China’s dramatic passage from the Qing Dynasty to the new republic period and the rise of socialism,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “Renowned as the people’s artist, Qi declined to enjoy retirement. Instead, he tirelessly explored ink art in his later years, aiming to share his love of nature among a wide audience and help them find enlightenment in everyday life.” Zhang added that the artist’s “technical abilities and expressionistic approach imbue his art with a spiritual quality, inviting viewers to contemplate the deeper significance of everyday motifs.” “His work resonates so widely with audiences because he not only captures his subjects but also seeks to express their spirit through calligraphic, spontaneous strokes, something that requires master brushwork,” Zhang said. In 1960, Baishi became the first Chinese artist to have a solo exhibition at the de Young Museum in San Francisco. Although he has humble roots, his pieces have achieved record-breaking prices at auctions worldwide, with his “Twelve Landscape Screens” (1925) selling for a $141 million in 2017. “His ability to capture the beauty in the ordinary contributed to his growing popularity inside and outside of China, a legacy that continues to thrive today,” said Rob Mintz, Chief Curator at the Asian Art Museum. “Qi Baishi’s quotidian subject matter and whimsical, playful style made his art incredibly accessible to audiences at the time, making him the first Chinese painter to capture the attention of American audiences,” Mintz added. The exhibition will be on view through April. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/ qi-baishi-inspiration-in-ink/ to learn more and to purchase museum tickets. articles.text: Via’s perspective gives the movie a dimension that could easily have been left out. Instead, it brings to the film a conflicted complexity that adds to its sense of reality. Wonder doesn’t dwell on Auggie’s past medical experiences, nor does a doctor appear to give sage diagnostic advice. This is a family’s story, one that is imperfect and at moments heart wrenching. But for all of its emotive power, it is also about the resilience of the human heart. For though Auggie is bright and understands the reactions of his fellow students, he also realizes that he is fearful and untrusting of anyone who approaches him with an outstretched hand. To its credit, Wonder is, from the first frame, understated. It is subtle and subdued, while gently presenting a narrative that draws you not only into Auggie’s world but also into that of his family. The audience is asked, repeatedly, to look beyond Auggie’s mask and truly see who this young boy really is as he struggles with his isolation. There’s a line in the film that resonates from beginning to end: “When given a choice between being right and being kind, choose kind.” That alone sums up this film. Wonder. Directed by Stephen Chbosky. Starring Julia Roberts, Owen Wilson, Jacob Tremblay. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Streaming on Fandango/ prime/ apple tv/Metflix. Set in Nazi occupied France during WWII, White Bird is a compelling story of courage and kindness. The story authored by R.J. Palacio is considered to be thematically connected to the author’s first book and film, Wonder. The film opens in the present with a middle school boy Julian (Bryce Gheisar) coming home from school to what he thinks is an empty house. Instead he is surprised by his grandmother, Sara (Helen Mirren), who tells him that she is aware of his expulsion from his previous school for bullying a classmate. She asks him to sit down in the dining room and tells him a story that takes place during the Nazi occupation of France in World War II. And so her narrative begins. Sara (Ariella Glaser), a young Jewish girl on the cusp of adolescence, is counseled by her parents regarding the possible dangers for Jews. She barely grasps the full significance of the Nazi’s presence in their town. One of her classmates is Julien, his right leg crippled by childhood polio, and therefore walks awkwardly with a crutch. He is often the subject of gossip and cruel taunting by the older boys. On one singular school day Sara’s life would change forever. Nazi troops arrive at her school with the intention of identifying and removing just the Jewish students. Terrified (there are perhaps a dozen), betrayed by other students, they try and escape. Unexpectedly, Sara is rescued by Julien who leads her through an underground tunnel out of the school to safety. He then explains that she must hide in an old barn on his parents’ property. Julien’s act is extraordinary (supported by his mother), considering the risk involved; the Nazis were lethally unforgiving to anyone assisting the Jews. And thus begins the essence of the narrative: Sara will spend a harrowing year hidden in the barn with Julien as her only contact with the outside world. Their friendship slowly evolves, and is Orlando Schwerdt and Ariella Glaser in White Bird the fulcrum of the story. White Bird is a remarkable film, and together with the film Wonder poses important questions about the courage required to choose kindness. White Bird. Directed by Marc Forster. Starring Helen Mirren, Ariella Glaser, Orlando Schwerdt. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released in 2024. Streaming on prime/Fandango/apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS White Bird a remarkable film

articles.text: Wonder is a touching family film that focuses on a 10-year-old boy, Auggie (Jacob Tremblay), who since birth has suffered with a craniofacial genetic disorder, an affliction that has distorted his face (he has endured some 27 surgeries). For so many reasons this story is life-affirming and brims with a surprising humanity. Auggie has always been homeschooled by his mom, Isabel (Julia Roberts). But now he finds himself confronting leaving the safety and embrace of his home and family, which includes his father Nate (Owen Wilson) and his sister Via (Izabela Vidovic). He is about to begin his first year in middle school, a place where he will confront for the first time the judgment of his peers. As Isabel and Nate walk him to school, Isabel utters a quiet prayer, saying, “Please, don’t let the kids be cruel.” And yet she knows that by definition that cruelty can define so many aspects of middle school. So, Wonder is about how Auggie strives to adjust to an environment for which he is profoundly unprepared. But to this film’s credit, it is never overly sentimental or maudlin; rather it inserts into the story other points of view. An example would be Via, who for much of her life has felt on the periphery of the family, understanding intellectually why Auggie has required so much of her parents’ attention. Owen Wilson, Izabela Vidovic (back), Jacob Tremblay and Julia Roberts in Wonder

Sara (Ariella Glaser), a young Jewish girl on the cusp of adolescence, is counseled by her parents regarding the possible dangers for Jews. She barely grasps the full significance of the Nazi’s presence in their town. One of her classmates is Julien, his right leg crippled by childhood polio, and therefore walks awkwardly with a crutch. He is often the subject of gossip and cruel taunting by the older boys. On one singular school day Sara’s life would change forever. Nazi troops arrive at her school with the intention of identifying and removing just the Jewish students. Terrified (there are perhaps a dozen), betrayed by other students, they try and escape. Unexpectedly, Sara is rescued by Julien who leads her through an underground tunnel out of the school to safety. He then explains that she must hide in an old barn on his parents’ property. Julien’s act is extraordinary (supported by his mother), considering the risk involved; the Nazis were lethally unforgiving to anyone assisting the Jews. And thus begins the essence of the narrative: Sara will spend a harrowing year hidden in the barn with Julien as her only contact with the outside world. Their friendship slowly evolves, and is Orlando Schwerdt and Ariella Glaser in White Bird the fulcrum of the story. White Bird is a remarkable film, and together with the film Wonder poses important questions about the courage required to choose kindness. White Bird. Directed by Marc Forster. Starring Helen Mirren, Ariella Glaser, Orlando Schwerdt. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released in 2024. Streaming on prime/Fandango/apple tv.

articles.text: It was another great mid-winter weather day on January 15 for the Walking on Wednesdays group, with an energetic group of 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends on hand. It had been a while since the group had gone to the “Five Way Stop” that brings Wildwood, Windsor, Warfield Avenues, and Wallace Road together, and to the streets below Wildwood School in the southwest part of Piedmont and Meghan Bennett shared some historical information. The current Wildwood Avenue was called Highland Avenue in 1903. The road ended at what was then called “Piedmont Avenue,” and it ended at “Pleasant Valley Road,” which is now Grand Avenue. Today’s Winsor Avenue was named “Buttercup Avenue.” Isaac Requa was born in 1828 in Westchester County, New York. In 1850, after hearing of the discovery of gold in California, he sailed to San Francisco around Cape Horn by clipper ship to try his hand at mining. He went immediately to the gold country and was successful. In 1861 he traveled to Virginia City, Nevada to work on the silver Comstock Lode, and became superintendent of a mining company and a director in other big mining concerns. He returned to California and became a prominent West Coast financier in railroads with the Huntington, Stanford, Crocker and Hopkins combine. He was also president of the Central Pacific Railroad Company and a director in other Huntington lines. For many years Requa was active in California politics, first as a “Whig” and later as a Republican. He was a long-time chairman of the Republican State Central Committee and was once offered its nomination for Governor, but he declined. In his later life Requa was devoted mainly to banking and the Oakland Bank of Savings, of which he was president. In 1877 Requa acquired about 80 rolling, unimproved acres in what became Piedmont. In the 1880s there were only seven houses where the City of Piedmont is today. Requa and his wife Sarah developed “The Highlands,” an estate built around a house that overlooked Lake Merritt, the Bay, and the San Francisco Peninsula. “The Highlands” was among the first impressive houses to be built in Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, January 22, 2025 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers learn history of Requas By Dick Carter It was another great mid-winter weather day on January 15 for the Walking on Wednesdays group, with an energetic group of 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends on hand. It had been a while since the group had gone to the “Five Way Stop” that brings Wildwood, Windsor, Warfield Avenues, and Wallace Road together, and to the streets below Wildwood School in the southwest part of Piedmont and Meghan Bennett shared some historical information. The current Wildwood Avenue was called Highland Avenue in 1903. The road ended at what was then called “Piedmont Avenue,” and it ended at “Pleasant Valley Road,” which is now Grand Avenue. Today’s Winsor Avenue was named “Buttercup Avenue.” Isaac Requa was born in 1828 in Westchester County, New York. In 1850, after hearing of the discovery of gold in California, he sailed to San Francisco around Cape Horn by clipper ship to try his hand at mining. He went immediately to the gold country and was successful. In 1861 he traveled to Virginia City, Nevada to work on the silver Comstock Lode, and became superintendent of a mining company and a director in other big mining concerns. He returned to California and became a prominent West Coast financier in railroads with the Huntington, Stanford, Crocker and Hopkins combine. He was also president of the Central Pacific Railroad Company and a director in other Huntington lines. For many years Requa was active in California politics, first as a “Whig” and later as a Republican. He was a long-time chairman of the Republican State Central Committee and was once offered its nomination for Governor, but he declined. In his later life Requa was devoted mainly to banking and the Oakland Bank of Savings, of which he was president. In 1877 Requa acquired about 80 rolling, unimproved acres in what became Piedmont. In the 1880s there were only seven houses where the City of Piedmont is today. Requa and his wife Sarah developed “The Highlands,” an estate built around a house that overlooked Lake Merritt, the Bay, and the San Francisco Peninsula. “The Highlands” was among the first impressive houses to be built in Piedmont. The Highlands was on a knoll where the present Hazel Lane and Requa Road meet. The house had 22 bedrooms, an adjoining wing for domestic help, and 11 hired hands had other quarters on the estate. Since it was a long trip in horse-drawn vehicles to Oakland via Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue), Moraga Road, and Piedmont Avenue, The Highlands was all but self-sufficient. It had its own vegetable gardens, orchard, berry patches, dairy herd of 11 cows, stable with seven stalls, and an independent water supply from the wells on the property. The house was painted a yellow that was called “buttercup yellow.” Its beacon-like quality with no trees on the hills around it made the mansion a prominent landmark, easily visible from San Francisco and ferry boats. Requa died at home in 1908 at the age of 80 and in 1923 the mansion was demolished. Today’s Highland Avenue is named after Requa’s estate. It is interesting to note that Piedmont High School’s mascot is the “Highlander,” and the school colors, purple and white, were purported to have been Sarah Requa’s favorite colors. On the weekly walk the group headed off going through Piedmont Park to Guilford Road and a path to Hazel Lane and up to the Requa Place cul-de-sac. This was the site of The Highlands. Chuck Oraftik recognized two pillars that marked the entrance to the estate. They are all that remains of it. The group retraced their steps and went down Requa Road to Wildwood Avenue past Wildwood School. The walkers came to the “Five Way Stop” where they took a group photo. Then it was up Warfield onto Boulevard Way and the border of Oakland. Time was getting short so Sherry Jacobs pointed out a hidden path up to the end of Sylvan Way, a steep hill that goes down to Wildwood Avenue. The walkers were up to the challenge and made it safely down the hill before going up Wildwood to Windsor, Park View, and Magnolia Avenues for an on-time noon return to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Group strength and conditioning session at BodyFit Training Rockridge We are bombarded with fitness program ads this time of year. Strength training, fueled by recent advances in sports training and medicine, is a hot topic today, with gyms changing their marketing to get in on the buzz. Real strength training, however, is an intentional program that builds foundational stability and resilience in all movement planes and using all muscle types. Older modes of exercise, like cardio-driven HIIT (high-intensity interval training), optimize short term calorie burns, while strength training impacts are broader and last long beyond your workout. What is real strength training? A true strength program focuses on programatically stimulating muscle and nervous system adaptations to build overall strength and health. This systematic approach contrasts with random circuit training or “toning” workouts, which often use weights but focus on calorie burn or aesthetics. Real strength training has four key pillars: 1. Progressive Overload: Increasing the demands on your muscles over time by lifting heavier weights or improving efficiency. This principle drives muscle growth and neuromuscular efficiency. Lighter weights and high-rep workouts may improve endurance and tone, but don’t deliver the stimulus needed for gains in strength and stability. 2. Compound Movements: Full body exercises like squats, deadlifts, presses, and pullups engage multiple muscle groups, promoting overall strength and functional movement. These multi-joint exercises require coordination and core stability, unlike isolation movements often used in floor workouts or circuit training. Accessory movements are also used to help build mobility and strengthen the muscle groups. 3. Balance of Rest and Intensit y: Strength training involves lifting heavy weights (70–90% of one-rep max) with proper form. Rest periods between sets (1.5-3 minutes) allow recovery for maximum effort set to set. In contrast, circuit training prioritizes cardiovascular endurance by minimizing rest and focusing on heart rate zones. 4. Periodization and Recovery: Structured progressions balance load, intensity, and volume, ensuring steady improvements while preventing plateaus, overuse injuries, or boredom! Recovery—through rest days, sleep, and nutrition—is essential for muscle repair and growth. GOOD THROUGH FEBRUARY 2025 GOOD THROUGH FEBRUARY 2025

articles.text: Are you changing jobs soon? If so, you’ll obviously be interested in your new salary — but you’ll also want to look at other financial considerations. Here are some of the most important ones: • 401(k) If you had a 401(k) plan through your previous employer, you’ll need to decide what to do with it once you’ve joined a new employer. You could just cash it out, but you’d pay taxes and possible penalties. You could leave your 401(k) with your previous employer, if allowed, and if you have been happy with your plan’s performance. Or you could move your 401(k) into your new employer’s plan, which might be a good choice if the new plan has lower fees and attractive investment options. You’d also want to ask whether the new employer offers matching contributions. Finally, you could roll over your old 401(k) into a traditional IRA, which would give you more investment choices. • HSA/FSA If your new employer offers a health savings account (HSA) as part of a high-deductible health plan, you may want to take advantage of it. Your contributions are made with pre-tax dollars, your earnings generally grow tax deferred and your withdrawals are tax free, as long as they’re used for qualified medical expenses. Plus, you can carry unused funds through retirement, when you can still use them for qualified medical expenses. Your employer might also offer a flexible spending account (FSA), which can pay for a variety of health care costs, such as deductibles, co-payments and co-insurance. Generally, if you’re contributing to an HSA, you can’t fund an FSA in the same year, except for a limited purpose FSA. • Waiting period for health benefits You’ll want to ask your new employer if there’s a waiting eligibility period to enroll in its benefits plan — health insurance, dental, vision, and so on. If so, you may need to get COBRA coverage for a few months to stay in your old plan, unless you can be added to a spouse’s plan. When you go on your new employer’s health care plan, make sure you know what it covers. Depending on your situation, you might want to add supplemental health insurance. • Life insurance When you leave a job, your employer-sponsored life insurance will end, unless you have the option to convert your group term life policy into an individual permanent cash value policy. So, you’ll want to be sure your new employer offers at least the same insurance coverage as your old one. But you should also determine whether the group policy offered by your employer is sufficient for your needs. Depending on several factors, such as your income, spouse’s income and family size, you may need to supplement your employer’s policy with an individual term life insurance policy. • Other benefits Review your new employer’s benefits package carefully to see what’s available. Many employers offer tuition reimbursement for their employees, and some even provide college planning assistance for employees’ children. For example, your employer might offer matching contributions to a tax-advantaged 529 education saving plan, which can be used for college, some K-12 expenses and some trade/vocational school programs. Changing jobs can provide you with an opportunity to expand your career, learn new skills and broaden your social network. And it can certainly be financially rewarding, too — so make sure you know all the benefits involved. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a Financial Advisor in the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue, Suite 201, Piedmont, tel. (510) 547-4589.

articles.text: As the Lighting Ceremony in Piedmont Park approaches each year, Piedmont residents are invited to send holiday greetings to their neighbors through donations to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s (PBF) Holiday Greeting Fund. This year, in addition to PBF’s regular funding initiatives, donors had the opportunity to support the reforestation of Dracena Park. PBF is delighted to report that the community responded with great generosity. Nearly $35,000 was raised in total, including $17,700 specifically designated for the reforestation project. Since July 1, PBF has also received more than $23,000 in donations for tributary trees and benches, given in honor of and in memory of Piedmont citizens. articles.text: Nancy Kent (left), Cathy Glazier, Patty Dunlap, Cameron Wolfe, Betsy Andersen, Tom Ramsey, Julia Burke, Jennifer Long, Nancy Bishop, Lorrel Plimier, Conna McCarthy, Rosanna Bayon Moore The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) celebrated its 60th Anniversary at the City Council Meeting on January 21. President Patty Dunlap, along with other PBF Trustees and Advisors, presented Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen and the City Council with a $60,000 check in recognition of the milestone. The funds are designated for refreshing and enhancing many of the projects PBF has completed in partnership with the City over the past six decades. Mayor Andersen responded with a Proclamation expressing gratitude to PBF “for its vision, leadership, and generous partnership.” The Proclamation officially recognizes and celebrates the Foundation’s 60th Anniversary. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation was established in Spring 1964 when the Piedmont Garden Club proposed creating a trust with the City to ensure a permanent source of funds for beautifying parks, the Community Center, street plantings, and other civic improvements. The City Council embraced the idea, and on May 13, 1964, PBF was incorporated with eight Trustees: three appointed by the City and five by Piedmont Garden Club. The Foundation’s first President was Mrs. Herbert Dunn. A Legacy of Leadership Over the years, PBF has benefitted from a strong partnership with the City. Typically, the Mayor, Vice Mayor, and Chair of the Park Commission have been among the City-appointed Trustees. In total, 31 members of the Piedmont Garden Club have served as PBF President, supported by countless other club members who served as Trustees or Advisors. Many PBF leaders have also held key roles within the City. Currently, four former or sitting Mayors serve as Trustees or Advisors: Betsy Smegal Andersen, Jen Cavenaugh, Bob McBain, and Valerie Matzger. President Patty Dunlap is a past Chair of the Park Commission, and other Trustees and Advisors with ties to the City or schools include Tom Smegal, Susan Herrick, Nancy McHugh, Bobbe Stehr, Patty Siskind and Cameron Wolfe, Jr. ects throughout the City, including improvements to City Hall, Piedmont Park, the Tea House, the Hall Fenway, the Exedra Gates and surrounding area, the Linda, Kingston Triangle, the Ramona Triangle and installation of the Bufano Bears Sculpture in Crocker Park”. More recently, PBF has contributed to safety and sustainability initiatives, including one of the largest donations to the new swimming pool project, second only to that of PRFO. This donation will fund environmentally appropriate landscaping around the pool. Endowments for the Future PBF established its first Endowment Fund in 1991, with an initial gift from Winifred Brown Bell. PBF has worked hard to grow this fund substantially, safeguarding existing and future projects and ensuring funds during lean times. In 2017, a second Endowment Fund was created, thanks to gifts from John Bates, Jr. and Charles Bates, to provide ongoing maintenance for the City’s sports facilities. Impactful Projects As Mayor Andersen noted in her Proclamation, “PBF has successfully partnered with the City to complete scores of projHonoring Key Leaders No discussion of PBF history would be complete without nods to two of its most prolific Presidents, Barbara Magee and Jean Brown Wolfe. Both women served four years instead of the typical two and oversaw some of PBF’s most impactful projects. Their contributions are commemorated on City property: Barbara Magee at the Exedra overlook area and Jean Brown Wolfe at the garden surrounding the Tea House. A Year of Celebration To mark its 60th Anniversary, PBF has planned a series of events and activities. Over the next month, news articles will highlight PBF’s key projects, accompanied by games such as word finders, crosswords, and spelling bees. The Wednesday Walkers group will visit various PBF project sites over three weeks, and a walking map will be published to guide residents to these locations. President Patty Dunlap expressed her excitement: “We hope everyone will find a way to participate in the celebration of PBF’s 60 years and support our future endeavors.” PBF President Patty Dunlap (left) presents $60,000 check to Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen

We want to restart our co-ed Sea Scouts program and we’re looking for interested youth and adults to serve as program leaders. Adults, if you haven’t led a group of kids and young adults before, that’s OK, as we can train you! Sea Scouts is an aquatics-based Scouting program in which young men and women learn seamanship, leadership, service, and teamwork. And, they have lots of fun, too. Scouts are recognized and rewarded for the things they learn and do. They can earn certifications in SCUBA, boating safety, lifesaving, and CPR. Like other Scouting programs, Sea Scouts is Scout-led (with adult mentoring), so Scouts are empowered to make the program what they want. In Sea Scouts, you build your own adventure! Want to know more? We’re holding an information session on Thursday, February 6, 2025 at the Scout office located at 10 Highland Way. By 2024, average sales prices remained higher than they were five years ago in every market except in Piedmont, where a decline was partly due to fewer total sales over $4 million. articles.text: Piedmont Finance Director Michael Szczech Piedmont’s Finance Director Michael Szczech is preparing to retire from his position, with his last day on Thursday, January 23. A long-time resident of Piedmont, Szczech served as Finance Director for over seven years. As Finance Director, Szczech administers the City’s fiscal operations, including budgeting, investments, financial transaction processing, record-keeping and reporting, payroll, accounts payable and accounts receivable. He oversees a three-person staff in the Finance Department – City Accountant Ken Lee, Human Resources Administrator Stacy Jennings, and Administrative Services Technician Melisa Mariano-Reyes. Originally from Chicago, Szczech is a 27-year resident of Piedmont and has two daughters. He moved to California in 1989, motivated to move after visiting an uncle in the Bay Area during the winter. After enjoying 60-degree temperatures during his visit and then returning to Chicago where it was 10 degrees below zero, he decided it was time for a change and started looking for jobs. Szczech joined the city’s staff as Finance Director in July 2017 after a long career in the private sector. He came to the City from Café Press, a San Mateo-founded shopping company where he worked for 10 years as Vice President. Prior to Café Press, Szczech worked at Leapfrog, an educational software company based in Emeryville. Szczech was recruited to apply for the role of Finance Director by former Mayor Bob McBain, who pointed out the advantages of being able to walk a few blocks to work each day. After retiring, Szczech said he is looking forward to spending more time traveling, and has trips planned this spring to the Florida Keys and to Washington DC. Further ahead, he’s looking forward to his first trip to Asia, where he hopes to see Japan, Thailand, and Hong Kong. Szczech is pleased to be leaving the City in strong financial shape, noting that Piedmont has never used deficit spending in his time as Finance Director. He also lauds the Council for the fiscal discipline during the recent multi-year period of high transfer tax receipts. Unlike many neighboring cities, Piedmont never used these surpluses to fund day-to-day operations. Instead, these funds went to building up reserves and capital funds, allowing the City to invest in infrastructure. During his time with the City, Szczech is most proud of these accomplishments: • Implementing a new financial software system for the city in 2020, modernizing City practices and ending paper-based processes for accounts payable and payroll. • Establishing the PARS (Public Agency Retirement Services) Fund in 2018. By funding and actively managing this fund now, the City hopes to mitigate the impact of increased pension costs projected in future years. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department has sent a fire engine and crew of four firefighters to Southern California to provide aid for the ongoing Los Angeles fires. Captain Mike Carlisle, Engineer Sandor Lengyel, and Firefighters Tariq Harless and Kevin Sauder arrived in LA last Wednesday morning, January 8. Fires have been raging out of control in the Los Angeles area since Tuesday, January 7. At least five fires broke out due to dry conditions and powerful winds and have destroyed thousands of homes and caused the deaths of 24 people in the Los Angeles area. A Piedmont Firefighter works to put out a house fire in Southern California.

articles.text: Big crowd in fundraising event for Havens School The Havens Dads Club hosted their 17th annual Poker Night on Friday, January 10 at the Veterans Hall with 150 players enjoying an authentic Texas Hold-Em tournament. By the time Havens Dad Luke Schloegel won the final hand, over $62,300 had been raised for Havens Elementary School. “It started somber right at the beginning and then it became really fun and it reflected the motto of the ‘all-in for the kids.’ I did feel like people were all-in on it and that’s reflected in the re-buys,” said Havens Dad Babak Sanii who was in charge of the event’s financials, check-in booth and photography. The event allowed for eliminated players to buy back in, a feature which benefited Havens school to the tune of $30,000. Food at the tournament made it a challenge to keep the grease off the chips, as passed hors-d’oeuvres from Chef Robert Dorsey, a taco bar and multiple round of pizza deliveries from Arthur Mac’s fed the masses. Oakland United Brewing provided the suds with many beer options on tap. articles.text: The outfield at Hampton Park’s baseball diamond is fenced off to allow grass seeds to germinate. Coaches and Hampton Fields are closed for repairs and re-sodding until February 21, in preparation for the upcoming Spring sports and soccer season. The popular fields are closed every year in the winter to repair damaged turf, level out mud holes, re-seed grass, and aerate and re-sod the terrain for safety and quality of play. Depending on the weather, the germination of new seeds may vary. “If the weather cooperates, we get good results,” said Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent. “If the weather is super wet or cold, the seed doesn’t germinate as well or the sod doesn’t take hold as well.” While growing new grass and re-sodding the fields, people have to be kept off the field to allow the turf repairs to settle properly and new seeds to germinate. Taking advantage of the gap in outdoor youth sports in winter, the City uses December and January to make its repairs. “Ideally, we would be doing these renovations during warmer months, but that’s when everybody wants to use the field,” said Kent. At Hampton Park, the baseball outfield is fenced off to allow new seeds the chance to germinate. Both fields are scheduled to complete repairs and re-open by February 21. In fact, as a political science professor at the University of California, Berkeley, I regularly teach about such cases in my undergraduate and graduate courses. In such scenarios, the research tells us that people tend to underinvest in the positive action, in this case brush clearing and home hardening. A short walk around some of the hillier, more forested parts of our city reveals that Piedmont is no exception to this general rule: dead branches, fallen leaves, and even toppled tree trunks abound. I say this not to shame negligent homeowners – though research also suggests that a little shame can be an effective motivator in certain cases. On the contrary, it is entirely rational for a property owner to underinvest in clearing dried brush and flammable debris when they reason that the likelihood of their house burning down is just as, if not more, dependent on what their neighbors decide to do with their own yard detritus. This is precisely why such a case warrants government participation. Given that all of us in Piedmont jointly benefit when our neighbors invest in preparing their properties for fire season, it stands to reason that we should jointly contribute to the costs of that investment. I propose that Piedmont set up a small fund that can be distributed annually as an inducement to homeowners to clear dried brush and take other protective measures around their homes. This fund could be financed using existing city money earmarked for wildfire preparedness or using new money raised via a nominal tax on property owners. Homeowners in high-risk areas would receive priority for fund distributions, with remaining money allocated based on secondary risk. Notably, this money would not cover the full cost of home hardening but instead offer enough incentive to encourage homeowners to take steps they otherwise might not have taken. Small sums of money could be paid out annually for brush clearing activities, while larger grants could be distributed on a lottery basis, much like the statewide Earthquake Brace and Bolt Seismic retrofit program, which offers grants of up to $3,000 for home retrofitting. An initial pilot program could help Piedmont determine the minimum level of financial inducements needed to create results while also offering proof of concept. Moreover, none of this would be at the expense of other, more traditional means of community preparation. City staff are currently engaged in hazard mitigation planning. Given that, and given the saliency of the LA fires, there is no better time to encourage our local representatives to consider ambitious and creative solutions to wildfires. We risk everything by not bracing ourselves for the next fire. We cannot count on individuals alone to take the necessary preemptive steps to reduce wildfire spread. Let’s collectively invest in protecting our community from future disaster. Rebecca Perlman is a Piedmont resident and assistant professor of political science at the University of California, Berkeley. Her research focuses on the politics of regulation and climate change. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to approve the first reading of a new ordinance designed to stay on top of new state housing laws at their Monday, January 6, council meeting. The laws make changes to the approval process for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and junior accessory dwelling units (JADUs), more commonly known as granny flats, in-law units, backyard cottages, garage/basement apartments, or secondary units. The recommended revisions to Piedmont’s ADU ordinance would make city code consistent with three recent state laws that went into effect on January 1, 2025. The laws governing the changes are Assembly Bill (AB) 2533, Senate Bill (SB) 1211 and AB 1332. AB 2533 legalizes all previously unpermitted ADUs and JADUs constructed before January 1, 2020. Permits for such ADUs/JADUs can only be denied if they fail to meet the required Health and Safety regulations. The newly legalized units will contribute toward housing production goals for the city, and Mayor Besty Anderson said she hopes that this step will help encourage community members with currently unpermitted ADUs and JADUs to acquire permits. SB 1211 allows uncovered parking spaces to be converted into ADU/JADUs and increases the maximum number of ADUs on a property to eight, as long as the number of ADUs is not higher than the amount of multi-family units. AB 1332 requires the City to create a system for pre-approved ADU design plans to be used by citizens seeking to build their own ADUs. Design plans would be submitted and approved by the City, after which citizens could pay a fee to use the already approved plans. When asked by the Council how these laws would affect the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan (the City’s plan to provide space for housing development in Moraga Canyon), Kevin Jackson stated that the City would be able to specify the number of ADUs that could be built in the development agreement with a potential housing developer. Piedmont’s Planning Commission recommended that the City Council adopt the proposed amendments to the zoning ordinance after a public hearing at their meeting on December 9, 2024. The Council will review the updates for approval at its January 21 council meeting. articles.text: At-risk Pittie mix Potpie is hoping the New Year will bring him a new home. Oakland Animal Services staff say this big boy of 70 pounds is big hearted and a true softie. He’s a playful, affectionate dog who loves to wiggle and bounce around with excitement and show off his silly side. While 4-year-old Potpie has had minimal training, he’s eager to please and is motivated by treats, making him an excellent candidate for positive reinforcement training. He knows the all-important sit command, takes treats gently, and is working on leash manners. He would get on with a dog who matches his gentle play style, or as your one and only pooch. Potpie would be an affectionate companion and happily sit by your side for some love. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is seeking feedback from community members on proposed changes to business permitting on Grand and Highland Avenues. Residents can provide input on the proposed performance standards by completing a brief online survey that will remain open until January 20. The goal of the proposed changes is to streamline the permitting process for new businesses in Piedmont’s commercial areas. Currently, any new business wanting to open in Piedmont must go through public hearings before the Planning Commission and City Council in order to obtain a conditional use permit (CUP). The City’s Planning & Building Department have developed a proposed list of business types that would be permitted “by right,” meaning that they would be able to open in commercial areas without a public hearing process – as long as they conform to certain standards covering hours of operation, number of employees, and other limitations designed to ensure that new businesses are compatible with the surrounding neighborhood. The proposed standards would apply for future restaurants, cafes, hair salons, fitness studios, and other businesses along Grand and Highland Avenues and would apply only in areas already zoned for commercial and mixed-use activity. The initial proposed list of business types eligible for “by right” permits includes: • Food and beverage sales: Wine shops, Limited service restaurants and cafes, Bakery • Nurseries and garden supplies: Florist shops, Plant nurseries, Garden supply stores • Neighborhood serving retail: Clothing store, Art and Craft store, Book store, Bike shop, Hardware store • Office: Architecture, Engineering, Medical, Dental • Professional Services: Hair salons, Barber services, Yoga studio, Dance studio, Martial Arts studio, Photography studio, Tutoring Center • Other: Fitness center Businesses that do not fit into one of these categories would still be able to open in Piedmont, but they would need to go through a public hearing process and receive individual approval from the Planning Commission. These proposals were developed based on a series of Planning Commission and City Council study sessions in July-August 2024, as well as input from community members via an online survey conducted in summer 2024. The findings from the initial survey were presented in a study session at the Planning Commission Meeting on October 14, 2024. With information from the new survey, Planning staff seeks to further refine the proposed list of permitted uses and performance standards. When complete, the revisions would be considered for approvals at public hearings by the Planning Commission and City Council. Responses to the survey are available at piedmont.ca.gov/BusinessStandardsSurvey and will remain open until January 20. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/PermittedCommercialUses. To provide input via email, contact Associate Planner Gopika Nair at gnair@piedmont. ca.gov.
articles.title: City seeks residents’ input on possible new businesses on Grand Ave.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works Department completed a project to update signage and striping on San Carlos Avenue on December 20, 2024. The new signs and paint seek to make the divided street’s one-way roads safer and more clear. Public Works looked into the street’s signage after they were contacted by a community member, concerned that they saw a lot of people turn their cars down the wrong way of the one-way streets. The complaint was reviewed by a Traffic Safety Working Group composed of Piedmont police and public staff. The group meets once per month to review any complaints received and traffic incidents to find out if there is anything that can be done to make Piedmont streets safer. After reviewing the complaint, the Traffic Safety Working Group brought in a traffic engineering firm to assess the intersections and make recommendations. The City then implemented the firm’s recommendations, updating the street with a new “Keep Right” directional arrow sign and fresh paint spelling out “DO NOT ENTER” at the exits of the one-way avenue roads. articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works team responded to a report of a fallen tree on Moraga Avenue on Saturday evening, January 11. Dispatchers received a report about the tree at 5:30 p.m. on Saturday to which Public Works staff responded immediately. On Moraga Avenue, workers found a large eucalyptus blocking the road. It had fallen from the Mountain View Cemetery property. Working with the tree contractor they were able to clear the massive tree and reopen the road at 8:15 p.m., within three hours of the first report. articles.text: The Lake School has been a pioneering play-based educational institution in the East Bay for the past 44 years. Recognized for its commitment to providing a stimulating and supportive environment for young children. The Lake School is open for play with learners from ages two to six years old. In the past, the school has only offered a part time schedule for preschoolers. For the 2025-26 school year, The Lake School will offer flexible options for children ages 2-6 years old from two to five days per week, with dismissal between 12:45 p.m. and 5 p.m. Campus tours for 2025-26 enrollment will be held on January 24, February 21, and March 21 at 9:30 a.m. This is a great opportunity to see our program in action and to learn how all of a child’s developmental milestones can be reached through engaging play. You will also get to explore our newly renovated classrooms and updated outdoor play facilities, meet our furry, feathered, and scaled pets, and ask any questions about the preschool experience for your child. To RSVP for the tours, contact Maia Gallo, the Head of School, at director@ thelakeschool.net or call 510-839- 4227. You are also welcome to join us on Thursday, January 23, from 7-9 p.m. online for a Transitional Kindergarten Information Night. The insightful session is designed to highlight the importance of this developmental year for your child. Hear from The Lake School teachers and parents who will share their expertise and learn why The Lake School is an exceptional choice for your child’s preparation for kindergarten. If you are a parent or caregiver or a 3-4 year old child, this event will offer valuable knowledge and support. Don’t miss out on this opportunity to set your child up for success! Contact Maia now to secure your spot. We are hopeful that our expanded hours will allow more families to join the wonderful Lake School community. Contact us today to learn more about what makes The Lake School unique. The school is located at 304 Lester Avenue in Oakland. Lake School campus tours for 2025-26 enrollment will be held on January 24, February 21, and March 21 at 9:30 a.m.
articles.title: Lake School expanding hours in 2025

articles.text: At the January 8 school board meeting a second reading was held for a proposal of six new classes to be offered at Piedmont High School. Aside from AP Physics C, all the new classes are honors versions of existing Visual Arts and Performing Arts classes and will be offered next year. New classes of instruction, which grant an extra grade point, will now be offered for AP Physics C, and the Honors versions of: Acting, Jazz Band, Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Dance. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich and PHS Principal David Yoshihara gave the first reading on December 11 and again were on hand to further explain the courses, give data and discuss the impact upon students. “Do we have students say ‘I love the arts, I want to continue in the arts, but I’m not taking that next class, because I’m worried about my college apps’? Oh my lord, yes,” said faculty member Elise Marks. Marks called the decision to move away from favorite topics of study as heart breaking and quite common. The five new arts classes should help students avoid having to move away from their passions to take more AP and honors classes. “We already have students who are doing all these amazing extra things within the classes. They are teaching other students, student directing, they are already doing the work and getting no reward for it,” Marks added. AP Physics C will be calculus-based and for juniors and seniors. The course content will cover Mechanics and Electricity & Magnetism. Board members, teachers, students and community members concurred that the change would be beneficial. “Because these classes do exist within classes that already exist, they don’t impact our master schedule in any way. There really is no downside,” said Marks.
articles.title: 6 new Honors and AP classes approved

articles.text: Piedmont School District invites families to learn more about the Transitional Kindergarten (TK) program at an Information Night 7:00 p.m. this Thursday, January 16, at Beach Elementary School. TK blends preschool and readiness standards for kindergarten with a focus on hands-on and experiential learning. In 2025-26, children who turn five years old after September 2, 2025 and before September 1, 2026 are eligible for TK. TK is the first year of a two-year kindergarten program designed to meet the specific needs of four and five-year-old children. TK does not replicate preschool or kindergarten; it uses developmentally and age-appropriate practices. TK addresses the child’s language, literacy, and pre-math skills with an emphasis on social and emotional development and learning through inquiry and play. The TK program is taught by credentialed teachers with specialized training in early childhood. It runs five days a week. Children are enrolled in either an AM (8:20-11:45 a.m.) or PM (11:45 a.m.- 3:10 p.m.) session. TK offers a developmentally appropriate curriculum that allows students to explore, create, and learn through purposeful play-based activities. Social emotional, fine motor, and academic skills are all integrated in this hands-on program to build a strong foundation for kindergarten the following year. To read more about our TK program, please visit Piedmont. k12.ca.us/about/enrolling/enrolling-info
articles.title: Transitional Kindergarten

articles.text: On Sunday, January 12, the Oakland, Emeryville and Piedmont Girl Scouts kicked off the 2025 cookie season at St. Leo Catholic School with a Cookie Rally. Northern California Girl Scouts changed bakeries this year, so the event allowed girls to review continuing cookies, learn about new cookies and prepare for the season. Girl Scout volunteers hosted different stations to review all the skills the girls will need for success. At the rally, Girl Scouts practiced how to speak to customers, how to multiply and total orders, learned about vegan cookies, and cookies with peanuts. “It made me pretty excited for the start of cookie season, and now I want to sell 2,000 boxes of cookies,” said Brownie Winnie Pickavance. Thin Mints are back, but several cookies have different names and there are some new cookies in town. Cookie Season started January 13 and continues until March 16. Find cookie booths at ilovecookies.org. Cadette Charlotte Phung hands out this year’s cookies to younger Girl Scouts for taste testing and diligent review.
articles.title: Girl Scout Cookie season begins

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club will host its 38th annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 8, at the Veterans Hall. Tickets are still available for the celebration with unlimited crab, sides, beer and wine that runs from 6:00- 11:00 p.m. The fundraising event that benefits the 101-year-old Wildwood Elementary School involves dozens of volunteers and sponsors to put on the popular production which procures upwards of 250 pounds of crab for 150 guests. Co-leaders of the event are former Dads Club President Scott Zengel and Sergio Serna, and they aim to make the event accessible to every community member this year. “This year we lowered the price, because we wanted to attract as many people as possible who have never been to one,” said Serna. Purchase includes all-you-caneat fresh crab cooked two ways, oven-baked salmon, and sides like New Orleans spicy spinach, creamy mac ‘n cheese, Tunisian spiced corn, desserts, and coffee. Tickets include bottomless beer and wine, with specialty cocktails available for purchase at the bar. Live entertainment will be provided by Dads Club DJ Ben Anderson selecting the chunkiest tracks to wind up and close down the evening. This year’s theme is “Island Vibes,” so anything from a Hawaiian shirt to full-body porpoise or pirate costumes will be acceptable. “If your outfit conjures an island paradise, your favorite sea animal or the beach bum life you’re on the right track,” the dads state on their website. This is an adults-only event. Proceeds from the event will go to the Wildwood Dad’s Club to fund capital and infrastructure improvements to Wildwood Elementary School. The fun starts when doors open at 6:00 p.m. and the crab fest starts at 7:00 p.m. Visit Wildwooddadsclub.org/ crab-feed for more details of what promises to be an unforgettable evening of food, drinks, and festivities. Former Wildwood Dads Club president Scott Zengel dresses as Crab Daddy to promote the annual Crab Feed on February 8.
articles.title: Wildwood Dads Crab Feed on Sat. Feb. 8

TK blends preschool and readiness standards for kindergarten with a focus on hands-on and experiential learning. In 2025-26, children who turn five years old after September 2, 2025 and before September 1, 2026 are eligible for TK. TK is the first year of a two-year kindergarten program designed to meet the specific needs of four and five-year-old children. TK does not replicate preschool or kindergarten; it uses developmentally and age-appropriate practices. TK addresses the child’s language, literacy, and pre-math skills with an emphasis on social and emotional development and learning through inquiry and play. The TK program is taught by credentialed teachers with specialized training in early childhood. It runs five days a week. Children are enrolled in either an AM (8:20-11:45 a.m.) or PM (11:45 a.m.- 3:10 p.m.) session. TK offers a developmentally appropriate curriculum that allows students to explore, create, and learn through purposeful play-based activities. Social emotional, fine motor, and academic skills are all integrated in this hands-on program to build a strong foundation for kindergarten the following year. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Highlanders beat California, San Leandro, Liberty Staff Photos Saniyah Johnson made her debut against San Leandro. She scored five points and four rebounds on the Pirates, along with eight points and eight rebounds on Liberty. Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued rolling, picking up three wins at Binks Rawlings Gym over the past week to improve its record to 12-1. The Highlanders defeated Liberty 69-11 on Saturday, January 11, beat San Leandro 72-25 on Thursday, January 9 for their first Western Alameda County Conference win, and claimed a 60-55 comeback win over California HS on Tuesday, January 7. Making her debut against San Leandro was junior forward Saniyah Johnson, giving coach Bryan Gardere eight players who can make a difference after having just one bench player on last year’s roster. “Last year was tough on numbers, so it’s nice to have more players available. It keeps the energy up, Some days you just need people to get things going,” Gardere said. Piedmont played its biggest game of the season thus far on Tuesday, January 14 when hosting Bishop O’Dowd, but results were not complete by the time of publishing this week’s Post. Gardere reflected on getting his cast ready for a crucial rivalry game, knowing that all but Shakila Zuberi of PHS’ roster are new to the varsity program. “You and I know there is a lot of energy behind this game. We just have to keep them composed and have them lock in for these big games. You try and stay in the moment, everyone is going to make it a big deal around the school, parents, families, friends, on social media – everything. You have to stay grounded, have fun with it, and avoid making it too big,” Gardere said. 69-11 win vs. Liberty Piedmont never allowed more than five points in a quarter, leading 24-1 by the end of the first and 50-3 by halftime. They extended the lead to 62-6 in the third, adding seven points in the final going. Final stats: Andrea Martin had 11 points, seven rebounds, two blocks and a steal. Savannah Dennig had six points, five rebounds, four assists, and two steals. Jenelle Solis had 14 points, five assists, and two steals. Zuberi had six points, five rebounds, and three assists. Taylor White had six points, eight rebounds, four assists, and three steals. BriAndrea Martin, a freshman, fights through contact. She had 22 points in their 60-55 win over California. Cleo Afsar put up 20 points on San Leandro. ana Webb had 11 points, eight rebounds, two assists and two steals. Cleo Afsar had seven points and two rebounds. Johnson had eight points, eight rebounds, and one assist. three steals, and three blocks. Zuberi had two points and two rebounds. 72-25 victory over San Leandro Piedmont didn’t allow a single point until 4:57 left in the second quarter, leading 27-0 in the first quarter and 43-13 by halftime. They added 15 more points in the third quarter, 58-19, and 14 more points in the fourth. Final stats: Afsar led with 20 points, four steals, and a rebound. Webb had 15 points, six rebounds, two steals, one block and assist. Solis had 10 points, six assists, and four steals. Martin scored nine points, four rebounds, two assists, two steals, and a block. Dennig had eight points, eight rebounds, two assists, and a steal. White had six points, seven rebounds, and a block. Johnson had five points, four rebounds, 60-55 important win over California California jumped out to a 24-13 lead in the first quarter, but Piedmont limited the Grizzlies to two points in the second quarter to take a 27-26 lead by halftime. Cal inched ahead in the third, 32-31, but Piedmont outscored the Grizzlies 19-13 in the fourth quarter to win 60-55. It was a critical game for Solis, who scored 18 points including knocking down three 3-pointers in five attempts, along with having eight assists. Final stats: Solis had 18 points, eight assists, and three steals. Martin had 22 points, six rebounds, and two assists. Dennig had two points, two rebounds, two steals, and an assist. Webb had 14 points, five rebounds, three assists, and two steals. White had two points, six rebounds, and a block. Zuberi had two rebounds, two assists, and a steal. Tuesday vs. Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont hosted Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, January 14. Results were not complete by post time, see next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (12-1 overall, 1-0 league) faces Menlo School on Saturday, January 18 at 3:00 p.m. in the MLK Shootout hosted by St. Mary’s of Stockton. They also face Centennial of Corona on Monday, January 20 for the MLK Shootout at Bishop O’Dowd at 10:30 a.m.

articles.text: It was a big week for Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team. On Saturday, January 11, the Highlanders claimed reversal of last year’s Div. 3 North Coast Section Championship loss to University, beating the Red Devils 82-79 in overtime at their home gym. Two days earlier, PHS beat San Leandro 49-39 at Binks Rawlings Gym in their first Western Alameda County Conference game of the season. Coach Ben Spencer feels their overtime win over University was among the best games of his six years at the school. “That was a top-five win in program history,” he said. ”We haven’t beaten them since the NCS semifinals in 2020 and we’ve never beaten them on the road.
