articles.text: Gianluca Bini scored four goals against Encinal. Bosco Lorin had three goals in the 10-0 shutout of Encinal. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team returned from winter break in a big way, toppling the Encinal Jets by a resounding 10-0 shutout victory under the lights at Witter Field on Friday, January 10. It put an end to a five-match winless run going back to December 5. “It was definitely a great way to start the year, it’s good to see the boys shake off the cobwebs. We still have to be relative; we’re going to have tougher challenges. But, it’s good for them to show success. We want to build on tactical concepts and adjust those concepts based on the opponent,” said coach Ben Russell. The brilliant offensive display featured two players gaining hat tricks with Gianluca Bini scoring four goals and Bosco Lorin with three. “It definitely build confidence for the team. Hopefully we can translate that to league against teams like Berkeley, Castro Valley, O’Dowd, and Alameda – those are going to be really tough games. Our discipline was lacking at the start of the season. If we can execute what we can do, I know we’re a really good team,” Bini said. “We’ve been lacking a lot in goal scoring and finishing. Getting this result is hopefully a good push in the right direction. The last couple of games we tied when we should’ve performed better. We went into this game knowing we had to compete and get a bunch of goals,” Lorin mentioned. Piedmont has a busy week ahead with three matches in seven days, visiting San Leandro tonight, January 15, then hosting Berkeley on January 17 and Castro Valley on January 21. Match Recap Piedmont led 5-0 at halftime and added another five goals in the second half. Their first goal was scored by Bini in the eighth minute after recovering a loose ball in the Jets’ penalty area, dribbling toward the net before slotting in a shot. Two minutes later, Henry Devan sent a perfect cross to Lorin running into the box, looping a well-placed header into the net. Then in the 15th minute, Bini scored again, this time sending in a laser after a ball fell to him around the top of the penalty area. Lorin made it 4-0 in the 25th minute, recovering a ball in the area to take a shot from close distance. Logan Faucher then made it 5-nil on a slick counter attack, where Niko Markopoulos sent a nice pass to Faucher running free in the box. Bini got his hat trick nine minutes into the second half, this time on a nice assist from Jacob Staff photos Henry Devan sends an assist to Bosco Lorin in the first half against the Jets. Rodriguez. Bini then scored his fourth goal on a shot from outside the box in the 59th. Lorin got his hat trick in the 63rd minute when holding off a defender to retain possession after receiving a ball over the top. Freshman Eli Dao-Hoang scored in the 70th minute when fellow freshman Russell Pan sent a slick low cross off of the end line to Doa-Hoang running at the near post. Sophomore Roman Ahearn scored via a free kick in the final minute of play on a shot about four yards above the penalty area. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-3-4) travels to San Leandro tonight, January 15, at 6:30 p.m. They also host Berkeley on Friday, January 17 and Castro Valley on Tuesday, January 21, both matches start at 7:30 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont tied league rival Berkeley 1-1 on Thursday, January 9 at Witter Field, marking the first clash of the season between the WACC powers. It was a result that left coach Dan Chubbock feeling like they missed out on three points after going into halftime holding a 1-nil lead. “I’m happy with the performance, but we want to be winning these games. We’re at home and I don’t think Berkeley is as strong as they were in the past. We just couldn’t find the net, and I think we had enough to win,” Chubbock said. The Highlanders scored in the 29th minute when midfielder Juliana Thornborrow whipped in a low cross near the end line targeting Elsa Wallway, who made contact to redirect the pass toward the goal in close distance. It officially goes down as an owngoal on Berkeley, but Wallway’s shot was likely going into the net regardless. Berkeley tied the match with 19 minutes left in the game on a wellworked play, where a cross from the right wing set up a shot and rebound opportunity for the score. Despite dropping points, it’s a positive result given that Piedmont is without multiple defenders due to injuries. The injuries to the center back rotation allowed freshman Teah Suhr to step in as a starter. “I normally play a different position, but knowing we have injuries, I try to adjust to how we’re playing. The coaches are helping me play center back again and they’ve made things very easy,” Suhr said. Chubbock is also relying on freshman Ayla Blanford to get quality minutes on the wing, after getting minutes as a fullback in Thursday’s draw. “The injuries have been difficult; I’ve been playing outside back because we also have a lot of injuries there. But it’s been easy to adjust because our team is so nice and the coaches are really helping us,” Blanford said. The tie brings PHS’ record to 3-2-3 (W-T-L). They look ahead Staff Photos Juliana Thornborrow had a strong performance against Berkeley, setting up Piedmont’s first-half goal. Elsa Wallway helped set up Piedmont’s goal against Berkeley, getting on the end of a sharp pass from Juliana Thornborrow.

articles.text: Award-winning flutist, bandleader, and composer Jamie Baum brings her quartet to SFJAZZ for the first time for two evening performances on Friday, January 24. Baum’s quartet will focus on the traditional jazz format of wind instrument with rhythm section and perform music ranging from Baum’s arrangements of both classic and modern jazz tunes. The flutist’s most recent recordings are a blending of South Asian, Near Eastern, and sacred Jewish traditions, with her newest release, What Times Are These, being the fifth with her expanded ensemble. Jamie Baum Baum was born into a musical family and attended the New England Conservatory of Music’s Third Stream program where she learned to master both jazz and classical music. Baum later said she was particularly fond of jazz music and graduated from the jazz department. She then received a master’s degree in jazz composition from the Manhattan School of Music. Baum studied under jazz multi-instrumentalist Jaki Byard at the New England Conservatory of Music, where she began the Yard Byard Project consisting of scores she received from him when she was a student. She founded the Jamie Baum Septet in 1999 with Ralph Alessi, George Colligan, and Jeff Hirshfield and has been an active flutist for over three decades. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/24-25/jamiebaum/ to purchase tickets and for more information.
articles.title: Acclaimed flutist Jamie Baum performs at SFJAZZ Jan. 24

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s production of the hit musical Jesus Christ Superstar opens February 21 and will be performed on stage through March 30. The show features Deanalís Arocho Resto as Jesus and Sydney Jacobs Allen as Judas. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s rock opera recounts the final days of Jesus’ life and chronicles the relationship between him and key biblical figures, including Judas, Mary Magdalene and his disciples. The majority of the plot focuses on Judas, one of Jesus’ twelve apostles who is dissatisfied with the direction in which Jesus is steering his disciples. The musical opened on Broadway in October 1971 and was nominated for five Tony Awards including Best Score, despite opening to mixed reviews. “Jesus Christ Superstar tells the deeply passionate, personal stories of humans trying to love each other, battle their own demons, and falter in the face of their own grappling questions of what is true and right,” said Director Kimberly Dooley. Dooley added that she and the Berkeley Playhouse creative team see this show “as a movement opera, a sort of pulsing ball of energy and passion told through gesture and music.” “As we look into the kaleidoscope of the last seven days of Jesus’ life, we witness the hierarchies of power and politics juxtaposed against the radical love and compassion Christ represents,” she said. “We want to sweep the audience up with us and take them on this powerful visceral journey that explores radical love, the dangers of power, and the power of perspective.” Performances run Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings from February 21 to March 30. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. All performances at Berkeley Playhouse located at 2640 College Ave., Berkeley, CA 94704. Photo by Ben Krantz Studio Sydney Jacobs Allen (Judas) and Deanalís Arocho Resto (Jesus) will perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Jesus Christ Superstar.
articles.title: Jesus Christ Superstar opens at Berkeley Playhouse Feb. 21

articles.text: Join art historian Michael Stehr as he presents an illustrated lecture celebrating the art of Mary Cassatt, whose exhibit is now featured at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco. His illustrated lectured at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will be on Thursday evening, January 16 beginning at 7 p.m. ($20, cash only, at the door). The Impressionist movement of the late 19th century launched notable challenges to the art establishment in France. The bright, luminous renderings of contemporary life were a stark contrast to the highly finessed history paintings of the academic tradition. Not only were the canvases a stark departure from the status quo, but the roster of participants was as well. The Impressionist movement would be the first major revolution in Western Art that would have women playing a major role. One of these women, Mary Cassatt, would be the lone American participating in the movement. While overcoming great social obstacles, Cassatt offers substantial contributions celebrating the lives of women – both their work and their pastimes. While depicting images of work was nothing new, what was ground- breaking was the celebration of the work of women in the home, including child care, bringing a new-found focus to a labor that had previously been undervalued. Cassatt’s commitment to her subject was matched by her dedication to her trade. Bucking the expectations in her day of her class and gender, Cassatt was determined to be a professional artist; this was not a pastime, nor a hobby. Constant throughout her lifetime was her ambition and her devotion to work. Mary Cassatt’s “Mrs. Robert S. Cassatt, the Artist’s Mother” ca. 1889 ®
articles.title: Michael Stehr lecture at PCA on art of Mary Cassatt

articles.text: The largest and most comprehensive exhibition of American portraitist Amy Sherald’s work to date is on display at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) through March. Georgia-born Sherald is wellknown for her portrayal of prominent African American figures as intimate portraits. The exhibition, entitled American Sublime, features nearly 50 paintings made from 2007 to present, including iconic portraits of Breonna Taylor and former first lady Michelle Obama. In 2018, the artist was selected by the first lady to paint her portrait as an official commission for the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. Another highlight of the exhibition is For Love, and for Country (2022), which SFMOMA recently acquired for its permanent collection. “Amy Sherald is one of the most important artists working today and we are honored to present her first mid-career survey at SFMOMA,” Museum Director Christopher Bedford said. “Sherald’s vision deeply resonates with the museum’s goals to share and to champion a more expansive art history in our galleries. Her unique and exquisite renderings of her subjects encourage close looking, curiosity, and awe.” American Sublime is curated by Sarah Roberts, SFMOMA’s Head of Painting and Sculpture. “Sherald has invented an entirely new form of figurative painting. Her approach goes beyond portraiture to enact new conditions for seeing, feeling, and understanding shared humanity,” Roberts said. “In the spirit of great American artists like Edward Hopper, Alice Neel and Kerry James Marshall, Sherald’s works reframe our understanding of American culture.” Roberts added that Sherald’s portraits “invite viewers to recognize and move beyond preconceived ideas and engage in more expansive thinking about race, representation and the wide-open possibilities and complexities of every individual.” The exhibition will be on display through March 9. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/amy-sherald-american-sublime/ to learn more.
articles.title: Amy Sherald exhibit at SFMOMA open until March

articles.text: Preview gala benefiting SFMOMA is Jan. 22 FOG Design and Art Fair will be held at Fort Mason Festival Pavilion in San Francisco from January 23 through 26. The annual fair celebrates current and significant contributors to the worlds of design and visual arts. The 2025 fair brings together 59 exhibitors and 15 galleries participating for the first time this year, including Galerie Maria Wettergren (Paris), Herald St (London), Kiang Malingue (Hong Kong), Lisson Gallery (London), Peter Blum Gallery (New York), SIDE GALLERY (Barcelona), Southern Guild (Los Angeles), and Venus Over Manhattan (New York) in Pier 3, Charles Moffett Gallery (New York), Chris Sharp Gallery (Los Angeles), Fernberger (Los Angeles), François Ghebaly (Los Angeles), House of Seiko (San Francisco), Municipal Bonds (San Francisco), and Superhouse (New York). Sydney Blumenkranz joined the fair as its inaugural director this fall, after leading the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) events team for nearly six years. “FOG Design and Art has always been about celebrating our creative community and fostering connections within the art and design world,” Blumenkranz said. “I am honored to take on this role and look forward to finding new and impactful ways to push the fair in new directions, and to find more opportunities for engagement with the arts community regionally and around the world.” A special preview gala benefiting the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will be held Wednesday, January 22. The preview gala provides support to SF MOMA’s exhibitions and education programs, which serves over 89,000 students, teachers, and families with online and in-person resources, programs, and visits each year. Food and beverages will be served and preview gala guests gain exclusive early access to the fair’s vast range of design objects, furniture, and fine art before it opens to the public the next day. The fair is open at Fort Mason from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Thursday through Saturday, and from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sunday, January 26. 2023 display at FOG Design and Art Fair at Fort Mason

Green Bay Packers football coach Vince Lombardi Murray. He didn’t write so much about sports as he saw it. The fact is, he had terrible eyesight. Murray commented on sports more from a philosophical standpoint. His criticism could be biting but it was written in such a way that no one was offended. Modern society has much to learn from people like Jim Murray. Paganini comes next. His accomplishments in music are legendary. He is often considered the greatest violinist of all time. But he was much more than that. He was the prototype for every entertainer who came after him. Without Paganini there would have been no Frank Sinatra, no Elvis, no Beatles, no Mohamed Ali. Paganini invented publicity. I would also include Enrico Caruso, perhaps the greatest tenor of all time. He also had a great work ethic and was a great colleague. Did you know that he was a composer and a famous artist? Jascha Heifetz is in contention as the greatest violinist of all time. Sadly, he is one of the most misunderstood and maligned performers of all time. He was accused of cold and mechanical perfection. This is simply not true. His 100% sincerity was misunderstood as coldness. His mantra was to give his very best at all times or die in the attempt. No performances were identical. He always observed the reactions of the audience. If he felt he was losing the attention of an audience, he felt he had to do something out of the ordinary. articles.text: Thursday, January 16, 7:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture Join art historian Michael Stehr as he discusses the importance of the current show at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, entitled Mary Cassatt at Work. Too often dismissed as a sentimental painter of mothers and children, Mary Cassatt (1844– 1926) was in fact a modernist pioneer. Her paintings, pastels, and prints are characterized by restless experimentation and change. Cassatt was the only American to join the French Impressionists, first exhibiting with the group at Degas’ invitation in 1879, and quickly emerged as a key member of the movement. The illustrated lecture will last approximately one hour; please pay $20 per person, cash only, at the door. Note that the Legion of Honor exhibit will close on January 26, 2025. He didn’t write so much about sports as he saw it. The fact is, he had terrible eyesight. Murray commented on sports more from a philosophical standpoint. His criticism could be biting but it was written in such a way that no one was offended. Modern society has much to learn from people like Jim Murray. Paganini comes next. His accomplishments in music are legendary. He is often considered the greatest violinist of all time. But he was much more than that. He was the prototype for every entertainer who came after him. Without Paganini there would have been no Frank Sinatra, no Elvis, no Beatles, no Mohamed Ali. Paganini invented publicity. I would also include Enrico Caruso, perhaps the greatest tenor of all time. He also had a great work ethic and was a great colleague. Did you know that he was a composer and a famous artist? Jascha Heifetz is in contention as the greatest violinist of all time. articles.text: It’s become a genre unto itself: coming of age films that focus not on adolescents, but on those twenty-something boy-men who are grappling with and resisting the prospect of actually having to grow up. As if adulthood, and all it represents – responsibility, commitment, employment – should be, if not avoided, at least postponed. How long is never made clear. Adventureland is the antidote. It’s not a shallow knockoff, and it easily could have been. Set in a tacky amusement park, in 1987, spanning one summer, it might have wallowed in gratuitous, comedy-porn dialogue, seasoned with nonsensical slapstick. It doesn’t. It reaches for more. True, the film focuses on young people. But it does so with insight and sensitivity. It’s well written and wonderfully acted with a solid ensemble, each getting it just right. The setup finds one James Brennan (Jessie Eisenberg), just graduated from college, hoping to spend the summer in Europe, followed by grad school at Colombia in the fall. His plans are derailed when the family hits a financial rough patch. Instead of Europe, he ends up working at Adventureland, running one of the many game booths On his first day as a carney, James meets Em (Kristen Stewart), a student at NYU, attractive, enigmatic and seemingly out of Jesse Eisenberg and Kristen Stewart in Adventureland reach. With the introduction of Em, the film shifts focus, giving her equal time, and thus creating a much stronger and far more interesting movie from the standard guy-centric fare. From the first moment James and Em meet, it is clear that he is drawn to her. But this isn’t simply a courtship film wherein the guy pursues and then reports back to his buds, giving them way too much information. To its credit, Adventureland involves more than one focus allowing a number of characters to emerge, but never as caricatures. Each is interesting, and each has a story. Kristen Steward is a remarkable actress, recognizable from her early work in Twilight. She infuses Em with subtlety and nuance and all but steals the film from Jesse Eisenberg, so strong is her performance. Adventureland is a sweet film, satisfying and entertaining to the end. And don’t be mislead by the title. This is an adventure to be sure, but one of the heart. Adventureland. Written and directed by Greg Mottola. Starring Jesse Eisenberg, Kristen Stewart, Martin Starr, Kristen Wiig and Ryan Reynolds. 1 hr., 46 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Streaming on Fandango/Roku/ prime. She went on to run a milt-million dollar empire of high stakes poker for close to a decade, drawing some of the richest and powerful players worldwide until she is arrested in the middle of the night Using seamless flashbacks Molly’s gripping story unfolds, involving scene after compelling scene in which she ultimately realizes that she must hire a toptier attorney. She finds Charlie Jaffey (Idris Elba). At first reluctant, then puzzled, he attempts to understand why Molly is unwilling to act in her own best interest regarding the federal charges that would likely result in her incarceration. I found this film compelling and complex, with exceptional performances by Chastain, Elba, and Costner.. However, as I reflected on its narrative structure (I watched the movie several times), and it wasn’t until the concluding scenes between Molly and her father, as well as a monologue delivered by Jaffey, directed at two government attorneys, that I understood what made this movie so remarkable. articles.text: Films such as The Karate Kid are unabashedly morality plays wherein the field of play is the context of choice. sports are so ideally suited to this predictable yet compelling narrative: adversity is confronted and overcome, the athlete prevails. The came cuts to scenes of cheers, raised arms, and gets ready for a warm glow. The wildly popular 80s martial arts classic of the same name, starring Pat Morita and Ralph Macchio, was set in Los Angeles. The more recent incarnation, released in 2010, takes place, interestingly enough, in Beijing and the sport is not karate but kung fu. Actually, it’s wushu, a more aggressive form of kung fu, involving punching and hard body contact. The template is familiar and the changes regarding geography and culture, when it comes to the core story, superficial. A young kid, Dre (Jaden Smith), from the streets of Detroit, arrives in China with his single mom, Sherry (Taraji P. Henson), who has a job with a car company. Dre is the new kid on the unfamiliar block and soon becomes the target of some local school bullies who are schooled by a cruel sensei in the art of kung fu. Dre’s life quickly becomes intolerable until he is rescued, literally, by the unassuming Mr. Han (Jackie Chan), the apartment building maintenance man, generally laconic, and yet deeply schooled in the martial arts, which he quickly makes obvious when Dre is attacked. Of course, there is a tween love interest, Mei Ying (Wen Wen Han), a gifted violinist, who befriends Dre. And so Dre’s training begins, including the familiar wax on, wax off, only involving a jacket. Jacket on, hang up, jacket off. Rinse and repeat. Dre is undisciplined and angry, wants to go home, and feels like a stranger in a strange land. He is, nevertheless, quietly and firmly instructed in the lessons of Kung Fu and, of course, in the lessons of life, all leading to the familiar climactic match where he meets his nemesis, Cheng, on the mat. The ending is foregone, the building tide of good feelings and anticipation are finalized with Dre performing a slo-mo kicking somersault that is the money moment in the film. As for Jaden Smith as Dre, well, he’s the son of Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith, the film’s producers. His debut role was with his father in The Pursuit of Happyness, a movie filmed in part in Piedmont. It must be nice to have a mom and dad who can gift wrap a movie and let you carry it on your pre-teen shoulders. Of course, Jackie Chan’s crew helped with Jaden’s intense training. Tweens will love the story, for them fresh and interesting as well as a nice introduction to China. To the filmmakers’ credit, the neighborhoods of Beijing are not scrubbed, but nicely frayed and crowded giving a solid sense of the bustling and crowded Beijing. It feels like the real deal. And so, once again, does the movie. The Karate Kid. Directed by Harald Zwart. Starring Jaden Smith, Jackie Chan, Taraji P. Henson, Wang Zhenwei and Wen wen Han. 2 hrs., 20 min. Rated PG. Released 2010. Streaming on prime/Fandango/apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Astro Boy (the movie) The character Astro Boy was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books) and animé (movie and television animation), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries, and finally Astro Boy debuted, a much anticipated feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh, and they will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. Initially, the story explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment, conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy (soon to be called Astro) superhuman. He can fly, has machine guns in his butt, x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. Astro, at first unaware he’s a robot, sets out to find his place in the world, meaning, Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City, all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. And so the story goes. articles.text: A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Dear Abby: I ran into a cute Pomeranian named Shortbread the other day at Pet Food Ex and as I said hello and pet her, I noticed severe bald spots on her back. I asked her owner what they were and he said she had developed alopecia and had it for over a year. He said the only thing their Vet had said was to add a specific Fish Oil to her food. Afterwards, I wondered if it was infectious and if I could give it to my dog simply from petting that cutie Shortbread? Don’t worry. I washed my hands for two hours before touching Frank. –Jo and Frank the Tank Dear Jo and Frank the Tank, Alopecia, or hair loss, can occur with dogs due to a number of possible reasons: 1. Allergies: Dogs can be allergic to food, dust mites, mold, pollen, or other environmental factors. 2. Skin infections: Fungal infections like ringworm or yeast infections can cause hair loss. 3. Parasites: Fleas or mange mites can cause alopecia. 4. Diet: A lack of protein in a dog’s diet can lead to contracting alopecia. 5. Genetics: Some types of alopecia, like follicular dysplasia, are primarily genetic. 6. Hypothyroidism: This is the most common cause of non-inflammatory alopecia that appears symmetrically on a dog’s body. So yes, alopecia can be infectious but it’s unlikely. Often it develops from something in the dog’s makeup, an allergy or sensitivity to a particular food but be careful if you run into a dog that has it…I’m glad you washed your hands for two hours before petting Frank.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group tries to walk every Piedmont street each year, but in 2024 they didn’t get to the upper portion of Grand Avenue between Kingston and Greenbank Avenues. This roadway is well traveled by car, but not by foot, and the walkers know to really see a street you need to walk it. A large turnout of 56 walkers and three K-9 best friends were at the Exedra ready to go. The walkers went on Latham Street, the only Piedmont roadway named a “street.” There are only three houses on this oneblock street. They are long and narrow, built in 1960 and 1961 on right-of-way land that became available when the Key System C Line commuter trains to San Francisco were discontinued in 1958. The group went down Cambridge Way and over to Holly Place and its two houses, then to Lower Grand Avenue. The homes in this neighborhood were all built in the 1910s and 1920s. The group went up Lower Grand, came out on Arroyo Avenue, and went up to busy Pleasant Valley Road/Grand Avenue. A group photo was taken, and some roadway history was shared. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road, which described the area well. It ran from Lake Merritt to the Piedmont hills. Today, the roadway in Piedmont is Grand Avenue until it crosses the Oakland city line where it goes back to being Pleasant Valley again. The group crossed the street at the stop light and made their way, three quarters of a mile, down Grand to the Piedmont/Oakland city line at Wildwood Avenue. On the way, they noted homes that were also built in the 1910s and 1920s, but were impressed by a new house with an ADU at its base that was completed around 2020. It was built on a lot that was long thought to be unbuildable. The group liked its modern design and construction. It is a large home, built with lots of concrete, up a steep incline. Architect Jim Kellogg said with all the concrete in its base it has nothing to worry about in an earthquake. The house is new, different, and beautiful. Jim liked it and so did the rest of the group. The walkers stopped at Grand and Linda Avenues where in 1892 there was a restaurant named “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle). It was built by Axel R. Gruggel. Over time, it had a number of owners and a trouble history with the City and police because of owner and patron behaviors which included no liquor licenses and gambling. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company and in 1922 the Del Monte Market. In the 1930’s Piggly Wiggly, as a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store up the street at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand. It was stiff competition. The Del Monte Market floundered and closed, and the A Mon Chateau building was torn down. A series of gas stations later occupied the site. Finally, in 1987 the current, block-long Piedmont Financial Center was built there. Further down the street, some longtime Piedmonters remembered the site as a not-very-successful “Big T” grocery store, which eventually became today’s Ace Hardware, and a nearby hamburger restaurant. The group crossed Grand and noted that nothing much has been done to the former Shell gas station site since their visit last month. Someday it will be a Shell Recharge station. On the other side of Grand they could see an Oakland City Limits sign that confirmed they had walked the entire Piedmont length of Grand Ave. The walk had taken a little longer than usual, and it was time to climb back to the Exedra via Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers gather for a photo on Grand Avenue on January 8. articles.text: It was a sunny afternoon on January 6th when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their first discussion of 2025. There was a big turnout of 24 readers The group was there to talk about A Farewell to Arms, a novel by American writer Ernest Hemingway, that was first published in 1929. The story is set during the Italian campaign of World War I and is a first-person account of Lieutenant Frederic Henry, an American serving as a volunteer lieutenant in the Italian army ambulance corps. The novel tells the story of Henry’s love affair with an English nurse, Catherine Barkley, and is divided into five sections, or “books,” that are narrated by Henry. A Farewell to Arms is considered an American classic and it established Hemingway as one of the greatest modern American writers. The book was his first best-seller and has been called the premier American war novel from World War I. The story has been adapted several times, initially for the stage in 1930, as films in 1932 and 1957, and as a three-part television miniseries in 1966. It had been a long time since many of the readers had read the book. For most it was in high school, and there were differing opinions about how well the book has held up over the decades. Hemingway was a great writer without question. He described situations in detail, but still allowed readers to create their own images in their minds. This ability to be descriptive but evocative at the same time, was recognized by the group to be a gift. Hemingway’s style was also innovative and broke the writing rules of his time. It worked then and continues to work now. As a child Hemingway loved Bach and classical music, and the melody of his prose – short sentences, and repetition – created a lyrical beat that engaged the readers. The group felt the book is a classic because it has great weight and importance in many ways. It is a love story set in a time of war. It also presented a view of life in a challenging time. While the readers didn’t contest Hemingway being a great writer, there were some members of the group who didn’t care for the book. It just didn’t play well for them today. It was shared that Hemingway wrote 47 different endings with 40 different chapter titles for the book. Many readers liked the ending Hemingway used, but others felt it was completely predictable and disappointing. Even more disappointing for some was the portrayal of Catherine Barkley’s adoring love for Henry. Her constant acceptance of anything associated with her “darling” was just too much for these readers. It was recognized that the book may be a period piece, but the dialogue still tired them. Some readers thought the book could be written and accepted today as a classic, but others didn’t. After the discussion was completed, it was noted that concern had been previously expressed that the group has grown so large and that having more participants might not allow everyone to share their thoughts. However, the 24 participants said that this was not the case in this discussion. They enjoyed the range of opinions and felt they were able to participate as they desired. The readers also agreed that A Farewell to Arms by Ernest Hemingway it is good for the group to read classics, like A Farewell to Arms, along with the contemporary fiction and non-fiction titles they usually select. This is a good mix that the readers enjoy and it expands their literary horizons. Future books The group had previously selected Endurance by Alfred Lansing for their February book and James by Percival Everett for March. After Dick Carter’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates, the group selected Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz for their April book. With all their business done, the group went outside the Community Hall for a group picture in the sunshine. The group’s next discussion will be on February 3rd at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. There is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 15, 2025 23 AMERICANS IN PARIS The Passion of Eugène Delacroix By Patricia Forsyth Privously printed in the Piedmont Post on March 2, 2022 The wood-frame home and studio of the painter Eugène Delacroix was purchased for preservation a century ago by the Foundation of the Delacroix Museum, and it remains a humble attraction at Place Fürstenberg on the Left Bank. The studio is a separate building behind the simply constructed, spare four-room residence, where the artist lived and worked on his final project – decorating the walls and ceilings of the nearby Church of SaintSulpice. This small museum’s collection consists of prints, writings, memorabilia, and minor oil paintings, takes about an hour to tour. But it’s not murals that Delacroix is remembered for, but the exhilarating, bold canvases he created as a young artist in his twenties and thirties. He was influenced by the great Théodore Gericault who painted Raft of the Medusa (1819). Gericault, only seven years his senior, was part of the Paris art commune; and Delacroix while still in art school posed as one of the corpses sliding off the raft. Delacroix is known for three massive paintings hanging in the Louvre, particularly Liberty Leading the People, the most often reproduced painting in French art. He submitted his first painting to the Paris Salon when studying at École Beaux-Arts. The Barque of Dante, a scene from Dante’s Inferno, shows demons attacking the boat as the Roman poet Virgil leads Dante across the River Styx into Hell. It created quite a stir; he was just 24 years-old and an art school nobody. The painting seemed startlingly intense to some but was generally received as a welcome departure from the staid Neo-Classicism works in vogue. The poet and art critic Charles Baudelaire referred to Delacroix as “passionately in love with passion.” Delacroix was a serious student of painting, and a devotee of the 16th-17th C. masters, particularly Rubens and Titian. He dutifully copied their canvases as part of his student work at the Louvre. His style was notably derived from the Baroque style of Peter Paul Rubens. Romanticism had nothing to do with romance in the modern sense; but artists Musée Delacroix preserves the atelier and home at 6 Rue de Fürstenberg, 6th arr. sought to convey human struggles in desperate situations to evoke powerful reactions. Romanticism valued emotion over logic, and the individual over the collective. Delacroix painted what moved him, taking his themes from religion, literature, history, and societal injustice. By age 40, he had emerged as the leader of Romanticism, though he wasn’t fond of that or any other label. The artist worked alone in his various studios and died “without heir or pupil.” His works were sold off and scattered around the world. It is fortunate that the Louvre purchased Delacroix’s greatest paintings available for viewing in the permanent collection. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris as tourists in The City of Light. Comments to pkf.empower@ gmail.com. Galerie d’Apollon, ceiling murals by Delacroix. Louvre Musical Gourmet Continued from page 16 of yesteryear. Violinists of today actually exceed the perfection of Jascha Heifetz. I’ll tell you a little secret; if you listen to some of his recordings, there are places where he really messes up. But he actually wanted those to be included on his recordings. He was human. He had great integrity and sincerity, something I can personally confirm. Today’s players remind me of automatons. They are perfect today, yesterday and ditto tomorrow. Every performance is exactly the same. In the headlong quest for uniform perfection, however, they have lost their humanity. They make up for it with uniformity. Instead of looking within to their souls. We often read in the major newspapers that the musical performer “attacked the instrument”. Attacking the instrument is real big these days. So is “tearing into the instrument”. Loud is good, louder is better, some say. I am reminded of one of the great violinists of the past, Mischa Elman. When he was praised for his powerful tone, Elman always replied the same way: “the violin is not a trumpet. You say I have a big tone. That is only half the story. The other half is that I can play softer than anybody else.” It is that contrast which made Elman so marvelous. How important is nuance to art these days? Unique personalities and national differences made the old performers individual and unique. I much prefer that to the uniformity and predictability of today’s performers. Perfection they have. That is marvelous in its way. But the cost in humanity is lamentable. And so it goes in the world of music. Democracy is not a spectator sport! With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park n the sside of Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook. In our five miles of hiking, we passed just 27 hikers. Another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the China Wall. To access this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook on their GPS devices for common starting areas. Remember to return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and for a hike to Donner Peak. A long tunnel through the mountains is part of a second China Wall above Lake Donner. When the fire department provides staff for mutual aid, the City is reimbursed for costs by the state. Piedmont’s current crew in Los Angeles will be replaced by a fresh crew on Thursday, January 16. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board reorganized its leadership positions on Tuesday, December 17, resulting in the election of Lindsay Thomasson as its new President through December 2025. Ruchi Medhekar will be the new Vice President. Newly elected board members Max Roman, Michael Malione and Susy Struble were also sworn into office replacing Cory Ruchi Medhekar is now the Vice President for the school board. Lindsay Thomasson is the new Piedmont School President Smegal who termed out, and Hilary Cooper and Veronica Anderson Thigpen who did not seek reelection. Thomasson and Medhekar were elected to the school board two years ago. Thomasson has experience running meetings in-person on dates when former President Anderson Thigpen participated remotely. The newly formed board will hold its first meeting tonight, January 8, in City Hall at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Last week the Post covered events that occurred in or that were relevant to Piedmont schools from January through May 2024. The chronology stopped for the summer break. It was also a time that coincided with the end of teacher salary negotiations. Education in Piedmont spans all ages, from preschool to adult school, and its importance cannot be overstated. The following is the second half of the chronology which aims to recount “how we got here,” and should orient the reader to be all caught up for the new year. Today, Wednesday, January 8, 2025, marks the first day back at school after the winter break for Piedmont teachers, students, administrators, and CSEA classified staff, and a new chapter, entitled 2025 begins. JUNE June 1: The Wildwood Dads Club’s softball team, the Wild Things, won the annual Buzz Redford, Tri-School Softball Tournament. June 12: Piedmont’s school board officially ratified new teacher contracts at the school board meeting, which run through the 2025-26 school year. June 12: Piedmont’s Title IX Task Force announced that Piedmont High School had an equal number of boys and girls playing on sports teams. This metric of equity represented the countless hours of hard work put in by parents, board members and student-athletes advocating for girls in sports. June 26: An increase in enrollment of approximately 100 students for the 2024-25 year was projected in a school board meeting. The upward change in the enrollment trajectory bucked the trend of declining enrollment seen recent years. AUGUST August 8: PMS teachers Ted Scherman and Tim Wisniewski hosted the, always popular, 6th Grade Boot Camp to help students find their way on the new campus. August 9: Original deadline for school board candidates to fill three soon-to-be vacant seats on the board. Date was extended after eligible incumbents chose not to run again. August 12: Witter Field’s track is completed, signaling the end of the construction project that was supposed to finish nine months prior. August 12: First day of school. Piedmont schools welcomes new administrators: PHS Principal David Yoshihara, PHS Athletic Director Tyler Small, Director of Special Education Jean Fagin and Jamie Van Kleeck is promoted to PMS Assistant Principal. August 14: Four school board candidates submitted papers to run in November elections. Michael Malione, Susy Struble, and Max Roman were on the ballot for three seats with Victoria Rosenbaum. Soon after, Rosenbaum endorsed the other three and unofficially withdrew her candidacy. This metric of equity represented the countless hours of hard work put in by parents, board members and student-athletes advocating for girls in sports. June 26: An increase in enrollment of approximately 100 students for the 2024-25 year was projected in a school board meeting. The upward change in the enrollment trajectory bucked the trend of declining enrollment seen recent years. AUGUST August 8: PMS teachers Ted Scherman and Tim Wisniewski hosted the, always popular, 6th Grade Boot Camp to help students find their way on the new campus. August 9: Original deadline for school board candidates to fill three soon-to-be vacant seats on the board. Date was extended after eligible incumbents chose not to run again. August 12: Witter Field’s track is completed, signaling the end of the construction project that was supposed to finish nine months prior. August 12: First day of school. Piedmont schools welcomes new administrators: PHS Principal David Yoshihara, PHS Athletic Director Tyler Small, Director of Special Education Jean Fagin and Jamie Van Kleeck is promoted to PMS Assistant Principal. August 14: Four school board candidates submitted papers to run in November elections. Michael Malione, Susy Struble, and Max Roman were on the ballot for three seats with Victoria Rosenbaum. Soon after, Rosenbaum endorsed the other three and unofficially withdrew her candidacy. articles.text: Gardens for a Changing Planet discussion on Jan. 15 Piedmont Garden Club welcomes the community to attend a discussion by Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden, on “Gardens for a Changing Planet: Towards a 21st Century Botanic Garden”. He will be the guest speaker on January 15 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Botanic gardens are more than just beautiful public parks. They play important roles in plant science and conservation. Novy, an internationally recognized leader in the horticultural world, will show how botanic gardens are adapting as the climate changes, He will share how these important green spaces are the sites of research into medicinal, native, and food and agricultural plants. In addition to his role at the Garden, Novy is an active researcher, holding an appointment as Adjunct Associate Professor at Salk Institute for Biological Studies. He is the founding co-chair of the Food and Agriculture Professional Section of the American Public Gardens Association and has served on task forces and advisory panels for diverse groups including the White House Council on Environmental Quality, the Cornell Alliance for Science, Botanic Garden Conservation International, Rock Creek National Park, the Garden Club of America, the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization, and many others. In 2024, he became an honorary Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden member of the Garden Club of America. Piedmont Garden Club was founded in 1923 and has been a part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. articles.text: At-risk Pittie mix Potpie is hoping the new year will bring him a new home. Oakland Animal Services staff say this big boy of 70 pounds is a true softie. He’s a playful, affectionate dog who loves to wiggle and bounce around with excitement and show off his silly side. While 4-year-old Potpie has had minimal training, he’s eager to please and is motivated by treats, making him an excellent candidate for positive reinforcement training. He knows the all-important sit command, takes treats gently, and is working on leash manners. He would get on with a dog who matches his gentle play style, or as your one and only pooch. Potpie would be an affectionate companion and happily sit by your side for some love. Come meet Potpie at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12-7 p.m., or Meet Potpie, an at-risk Pittie mix. this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Potpie must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites community members to an Open House this Sunday, January 12, at 3:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Ave. This free event is an opportunity to meet local League leaders and members, learn about the organization’s projects and programs, and discover ways to get involved in fostering informed and active participation in democracy. The Open House will feature: • Networking: Connect with like-minded individuals committed to making a difference. • Program Plans for 2025: Learn about the League’s advocacy efforts, voter education programs, and community engagement activities. • Volunteer Opportunities: Explore how you can contribute to voter empowerment and civic education. Light refreshments will be served. This family-friendly event welcomes individuals of all ages who are passionate about civic engagement and strengthening democracy at the local level. “We’re excited to open our doors and engage with the community,” said Anita Stapen of the LWV Program Committee. “This event is a chance for us to celebrate the power of collective action and inspire more people to join us in our mission to create a stronger, more inclusive democracy.” The League of Women Voters, a nonpartisan organization, has been a vital part of the Piedmont community, working to empower voters and advocate for effective public policies for over a century. The Open House will highlight the importance of local engagement in addressing today’s pressing issues. RSVPs are encouraged but not required. For more information, please visit https://www.lwvpiedmont.org or contact Lisa Gardner via email Lgardner555@gmail. com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Tyler Kintz, Construction Superintendent, examines plans at the Dispatch Center construction site. Piedmont city staff gave an informational update at the City Council meeting on Monday, January 6, with updates for the ongoing construction of Piedmont’s 9-1-1 emergency dispatch center. The presentation was given by Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales and Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, According to their report the project has encountered no significant delays and its budget remains on track. Building security and services have been maintained despite a 75% reduction in floor space during the construction process. The project, which started in June 2024, will relocate the dispatch center into the space that formerly served jointly as the City’s Emergency Operations Center and the Police Department’s conference and interview room. Dispatch functions as the nerve center for the Piedmont community’s access to public safety services, fielding over 13,000 calls annually for the Police and Fire Departments. According to the City, the former space was severely undersized, unable to accommodate modern technologies, and located in an area that has not been seismically retrofitted. Additionally, the project includes infrastructure upgrades that benefit the entire Police Department, including an independent electrical system with a backup generator that can provide power for the entire building. Since the construction began last June, concrete has been poured throughout the interior, and for the patio space. Council member Tom Ramsey applauded the construction efforts at the meeting. “If you walk through that small space, you notice there is structural steel, there’s concrete, there’s shock-crete, there’s wood, there’s metal framing, there’s wood framing… that just speaks to the complexity, not only of the systems that are going into, but of the space that [they] are working in.” Contractors aim to complete the installation of structural steel beams by the end of January. Installation of electrical equipment, including the generator, is expected to begin when the equipment arrives in February. Interior architectural work is scheduled to start in March, with the dispatch center being fully operational by June 2025. The workload for the Dispatch staff has increased significantly over the last decade and will continue with the implementation of Next Generation 9-1-1 capabilities. Concurrent with the physical space improvements, the City recently augmented dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978. Two new dispatcher positions were added in the last year, a staffing increase made possible by the March 2024 passage of Measure F. Renovation of the 9-1-1 dispatch center was identified by the City Council as the best use for American Rescue Plan Act funding in October 2021. Design work for the relocated dispatch center began in 2022, and the City Council awarded a $1.8 million construction contract for the project in March of 2023. The project is now roughly 50% complete according to the report by City Staff. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers also mentioned wanting to share the upgrades and new services of the dispatch center with community members. “We definitely want to have an opportunity for the public, before we’re fully operational in June, to allow the public to see it as well,” said Bowers. “We really want our community to see the investment that they made in this project.” Tyler Kintz shows the interior of the in-progress dispatch center. A trench was dug as part of construction to lay the groundwork for electrical equipment.
articles.title: Dispatch Center is on-budget and on-time

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department introduced a new department member and honored the promotion of a long-time staff member at the City Council meeting on Monday, January 6. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers welcomed the new Support Services Commander Brandi Marin-Morris at the meeting, as well as recognizing Mercedes Bolds for her promotion to Dispatch Supervisor. Marin-Morris was hired after a lengthy interview process to fill the role of Support Services Commander Lisa Douglas after her retirement, which was announced through social media in December last month. As Support Services Commander, Marin-Morris will oversee daily operations of support functions in the department, including Records, Communications, Property and Management, and working with the City’s Communications Director on social media posts and information. “Support Services Commander is one of the most essential and critical positions in our organization… It’s absolutely essential,” said Bowers. Marin-Morris joined Piedmont Police from Cal Poly San Luis Obispo Police Department where she had worked since 2007. Marin-Morris eventually became the lead in San Luis Obispo’s dispatch and records divisions. Marin-Morris was joined at the ceremony by her children Brooklyn and Eli, her husband Josh, and her father Mike. “I’ve only been in Piedmont for a couple of months, but it’s been wonderful,” said Marin-Morris at the meeting. “I feel very welcomed and supported, and I am very grateful to be here and be a part of this community.” Next to be honored at the meeting was Dispatch Supervisor Mercedes Bolds. Bolds first joined the Piedmont Police Department as a parking enforcement officer in 2008. She was later appointed as a part-time dispatcher in 2009. Her work continued in Piedmont until 2012 when she earned a full-time dispatch position with the City of Emeryville. In 2014, when Piedmont was able to offer her a full-time dispatch position, Bolds came back home and rejoined the PPD. Support Services Commander Brandi Marin-Morris was honored with a badge, pinned on by her father, Mike. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers (left) speaks about Mercedes Bolds (right) and her qualifications as she is promoted to Dispatch Supervisor. Dispatch Supervisor Mercedes Bolds receives her badge, pinned on by her daughters Kylie and Aubrey.
articles.title: Piedmont Police introduce new commander, promote new dispatch supervisor

Marin-Morris was hired after a lengthy interview process to fill the role of Support Services Commander Lisa Douglas after her retirement, which was announced through social media in December last month. As Support Services Commander, Marin-Morris will oversee daily operations of support functions in the department, including Records, Communications, Property and Management, and working with the City’s Communications Director on social media posts and information. “Support Services Commander is one of the most essential and critical positions in our organization… It’s absolutely essential,” said Bowers. Marin-Morris joined Piedmont Police from Cal Poly San Luis Obispo Police Department where she had worked since 2007. Marin-Morris eventually became the lead in San Luis Obispo’s dispatch and records divisions. Marin-Morris was joined at the ceremony by her children Brooklyn and Eli, her husband Josh, and her father Mike. “I’ve only been in Piedmont for a couple of months, but it’s been wonderful,” said Marin-Morris at the meeting. “I feel very welcomed and supported, and I am very grateful to be here and be a part of this community.” Next to be honored at the meeting was Dispatch Supervisor Mercedes Bolds. Bolds first joined the Piedmont Police Department as a parking enforcement officer in 2008. She was later appointed as a part-time dispatcher in 2009. Her work continued in Piedmont until 2012 when she earned a full-time dispatch position with the City of Emeryville. In 2014, when Piedmont was able to offer her a full-time dispatch position, Bolds came back home and rejoined the PPD. See Police Promotions on page 27 Support Services Commander Brandi Marin-Morris was honored with a badge, pinned on by her father, Mike. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers (left) speaks about Mercedes Bolds (right) and her qualifications as she is promoted to Dispatch Supervisor. Dispatch Supervisor Mercedes Bolds receives her badge, pinned on by her daughters Kylie and Aubrey.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont’s Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee will host the 28th annual Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 20, at the Alan Harvey Theater at 11:00 a.m. The theme of this year’s celebration is “Separate is Never Equal: Fight Injustice.” It comes from a speech that Dr. King gave in 1966, when he called on people to never feel comfortable with any form of segregation, tyranny, or supremacy. “I never intend to adjust myself to segregation and discrimination,” King said. “I never intend to become adjusted to religious bigotry. I never intend to adjust myself to economic conditions that will take necessities from the many to give luxuries to the few.” This year’s event, incidentally, will take place on the same day as the presidential inauguration. The program will feature keynote speaker Ericka Huggins, an educator, leading Black Panther Party member, former political prisoner, human rights advocate, and poet. For more on Huggins visit Erickahuggins.com The celebration will also include performances by the Oakland Youth Chamber Chorus and Destiny Arts Junior Dance Company. Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust will offer a land acknowledgement. Admission is free. Tickets can be reserved at: Events.humanitix. com/28th-annual-dr-martin-luther-king-jr-celebration

articles.text: A quick note of advice: undersell your aspirations As soon as that dreaded clock ticks into place, people scramble to write down their resolutions as if their life depends on their ability to best predict the goals they won’t follow through with. It’s a running joke throughout lifestyle magazines and the New York Times that New Year resolutions are rarely reached as a universal truth. So, what’s the point of “writing resolutions” as an official way to celebrate the New Year? For me, New Years represents a fresh start – the opportunity to become a better version of the person I’ve become over the past twelve months. I believe we put too much pressure on ourselves to accomplish unreasonable goals leading only to the guilt that we reap from not following through on our promises to ourselves. This creates an invisible barrier that if we don’t completely overhaul our lives, we’re complete failures. There’s a reason why only about 25 percent of people stick with their resolutions after just 30 days, and only nine percent who stay with their goals throughout the year. According to the Pew Research Centre, around 79% of resolution makers have one resolution centered on diet or health, often long-term goals. People are so afraid of even attempting to tackle overly ambitious goals that they become frustrated and ultimately give up on their long-term aims. So, what’s the alternative? Everyone is ready to create meaningful change in their life, to turn over a new leaf and feel the beauty of a fresh start. If you’re one of the nine per cent who feels they can stick to a resolution, that’s great. That works for you, and you’re creating change that helps you become a better version of yourself. Unfortunately for a large majority of people, sticking to your resolution is too overwhelming. Even if you’re adamant about writing out your resolutions, let me offer a quick note of advice: undersell your aspirations. Scale back, look at your goals and ask, ‘Is this honestly, truly achievable by me?’. Even better, ditch the resolutions entirely. What I propose: quarterly goals. Small, achievable steps you can take every quarter, every three months. You’ll find that by cutting down the time span, you can also reflect on your goals at the end of each period and see what worked and what didn’t It might allow you to create more attainable or ambitious goals for the next quarters. This forces you to choose a smaller timeframe, allowing for smaller, more manageable goals. You can even go smaller monthly resolutions, or even weekly. Consistency is, as it often is, key to maintaining a path that is both possible and rewarding. With this article, I hope to shed some light on reality. While often cruel it can be a way to find more fulfilling ways of accomplishing your goals. By setting your goals and reaching higher aspirations for the next quarter. Whatever you choose to do, I wish you all the best of success and hope that you can achieve those goals this year. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen who got really frustrated she didn’t manage to reach her resolutions last year.
articles.title: A look at the failure of New Year resolutions

articles.text: The Havens Parents Club is hosting its annual poker tournament with a theme of “All In for the Kids.” It will be held in the Veterans Hall this Friday, January 10, beginning at 6:00 p.m. This is the 17th year of turning the hall into a Las Vegas poker hall for an evening until a winner is crowned at the end of the night. Food at the tournament will include passed hors-d’oeuvres from Chef Robert Dorsey, pizza from Arthur Mac’s, and an impressive open snack bar. Cocktails, beer, and wine will also be available at the bar and will provide a colorful barroom atmosphere. As of publishing time, tickets were still available at: Eventbrite. com/e/17th-annual-havens-poker-night-all-in-for-the-kids-tickets-1077652951989 Buy-in to the Texas Hold-em tournament costs $173.80, and a bottomless pint option is available for $60 online and at the door. For a little over $200 tournament players can enjoy both. As always, players can stay in the game with a re-buy-in option, to get more chips and continue to support the schools by slow playing aces, bluffing with nothing, and being saved on the river. All funds support Havens Elementary School. In prior years the event has raised in excess of $50,000 for the school. The 2024 event finished with Havens dad Jeff Hoffman defeating Melissa Clark in the final hand with two pair, Queens over Twos. Act now to get into the field of 150 players, before the first hand is dealt at 6:30 p.m. Join the fun evening which ends about 11:00 p.m. The poker tournament takes place at 401 Highland Avenue.
articles.title: Last chance to get tickets for Havens Poker Night on Friday

articles.text: Highlanders enter January with a 10-1 record Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its great start to the season, improving its record to 10-1, They recently beat Clayton Valley Charter 61-52 in overtime at the Sabrina Ionescu 20 Showcase at Carondelet in Concord on Friday, January 3. They also won three of four games at the San Diego Holiday Classic tournament at Torrey Pines HS from December 26-30. In tournament, results they opened with a 72-26 win over Canyon of Anaheim, lost 68-55 to Mission Hills of San Marcos, beat Cal High of San Ramon 74-50, and won 51-45 over Oak Ridge of El Dorado Hills to close. Freshman Jenelle Solis made the San Diego Holiday Classic All-Tournament team. “I feel like we’re watching the growth of the team right before our eyes. We’re starting to meet teams that match us. It showed a lot tonight [against Clayton Valley],” coach Bryan Gardere said. The last group of games marked the official start for Senior Briana Webb is proving to be a vital part of this year’s team. She had a double-double against California. transfer students Briana Webb and Taylor White. Both come to Piedmont after spending time at Moreau HS in Hayward. “It’s about our chemistry; we’re really coming together as a team,” said White. “When we’re down, we pull each other up. We have great potential, we’re young but we’re mighty. Tonight was really about defense and focusing on their best player.” . “I think we’re coming together really well,” added Webb. “I’m trying to help out with communication because a lot of the girls are so young, so I try to speak up and help them figure things out with their roles and where to be. My approach is to play well defensively because if I can get steals, force turnovers, and get rebounds, I know it will transfer to the offensive side.” In the victory over Clayton Valley Charter, Piedmont trailed by 11 points at the half but rallied for a strong second half performance. “We’re playing together and not forcing anything. Coach gave us a hard talk at halftime. We didn’t play scared and just stayed together, said Andrea Martin. 61-52 over Clayton Valley in overtime Piedmont trailed 17-11 by the end of the first quarter and 32-21 by halftime. The comeback began in the third quarter with PHS taking its first lead of the game, 33-32, with 3:25 left in the third, but Clayton Valley quickly got back ahead to start the fourth period leading 38-36. There were three lead changes in the fourth quarter, including White hitting a 3-pointer with 50 seconds left to go up 47-45, but CV scored the tying basket with six seconds left to force overtime. Although CVC took an initial 48-47 lead in overtime on a free throw, Savannah Dennig put Piedmont back up 49-48 and the Highlanders never looked back., They scored five unanswered points to lead 54-48 with 2:15 left. CV clawed away to make it 54-52 with 1:39 remaining, but it was their last score of the game. Piedmont closed it out with seven more points, including four by Martin. Final scorers: Martin had 23 points, Webb had 13 points, White had 12 points, Solis had five points, and Dennig had four. 51-45 win over Oak Ridge Piedmont held a narrow 11-6 lead and went up 24-13 by halftime. Oak Ridge outscored PHS 17-10 in the third to clip away at PHS’ lead 34-30, but the Highlanders held on with 17 points to OR’s 15. Final stats: Martin led with 17 points, seven rebounds, one assist, three steals, and four blocks. Solis scored 16 points, five rebounds, five assists, and one block. Webb had eight points, eight rebounds, and two assists. Dennig scored three points, three rebounds, and one assist. White had six points, six rebounds, two assists, and one steal. 74-50 blowout of California Piedmont t railed 19-16 through the first quarter, but went up in the second quarter to lead 33-29 by halftime. PHS then outscored the Grizzlies 19-7 in the third to take a commanding 52-36 lead into the fourth, adding 22 more points in the final going. Final stats: Martin scored 24 points, 10 rebounds, two assists, two steals, and one block. Solis had 19 points, seven assists, three Staff Photos Sophomore Taylor White is making an impact in her first games with Piedmont. rebounds, and one steal. Webb had 16 points, 12 rebounds, two assists, and two steals. Dennig had six points, two rebounds, two assists, and a steal. White had seven points, seven rebounds, four assists, and four steals. 68-55 loss to Mission Hills In Piedmont’s only loss if the season, Mission Hills led 20-15 through the first quarter and 28-25 by halftime. MH then scored 23 in the third to lead 51-36 entering the fourth, scoring 17 more in the final quarter. Final stats: Martin had 21 points, eight rebounds, one assist, one steal, and one block. Dennig had four points, one rebound and assist. Solis scored 14 points and six assists. Shakila Zuberi had two points and three rebounds. White had 10 points and three rebounds, Webb had four points, five rebounds, and three assists. 72-26 drubbing of Canyon Piedmont led 25-10 through the first and 49-13 by halftime. With a running clock, PHS led 61-22 through the third and added 11 more in the final going. Final stats: Solis led with 29 points, six assists, and three steals. Webb had 25 points, four rebounds, three assists, and two steals. Martin had eight points, six rebounds, two assists, five steals, and a block. Dennig had two points, three rebounds, three assists, and two steals. White had six points, six rebounds, two assists, and one steal. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-1) hosts San Leandro for its first Western Alameda County Conference game tomorrow, Thursday, January 9 at 5:30 p.m. They also host Liberty on January 11 at 3:00 p.m. and Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, January 14 at 5:30 p.m. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Freshman Andrea Martin continues her strong debut season. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team continued its strong run before the turn of the New Year, tying Las Lomas 1-1 at Witter Field on Friday, December 20. Their draw comes against a Division 2 North Coast Section school, while Piedmont competes in Division 4. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 3-1-2 (W-T-L) to start the second half of its 2024/2025 season. Moreover, the Highlanders are now on a three-match unbeaten run against stout teams, including 2-1 wins over D4 opponent Cardinal Newman and D1 school California. It also marked the fourth straight game for sophomore forward Elsa Wallway to contribute a goal, scoring the game’s only goal in the first half. The Highlanders look ahead to the start of its Western Alameda County Conference schedule as they push for a league title. They host Berkeley on Thursday, January 9 before bringing in Castro Valley on Tuesday, January 14. Match Recap Piedmont had the first offensive action of the contest with a long shot from a free kick by Louisa Symkowick. From about 16 yards above the penalty area, Symkowick’s shot was caught by the Las Lomas goalkeeper and briefly fumbled for a nervy moment. Ryo Woltag also had a shot loop high after receiving a nice pass off of the end line by Kyla Williams moments later. At the 15-minute mark, Wallway won a free kick a few yards above the penalty area. Taking the spot kick, Wallway whipped a shot above Las Lomas’ wall of defenders but her shot went narrowly wide of the right post. Piedmont’s goal by Wallway came around the 20th minute. It happened when a pass by Symkowick bounced off of the turf and a defensive header caused the ball to loop high into the air. Holding off a defender, Wallway allowed the ball to bounce, then instinctively spun around the ball-watching defender. Wallway took one touch past the out-rushing keeper, slotting her shot into the empty net with a left-footed shot. In the second half, Las Lomas maintained an aggressive press to limit more opportunities. The Knights found its equalizer around the 60th minute on a desperation long shot from 35 yards out of goal—where the shot was inch-perfect above the outstretched leap of Piedmont’s goal keeper Friedie Schickedanz. PHS stayed aggressive in the Staff Photos Elsa Wallway scored Piedmont’s goal in its 1-1 tie with Las Lomas. Juliana Thornborrow nearly scored the game-winner against Las Lomas.

articles.text: PHS beats El Cerrito, loses to St. Joseph in OT Staff Photos Dillon Casey scored 24 points against El Cerrito and 25 against St. Joseph. The Highlanders’ boys’ basketball team split its first two games of the New Year, defeating El Cerrito 65-57 in the Gauchos’ home gym on Monday, January 6, and losing a heartbreaker 70-68 in overtime to St. Joseph at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, January 8. Their recent win snapped a three-game losing streak and brough its record to 6-5. The loss to St. Joe came after the Pilots sank a buzzer-beater to force overtime, followed by another buzzer-beater basket to win the game. “We’re a young team that hasn’t been in a lot of situations like St. Joe. We had some jitters in the first quarter, but we were good for most of the game,” said coach Ben Spencer. Piedmont did well to deal with an aggressive press by El Cerrito for the entire second half. “Despite being a bit tired from that overtime game. We handled the ball pretty well in the third quarter and not too many turnovers. It wasn’t until the fourth quarter until their press started making an impact. With a young team that’s going to happen. We let them play through it and they knew what they had to do. These games will get us ready for league play and the postseason,” Spencer said. Monday’s game was also a strong performance by sophomore Lucian Fang-Ring, who hit two 3-pointers in the third quarter and another in the fourth to help put the game away. After getting limited minutes toward the end of his freshman season, Fang-Ring is in his first season of a full varsity role. “It felt like our energy was falling away and I wanted to shoot the big shot. It feels good to have the upperclassmen trust me, It’s good to bounce back and snap out of that three-game losing streak,” Fang-Ring said following their win over El Cerrito. Piedmont looks ahead to the start of a busy week. They begin their Western Alameda County Conference schedule tomorrow, January 9 with a game against San Leandro, then a game at University in San Francisco on January 11, and a game at home against Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, January 14. 65-57 win vs. over El Cerrito Piedmont trailed early before taking the lead at 11-10 with 1:02 left in the first quarter when Ravi Silverberg converted a threepoint play. They never relinquished their advantage from then on, ending the opening quarter with a narrow 14-13 lead. Sophomore Lucian Fang-Ring had a big second-half in Piedmont’s win over El Cerrito. In the second quarter, Silverberg opened things with another three-point play after Fang-Ring nabbed an offensive rebound and sending a slick pass to Silverberg under the rim for the lay-up and foul. After El Cerrito made a free throw to make it 17-14, PHS went on an 8-1 scoring run to take a 25-15 lead. Dillon Casey knocked down a 3-pointer on an assist from Silverberg to close the quarter, making it 28-19 at the half. Piedmont opened the third quarter with a 7-2 scoring run to build a 35-22 advantage. The Gauchos cut the deficit to four points at 38-34, but Fang-Ring hit a big 3-pointer to make it 41-34. After four more points by El Cerrito, P.J. Brayer hit another 3-pointer to end the quarter, leading 44-38. Their recent win snapped a three-game losing streak and brough its record to 6-5. The loss to St. Joe came after the Pilots sank a buzzer-beater to force overtime, followed by another buzzer-beater basket to win the game. “We’re a young team that hasn’t been in a lot of situations like St. Joe. Piedmont did well to deal with an aggressive press by El Cerrito for the entire second half. “Despite being a bit tired from that overtime game.
