articles.text: Both the girls’ basketball and girls’ soccer teams had strong performances in December. The basketball winning eight games throughout the month while soccer took two wins and a draw against stout competition. We’ve named Andrea Martin of basketball and Elsa Wallway of soccer our Athletes of the Month for December, with honorable mentions to Jenelle Solis of basketball and Louisa Symkowick of soccer. Andrea Martin has caught everyone’s attention as one of three freshman starters on the basketball team. She has helped lead the team to a 10-1 record in the squad’s first full month of action. In the 10 games through the month of December, Martin has led the team with 175 points while providing a presence on the boards and defensively. She had a double-double in nearly every game and put together big performances against solid teams. She recorded 24 points and 10 rebounds in Piedmont’s 74-50 win over California, a Division 1 North Coast Section school. Piedmont’s only loss this season came against Mission Hills, the defending San Diego Section’s Open Division champions. In that game, she recorded 21 points and eight rebounds. Elsa Wallway, a sophomore soccer player, returned to Piedmont’s lineup on December 7 and scored the team’s only goal in a narrow 2-1 loss to Archbishop Mitty, the defending D1 State Champions. Since then, PHS had 2-1 wins over D4 foe Cardinal Newman and D1 playoff contenders California while also Staff Photos Piedmont freshman Andrea Martin was named Athlete of the Month for December. Piedmont sophomore Elsa Wallway also was named Athlete of the Month for December. drawing 1-1 with D2 NCS school Las Lomas. She scored against Freshman Jenelle Solis earns an Honorable Mention for December’s Athlete of the Month. Senior captain Louisa Symkowick earns Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Month in December. Las Lomas, Mitty and California, also sending the game-winning own-goal on the California Grizzlies and the game-winning assist versus the Cardinals. Her goal against Las Lomas came on an amazing play. She allowed the ball to bounce high over her defender before heading the ball past the goal keeper to herself in close distance before uncorking a left-footed laser shot into the net. Honorable Mentions Jenelle Solis earns our honorable mention after being a big part of the Piedmont basketball team’s success as a slick ball handler, creative passer, and knockdown shooter. She was named to the San Diego Holiday Hoops’ All-Tournament team. The freshman starter had 16 points, five rebounds and five assists in their tournament win over Oak Ridge and scored 19 points and seven assists in their win over California. She also had an impact in their loss to Mission Hills, scoring 14 points and six assists. Louisa Symkowick receives our honorable mention as senior captain of the girls’ soccer team and making an impact as Piedmont’s midfield general to facilitate the operation in the school’s 3-1-2 (W-T-L) start to the season. Symkowick is a central midfielder, and the attack often starts with her passes to wide runners and making tackles to initiate the offense. She will continue being a focal part of the Highlanders’ success.

Although visitors of the coast should be wary of their surroundings during this time of year, swells typically are roaring through the winter months; attracting big-wave lovers from all over the world to gaze at the Pacific Ocean’s moving-mountains of water. Tomales Point Taking the 9.7 out-and-back Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay, It overlooks remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific Coast and Tomales Bay. The hike starts at Pierce Point Ranch, a historic farmstead of the Pt. Reyes Peninsula that has informative markers to describe Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Preserve. Tule Elk are considered the smallest subspecies of elk. Tomales Point in Western Marin has 10+ foot waves forecasted on Saturday, January 11. Staff Photos the early dairy farming culture of the area. The near five mile walk to Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Reserve, where herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves are roaming. The ending is a bluff overlooking tide pools and a common array of birds: pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while red-tailed hawks and turkey vultures are often spotted looking for food as well. According to wave forecasts, the area will be hit with expected 10-foot swells on Saturday, January 11. Waves will taper to sixfeet by Monday. It is a popular trail; expect to span over 100 other patrons on a typical weekend hike. Muir Beach & Tennessee Valley Beach Muir Beach and Tennessee Valley Beach are among the most popular destinations in Marin County. While Muir Beach has a parking lot for beachgoers, hiking to Tennessee Beach is a 1.8 mile out-and-back along the Tennessee Valley Trailhead. articles.text: The Thing About Jellyfish, based on the novel of the same name will be performed at Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Roda Theatre from Friday, January 31 through Sunday, March 9. Based on the novel by Ali Benjamin and adapted for the stage by Keith Bunin, the play follows 12-year-old Suzy Swanson who is devastated to learn that her best friend, Franny, has drowned and died. The coming-of-age story narrates Suzy navigating this tragic loss, delving into themes of love, loss, friendship, and a young girl’s imagination. Playwright Bunin said he is thrilled to return to the East Bay, where he spent “three wonderful years” working on the Pixar movie Onward. This will be his first production on the Berkeley Repertory Theatre stage. The world premiere of The Thing About Jellyfish is directed by Tyne Rafaeli. The play features Matilda Lawler in the role of Suzy, and includes Jasper Bermudez, Cassidy Brown, Christiana Clark, Sydney Walker Freeman, Andy Grotelueschen, Maxwell Hamilton, Stephanie Janssen, Colby Kipnes, Lexi Perkel, Rebecca Schweitzer, Robert Stanton, Kayla Teruel, and Antonio Watson as supporting actors. Matilda Lawler is featured in the title role of Suzy Swanson at Berkeley Rep. “Ali Benjamin’s astonishing novel The Thing About Jellyfish is a story about the most essential of human experiences” said Rafaeli. “Through the eyes of the singular Suzy Swanson we are taken on a journey that allows us to reflect on the extraordinary gift of being alive.” “It’s a thrilling and vibrant story for audiences of all ages, and I’m thrilled to collaborate with the incredible director Tyne Rafaeli to bring it to the stage,” Bunin added. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org to purchase tickets, or call the box office at 510-647- 2949 Tuesday through Sunday, 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. ®
articles.title: World premiere of The Thing About Jellyfish comes to Berkeley Rep stage Jan. 31

articles.text: The Tony award-winning musical Some Like it Hot is showing at San Francisco’s Orpheum Theatre now through January 26. Set in Chicago during the prohibition era, the musical comedy follows two musicians who take up new identities and go on the lam after witnessing a mob hit. With gangsters hot on their heels, they board a cross-country train and begin a life-changing trip, ultimately meeting a dazzling young singer who captures one of their hearts. Cast includes Matt Loehr as Joe/Josephine, Tavis Kordell as Jerry/Daphne, Leandra Ellis-Gaston as Sugar, Edward Juvier as Osgood, Tarra Conner Jones as Sweet Sue, Jamie LaVerdiere as Mulligan, Devon Goffman as Spats, and Devon Hadsell, who was a member of the original Broadway production, as Minnie. Visit https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/some-like-it-hot/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Some Like it Hot at Orpheum Theatre now through Jan. 26

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet premiere of Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon opens the company’s 2024-25 Repertory Season on Friday, January 24. Inspired by the 1731 novel Manon Lescaut by Abbé Prévost, Manon is considered one of MacMillan’s most notable and widely-celebrated works. The ballet chronicles the rise and fall of its titular heroine, beginning near Paris and ending in New Orleans. The three-act ballet was first performed by The Royal Ballet in London in 1974 with Antoinette Sibley and Anthony Dowell in principal roles. “MacMillan was an artist who infused novelty and depth into his choreography,” San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo said. “Manon exemplifies how he brought new life to a classic story, transforming it into a timeless narrative.” Principal casting for Manon includes Dores André, Jasmine Jimison, Sasha De Sola, with Nikisha Fogo as Manon, and Harrison James, Max Cauthorn, and Aaron Robison as des Grieux. San Francisco Ballet welcomes principal guest artist Alban Lendorf to the War Memorial Opera House stage for select performances as des Grieux. The War Memorial Opera House bars will serve a specialty cocktail inspired by the themes of Manon and 18th-century France. Manon will be performed through February 1. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling ticket services at 415-865- 2000, open Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Scene from San Francisco Ballet’s production of Manon

The play features Matilda Lawler in the role of Suzy, and includes Jasper Bermudez, Cassidy Brown, Christiana Clark, Sydney Walker Freeman, Andy Grotelueschen, Maxwell Hamilton, Stephanie Janssen, Colby Kipnes, Lexi Perkel, Rebecca Schweitzer, Robert Stanton, Kayla Teruel, and Antonio Watson as supporting actors. Matilda Lawler is featured in the title role of Suzy Swanson at Berkeley Rep. “Ali Benjamin’s astonishing novel The Thing About Jellyfish is a story about the most essential of human experiences” said Rafaeli. “Through the eyes of the singular Suzy Swanson we are taken on a journey that allows us to reflect on the extraordinary gift of being alive.” “It’s a thrilling and vibrant story for audiences of all ages, and I’m thrilled to collaborate with the incredible director Tyne Rafaeli to bring it to the stage,” Bunin added. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org to purchase tickets, or call the box office at 510-647- 2949 Tuesday through Sunday, 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Ballet premiere of Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon opens the company’s 2024-25 Repertory Season on Friday, January 24. Inspired by the 1731 novel Manon Lescaut by Abbé Prévost, Manon is considered one of MacMillan’s most notable and widely-celebrated works. The ballet chronicles the rise and fall of its titular heroine, beginning near Paris and ending in New Orleans. The three-act ballet was first SF Ballet premieres Manon to open season Jan. 24 performed by The Royal Ballet in London in 1974 with Antoinette Sibley and Anthony Dowell in principal roles. “MacMillan was an artist who infused novelty and depth into his choreography,” San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo said. “Manon exemplifies how he brought new life to a classic story, transforming it into a timeless narrative.” Principal casting for Manon includes Dores André, Jasmine Jimison, Sasha De Sola, with Nikisha Fogo as Manon, and Harrison James, Max Cauthorn, and Aaron Robison as des Grieux. San Francisco Ballet welcomes principal guest artist Alban Lendorf to the War Memorial Opera House stage for select performances as des Grieux. The War Memorial Opera House bars will serve a specialty cocktail inspired by the themes of Manon and 18th-century France. Manon will be performed through February 1. articles.text: The San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park will host an artist reception with photographer Mark Citret on Saturday, February 8. Citret, a San Francisco native, began photographing in 1968 and in the 1980’s produced a large body of work titled “Unnatural Wonders”, which is his personal survey of architecture in national parks. The February 8 event highlights the artists’ latest collection of works, entitled Structural Beauty: Photographs of the San Francisco Botanical Garden. In this new exhibition, Citret captures the physical beauty of plants through black and white photographs, his preferred medium. Citret received both his BA and MA in Art from San Francisco State University, and has taught photography at the University of California Berkeley Extension since 1982. Structural Beauty: Photographs of the San Francisco Botanical Garden is on exhibit at the Helen Crocker Russell Library in the San Francisco Botanical Garden February 8 through May, 2025. The reception is from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. and is free to the public. Reservations are encouraged. Visit https://gggp.org/event/artistreception-with-mark-citret/ for more details. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum will host an expert-panel discussion on Yerba Buena Island’s natural history this Saturday, January 11 at 10 a.m. Yerba Buena Island is the second largest natural island in San Francisco Bay, and its development and restoration is an on-going and multi-phase effort, much like the larger, man-made Treasure Island. Yerba Buena Island was historically used as a naval base and training center and its native ecosystems have been replaced by invasive species. Significant and biodiverse natural areas still remain, and ongoing redevelopment of Yerba Buena Island and Treasure Island provided the opportunity to restore native ecology. Both islands have been planted with over 50 species of native plants, including flora and fauna that are native to the ecosystem. According to Treasure Island Museum staff, the design and planning for these spaces involved a unique and collaborative effort between developers, the City of San Francisco, ecologists, local nurseries and landscape architects. Peter Brastow, from the San Francisco Environment Department and Will Benge, Senior Associate with CMG Landscape Architecture will be onsite to discuss restoration efforts. Tickets are free, but reservation is required. Visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum.org/ event-details/restoration-of-yerba-buena-island-weaving-ecology-with-place-and-infrastructure to register. articles.text: “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light,” an exhibit showcasing the work of Italian father-son photographers Elio and Stefano Ciol, is on view at Museo Italo America in San Francisco now through February 2. Both photographers, hailing from Casarsa della Delizia in the Italian region of Friuli Venezia Giulia, are known for works that highlight their masterful use of light, balance of geometric lines and angles, and impeccable photographic composition. These three essential aspects enabled the father-son pair to create visually captivating and highly structured pieces that stand the test of time. Elio, born in 1929, lived his formative years during Nazi occupation and is now renowned as one of the foremost European masters of landscape photography. Many of his predominantly black and white shots have been featured in over one hundred solo exhibitions. “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light” showcases a collection spanning over sixty years. Museum hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. and Sunday, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The exhibit is free on Thursdays. Museo Italo Americano is the first museum in the United States devoted exclusively to Italian and Italian-American art and culture, located in San Francisco’s historic Fort Mason. Visit https:// sfmuseo.org/exhibition/elio-andstefano-ciol-into-the-light/ to learn more. Patrons view “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light” at Museo Italo Americano in San Francisco.

articles.text: Thursday, January 16, 7:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture Join art historian Michael Stehr as he discusses the importance of the current show at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, entitled Mary Cassatt at Work. Too often dismissed as a sentimental painter of mothers and children, Mary Cassatt (1844– 1926) was in fact a modernist pioneer. Her paintings, pastels, and prints are characterized by restless experimentation and change. Cassatt was the only American to join the French Impressionists, first exhibiting with the group at Degas’ invitation in 1879, and quickly emerged as a key member of the movement. The illustrated lecture will last approximately one hour; please pay $20 per person, cash only, at the door. Note that the Legion of Honor exhibit will close on January 26, 2025. Saturday, January 18, 4:30 p.m. Boon Hiker Band The Boon Hiker Band includes John Bidwell, Clare Broussard, J.T. Devine, Robin Eschner, Dennis Hysom, Natasha Haugnes, Chris Smith, and John Tuttle. These eight group members bring dynamic vocal harmonies to the heart of the original compositions and the arrangements of covers – all supported by various combinations of guitar, bass, keyboard, banjo, accordion, dobro, lap steel, and percussion. The songs lean toward Americana/Folk/Indie traditions, with energetic and vibrant musicianship provided by the three East Bay members – and the five North Bay members enhance the vocal textures and harmonies with their choral backgrounds. Advance tickets for this concert can be found at https://bpt.me/6383991. Doors will open at 4 p.m. Saturday, January 25, 7:30 p.m. Italian Cristiana Pegoraro solo recital Returning to PCA after several years, Italian-born pianist and composer Cristiana Pegoraro honors Piedmont and PCA with another stellar, inspired solo performance on our Steinway grand piano! This renowned pianist will perform the same program she played at Carnegie Hall’s Weill Recital Hall in mid-November! Acclaimed as one of the most gifted musicians of her generation, since her formal debut in Messina at age 10 she has received more than forty international awards, has released over thirty CDs, of which six are of her own compositions, and has performed with major orchestras and in renowned concert halls all over the world, including Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall. In addition to a full-time teaching schedule in Rome and New York, she has written books, is the founder and President of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of the annual Narnia Festival, both in her hometown of Narni in Umbria, Italy. Discounted tickets for this special concert are available at https:// bpt.me/6504559. Sunday, January 26, 4:00 p.m. Mads Tolling, with Kenny Washington Danish-born jazz violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with jazz pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington. Although all three are celebrated names in the Bay Area, this marks their first time performing together. Mads and John will feature music from their 2023 album, Ramblin’, which includes songs ranging from Toto and The Beatles to John McLaughlin and Chick Corea, along with a few original compositions. Kenny Washington, one of the world’s premier jazz vocalists and a frequent performer at Wynton Marsalis’ Jazz at Lincoln Center, will join them. Jazz writer Andrew Gilbert has dubbed Kenny “The Superman of the Bay Area Jazz Scene.” Together, the three will perform American Songbook tunes by Duke Ellington, Thelonious Monk, and George Gershwin. Tickets for this performance can be purchased at https:// bpt.me/6504543. articles.text: As humans we are always on the lookout for adventure and beauty. Some look for it in the misfortune of others. Fortunately, the great majority of us look into the sunset for beauty. It seems that every December is a month of beauty. Let’s see if you agree. In the “old days“ a musical soirée came before a fine meal, and that’s the way it was at the French Club in San Francisco in mid-December. Some friends invited my string Quartet to play background music before the banquet. That was our pleasure, to say the least. And then we feasted. The entire meal was memorable, but here are a couple of items that you can make yourself: The main course was roasted quail with truffles, but maybe you could try to make the first course. Above a creamy bed of cauliflower was a mixture of wild mushrooms. If you don’t want cream of cauliflower, I would recommend a bed of polenta. Sauté some wild mushrooms and sprinkle them above the bed of cream cauliflower or polenta. The banquet featured 10 carefully selected wines which served to increase the delight of the foods. At the end was a great surprise – a Madeira wine vintage 1908. I wonder if royalty ever ate as well. Loss of two sports heroes The year 2024 saw the passing of two notable athletic heroes, Willie Mayes and Ricky Henderson. Willie Mayes was a great gentleman to match his athletic prowess. Unique he was in every way. So was Ricky Henderson… but ever so different. There was a charming ego to match his ability. I wonder if he took himself seriously. His super competitiveness was matched by his generosity… all delivered with a self-deprecating smile. Looking back a long time we find that Al Jolson was a character something similar to Ricky Henderson. Everyone knows his famous declaration: “you ain’t heard nothing yet.” Most people do not know the origin of this. Early in the First World War there were rallies to encourage people to buy war bonds.. The greatest entertainers of the time were featured. Early in the concert, the greatest operatic tenor Enrico Caruso would sing. Soon after that, the great Irish tenor John McCormack was featured. And then came Al Jolson, whose first words to the audience were “you ain’t heard nothing yet.” Sounds like a serious condition called… Ego unbounded. In reality, Al Jolson was not pompous, but extremely generous. His generosity is not as well known as it needs to be. articles.text: A scene from Disney/Pixar’s Inside Out 2 The genius of Pixar Animation Studios resides with its spot-on sense of audience. It consistently demonstrates imaginative storytelling featuring characters that resonate, plus plots that compel. Clearly, Pixar also possesses a deep bench of extraordinary animators who, in feature after feature, create vibrant, rich images. I would judge that Inside Out 2 represents all of the above, and surely must have been a challenge for both the writers and the animators. Riley Anderson, previously a tween in Inside Out, finds herself on the precarious cusp of adolescence and all that it entails. Where once life was relatively calm, involving lingering residuals of childhood, well, being a newbie teen can feel as if you are abruptly unmoored, adrift, often steeped in uncertainty. Early cartographers labeled those area yet to be explored as places where “there be dragons.” Indeed. Riley’s parents are, of course, one barometer of her surprising mood swings and unpredictable intensity. What is the sound of a bedroom door slamming? Or how to understand the “DO NOT ENTER” sign on the door? Of course, most often stories that depict the onset of teendom focus on the external stuff that features a panoply of new behaviors, as if this stranger is taking a ride on a roller coaster or is engaged in bumper cars. Both are easy metaphors for unanticipated emotions suddenly made manifest. But Pixar has done something extraordinary in its storytelling explanation of Riley’s conflicted reactions: relying on the remarkable license offered by animation, they have used personification to depict a deep bench of characters, each an inspired representation of Riley’s familiar emotions as well as those rookies who have only recently appeared in the lineup. To make all of the above interesting, Riley and her buds are off to hokey camp where her veteran and new squad of feelings will be put to the test. Taking the familiar lead is Joy (Amy Poehler), calm and caring, who has always been in charge of a NASA-like emotions central panel. That is until Anxiety (Maya Hawke), frazzled, bug-eyed, wild hair, red everything steps up to reaction central, and begins to dominate, opening the door to Embarrassment, Envy, mixed with the old school Sadness, Anger, Fear, and even Ennui (lassitude). Riley confronts her desire to be popular, to be liked by the older hockey camp girls, while the word “cool” swirls. Plus an confronts an unfamiliar desire to fit in and so transforms herself and thereby gain the approval of those who have already achieved “cool.” This results in Riley becoming a person that her friends, and ultimately even Riley herself, no longer recognize. Meanwhile, back at the emotive control panel, a struggle develops between Joy, and the frenetic, unrelenting Anxiety who is buttressed by Envy. Ultimately, the question begged is: will Riley return to her core values, and to her faithful friends? Or will Anxiety prevail, causing Riley to abandon the person she truly is as personified by Joy, and instead choose trendy popularity and facile coolness? Regarding the writers, choosing hockey camp as the setting is inspired. It is a kaleidoscope of new challenges for Riley. And regarding the teen vernacular/ interactions it’s perfect. Considering perfect, the animation is remarkable, the intensity of hockey nailed. Plus the emotions (determination, disappointment, desire to win not only the game but the approbation of the team), are exceptional. As am aside, Inside Out 2 was nominated for a Golden Globe award, and though it didn’t win, the Golden Globes are often a reliable precursor to the coming Oscars. Inside Out 2. Pixar–Disney animation. Directed by Kelsey Mann. Starring Amy Poehler, Maya Hawke, Phyllis Smith. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2024. Streaming on prime/Disney+.

articles.text: From the world renowned Japanese Studio Ghibli, The Secret World of Arrietty was co-written by two of its principal storytellers, Hiromasa Yonebayashi and Hayao Miyazaki. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule, even law, is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, alas, the Borrowers, they believe, are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure to be sure for she is fascinated by the sheer size of the bean world, something she views in all its gigantic splendor and potential danger. But, as it turns out, she is also drawn into Shawn’s personal world and is soon discovered by the bean boy. Surprisingly these two most disparate characters fashion a friendship and a bond of trust. Of course, one of the beans, an elderly housekeeper, Hara (Carol Burnett), is ever on guard, intent on ridding the bean’s home of any “pests.” The danger to Arrietty and family is palpable. The Secret is a wonderful tale, lush and beautiful, hand drawn animé that brings to life this contrasting world of Borrowers and beans. It is also a coming-ofage story featuring a strong and courageous newbie-teenage girl who years to expand her horizons above the floorboards and exhibits a focused fearlessness and kindness, qualities that are endearing. This film tells a tender story and is a visual stunner while avoiding the fantastical, extraordinary, shape-shifting characters that are often part of the Ghibli world. The Secret World of Arrietty. Animaé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hiromasa Yonebayashi. With the voices of David Henrie, Bridget Mendler, Amy Poehler and Carol Burnett. Walt Disney – Studio Ghibli. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated G. Released in 2019, Streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty

articles.text: It was New Year’s Day and the Walking on Wednesdays group started 2025 looking back at one of the city’s treasures, Piedmont Park. Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi and Piedmont historian Meghan Bennet’s research, along with the Piedmont Park History Trail markers were guides for them. The Ohlone are the area’s original, predominant Indigenous group. They lived here for 10,000 years before Spanish explorers arrived in 1769 and later colonized the area. In 1820 the Spanish Crown gave Luís María Peralta a 44,800-acre land grant in recognition of his 40 years of military service. His Rancho San Antonio stretched from what is now San Leandro to Albany. The annexation of California in 1848 and the Gold Rush of 1849 had a tremendous impact on the Peraltas and other “Californios.” Walter Blair came to California in 1852 and one year later purchased land in what became Piedmont from the US Government, which then owned most of the Peralta land. Blair’s property ran from the Mountain View Cemetery wall on Moraga Avenue to beyond Blair Avenue. In about 1867 pink minerals oozing from the creek in Bushy Dell Canyon started to attract visitors. It was believed the minerals had therapeutic benefits. From 1868 to 1870 there was a “boom,” and Piedmont lands became sought after. However, this soon died and little attention was paid to the area, except for the springs. Walter Blair built his Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 and in 1884, he also developed a 75-acre amusement park in Moraga Canyon. Blair died suddenly in 1888 at the age of 57, but the hotel thrived until 1892 when it was destroyed by a fire. Additionally, a boy fell to his death from a hot air balloon in 1897 at the park. The land was felt to be cursed and developer Frank C. Havens’ Realty Syndicate swooped in to buy it. Havens developed Piedmont Park in 1898 and through the early 1900s to draw people to Piedmont. However, by 1916 Havens was in financial trouble, and wanted to sell the park. The Piedmont School Board wanted to purchase 13 acres of the park for a new high school, but Havens wouldn’t sell less than its entire 27 acres, and the City didn’t have money to purchase the remaining park land. Havens died in 1918, and the land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others purchased the land from Havens’ widow. Voters later passed a bond issue to reimburse them. The walkers’ first destination on the first Wednesday of 2025 was the Piedmont Park History There was a large turnout of walkers on New Year’s Day. A total of 51 walkers and four K-9 best friends were on hand last week. . pages.text: Wednesday, January 8, 2025 19 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Piedmont Park for its history By Dick Carter It was New Year’s Day and the Walking on Wednesdays group started 2025 looking back at one of the city’s treasures, Piedmont Park. Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi and Piedmont historian Meghan Bennet’s research, along with the Piedmont Park History Trail markers were guides for them. The Ohlone are the area’s original, predominant Indigenous group. They lived here for 10,000 years before Spanish explorers arrived in 1769 and later colonized the area. In 1820 the Spanish Crown gave Luís María Peralta a 44,800-acre land grant in recognition of his 40 years of military service. His Rancho San Antonio stretched from what is now San Leandro to Albany. The annexation of California in 1848 and the Gold Rush of 1849 had a tremendous impact on the Peraltas and other “Californios.” Walter Blair came to California in 1852 and one year later purchased land in what became Piedmont from the US Government, which then owned most of the Peralta land. Blair’s property ran from the Mountain View Cemetery wall on Moraga Avenue to beyond Blair Avenue. In about 1867 pink minerals oozing from the creek in Bushy Dell Canyon started to attract visitors. It was believed the minerals had therapeutic benefits. From 1868 to 1870 there was a “boom,” and Piedmont lands became sought after. However, this soon died and little attention was paid to the area, except for the springs. Walter Blair built his Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 and in 1884, he also developed a 75-acre amusement park in Moraga Canyon. Blair died suddenly in 1888 at the age of 57, but the hotel thrived until 1892 when it was destroyed by a fire. Additionally, a boy fell to his death from a hot air balloon in 1897 at the park. The land was felt to be cursed and developer Frank C. Havens’ Realty Syndicate swooped in to buy it. Havens developed Piedmont Park in 1898 and through the early 1900s to draw people to Piedmont. However, by 1916 Havens was in financial trouble, and wanted to sell the park. The Piedmont School Board wanted to purchase 13 acres of the park for a new high school, but Havens wouldn’t sell less than its entire 27 acres, and the City didn’t have money to purchase the remaining park land. Havens died in 1918, and the land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others purchased the land from Havens’ widow. Voters later passed a bond issue to reimburse them. The walkers’ first destination on the first Wednesday of 2025 was the Piedmont Park History Trail marker summary in front of the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building. There they learned that when Piedmont celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2007 a public/private partnership was developed to preserve the history of Piedmont Park and to create a self-guided walking park tour with nine markers. The walkers went to the first marker just up Vista Avenue past the City Hall in the shaded, somewhat secluded courtyard at its right front. They read the Last Original Park Bench marker with a photo of a rustic wood bench near the spring’s grotto. The group exited the courtyard and went down Vista to Bonita Avenue, then turned up Magnolia Avenue with the second marker at the Exedra. This one told how Blair built the Piedmont Springs Hotel. Next, the walkers went behind the Exedra to the upper edge of the park where a marker told the story of Havens opening his Piedmont Springs Park in 1898. The walkers continued past the Community Hall to the Japanese Tea House. This is not the original tea house that Havens built in 1907 as a park attraction. When the City acquired the park in the 1920s, the tea house was torn down to make room for a new civic center master plan. In 1976 when the Leander Redmon estate at Hillside and Magnolia Avenues was razed to build the new Piedmont Middle School its tea house was donated to the City of Piedmont was moved to its current site. The group’s next stop was outside the park tennis courts. Here Havens had built a world class art museum in 1907. The walkers went behind the Community Hall into the park and took the lower path that followed Bushy Dell Creek to the Cascade marker. This was “a lush tropical paradise” and an artificial waterfall. The next stop was the marker for the Sulphur Springs Grotto which told how Mark Twain was there in 1867. The group continued to the Eucalyptus Amphitheater that was built in 1908 and where the PHS softball field is today. Finally, after climbing to the steps above Witter Field, they read the marker telling the story of the maze which is where Witter Field is now located. The walkers had read all nine markers and shared lots of Piedmont Park history. They returned to the Community Hall through the upper path, appreciating the park even more. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. There was a large turnout of walkers on New Year’s Day. A total of 51 walkers and four K-9 best friends were on hand last week. . articles.text: Rustic Portuguese-Style Potato-Kale Soup with Sausage. Here is a hearty, rustic soup that comes together quickly, is ideal for swapping out ingredients, and perfect for winter. Home cooks have to be flexible these days, preparing dishes based on what’s at hand. This recipe can be the start of many improvisations on its theme. I always appreciate an easy, mix-and-match recipe that’s built for flexibility depending upon what might be on hand. Even a trip to the store doesn’t guarantee they will have everything on the grocery list, and given wait times and lines, most of us are not store-hopping to multiple locations these days to hunt down a specific item. This soup should fly to the top of the list for a warming and satisfying soup when the mood strikes. Rustic Portuguese-Style Kale and Potato Soup with Sausage Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • 1 package Portuguese-style Linguica, 12 ounces, halved lengthwise and sliced ¼-inch thick; substitute any smoked sausage such as Spanish chorizo, Italian, kielbasa, etc. 1 pound Yukon Gold potatoes, halved or quartered lengthwise then sliced ¼-inch thick; substitute any potato you prefer, even a sweet potato 1 to 1½ bunches kale, thinly sliced; substitute any variety of kale, collard greens, cabbage 1 medium onion, about 1 cup diced; Spanish, yellow or white 2-stalks celery, about 1 cup diced; include leaves if desired 4 – 6 cloves garlic, minced 1 – 2 bay leaves, fresh or dried ½ – 1 teaspoon smoked paprika Red chile flakes to taste Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste 1 quart low-sodium chicken broth Optional: Add1 can white or garbanzo beans, rinsed and drained; and 1 can diced tomatoes with their juices INSTRUCTIONS 1. Use a stock pot of at least 4-quart capacity, add the sliced linguica and slowly brown over medium low heat; stirring occasionally to brown both sides as the fat begins to render. Depending on the diameter of your pot, this will take about 5 minutes. Remove the linguica with a slotted spoon or spatula to a plate and set it aside. 2. Increase the heat to medium, then add the celery and onions. Stir occasionally until they begin to soften, about 2 minutes. Add the garlic and cook another minute or so until the garlic softens. Add the sliced potatoes and mix to combine. Add the bay leaves, smoked paprika, red chile flakes and a slight amount of salt and pepper. Stir well to distribute the spices, then add the chicken stock. 3. Cover and bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to barely a simmer. Cook until the potatoes are barely tender. Return the browned linguica and add the sliced kale. Cook at a slow simmer for another 10–15 minutes until kale is softened. 4. Taste and adjust seasonings accordingly. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil if desired. Options: • For a thicker soup, use an immersion blender and blitz a few times when the potatoes Cathead Biscuits

articles.text: For light, fluffy easy-to bake biscuits, I recommend Cathead Biscuits, as adapted from Cooks Country April/May 2010 edition. Makes 6 very large biscuits INGREDIENTS • 1½ cups all-purpose flour • 1½ cups cake flour • 1 tablespoon baking powder • ½ teaspoon baking soda • 1 teaspoon table salt • 8 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into ½” pieces and softened • 4 tablespoons pork leaf lard, cut into ½” pieces (Substitute vegetable shortening if you insist) • 11̸8 cup buttermilk INSTRUCTIONS 1. Adjust an oven rack to upper-middle position and heat oven to 425°F. Butter a 9” round cake pan. 2. Combine flours, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a large bowl. Rub the butter and shortening into flour mixture until it resembles coarse meal. Stir in buttermilk until combined. 3. Use a buttered ½ cup measuring cup or scoop to transfer 6 heaping portions of dough into prepared pan. Place 5 portions around the perimeter and 1 in the center. 4. Bake until puffed and golden brown, 20 – 25 minutes. Cool in pan for 10 minutes then transfer to a wire rack. Notes: • In a pinch, you can substitute the buttermilk by combining 1-1/8 cups milk with 1 tablespoon lemon juice and letting it sit for about 10 minutes until it thickens slightly. • The dough is fairly moist. Take care to not overmix, as this will result in a denser biscuit. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 8, 2025 Rustic Portuguese-Style Potato Soup with Sausage Rustic Portuguese-Style Potato-Kale Soup with Sausage. By Deborah Quok Here is a hearty, rustic soup that comes together quickly, is ideal for swapping out ingredients, and perfect for winter. Home cooks have to be flexible these days, preparing dishes based on what’s at hand. This recipe can be the start of many improvisations on its theme. I always appreciate an easy, mix-and-match recipe that’s built for flexibility depending upon what might be on hand. Even a trip to the store doesn’t guarantee they will have everything on the grocery list, and given wait times and lines, most of us are not store-hopping to multiple locations these days to hunt down a specific item. This soup should fly to the top of the list for a warming and satisfying soup when the mood strikes. Rustic Portuguese-Style Kale and Potato Soup with Sausage Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • 1 package Portuguese-style Linguica, 12 ounces, halved lengthwise and sliced ¼-inch thick; substitute any smoked sausage such as Spanish chorizo, Italian, kielbasa, etc. 1 pound Yukon Gold potatoes, halved or quartered lengthwise then sliced ¼-inch thick; substitute any potato you prefer, even a sweet potato 1 to 1½ bunches kale, thinly sliced; substitute any variety of kale, collard greens, cabbage 1 medium onion, about 1 cup diced; Spanish, yellow or white 2-stalks celery, about 1 cup diced; include leaves if desired 4 – 6 cloves garlic, minced 1 – 2 bay leaves, fresh or dried ½ – 1 teaspoon smoked paprika Red chile flakes to taste Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste 1 quart low-sodium chicken broth Optional: Add1 can white or garbanzo beans, rinsed and drained; and 1 can diced tomatoes with their juices INSTRUCTIONS 1. Use a stock pot of at least 4-quart capacity, add the sliced linguica and slowly brown over medium low heat; stirring occasionally to brown both sides as the fat begins to render. Depending on the diameter of your pot, this will take about 5 minutes. Remove the linguica with a slotted spoon or spatula to a plate and set it aside. 2. Increase the heat to medium, then add the celery and onions. Stir occasionally until they begin to soften, about 2 minutes. Add the garlic and cook another minute or so until the garlic softens. Add the sliced potatoes and mix to combine. Add the bay leaves, smoked paprika, red chile flakes and a slight amount of salt and pepper. Stir well to distribute the spices, then add the chicken stock. 3. Cover and bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to barely a simmer. Cook until the potatoes are barely tender. Return the browned linguica and add the sliced kale. Cook at a slow simmer for another 10–15 minutes until kale is softened. 4. Taste and adjust seasonings accordingly. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil if desired. Options: • For a thicker soup, use an immersion blender and blitz a few times when the potatoes • are just tender, before adding the linguica and kale. Take care to not over blend and leave plenty of sliced potatoes to enjoy in the soup. Add a 15-ounce can of diced tomatoes, cooked white beans or garbanzo beans when you add the linguica and kale. Fresh biscuits – a must for homemade soup For light, fluffy easy-to bake biscuits, I recommend Cathead Biscuits, as adapted from Cooks Country April/May 2010 edition. Makes 6 very large biscuits INGREDIENTS • 1½ cups all-purpose flour • 1½ cups cake flour • 1 tablespoon baking powder • ½ teaspoon baking soda • 1 teaspoon table salt • 8 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into ½” pieces and softened • 4 tablespoons pork leaf lard, cut into ½” pieces (Substitute vegetable shortening if you insist) • 11̸8 cup buttermilk INSTRUCTIONS 1. Adjust an oven rack to upper-middle position and heat oven to 425°F. Butter a 9” round cake pan. 2. Combine flours, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a large bowl. Rub the butter and shortening into flour mixture until it resembles coarse meal. Stir in buttermilk until combined. 3. Use a buttered ½ cup measuring cup or scoop to transfer 6 heaping portions of dough into prepared pan. Place 5 portions around the perimeter and 1 in the center. 4. Bake until puffed and golden brown, 20 – 25 minutes. Cool in pan for 10 minutes then transfer to a wire rack. Notes: • In a pinch, you can substitute the buttermilk by combining 1-1/8 cups milk with 1 tablespoon lemon juice and letting it sit for about 10 minutes until it thickens slightly. • The dough is fairly moist. Take care to not overmix, as this will result in a denser biscuit. Just before summer vacation a deal was struck, and the parlay between Piedmont Unified School District and the Association of Teachers reached a resolution. It was also a year in which Wildwood Elementary celebrated its 100 year anniversary on the field below the school. Witter Field finally reopened one year late. When fall classes resumed in August 2024, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and the school board were faced with paying for raises and for accounting for shortfalls from made by the district’s previous leadership. PUSD proposed budget cuts to balance the budget and the community responded in droves to fight for the music, the arts and other programming being cut. Cuts to certain positions were walked back, and a solution was proposed: increase the parcel tax in the 2024 November General Election. Residents showed their unwavering support for schools and handily passed Measure P, to fund teacher and staff salaries with 81% in favor. articles.text: As the Post celebrates its 27th year of publication, it may bring a smile to the faces of our readers as they see a list of the top newspapers in the country. 1. The Wall Street Journal is read by the people who run the country. 2. The Washington Post is read by people who think they run the country. 3. The New York Times is read by people who think they should run the country and who are very good at crossword puzzles. 4. USA Today is read by people who think they ought to run the country, but don’t really understand The New York Times. They do, however, like their statistics shown in pie charts. 5. The Los Angeles Times is read by people who wouldn’t mind running the country if they could find the time, and if they didn’t have to leave Southern California to do it. 6. The Boston Globe is read by people whose parents used to run the country and did a poor job of it, thank you very much. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. The New York Daily News is read by people who aren’t too sure who’s running the country and don’t really care as long as they can get a seat on the subway. The New York Post is read by people who don’t care who is running the country as long as they do something really scandalous, preferably while intoxicated. The Miami Herald is read by people who are running another country but need the baseball scores. The San Francisco Chronicle is read by people who aren’t sure if there is a country, or that anyone is running it; but If so, they oppose all that they stand for. There are occasional exceptions, such as if the leaders are handicapped minority feminist atheist dwarfs who also happen to be illegal aliens from any other country, or galaxy, provided, of course, that they are not Republicans. The National Enquirer is read by people trapped in line at the grocery store. The Piedmont Post is read by people who quietly run everything but the country, and who prefer a smaller newspaper for Where In the World Are We photo ops when they travel.

pages.text: 2 Thursday, January 2, 2025 Opinion RELIGION CORNER All the journeys of Christmas By Pastor Jim Hopkins It was well known that the Christmas season is one of the busiest travel seasons of the year. Traffic is heavy. Airports are jammed. People are on the move. “Over the river and through the woods to grandmother’s house we go,” is a fitting song for the season. In the birth narratives of the New Testament people are on the move. In fact, the biblical accounts of Jesus birth are full of journeys. Angels journey to earth with messages of good news. Mary and Joseph journey to Bethlehem. The shepherds journey to the manger. The Magi, following the star, journey from the East. The Holy Family, fleeing the wrath of Herod, journeys to Egypt. The biblical Christmas journeys can be divided into four main types: 1. Searching for Jesus 2. Carrying Jesus 3. Having Jesus carried to us 4. Retracing our steps when we misplaced Jesus Searching for Jesus The journey of the Magi following the star is an example of this kind of journey. Unsure of where they are going, trusting that joy awaited and following the star, they came from the East. Their journey is one many of us can relate to. We long for grace and truth and so we set out, step by step by step. Carrying Jesus Mary and Joseph traveling from their home in Nazareth to Bethlehem while Mary was pregnant with Jesus represents this type of journey. From Bethlehem, his parents carried Jesus to Jerusalem, to Egypt, into the world. With Mary and Joseph, we who identify as followers of Jesus, are given the assignment to carry Jesus, in word and deed, action and attitude, into the world. articles.text: The City Hall fountain is illuminated at night once again, showing its brand new tiles. The Piedmont Public Works Department has completed its project to replace tiles on the city’s two fountains – in front of City Hall and on the back side of the Exedra. The work included replacing existing tiling, adding tile to previously untiled vertical faces on the Exedra, replacing the lighting with energy efficient LEDs, and repairing lighting on the City Hall fountain that had not been illuminated in more than 10 years. The City Hall fountain was built in the mid 1980s. Originally untiled, tiles were added in the 1990s. The Exedra fountain and plaza was dedicated in honor of Piedmont resident Matthew Lempres in 2002. Both the City Hall and Exedra fountains had been in need of repair for several years – tiles were chipping and coming loose at an increasing pace. Every time the fountains were drained for cleaning, more tiles would need to be removed. Funding was included in the City’s budget for 2024 to retile both fountains. Pool tiles were used for the repairs since they are designed to be used underwater and are expected to be more durable than the previous tiles. The City Hall fountain restoration is complete. The Exedra fountain retiling is also complete, but Piedmont Public Works is awaiting delivery of a transformer before the fountain can be refilled with water. The Exedra fountain is being restored. articles.text: After holiday celebrations end, residents may dispose of their Christmas trees by using Republic Services curbside pickup or by cutting it up and placing it in a recycling cart. Holiday trees can quickly dry out and become a fire hazard. Once you are done with your tree, you should not leave it in your home or garage or lean it against your home outdoors. Curbside collection Curbside collection for natural trees is available December 26 through January 10. Republic Services will collect natural, unflocked trees until January 10. These trees will be turned into valuable compost and mulch. Put your tree out on your regular service day. Before placing your tree on the curb: • Remove everything from the tree: lights, decorations, tinsel, ornaments, and the tree stand. • If your tree is more than six feet tall, please cut it in half. Flocked or artificial trees Flocked, or “snow covered” trees are not compostable or recyclable. To dispose of a flocked or artificial tree, cut it up so that it fits in your black waste cart with the lid closed. Alternately, Republic Services will collect non-compostable trees curbside by request. Call 800-320-8077 to schedule a pickup: • There is a $33.33 disposal fee for curbside collection of non-compostable trees. • You can also use your annual Bulky Item Clean-ups for non-compostable trees in lieu of the pick-up fee. When placing non-compostable trees for curbside pickup, cut them into four foot or shorter pieces. For questions about holiday tree collection, email piedmont@ repsrv.com or call (800) 320-8077. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Gardens for a Changing Planet discussion on Jan. 15 Piedmont Garden Club welcomes the community to attend a discussion by Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden, on “Gardens for a Changing Planet: Towards a 21st Century Botanic Garden”. He will be the guest speaker on January 15 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Botanic gardens are more than just beautiful public parks. They play important roles in plant science and conservation. Novy, an internationally recognized leader in the horticultural world, will show how botanic gardens are adapting as the climate changes, He will share how these important green spaces are the sites of research into medicinal, native, and food and agricultural plants. In addition to his role at the Garden, Novy is an active researcher, holding an appointment as Adjunct Associate Professor at Salk Institute for Biological Studies. He is the founding co-chair of the Food and Agriculture Professional Section of the American Public Gardens Association and has served on task forces and advisory panels for diverse groups including the White House Council on Environmental Quality, the Cornell Alliance for Science, Botanic Garden Conservation International, Rock Creek National Park, the Garden Club of America, the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization, and many others. In 2024, he became an honorary member of the Garden Club of America. Piedmont Garden Club was founded in 1923 and has been a part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. Other activities include hands-on workshops, field trips and work projects.
articles.title: Piedmont Garden Club event for community

articles.text: With a CBS news crew at the South End Rowing Club on Sunday morning, December 14, it was a bit more lively than usual. But once we began our ritual it was a typical pre-winter morning. I keep my swim parka on to the last possible second, then we headed to the beach. The water is getting very cold now, bitter biting cold actually, and I had to force my breathing as I waded in. One big exhale and I was off. The first “2 minutes of misery” is really a test of resolve, and the only way to get through it is knowing that you’ll get used to it in a couple of minutes. Our pod headed west in the dark into a strong flood. I breathed on my left and kept watching the festive lights at Ghirardelli Square. As the first hint of light dawned in the east, we went under Muni Pier at Farnsworth Gap, and with a king tide we made it under without scraping any rocks or pilings – a painful hazard. Protected from the flood tide by Fort Mason pier, we cruised across the glassy channel and rendezvoused at the end of the pier. The Golden Gate was spectacular in the dawn’s early light. A couple of guys decided to head back from there while the rest of us pushed on to Gas House Cove against the flood. Looking back, I could see a spectacular day breaking over the city with Coit Tower and the Transamerica Pyramid in silhouette, and the Bay Bridge lit up with twinkling lights. The Ferry Building was red and green for Christmas. It was still quite dark and the only way I could recognize my pod mates was by the color of Josh Bernstein in San Francisco Bay on a chilly December morning. their blinking lights. Once we got to Gas House, we could really feel the flood moving the water. Heading east now with each breath I could see Alcatraz, Angel Island and Sausalito and Tiburon. The water was pretty smooth. With the swift tide we flew back to the cove opening then pressed on for Creakers at the end of the breakwater. There’s always a strong smell of fish along the breakwater, along with a high likelihood of seeing harbor seals or sea lions, so we kept our eyes peeled and rested up for a fight against the tide once we rounded the corner of Creekers. We bargained for a fight and that’s what we got. So we put our heads down and swam hard to beat the flood. The old ships at Hyde Street Pier are always a magnificent sight. my extremities, but inside my thermal cap, my head was toasty. As we swam further along the curve of the breakwater, the flood let up and we passed the end of the breakwater and headed for home. We had been in the water for an hour this morning. One of the guys from another pod passed out in the locker room from hypothermia. We helped him into the sauna, got him warm, and he recovered quickly. I guess I’m acclimated now because I was fine, even after a long swim in the cold water and cold weather. For those who think it’s crazy to swim without a wetsuit, all I can say is that it’s beautiful, it’s invigorating, it’s fun, and you can’t beat the camaraderie. Josh Bernstein is a Piedmont resident and lifelong swimmer. His parents were among the founders of the original Piedmont Swim Club. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites community members to an open house on Sunday, January 12, from 3:00 to 5:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. This free event offers an opportunity to meet local League leaders and members and learn about LWV projects and programs. Find out how to get involved in fostering informed and active participation in democracy. The Open House will feature: • Networking: Connect with like-minded individuals committed to making a difference. • Program Plans for 2025: Learn about the League’s advocacy efforts, voter education programs, and community engagement activities. • Volunteer Opportunities: Explore how you can contribute to voter empowerment and civic education. Light refreshments will be served. This family-friendly event welcomes individuals of all ages who are passionate about civic engagement and strengthening democracy at the local level. “We’re excited to open our doors and engage with the community,” said LWV Program Committee member Anita Stapen. “This event is a chance for us to celebrate the power of collective action and inspire more people to join us in our mission to create a stronger, more inclusive democracy.” The League of Women Voters, a nonpartisan organization, has been a vital part of the Piedmont community, working to empower voters and advocate for effective public policies for over a century. In addition to his role at the Garden, Novy is an active researcher, holding an appointment as Adjunct Associate Professor at Salk Institute for Biological Studies. He is the founding co-chair of the Food and Agriculture Professional Section of the American Public Gardens Association and has served on task forces and advisory panels for diverse groups including the White House Council on Environmental Quality, the Cornell Alliance for Science, Botanic Garden Conservation International, Rock Creek National Park, the Garden Club of America, the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization, and many others. In 2024, he became an honorary member of the Garden Club of America. Piedmont Garden Club was founded in 1923 and has been a part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Open water swimmers brave winter waters By Josh Bernstein, DDS With a CBS news crew at the South End Rowing Club on Sunday morning, December 14, it was a bit more lively than usual. But once we began our ritual it was a typical pre-winter morning. I keep my swim parka on to the last possible second, then we headed to the beach. The water is getting very cold now, bitter biting cold actually, and I had to force my breathing as I waded in. One big exhale and I was off. The first “2 minutes of misery” is really a test of resolve, and the only way to get through it is knowing that you’ll get used to it in a couple of minutes. Our pod headed west in the dark into a strong flood. I breathed on my left and kept watching the festive lights at Ghirardelli Square. As the first hint of light dawned in the east, we went under Muni Pier at Farnsworth Gap, and with a king tide we made it under without scraping any rocks or pilings – a painful hazard. Protected from the flood tide by Fort Mason pier, we cruised across the glassy channel and rendezvoused at the end of the pier. The Golden Gate was spectacular in the dawn’s early light. A couple of guys decided to head back from there while the rest of us pushed on to Gas House Cove against the flood. Looking back, I could see a spectacular day breaking over the city with Coit Tower and the Transamerica Pyramid in silhouette, and the Bay Bridge lit up with twinkling lights. The Ferry Building was red and green for Christmas. It was still quite dark and the only way I could recognize my pod mates was by the color of Josh Bernstein in San Francisco Bay on a chilly December morning. their blinking lights. Once we got to Gas House, we could really feel the flood moving the water. Heading east now with each breath I could see Alcatraz, Angel Island and Sausalito and Tiburon. The water was pretty smooth. With the swift tide we flew back to the cove opening then pressed on for Creakers at the end of the breakwater. There’s always a strong smell of fish along the breakwater, along with a high likelihood of seeing harbor seals or sea lions, so we kept our eyes peeled and rested up for a fight against the tide once we rounded the corner of Creekers. We bargained for a fight and that’s what we got. So we put our heads down and swam hard to beat the flood. The old ships at Hyde Street Pier are always a magnificent sight. By now, the cold was affecting my extremities, but inside my thermal cap, my head was toasty. As we swam further along the curve of the breakwater, the flood let up and we passed the end of the breakwater and headed for home. We had been in the water for an hour this morning. One of the guys from another pod passed out in the locker room from hypothermia. We helped him into the sauna, got him warm, and he recovered quickly. I guess I’m acclimated now because I was fine, even after a long swim in the cold water and cold weather. For those who think it’s crazy to swim without a wetsuit, all I can say is that it’s beautiful, it’s invigorating, it’s fun, and you can’t beat the camaraderie. Josh Bernstein is a Piedmont resident and lifelong swimmer. articles.text: Calling all young men and women ages 14-20 who love water activities. If you enjoy kayaking, sailing, rafting, and being on the water, this is for you. We want to restart Sea Scouts in Piedmont, and we’re looking for interested youth and adults to serve as program leaders. Adults, if you haven’t led a group of kids and young adults before, that’s okay. We can train you. Sea Scouts is a co-ed aquatics-based Scouting program in which youth learn seamanship, leadership, service, and teamwork, in addition to making friends and having lots of fun. Sea Scouts are recognized and rewarded for the things they learn and do. Scouts can earn certifications in SCUBA, boating safety, lifesaving, and CPR. Like other Scouting programs, Sea Scouts is Scout-led with adult mentoring, so Scouts are empowered to make the program what they want. In Sea Scouts, you build your own adventure. An information session will be held on Thursday, February 6, at 7 p.m. at the Scout office, 44 Highland Way (next to Piedmont Community Church). articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Our annual sports recap of the year includes highlights of great accomplishments and accolades which student-athletes can reminisce upon with awe. Our top moments from 2024 are shown below. Natalia Martinez concludes illustrious PHS basketball career In February of 2024, Natalia Martinez concluded her high school career at Piedmont High among the best to ever grace the basketball court at Binks Rawlings Gym. She finished her prep career as a four-year starter and never missed a single game since coming to Piedmont in 2020. We named her our 2024 Athlete of the Year, becoming our first-ever candidate to receive back-to-back Athlete of the Year awards. She received the Post’s Staff Photos The girls’ soccer team had a strong 12-4-2 (W-T-L) record despite not having Witter Field for the season. We named Miranda Liu (left) our 2024 Sophomore of the Year and Elsa Wallway (right) our 2024 Freshman of the Year. The boys’ soccer team went 12-3-3 and reached the D3 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 2 seed. Staff Photos Boys’ soccer head coach Todd Sullivan resigned from the school after eight years. He was a two-time NCS winner, three-time WACC Shoreline winner, and won 87 matches. end-of-year awards in each year of her high school career – Freshman of the Year in 2021, Sophomore of the Year in 2022, and Athlete of the Year as a junior in 2023. Martinez led the Highlanders to a 20-8 overall record and 7-1 league record to share the WACC league championship (WACC) with Bishop O’Dowd, marking Piedmont’s second consecutive league banner. PHS received the No. 6 seed in the North Coast Section Open Division and lost to No. 3 Carondele in the first round on February 15. They automatically qualified for the Div. 1 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed, and lost to No. 8 Whitney 53-41 in the first round on February 27. Martinez earned her second straight WACC Player of the Year award and was elected for a second time to the SF Chronicle’s All-Metro first-team. CalHiSports named her to the second-team Open Division. It was a magnificent scoring year for Martinez, putting up record numbers throughout the season. She concluded her high school career with 2,272 total points, including the school-record for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28. articles.text: the second half. Wallway was our 2024 Freshman of the Year for her instant impact, showing rare footwork and technical ability at the high school level. She received firstteam All-League honors last winter, while she also competed on the track team in the spring. Miranda Liu was named the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2924 after winning Freshman of the Year in 2023. Despite missing the first portion of the soccer season due to her club schedule, Liu earned second-team All-League honors as the team’s leading center forward. The boys; soccer team finished their season 12-3-3 overall and qualified for the D3 NCS playoffs as the No. 2 seed. PHS bashed No. 15 Novato 6-1 in the opening round on February 13, but was upset 3-1 by No. 7 Archie Williams in the quarterfinals three days later. They challenged for the Foothill Division title, notably claiming a 1-nil win over Berkeley, which marked the first time in eight years for the Highlanders to be victorious over the Yellowjackets. PHS received seven AllLeague selections, including Enzo Bernales and Ben Elmquist earning first-team honors, Andrew McLaughlin, Axel Saldanha and Aiden Woolwine were second-team selections, while Harper Mand and Bosco Lorin were honorable mentions. Todd Sullivan resigns as boys’ soccer coach Following the winter of 2024, boys’ soccer head coach Todd Sullivan announced his resignation from his role after eight years, leaving Piedmont High after reviving the program. His teams finished on top of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division in 2019, 2021, and 2022, which earned them a promotion to the Foothill Division. Sullivan’s finest accomplishment was winning back-to-back Division 4 North Coast Section titles in 2022 and 2023. The first title came in a 1-0 win over No. 2 University as the No. 1 seed at Witter Field, while the second was another 1-nil win over No. 2 University, this time coming as the tournament’s Cinderella story as the No. 8 seed. The 2019 league title marked the school’s first in 10 years. That February night when Piedmont claimed the WACC banner appeared to be the turning point of the program. Sullivan signed on as head coach for the winter of 2016/2017, replacing Rory O’Connor, who in four years had only one NCS win and finished with a positive winning percentage just one time. PHS went 9-2-9 (W-T-L) in Sullivan’s first year and 7-2-13 his second year when still developing a system change—creating the high-pressing and possession style. He finished his time at Piedmont with 87 wins and 155 matches as head coach. He closes with a record of 87 wins, 19 ties, and 49 losses. Girls Lacrosse wins league title Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team won its first WACC Title since 2019 with a heated 8-7 victory over rival Bishop O’Dowd on April 26. It was a fitting championship match, as O’Dowd had won the last two league titles. Piedmont responded to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but the Highlanders won the day after a goal by Friedie Schickedanz and two by Ruby Guzdar. Holding the 8-7 lead, PHS consumed nearly three minutes of possession to win the game. It was a big game for goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter who recorded 12 saves. The Highlander season came to an end on May 2 at No. 4 Acalanes in Lafayette where they lost 9-7 in the D2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 5 seeded school. articles.text: East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) confirmed in February that workers used glyphosate chemical sprays to eliminate weed growth near Reservoir Number One, an out of commission reservoir on Blair Avenue, much to residents’ dismay. “I think residents’ astonishment and anger is not unwarranted,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “It was essentially a heavy-duty version of Roundup.” Interest in EBMUD’s use of glyphosate in Piedmont began after former City Parks Commissioner Jukka Valkonen noticed signs in his neighborhood about the spraying and confirmed that the chemicals were sprayed outside the fence of the reservoir, which is near an area with frequent foot traffic from joggers and dog walkers. The City of Piedmont confirmed that it was not aware of EBMUD’s plans to use glyphosate chemical sprays. *** Workers from Piedmont’s Public Works Department were called into action on February 9 to enforce compliance with local stormwater laws at the Shell Photos by Piedmont Fire Department

Piedmont resident Shannon Fierro saw the fire and called 911, and a fire engine with five firefighters arrived to put out the blaze. Two other arson incidents occurred the week before on Grand Avenue, both of which resulted in arrests. Police Captain Chris Monahan said it was unusual to have so much activity, but that the events on January 24 (grass fire) and January 26 (trash can fire) were unrelated to the fire on Ranleigh. *** The Piedmont Police Department welcomed two new officers in January after completing their field training. Jessica Morey, a former teacher, and Ashley Gallion, a Psychology graduate from San Jose State University, joined Piedmont Police as close friends. The Piedmont Fire Department also welcomed Viktoriya Franzen and Lucas Romero in January as new recruits. February East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) confirmed in February that workers used glyphosate chemical sprays to eliminate weed growth near Reservoir Number One, an out of commission reservoir on Blair Avenue, much to residents’ dismay. “I think residents’ astonishment and anger is not unwarranted,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “It was essentially a heavy-duty version of Roundup.” Interest in EBMUD’s use of glyphosate in Piedmont began after former City Parks Commissioner Jukka Valkonen noticed signs in his neighborhood about the spraying and confirmed that the chemicals were sprayed outside the fence of the reservoir, which is near an area with frequent foot traffic from joggers and dog walkers. The City of Piedmont confirmed that it was not aware of EBMUD’s plans to use glyphosate chemical sprays. *** Workers from Piedmont’s Public Works Department were called into action on February 9 to enforce compliance with local stormwater laws at the Shell Piedmonter Shannon Fierro called 911 to report what appeared to be an arson fire, then used a garden hose on the fire. An inspection by the Public Works Department determined that large amounts of mud caused by on-site drilling were traveling into nearby storm drains in violation of the Municipal Regional Permit (MRP), which mandates stormwater pollution prevention activities. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that workers from his department were sent to “remediate the site to the proper level of care,” following an unsatisfactory cleanup by contractors, and that Public Works would be billing either Shell or their contractors directly for the department’s services. March Piedmont voted to pass Measure F in the March primary election with more than 75% of the vote. Measure F increases the previous city parcel tax, also known as the City Services Tax, by 20% (an additional $11-$19 per month for most households). It also changed the tax’s renewal period from every four years to 12 years. *** The Piedmont Public Works Department completed a new ADA-compliant access ramp at Dracena Park on March 7. The ramp provides a low-incline pathway connecting Dracena Avenue to the main body of the off-leash dog area in the park. *** Piedmont resident Maryann Phelps tripped on the recently constructed bulb-out on the corner of Oakland Avenue and El Cerrito Avenue, forcing her to spend the night of March 13 in the hospital. “It all happened so fast. I just went down,” she recalls of the incident. After her fall, two over the years since I’ve been here, it’s been a pleasure watching you develop and grow and mature into the leader that you are today,” said Bowers. *** The Piedmont Fire Department responded to a “high stakes” house fire at 660 Blair Avenue on the night of April 9. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan stated that when his crew arrived, the fire was “hazardous” and “devastating” due to the severity of the damage sustained and the fact that the fire had begun to spread to a neighboring home. The complexity and size of the fire required mutual aid from neighboring agencies, including an engine from Berkeley Fire Department and on-site support from Oakland Fire Department. “We train daily for situations like this,” said Brannigan, “and it’s a testament to that work that this challenging operation went off without a hitch.” The weather was hot enough for tank tops at the 3rd annual Piedmont Food Fest on April 20. More than 2,300 people came out to enjoy diverse and unique foods from Bay Area restaurants, local breweries, and wineries, making it one of the largest public events in Piedmont. Although the Food Fest was brimming with a smorgasbord of exciting eats, food wasn’t the only attraction at the event. A diverse cast of performances entertained festival goers, including the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, the Oh Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance School from Brisbane, and Oakland Taiko. *** A man was arrested by the Piedmont Police Department following an assault at Ace Hardware on April 26. At this meeting, the City also announced that it would seek up to 199 new housing units rather than the previously planned 132 units. The project’s initial goal was to build 60 low-income housing units and 72 market-rate units. All new housing units added to the plan would be market rate, with 60 low-income housing units and up to 139 potential market-rate units in total. *** The Piedmont City Council voted unanimously in their March 18 meeting to award a $1,815,400 contract to Giant Construction LLC to build a new emergency dispatch center at the Piedmont Police Station. This project had been long overdue for officers and firefighters, with Police Chief Jeremy Bowers citing two primary reasons for the need for a new dispatch center: a lack of space and current technology. April Piedmont Police Officer David Cutler was promoted to the rank of Sergeant in a pinning ceremony at the April 1 City Council meeting. Cutler was honored for his promotion alongside Officer Jehan Liles, who was being recognized for his achievement in the department.
