articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s newest production Waitress is playing onstage now through January 18. Susi Damilano’s revision of the motion picture Waitress, written by Adrienne Shelly, features music and lyrics by pop singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles. The play first premiered in 2015 at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and then transferred to Broadway in 2016, where it went on to receive 3 Tony Award nominations including Best Musical and Best Original Score. Waitress features protagonist Jenna, a diner waitress and expert pie maker, who is stuck in a small town and a loveless marriage. Jenna worries she will have to abandon her dream of opening her own bakery when she becomes unexpectedly pregnant, until she enters a baking contest and meets the soon-to-be love of her life. Ruby Day plays Jenna, and is supported by Zeke Edmonds, who plays Jenna’s love interest Dr. Pomatter. Supporting characters include Louis Parnell, Dorian Lockett, Tanika Baptiste and Sharon Shao. Music Direction is by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. Waitress is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through January 18, 2025. The venue is located at 450 Post Street in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. The show is on stage six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/2024-2025-season/waitress/ to purchase tickets. Cast of Waitress Photo by Jessica Palopoli

articles.text: A patron views the Mary Cassatt at Work exhibit at the Legion of Honor. An exhibition featuring the work of Impressionist painter Mary Cassatt is on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco through January 26. Mary Cassatt at Work is the first North American retrospective of Cassatt’s work in 25 years. The exhibition, which includes 93 objects on loan from institutions including the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, focuses on the roles of women and children in the late 19th century. Cassatt’s paintings often depict ‘women’s work,’ including knitting and needlepoint, bathing children and nursing infants. “Mary Cassatt at Work disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “It is fitting that this exhibition, which celebrates Cassatt’s daring and modernity, will open our yearlong centennial celebration of the Legion of Honor. The Legion of Honor was cofounded in 1924 by another intrepid female pioneer, Alma de Bretteville Spreckels, who shared Cassatt’s deep attachment to French culture and bold vision for the future of art in America,” Campbell said. The exhibition presents a group of distinguished works, including Cassatt’s magisterial oil portrait of her mother and recently acquired pastels from the Fine Arts Museums’ collection. Organizing curator Emily Beeny said the mother-and-child theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. “Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sweet or sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever more experimental handling of paint,” Beeny said. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state. The ambition and scope of her career were, alas, quite incompatible in the late 19th century with marriage and childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” Visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/mary-cassatt?mc_cid=f4db3a4148&mc_ eid=573801a180 to learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum.

articles.text: Meet the artist on Jan. 6 Bermuda-born artist Soleé Darrell’s solo exhibition Cosmic Ceremony is on display at the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco now through February 2. The artist said that being from Bermuda and living in the United States has given her the unique perspective of embracing multiple identities. Darrell, now based in Northern California, creates silk velvet paintings that explore color, sound, and texture as tools for healing and self-discovery. The exhibition features seven paintings and a single sculpture using various mediums, but most frequently delicate silk. Her paintings often mimic galaxies, star formations, and supernovae. Darell’s new works displayed at MoAD, including Within the body are gardens (2024) and Blessed are they who remember (2024). They are organic forms that blend free-flowing colors, while her large-scale sculpture Ritual is all we have (2024) uses silk velvet, boat rope, velvet ribbon, and found trimmings to create a nearly-symmetrical form in clashing pigments. Visit the museum on Monday, January 6 at 6:30 p.m. for a conversation and reception with Darrell, an Emerging Artist Program awardee. She will be in conversation with Oakland artist Angela Hennessy. Visit https://www.moadsf.org/ exhibitions/cosmic-ceremony to learn more. Artist Solee Darrell Soleé Darrell solo exhibition. “Cosmic Ceremony”

articles.text: Treasure Island Museum will host a panel discussion on Yerba Buena Island’s natural history. On Saturday, January 11 at 10 a.m. It is free to the public. Yerba Buena Island is the second largest natural island in San Francisco Bay, and its development and restoration is an on-going and multi-phase effort, much like the larger, man-made Treasure Island. Yerba Buena Island was historically used as a naval base and training center and its native ecosystems have been replaced by invasive species. Significant and biodiverse natural areas still remain, and ongoing redevelopment of Yerba Buena Island and Treasure Island provided the opportunity to restore native ecology. Both islands have been planted with mor than 50 species of native plants, including flora and fauna that are native to the ecosystem. According to Treasure Island Museum staff, the design and planning for these spaces involved a unique and collaborative effort between developers, the City of San Francisco, ecologists, local nurseries and landscape architects. Peter Brastow, from the San Francisco Environment Department and Will Benge, Senior Associate with CMG Landscape Architecture will lead a discussion of restoration efforts. Tickets are free, but reservations are required. Visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum.org/ event-details/restoration-of-yerba-buena-island-weaving-ecology-with-place-and-infrastructure to register. View from Yerba Buena Island

articles.text: Visit historic Filoli House and Garden in Woodside now through January 12 to see the 16-acre estate decorated for the holidays. Filoli’s team has installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, with more than 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceiling create an appropriate location for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest tree on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debutante balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreated the original holiday placement used by Agnes and William Bourn, Filoli’s first owners. Original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene is now on display in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively during the day. Daytime admission allows visitors to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. through January. To learn more about holidays at Filoli and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/.
articles.title: Celebrate the holidays at Filoli House & Garden

By Allyson Aleksey An exhibition featuring the work of Impressionist painter Mary Cassatt is on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco through January 26. Mary Cassatt at Work is the first North American retrospective of Cassatt’s work in 25 years. The exhibition, which includes 93 objects on loan from institutions including the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, focuses on the roles of women and children in the late 19th century. Cassatt’s paintings often depict ‘women’s work,’ including knitting and needlepoint, bathing children and nursing infants. “Mary Cassatt at Work disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “It is fitting that this exhibition, which celebrates Cassatt’s daring and modernity, will open our yearlong centennial celebration of the Legion of Honor. The Legion of Honor was cofounded in 1924 by another intrepid female pioneer, Alma de Bretteville Spreckels, who shared Cassatt’s deep attachment to French culture and bold vision for the future of art in America,” Campbell said. The exhibition presents a group of distinguished works, including Cassatt’s magisterial oil portrait of her mother and recently acquired pastels from the Fine Arts Museums’ collection. Organizing curator Emily Beeny said the mother-and-child theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. “Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sweet or sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever more experimental handling of paint,” Beeny said. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state. The ambition and scope of her career were, alas, quite incompatible in the late 19th century with marriage and childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” Visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/mary-cassatt?mc_cid=f4db3a4148&mc_ eid=573801a180 to learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum. articles.text: After reflecting on the year past, my sense is that if the mood of the country were a weather report I would judge it to be overcast, dark clouds on the horizon, often stormy. To continue the metaphor, at times it can feel like trying to fly a kite in a hurricane of cynicism. As an antidote to 2024, or as a reminding that decency and good will are still embedded in our culture, I would recommend three films: Frank Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life, Nora Ephron’s Sleepless in Seattle, and The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn (all streaming). Each is an extraordinary example of the ability of movies to remind us of who we are or wish to be, all while using the wondrous confluence of imagery, dialogue and sound track. It’s a Wonderful Life, is set in Bedford Falls, NY, the year is 1928. It focuses on George Bailey (James Stewart), first as a boy, then as a young man who is filled with dreams of leaving his small town behind and traveling to exotic places worldwide that only he can imagine. But circumstances – his sense of duty and commitment, his innate decency, and, of course, love - redefine George’s dreams while years slip away (the Great Depression followed by WWII). This heartfelt story is told through the prism of director Frank Capra who demonstrates a belief in the inherent integrity and goodness of people, qualities often lost in many of our more contemporary films. It’s a Wonderful Life. Directed by Frank Capra. Starring James Stewart, Donna Reed, Lionel Barrymore. Streaming on Fandango/prime. Released into Theater in 1946. Rated PG. 2hrs 9min Sleepless in Seattle, at least initially, is framed by grief and loss. Written and directed by Nora Ephron, who turns the profound sadness of a young architect, Sam Baldwin (Tom Hanks), and his 10-year-old son Jonah (Ross Malinger), into a compelling story, set in Seattle, someJames Stewart in It’s a Wonderful Life Sidney Poitier and Mary-Louise Parker in The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks in Sleepless in Seattle time in the 1990s. Sleepless is actually two parallel stories, one involving a young journalist, Annie Reed (Meg Ryan), recently engaged to Walter (Bill Pullman). Unexpectedly, she finds herself redefining her dreams of what love should be, while wondering if her relationship with Walter truly touches her heart. This nudging doubt is revealed one night as she is driving to her home in Baltimore. While listening to talk radio, a call-in show hosted by psychologist Dr. Marcia, she hears Jonah telling the “shrink” about his dad, Sam, who deeply misses his wife, as Jonah feels the absence of his mother. This moment, with Jonah’s voice filling the darkness, is the sweet spot of the narrative, and is slowly revealed and embellished in scene after remarkable scene (some moving and others comedic). We soon come to realize that Sleepless is a love story though Sam and Annie never meet until that much anticipated encounter on top of the Empire State Building takes place on St. Valentine’s Day. Of course, this occurs with the help of Jonah. And not to forget the recurring reference to the 1940s film An Affair to Remember. A brief comment about the Sleepless soundtrack: it is so good. The song choices made by Norah Ephron are inspired, and help tell the story, opening with the voice of Jimmy Durante (actor/comedian from the 1940s). Sleepless in Seattle. Written and directed by Nora Ephron. Starring Tom Hanks, Meg Ryan, Bill Pullman. Rated PG. 1hr 44min. The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn verges of being a heartwarming allegory about a mysterious man named Noah Dearborn (Sidney Poitier), who lives alone on a bucolic farm on the outskirts of a small southern town. He is a gifted carpenter, woodworker, generous to a fault, and seems ageless. soon becomes clear that the denizens of the town keep Noah’s presence a well-kept secret, understanding that it’s his preference to live quietly, go about his work, and be left undisturbed. In countless ways his life is so spare and timeless it seems as if the 20th century has passed him by. And so it has, until a cohort of land developers arrive and decide that in order to build a shopping center they need Noah’s acreage. Driven by greed, they set up an office in town and send slick and fashionable Christian Nelson (George Newbern) out to pay Noah a visit, prepared to make him an offer for his property that, given the amount, he certainly cannot refuse. articles.text: Sunday, January 5, 2025, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz and Pop Piano Trio Join Bill Jackman, Albert Brooks, and Michael Jones in our comfortable, relaxed classic jazz club to celebrate the New Year 2025 with some classics from the 20s, 30s, and 40s, along with eight of your favorite Beatles songs. Sing along with Auld Lang Syne using Bill’s English translation of the traditional words. Enjoy complimentary refreshments with $25 tickets at https://bpt.me/6214927, or pay more at the door, cash/check Only. Thursday, January 16, 7:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture Join artist and art historian Michael Stehr, art historian, as he discusses the importance of the current show at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, entitled Mary Cassatt at Work. Too often dismissed as a sentimental painter of mothers and children, Mary Cassatt (1844–1926) was in fact a modernist pioneer. Her paintings, pastels, and prints are characterized by restless experimentation and change. Cassatt was the only American to join the French Impressionists, first exhibiting with the group at Degas’ invitation in 1879, and quickly emerged as a key member of the movement. The illustrated lecture will last approximately one hour; please prepare to pay $20 cash or check per person at the door. Note that the Legion of Honor exhibit will close January 26, 2025 Saturday, January 18, 4:30 p.m. Boon Hiker Band The Boon Hiker Band includes John Bidwell, Clare Broussard, J.T. Devine, Robin Eschner, Dennis Hysom, Natasha Haugnes, Chris Smith, and John Tuttle. These eight group members bring dynamic vocal harmonies to the heart of the original compositions and the arrangements of covers – all supported by various combinations of guitar, bass, keyboard, banjo, accordion, dobro, lap steel, and percussion. The songs lean toward Americana/Folk/Indie traditions, with energetic and vibrant musicianship provided by the three East Bay members – and the five North Bay members enhance the vocal textures and harmonies with their choral backgrounds. Advance tickets for this concert can be found at https://bpt.me/6383991. Doors will open at 4 p.m. Saturday, January 25, 7:30 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro solo piano Returning to PCA after several years, Italian pianist and composer Cristiana Pegoraro honors Piedmont and PCA with another stellar, inspired solo performance on our Steinway grand piano! This renowned pianist will perform the same program she played at Carnegie Hall’s Weill Recital Hall in mid-November! Acclaimed as one of the most gifted musicians of her generation, since her formal debut in Messina at age 10 she has received more than forty international awards, has released over thirty CDs, of which six are of her own compositions, and has performed with major orchestras and in renowned concert halls all over the world, including Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall. In addition to a full-time teaching schedule in Rome and New York, she has written books, is the founder and President of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of the annual Narnia Festival, both in her home town of Narni, in Umbria, Italy. Discounted tickets for this special concert are at https://bpt.me/6504559. Sunday, January 26, 4:00 p.m. Mads Tolling, with Kenny Washington Danish-born jazz violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with jazz pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington. Although all three are celebrated names in the Bay Area, this marks their first time performing together. Mads and John will feature music from their 2023 album, Ramblin’, which includes songs ranging from Toto and The Beatles to John McLaughlin and Chick Corea, along with a few original compositions. Kenny Washington, one of the world’s premier jazz vocalists and a frequent performer at Wynton Marsalis’ Jazz at Lincoln Center, will join them. Jazz writer Andrew Gilbert has dubbed Kenny “The Superman of the Bay Area Jazz Scene.” Together, the three will perform American Songbook tunes by Duke Ellington, Thelonious Monk, and George Gershwin. Tickets for this performance can be purchased at https://bpt.me/6504543.

articles.text: There were many reasons for the Walking on Wednesday group to be at Exedra last Wednesday. The group walks every Wednesday, rain or shine, but it was Christmas and Hanukkah. The last time the holidays were on the same day was in 2005. It won’t happen again until 2035. It was also the last Wednesday of the year, so there was a good turnout of 19 walkers and one K-9 best friend to celebrate this special morning together. The group was mindful of the services provided by the Piedmont Police and Fire Departments, and especially appreciative of the people who were on duty this holiday morning. The walkers went to the police station where they met officer Hugo Diaz, then next door to the fire station where they met firefighters Chad Walker, Brittany Burges, and Lucas Romero. Both the police and fire personnel were thankful for the group’s gift of donuts. After the visits the group was off to see the homes in the central part of Piedmont that are decorated with representations of the 12 Days of Christmas gifts. As a holiday tradition, some residents of Highland, Caperton, and Sheridan Avenues display the items of the 12 Days of Christmas carol in their windows or entryways. It was shared that 12 Days of Christmas is an English Christmas carol, however it may have also been a catechism song for young Catholics during the 16th through early 19th Centuries. During this period Roman Catholics in England were not permitted to practice their faith openly. Someone may have written this carol with two levels of meaning. One is the surface meaning, but the other may have been known only to Church members. Each gift in the carol may have been a code for a Catholic religious concept which the children could remember. The walkers went down Guilford looking for decorated houses. They didn’t find any, but on Highland they soon found a partridge in a sparkling pear tree in a front window. The walkers continued, finding two turtle doves, three French hens (drawn by the family’s s three children), and four calling birds. The group turned up Caperton Avenue and found five golden rings, six geese a-laying, and ten lords a-leaping. They arrived at Sheridan Avenue searching for eleven pipers piping and twelve drummers drumming. Going back towards Highland, they found them in two more windows. The group’s search and walk were complete. It was time for them to wrap up 2024 and go home to continue their holidays. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. On hand for last week’s walk on Wednesday were Albert Chen, Vicki Trimbach, Sherona and Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Phil Witte, Elizabeth Richter, Denny McGee, Peggy and Dana Shultz, Pat and Greg Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Bonnie Sherwood, Mark Davis, Dick and Mary Carter, Irene Thompson, Jim Kuo, and Marianne Jakus.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup is a great dish for a cold winter day. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 4, 2024. It is never too soon to be proactive about your health and longevity. As we ring in the New Year, many of us have considered that healthy lifestyle goals and the meals we consume are a large part of it. Gigantic Royal Corona beans are the stars of this soup. They cook up tender and, dare I say, “meaty” owing to their size and toothsomeness. They’re as fun to eat as they are impressive to those new to them. Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup Adapted from Diane Kochilas’ Fasolada – Bean Soup with Pumpkin & Corn Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 1/2 pound giant beans such as Royal Corona or Greek gigantes • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided, preferably Greek • 1-1/2 red onion, coarsely chopped, about 1-1/2 cups • 2 tablespoons fresh garlic, minced, divided • 1 tablespoon tomato paste • 1 14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes • 1 bay leaf • 1/2 teaspoon dried oregano, or 2 sprigs fresh • 1 3-inch-long strip of fresh orange peel • 1 cup corn kernels • 1 cup cubed delicata or butternut squash • 1/4 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped • 1 – 2 teaspoons honey, preferably local • 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar, scant measure to taste • 1/2 – 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • A few grinds black peppercorns, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Check the beans for debris, rinse and then soak overnight; drain and discard the soaking water. Soaking is optional but will decrease the cooking time considerably. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large soup pot over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5–10 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent scorching. Stir in 1 tablespoon of the minced garlic (set remaining 1 tablespoon aside for later), give it a quick stir; then add the tomato paste. Stir again to incorporate the tomato paste well. Add the drained beans, canned tomatoes, bay leaf, oregano, and orange peel. Top off with enough water to cover by 2 inches. Bring to a boil then reduce to a simmer until the beans are very tender, about 1-1/2 to 2 hours. When the beans are tender, scoop out about 1 cup of the soup and puree in a food processor or blender/immersion stick blender, then return to the pot. This blending step is optional but will add a bit of body to the soup. Meanwhile, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the squash and corn until lightly browned, then add the remaining garlic and sea salt. Mix well then add to the soup pot once the beans have cooked through and the pureed portion has been added back to the pot. Return the soup to a simmer and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper. Just before serving remove the orange peel and bay leaf. Stir in the chopped parsley, honey and balsamic vinegar. Serve with an additional drizzle of high-quality, extra-virgin olive oil and a few sprinkles of parsley. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok at: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: These concept sketches were made by Mark Becker, in the very early stages of his design for Piedmont’s Havens Elementary School. Certainly not all details are (yet) shown, but these rough drawings can be considered the blueprint for all the design and construction work that was to follow for this wonderful job. This column appeared in the Post originally on August 3, 2022. As a tribute to the late Will Adams, it is being reprinted. It was his 49th column in his biweekly observations and comments on the architecture of Piedmont with examples with photos and sketches from around the world. Will Adams was a talented Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who lived in Piedmont for 30 years. All good designs have at their source a strong, clear vision, or concept. This can be defined as the overall main idea – a view into the future of what the project should look like, feel like and how it will function. The built environment around us – the places we work, live, play and interact with each other – is in reality an ongoing design process that has an important effect on all of our lives, often much more than we realize. As we must continually upgrade, accommodate, and adapt to the new, this process especially requires a strong vision. Walking around Piedmont and looking at the various finished buildings, landscapes, urban designs and planning decisions at various different scales, it is instructive to judge how clear the initial visions were, and how well they were adhered to during the often lengthy design and construction processes. It makes us ask how strong will be our evolving city vision(s) going forward in the next months, years and decades? Inspiration for concept direction in the built environment can be derived from many sources, such as the local architectural history of a place, the logical transportation connections, the solar orientation, a response to a dramatic view, or surrounding existing geographical features. Vision can also be inspired by a need for change, an opportunity to accommodate current needs by adjusting existing patterns to enhance function, aesthetics and/ or to build and strengthen the community. In most cases there are a number of considerations, sometimes competing, that make up a vision. For effective implementation, the best concepts and resulting designs will have a clear hierarchy of importance assigned to each of their parts. It is a way to prevent small or unimportant aspects from controlling the big picture and compromising the vision. This somewhat more developed, more detailed concept drawing was made to provide an upgraded vision statement for a multifamily island housing boating community in the Caribbean.
articles.title: The importance of vision for the built environment

pages.text: Thursday, January 2, 2025 25 The importance of vision for the built environment Vision statements in environmental design can be thought of and used in much the same way artists attach theme sketches or photos to their easels: to provide a constant reminder and reference to an overall concept during the course of the work. Communicating a vision is essential for success. It should be clear enough to be stated, drawn or written. I used to have as a client Jim Thompson, who ran Vail Resorts. He astutely insisted that with any project, the concept and goal should be able to be stated in one concise sentence. He was absolutely right! Not only does this clarify the idea, but it also makes it easier for everyone concerned to continually evaluate the design and construction process for adherence to the stated purpose. As the number of participants associated with a project grows as it progresses, it is easy to confuse, forget, or dilute the primary concept. One of the principal tasks of the design professions, the owners, as well as the concerned public should be guarding and protecting the main vision of a project through all phases to completion. articles.text: On Friday, December 20, Piedmont Community Church hosted its second annual Snow Day – transforming the parking lot and Courtyard into a winter wonderland. An estimated 1,000 people from Piedmont and surrounding communities participated in the event which featured 23 tons of snow, bounce houses, face painting and treats. Photos by Michael Barber An employee with San Jose Ice Company waits for bags of ice to be transformed into snow before blasting a sledding hill made of hay in the church parking lot. It took about two hours to deliver 23 tons of snow. Nighttime falls upon the church Courtyard as the second annual Snow Day event winds down. Multiple trucks hauling bags of ice are used to deliver snow to the sledding hill and the children’s play area in the church Courtyard. Children dressed in winter wear and shorts wait for their turn on the sledding hill. Leon Coffey Midili, 10, ducks after throwing snowballs from the Courtyard wall onto people below as friend Austin Gray, 10, looks for their next mark. Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted shovels large quantities of snow into wheelbarrows to be shuttled into the church Courtyard where it covered a children’s play area. Jeff Hiller gives a pint-sized sledder a needed push. Henry Jobst, 11, and Ember McCall, 11, secure a pile of snowballs far from the snow site in order to properly stock a boys vs girls snowball fight. Suzie Skugstad brings enthusiasm, along with a can of Reddi-Wip for hot cocoa, to her role as Mrs. Claus. Carolyn Chun and her granddaughter, Mia, 2, laugh after taking a tumble at the end of the sledding hill. Corubella Gonzales, 8, enjoys being first in line to have her face painted.

articles.text: With profound sadness, the family of Harvey Anderson has confirmed his sudden passing on December 19, 2024 at the age of 61. Harvey James Anderson II was a proud father and husband, an accomplished lawyer, a dedicated sponsor and mentor, a cherished friend and an avid surfer, who led his life with love and light. Born in Washington, DC, Harvey was raised by his parents, Joan and Harvey. Andersson, who instilled in him a strong sense of family, community, and faith that guided him throughout his adult life and career. Harvey progressively followed a call west starting with Milwaukee, Wisconsin where he completed his Bachelor’s Degree in Engineering at Marquette University and built friendships that would prove to be lifelong. Upon graduation, he continued on his westward path, finally settling by the ocean he loved so deeply in the San Francisco Bay Area, which he called home for more than 35 years. There, he studied law at the University of San Francisco School of Law, which set him on course for a prolific career, throughout which he was known and admired for his strategic vision and commitment to doing the right thing. His work ethic and talent brought him to the most senior offices at the intersection of tech, law, and policy. He led the legal and policy functions at HP as the Chief Legal Officer, successfully navigated the business, legal and policy needs of AVG, and used his innovative thinking to create some of the most impactful policy and business programs at Mozilla. After retirement, Harvey dedicated himself to beginning a new adventure as an Adjunct Professor at University of California Berkeley School of Law on the “business of law.” He served on the Board of Trustees for Marquette University, was a member of the board of Common Sense Media, and was a strategic advisor and board member for startups throughout his career. Less formally, he always freely and enthusiastically gave wisdom and advice to anyone who sought him out for mentorship or career guidance - even if his sons sometimes gave him feedback that his lessons took too long. His intellect, judiciousness, and talent as a leader and lawyer made him an incredible force in the workplace but his greatest gifts to the world were his spirit of warmth, generosity, and devoHarvey Anderson died suddenly on December 9 at age 61. tion to his family and community. As someone guided deeply by his faith, Harvey was committed to service and driven by a sense of responsibility to share the goodness that life bestowed upon him with others. He found every opportunity to give to those in need, either donating time at local organizations, building houses annually for underserved communities in Mexico, or even just being an available ear to listen and support as someone who battled life’s challenges. Harvey proudly achieved 35 years of sobriety through hard work, dedication and support from members of the Program. His commitment to the Program was unmatched as he served as a guiding light and sponsor to countless men and women, supporting their journeys to not only reach sobriety, but to thrive. Harvey had a rare gift to make someone feel seen, heard, and understood. But Harvey was at his happiest when spending time with his wife, Denelle, and their five sons, Luke, Cole, Dylan, Trevor, and Jax. Harvey and Denelle’s journey to each other took time, but when they found each other and blended their families, Harvey embraced every moment spent together and lived his most core values to ensure their home was joyful, supportive, and welcoming. He was there to cheer them on at events whether sports performances or, in Denelle’s case, speaking engagements (for which he had a front row seat for her speeches from Rome to Nairobi), He was there to play any and all games together from board games and trivia to pickleball and paintball, to spend holidays in their favorite places always trying to get to surfing (especially Hawaii), or just quiet time together. His family was the center of his world and he was immensely proud of his wife and sons. Harvey will be remembered for always saying yes to life – yes to fun, yes to sharing his good fortune, yes to anything with his boys and wife, yes to putting his feet in the ocean, yes to discovering the world, yes to listening, yes to being there for those who asked or needed him – and always yes to surfing. Harvey was the embodiment of someone who lived his life to the fullest and in service of those he loved and his community. In doing so, he managed to touch so many lives, inspiring each one to carry on his legacy. He leaves behind his loving family, mother Joan Fowler Anderson, wife Denelle Dixon, and their sons Cole Anderson, Luke Anderson, Dylan Thayer, Trevor Thayer, and Jax Thayer. He is predeceased by his father Harvey James Anderson A memorial service will be held at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont, on January 9, 2025 at 7:00 pm. A celebration of Harvey’s tremendous life will be held on January 11. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to: Marquette University (https://www.givecampus.com/campaigns/28093/ donations/new?a=9077221), and Surfrider Foundation (https:// www.surfrider.org/?form=memorial).

articles.text: and seasons in our lives when we need others to carry Jesus to us. The ability to receive the gifts others bring is, in itself, a gift. Retracing our steps when we have misplaced Jesus Luke bridges the story of Jesus birth with the story of the journey Jesus’ family took to Jerusalem when he was twelve years old. There, they misplaced him. They were well on their way home before they realized he was not with them. They then retraced their steps and found him still in Temple, discussing important matters with the leading teachers of the day. Once again, we do well to follow the example of Jesus’ parents. Life gets busy. We lose focus. Despite our best intentions, we misplace Jesus. When this happens, we do well to go back to where we saw him last. This could be the manger. It could be the Temple. It could be the cross. It could be the garden outside the empty Tomb. Fortunately, when we misplace Jesus, we have some reliable places to return to. even as we journey into 2025. Rev. Jim Hopkins is senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard, Oakland. And so the story develops, filled with charming moments and an outstanding performance by Dianne Wiest. She was nominated for an Emmy for Best Supporting Actress, delivering a superb portrayal of Sarah McClelland, a neighbor who lives just down the road from Noah and constantly searches for reasons to have him repair something while thanking him with a homemade pie. And, of course, there’s Sidney Poitier who will be deeply missed. The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn. Directed by Greg Champion. Released in 1999. Streaming on Fandango/Prime/ Apple tv. Starring Sidney Poitier, Dianne Wiest, Mary-Jane Parker. 1hr 36min. Rated PG In summary, I would suggest in the best possible way that each of the three films are allegories or parables. Each replaces cynicism with hope, buttressed by kindness, each a gift of sorts to reflect upon as we go forward into 2025. Best wishes.

articles.text: Piedmont residents voted on new City Council members in 2024, electing Conna McCarthy to a second term on the Council and welcoming new Council member Lorrel Plimier. Betsy Andersen was named the city’s new mayor succeeding Jen Cavenaugh who served two terms on City Council. Piedmont voters approved Conna McCarthy for a second 4-year term on City Council and confirmed Lorrel Plimier as a new member of the council. McCarthy won 4,799 votes and Plimier won 3,605 votes, placing them at 43.43% and 32.62% of the vote respectively. Plimier was sworn into office on December 16 to join four other members of Piedmont’s City Council, and McCarthy was confirmed for a second four-year term. The special city council meeting took place in the Community Hall and included the swearing in of three new school board members. At the ceremony the city council voted to name Betsy Andersen as Mayor and Conna McCarthy as Vice Mayor. “I have been sharpening my scissors,” said Andersen, with hopes of cutting many ribbons in her upcoming mayoral term. Piedmont’s new City Council will hold its first meeting of the new year on January 6, 2025 at 6:00 p.m. at City Hall. Betsy Smegal Andersen speaks after being named Piedmont’s new mayor.
